Your Excellencies, Heads of State and Government,

Distinguished Delegates,

Allow me to congratulate His Excellency Khalilur Rahman on his  election  as  President  of  the  Eighty-first  Session  of  the United Nations General Assembly, in the hope that, with his vast  experience  and  profound  knowledge  of  our international  organization,  he  will  render  valuable  service to the United Nations, which faces complex challenges that must  be  overcome  in  order  to  resume  its  central  role  in addressing  the  major  issues  of  contemporary  international relations.

I  also  congratulate  Ms.  Annalena  Baerbock,  who  preceded you  in  the  discharge  of  these  noble  duties  and  spared  no effort,  during  the  term  she  carried  out  with  undeniable competence,  to  preserve  the  role  of  the  United  Nations  in addressing  the  issues  that  most  concern  the  international community today.

I  would  also  like  to  congratulate  His  Excellency  the Secretary-General, António Guterres, who has been working tirelessly and devoting himself with persistent dedication to the great global causes, building bridges for dialogue in the

search  for  peaceful  solutions  to  the  problems  facing humanity today.

We  highlight  his  exemplary  contribution  as  a  man  of dialogue,  an  advocate  of  the  United  Nations  Charter  and  of International Law, a tireless advocate of the need to protect the planet from the harmful effects of climate change, and a champion  of  the  global  debate  on  the  global  governance  of artificial intelligence.

The United Nations General Assembly is  always held in the month  of  September;  this  year's  session,  however,  takes place 25 years after the terrorist act that destroyed the twin towers  in  New  York  and  struck  other  targets  on  American territory, causing thousands of civilian deaths and injuries, some  of  whom  continue  to  bear  physical  and  emotional scars to this day.

I take this opportunity once again to condemn terrorism in all  its  forms,  wherever  it  occurs.  In  addition  to  terrorism, which  remains  active  in  some  countries,  particularly  in Africa,  the  situation  of  global  peace  and  security  has  been worsening  year  after  year,  bringing  us  to  the  present moment, in which we note with deep concern that the world has taken a course that brings it alarmingly close to a global conflict.

Over the years, Angola has sought to make its contribution to  the  building  and  consolidation  of  peace  in  Africa  and  in the  world,  but  the  current  situation  in  no  way  reflects  the aspirations  of  peoples  for  harmony  and  understanding among nations.

Among  these  contributions  to  peace  are  several  initiatives undertaken  in  Africa,  of  which  I  highlight  the  “21st the  African  Union  on Extraordinary  Conference  of Strengthening  Conflict  Prevention  and  Resolution  Mechanisms in Africa”,  recently  held  in  Luanda,  which  opened  a  serious and  sound  prospect  for  resolving  the  problems  affecting peace and stability on the African continent.

Also deserving particular attention is the holding, in July of this year in Luanda, in partnership with the United Nations Alliance  of  Civilizations,  of  the  Third  Edition  of  the “Initiative  Call  for  Peace,  an  End  to  Wars  and  Respect  for International Law”.

In  this  same  context,  Angola  will  host  next  October  the “Pan-African  Forum  for  the  Culture  of  Peace  and  Non-Violence, Luanda Biennale”.

My  country  takes  seriously  our  commitment  to  matters through the  conflicts concerning  peace, dialogue,  respect  for  the  norms  governing  international relations  and  the  defence  of  International  Law,  sparing  no effort to bringing the conflicting parties closer together and build consensus in Africa.

resolution

We  remain  available to  render  our  attention  and contribution  to  resolving  the  conflicts  that  persist  on  the continent.

Our  paradigm  for  peacebuilding  initiatives  is  based  on  the search  for  realistic  and  sustainable  solutions,  within  the principle of African solutions to conflicts in Africa.

We call for the effective implementation of Security Council Resolution  2719,  which  must  ensure  predictable,  adequate and  sustainable  financing  for  African  Union-led  peace support  operations  authorized  by  the  United  Nations Security  Council,  because  investing  in  Africa’s  capacity  to prevent  and  resolve  conflicts  is  also  an  investment  in international peace and security.

This  session  of  the  General  Assembly  is  of  particular significance  to my  country,  as  it  is  taking  place  in  the  year in  which  we  celebrate  the  fiftieth  anniversary  of  the Republic  of  Angola’s  admission  as  a  full  member  of  the United Nations Organization, in December 1976.

At  that  time,  it was  a  historic  achievement  for  the  Angolan people, who waited more than twelve months from the date of the proclamation of their National Independence for the country  to  be  accepted  as  a  full-fledged  member  of  the international community.

That  event,  of  great  significance  for  the  history  of  my country,  took  place  in  a  global  context  in  which  Angola became  a  victim  of  confrontation  between  the  world powers,  in  the  struggle  for  control  of  spheres  of  influence within the spirit of the Cold War.

Our entire journey towards the attainment of peace in 2002 was  closely  linked  to  the  disputes  of  that  period,  which hampered  the  fulfilment  of  the  dreams  of  Angolans  and their  plans  to  build  a  prosperous  nation  committed  to  its development.

These  facts  belong  to the  past,  but  they  have  left  us  with  a wealth of  experience  and lessons that we have drawn  upon

to build peace,  understanding and reconciliation among all Angolans and to chart the course of our foreign policy.

Peace and national reconciliation is now a reality, as shown demonstrated  through  concrete  gestures,  including  the holding  of  award  ceremonies  honouring  the  main  political leaders  of and representative  members  of  all  segments  of  civil  society, within  the  framework  of  the  50th  anniversary  of  National Independence.

struggle

Still  within  this  framework,  a  monument  in  memory  of  all victims  of  the  political  conflicts  that  occurred  in  Angola, from  the  proclamation  of  National  Independence  until  the achievement  of  peace  in  April  2002,  will  be  inaugurated next October in Luanda.

In our time, we are witnessing a downgrading and violation of the rules governing international relations, with the logic imposition  of  values of  force, stemming  from  the  unilateral  vision  of  certain  countries prevailing in the defence of their exclusive interests.

intimidation  and  the

Instability  being  experienced  in  various  regions  of  our planet  is  a  direct  consequence  of  this  stance,  as  it  can  be seen  in  the  conflicts  currently  unfolding  in  Europe,  the Middle  East,  the  Persian  Gulf  and  Africa,  while  tension  is mounting in the Asia-Pacific region.

From  what  we  have  observed,  we  do  not  discern encouraging signs regarding the likelihood of reaching any peace  agreement  in  the  near  future  in  the  wars  between Russia and Ukraine, in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict in the Middle East and in the Persian Gulf.

We condemn the genocide against defenceless populations, the  elderly,  women,  children,  bedridden  patients,  health professionals,  journalists  and  workers  of  international humanitarian  organizations,  who  are  often  deprived  of access  to  the  most  basic  human  rights  and  to  essential goods for life, such as water, food and medicines.

The  expulsion  of  the  Palestinians  from  their  homes  and lands  through  the  expansion  of  Jewish  settlements  in  the West  Bank  must  elicit  the  strongest  international  outrage and condemnation.

Attempts  to  dominate  entire  countries  and  regions  of  the globe  by  force  of  arms  are  leading  the  world  towards catastrophe.

The  food  security,  energy  and  humanitarian  situation  of countries  and  of  the  world  in  general  has  deteriorated considerably  following  the  outbreak  of  the  wars  against Ukraine and, more recently, against Iran.

is  disastrous,

The  toll  of  the  wars judging  by  the consequences  arising  from  the  strangulation  of  freedom  of maritime  navigation  through  the  Strait  of  Hormuz  and  Bab al-Mandab,  a  situation  that  has  created  a  serious  risk  of disruption to logistics supply chains in general, and to food and  energy  supply  chains  in  particular,  with  devastating effects on the most vulnerable countries.

Today,  we  live  in  an  environment  of  global  anarchy  in which the use of force prevails over the force of reason and of  law,  in  blatant  opposition  to  the  norms  governing international relations.

In  view  of  this,  there  is  every  need  for  profound  reflection within the United Nations, the only institution on the planet with legitimacy and which brings together all the nations of the  world,  in  order  to  find  the  best  solutions  for  achieving global peace.

Our  appeal  is  for  us  to  act  with  wisdom  and  courage  to restore  the  central  role  of  the  United  Nations  in  its responsibility  and  irreplaceable  mission  in  maintaining world peace.

Ladies and Gentlemen

We are concerned by the unjust manner, indicative of great human  insensitivity,  in  which  Cuba  has  been  treated  over decades,  as  a  victim  of  an  embargo  that  continues  and worsens the living conditions of the Cuban people.

Cuba  is  not  a  terrorist  State;  it  neither  produces  nor possesses  nuclear  weapons,  chemical  or  bacteriological weapons that could constitute an imminent or real threat to the  national  security  of  other  countries, including neighbouring countries.

On  the  contrary,  Cuba  contributed  to  the  fall  of  South Africa’s  racist  and  segregationist  apartheid  regime,  a regime  broadly  and  unanimously  condemned  by  the international  community  and  consequently  became  one  of the  signatories  to  the  Quadripartite  Agreements  of  New York of 22 December 1988.

As  the  embargo  is  chiefly  responsible  for  the  calamitous situation  in  which  Cuba  and  the  Cuban  people  find themselves, and since it is inhumane, unfair and violates all the  principles  and  norms  of  International  Law,  we  once again call for an end to the embargo against Cuba.

Today,  we  are  witnessing  the  direct  involvement  of  certain permanent members of the United Nations Security Council in  the  bloodiest  and  most  destructive  conflicts  of  our  time in Europe and the Persian Gulf, which is a cause for concern and a bad example for the rest of the world. Those  countries  rendered  a  great  service  when  they  freed humanity  from  the  horrors  of  Nazism,  fascism  and  the Holocaust,  and  should  therefore  preserve  that  capital  and legacy as liberators.

At  a  time  when  good  governance  of  countries  is  widely advocated,  the  governance  of  the  world  likewise  calls  for  a new, more democratic and just world order, one that is not based solely on the power of the restricted club of victors of a war that took place eight decades ago.

Since then, the World has come to know a different reality: new  countries  have  emerged,  which  at  the  time  were colonies  and  which  today  are  strong  economies  with significant advances in science and technology.

It is therefore becoming increasingly pressing and urgent to undertake a profound reform of the United Nations Security Council,  in  which  Africa,  Latin  America  and  Asia  should  be

adequately represented as permanent members with all the powers inherent therein.

In  this  context,  the  Republic  of  Angola  reaffirms  its  full support  for  the  common  African  position  enshrined  in  the Ezulwini Consensus and the Sirte Declaration.

The voice of Africans must be heard in all circumstances, at all  times,  in  strategic  decision-making  processes  on  issues of peace, global security, financing for development, as well as  climate  issues  and  the  global  governance  of  artificial intelligence.

Peace  and  development  are  inseparable,  which  compels  us to  consider  strategies  that  can  help  accelerate  the implementation of the 2030 Agenda.

The  important  decisions  adopted  under  the  Pact  for  the Future  and  the  Seville  Commitment  can  help  advance development programmes in Africa.

transfer,

capacity-building

However, in order to achieve concrete results in this area, it is  essential  to  ensure  affordable  financing,  debt  relief, technology and  greater participation in international financial institutions. African  countries  spend  far  more  resources  on  the exorbitant  costs  of  debt  servicing  than  they  are  able  to invest in health, education and infrastructure development programmes.

This  situation  obviously  limits  productive  investment, deepens inequalities  and  economic  disparities,  and threatens economic and social stability.

In view of this, it is imperative to correct these distortions, and  I  therefore  reiterate  the  call  for  the  immediate  reform of the international financial architecture, in order to make it fairer, more equitable, democratic and geared towards the progress and well-being of humankind.

These  challenges  are  inherently  complex  and  are  further exacerbated  by  climate  change,  which  has  a  severe  impact on  Africa,  with  severe  and  prolonged  droughts,  floods, desertification, population displacement.

This  situation  clearly  illustrates  the  need  to  establish predictable,  affordable  and  additional  climate  financing, without  further  aggravating  the  debt  of  developing countries.

Today,  peoples  and  nations  have  an  opportunity  to make  a qualitative  leap  in  their  overall  living  conditions,  through fair mechanisms to support development and the tools that artificial intelligence provides to improve education, health, agriculture,  public  services,  scientific research  and economic productivity.

In  this  regard,  I  consider  that  the  Global  Digital  Compact opens  new  prospects  for  cooperation  to  bridge  the  digital divide,  expand  digital  public infrastructure,  promote training and innovation, strengthen cybersecurity and build more  inclusive,  secure  and  human-centred  governance  of artificial intelligence.

To that  end,  I  believe  there  is  a  need  to strengthen  North-South, South-South and triangular cooperation, in order to make  the  digital  revolution  an  instrument  of  inclusion, sovereignty  and  development,  rather  than  a  source  of dependence and inequality.

We are drawing close to the end of the tenure of the current Secretary-General and the appointment of the next one, an act of great importance, given that the person chosen must integrity, possess competence  and  courage  to  build  consensus,  uphold  the Charter,  promote  conflict  prevention,  lead  the  necessary reforms  and  seek  solutions  to  address  the  Organization’s financial crisis.

independence,

The  Republic  of  Angola  reaffirms  its  commitment  to  the United  Nations,  convinced  that  only  at  the  level  of  this institution will it be possible to safeguard the achievements of recent decades in respect for International Law.

Only  within  the  framework  of  the  United  Nations  can  we make progress in seeking peaceful solutions to the conflicts ravaging  the  world,  within  a  framework in  which multilateralism  serves  as  the  mechanism  for  bringing together  ideas,  political  will  and  initiatives  conducive  to global peace.

We,  political  leaders  and  rulers  of  today,  will  be  judged  in the  future  by  our  ability  to  replace  confrontation  with cooperation, dialogue,  predatory

competition  with

exclusion  with  solidarity  and  the  force  of  arms  with  the force of law.

Only  in  this  way  will  we  build  a  more  just,  peaceful  and inclusive  international  order,  capable  of  ensuring  progress and well-being of humankind, leaving no one behind.

No  weapon  is  more  powerful  than  diplomacy,  since  all others are used only to destroy lives, infrastructure, dreams and  life  plans,  whereas  diplomacy  is  the  only  weapon  that exists to unite, repair, build and save lives, peoples, nations and humanity.

For  this  reason,  the  United  Nations  Organization  must equip  itself  with  the  appropriate  tools  and  means  to  fulfil the  theme  of  this  81st  session  of  its  General  Assembly, namely,  “Restoring  Trust,  Managing  Transformation  and Empowering It to Become an Organization That Delivers for All”.

Mr. President, Dear representatives of the Peoples of the United Nations,

Gunpowder changed the battlefield.

Nuclear fission changed the meaning of human survival.

Artificial intelligence is changing something even more intimate: who can enter the mind of a citizen, imitate a trusted voice, manufacture a reality calibrated to one person’s fears, and do so millions of times at once.

Albania is not a developer of frontier models. But we are a nation that has already lived the future others are still debating.

And I have come here with a simple message:

The greatest immediate danger is not that artificial intelligence will stop obeying humanity.

The greatest danger is that it will obey the wrong human beings perfectly.

The challenge comes in three layers: what artificial intelligence does instead of us, what it does to us, and who gains the power to reach us.

First, what it does instead of us.

The public debate imagines machines that awaken, acquire ambitions and turn against their creators.

But the systems confronting us today do not wake up with hatred in their hearts. They multiply ours.

They have no ambition of their own. They serve the ambitions of others.

They carry no flag. But they can be deployed by a state.

They tell no lie for their own benefit. But they can tell a billion lies on our behalf.

The machine has no conscience, but it can borrow the reach of a government, the precision of a weapon and the intimacy of a friend.

At the same time, the economic incentives surrounding artificial intelligence increasingly reward the replacement of human effort, rather than the enlargement of human capacity.

Write the code so that I do not have to understand it.

Draft the report so that I do not have to think through it.

Make the judgment so that I do not have to assume responsibility for it.

When success is measured only by how much work the machine removes from the human being, we may create more efficient institutions but less capable people.

A civilisation that outsources effort may eventually outsource knowledge.

A civilisation that outsources knowledge may eventually outsource judgment.

And a civilisation that outsources judgment will discover that it has also outsourced responsibility.

This is not inevitable. It is a choice.

We can build artificial intelligence that teaches rather than merely answers, guides rather than commands, and strengthens the human being instead of

making the human being dependent upon it.

The question cannot be only: How quickly did the machine complete the task?

We must also ask: What did the human being learn? Who understood the decision? Who can challenge it? And who answers when it is wrong?

Albania became the first country to bring an artificial intelligence instrument into the architecture of government through Diella, our artificial intelligence minister.

We did not do this to transfer sovereignty from people to a machine. We did it to make public services more accessible, procedures more transparent and the state more accountable.

No machine possesses democratic legitimacy.

No algorithm inherits constitutional responsibility.

Behind every consequential public decision there must remain a legal mandate, a human institution and a name that can be called to answer.

The second layer is what artificial intelligence can do to us.

Artificial intelligence inside an accountable state can reduce the distance between citizens and public services.

Artificial intelligence outside accountability can eliminate the distance between a lie and the human mind.

Albania experienced this directly.

A fabricated narrative of an Israeli invasion of the Albanian coast, an invasion that had never occurred, was manufactured, personalised and delivered through voices, pages and channels citizens already trusted.

One citizen received a story of national betrayal.

Another received a story of religious provocation.

Another received a conspiracy of foreign occupation.

Different fabrications entered different emotional worlds, all serving the same strategic lie.

The consequences were real.

Citizens protested against a phantom enemy. Antisemitic tropes entered our public discourse. Fear became anger, anger became mobilisation, and fabrication became political reality.

This was not a laboratory experiment.

It was not science fiction.

It was a Tuesday in Tirana.

The algorithm did not invent the objective. A human actor did.

The algorithm did not develop hatred. It discovered how to activate ours.

This is systematic fraud as a service.

Election interference no longer requires one television station or one piece of propaganda repeated to an entire population. It can now operate at the resolution of one voter.

Two neighbours may stand in the same street, vote in the same election and inhabit entirely different realities, each manufactured specifically for them.

When that happens, democracy does not merely lose a debate.

It loses the common ground on which debate is possible.

Sovereignty no longer erodes only at the border.

It erodes in the feed.

In the twentieth century, sovereignty meant control over land, territorial waters and national airspace.

In the twenty first century, it must also mean the capacity of a free society to defend the conditions under which its citizens form their own judgments.

And then comes the third layer: reach.

For centuries, the great threat to freedom of speech was censorship.

Today, freedom of speech is also threatened by the weaponisation of freedom of reach.

Speech is the right to express an idea.

Reach is the power to place that idea before millions of people.

Speech belongs to human beings.

Reach can be purchased, automated, manipulated and secretly assigned by platforms, corporations, criminal networks and foreign states.

The right to speak is universal.

But there is no universal right to anonymous, unlimited and artificially amplified reach.

When one lie can be multiplied a billion times, truth does not need to be censored. It can simply be buried.

The citizen remains formally free to speak, but speaks into a storm that no human voice can match.

Freedom of speech can therefore be defeated without banning a single book,

imprisoning a single journalist or deleting a single post.

The answer to bad speech remains more speech.

But the answer to covert, industrial amplification must be exposure.

Who created the message?

Who paid for it?

Was it spread by people or machines?

Why was this citizen targeted?

Was the apparent public reaction authentic, coordinated or foreign-directed?

Defending democracy does not mean controlling what people are allowed to think.

It means revealing the hidden powers seeking to control what people are made to see.

If we protect freedom of speech while leaving the control of reach completely opaque, we defend the door while surrendering the room.

Some respond by demanding that artificial intelligence be slowed or stopped.

Albania respectfully disagrees.

A pause by democracies will not produce a pause by dictatorships.

A moratorium observed by responsible states will not restrain hostile powers, criminal networks or industries of manipulation.

We cannot regulate ourselves into helplessness.

On this essential strategic question, President Donald Trump is right: we cannot stop. We must accelerate.

But acceleration must have a direction.

We need artificial intelligence that is verifiable, transparent and accountable, built by free societies, shared among allies and placed in the service of citizens.

The answer to weaponised automation is not technological surrender.

It is democratic capacity.

It is sovereign capability.

It is better artificial intelligence in the hands of those who remain accountable under law.

Sovereign artificial intelligence does not mean isolation. It means that no nation should be helpless before systems it cannot understand, inspect or challenge.

Every country must be able to protect its language, authenticate public communications, detect coordinated manipulation, preserve evidence and inform its citizens without depending entirely on the commercial priorities of a distant corporation.

This is why Albania is building an artificial intelligence based digital Mirror.

The Mirror will identify manipulation in real time, test claims against authoritative information, reveal coordinated patterns and help citizens understand not only what they are

seeing, but also how and why it reached them.

It will not tell citizens what they must think.

Truth cannot be decreed by a government. It must be evidenced, sourced, tested, challenged and defended in the open.

The Mirror is not intended to become an arbiter of opinion.

It is intended to become an infrastructure of transparency.

It does not seek to create a ministry of truth.

It seeks to defend society against an industry of lies.

Albania therefore calls for an international compact for sovereign and democratic artificial intelligence.

First, citizens must know when politically consequential content has been artificially generated or materially manipulated.

Second, the architecture of reach must become transparent. Citizens and states must be able to know who created, financed, targeted and artificially amplified consequential political content.

Third, every consequential use of artificial intelligence by a public institution must preserve a clear chain of human and legal accountability.

Fourth, democracies must create a shared early warning system so that evidence of artificial intelligence driven

manipulation can travel between allies as quickly as the manipulation itself.

And smaller nations and smaller languages must not be abandoned outside this protective architecture. Digital sovereignty cannot become a privilege reserved for the richest states.

Lies travel without visas.

Algorithms cross borders without passports.

Those attacking our societies already cooperate across jurisdictions. Our democracies must learn to do the same.

This is not ultimately a contest between humanity and machines.

It is a contest between different human purposes, each amplified by machines.

Between those who use artificial intelligence to enlighten and those who use it to obscure.

Between those who use it to empower citizens and those who use it to manipulate them.

Between those who accept responsibility and those who hide behind automation.

We should not fear that machines will become too human.

We should fear that human beings will become invisible behind machines.

Excellencies,

Every generation is called upon to defend freedom in the territory where freedom is most threatened.

For one generation, that territory was the battlefield.

For another, it was the ballot box.

For ours, it will increasingly be the human mind.

Let us ensure that no citizen is left alone before an algorithmic army.

Let us ensure that no small nation is forced to rent its understanding of reality from beyond its borders.

Let us ensure that no democracy wakes up after an election to discover that its people exercised their freedom of choice inside a world secretly designed for them by someone they could not see.

Artificial intelligence will not decide whether this century belongs to liberty or manipulation.

We will.

The machine will obey.

The question is whom it will obey, under what law and in the service of what human purpose.

Albania has made its choice.

We choose acceleration, but not surrender.

We choose innovation, but not abdication.

We choose augmentation, not the atrophy of human capability.

We choose sovereignty, but not isolation.

We choose freedom of speech. And precisely because we choose it, we refuse to confuse it with the unchecked freedom of machines, money and foreign powers to reach everyone, everywhere, without disclosure.

We choose truth, not because truth is always easy or comfortable, but because without a shared commitment to reality, there can be no shared public life.

And without a shared world, there can be no United Nations.

Thank you.

Mr. President,

Mr. Secretary-General,

There is an idea that has accompanied Andorra for more than two hundred and seventy years

and that continues to shape the way we understand politics. The Manual Digest, one of the

great works of our institutional heritage, through which Antoni Fiter i Rossell condensed

and recounted the essence of Andorran identity, reminds us that the legitimate exercise of

power only makes sense when it places the common good above any other interest.

This  idea,  written  in  1748,  long  before  modern  international  organizations  came  into

existence, remains remarkably relevant today, because multilateralism is nothing more than

the application of this same principle to relations among nations: the understanding that the

common good of the international community is inseparable from the well-being of each of

our countries.

In Andorra, this approach to politics has enabled us to preserve more than seven centuries

of peace, dialogue and coexistence. Not because history has been easier for us, but because

we have learned that the best way to protect freedom is to build trust, seek balance and make

compromise a form of governance. Perhaps it is precisely this experience that a small country

such as ours can share with this great Assembly today.

Mr. President,

Allow me to congratulate you on your election as President of the eighty-first session of the

General  Assembly.  I  am  convinced  that  your  experience  in  multilateralism  will  help

strengthen the role of the United Nations at a particularly decisive moment for the world

and for this Organization itself.

The theme you have chosen for this session, “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation:

An Effective and Inclusive United Nations for All,” accurately captures the challenges of our

time.

The crisis we face is not only geopolitical, economic, climatic or technological. Above all, it

is a crisis of trust: among States, between institutions and citizens, and above all in the ability

of the international community to fulfil the promise that gave meaning to the creation of the

United  Nations:  to  save  succeeding  generations  from  the  scourge  of  war,  to  uphold  the

inherent dignity of every human being, and to promote an international order founded on

human rights.

Trust is an intangible asset, perhaps the most valuable of all. It takes great effort to build, yet

very little to destroy.

When international commitments are relativized; when the Charter of the United Nations

ceases to serve as the shared framework guiding the actions of States; when international

humanitarian law is violated with a frequency that risks normalizing horror; or when civilians

cease to be protected and instead become targets, what is weakened is not only peace itself,

but also confidence in the international order and in all the organizations that represent and

promote it.

From this Assembly, Andorra wishes to reiterate a conviction it has upheld for more than

three decades: for small States, multilateralism is not a strategic option but a guarantee that

all countries, regardless of their size, can make their voices heard on an equal legal footing.

It is the clearest expression of the principle that the force of law must always prevail over the

law of force.

It is precisely for this reason that we continue to firmly defend the need to uphold the Charter

of the  United Nations, international law and international humanitarian  law. We  support,

more than ever, the efforts of the International Criminal Court to identify those responsible

for the gravest crimes and we condemn any act of aggression that violates the sovereignty

and territorial integrity of a State.

In this sense, we continue to express our solidarity with the people of Ukraine in the face of

The effects of global warming are being felt across many regions of the world, from coastal
