Excellencies, president of the 81st session of the General Assembly. Mr. Secretary General, your excellencies, heads of State and government, distinguished delegates. Ladies and gentlemen allow me to. Before delivering the message of His Excellency Denis Sassou-nguesso, president of the Republic of the Congo, please allow me to express my very deep gratitude for the honour he has bestowed upon me by entrusting me with this mission, and I carry it out with respect, loyalty, and a sense of duty. Fully aware of the significance of faithfully conveying the national message entrusted to me today. Your excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, the Republic of the Congo congratulates the election of His Excellency Mr. Halilu Rahman as president of the 81st session of the General Assembly.

We also pay tribute to Her Excellency, Miss Annalena Baerbock for her contribution to our work, and we further express our profound gratitude to His Excellency Mr. Antonio Guterres, Secretary general of the United Nations, for his advocacy. Advocacy on behalf of Africa, his constant commitment to the Congo Basin and his support to the peace, mediation and dialogue efforts undertaken by our country. And in this regard, the Republic of the Congo is following very closely the selection process for the next UN Secretary General. We believe that Africa a continent at the centre of many UN challenges and global geopolitical issues, must remain at the heart of the future. Secretary-General's agenda. The next Secretary General must embrace a truly universal vision of the United Nations, one that leaves no continent continent at the margins and which fully takes into account Africa's place, responsibilities and legitimate interests.

Your excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, for the Republic of the Congo. Restoring trust and managing transformation of our international institutions is a collective imperative. The theme of this session, Restoring Trust and Managing Transformation, resonates as a call for clarity and courage. In a world where trust is eroding, tensions are rising and double standards and relationships of fourths threaten to replace both the spirit and the letter of the UN charter. Humanity has never needed a renewed, inclusive and representative multilateralism more than it does today, a multilateralism that can reflect the realities of a multi-polar world in which Africa occupies its rightful place. This renewal requires a deep reform of international institutions.

Foremost amongst them the Security Council. Africa, strengthened by its history, its demographic dynamism and geopolitical importance, can no longer remain on the sidelines of decisions that shape its destiny. It must become a full and legitimate actor in accordance with the consensus. Africa's demand for two permanent Security Council seats with veto power is not a request, but a right, a legitimate right. Grounded. Which reflects the realities of the 21st century.

The world has changed and our institutions must evolve with it. This is an imperative, and Africa is not asking for a favor. It is claiming its rightful place. The Republic of the Congo is a member of the Committee of Heads of States and Governments of the African Union on Security Council reform. The C10 Committee will not compromise on this shared demand. Your Excellency, ladies and gentlemen, the Republic of the Congo reiterates its willingness to serve the international community.

With your support, we renew our aspiration to serve as a non-permanent member of the UN Security Council for the 2030 2031 term. This candidacy of ours is rooted in a long diplomatic tradition. Our sustained commitment to peace and a strong sense of international responsibility. For more than five decades, our diplomacy has contributed constantly and effectively to numerous peace processes on our continent, and which also had global implications. And let me quote the following our contribution to supporting Namibia's liberation, and then the withdrawal of Cuban troops from Angola through the 1988 Brazzaville Protocol. The efforts to end hostilities in the Central African Republic, the initiatives to promote reconciliation in Libya, where my country leads the African Union High level Committee.

Also, the peace efforts in the Great Lakes region. Our diplomacy is not a diplomacy of confrontation. It is diplomacy based on dialogue, mediation, mutual respect and African solutions to African problems. We reaffirm here and now the Pan-African vocation of our diplomacy and our commitment to international law. Your excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, sovereignty is not a rejection of cooperation. Sovereignty is the ability of a people and a nation to freely determine their priorities, to defend their legitimate interests, to choose their partners, and to preserve their independence in decision making And this is the understanding of sovereignty that the Republic of the Congo upholds.

And we intend to continue pursuing a foreign policy based on non-alignment, diversification of partnerships mutual respect among states, and the rejection of any foreign interference in domestic affairs. We are open to the world, but we intend to remain masters of our choices and our destiny. The Republic of the Congo does not seek to choose one camp against another Rather, we seek to be a bridge between nations. Your excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, the Republic of the Congo has embarked upon a profound transformation through our national roadmap, which is called Let's Accelerate the March towards Development. And it includes the following priorities investing in human capital, promoting youth employment, strengthening public governance, diversifying the economy, modernizing agriculture and industry, expanding infrastructure, accelerating digital transformation and innovation, and consolidating peace and social cohesion. We are building a Congo that does more than export raw materials.

We aim to process and add value to our resources domestically, and this explains our interest in special economic zones because we think political sovereignty must go hand in hand with economic sovereignty. Our vision, I would like to point out, aligns with the Sustainable Development Goals, the SDGs and the 2063 African Union agenda, the Africa we want. But let's be lucid and pragmatic here. The ambitions of our development of the Republic of the Congo and many other African countries are impeded by the burden of debt inequalities in the international financial system and the consequences of climate change. For years before the 2030 SDG deadline, we cannot afford another collective failure. The Republic of the Congo, therefore, calls for an ambitious international action on the issue of developing country debt, including through debt relief and, where appropriate, debt cancellation measures to free resources for SDG related investments.

Your excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, Africa is not the world's periphery. It is one of its centers of gravity and a source of multilateral renewal. When Africa speaks with one voice, it advances the international agenda and inspires the world and opens new perspectives. Three major initiatives by my country illustrate this the United Nations Decade for Afforestation and Reforestation 2027 to 2036, which was promoted by my country, the Republic of the Congo. Resolution 8250 on the transatlantic slave trade, recognizing it as a crime against humanity, which was promoted by Ghana and the correct the Map resolution promoted by Togo. These initiatives show that Africa contributes towards defining the international agenda.

It is in this spirit that the Republic of the Congo will continue with its commitment to Africa. The removal of the visas as of the 1st of January 2027 for Africans promotes free movement, Intra-african tourism and solidarity amongst African people. Making our trade more inclusive all the while promoting the African Continental Free Trade Area. Ladies and gentlemen, Your Excellencies, the duty of memory also forces us to look at our history in in squarely in the eye. And we are working on a major historical memorial. The longer Bay Memorial Memorial.

From this region. Countless people were torn from their families and homeland. Through the transatlantic slave trade, Luongo must become a place of truth, remembrance, reflection, but also a place of renewal. And our ambition here is to make Luongo like a Gorée in Senegal, like Cape Coast in Ghana or Ouidah in Benin, should become a bridge between Africa and its diaspora. The people of African descent worldwide can reconnect with their history, identity and dignity there. This is also the rationale of our 2025 meetings in Harlem with people of African descent.

Your Excellency, ladies and gentlemen, we also re affirm our determination to mobilize Congolese living abroad. Our diaspora is a human benefit and intellectual one, scientific and economic one. Its competencies, its experience, its investments, commitment are needed to accelerate our own development. We need all of our children for a. To realize our human capital. The Republic of the Congo, is a land of opportunity.

It's endowed with natural resources, with critical minerals, with agricultural potential, with tourism potential, which has not yet been developed. Our expanding infrastructure and a strategic location at the heart of Central Africa. And we invite investors and development partners to join us through, for example, mutually beneficial public private partnerships. We want the partnerships that create added value, develop our national competencies, promote technology, transfer, respect our interests, and help us manage and develop our economy. Your excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, the Republic of the Congo also bears a special responsibility for the Congo Basin, which is the world's second largest environmental Lung. This exceptional ecosystem contains, contains immense biodiversity and plays a crucial role in regulating the global climate.

The Congo Basin is one of Africa's principal contributions to the fight against climate change. We cannot continuously accept that countries preserve these ecosystems on their own and bear the cost alone. Conservation has a cost and international solidarity. Solidarity must also have a value. We therefore call for fair and predictable compensation for ecosystems and carbon services for innovative, sustainable financing mechanism increased capitalisation of the Blue Fund and for the recognition of the Congo Basin as a global priority, and for the strengthening of international cooperation aimed at preserving it. We.

Support a United Nations institution in the Republic of the Congo dedicated to the preservation of the basin. We also are asking for launching of a decade of the United Nations on afforestation, reforestation and national plans for the implementation. Excellent. Ladies and gentlemen, um. Above and beyond our rivers and forests. The tourist of the territory of the country is more than a geographical space.

It is the foundation of our nation, the basis of our identity, the territory for our sovereignty. The Republic of the Congo will always defend the integrity of its territory, the security of our borders, mastering our resources, and the freedom of our strategic choices. Our sovereignty is not negotiable. It is the responsibility that we owe to future generations, the inheritance that we need to bestow on future generations. Your excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, we are a defender of peace internationally, and we are therefore call for negotiations between Russia and Ukraine for de-escalation in the Strait of Hormuz, a just and lasting political solution in the Middle East and in Palestine. We call for the stabilization of Eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo.

Return of the lasting peace in Sudan, continued reconciliation in Libya, lifting of the embargo against Cuba, restoring of peace and stability in the Sahel. We reaffirm that peace is not weakness, that negotiation is not surrender. The dialogue is not capitulation. And in this spirit, we will continue to prioritize mediation, dialogue and looking for peaceful political solutions so as to build Africa, which is prosperous and peace. From Libya to Sahel, from Sudan to Great Lakes. We reiterate the fact that we are available to accompany our brotherly countries in their work to achieve return to peace and stability through our history.

We know that peace is difficult to build, but it is the only victory that benefits one and all. Ladies and gentlemen, Your Excellencies, guided by the same sense of responsibility, the recurring Ebola outbreaks and repeated pandemics have shown that global threats are no longer solely military or economic. Health security has become an essential component of collective security, and here we will continue supporting. The strengthening of the World Health Organization Regional Office for Africa in Brazzaville and will shoulder all of its responsibilities in accordance with the 1952 Headquarters Agreement. We also call for international governance of artificial intelligence and outer space. These technologies must remain in the service of humanity, progress and the empowerment of peoples technological progress must not become a new instrument of domination.

Africa must also be a center of creativity, innovation and digital sovereignty. Your excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, to conclude, the Republic of the Congo remains faithful to its principles peace, development, sovereignty, good neighbourliness, dialogue, cooperation and mutual respect amongst nations. We will continue to defend our national interests while fulfilling our international responsibilities. We will continue to believe in Africa and in our shared destiny, and we will continue to choose the United Nations as a privileged space for dialogue amongst people. I thank you. I thank the Minister of Foreign Affairs, La Francophonie, and Congolese abroad of the Congo.

Mr. Secretary general, Mr. Vice president of the General Assembly, heads of State and government. Excellencies, ambassadors. Ladies and gentlemen, I appear today before this assembly representing the president of the Republic of Colombia, Abelardo de la Espriella, who has asked me to be here on his behalf and bring before you a message written by him. From this moment on, what you will hear are the words of the president of the Republic of Colombia. I have asked the Vice President of the Republic, José Manuel Restrepo, to read this message on my behalf. I have done so because I assured the Colombian people that I would not leave the country during the four years of my term, and I am keeping that promise.

47 days ago, a new government took office in Colombia. Three days later, at 7:34 a.m., the earth shook. A 7.4 magnitude earthquake struck my country in a matter of seconds. Homes, hospitals, schools, roads and bridges had been totally destroyed or severely damaged. The Colombian Geological Service confirmed that this was the strongest magnitude earthquake recorded in Colombia so far this century Hundreds of Colombians lost their lives. 4500 were injured and more than 452,000 people were affected.

36,000 homes were totally destroyed. They represented the life savings assets of these people. The government that had barely started its work was forced to confront one of the greatest natural disasters in our recent history. There was no time to ask whether we were ready. We had to act, and we did so. From the very outset.

I gave one unequivocal instruction we had to save human lives. There was time for everything else. Appointments to posts could wait, meetings could wait. But my fellow fellow Colombians trapped underneath the rubble could not. The government deployed to the affected areas alongside the security forces, emergency services, volunteers and rescue workers. And from the very beginning, we started receiving the generous assistance from friendly countries and international organizations such as all of you.

And today, from this rostrum, I wish to express the profound and sincere gratitude of the Colombian people to all of you. The earthquake claimed the lives of many of our fellow Colombians and destroyed thousands of homes and buildings and much infrastructure. But it also reminded us once again of something that Colombians are very familiar with. We might fall, we might suffer, and we might weep. But what we cannot and what we do not know how to do is give up. But I'm not only going to talk to you about this tragedy.

I want to refer to what Colombia decided to do in its aftermath. On the 7th of August, I took over a country that had begun to lose something far more difficult to rebuild than a road or a building. That is trust. Trust in the law that should protect our citizens. Trust that working, studying, and doing things well are worthwhile. Trust in a state that lives up to its duty.

No country, no country can prosper when its people cease to trust in it. That's why the government that I lead has tasked itself with taking up every possible decision to enable Colombia to believe in itself again, and to ensure that the world can believe in Colombia again. And I call that overarching purpose the patria milagro, the miracle nation. The first step is a basic one restoring security. For far too long, Colombians have had to live alongside situations that no society should accept as normal. A rural farmer having to ask permission from a terrorist group to work on his land, a shopkeeper having to hand over part of the fruits of his labor to extortionists, a mother increasingly gripped by fear every time their child goes out to play in the park.

That is not, and it cannot become the norm. Consequently, from the very beginning of my government I gave the security forces one clear instruction to regain territorial control, to fully restore the state's authority and to confront the structures using terrorism. My government is determined to do away with euphemisms. Organizations that murder, that kidnap, that use explosives, that recruit children, and that deliberately resort to terror to subjugate a society are terrorist groups. That is what we call them, and we are facing up to them with the full, legitimate force of the state, within the Constitution and within the law But there is another reality that is very often overlooked. The illicit drugs produced in Colombia don't end up in Colombia.

Drugs trafficking is a transnational criminal enterprise. Its routes cross borders. Its money moves through international financial systems, and its networks operate across numerous countries. I will do everything necessary to combat that scourge, but a transnational threat requires the international community to play its part as well. Security, while essential, is not enough. A territory that provides no opportunities remains vulnerable.

My administration is therefore also focused on ensuring that Colombia grows again. For years, we have discussed how to better distribute what we have. That is a legitimate, necessary discussion, but it's absolutely not enough. We also need to ask ourselves, how are we going to produce more? In the end? Governments can't decree economic growth.

What they have to do is lay the foundations for it to occur. In our miracle nation, we want an idea to be able to come, a business, a business to create jobs, and for jobs to become well-being for our people. To those of you anywhere else in the world who are wondering where to invest, I would like to invite you to look at Colombia. It's a country with access to two oceans, productive land, energy resources, enormous biodiversity, an excellent geographical position, and a government that champions private enterprise. But above all, look at our people. Colombia does not want to watch the technological transformation of our time from the sidelines.

We want to be a part of it. We want to train young people for super intelligence, for robotics, for data science, for agro industry for engineering, and for the new economy. Millions of Colombians are not asking the state to sort out their lives. They're asking the state to give them the opportunity to build those lives. And that is what gives meaning to what I have called the miracle nation. This isn't the name of a government, nor is it a naive promise that our problems will just disappear.

No, that's not it. This is the country that we're going to build. It's a country where security allows us to reclaim our territories threatened by terrorism, where trust attracts investment, where investment creates jobs, and where growth leads to better living conditions. It is a schoolteacher in Mompos Bolivar, teaching with the tools of the 21st century. It is a rural farmer in Ubaté Cundinamarca who can now so sell and prosper thanks to his work. It's a.

A young woman in Pasto, Narino, preparing to be a part of the future industries This is the miracle nation that we've already started to build. I'm well aware that 47 days is far too little time to change a country, but it is enough time to change the course of a country. And I want Colombia to once again enjoy strong growth. That growth should lead to a job for a young person, a home for a family, timely access to medicines, a harvest that finds a market, and Colombians who, thanks to their own efforts and dedication, can escape poverty. This is our miracle economy, an economy that grows so that people can grow with it Our relationship with the world is also a part of this purpose. Over the last few weeks, we have seen this very tangibly.

When friendly countries and international organizations came to our aid following the earthquake. This solidarity makes full sense when it reaches people, when it solves problems, and when it produces results. And it is precisely because I recognize the value of that cooperation that today I want to speak frankly about the UN. I've been critical about this, of this organization. I was critical of it before I became president, and it would be inconsistent to address this Assembly today and conceal my attempt to seal my convictions. This criticism isn't born out of whim or hostility towards the United Nations.

It's based in political, institutional, doctrinal considerations. I believe in the UN as an organization, and it is precisely for that reason that I believe it's legitimate to ask whether the institutions that we've been building are effectively responding to the problems that that it was created to address. The charter itself is very clear here. This organization was born to maintain international peace and security, to foster friendly relations among nations, and to promote cooperation in resolving the major common problems. Eight decades on, the question cannot be whether those purposes remain valid. Of course they do The questions have completely changed, though.

Is the UN fulfilling those purposes with the effectiveness demanded by today's world? Are there bureaucratic structures that have become excessively cumbersome? Are we dedicating too many resources, too much energy to administering procedures and or too little to resolving problems? Are we measuring our results rigorously enough? Another matter that I wish to address is human rights. Colombia defends human rights and will continue to do so.

But my country believes that protecting human rights loses credibility when it becomes subjected to political calculation. I categorically reject human rights being used as a banner raised against some and lowered against others. Nor can human rights become an instrument rewarding friends, punishing adversaries, or, worse still, remaining silent in line with the political circumstances of the time. Our duty is to prevent politics from weakening the defense of human rights. If we want the system to be respected, it needs to be serious, consistent and equally demanding on all of us. My country is consistent, and therefore we want to ensure that we have a credible defense of human rights.

And in this, just as in so many other areas, the United Nations still has some room for improvement in that connection. We trust in a democratic transition in Venezuela, a swift, safe, far reaching transition. There's another doctrinal concern that I wish to raise just as honestly globalism. Allow me to begin by clarifying what I mean by that. I'm not talking about international trade or cooperation among states, nor am I talking about a humanity that shares common problems and responsibilities. All of those things are absolutely necessary I'm talking about a concept according to which nation sovereignty, distinct identities, traditions, and the values of peoples are obstacles that gradually give way to increasing political and cultural uniformity decided by supranational bodies.

I don't share in that doctrine, which I consider perverse and harmful. For me, multilateralism isn't about dissolving nations, but rather about facilitating cooperation among them. Loving one's homeland isn't compatible with respecting others, defending history, culture, values, and traditions doesn't mean disparaging those of another. International cooperation is richer when those who sit around this table know who they are, where they come from, and what the people in whose name they speak represent. Several of the questions that I've asked are not unfamiliar to this organization. The UN 80 initiative has placed on the table issues of duplication, fragmentation, administrative burden, and the way mandates function as part of an effort to make the United Nations more efficient and more effective.

President, Secretary general, heads of State and government. Excellencies. Acknowledging an institution's imperfections doesn't mean overlooking its value. On the contrary, it might be a way of strengthening it. It has never been my style to hide behind political correctness or to tell my interlocutors what I imagine they want to hear. I'm not looking to please anyone, but rather to set out the position of the Republic of Colombia respectfully, cordially and clearly.

No human institution is perfect. All can be improved perfected, and the United Nations is no exception. There is one specific area that Colombia wishes to reflect on further. That is the international fight against terrorism. This organization has done significant work here. Since 1963, the international community has developed 19 universal legal instruments aimed at preventing different terrorist acts.

However, after decades of discussion, there is still no legal definition of terrorism that is universally agreed by member states. The UN Office of Counterterrorism itself has recently flagged that the lack of a universally agreed definition begets legal uncertainty. Discrepancies among national laws and causes difficulties in international cooperation. The Republic of Colombia believes that the time has come to move ahead. We need a common international definition that is sufficiently clear and precise, compatible with international law and fundamental safeguards, but also useful enough so that states can cooperate effectively in combating acts of terrorism. A serious definition should avoid two extremes.

On the one hand, a political disagreement being arbitrarily characterized as terrorism, and on the other hand, allowing an organization to hide murders, kidnappings, bombings, or deliberate attacks against civilians behind a political label in order to evade the legal consequences of its actions. Terrorism must be condemned regardless of the perpetrator, where it is committed or the cause they invoke. The United Nations has repeatedly reaffirmed that terrorism, in all its forms and manifestations, represents one of the most serious threats to international peace and security. Now, a better definition is not enough. States need better tools to combat this phenomenon. We need faster mechanisms for exchanging information and intelligence.

We need better judicial cooperation, effective tracing, freezing, seizing instruments for assets related to terrorist financing. And we need closer cooperation to deal with networks that operate simultaneously across different countries. Colombia stands ready to participate actively in that discussion. My country wants to see United Nations, where the effectiveness is measured less by the volume of documents it produces, and far more by the results that it delivers. A UN that is less inclined to multiply processes and more determined to translate international cooperation into concrete action. That is the sort of multilateralism that Colombia is ready to defend, one that respects the sovereign equality of states as the charter itself provides, but one that is also capable of acting effectively when threats recognize no borders, drugs, trafficking, terrorism, transnational organized crime and illicit economies are precisely those threats.

Specifically, my government's foreign policy is guided by national interests by the defense of our sovereignty, and by the pursuit of results. That national interest I refer to also has a specific objective that is ensuring the prosperity of our people. Foreign policy should serve to create jobs, to attract investment and technology, to open markets, and to create opportunities for Colombians. With that goal in mind, I wish to extend an invitation to the world. Come to Colombia, invest in Colombia grow and prosper with Colombia Believe in Colombia. I don't promise you a perfect country, but I can assure you that I am working tirelessly to build you a nation that is, to build a nation that is safer, more prosperous, and with more opportunities for its people.

Colombia does not come before the world today to ask others to do for us what it is our responsibility to do for ourselves rebuilding our country, restoring security, growing the economy, protecting our institutions, and giving opportunities back to millions of people are first and foremost responsibilities that fall to Colombians. But we also know that no nation can turn its back on the world. We need partners and friends with whom we can trade, invest, exchange knowledge, and address common threats. That is the Colombia that I present to you today, a country that is well aware of its difficulties, but also of its enormous potential. A country that doesn't try to hide its problems, but rather to confront them. A country that is getting back on its feet and knows where it wants to go.

To the nations represented here, I extend my hand respectfully and through friendship. Colombia wants to work with you on everything that we can build together. I want within a few years, when the world looks again at my country, I want them to see a nation that is safer, more prosperous, more well respected and above all, far more confident in its own abilities. And if that is the Colombia that the world sees, there'll be no need to explain what I meant when I spoke of the Patria Milagro, the miracle nation. Thank you very much.

Mr. president of the General Assembly, your Majesties, Your Highnesses. The United Nations Secretary General, your excellencies, heads of State and government, your excellencies, heads of delegations, distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen. Peace be upon you. At the outset, I would like to. On behalf of the Comorian delegation, I wish to express our sincere gratitude to the authorities of the United States. We thank them for the hospitality and arrangements extended to us since our arrival in New York.

For this 81st session of our Assembly. Allow me to also congratulate His Excellency Doctor Khalilur Rahman on his election as president of the session, and to wish him every success in his noble mission. I would also like to pay a well-deserved tribute to Her Excellency, Miss Annalena Baerbock, for her work and her wisdom in guiding the previous session. I would also like to pay tribute to the leadership of His Excellency Antonio Guterres, Secretary general of the United Nations, and commend his commitment to peace and development at a time when the international order is under severe strain. As he prepares to hand over the leadership of our organization and an international context marked by tension and uncertainty. I extend my best wishes.

To his successor. At a time when confidence in international institutions is declining, and they are often perceived as favoring power politics over law. Our organization must rise above partisan interests. God willing the next leadership will embody unity and the renewal of a more credible multilateralism, and this will have the full support of the Comoros. He will be essential for that voice to defend the aspirations of developing countries, particularly small island and vulnerable states, and to foster collective responses to the challenges we share. For 81 years, this General Assembly.

Has remained the central pillar of multilateralism. And now that we are meeting in New York, humanity is at a crossroads. Despite our efforts the Sustainable Development Goals of the 2030 agenda remain unfortunately out of reach. Growing inequalities, the climate emergency, the fragility of international peace all require renewed clarity and determination on our part. Restoring trust, mutual respect and equality before the law is our collective responsibility. During this 81st session.

Mr. president, distinguished participants, a year ago, we called in this very hall for peace to be the foundation of development and human rights. 12 months later, we must acknowledge that the gap between our commitments and reality remains evident everywhere around the world, from the Middle East to the Sahel, through the Great Lakes region, in Eastern Europe and Latin America, civilian populations continue to pay the high price of conflict, driven by interests that are often hidden. The devastating war in the Middle East, marked by massive civilian losses and destruction of critical infrastructure. Mr. President of the General Assembly, Mr. Secretary-General of the United Nations,

It is a pleasure to be here, representing Cabo Verde, in this forum where the world comes together to discuss the challenges we share and the future we want to build.

I come from a country made up of ten islands in the Atlantic. A country aware of its vulnerabilities, but one that has learned that the size of a territory must never determine the size of our dreams.

The history of Cabo Verde is also a history of learning. We have learned to confront  drought  and  scarcity,  to  transform  the  sea  from  a  barrier  into  a bridge, but, above all, we have learned that a nation’s greatest wealth lies in its people. We even have a word for this wealth, which is "morabeza", a term that defines the cordiality, determination, and kindness of our people, which the whole world was able to witness a little during this year's Football World Cup.

Amílcar Cabral, one of the great figures of our history, left us a lesson that continues to resonate across generations:

“Learn in life, learn from our people, learn from the books and from the experiences of others. Learn always.”

Perhaps this is an ability that the world must rediscover: the ability to learn from history, to learn from one another, and to understand that there can be no lasting development without peace, just as there can be no lasting peace where poverty, exclusion and lack of opportunity persist.

In this spirit, Cabo Verde reaffirms its faith in the United Nations, in dialogue among nations, in cooperation among peoples, and in the primacy of Law over the use of force.

In  the  face  of  the  wars,  inequalities,  and  crises  confronting  our  world,  we reaffirm our unwavering commitment to the Charter of the United Nations, to the sovereignty and territorial integrity of States, to the protection of civilian populations, and to the peaceful resolution of conflicts.

International Law and International Humanitarian Law cannot be applied in a selective manner. They will only be truly strong and fulfill their role when they are respected and upheld by all.

In  our  region,  terrorism,  violent  extremism  and  transnational  crimes  also remind  us institutions  and cooperation.

that  peace  requires  prevention,  strong

And requires opportunities.

Africa is the continent with the youngest population in the world. Therefore, investing  in  our  young  people,  in  education,  in  knowledge,  and  in  the possibility of building a dignified life means also investing in peace.

Learning also means embracing change.

The world of today is not the world of 1945.  The institutions we created to respond to the challenges of that time need to learn with the world that has changed.

Cabo Verde therefore supports a United Nations that is more effective, more transparent,  and  more  representative.  The  UN80  Initiative  presents  an opportunity  to  modernize  this  Organization  and  strengthen  its  response capacity.

In this spirit, we also support the reform of the Security Council.

Africa  is  home  to  nearly  one-quarter  of  the  Member  States  of  this Organization  and  represents  approximately  one-fifth  of the  world’s population, and yet it still lacks the representation it deserves on this Council.

Therefore,  we  support  a  more  equitable  African  representation, accordance with the Ezulwini Consensus and the Sirte Declaration.

in

A fairer international order also requires fairer and more inclusive institutions.

The  election  of  the  next  Secretary-General  should  reflect  the  same principles: transparency, inclusion, merit and equal opportunities.

But the United Nations is not just a place where we discuss crises. It is also the space where we build common paths.

The  2030  Agenda,  the  African  Union's  Agenda  2063  and  the  Pact  for the Future point us in one direction: sustainable development, centered on the people, capable of transforming global commitments into concrete changes in the lives of populations.

This is also the mission of the new Government of Cabo Verde: to concretely improve the lives of its people.

And we have placed education at the heart of this mission.

Because  the  school  is  where  a  society  begins  to  shape  its  future.  And Education is a powerful development strategy.

We seek to transform knowledge into innovation, decent employment, and opportunities;  to  strengthen  our  education  and  health  systems;  and  to advance  progress  in  digital  transformation,  gender  equality,  the  energy transition, water security, and the blue economy.

We  want  to  create  more  opportunities  for  our  young  people  and  build  an economy capable of transforming people’s talent into development.

Development is transforming knowledge into opportunity and opportunity into dignity.

For  Cabo  Verde  and  other  Small  Island  States,  the  climate  crisis  is  not  a distant threat; it is a present reality - it’s here: the droughts, desertification, water scarcity, ocean acidification, and rising sea levels.

Just look at what is happening on the island of Sal, where, only two days ago, rising sea waters flooded the avenue in front of the hotels.

It is also a question of justice, because those who have contributed the least to this crisis cannot continue to bear some of its most serious consequences.

Science has shown us the way forward. We must now translate this valuable knowledge into decisions and actions.

Cabo Verde has tried to do its part.

In September 2024, Cabo Verde launched  a call for a Global Compact for

Climate  Mobility,  and  in  June,  in  Berlin,  57  countries  endorsed  the  Global

Consensus on the Principles to Address Climate Mobility.

At the United Nations, Cabo Verde co-facilitated negotiations on the Political Declaration of the Third Conference on the Oceans and the Declaration on Sea Level Rise.

For  a  country  made  up  of  islands,  protecting  the  ocean  is  not  just  an environmental policy.

It is protecting the national territory, the economy, the culture, and the future.

In January 2027, Cabo Verde will take over the Presidency of the Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS). We will take on this responsibility by working for the unity of Small Island States, the implementation of the Antigua and

Barbuda Agenda, for fairer financing, for climate adaptation, and for ensuring that the oceans remain at the heart of the global agenda.

And in 2034, we will host the Fifth International Conference on Small Island Developing  States,  providing  an  opportunity  to  share  experiences,  build common responses, and transform vulnerabilities into opportunities.

There is also pedagogy in the relationships between Nations.

It begins with the ability to listen.

It  entails  the  humility  to  recognize  that  no  one  country  alone  has  all  the answers.

And it makes sense when what we learn together is translated into action.

This, after all, is the essence of multilateralism.

In a time of fragmentation, we need to regain trust. In a time of confrontation, we need to strengthen cooperation. In a time when force so often prevails, we need to reaffirm the Law.

But our history has taught us to engage in dialogue, to build bridges, and to seek consensus.

It also taught us that no country is too small to have a voice and no challenge is too big to tackle when we work together.

The  United  Nations  must  continue  to  be  the  space  for  this  collective endeavor.

And I will recall what Amílcar Cabral taught us: “Learn always.”

Today,  learning  also  means  understanding  that  educating  a  child, providing  opportunities  for  young  people,  protecting  the  planet,

fighting poverty, promoting development, and building peace are not separate missions.

They are, indeed, different ways of caring for the future.

And perhaps this is the greatest lesson that our times require of us: the future is not simply what we receive.

Rather, it is what we are able to teach, learn, and build together.

Thank you

text:
Mr. president. With a great sense of humility and respect, I address you and the excellencies here in this illustrious hall. More than eight decades ago, the founders of the United Nations understood that no peace built on brute force could stand the test of time. They opted instead for law, cooperation, and dialogue as pillars of a new international order. Today, this conviction is facing one of the toughest tests it has faced since the organization's foundation. The world stands in a period of deep rooted fragmentation.

The world is deeply polarized. Armed conflicts are dragging on longer than before. Transnational organized crime is broadening its capacity to act. Its tentacles are growing longer. The effects of climate change are growing. Ever more intense development divides remain, and the technological transformation is posing unprecedented challenges to our institutions.

At the same time, trust in multilateralism is waning precisely when we need it most. Standing before this landscape, Costa Rica reaffirms its belief that no state, no state can alone address challenges that are common to us all. Multilateralism is a prerequisite for the preservation of peace, to promote sustainable development and to protect human dignity. However, multilateralism will only preserve its dignity if it proves able to yield tangible results. Specific results for people for human beings. Costa Rica champions a United Nations which is more agile, more efficient, more transparent and more accountable to its member states.

Our organization should establish priorities, do away with overlaps, make prudent use of its resources, and measure its results. President, international peace and security are facing increasingly complex threats transnational organized crime, drug trafficking, trafficking in persons, weapons smuggling, asset laundering, cybercrime and illegal mining transcend national borders and undermine democratic stability, development and the rule of law Costa Rica has first hand experience of these threats. Illegal mining, spearheaded by transnational, organized, transnational criminal organizations on our border with Nicaragua, has wrought havoc on the environment and is producing risks to public health, the economy, and regional security. These organizations dispute territory They fuel illegal economies. They wage attacks against democratic institutions and directly affect the rights and dignity of persons. Artificial intelligence can boost cyber terrorism and other crimes that we cannot yet envisage.

Costa Rica, according to Microsoft's system use data, is the Latin American country that makes greatest use of artificial intelligence. We use it 58% more. Than the. Other than the world. On average, these threats require greater international cooperation, information exchange, stronger institutions, and a renewed commitment to international law and international humanitarian law. Mr. president, Costa Rica has demonstrated that environmental leadership is not measured by the size of a country's territory, but rather by how unstinting its commitment is to both present and future generations.

For decades, we have championed a vision whereby economic prosperity and the protection of nature are not mutually exclusive goals. Rather, they complement each other. Climate change is dealing a particularly heavy blow to the most vulnerable among us. At the same time, biodiversity loss is picking up pace, as is ecosystem degradation, the pollution of our water resources and the pressures on our oceans. These are not isolated challenges. They converge in one global crisis that is imperiling food security, public health and development opportunities for millions and millions of people President, there can be no lasting security.

In a world where we see the erosion of democratic institutions, there can be no sustainable development. When we violate human rights, our response must have human beings at its heart. Costa Rica will continue championing the dignity and human rights of all persons, paying particular attention to the inclusion, autonomy, empowerment and effective participation of persons with disabilities, including of persons with autism. Against this backdrop, we reiterate our grave concern at the situation in Nicaragua the erosion of fundamental freedoms, the persecution of dissenting voices, the shutdown of civic space, religious persecution and reports of human rights violations continue to draw the country further and further away from democratic principles As a neighboring nation that has welcomed hundreds and hundreds of thousands of Nicaraguan citizens, we remain staunchly committed to defending their rights and to the restoration of the rule of law in Nicaragua. We also note the situation in Cuba with concern, and we once again hear appeal for the full respect of human rights and fundamental freedoms. We also continue to closely follow the situation in Venezuela.

As it unfolds, we harbor the hope that dialogue will prevail along with the respect for the people's will, the restoration of democratic institutions, and the provision of care and services to particularly vulnerable individuals. President, 8081 years after the adoption of the charter, the best way to defend the United Nations is to defend its ability to discharge its mandates. We need a U.N. which is more effective, transparent and agile, able to prevent conflicts, forge consensus even in times of deeply rooted polarization. We need a UN able to offer tangible responses to the challenges of the 21st century. For this reason, Costa Rica has presented the candidacy of Miss Rebecca Greenspan to the position of Secretary general of the United Nations. She is a Latin American woman with a woman with a wealth of political, economic experience and experience in the multilateral arena.

She has a proven track record of leadership. She knows the United Nations from the inside and from outside, and she understands that knowing an institution intimately and serving it also involves having the courage to reform it. Her candidacy is rooted in a simple but powerful idea. Defending the United Nations means and requires having the courage to reform it. Today, we need a leader able to unite the membership, strengthen the organization, and renew trust in international cooperation. We need a UN that does what it is called upon to do in its founding charter, that is, maintain international peace and security, ensure respect for human rights and advance development.

Costa Rica firmly believes that the next secretary general must be a Latin American woman. More than that, it must be Rebecca Greenspan. Costa Rica abolished its army more than seven decades ago. We did that because we believed that international law could offer greater security than weapons. I wish to repeat that Costa Rica abolished its army more than seven decades ago, because it believed that international law could offer greater security than weapons. We will continue to build bridges, crafting consensus and defending the conviction that was the very life force behind this organization.

That is, that dialogue will be more powerful than belligerence. What will last longer than brute force and cooperation is the only way that we can achieve genuine, lasting peace. The future of the United Nations will not depend solely on the strength of its charter. Rather, it will depend upon our collective courage to implement and uphold that charter. To conclude, President Excellency's one and all, Costa Rica wishes peace, health and blessings to each and every one of you, and we extend to you brotherly greetings. That is you, the Costa Rican people.

Thank you.
