a dialogue with the government of the United States to try to find a

solution to bilateral differences, on the basis of responsibility, respect,

sovereign equality, the observance of International Law, without any

interference in the internal affairs of States and without preconditions.

We know that we count on the support of the international community

and the solidarity of millions, among them, an increasing number of

US citizens.

That is reflected in the numerous gestures and statements in support

of  Cuba  and  against  the  abusive  aggression.    It  is  reflected  in  the

fraternal  material  assistance  received  by  our  people,  seeking  to

mitigate the huge damage caused to the Cuban economy and society.

That  spirit  of  solidarity  and  empathy  is  expressed  with  particular

emphasis  among  Cubans  who  reside  permanently  or  temporarily

outside the national territory and among their descendants, even here

in the United States.

Mr. President;

We  reject  the  Monroe  Doctrine  and  its  Corollaries  as  much  as  we

refuse  every  attempt  of  imperialist  militarization,  intervention  or

domination  in  Latin America  and  the  Caribbean,  a  region  that  was

proclaimed as a Zone of Peace in 2014 in Havana.

As  a  Small  Island  Developing  State,  we  stand  in  solidarity  with  our

brothers  and  sisters  who  share  a  similar  condition  and  the  warning

about the worrying and inexorable advance of climate change.

It is necessary to promote a governance that makes a more intensive

use of the new ICTs, particularly the disruptive technologies, such as

artificial intelligence.

We  reject  the  implementation  of  unilateral  coercive  measures.    We

express our support to and solidarity with the nations which are victim

of them.

We ratify our solidarity with the Government of National Reconciliation

and Unity of Nicaragua.

We  reiterate  our  support  to  the  inalienable  right  of  the  people  of

Puerto Rico to self-determination and independence.

The  sister  nations  of Africa  and  the  Caribbean  deserve  a  fair  and

differentiated treatment, as well as the reparations for the horrors of

colonialism and the transatlantic slave trade.

We reaffirm our solidarity with the Saharan people and their right to

self-determination.

We ratify our support to the “One China” principle.

We strongly believe that the current trend of international relations of

disrespect  for  International  Law  and  the  United  Nations,  the

imposition of the unilateral will of the mightiest over other countries by

means of intimidation and coercion, is dangerous and unsustainable.

The law of the jungle cannot be the future of humanity.

To prevent those practices, in addition of promoting peace and justice,

the  preceding  generations  founded  the  United  Nations  and  for

decades  developed  and  enriched  its  activity.  Let  us  recover  its  role

today, when we are perhaps in time to do so, before the Organization

goes down in history as an unrealized dream of great promises.

In the year of the centennial birthday of Fidel Castro Ruz, the historical

leader of the Cuban Revolution, let us be confident, as he was, that if

we struggle with resolve, a better world will be possible.

Homeland or Death, We Shall Overcome!

Mr. President,

As the UN Secretary-General reminded us a few years ago, "The

United Nations is the product of HOPE."

Eighty-one years after its birth, that HOPE is being tested.

Technology, including Artificial Intelligence, is advancing at rapid

speed.  Climate  change

is  reshaping  our  societies.  The

international  landscape  is  becoming  more  complex,  more

contested and more unpredictable.

The international order is not simply changing. It is being tested

in an unprecedented manner.

But, it is in such times of uncertainty, that the foundational values

of Multilateralism must be protected:

International Law. The UN Charter. Respect for Sovereignty and

Territorial Integrity. The peaceful settlement of disputes. Respect

for human rights. The equality of States.

All these are not principles of the Past.

They are principles that transcend time. The essential ingredient

for the Present and for the Future.

The  challenge  before  us  is  therefore  clear:  as  the  World

changes, our Institutions must be able to respond to new realities

and threats. While guided by the painful lessons of history AND

the vision of the founding fathers of this Organisation.

This is the essence of the theme of the 81st General Assembly:

“Restoring trust, managing transformation: a United Nations that

delivers for all.”

Transformation is inevitable. What must remain  constant is the

UN Charter as our compass.

It directs all of us. Irrespective of Power, Size and Leverage.

For  small-sized  countries,  the  principle  of  equality  of  States  is

fundamental. And it has formed the binding Trust between us.

We  rely  on  an  International  System  in  which  sovereignty  and

territorial integrity are respected.

We  expect  International  Law,  including  the  UN  Convention  on

the Law of the Sea, to be applied consistently.

We believe in the peaceful resolution of disputes.

AND we demand that the rights of every state are protected.

These, are the integral elements of our Collective Trust. And this,

is the code of conduct of Cyprus’ diplomatic engagement.

And in a rapidly changing world, small and medium-sized States

must  seek  synergies,  while  continuing  to  pursue  strategic

autonomy.

Preserving  Trust,  also

requires

Institutions  capable  of

responding to the World as it is today: The United Nations must,

therefore, continue to evolve.

The UN80 Initiative is an important part of this effort. The Pact

for  the  Future,  and  the  2030  Agenda  and  its  Sustainable

Development  Goals,  are  also  part  of  the  effort  to  ensure  that

Multilateral Cooperation can respond to the needs of our time.

This  moment  of  Reform  also  comes  as  Secretary-General,

António  Guterres,  approaches  the  completion  of  a  decade

leading  this  Organization.  Cyprus  wishes  to  acknowledge  his

leadership during a period of extraordinary global developments,

his  steadfast  commitment  to  multilateralism AND  his  efforts  to

strengthen and reform the UN.

But  reforming  our  structural  set-up  is  only  part  of  the  answer.

What  is  also  needed,  is  the  genuine  willingness  of  Member

States to contribute and protect the Multilateral System.

After  all,  States  bring  different  Capabilities,  Experiences  and

Perspectives.

Great powers have scale. Smaller states must have persuasion.

We  cannot  compel.  But  we  can  coalesce.  We  cannot  dictate

outcomes. But together, we can help shape them.

There  is  no  doubt  that  the  challenges  of  today  require

cooperation and partnerships based on the knowledge of regions

and of their realities. AND

The  Republic  of  Cyprus  has  consistently  sought  to  do

exactly that. And it has built the capabilities for it.

Our geographical position, at the crossroads of Europe, Asia and

Africa, places us close to some of the most complex dynamics

of  our  World. At  the  same  time,  it  gives  us  the  opportunity  to

actively contribute to address them.

Following the Hamas terrorist attack of October 7, 2023, and the

devastating humanitarian situation in Gaza, Cyprus, in addition

to  having  dedicated  more  than  25%  of  its  humanitarian

assistance  budget  to  Palestine,  has  put  forward  the  Amalthea

Maritime Humanitarian Corridor.

Cyprus could offer something specific: its geographical position,

its infrastructure,  its excellent relationships with all countries in

the region and the will to engage with international partners.

Through  cooperation,  including  with  the  UN2720  Mechanism,

that  idea  became  a  proposal,  and  evolved  into  a  functioning

humanitarian route. One that keeps delivering as we speak.

Cyprus  has  ALSO  played  a  constructive  role  in  times  of

Emergency.  When

third-country  nationals  needed

to  be

evacuated from our neighbourhood, my country has served, time

and  time  again,  as  a  safe  harbour.  Our  infrastructure  and  our

resources, have been made available in order to facilitate safe

passage for people in danger.

In the last three years alone, we helped evacuate thousands of

citizens from 70 different countries.

AND  through  CyprusAid,  we  have  provided  humanitarian

assistance  to  countries  facing  natural  disasters.  Cyprus  was

among the first responders following the catastrophic earthquake

in  Venezuela  and  the  flashfloods  in  Nepal.  The  devastating

humanitarian situation in Sudan, and in the wider Sahel region,

have also been a priority for my country, with a large percentage

of our available earmarked resources directed to the region.

Rising  Temperatures,  Water  Scarcity  and  Extreme  Weather

affect us all. Transcending borders and politics.

In  the  Eastern  Mediterranean  and  the  Middle  East,  the

interwoven  political  realities  that  we  are  facing,  are  further

amplified by the climate crisis.

Cooperation is therefore the only answer.

This  is  the  purpose  of  Cyprus’  Regional  Initiative  on  Climate

Change:  to  bring  together  countries  of  our  region,  thus

strengthening  our  collective  capacity  for  adaptation,  mitigation

and resilience.

ANOTHER manifestation of this, is the Cyprus Regional Aerial

Firefighting Station. Hosted at Paphos Air Base  and supported

by  the  European  Union,  it  offers  an  operational  hub  for  aerial

firefighting and rapid response, and a Centre of Excellence for

training,  interoperability  and  capacity-building.  Reflecting  its

emphasis on regional ownership, it brings together partners from

the Middle East, North Africa and the Gulf.

This  commitment

to

regional  engagement

is  ALSO

demonstrated through the Cyprus Center for Land, Open Seas

and  Port  Security,  jointly  created  with  the  United  States.  In  its

four  years  of  operation,  it  has  provided  specialized  training  to

thousands of government officials from more than 50 countries,

from the Middle East, Africa, Central Asia, and Europe.

The ability to bring different interests together was ALSO at the

heart  of  Cyprus’  Presidency  of  the  Council  of  the  European

Union, during the first half of this year.

For  six  months,  a  country  of  fewer  than  one  million  people,

assumed the responsibility of steering the work of a Union of four

hundred and fifty million European citizens.

For Cyprus, this was both a Responsibility and an Opportunity:

to  listen,  to  negotiate,  to  build  consensus.  And  to  help  the

European  Union  and  its  Member  States  move  forward  on

common priorities.

Our size did not diminish the responsibility to lead.

Nor did it diminish our ability to fulfil it.

Our position is CLEAR:

In an era of polycrises, isolation is the antithesis of Responsibility

and a Luxury we cannot afford.

Cyprus  proved  to  be  an Active  and  Responsible  party  of  the

international community. A contributor in crisis management, an

actor  in  humanitarian  assistance,  a  proponent  of  regional

synergies and a defender of the protection of human rights and

multilateralism.

Esteemed Delegates,

In these times of transformation, the Credibility of the UN must

be safeguarded.

And  credibility  requires  consistency  in  the  application  of

International Law.

For my country, Cyprus, this is not an abstract principle. It is a

painful, existential reality.

Fifty-two years have passed since the illegal Turkish invasion of

Cyprus. An act of aggression, violating the core principles of the

UN Charter.

An  ongoing,  flagrant  violation  of  International  Law,  with  more

than a third of the territory of the Republic of Cyprus remaining

under Turkish occupation.

For fifty-two years, the tens of thousands of displaced and their

descendants are prevented from returning to their homes.

For fifty-two years, Varosha remains sealed off, with Turkey still

in  defiance  of  its  clear  and  specific  obligations  set  out  in  the

relevant UN Security Council Resolutions.

For

fifty-two  years,  we  are  experiencing  violations  of

fundamental  human  rights;  the  destruction  of  religious  and

cultural  heritage;  AND

the  organized

transfer  of  settlers

amounting to demographic change.

Pain and immense suffering are the daily reality of the relatives

of the missing persons, that to this day are demanding answers

as to the fate of their loved ones.

AND for fifty-two years, the principles at stake have remained the

same.

Respect for Sovereignty and Territorial Integrity are not rhetorical

vehicles.  Nor  are  they  to  be  applied  selectively,  depending  on

who the perpetrator is.

These principles do not become less important with the passage

of time.

Nor do the Resolutions of this Organization.

UN Resolutions cannot be upheld in one case and disregarded

in another.

And  the  Sovereignty  and  Territorial  Integrity  of  a  state  cannot

depend on its Size, its Power or the Passage of time. AND

This is not only a question for Cyprus.

It goes to the credibility of the International System itself.

If we ask states to believe in Multilateralism, if we expect them

to be active contributors, then they must be able to Trust that the

principles and decisions of our Institutions will be upheld without

exception.

This consistency matters, particularly for States whose security

rests on the protection afforded by International Law, rather than

on the Balance of Power.

I  listened  very  carefully  to  the  speech  of  President  Erdogan

yesterday: references to International Law, to the respect for the

sovereignty  and  territorial  integrity  of  all  states,  to  illegal

occupation, to the drama of refugees.

Yet, in relation to Cyprus, Turkey is doing exactly the opposite.

Hypocrisy of the highest form.

President  Erdogan  also  quoted  extensively  from  the  UN

Charter. But politicians are judged not by their words but by their

deeds.

Mr. Erdogan, if you want to quote from the Charter, you must first

apply it.

The UN Security Council has established the framework for the

settlement of the Cyprus problem. That framework, of a Bizonal

Bicommunal Federation with political equality remains the ONLY

basis, on which a comprehensive settlement must be reached.

I  remain

fully  committed

to  achieving  a  comprehensive

settlement.

I am ready to resume negotiations from where they were left off

in 2017, building on the substantial work already achieved, within

the agreed United Nations framework.

The  common  ground  is  there:  the  relevant  Resolutions  of  the

United Nations Security Council, International Law, and the laws,

values, and principles of the European Union.

What is now required, is Political Will by all parties.

A genuine willingness to return to meaningful negotiations.

To engage seriously.

To build on the body of work already achieved.

AND  to  reach  a  settlement  that  reunifies  our  country  and  our

people.

A  settlement  that  allows  Greek  Cypriots,  Turkish  Cypriots,

Maronites,  Armenians,  and  Latins,  to  live  together  in  Peace,

Security and Prosperity.

On my side (let me REPEAT it), I am fully committed.

Because Division will not be accepted. This cannot and will not

be  the  future  for  my  country  and  my  people. Ever.  Our

determination to reunify our island is firm.

I therefore call on my Turkish Cypriot compatriots to perceive our

future together as the opportunity for prosperity.

AND  I  call  on  President  Erdogan  to  give  the  green  light  for

substantive negotiations within the UN-agreed framework.

I mentioned several times how Change is inevitable.

But the Choices we make in response to Change, are ours.

For countries like Cyprus, the answer must be cooperation with

purpose.  Partnerships  that  deliver  when  they  are  needed.

Formed by the belief that in times of need, we must act together.

This is the choice to make.

We  can  allow  divisions  to  weaken  the  Institutions  we  built

together.

Or, we can choose to strengthen them.

We  can  allow  differences  in  power  to  determine  whose  voice

matters.

Or, we can reaffirm the principles on which this Organization was

founded.

For Cyprus, there is no such dilemma:

We believe in a United Nations that protects the principles of its

Charter and has the capacity to act upon them.

We believe in a Multilateral System in which every state has both

rights and responsibilities.

AND we believe that small-sized states have a particular role to

play:  NOT  on  the  margins of  international  affairs  but  as  active

participants in shaping our common future.

For the Republic of Cyprus, that means Defending the principles

on which we depend,  Contributing to the institutions in which

we believe, Building partnerships for the common good, Taking

initiatives  to  create  useful  synergies,  and  Acting  responsibly

where we can affect change.

Your Excellencies,

Despite the challenges because of the Turkish occupation,  we

remain  resilient  and  steadfast  in  our  faith  in  the  Multilateral

system.

Because in the end, the strength of Multilateralism is measured

by whether every Member State believes that its voice matters,

its rights are protected and its contribution has value.

That is how we restore Trust.

That is how we manage Transformation.

And that is how we build a United Nations that truly delivers for

All.

Thank you.

Mr. President, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen,

it is my honour to return to this Hall and to address the 81st session of the General Assembly on behalf of

the Czech Republic.

“Restoring trust, managing transformation” is a fitting theme for this year’s session. It reflects both the

scale of the changes our world is undergoing, and the need to navigate them responsibly.

After the Second World War, a robust multilateral system based on rules and global cooperation was built,

spanning security, human rights and economic development. For decades, shifts in global power unfolded

within this largely predictable framework.

Power has always been unevenly distributed. Today, however, we are witnessing profound changes that

are reshaping the post-war system. The task of the international order is not to resist these changes, but

to manage them peacefully.

Our shared ambition should be to draw inspiration from the founders of the United Nations: our goal

should be to prevent war and destruction, and to build a predictable international order capable of

adapting to change, while providing fairness and stability.

This is precisely why we need forums like this one, places where dialogue can prevail and diplomacy can

work.

This is why we need rules. Not because all states are equally powerful, but precisely because they are

not. Rules have value only if they bind everyone, especially those powerful enough to break them.

When rules are cast aside, raw power fills the vacuum. A world dominated by great-power competition is

a volatile world, less able to address the most pressing challenges of our time. It is a world where a single

spark can ignite a fire.

Instead, we should insist that with greater power comes greater responsibility.

Responsibility in the use of force. Responsibility to exercise restraint. But also responsibility to use one’s

influence to prevent force from becoming necessary in the first place. This applies particularly to

permanent members of the UN Security Council.

China has the power, influence and responsibility to help prevent conflicts, de-escalate tensions and

contribute to ending wars. This includes using its influence to help bring Russia’s aggression against

Ukraine to an end.

That aggression was launched, and continues to be waged, by another permanent member of the UN

Security Council – Russia – in violation of the UN Charter and fundamental principles of international law.

Russia’s aggression continues to inflict enormous suffering on the Ukrainian people. Civilians and civilian

infrastructure continue to be attacked indiscriminately.

And the risks are growing day the day. Russia’s aggressive posture poses a direct threat to European

security as a whole.

The immediacy of that threat was starkly illustrated by the recent attempted Russian drone attack on

Leipzig/Halle Airport in Germany, only 150 kilometres from the borders of the Czech Republic.

The consequences of aggression reach far beyond Europe.

Russia’s war has undermined global food security, disrupting agricultural production, exports and supply

chains. Its effects are felt in my country, but even more acutely in parts of Africa and elsewhere,

particularly in countries that depend on stable and affordable food supplies.

While we need to raise the costs of war for Russia, we must give serious diplomatic efforts a genuine

chance.

Diplomacy matters most not between friends, but between adversaries. That is where the United Nations

remains indispensable: as a forum for dialogue, even when agreement seems very distant.

The UN was founded on principles. These principles matter in Ukraine. They matter in the South China

Sea and across the Taiwan Strait. And they also matter in the Middle East, in Sudan or the DRC.

The current developments in Yemen and Saudi Arabia demonstrate what happens when rules give way to

force and coercion, when might replaces right – and how a regional conflict can, in an instant, have

consequences for the entire world.

Ladies and Gentlemen,

as Secretary-General António Guterres nears the end of his mandate, we commend his efforts to reform

and modernize the United Nations.

The next Secretary-General will face a defining task: adapting the United Nations to a world of growing

geopolitical rivalry and fragmentation. We expect her or him to carry forward the UN80 agenda and turn

reforms into results.

The success of UN reform will be judged not by new structures or new language, but by whether the

multilateral system can deliver, uphold international law and make its rules matter. The future legitimacy of

the United Nations will depend on it.

Nowhere is this more important than in peace and security. The international community must become

better at preventing crises, protecting civilians and defending the rules it has agreed to uphold.

The Czech Republic is ready to do its part. Let me reiterate that we are seeking a non-permanent seat on

the United Nations Security Council for 2032–2033. If elected, we will contribute actively to its work and

shoulder our share of responsibility.

We will continue to help preventing and resolving conflicts through political engagement, humanitarian

assistance and practical cooperation. We will stand for the protection of civilians and critical infrastructure,

and for accountability when international law is seriously violated.

And we will remain a strong advocate for human rights and democracy. We willsupport independent

human rights mechanisms, peaceful assembly and free and fair elections. And we will work to ensure that

new technologies strengthen our societies rather than weaken them.

Mr. President,

this is also the moment to confront the extraordinary pace of advances in artificial intelligence. In recent

days, the debate has acquired a new sense of urgency and gravity.

The message from the UN’s Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, researchers in leading AI

companies, and independent experts is increasingly clear: our ability to govern this technology is not

keeping pace with its development.

AI can bring enormous benefits to humanity. But without effective safeguards, it can also cause immense

harm.

We must therefore hold on to a basic principle: human beings must remain in control of technology, not

become subject to it. Technology should advance our common goals, and no system should ever operate

beyond human responsibility and accountability.

Nor can we allow an unchecked race to determine the future of AI, with the pressure to move first pushing

safety, oversight and responsibility aside.

More than eighty years ago, the Manhattan Project showed how rapidly a scientific breakthrough can

transform the balance of power – and how difficult it is for politics and international rules to catch up.

Artificial intelligence confronts us with a different technology and different risks, but with a similar lesson:

governance that comes only after the fact may come too late.

If AI is to serve humanity, it must develop within a framework of international rules. No country, and no

company, can meet this challenge alone.

We need common standards, meaningful public oversight and clear mechanisms of accountability. The

choice is not between innovation and rules. It is between innovation governed by rules and innovation

governed by the logic of the race.

Ladies and Gentlemen,

artificial intelligence is not the only challenge that no country can manage alone. The same is true of

climate change.

This year has once again reminded us of the growing impact of extreme weather, affecting people and

communities across the globe.

In many regions, climate-related challenges are threatening homes and livelihoods. They are putting

pressure on public health, food and water security, increasing living costs and, in some cases,

contributing to instability and conflicts. The most vulnerable are often hit hardest.The Czech Republic has

offered its support and stands with those working to rebuild their communities. But support after disaster

is not enough.

We need concerted global action – both to limit further damage and to adapt to changes that are already

affecting our lives and will shape the lives of future generations.

Mr. President,

let me finish with a message that has not changed over the past year:

Most of the challenges we face are global. No nation can meet them alone.

That is why we need more dialogue, more cooperation and more collective action.

And that is why we must make multilateralism work. It is my common goal.

Thank you.

Mr President,

Imagine if nuclear weapons were developed by private companies.

If stockpiles were located on company grounds. And launch codes locked away in a safe in a CEO’s office.

It´s a disturbing thought.

When a technology has the power to fundamentally change the world, possibly even determine the fate of humanity – we need to ask:

Who controls it?

Who sets the rules?

Who is accountable?

Today humankind faces another technological revolution that raises exactly these questions.

Engineers have developed a technology that does not need to be launched from a rocket or a submarine to change the course of history.

I am, of course, talking about artificial intelligence.

A technology with seemingly unlimited power.

In the wrong hands, it can upend our economies and threaten our livelihoods.

It has the potential to erode trust within our societies by spreading information that appears real but is, in fact, fake.

A.I. can endanger the infrastructure that keeps our societies running.

And ultimately, it can influence decisions that determine global peace and security.

At the same time, artificial intelligence holds extraordinary promise.

It can accelerate scientific discovery.

Improve healthcare and education all over the world.

Provide opportunities for economic development, overcome inequalities and help us address challenges that no country can solve alone.

Just imagine a world, where with the help of A.I. we can prevent famine and cure cancer.

This is precisely what makes AI so powerful – for better or for worse.

But there is a critical tension.

Only two major countries are home to the companies holding the vast majority of all global A.I. patents.

That puts an enormous amount of influence in the hands of a very few.

Such power carries responsibility – not only towards customers, shareholders or governments. But also to humanity.

And whenever power becomes global, responsibility must become global, too.

The United Nations was created precisely for a moment such as this.

When a challenge is too large for any one nation to address alone.

When risks need to be managed to protect people all over the world, and when opportunities need to be exploited in a way that benefits the largest and the smallest, the richest and the poorest member states.

But today, the United Nations itself is under pressure.

There are great powers that believe they fare better if they ignore the rules enshrined in the UN Charter.

The erosion of international law jeopardises the enormous civilisational progress that the United Nations stands for.

The commitment to peace.

The principle of sovereign equality of all states.

The belief in norms and rules.

The conviction of the dignity inherent in every human being.

The erosion of these principles may serve the interests of a few. Who believe themselves powerful enough to survive in a world without norms – or to write their own rules.

For us, for the overwhelming majority of the 193 states represented in this General Assembly, this is harmful.

We know that the people of this world will pay the price if the respect for international law erodes. And if its institutions are under attack.

For some of us, this erosion of the international order is already catastrophic. If it continues, we all stand to lose.

But this pressure on the international order does not come from political actors alone. It also comes from the forces of technological revolution.

This poses a crucial question: how do we enable our international institutions to keep pace with the technologies that are reshaping our world?

Faced with this question, it will not be enough to invoke what we still have – or once had – in the United Nations.

Nor will it help if we ignore its weaknesses.

What we need is honesty, realism and cooperation.

Honesty in our analysis, realism in our ambition and cooperation as our method.

We must acknowledge that many of the beams of this common house cannot carry the burden we put on them. We must decide: which parts of the house do we preserve, and which do we rebuild?

For this endeavor to succeed we need the new Secretary-General to lead a profound process of reform.

Above all, we must close the gap between what we expect from the United Nations and the capabilities we give to the organisation.

First, we need a functioning UN that plays an active role in resolving conflicts – rather than merely managing them.

In times when the Security Council, as the central decision-making body, is paralyzed, this is more difficult than ever.

We need to keep its reform high on our agenda.

Germany stands up for peace and security.

Today, more people than ever are affected by violent conflict. At the same time, for every member state, resources are limited.

Thus, we have to join forces to bring conflicts to an end.

Today, Germany is the largest supporter of Ukraine in its defence against Russian aggression. This aggression has been condemned consistently by an overwhelming majority here in the General Assembly.

Russia’s war targets the lives of millions of innocent people, the existence of the Ukrainian state and culture and the European peace order. It puts vital grain deliveries for millions of people at risk, particularly in Africa, Asia

and the Middle East. It shows contempt for the Charter and for the common order on which we stand.

That is why we will continue to urge Russia to finally come to the negotiating table. I call on every member state to join us in convincing Russia that the future is built at the negotiating table, not on dead bodies in cities and villages. The day when negotiations finally begin will be a good day for the United Nations.

Germany is also taking on responsibility for peace and security beyond Europe – for example, in Haiti, where we have significantly increased our contribution to the international mission to combat gang crime.

Also, we shall not forget Sudan. At the Sudan conference in Berlin in April, together with our partners we mobilized more than 1,7 billion Dollars to alleviate the biggest humanitarian catastrophe of our time.

Second, we stand for international cooperation that is peaceful, fair and based on equality.

A new nationalism would be a misguided path. Whatever its prophets may preach, the truth is, that it would make our lives narrower, poorer and less secure.

Instead, global trade relations need to be diversified and deepened – in the framework of a fair trading order.

No country should have to accept raw materials being used to force obedience.

Or supply chains becoming instruments of pressure.

None of us is powerless in the face of this. Where we cooperate, we free ourselves from one-sided dependencies and open up new spaces of freedom.

With our partners in the European Union, we have begun this work through new trade accords, cooperation agreements and partnerships. These partnerships are built on mutual respect, on common rules and a shared respect for international law.

They also take into account the fortunate fact that many countries of the Global South are developing with extraordinary success.

The same principle of partnership and cooperation also applies to technology.

Access to computing power, data, expertise and infrastructure will increasingly shape who can innovate – and who merely has to accept the rules set by others.

Cooperation must therefore create capabilities, not new dependencies.

Third, we want to answer the great global questions of our time together. No one here – not even the largest among us – can do this alone.

Together with all those who are willing to do so, we will continue our work to address human-made climate change and its devastating effects swiftly and effectively.

We are forced to chart new courses, and we must do it with speed.

But nowhere is the need more pressing than in the area of artificial intelligence. It is our collective responsibility to ensure that this technology serves human dignity.

This is particularly urgent because technologies are already changing the foundations of our societies.

A.I. is not waiting for our institutions to catch up.

Our institutions have to catch up with reality.

At the beginning of my remarks, I asked three questions: who controls new technologies? Who sets the rules? And who is accountable?

We cannot answer them by simply trusting that those with the greatest capabilities will always act in the interest of everyone else.

We need to ensure that technological progress is guided by a framework that we all have a say in shaping.

That means building the capacity to understand and assess increasingly capable A.I. systems.

It means making sure that all regions can participate in shaping the rules.

And it means moving from voluntary commitments towards increasing transparency, as well as developing common standards.

That is why Germany calls on UN member states to work towards common safety requirements for the most capable A.I. models.

Providers should be required to test these models before release and report serious safety failures.

These requirements should be supported by effective national and regional oversight.

The A.I. industry will have to play its role in this and continue to bear a responsibility in shaping the trajectory of this technology.

At the same time, we need to ensure accountability, in particular when global peace and security are potentially affected.

In the course of this week, we have intensified our conversation about these questions.

How we address A.I. together, is one of the clearest tests of whether we have the strength and the will to build a United Nations for today’s world.

The next Secretary-General can count on Germany along this path.

Our history, our geography and our constitution bind us to the UN Charter and to the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. This is at the very core of our statehood.

The technologies may change.

But one principle will remain: power must be bound by responsibility.

And progress must serve human dignity.

The world has long been in a mode of permanent escalation.

And with it, the UN is navigating stormy waters.

We must decide: are we truly willing to let the boat we all share drift toward capsizing, or will we pool our strength and steer it back on course?

The tools are in our hands.

Together, we can push for renewal and build a peaceful future for generations to come.

speaker_post: Minister for Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation
text:
At the outset, I should like to convey to this August Assembly the greetings of His Excellency Ismail Omar Guelleh, president of the Republic of Djibouti. Mr. president, allow me, on behalf of the Republic of Djibouti, to extend my warm congratulations to His Excellency, Mr. Khalilur Rahman of Bangladesh on his election as president of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, and to wish him every success in carrying out his mandate. I would also like to pay tribute to Her Excellency Madam Annalena Baerbock for her leadership. During the last session, which marked the 80th anniversary of our organization the Republic of Djibouti welcomes the choice of the theme for this session Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation. A United Nations that delivers for all. This theme is particularly relevant in the current international context.

We are living through a critical juncture, exacerbated by the proliferation of conflicts, deepening existing crises, and the emergence of conflicts, and the emergence of new crises with devastating political, economic, humanitarian and security consequences. In the face of these challenges, we must reaffirm the essential mission of the United Nations and strengthen a renewed, more inclusive and more effective multilateralism that takes full account of the interests of all states, large and small. The region that is home to my country also continues to face crises, the consequences of which extend beyond our national borders. Djibouti is following the situation in Yemen with grave concern. We are indeed directly experiencing its effects. With the recent arrival in our territory of several thousand people fleeing the violence.

This situation is already placing considerable pressure on host communities in the Obock region, as well as on the reception capacity of the Marcus II site. Djibouti alone cannot meet the growing needs for shelter, food and essential services. Therefore, we reiterate our appeal to the international community to step up its support so that we can respond adequately to this influx, which, according to UN estimates, could reach up to ten 000 people in order to prevent this humanitarian crisis from becoming protracted We renew our call for de-escalation and for a lasting political solution in Yemen to preserve human life. Turning now to Somalia, we remain fully committed to the Somali people and government in their quest to consolidate peace and stability. The international community must preserve the security gains that have been made, and continue to support the Somali authorities in fully shouldering their responsibilities and protecting their institutions. In this regard, we recognize the crucial role played by awesome in stabilizing the country, as well as the crucial support provided by the United Nations, particularly through Nsos.

We hope that the international community will stand mobilized so as to enable Somalis to. Assume lasting responsibility for their security, sovereignty and the preservation of the integrity of their national territory. Turning now to Sudan Djibouti, in its capacity as current chair of Egad, welcomes the return of that kindred country to full participation in our regional organization, of which is a founding member. We call for de-escalation and the resumption of talks to be prioritized only an inclusive political solution that places the Sudanese people at the heart of every initiative will make it possible to restore lasting peace and stability. We also call on foreign actors to refrain from fueling this war through harmful interference. Once again, we extend a hand to our Eritrean neighbour.

Djibouti remains convinced that dialogue and negotiation in full respect for international law, represent the only path towards a peaceful and definitive settlement of our border dispute and the return of our prisoners of war, who have been held incommunicado for more than 18 years. The Republic of Djibouti further reaffirms its unwavering solidarity with the Palestinian people and its full support for their legitimate rights, in particular their inalienable right to the establishment of an independent and sovereign state. We reaffirm our commitment to a two state solution based on the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as the capital of the State of Palestine, as the path towards a just and lasting peace. We roundly condemn illegal settlement activity, violence committed against civilians, including by Israeli settlers in the West Bank, forced displacement placement and any policy aimed at altering the demographic and territorial reality of the occupied Palestinian territory. The humanitarian situation in Gaza remains a tragedy, requiring an immediate response from the international community. The protection of civilians must be guaranteed.

Humanitarian assistance, must reach those in need without hindrance, and violations of international humanitarian law must cease and be condemned. Djibouti will continue to support efforts to bring an end to the suffering of the Palestinian people, and to ensure that justice, peace and international law prevail. Preserving freedom of navigation in the Red sea and more particularly through the Bab el Mandeb Strait, is a major geopolitical and economic issue for regional and global stability. This strategic maritime passage is a vital artery for international trade and any obstruction to free movement of shipping could seriously affect supply chains and energy security. Although Djibouti has observed no disruption to passage through the strait to date, my country's authorities remain particularly watchful with regard to the current tensions affecting the region. Mr. president, the climate emergency is one of the most pressing challenges facing our international community.

For Djibouti as an African coastal country, this emergency is indivisible from development. Rising sea levels pose a direct and growing threat to our populations and ecosystems. Djibouti, like many developing countries, makes only a marginal contribution to global emissions, yet remains particularly exposed to the consequences of climate disruption. This situation highlights a profound injustice Those countries that have contributed least to climate change are often those that suffer its most severe consequences. We must therefore accelerate the implementation of the Paris Agreement and strengthen our adaptation and resilience efforts, including through resilient coastal infrastructure, better protection for marine and coastal ecosystems, early warning systems, and simplified predictable and equitable access to climate finance for Djibouti. Climate action must not be separated from development.

On the contrary, it must help to transform our economies, develop renewable energy, create jobs and open up new opportunities for investment and innovation. And it's in this spirit that the government is working to operationalize the mechanisms provided for under article six of the Paris Agreement through a robust, transparent and credible national framework for carbon markets with a view to mobilising new resources, attracting investment, promoting technology transfer and strengthening national capacities. This transformation however, requires resources. Developing countries continue to face high financing costs, external vulnerabilities and limited fiscal space. Access to climate finance and reform of the international financial architecture therefore remain essential. In this regard, the severe commitment represents an important step forward whose commitments must now be translated into tangible results, including through improved access to concessional financing, enhanced debt sustainability and increased mobilisation of public and private capital for development We must also strengthen South-South and triangular cooperation in order to share technologies, knowledge and solutions tailored to the realities of our countries.

Africa must not be viewed solely as a region vulnerable to climate change. It should be recognised as an actor that is capable of innovating, proposing solutions and contributing to the transformation of the global economy. Beyond climate action, the 2030 agenda remains at the heart of our development vision Djibouti's economy is demonstrating resilience, driven in particular by port and logistics activities, trade telecommunications, energy and investment. Djibouti intends to consolidate its role as a regional hub while accelerating the diversification of our economy. This ambition can be seen just as recently as this week with the launch of construction work on modern petroleum product storage facilities and transport infrastructure, including oil and gas pipelines in Djibouti linking Djibouti and Ethiopia. These projects illustrate our ambition to achieve energy sovereignty and security, regional integration and economic transformation.

But above all, growth should translate into jobs, social progress and opportunities, particularly for women and young people. We are continuing to invest in education, health. And to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals and implement the African Union's Agenda 2063 Both require a collective surge of action. The climate emergency demands action. Development demands investment and peace and humanitarian crises demand solidarity. The digital transition and artificial intelligence also offer new opportunities to accelerate development and improve the capacities of our states.

Their potential, however, will only be fully realised if we are able to bridge the digital divide, facilitate technology sharing and build the capacities of developing countries. And with that in mind, Djibouti supports the beyond GDP intergovernmental process. This seeks to complement traditional economic indicators with measures that better take into account people's wellbeing, social inclusion and environmental sustainability. Djibouti supports efforts to adapt the UN to contemporary challenges and enhance its effectiveness, but we must make it clear that our organisation does not exist merely to balance the books. Rather, it is here to serve our peoples and to give effect to the decisions that we take together Any reform should continue to be guided by the mandates established by member States, and should preserve the balance between the three pillars peace and security, development and human rights. As the mandate of the outgoing Secretary General, His Excellency António Guterres draws to a close.

I should like on behalf of my president, His Excellency Ismail Omar Guelleh, to express our profound gratitude for his years of service to the UN. We wish him every success and we sincerely thank him for his invaluable contribution to global peace and justice. Finally, we are following very closely the process to identify the most qualified person to serve as the next Secretary General of the UN. That selection must be guided by competence, professional integrity and unequivocal commitment to respect for international law and the ability rigorously to implement the reforms on which member states have collectively agreed. Thank you. I thank the Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Government's spokesperson of Djibouti.

Mister President

Distinguished Delegates,

Mabrika, good afternoon.

I bring greetings to this Assembly from the People and Government of the

Commonwealth of Dominica. I congratulate you, Mr. President, on your

election  and  on  the  theme  chosen  for  this  eighty-first  session  of  the

General Assembly:

“Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations That

Delivers For All.”

This theme speaks directly to the defining challenges of our time.

We are living through an age of profound transformation. Technology is

changing how we work, communicate and understand the world. Climate

change  is  reshaping  economies,  communities  and  entire  ecosystems.

Conflicts  are  destroying  lives  and  displacing  families.  Economic

uncertainty is deepening inequality, while progress towards achieving the

Sustainable Development Goals has stalled.

These challenges are not unfolding in isolation. They are interconnected,

global in scale and beyond the capacity of any one nation to address alone.

They  demand  stronger  cooperation  and  renewed  confidence

in

multilateralism.

Yet,  Excellencies,  at  the  very  moment  when  collective  action  is  most

urgently needed, this Organization stands at a crossroads.

The  question  before  us,  therefore,  is  whether  we  possess  the  courage,

solidarity  and  political  will  to  shape  that  change  and  guide  our  world

towards peace, justice and shared prosperity.

The UN already Delivers for All.

I strongly believe that most right-thinking individuals would agree that

the  UN  System  has  substantially  delivered  for  all  countries  over  the

several decades of its existence.

For more than eighty years, this organization has embodied humanity’s

highest collective aspiration, that countries, large and small, rich and poor,

can work together to prevent conflict, protect human dignity and improve

the lives of their people.

The  United  Nations  provides  shelter  and  protection  to  people  enduring

conflict,  displacement  and  natural  disaster.  It  supports  education,

healthcare, peacekeeping, elections and development in communities that

might otherwise be forgotten.

These achievements matter and must never be dismissed or diminished.

What the United Nations does not currently do enough, is deliver at the

transformative level.

Too often, humanity, and the institutions we have created to serve us, have

had to concentrate on managing one crisis after another, without giving

enough attention to the conditions that allow them to persist.

Excellencies,  there  is  no  question  that  managing  crises  is  necessary.  It

brings relief, restores hope and saves lives. But we cannot stop there. Our

responsibility must also be to address the root causes of these problems

and  build  systems  that  are  fairer,  stronger  and  better  able  to  serve  our

people.

The  true  test  of  this  Organization,  therefore,  is  not  only  how  well  we

respond  after  people  have  suffered.  It  is  also  whether  we  can  work

together to prevent that suffering in the first place.

This is not to dismiss what has already been achieved. It is a call for us to

build  on  that  progress,  strengthen  our  cooperation,  and  deliver  the

meaningful change that our people expect from us.

A  fundamental  question  that  one  must  ask  is  “Can  the  international

system still deliver?”

For Dominica, this is not an abstract question. When a hurricane destroys

our infrastructure, when international energy prices rise, when access to

capital becomes more expensive, when global markets  change or when

climate  finance  remains  beyond  our  reach,  the  consequences  are  felt

immediately  -  in  our  homes,  in  our  businesses,  in  our  schools  and

hospitals, and in the very lives of our people.

Yet, Mr. President, I do not come before this Assembly to speak only of

vulnerability. I wish to speak of transformation and resilience.

Dominica has made a choice. We have chosen not  only to rebuild after

disaster,  but  to  build  differently,  build  better,  build  stronger.  We  have

chosen not only   to adapt to climate change, but to demonstrate what a

climate-resilient economy and country can look like. And we have chosen

to move from dependence to greater self-reliance.

FROM VULNERABILITY TO RESILIENCE

Mr. President,

In 2017, Category Five Hurricane Maria demonstrated with devastating

force the vulnerability of small island states like Dominica. The economic

and human consequences were enormous.

Hurricane Maria however, also taught us an important lesson: Resilience

should  never  begin  after  the  disaster.  Resilience  must  begin  before

disaster.

The  international  community  must  therefore  move  from  a  model  that

primarily  finances  reconstruction  after  catastrophe,  to  one  that  invests

systematically in resilience before disaster strikes.

For Dominica, this means resilient roads and bridges, resilient buildings,

reliable  communications,  modern  water  systems,  strengthened  health

infrastructure and disaster-ready communities.

But resilience is not only physical. A resilient country must have resilient

institutions. It must have resilient public finances. It must have resilient

energy systems and must have resilient food systems.

Above all, a resilient nation must have people who possess the skills and

confidence to withstand shocks and move forward.

That is the Dominica that we are building.

THE ENERGY TRANSFORMATION

Dominica has begun the transition from imported fossil fuels to renewable

energy. Our geothermal power plant is now in commercial operation, and

increasing

the  renewable  share  of  our  electricity  generation

to

approximately  84  percent.  We  are  well  on  our  way  to  achieving  100%

renewable energy by 2030.

This  is  more  than  an  energy  project.  It  is  economic  transformation.  It

demonstrates that small states can lead in the transition to clean energy.

Every  barrel  of  oil  that  we  no  longer  need  to  import,  strengthens  our

resilience to international price shocks. Every unit of clean electricity we

produce strengthens our energy security.

Affordable, reliable renewable energy can become a foundation for new

industries,

new

investment,

new

employment

and

greater

competitiveness.

The lesson is important beyond Dominica. We need international finance

that recognises the transformative nature of renewable energy investment

in vulnerable countries.

We need financing mechanisms that allow countries such as Dominica to

move faster. And we need partnerships that allow the energy transition to

become an engine of economic development and growth.

Our ambition is not merely to generate clean electricity. Our ambition is

to use clean energy to transform our economy.

Finance Must Change

The  international  community  has  become  very  good  at  recognising

vulnerability.  We  have  become  less  successful  at  financing  the

transformation that vulnerability requires.

Too  often,  the  cycle  is  predictable:  A  disaster  occurs.  Infrastructure  is

destroyed and economic activity collapses. We then mobilise resources to

rebuild  what  was  lost,  often  through  borrowing  that  substantially

increases debt to rebuild what we  could have made more resilient  from

the outset. This is not an efficient financial model.

The best time to build resilience is before disaster. The best time to finance

transformation  is  before  crisis.  And  the  value  of  resilience  should  be

measured not only by what we build, but by what we prevent from being

destroyed.

Dominica does not come to the United Nations asking to be treated as a

victim of vulnerability. We come asking to be recognised as a partner in

transformation.  We  must  finance  potential  -  not  merely  manage

vulnerability.

And  this  is  not  only  about  Dominica.  It  is  about  whether  the  global

financial system is capable of recognising a different development model.

A  model  in  which  resilience  is  an  investment.  Nature  is  an  asset.

Connectivity  is  productive  infrastructure.  Clean  energy  is  economic

opportunity. And prevention is financially smarter than reconstruction.

That is the proposition we place before this Assembly. It is time that the

international financial architecture evolves. Dominica joins its voice with

those countries that continue to advocate for the use of multidimensional

vulnerability  as  a  practical  and  fair  basis  in  determining  access  to

development finance.

We call for greater and easier access to concessional financing and grants

for adaptation.

We call for stronger disaster clauses in sovereign debt instruments.

We  call  for  financing  mechanisms  that  can  be  activated  rapidly  when

disasters strike.

And  we  call  for  a  fundamental  shift  in  the  way  the  international

community views investment in resilience.

Every dollar spent preventing the destruction of a road, a hospital, a school

or a water system is an investment in  future development. Dominica is

prepared to serve as a demonstration country for this approach.

We are prepared to work with international partners to show what happens

when finance is designed around transformation rather than vulnerability.

Dominica has long spoken of becoming the world's first climate-resilient

nation.  Today,  I  wish  to  take  that  ambition  further.  We  invite  the

international community to partner with us in making Dominica a living

laboratory for climate resilience and sustainable development.

Bring us the technology; Bring us the research; Bring us the investment;

Bring us the innovation.

And together, let us demonstrate what a resilient small island economy

can  look  like.  Resilient  housing;  Smart  and  renewable  energy  systems;

Climate-smart  agriculture;  Modern  water  management;  Digital  public

services;  Resilient  infrastructure;  Nature-based  adaptation;  And  new

industries powered by clean energy.

This should not be a relationship based simply on donor and recipient. It

should  be  a  relationship  based  on  partnership,  innovation  and  shared

learning. Dominica has lessons to learn from the world. But we also have

lessons to offer the world.

Transformation Must Create Opportunity

Transformation  is  ultimately  about  people.  A  resilient  economy  must

create  opportunity  for  young  people.  Young  people  want  to  inherit  a

country that is not merely protected from disasters, but one in which they

can  build  businesses,  work  in  new  industries,  participate  in  the  global

economy, and build meaningful lives at home.

That

is  why  our

investments

in  energy,  connectivity,  digital

transformation,  tourism,  agriculture  and  resilience  must  ultimately

converge around one objective: creating opportunity.

The Wider Challenge to Multilateralism

The challenges before us extend beyond climate and finance. We meet at

a time when war continues to devastate communities and ruin lives. When

humanitarian  crises  are  multiplying.  When  international  law  is  under

pressure. When trust between nations is strained.

We  cannot  speak  about  development  without  speaking  about  peace.

Without peace, development is tenuous.

We believe in the principles of the United Nations Charter. We believe in

respecting the sovereignty and territorial integrity of states. We believe in

the peaceful settlement of international disputes. We believe in dialogue.

And we believe that international law must apply equally to all nations,

and must be applied consistently.

Small  states  must  never  become  collateral  damage  in  the  competition

among larger powers.  The security of a small nation is no less important

than the security of a large one.

The credibility of multilateralism depends on fairness. But it also depends

on delivery.

The true test of multilateralism is not whether we can agree in this room.

It is whether our agreements can transform lives outside this room.

Restoring Trust

That  is  why  I  welcome  the  central  challenge  of  this  81st  General

Assembly, “restoring trust”.

The  world  does  not  need  another  generation  of  promises  that  remain

unfulfilled. It needs delivery. It needs institutions that respond faster. It

needs  financing  that  reaches  vulnerable  countries  more  efficiently.  It

needs  partnerships  that  produce  measurable  results.  And  it  needs  a

multilateral system that people can believe in again.

For Dominica, restoring trust means closing the gap between international

commitments and the lived experience of our people.

It means ensuring that when the world says it supports climate resilience,

resources actually reach the communities that need them.

It  means  ensuring  that  when  we  call  for  sustainable  development,

financing mechanisms do not make sustainability harder to achieve.

And  it  means  recognising  that  the  challenges  confronting  small  island

states are not marginal issues. They are an early warning of the challenges

that the wider world will increasingly face.

The United Nations must remain a place where every country -  large or

small - can believe that its voice matters. But the United Nations must also

remain a place where ambition can become action.

We  must  also  confront  the  serious  challenges  facing  the  Sustainable

Development Goals.

The  SDGs  represented  a  promise  that,  by  2030,  we  would  make

meaningful progress in ending poverty and hunger, improving health and

education,  advancing  equality,  protecting  our  planet  and  building  more

peaceful and inclusive societies.

Today,  that  promise  is  at  risk.  Conflict,  climate  change,  debt  distress,

inflation and persistent inequality have pushed the  Goals further out of

reach for many developing countries.

But this is not the time to abandon the 2030 Agenda. It is the time to renew

our commitment and concentrate on delivering results that people can see

and feel in their daily lives.

For  Dominica,  we  have  incorporated  the  SDG’s  as  priorities  in  our

National Resilience Development Strategy 2030, our Climate Resilience

and Recovery Plan and our wider development agenda.

We see sustainable development in the homes we have built for vulnerable

families;  in  our  investment  in  geothermal  energy  as  cleaner,  more

affordable and reliable energy.

We  see  it  in  our  efforts  to  strengthen  education,  expand  technical  and

vocational training and better prepare our young people for the world of

work. We see it in our support for farmers, entrepreneurs, agro-processors

and tourism operators who are creating jobs and building stronger local

industries.

We also see it in our work to protect  our forests, marine  resources and

natural  environment.  For  Dominica,  these  resources  are  part  of  our

identity,  but  they  are  also  essential  to  our  food  security,  our  tourism

product and the livelihoods of our people.

The challenges before us cannot be overcome by any one country acting

alone.  They  require  a  strong  and  effective  United  Nations,  renewed

international cooperation and a firm commitment to multilateralism.

We need a United Nations that does more than respond to crises after lives

have been lost and communities destroyed. We need an Organization that

works  with  determination  to  prevent  conflict,  advance  sustainable

development,  confront  injustice  and  protect  those  who  are  most

vulnerable.

We need a system in which every country, regardless of its size, wealth or

influence,  has  a  voice  and  a  meaningful  place  at  the  table.  We  need

multilateralism  that  is  not  selective  in  its  concern  or  uneven  in  its

response, but fair, effective and responsive to the needs of all people.

Our  development  must  include  young  people,  women  and  girls,

Indigenous  Peoples,  persons  with  disabilities,

the  elderly  and

communities that have too often been left behind.

If the United Nations is to deliver for all, it must first see, hear and include

all.

Multilateralism  is  our  best  hope  for  addressing  challenges  that  cross

borders, threaten our shared future and demand collective action.

We  therefore  remain  committed  to  peace,  climate  action,  sustainable

development and the dignity of every human being. We remain ready to

work  with  all  nations,  in  a  spirit  of  mutual  respect  and  shared

responsibility, to build a fairer, safer and more resilient world.

Mister President

Let  this  Eighty-first  Session  be  remembered  as  the  moment  when  we

collectively renewed our faith in cooperation, and matched our words with

action.

Let  this  Eighty-first  Session  be  remembered  as  the  moment  when

vulnerability was met with solidarity, promises were honoured and trust

was rebuilt through meaningful delivery.

Above  all,  let  this  Eighty-first  Session  be  remembered  as  the  moment

when  this  family  of  nations  found  the  courage  to  act  together  and

recommitted ourselves to ensuring that no country, no community and no

person was left behind.

Ayahora, thank you.

I thank you

speaker_post: Permanent Representative to the United Nations
text:
Mr. President, Mr. Secretary-General, Excellencies,

distinguished delegates,

A compass does not change with the weather. It helps

you find the way; in fair weather as well as in storm.

Eighty-one years ago, the world gave itself a compass.

We named it the United Nations Charter. It has helped us

stay the course, even when the seas have been anything

but calm.

It has pointed us toward a world of equal rights, self-

determination of peoples and territorial integrity of all

states, large and small.

Toward a rules-based international order.

The progress has been real. More than a billion people

lifted out of poverty. Standards of living transformed.

Colonial empires brought to an end. Independent nations

emerged. Peoples gained the right to shape their own

future.

That progress was made possible because we kept

consulting the compass. Because, we stayed the course.

Today, it seems we are losing our way.

Wars and conflicts are at the highest level since World

War II. Extreme poverty is on the rise. Extreme weather

and climate-related disasters are hitting record highs.

Mistrust, polarisation and divisions are growing, both

among states and within societies.

Even the most basic principles of international law,

including international humanitarian law, are violated

with impunity.

To get back on track, we must turn our attention to the

compass.

Respect for the Charter, for human rights, for

international law, is not a courtesy we extend when

convenient. These are binding obligations we all agreed

to. Respecting them is the precondition for international

peace and security.

We see this clearly in Ukraine. Russia's illegal war of

choice could end tomorrow, if Russia withdrew to its

own territory and stopped trying to redraw borders by

force.

The vast majority of UN member states and the UN

Secretary General support calls for an immediate and

comprehensive ceasefire in Ukraine.

It is the only basis for good-faith talks aimed at a just and

lasting peace in line with international law, including the

UN Charter. Ukraine has been offering this for a year

now.

Denmark's support for Ukraine will remain steadfast.

This is not only a matter of helping Ukraine defend itself.

It is a matter of defending the universal principles upon

which this Organisation was built.

In Sudan, the war continues to inflict immense human

suffering.

Millions are displaced. Famine has been confirmed. And

the international community has been warned of mass

atrocities over and over again, but has failed to act. The

responsibility for this horrific war lies in the hands of the

warring parties. Yet, it is fuelled by outside actors and

permitted by international inaction.

We must act now to prevent further mass atrocities

against the Sudanese people. We must put our political

will and weight behind a stronger demand for peace and

accountability.

The warring parties must come to the negotiation table.

Engage in dialogue. And agree on a much-needed truce.

Denmark fully supports the Quintet’s efforts to advance a

civilian-led political process and welcomes the improved

coordination among mediators.

In Syria, the fall of the brutal Assad-regime offers a

historic opportunity to build a brighter future for all

Syrians. Denmark is committed to supporting the people

of Syria in a Syrian-led and owned transition. It is a

glimpse of hope in a troubled region.

And a stark contrast to the destabilizing actions of Iran,

whose consequences are felt far beyond the region.

Denmark’s position remains clear: Iran must never be

allowed to develop or acquire a nuclear weapon. We

strongly support continued diplomatic efforts to restore

effective international verification of Iran’s nuclear

programme. And we deeply regret the unwillingness of a

few Council members to acknowledge that sanctions

measures have been reinstated in full accordance with

Security Council resolution 2231.

At the same time, we urge Iran to comply fully with

resolution 2817. Cease attacks against countries in the

region and refrain from any actions or threats that

undermine freedom of navigation in the Strait of

Hormuz.

Last year, this Assembly endorsed the New York

Declaration – a roadmap toward the two-state solution. A

path to lasting peace and security for Israelis and

Palestinians.

Since then, the Comprehensive Plan to end the Gaza

Conflict has been endorsed by the Security Council. Now

it must be implemented in full. We call on all parties to

stay committed to the plan.

Yet in Gaza, civilians continue to pay the price. Far more

must be done to secure humanitarian access and long-

term peace.

And in the occupied West Bank, settler violence and

settlement expansion threaten the daily lives of

Palestinians – and undermine the prospects for a future

Palestinian state. This has to stop.

As an elected member of the Security Council, Denmark

strives to ensure that the Council fulfils its mandate.

At times, we succeed. This June, the Security Council

unanimously adopted resolution 2823 [Twenty-eight

twenty-three] on accountability for crimes against UN

peacekeepers – led by Denmark and Pakistan, and backed

by a record 153 member states. A clear signal of

commitment to the safety and security of the brave men

and women who serve under the UN flag.

And a clear demonstration that the Council can still come

together and speak with one voice.

Too often, however, the Security Council is blocked by

geopolitical divisions. Unable to act. Meanwhile, the

costs of inaction are felt by civilians across the world as

the disrespect for international humanitarian law is

allowed to fester.

Our collective inability to halt the killings, suffering, and

injustices in Gaza, Ukraine, Sudan and beyond, must not

prompt us to surrender to a world ruled by brute force.

On the contrary, it must inspire us to work harder to

sustain and strengthen the structures, instruments and

mechanisms, we have built over the past 81 years.

To Denmark, this includes maintaining our firm support

for the ICJ and ICC as core international justice

institutions. This year, Denmark nominated its first-ever

candidate for judge at the ICC, reaffirming our

unwavering support for the Court at a critical time.

It also means continuing to meet the UN target of

providing 0.7 per cent of GNI for official development

assistance.

For more than 45 years, Denmark has consistently

delivered on this goal. We do so, not as an act of

altruism, but because it is in our shared interest: It creates

jobs, opportunities and hope where people live, allowing

them to build a future at home, increasing stability and

mutual prosperity. We call on fellow member states to

join us.

At the current juncture, however, sustaining an order

with the UN at its core, means working for reform.

Reform is how we keep this Organisation fit for the

world we live in.

Denmark continues to call for fundamental Security

Council reform: we wish to expand the Council with

more members in both categories, including permanent

seats for underrepresented regions. And we wish to

commence text-based negotiations. Only then can we

begin to redress historical injustices.

Denmark also strongly supports the UN80 reform

process. We applaud the results so far and call for

ambitions to be raised. We must strive to build a more

efficient and inclusive UN.

A UN that delivers better – on its core mandates, and on

the ground, where it matters most.

To enable this, we call on all UN Member States to meet

their financial obligations to the UN. In full and on time.

Let’s be real. We need the UN, not for the sake of the

UN, but in order to address challenges that face us all.

Because no single country can manage climate change,

global health threats, or the governance of emerging

technologies on its own.

The climate crisis makes the point starkly. We see it in

droughts and wildfires. In record-breaking heat. And in

the growing pressure on food, water and energy

accessibility and security.

The challenge before us is no longer a lack of solutions.

We have the solutions. We know what is required. Now

we need to deliver.

Therefore, COP31 must be a COP of implementation.

Turning ambition into action and real-world results.

Delivering on the objectives of the Paris Agreement and

its 1.5-degree Celsius temperature goal.

With only four years left to 2030, we must also be honest

about where we stand with the Sustainable Development

Goals. Both in terms of achievements and challenges.

Let’s make the upcoming SDG Summit a turning point.

2030 must not be a missed deadline.

This year, we will be selecting a new Secretary-General.

Denmark thanks the outgoing Secretary-General Guterres

for a decade of dedicated service to this Organisation –

often under exceptionally difficult circumstances.

The next Secretary-General will take over an

organisation under strain and under scrutiny.

To bring the UN safely into the future, we must select a

person who can work to restore global trust in the UN

and among its member states.

In closing, I am happy to inform you that last week - in

this very building - Denmark, Greenland and the United

States signed an agreement on security, which

strengthens the defence of Greenland, the NATO area

and the American continent. The agreement is good for

Greenland, for Denmark, for the USA, and for NATO

and Europe.

Progress can still be made, when we consult the compass.

I thank you.
