First of all, an international mechanism within the framework of the UN to trace and freeze the illicit financial flows from transnational organized crime. The money is the fuel of these networks, so let us stop it in its tracks. Second, a permanent platform of information exchange between police forces, prosecutors' offices, and financial intelligence units that enables states to anticipate rather than react once it's happened. And the third concrete action: that the UN80 initiative include transnational organized crime as a priority for conflict prevention, and provide the organization with the capacity to support states that request it. These are proposals that Ecuador is prepared to support and drive forward alongside all countries that wish to join us. Excellencies, security is not an end in itself; it's a condition for a country to be able to flourish.

And today we are experiencing a crisis, a profound crisis. And recovering security means giving people back their future, for a young person to be able to choose university rather than being trapped by a criminal gang, for a family to open a business without fear, for a company to invest and create jobs, and for institutions to respond to the needs of citizens and not to illicit interests. Therefore, the success of an economy is not measured only by how much production grows, but rather how much it's able to reduce poverty. It's measured in young people with decent jobs and children with a better education, in citizens who are able to build their future with dignity. And this also must guide the agenda of international development. Middle-income countries face vulnerabilities that income per capita does not reflect.

We ask that access to cooperation and financing be defined using more fair vulnerability criteria, and that the international financial architecture support the efforts of those who are undertaking reforms. We believe in open, predictable, and equitable trade. When a producer can export, innovate, and grow, there's a family behind that can be lifted out of poverty. The best social policy is policy that generates opportunities. President, I come from a country that is small in size but great— huge in terms of our nature. The Galápagos Islands, where Darwin found evidence of the evolution of life, are a world heritage site for the whole of humanity, and today they are threatened by illegal fishing networks that operate with the same logic and the same financing of other organized crime groups.

The same is happening with illegal mining in the Amazon that's destroying forests and funding gangs. Protecting nature is also a matter of security. Ecuador will continue to fulfill our responsibilities and invite all of you to join us. Latin America and the Caribbean is a region with a lot of talent, energy, food, strategic resources, and above all, youth that is resolved to building a different future. It's a region that has not come to this Assembly to ask for solutions from the outside, but rather to offer up our solutions. And one of the greatest challenges of the future is artificial intelligence.

It can transform education, multiply productivity, and close historic gaps, but also entrench inequalities and serve those that seek to weaken our institutions. We need international governance that enables us to innovate without renouncing our values, and that does not leave those that have the least resources behind. They also need to be able to access this technology. Excellencies, confidence in the multilateral system is going through difficult times. Many citizens see a gulf between what we agree on here and what people experience on a daily basis. Closing this gap is the task of our organization.

A lot of citizens realize that this is the task that our generation must take up. And as a founding country, Ecuador believes in the United Nations, and it's precisely for this reason that we want an organization that's able to respond to the challenges of the world today, not of 1945. Supporting the organization, the United Nations, also needs to involve a willingness to transform the United Nations. And that's why we support the UN80 initiative and pose an essential question: what United Nations of the world needs today? We need an organization that's more efficient, with the ability to prevent conflicts, resolve crises, and support states to challenges that didn't exist when the organization was created. An organization whose legitimacy depends not only on the decision that we adopt, but the way that they adopt.

And we need the charter and international law to remain our common language. More than 80 years ago, countries understood that peace didn't depend on everyone's power, but rather is something that we built organizations to cooperate to achieve. This remains our main strength. The citizens of the world will not judge this organization by its declarations; they will judge it by its ability to turn commitments into peace and security, into respect for human rights, into real opportunities for development, and how many lives we really save. President, the criminal gangs already coordinate with each other. Now we need to do better.

Ecuador has come to this Assembly to defend collective solutions, because no country can build a safe, prosperous, and sustainable future alone. And because when international cooperation works, we are all stronger for it. Thank you very much.

Your Excellency Dr. Khalilur Rahman, President of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly,

Your Excellency António Guterres, Secretary-General of the United Nations,

Honourable Heads of Delegation, Distinguished Delegates, Ladies and Gentlemen,

I have the honor to present this statement on behalf of my President, His Excellency Isaias Afwerki, President of the State of Eritrea.

Allow me to join previous speakers to congratulate Your Excellency for your election to the Presidency of the 81st Session of the UN General Assembly.

On this auspicious occasion each year, the crucial questions that crop to mind, and that we ponder about, are the crucial and novel messages that we should focus on. Should our annual interventions be confined to sheer and rather routine accounts, or balance sheet, of developments that had transpired during that

particular year? Should the forum be seen as essentially and solely a congenial Public Relations platform for eloquent speeches and discourses?

Does the annual forum consist of structured agendas that have continuity and coherence? What is the context? What is the overarching mission? And how do we gauge progress? ... etc. etc.

In previous Summits, I have dwelt on the historical backdrop of the establishment of the UN; the popular aspirations of humanity for peace, growth, and prosperity that underpinned the creation of the UN; the economic injustices that prompted those aspirations in the first place; the innate mission of the UN? ... as well as its structure and operational modality as elaborated in the foundational precepts elabored below.

The first and foremost challenges of humanity are to redress economic injustices; create wealth; and more broadly and accurately, ensure fair distribution of wealth and income. The prevailing injustices stem from the denial of the rights, as well as enabling environment, for humanity to create and accumulate wealth without any encumbrances on the one hand; and, the usurpation of their right and opportunity for rational distribution of whatever nominal wealth they create under suppressive conditions on the other.

This is precisely the reason why the prevailing international order has become and is dubbed as a "zero-sum order".

In the event, the imperative for installing a new world order predicated on justice and rationality - and that jettisons the zero-sum system - remains humanity's fundamental individual and collective right.

In this respect, the overarching mission of the endeavor/struggle of mankind can be summed up in:

• To fairly own their economic resources and the produce of their work, and march on a sustainable path of generational progress and prosperity by accumulating wealth.

• To secure peace and stability in order to guarantee prosperity and economic growth.

• To ensure prevalence of fairness and justice as vital prerequisites for peace and stability.

• To promote mutual respect, complementarity and cohesion/integration so as to bolster widest regional and global peace and stability as well as mutual growth

• To establish appropriate legal executive structure and associated mechanisms for the implementation of these fundamental human aspirations.

The substance of the framework briefly described above evidently requires further expansion and elaboration. It is not otherwise controversial or novel by any metrics. In this respect, the main tasks of the annual UNGA Summits ought to focus on rigorous assessment of progress in achieving these goals.

Mr. President,

The events that have unfolded since the 80th Summit of the UNGA are important for gleaning appropriate lessons in comparative terms and within the reality of this international organizations. They cannot otherwise deflect the attention and focus of the peoples of the world from their chore mission and struggle.

As such:

• The impacts and ultimate ramifications that may ensue from President Trump's pronounced MAGA Doctrine; as well as the ongoing war in Iran that must be stopped;

The Ukraine war, with all its multi-layered ramifications must also be terminated;

• Global climate change and the imperative of finding enduring solutions for its control and reversal;

• The urgency of reversing the war and related acts of subversion unleashed in order to foment chaos in our broader neighborhood; i.e. the Nile Basin; the Horn of Africa; the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden and the Gulf States; the need to terminate

debilitating interventions under the rubric of "humanitarian assistance";... are some of the trends and developments that warrant attention.

Against this overall backdrop, it must be recognized that the prime victims of the "zero-sum" global order whose hallmarks are plunder, domination and deceit, are the African peoples who continue to seethe under subsistence economy. This disconcerting reality impels them to naturally stand at the forefront of the struggle for justice and fairness.

In the event, it behooves on them to formulate appropriate strategies for accomplishing their mission; remove stale and obstructive frameworks and mechanisms; and move forward with greater unity and rigour.

I thank you.

I have come to defend the principles and ambitions that inspired the creation of this organization 81 years ago. Principles and ambitions that different governments present here disregard or seek to dismantle. Eight years have gone by since I addressed this Assembly for the first time, and since then, several things have changed in the world. And I regret to say that things haven't changed—well, not many things have changed for the better, but for the worse. In 2018, the 193 countries that make up this body had just adopted the 2030 Agenda, and the majority of the leaders present here proudly showed off the SDGs logo. And we didn't do this because it was fashionable, nor because we thought that it would be an easy journey.

We did it because the majority of us believed in this common promise. Because we were convinced that peace, sustainability, equal opportunities were not ideological positions, but rather a comprehensive part of the future of humanity. Today, however, these ideas are not only being called into question; they are being attacked by political actors and governments that want to take us back to a dark past. And I don't need to point them out; we all know who they are and what their modus operandi is. They start by questioning the rules, then they break them, knowing full well that nobody will dare to hold them accountable. They cut their contributions to multilateral bodies like this one.

They point to their leaders and officials. They obstruct these organizations' ability to act, to then write them off as useless entities that we can do without. What they're doing, nevertheless, is a planned and coordinated demolition attempt that is presented as something that we can't stop and that's necessary. However, the reality is that it runs counter to the structural currents of history and is based on three misguided pillars. The first of these pillars is selfishness, the absurd belief that the world is a zero-sum game, where some winning must imply that others losing. The second pillar is ignorance, disregarding scientific evidence and assuming that there are countries that are so powerful that they can abuse all of the others and they don't need anyone else to prosper.

And the third pillar, the worst in my opinion, is cruelty. Cruelty that isn't even moved when it sees the ribs of a starving child or a hospital reduced to rubble. Over these 8 years, I've seen these selfish, ignorant, and cruel forces grow. I've seen how they took off their masks and seized power in many places. And then I saw them start illegal wars, massacre innocent civilians. I've seen them treat millions of human beings like livestock and take away aid from those suffering the most, from poverty and disease.

I've seen them pollute the atmosphere and also the ocean as if it's their own property, and conspire to destroy this organization and everything it represents. I'm saying this because bearing witness to these things has changed the way that I understand the world. However, it hasn't led me to lose hope. Because also, over these 8 years, I've seen wonderful things that allow me to still have confidence in humanity. For example, I've seen millions of people mobilized to defend nature, peace, and civil rights. I've seen thousands of activists and public servants confront these reactionary powers, knowing full well that they're putting their professional careers and even their own lives at risk.

I've seen scientists make progress that we thought was impossible. And I've seen many governments do things right, opting for cooperation, social justice, and environmental sustainability. All of this has taught me something that I want to share with all of you, and that is that humanity is not intrinsically good or bad. Humanity can actually be both. And every day, every year, and in each and every crisis, we must decide how to act. The United Nations is one of these spaces where these decisions are made at the highest level.

And the UN doesn't always do it well. Of course, I myself, on several occasions, have called out the contradictions and lackings of this body. However, with the same belief, I must call out the fact that the majority of the voices that today insist on criticizing the United Nations are not describing its failure; what they're doing is trying to cause its failure. And I must also say that multilateralism is the best tool that humanity has to manage its diversity and its interdependence, especially in a globalized and multipolar world like the world we're living in today. And this is why what we need to do is up- ramp up our trust in this organization. We must renew it and strengthen it so that this century it can play the same key role that it played last century.

And doing this will not be easy. However, the good news is that all of the guidance we need is right here, in the United Nations Charter. In this charter, they wrote the best chapters. Our forefathers wrote it, the men and women who saw the world burn, and even then, they died to imagine a better future. These men and women laid down their wisdom and their hope in this charter. And they didn't ask us to keep it in a glass case.

They asked us to fulfill it. They asked us to defend it, and for us to turn back to it in times of uncertainty and extraordinary difficulty. And today is one of those times. And therefore, it's our duty to rise to the courage and the ambition present in this text, in the United Nations Charter. And this is why, ladies and gentlemen, we need to reform the Security Council so that all of the regions in the world have fair representation, and so that we can do away with the right of veto of the permanent members. Because as the UN Charter sets out, no country should be judged in its own case, no matter how powerful they are.

We therefore need to strengthen all of the other main bodies and reorganize the agencies' funds and programs, and provide them with more resources and more executive capacity so that they can have a more decisive impact on the great challenges that beset humanity. We must strengthen bodies like the International Criminal Court so that they can investigate, prosecute, and punish those that break the rules. It took humanity centuries to replace might as right with the rule of law. And we must not be the generation that backtracks on this. It's for this very reason that we must rebuild the nuclear non-proliferation and disarmament architecture to avoid a poorly designed security policy that brings us back to another global conflict. And we must impose strict regulations on the tech oligarchs who control the functioning of social networks and the development of artificial intelligence.

Because at the end of the day, the future of our children is more important than the pockets of these tech oligarchs. And of course, doing all of these things will require compromise, time, strong leadership, being able to build agreements, to listen, to look beyond our known reality, and imagine a better alternative. And what I'm advocating for, for this leadership, is very clear. Nine men have served as Secretary-General of this organization in its 80 years of existence. Now it's time for a woman to serve, a Latin American woman. Because, ladies and gentlemen, how can an organization that claims to speak on behalf of the whole of humanity never have had a woman leading the organizations?

How can we represent all of the continents if, for 3 decades, we haven't let the third most populated continent have this role? The United Nations came to being with the promise that all human beings had their place in this house. Therefore, the time has come to fulfill the outstanding half. The time has come for a woman from Latin America to become United Nations Secretary-General. This is an historic debt that we must settle. And today, more than ever, when feminism is being attacked, when thousands of women are falling victim to machism, violence, and xenophobia, we must reaffirm this commitment.

And I want it to be very clear: I'm not saying this because I think that women have anything to prove. I'm saying it because it is the world that needs to show itself that on the road to equality, there's no going back. In my country, ladies and gentlemen, in Spain, it was women who were the first to show us that security could not be achieved through force but through social progress. It was brave women like Clara Campoamor, the first to defend in Parliament the rejection of war as a way of interacting with the world, and opting instead for empathy and peace. That should always be what we do. If only more of the leaders that came up to this rostrum this week had even half the courage and lucidity of Clara Campoamor.

Feminism, ladies and gentlemen, is one of the main forces of transformation and progress that the world has experienced in the last century. And it's time for this force to guide this institution in much more of a clear and robust way. And it's for these reasons, ladies and gentlemen, that I believe. I believe that in order to get off on the right footing in this new decisive step forward for the United Nations, the UN needs a female Latin American Secretary-General. And I believe, what's more, that in order for her not to be alone, she will also need the support of brave governments who are prepared to do things right, however high the price to pay may be. This, ladies and gentlemen, is the option and the way forward that Spain has chosen.

Over the last 8 years, my country has opposed all wars of aggression wherever they have started, whether it's in Ukraine, in Lebanon, or in Iran. We have refused to increase our military spending to 5% of GDP, and we've done everything possible to avoid aggressions that run counter to the UN Charter, placing sanctions on the Russian aggressors, imposing an arms embargo on the Netanyahu government in Israel, and prohibiting the use of our territory to deploy an aggression that was against international law, and unequivocally condemning the genocide that Netanyahu is still perpetrating in Gaza. We have also mobilized resources to do more. And in the face of the chainsaws that have cut close to a third of world development aid in just 2 years, Spain has doubled its investment in cooperation and has increased its contribution to the multilateral system by 60%. And we've done this always holding true to our principles, not even in the most difficult times, like the times being experienced by the Spanish city of Ceuta, where inequality, desperation, and disinformation has fed one of the most significant irregular migration crises in recent years. I know that in times like this, the temptation is to take shortcuts, to give in to fear, to turn migrants into the enemy, and to break the law.

However, my country, Spain, will not do this. And a Spanish city like Ceuta won't do it either, because their citizens are showing that we can tackle a crisis without compromising on decency, upholding the law, and respecting human rights. And we'll come out of this stronger, precisely for this reason, because Spain does not choose the easy route. We always choose the fairest route. And I also want to recognize that the world knows this. At the end of the day, the reactionary forces that want to destroy this multilateral order won't stop attacking us for it.

They want us to be intimidated. They want us to give up. They want us to end up believing that the SDGs are a lost cause, that defending the common good is naive, that cooperating is an act of weakness. Well, I'm here, and I've come up to this rostrum to tell you loud and clear that they are wrong and that we will not keep quiet. The Spanish people are not going back. We will not stop believing that humanity can continue to progress and that working together, we can build a better world.

And we're not going to do this because we believe that delivering for our children, because we know that in a few years, future generations will look back. They will study this decisive decade, and they will ask us what role each and every one of us played. They will ask us, what did we do when some countries started to break the rules and others decided to look the other way? They will ask us what we did when defending what we believed in started to cost us dearly. And when this happens, we want to be able to tell them that we did not give up the fight. Not us.

We want to be able to tell them that we gave everything to leave them a more peaceful, more sustainable, and of course, a fairer world. That's what we want to be able to tell them. And this is the commitment that I want to make here, at this rostrum, not in my own name, of course, but rather on behalf of the country that I represent, Spain. Thank you very much.

But  it  is  also  true  that  the  UN  requires  profound  reforms to be able to tackle the challenges of the 21st century.

As such, the question really is this: do we let the United Nations, together with its aims and founding principles, just slowly fall apart?  Or  do  we  start  facing  these  challenges  with  a  sense  of common responsibility, and genuinely try to reform the UN and start to use the only global framework we have in a responsible and sensible way? One  of  the  biggest  tests  for  the  UN’s  relevance  is  Russia’s aggression  against  Ukraine.  For  more  than  12  years  now, since the illegal annexation of Crimea and occupation of Eastern Ukraine in 2014, a permanent member of the Security Council – the  Russian  Federation  –  has  been  perpetrating  a  war of aggression at the very heart of Europe.

That  aggression  disregards  the  principles  of  the  UN  Charter to its very core: it violates the respect for the sovereignty and territorial  integrity  of  states  and  the  prohibition  on  the  use of force against another state.

The  consequences  of  Russia’s  aggression,  however,  extend far beyond Ukraine and Europe. For example, by increasingly targeting  Ukraine’s  Black  Sea  ports,  commercial  shipping, grain  infrastructure  and  alternative  export  routes,  Russia is putting global food security at grave risk.

As  such,  this  is  a  concern  for  all  of  us,  and  rightly  so. Russia’s  actions  have  been  condemned  by  a  large  majority of  this  Assembly. For  this  we  can  and  should  use  the  diverse  instruments at  our  disposal,  be  they  economic,  diplomatic  or  political. I  strongly  encourage  more  of  my  fellow  heads  of  state  and government  to  use  this  occasion  to  call  on  Russia  to  cease its aggression.

Those of you who have done so already, be it in the Global South or  North  –  you  have  my  appreciation.  The  principles of the UN Charter cannot be trampled on. It is our collective task to stand up for them.

Excellency Khalilur Rahman, President of the 81st Session of the United General Assembly; Excellency António Guterres, Secretary-General of the United Nations; Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. On behalf of Ethiopia, I wish to congratulate you, Mr. President, on your election as President of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly. I also wish to express my sincere appreciation to your predecessor, Her Excellency Ms. Annalena Baerbock, for her leadership during our 80th Session. Mr. President, we assemble at a historic moment for humanity. Sixty-three years ago, in 1963, Emperor Haile Selassie famously cautioned this global community by stating:" Lasting peace can be achieved only when nations recognize that their true strength lies not in the domination of others, but in cooperation anchored upon genuine equality." As a founding member of the United Nations, Ethiopia bears both the scars of historical betrayal and the unyielding conviction of a survivor.

When the League of Nations abandoned our appeal against Fashist aggression in the 1930s, we did not surrender to despair and desolation. We resolutely stood firm as champions of collective security, helping the birth of the very organization in which we stand for. Today, we call upon the Community of Nations to summon that same foundational courage to actively reinforce the very ideals that help prevent global conflict and the scourge of war. The question, therefore, is: how much longer shall we wait before the pillars of collective security fractured beyond repair? This is exactly what drives the significance of multilateralism, not as a diplomatic convenience, but as a living shield rooted in sovereign equality to address the shifting tides of power politics. Mr. President, I would like to thank the Secretary-General for placing before us the defining imperatives of our era, namely artificial intelligence, the climate crisis, and deepening global inequalities.

These are not only policy choices; they are the pivots upon which human destiny is determined. The United Nations has achieved remarkable victories against extreme poverty, but it has never been enough. While wealth accumulates in the hands of the few, billions endure the downside of structural deprivation. However, we believe that we are capable of charting the blueprint, the resources, and the wisdom to bridge this divide. What the global community lacks is not the means of implementation, but the moral courage to keep the promise we made eight decades ago. Poverty and systemic inequality also fuel ecological and environmental crises.

Excessive consumption of the few drives the emission that is currently choking our planet. Yet, delayed promises add a brutal toll on the loss of lives and the devastation of infrastructure. If we are to survive this crisis, we must act now, and act fast. Speaking of actions, my country, Ethiopia, will proudly host COP32 in November 2027. Ethiopia will help organize a vibrant and inclusive platform for the private sector and international stakeholders to pioneer tangible solutions to climate action. In this connection, I sincerely invite all world leaders to come to Ethiopia and leave their footprints at this important global climate summit.

With regard to the digital revolution and artificial intelligence, Africa is compelled to ask a very defining question: will the age of the AI become another instrument of global inequality, or will it be a catalyst for our collective growth? We must ensure that the Global South leads this technological revolution, rather than remain a helpless spectator. Nevertheless, some of the initiatives we see from the Global South give a beacon of hope that we indeed can attain technological advancement through foresight and leadership. A key point is Ethiopia's initiative of the Five Million Quarters program, and the soon-to-be-commissioned University of Artificial Intelligence reaffirms that our continent is ready to build the future. Mr. President, Ethiopia remains steadfast in its belief that the United Nations must be fundamentally reformed to best address the shifting global challenges. The UN reform must reflect our highest aspiration to witness an organization anchored in true equality and justice.

Africa has waited far too long in the shadow of global decision-making. Now it is demanding immediate justice through the comprehensive reform of the United Nations Security Council. With genuine political goodwill, how can a world with a right conscience justify the denial of 1.6 billion Africans the right to equal representation? That indeed is a generational quest for truth and for morality. Mr. President, Ethiopia has diligently worked to promote cooperation and regional integration through infrastructure development, trade, and people-to-people relationships in the Horn of Africa. We have achieved notable progress with several of our neighbors, in spite of attempts by reckless external actors who are habitually engaged in fueling instability.

Despite continued interference in our internal affairs by adversarial elements, we have exercised immense restraint and remained by the firm conviction of becoming one of the most prosperous and dynamic development engines in the Africa. Our message to forces of destruction and mayhem is loud and clear: we urge them to respect the sacred right of the people of the Horn of Africa to live in peace and prosperity. Turning to the wider region, Ethiopia has consistently supported efforts by subregional and regional organizations to bring durable and lasting peace in the Sudan. We firmly believe that a peaceful resolution can only be achieved through a Sudanese-led and Sudanese-owned peace process that reflects the true will and aspiration of the Sudanese people. Mr. President, Ethiopia will continue to commit to the realization of our overarching goal of building a democratic and prosperous country. The progress we have achieved so far on various facets of development reflects this firm and strong resolve.

We recently held a democratic election that laid a strong foundation for a free, fair, and transparent political dispensation. Equally, in our relentless pursuit of building national consensus, the National Dialogue Commission has convened the first historical summit where citizens from every corner of the country and from all walks of life deliberate on critical issues of national importance. It has now opened a glorious new chapter in our political history that helps strengthen our democratic institutions. A significant leap has also been achieved in attaining food security. As part of fulfilling our commitment to enhance resilience to climate shock, we were able to produce an improved climate-resilient wheat variety seed. In a very short period, we have transitioned from a wheat importer to one of the largest wheat producers in Africa.

At a time where food provision has become a political battleground and the global food supply hangs precariously in the balance, we send a clear message that Africa can feed itself. Since the launch of the Green Legacy Initiative in 2019, we were able to plant 56 billion trees, which is not only expanding our forest coverage but significantly restoring our ecosystem. At this stage, this initiative is expected to sequester approximately 1.2 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide annually. As one of the powerhouses of clean energy, with a total potential of 60,000 megawatts, Ethiopia targets to generate 13,000 megawatts by 2030, aiming also to scale up our energy supply across the East African power pool and beyond. In this regard, the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam stands as a monumental pan-African clean energy project, providing that our shared waters and resources can generate progress and development for collective regional prosperity. Moreover, adding to Ethiopia's growing portfolio of mega-project executions, the government is investing in an international airport worth 12.5 billion US dollars, which will handle 110 million passengers and about 4 million tons of cargo annually.

This project will play a catalytic role in the African continental free trade area. To sustain and scale up the success we have achieved in renewable energy, connectivity, food security, manufacturing, and urban development, Ethiopia calls for genuine and sustained regional and international cooperation. Despite this tremendous achievement, Mr. President, we have come to recognize that our efforts to build a strong economy cannot generate sustained development without reliable and dependable access to the sea. We believe that maritime access can be managed for the common benefit and progress of all countries in the region. It is upon this unwavering aspiration that we are pursuing all possible diplomatic avenues to secure access to and from the sea, to ensure Ethiopia's integration into a global trading system. Mr. President, as we attend this August Assembly, we are reminded not only by the ideals and values of our organization, but of the imperatives we must uphold as enshrined in the Charter.

We stand a better chance of surviving and succeeding if we continuously and collectively shape our collaboration. This will certainly revive multilateralism to meet the demands of the current and future generations. In conclusion, Mr. President, I give you my reassurance that Ethiopia remains steadfast, as it has always been, in its historic commitment in upholding human dignity, justice, and the unyielding solidarity of all free peoples. I thank you, Mr. President.

Speech by President António Costa at the 81st United Nations General Assembly - Consilium

Multilateralism is not an ideal of the past. It is the only realistic way to

address the problems of today.

Alone, no country can prevent a pandemic, stabilise the climate, secure

resilient supply chains, regulate Artificial Intelligence, ensure financial

stability or deliver sustainable development. Alone, no country, however

powerful, can build lasting peace.

This is why our message is clear: we need multilateralism.

Multilateralism that is strong, eﬀective, representative and capable of de-

livering for people. Multilateralism that protects human rights, strength-

ens democracy and advances gender equality.

Multilateralism equipped to address the defining challenges of today:

peace, the climate emergency, economic insecurity and Artificial

intelligence.

On artificial intelligence and its governance, we need an accountable,

transparent and regulated architecture. We need an AI that serves human-

ity, not controls it. We must always be in the driving seat. Setting a safe

and secure pace of innovation and development. The AI industry cannot

be regulated by a few major global companies.

The United Nations must play a central role in setting global standards

through the UN Global Digital Compact, the Independent International

Scientific Panel and the Global Dialogue on AI Governance.

The United Nations must remain at the centre of the multilateral system.

The United Nations is under pressure from geopolitical polarisation, fi-

nancial constraints and institutional shortcomings.

But the answer is not withdrawal. The answer is to reform, renew and

reinvest. The UN80 initiative oﬀers an opportunity to make the United

Nations more eﬀicient and more eﬀective.

The European Union also continues to call for a comprehensive reform of

the UN Security Council to make it more eﬀective, inclusive, democratic

and accountable. The European Union will continue to contribute to

strengthening the United Nations politically, financially and through con-

crete action.

Because the best argument for multilateralism is what it delivers: On

peace and security – with the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of nuclear

weapons. On climate action – with the Paris Agreement. On poverty and

health – with the Global Response to Covid-19.

The truth is: when we act together, multilateralism delivers for people.

That is why, this week the European Union has launched, together with

Australia, Barbados, Brazil, Canada, India and Kenya, the P4M: Partners

for Multilateralism, International Law, Peace and Prosperity.

Our initiative aims to be an open platform for partners from all parts of

That means safeguarding the institutions that give full meaning to these

Ukraine.

Speech by President António Costa at the 81st United Nations General Assembly - Consilium

Law over power.

Partnership over isolation.

Action over paralysis.

We are ready to work together with all those who share this conviction.

Mr President, Mr Secretary-General, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen,

Former Secretary-General Kofi Annan once said: “Whatever our differences, […] we stand or fall together.”

When we forget this, disorder is what happens.

Last year, from this very podium, I stated that foreign policy is based on three pillars: values, interests, and power.

This year, I come with something simpler. A choice. Co-operation or conflict.

In today’s world, co-operation is undermined by a lack of trust, disregard for rules, and the weakening of institutions.

Conflicts are spreading, bringing suffering, violence, and injustice.

According to some accounts, there are currently 65 active armed conflicts – more than at any time since the end of the Cold War.

Competition will always be there. Nations compete now harder than they did a generation ago. That doesn’t worry me. What does, is that more and more of them now compete against the rules on which the international order rests.

So, this speech defends the rules. And it calls for co-operation. Small nations need it to survive. Large nations need it to stay great.

Upholding the most basic rules, values and institutions is our best option to ensure that competition does not escalate into conflict. And that co-operation gains ground.

Now, I want to begin by analysing how the world is changing today. And as a pragmatic Finn, I will always try to deal with the world as it is, because it often helps in building a world that I wish we would have. In other words, a world we can build together.

I will then make a few suggestions about what we should do next.

We should all be steadfast defenders of multilateralism. As Strobe Talbott reportedly remarked, multilateralism is hell, and can be a real pain in the neck. But it is the best option for humanity as a whole.

We need multilateralism in order to address our shared agenda, ranging from armed conflicts and climate change to sustainable development and artificial intelligence.

Currently, however, we seem to be going the other way: towards a non-cooperative multipolar world order.

This order, as it turns out, is based on zero-sum deals, transactions, and unrestrained power. This is a short-sighted approach.

Tempting as it may be for some, such a multipolar order will ultimately lead to conflict. It will turn against us, whether you represent a great power, a middle power, or a small state, like Finland.

Between these two approaches, there is a third option: plurilateralism. It means building ad hoc coalitions when global co-operation is unattainable.

And this is my first observation today: the emergence of flexible forms of co-operation around different themes and interests. Be it in the economy, climate, defence, or technology.

Coalition-building can be a force for good. But with one condition: it should not challenge multilateralism, but build on it. It should support the UN system, not substitute it.

The Coalition of the Willing for Ukraine is particularly close to my heart. It is a group of countries working to end Russia’s war of aggression. The war is unlawful, unjustified and unprovoked. Its solution will have far-reaching consequences for Ukraine and beyond.

The Coalition works for a just and lasting peace in Ukraine in accordance with the UN Charter. It seeks to uphold the basic tenets of the international order.

My second observation is that everywhere I travel, I hear the word ‘realignment’.

Whether it is in Europe, Africa, the Middle East, Asia, or the Americas, nations are seeking new alliances and partnerships.

This is a logical consequence in times of uncertainty and transformation. You seek security where you can get it.

We are seeing an intensification of regional integration akin to what we saw in the immediate aftermath of World War II.

Regional organizations like the African Union, Gulf Cooperation Council, Mercosur, ASEAN or the EU build trust.

When integration is not feasible, other forms of co-operation can prove essential. We Finns are happy to point to the historic signing of the Helsinki Final Act in 1975. It brought together 35 nations in the midst of the Cold War and laid the foundations for what would later become the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe.

There was no trust. There were deep disagreements. And outright hostility. Yet there was room for a process that reduced tensions and built common ground.

I believe regions, such as the Middle East, where conflicts are raging today, may consider something similar.

Even in the face of conflict and grievance, a region may be able to agree on principles that foster co-operation and prevent further conflict.

My third observation is that a new economic world order is taking shape.

Instruments once used for economic integration – including trade, technology, energy, investment, and supply chains – have become instruments of geopolitical competition.

There was perhaps, at times, a naïve belief that interdependence would bring about stability and peace. Now, the focus on opportunities has been replaced by the focus on threats.

We have entered a world of coercion, where dependencies are vulnerabilities. Countries seek chokepoints that can be weaponized to pressure others.

But dependencies are complex. No nation, not even the biggest ones, can go it alone. All coercive actions come at a cost.

And even if a mightier state dominates in one domain, a smaller state can respond in another.

In the new geopolitical environment, the economic order of the post-World War II era is seeking new forms.

The new order must be based on a realistic understanding of the power balance in the world.

We in the West must acknowledge that the Global South and East are an expanding economic and political force.

Many nations around the world have made remarkable advances in competence and know-how. We should put this collective expertise to work for the global common good.

Countries are right to be wary of dangerous dependencies. But our focus on threats should not lead us to abandon co-operation.

We should strive for an economic world order built on institutions and agreements. Multilateralism is also needed in the global economy.

It is all well and good to diagnose the problem: too many nations now compete at the expense of basic rules, and that is why the world has slipped into disorder.

But it matters more to find a prescription which would bring us back to order, stability and co-operation.

Thus, I will offer you three remedies for a world in disorder. To begin with, we need to go back to the basics of international law.

On my recent visit to India, I came across a quote from Mahatma Gandhi: “The breach of one rule inevitably leads to the breach of other rules”. These words resonate all too strongly today.

We have moved back to a world defined by raw power and narrow self-interest.

Rules and values seem to be taking a back seat. Some are ready to throw in the towel, prepared to accept the defeat of the international rules-based order.

That is an exaggeration. International law has been questioned and challenged before. It has never been a perfect system.

But we must admit that we are at a critical juncture. Fundamental norms are being questioned in a way that erodes confidence in the entire multilateral system.

Therefore, the first remedy for a world in disorder is rule of law.

Today, international norms are often presented as an obstacle to the pursuit of national interests. This is both wrong and dangerous.

International law has never been merely an effort to achieve universal justice, but neither can it be reduced to a mere instrument of domination.

It is not only about values, nor only about interests, but about both.

Despite the rhetoric, no major power is likely to give up its ability to shape the rules.

Even when actors claim to abandon rules, they rather seek to replace existing rules with ones more to their liking.

Therefore, we will not face a world without rules. But we could be facing a world with less predictability, less restraint – a world based on rules that are more permissive for the powerful.

For the collective benefit of the nations in this Hall, we should continue to defend the rule of law and uphold its most fundamental principles. They include the independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity of nations; freedom of navigation at sea; and accountability for the most serious international crimes.

The second remedy is about humanitarian principles.

The world today has an unprecedented capacity to meet humanity’s most pressing needs.

Since the establishment of the United Nations, poverty has declined, access to basic education has expanded, literacy has increased, and child mortality has fallen.

Yet, we are witnessing tyranny, disregard for the vulnerable, and violence against civilians in many parts of the world. Poverty and distress are still widespread.

For example, Sudan is devastated by war. Millions have been displaced, and many face famine.

Gaza continues to be one of the world’s most acute humanitarian emergencies, marked by mass displacement, the destruction of infrastructure and a lack of essential services.

Haiti struggles with armed violence and extreme weather events, causing a displacement crisis, a hunger crisis, and a health crisis.

We must not grow indifferent to wars and human suffering, but instead channel our efforts into preventing conflicts, upholding human rights, and strengthening sustainable economies.

Our growing material prosperity should not come at the expense of our ethical responsibilities.

The third remedy is about language and the way we treat each other.

Unfortunately, there is no shortage of examples of those who use dismissive language to describe others and entire groups of people.

Too often, those with the most provocative rhetoric receive the greatest visibility.

Provocation is rewarded with attention. Excess is misinterpreted as courage. Exaggeration as the truth.

Language can foster co-operation, but it can also break trust and turn competition into conflict.

The recipe is simple, but necessary: avoid polarization, strengthen trust, and listen to others.

We need dignified foreign policy. And that starts here, at the United Nations.

Ladies and Gentlemen,

I would like to thank Secretary-General Guterres for his service and his dedication to reforming and rationalising the UN system. This work must continue.

Every Secretary-General is shaped both by their era and by their own actions.

I was reminded of this recently when reading the biographies of former Secretaries-General U-Thant and Kofi Annan, both highly influential leaders who navigated an era of great-power tensions.

Let me put forward a few suggestions for the new Secretary-General’s consideration, whoever she may be, and for the international community at large.

Since my first speech here two years ago, I have consistently called for a reformed Security Council. The world has changed, so should the UN.

There should be, at least, two new permanent seats for Africa, two for Asia-Pacific and one for Latin America.

No single state should have veto power. And, if a member of the Security Council violates the UN Charter, its voting rights should be suspended.

The world needs a functioning UN Security Council. To move forward, we need to break the impasse and be open for creative solutions.

The need for reform also extends to the global economic architecture. It, too, must be updated to reflect today’s power balance.

We have to make sure international economic co-operation continues to be rules-based, legitimate, and representative. Multilateral solutions are needed in an increasingly multipolar world.

We must also bring the United Nations back to peace mediation. The Secretary-General, as Mediator-In-Chief, will have a key role.

The UN’s legitimacy as a mediator is unique. Together, the UN and its Member States can accomplish what neither can achieve alone.

The UN needs to be at the centre of rule-making and institution-building. Regional integration and thematic coalitions can and should support it.

Artificial intelligence is the most consequential technology in the history of mankind. It will impact science, the economy, politics, security, and the very essence of our humanity.

Humans can and should be in the driver’s seat. We have a choice: we can compete, co-operate or slow down. For me, co-operation is the best way forward.

This is why Norway and Finland have, together with leaders from nations around the world, launched a call for companies, governments, regional organisations and the UN to develop mechanisms to control frontier models of AI.

My country, Finland, wants the United Nations to succeed and will remain strongly engaged in its work. Therefore, we are standing for election to the Security Council from 2029 to 2030.

We are motivated by our belief in the UN Charter and the values it stands for. We will prioritize peace, people, and partnerships.

We are willing to take on the responsibility of the Council membership at a time that calls for more peace. We want people and nations to thrive. We believe in dialogue and co-operation.

Finally, let me make a procedural proposal. The foundations of the United Nations were built in San Francisco over 80 years ago.

Today, we must restore balance to the world order. We must recommit to the fundamental principles of the international order. And we must embrace co-operation over conflict.

What the world needs now, is a new San Francisco moment. A moment where world leaders come together to chart the way forward. A process to achieve this should start with the new Secretary-General.

I bring warm greetings from the people of Fiji, and from

Assembly.  Fiji  assures  you  of  our  full  support  as  you

Honourable  Sitiveni  Rabuka,  joins  me  in  wishing  you

and  all  Member  States  a  peaceful,  productive  and

I  acknowledge  your  predecessor,  Her  Excellency

Annalena Baerbock, for her stewardship of the Eightieth

Session.

I pay tribute also to Secretary-General António Guterres,

who addresses this general debate for the last time in that

office.

Through  a  decade  of  turbulence  he  has  defended

multilateralism and stood with Small Island Developing

States. Fiji thanks him.

The theme of this session — “Restoring Trust, Managing

Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All”

— speaks directly to the condition of our world.

We face deepening geopolitical rivalry, armed conflict,

climate and environmental crises, economic uncertainty,

disrupted supply chains, rapid technological change, and

an information environment corroded by disinformation.

These  crises  do  not  remain  where  they  begin.  Conflict

raises the cost of fuel and food far beyond its borders.

Carbon emitted far from the Pacific takes our shorelines,

our homes and our sacred places.

For Small Island Developing States, distance no longer

insulates us from global shocks. Too often, it magnifies

their cost.

Trust, therefore, is not restored by declarations alone. It

is

restored  when  commitments  are  kept,  when

international

law

is  applied  consistently,  when

institutions listen, and when people can see and feel the

results of multilateral action in their daily lives.

PEACE, SECURITY AND THE RULE OF LAW

Fiji reaffirms an enduring principle: international law is

not  optional,  and  peace  cannot  be  secured  by  power

alone.

For  small  States,  the  principles  of  the  Charter  —

sovereign  equality,  territorial  integrity,  the  peaceful

settlement  of  disputes  —  are  the  safeguard  against  a

world in which size or military strength decides whose

rights matter.

When  the  world  asks  small  States  to  choose  between

competing  power  blocs,  Fiji  chooses  principles.  We

choose the Charter. We choose international law.

We choose dialogue over coercion, human dignity over

domination, and cooperation over confrontation.

Fiji  calls  for  the  peaceful  settlement  of  conflicts

wherever they occur.

We  urge  all  parties

to  protect  civilians,  respect

international  humanitarian  law,  and  return  to  the

negotiating table.

The Charter does not apply differently according to who

is involved, or where. Fiji asks the same of every party,

in every theatre.

Energy, food security and supply chains are inseparable

from  peace.  The  freedoms  of  navigation  guaranteed

under  international  law,  including  the  United  Nations

Convention on the Law of the Sea, must be respected.

Fiji  will  continue  to  serve  in  United  Nations  peace

operations. We ask only that they be properly mandated,

properly  financed  and  properly  supported  —  and  we

support  renewed  investment  in  prevention,  mediation

and  the  quiet  diplomacy  that  stops  wars  before  they

begin.

We  carry  a  simple  Pacific  conviction:  the  life  of  a

stranger is worth protecting, dialogue is worth pursuing,

and peace, however difficult, is always worth building.

THE BLUE PACIFIC AND REGIONAL

COOPERATION

The Pacific knows the cost of militarization and nuclear

testing.

Our  ocean  carries  the  memory  of  decisions  made

elsewhere but suffered by Pacific peoples. That memory

strengthens  our  determination  that  the  Blue  Pacific

remain a region of peace.

The  Ocean  of  Peace  Declaration  expresses  a  regional

vision grounded in sovereignty, international law and the

rejection of coercion.

Our message to all partners is clear: the Pacific welcomes

friendship,  investment  and  genuine  cooperation  —  but

our  ocean  must  not  become  a  theatre  in  which  others

settle their rivalries.

For  Small

Island  Developing  States,

regional

cooperation is not an optional layer of diplomacy.

It  is  a  practical  necessity.  Separated  by  vast  distances,

with small populations and narrow economic bases, what

is  difficult  alone  becomes  possible  together.  We  must

take  it  further  still  —  through  connectivity,  food  and

energy  security,  and  Pacific-led  financing  such  as

something the Pacific has built. The Pacific Resilience

Facility is the first climate and disaster financing facility

owned, governed and hosted by the States it serves.

Its treaty entered into force in May, it is seated in Tonga,

and its first grants are already reaching our communities.

It exists because a village seawall does not need a three-

year accreditation process. It needs money that arrives.

Its  initial  capitalisation  target  is  five  hundred  million

United  States  dollars  by  December,  of  which  one

hundred and seventy-three million has been pledged.

I thank those who have come forward, and I ask those

able to close that gap to do so.

Cooperation  of  this  kind  does  not  diminish  our

sovereignty. It strengthens our ability to exercise it.

RESTORING TRUST AT HOME:

CONSTITUTIONAL AND DEMOCRATIC

RENEWAL

The call to restore trust must also apply within our own

nations. Fiji's democratic journey has not been easy. We

have  known  political  upheaval,  constitutional  change

and  periods  of  deep  division.  We  cannot  change  that

history, but we can learn from it.

This year Fiji undertook a national review of the 2013

Constitution,  informed  by  consultations  across  the

country. On 1 September the Commission presented its

report  to  me  as  Head  of  State.  That  did  not  end  the

process; it began the next stage.

The report must now proceed through Parliament and the

democratic  processes,  transparently  and  in  accordance

with the rule of law.

What Fiji seeks is not a Constitution for a government, a

party or one generation, but a settlement that every Fijian

recognizes  as  their  own.  Alongside  it,  our  Truth  and

Reconciliation  process  continues.  Renewal  strengthens

institutions; reconciliation heals divisions.

Together

they  can  carry  Fiji  from  memory

to

understanding, and from division to trust.

A UNITED NATIONS THAT DELIVERS

If the United Nations is to restore trust, it must also be

willing to reform itself.

Fiji  supports  the  UN80  reform  agenda  to  make  the

Organisation more coherent, efficient and effective. But

reform must be judged by a single test: what it improves

for people and for Member States.

For  Pacific  Small  Island  Developing  States,  efficiency

must  not  mean  distance.  The  Multi-Country  Offices

serving our region are essential bridges between global

commitments and island realities.

Reform must strengthen, not thin, our capacity to deliver

where need is greatest.

This  Assembly  will  also  select  the  next  Secretary-

General.  Fiji  asks  for  a  process  that  is  transparent  and

merit-based  —  and  for  a  Secretary-General  who

understands the realities of small island States and will

act on them. For too long our circumstances have been

well diagnosed and poorly addressed.

The promise to “deliver for all” must also be measured

in  development.  With  2030  approaching,  too  many

Sustainable  Development  Goals  remain  off

track.

National  income  alone  cannot  capture  remoteness,

disaster exposure and the repeated burden of rebuilding.

The  Multidimensional  Vulnerability  Index  must  move

from adoption to application.

There  is  one  measure  of  delivery  that  reaches  Fijian

households  directly.  Remittances  are  now  Fiji’s  third-

largest source of foreign exchange. They pay school fees,

rebuild  homes  after  cyclones,  and  sustain  families

between harvests. They are not aid. They are the earnings

of Fijians abroad, sent home.

Yet Pacific corridors remain among the most expensive

in the world through which to send money.  In May, in

this  Hall,  we  recommitted  ourselves  to  bring  transfer

costs  below  three  per  cent,  and  to  eliminate  corridors

costing  more  than  five.  Pacific  corridors  are  among

those. Fiji asks that this be treated as an obligation and

not an aspiration.

Labour  mobility  must  also  not  become  a  one-way

transfer of the people we have trained.

Fiji does not begrudge any Fijian the chance to build a

life abroad. We ask only that those who recruit our nurses

and teachers invest in the systems that produced them.

And

this  belongs  beside  what  I  have  said  of

reconciliation. Not every Fijian abroad left in search of

work. Some left in seasons of upheaval, when they did

not feel that the country was theirs. They are Fijians still,

and so are their children.

A supreme law that belongs to every citizen must belong

to them also. Fiji’s door is open.

This  month,  Fiji  declared  a  national  HIV  emergency.

One in sixty of our adults is now estimated to be living

with the virus. Fewer than four in ten know it.

I say this plainly, because stigma and silence are how

this epidemic grew — and because the late Ratu Epeli

Nailatikau,  our  former  Head  of  State  and  UNAIDS

Goodwill Ambassador for the Pacific, spent his last years

telling us so.

This  is  also  a  security  question.  Methamphetamine

trafficked  into  our  region  by  transnational  criminal

networks is now driving transmission through injecting

drug  use.  Our  borders  are  ocean,  our  populations  are

small,  and  the  profits  at  stake  exceed  our  national

budgets.  A  country  of  under  a  million  people  cannot

interdict a global supply chain alone.

So Fiji asks three things: that treatment and diagnostics

reach small States at prices we can pay; that the Global

Fund and UNAIDS be resourced at a level that does not

force triage between regions; and that our partners treat

Pacific  narcotics  interdiction  as  the  shared  security

interest it is.

These are the same loss. A nurse who emigrates is a nurse

Fiji trained and will not have. A Fijian who dies at thirty-

five  of  a  treatable  virus  is  the  same  subtraction,  made

permanent, with the cost of care left behind. Small States

are not losing workers at the margin. We are losing the

capacity to staff our own future.

CLIMATE CHANGE AND THE OCEAN

Nowhere is the gap between promise and delivery more

consequential than in the climate crisis.

For the Pacific, climate change is not a future scenario.

It is saltwater entering farmland, coastal erosion moving

closer to homes, stronger storms damaging schools and

roads,  pressure  on  fisheries  and  food  security,  and

communities facing relocation.

This  is  a  question  of  science.  It  is  also  a  question  of

justice.

This Assembly has this week addressed the threats posed

by sea-level rise. For Fiji the legal consequences are not

abstract.  Statehood,  once  established,  continues.

Maritime zones, once lawfully established and deposited

with the United Nations, must remain — notwithstanding

the physical changes brought by sea-level rise. No State

should lose its rights, its identity or its seat in this Hall

because others have altered its coastline. Fiji urges this

Assembly  to  carry  that  principle  from  declaration  into

settled international law.

Fiji welcomes the Advisory Opinion of the International

Court of Justice on the obligations of States in respect of

climate change. It confirms that climate responsibility is

not only political or moral — it is legal.

The task now is implementation: obligations recognised

by the Court must be reflected in national commitments,

in  the  conduct  of  States,  and  in  the  outcomes  of  our

negotiations.

Climate finance must move from promise to access, and

from  announcement  to  disbursement.  The  Loss  and

Damage Fund must operate at a scale that reflects actual

need,  and  access  must  be  simplified  —  for  small

administrations, the cost of applying should never exceed

the capacity to apply.

In November, the world gathers in Antalya for COP31.

Before  that,  Fiji  hosts  the  Pre-COP,  and  Tuvalu  a

Leaders’ event, in early October.

To every delegation in this Hall: come to the Pacific. See

what a rising sea means to a village that has nowhere to

move.  Then  let  us  go  to  Antalya  and  deliver  —  on

adaptation, on finance, on loss and damage, and on the

transition away from fossil fuels.

As  a  Large  Ocean  State,  Fiji’s  identity,  economy  and

future  are  inseparable  from  the  ocean.  Illegal  fishing,

pollution, biodiversity loss and warming, acidifying seas

do  not  respect  national  boundaries  —  and  no  island

nation can meet them alone.

This year, the Agreement on marine biodiversity beyond

national  jurisdiction  entered  into  force  —  a  genuine

achievement  of  multilateralism.  Fiji  calls  for  universal

ratification,  for  a  first  Conference  of  the  Parties  that

delivers  a  functioning  institution,  and  for  capacity-

building and technology transfer that are real rather than

aspirational.

And in the deep sea we ask of others only the discipline

we  ask  of  ourselves:  that  no  exploitation  proceed  until

the  science  is  sufficient  and  the  rules  are  sound.  The

common heritage of humankind is an obligation owed to

those not yet born.

CONCLUSION: THE CHOICE BEFORE US

Fiji comes to this Assembly as a small island State, but

not with a small vision.

Our size does not diminish our voice.

Our vulnerability does not diminish our agency.

And  our  distance  from  the  centres  of  power  does  not

distance us from its consequences.

Transformation  will  happen  whether  we  manage  it  or

not. The real question is what kind of transformation we

choose.

Will it be governed by law, or by power?

And  will  this  Assembly  remain  a  place  where  we

describe  crises  —  or  become  an  institution  that  solves

them?

Let this Eighty-First Session be remembered not for the

depth  of  our  concern,  but  for  the  courage  of  our

decisions.

Let us build a United Nations that is trusted because it is

fair; relevant because it adapts; and respected because it

delivers.

Let us build a Pacific that remains an Ocean of Peace —

united  in  purpose,  confident  in  its  identity,  and  strong

enough to shape its own future.

And let us remember that the measure of what we do here

will  not  be  found  in  our  speeches.  It  will  be  found  in

whether a coastal community can remain on the land of

its  ancestors,  and  whether  a  young  person  can  trust

democracy and find a future at home.

That is the United Nations Fiji believes in.

And that is the trust we must restore — together.
