For the first time in the history of our species, we have created a

technology  that  openly  challenges  the  supremacy  of  the  human

mind  as  the  pinnacle  of  our  evolutionary  development.     I  will  not

dwell  on

the

transformational  potential  of

this  revolutionary

technology,  whether

in  disease  eradication,  productivity

enhancement, or fighting climate change.

However, it is simply impossible to ignore the fact that, at present,

the  risks  of  an  unchecked  and  unregulated  advance  in  artificial

intelligence could greatly outweigh its potential benefits.

When the people developing the technology tell us openly that, “left

unchecked AI could outrun our ability to control these systems” and

admit  that  “we  only  understand  a  tiny  fraction  of  what  goes  on  in

these models”, alarm bells should ring very loudly for all of us.

In simple words, AI bosses are telling us that they have no idea how

recursive  self-improvement,  the  ability  of  AI  to  constantly  create

better versions of itself, actually works.

Add to that the possibility of massive job destruction, the likelihood

of unprecedented wealth creation in the hands of very few, and the

impact that AI may have on the very nature of human relationships,

especially  for  our  kids,  and  you  have  all  the  ingredients  of  an

unprecedented political and social upheaval.

The  idea  that  the  big  tech  companies  will  find  some  voluntary

arrangement to self-regulate the development of AI is naive.  It flies

in  the face  of  everything  we  know  about  the  history  of  capitalism.

The prize for the winners is simply too great to believe that benign

consideration  for  the  wellbeing  of  humanity  will  outweigh  the

relentless drive of capital to constantly seek better returns.

Given that the leading AI models are being developed here in the

United States, this is primarily an issue  for the US government to

address.    Fortunately,  there  are  precedents  from  which  to  draw

lessons.

In the 1940s and 50s, the American government heavily regulated

another  technology  so  powerful  that  its  creators  believed  it  could

bring about either a golden age in human flourishing or the end of

the world.  That technology was nuclear.

The same needs to happen now.  And it needs to happen fast.  AI

companies  need  to  be  licensed  based  on  specific  requirements:

adherence  to  human  values,  transparency  and,  most  importantly,

safety.  In order for a new plane to fly, it has to undergo a myriad of

rigorous tests approved by the regulator.  But the same is not true

for a frontier artificial intelligence model.

At  the  same  time,  I  take  the  call  by  leading AI  executives  for  a

voluntary pause in the development of their models very seriously.

But  only  as  a  temporary  measure  to  buy  time  for  a  powerful

regulatory authority to be set up.

Liberal  capitalism  has  a  history  of  reining  in  market  excesses,

whether it was breaking up powerful monopolies or setting rules and

standards to allow the market to operate with an eye on the common

good.  The same needs to happen now.

And as much as the cooperation of China and the rest of the world

is  necessary  to  address  this  huge  challenge,  the  fate  of  artificial

intelligence and the impact it will have on humanity as a whole will

not be decided in Brussels, Tokyo, or Brasilia, but primarily here, in

the United States.

With great power comes great responsibility.  Let us hope our host

country will rise to the occasion.

Thank you.

speaker_post: Permanent Representative to the United Nations
text:
Distinguished Heads of State and Government, Mr. Secretary-General, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen,

Let me thank the Government and People of Grenada for this privilege bestowed on me. And thank Grenada’s visionary Prime Minister, Honourable Dickon Mitchell for the trust.

Grenada congratulates you Mr. President as President of the Eighty First Session of the General Assembly, and thank the former President, Annalena Baerbock.

One year ago, standing at this very podium, the Prime Minister of Grenada addressed this General Assembly not only as our Head of Government, but as a proud son of the Caribbean. He reminded us that our Region continues to literally and figuratively weather storms, yet continues to rise with resilience, dignity and hope.

Today,  as  I  stand  before  you  representing  the  people  of  Grenada,  I  speak  of transformation  -  Because  resilience  alone  is  no  longer  enough.  Our  task  cannot simply be to survive one crisis after another. We must transform the conditions that make  people  vulnerable  in  the  first  place.  We  must  renew  our  global  systems, strengthen our multilateral partnerships and summon the collective will necessary to build  a  world  worthy  of the  next  generation.  And  that transformation  must  begin with people.

Haiti: From Solidarity to Action

Grenada joins CARICOM in calling for the timely renewal of the mandate of the

Gang Suppression Force, its full and rapid deployment in close partnership with the

Haitian National Police, and the provision of the personnel, financing, equipment

and  logistical  support  necessary  for  it  to  fulfil  its  mandate  effectively  with

appropriate human-rights safeguards. These security efforts are essential to creating

the  conditions  for  credible,  free,  fair  and  inclusive  Haitian-led  elections,  the

strengthening  of  national  institutions  and  the  restoration  of  constitutional

governance.

Haiti is not a failed state. Haiti represents a promise yet to be fulfilled.

It is a promise to the Haitian people that the international community must honour, not with pity - but with purpose; not temporarily - but sustainably. And even as we respond to the security crisis, humanitarian assistance must remain at the centre of our efforts.

Cuba: Partnership Must Prevail Over Isolation

Grenada  remains  deeply  concerned about the  continuing  hardship  endured  by  the

Cuban  people.  Our  humanitarian  conscience  cannot  be  indifferent  to  the

circumstances  of  ordinary  households,  particularly  children,  the  elderly and  other

vulnerable persons, whose difficulties deepen with each passing day that the present

impasse remains unresolved. We call for constructive engagement that places the

well-being of the Cuban people at its centre and opens a path towards meaningful

relief, improved living conditions and renewed opportunities.

As we speak of transforming our multilateral system, we must also ensure that its

leadership reflects the diversity, experience and aspirations of the people it serves.

Grenada therefore proudly joins our CARICOM family in giving our unequivocal

support to the candidacy of Ambassador Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett of Guyana

for the position of Secretary-General of the United Nations. CARICOM Heads of

Government have endorsed her as the region’s candidate, recognising the experience

and leadership she brings to this important moment for global multilateralism. Her

distinguished service as Guyana’s Foreign Minister and Permanent Representative

to the United Nations, has demonstrated a deep commitment to diplomacy, dialogue

and international cooperation.

The Caribbean has long demonstrated that size does not determine the strength

of our ideas, the quality of our leadership, or the value of our contribution to

the  international  community.  We  believe,  Ambassador  Rodrigues-Birkett  is

eminently  qualified  to  serve  the  entire  United  Nations  membership.  Her  election

would  represent  a  historic  milestone  for  our  Caribbean  Region  and  a  powerful

affirmation  that  every  region,  including  Small  Island  Developing  States,  can

contribute to leadership at the highest levels of our multilateral system.

Restoring Trust Through Transformation

We meet at a time of significant global transformation.

The challenges before us are complex, but they also present an opportunity to renew our commitment to cooperation and create practical solutions that improve the lives of our people.

The theme of this session, “Restoring trust, managing transformation: A United Nations that delivers for all,” challenges us to move beyond declarations toward delivery.

For  Grenada,  restoring  trust  means  demonstrating  through  our  actions  that international cooperation produces results.

It means listening to one another.

It means respecting the voices of small states as much as those of large ones.

It means building genuine partnerships.

And it means ensuring that every country has the opportunity to pursue its legitimate development aspirations.

Grenada approaches this General Assembly in a spirit of partnership, optimism and constructive engagement.

We remain firmly committed to the purposes and principles of the Charter of the United Nations, international law, peaceful dialogue and the peaceful settlement of disputes.

In an increasingly interconnected world, cooperation is not merely desirable.

It is indispensable.

Vision 75: Grenada's Transformation

The  transformation  we  advocate  internationally  must  also  take  place  at  home. Grenada is advancing an ambitious long-term roadmap towards our 75th anniversary of independence.

Anchored  in  our  National  Sustainable  Development  Plan  2020–2035,  Vision  75 charts a transformational course for our Nation, rooted in sustainability, resilience, equity and opportunity.

At the heart of Vision 75 are five strategic pillars:

Education and Skills Training. Healthcare. Agriculture and Food Security. The Environment and Energy. And Housing.

These are not simply sectors of government policy. They are investments in people. We  are  investing  in  health  and  wellness,  education  and  skills,  food  security, renewable energy, digital innovation and environmental sustainability.

We are creating greater opportunities for our young people and preparing them not simply for the jobs that exist today, but for the industries that will define tomorrow.

For Grenada, transformation must always be people-centred.

It means building resilience while creating opportunity.

Expanding our economy while protecting our environment; and,

Embracing technology while safeguarding humanity.

SIDS, Climate and Resilience

As a Small Island Developing State, Grenada understands resilience. But experience

has also taught us that resilience cannot begin after disaster strikes.

We must invest before the storm.

Prepare before the emergency.

Build before the damage is done.

And finance resilience before countries are forced to borrow simply to rebuild what they have lost.

This  requires  greater  international  cooperation  in  climate  adaptation,  disaster

preparedness,  resilient  infrastructure  and  accessible  financing.  Small  Island

Developing States should not be viewed simply as victims of climate change. We

are also laboratories of resilience.

From Climate Vulnerability to Opportunity

Climate  action  remains  one  of  the  areas  in  which  collective  effort  can  make  a profound difference.

Grenada remains committed to strengthening resilience and advancing sustainable and  low-carbon  development.  But  ambition  without  implementation  is  merely aspiration.

For  vulnerable  countries,  climate  commitments  must  be  accompanied  by  reliable access  to  the  resources  required  to  deliver  them.  Climate  financing must  become more accessible, predictable and responsive.

Our objective should not simply be to help vulnerable countries recover from the next disaster.

Our objective must be to transform vulnerability into resilience and resilience into sustainable opportunity.

Financing Development Differently

This transformation must also take place in the international financial system.

Grenada welcomes growing recognition that development and vulnerability cannot be assessed by income alone.

The Multidimensional Vulnerability Index offers an important opportunity to better recognise the structural circumstances of Small Island Developing States.

Our  vulnerabilities  are  shaped  by  exposure  to  climate  change,  natural  disasters, external  economic  shocks  and  other  circumstances  that  cannot  adequately  be captured through income per capita.

therefore  encourages  Member  States,  development  partners  and Grenada international financial institutions to advance vulnerability-informed approaches to development financing.

Greater access to concessional financing, climate finance, disaster-risk financing and innovative  financial  instruments  can  help  countries  move  from  vulnerability  to resilience, and from recovery to sustainable growth.

Young People, Technology and AI

At the centre of all of this must be our young people. Their creativity, energy and ideas are among our greatest national and global assets. Our responsibility is to give them  the  education,  skills,  technology  and  opportunities  necessary  to  shape  the world they will inherit.

Digital transformation and emerging technologies, particularly artificial intelligence, offer  enormous  possibilities  for  education,  healthcare,  agriculture,  public administration and economic development.

But access must be equitable.

The technologies shaping humanity's future must not create another divide between those countries that can afford to innovate and those that cannot.

And access alone will not be enough.

As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly embedded in our economies and societies, we must develop credible AI governance frameworks that encourage innovation while protecting people, privacy, security, democratic values and public trust.

Technology must remain a tool for human development, not a replacement for human responsibility.

We must prepare young people not only to use new technologies, but to question them, govern them, and deploy them ethically.

Global Call to Action

Grenada approaches the future with confidence. We recognise the challenges before us, but we also see enormous possibilities.

Our  Vision  75  embodies  our  determination  to  build  a  stronger,  healthier,  more resilient  and  more  prosperous  Grenada.  Our  commitment  to  the  Sustainable Development Goals reflects our belief in shared global progress.

And our engagement in this United Nations reflects our conviction that partnership remains one of humanity's greatest sources of strength. But partnership must deliver. So let this Assembly send a clear message:

Let us restore hope in Haiti.

Let us protect children and civilians wherever conflict threatens their future.

Let us choose dialogue over division.

Let us allow cooperation with Cuba and with all nations to be guided by the interests and well-being of people.

Let  us  ensure  that  Small  Island  Developing  States  have  fair  access  to  the financing necessary to build resilience before disaster strikes.

Let us equip our young people to lead the technological transformation rather than become casualties of it.

Let us protect our oceans and our planet.

And let us transform our multilateral institutions so that they deliver not simply promises, but progress.

The measure of this United Nations cannot only be the resolutions we adopt.

It must be the lives we improve.

The children we protect.

The conflicts we help prevent.

The opportunities we create.

And the hope we restore.

Grenada stands ready to work with all Member States and international partners in advancing a future that is peaceful, resilient, inclusive and sustainable.

One year ago, Grenada came before this Assembly with a message about resilience and education.

Today, we build upon that message.

Resilience gives us the strength to endure. Transformation gives us the power to change. Partnership gives us the ability to do both.

Together,  through  renewed  trust  and  genuine  partnership,  we  can  build  a  United Nations that delivers.

A United Nations that protects. A United Nations that listens. A United Nations that acts.

And ultimately, a world in which no country, no community and no person is left behind.

May God bless the United Nations.

I thank you

Mr. president of the General Assembly. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, the international system that has guided our relations over recent decades is undergoing a profound transformation. Conflicts, geopolitical tensions, declining resources for development and the fragmentation of spaces for dialogue are testing the principles that have guided coexistence among nations. At the same time, democracy faces a twofold challenge the resurgence of authoritarian tendencies that seek to undermine the will of the people, and the spread of organised criminal networks that infiltrate institutions, corrupt justice systems, capture economies and territories, and erode public trust. Transnational organised crime is more than just a threat to public security. It is a direct threat to democracy the rule of law, and the ability of our peoples to freely determine their future.

Criminal networks do not recognize borders. They are linked through drug trafficking trafficking in persons, illicit arms trafficking, smuggling, extortion, money laundering, environmental crime and other illicit economies. They exploit institutional weaknesses, inequality, and a lack of opportunities. Wherever the state is weakened, these structures seek to replace it, intimidate it, or bend it to serve private interests. In the face of these realities, the fundamental principles that must guide our collective action have lost none of their relevance. Preserving peace, combating hunger and poverty.

Ensuring equal rights and opportunities, strengthening justice, protecting our planet, and consolidating democratic institutions remain shared responsibilities. The Sustainable Development Goals continue to provide an essential roadmap. It is precisely at moments such as this that international law, multilateralism and democracy show their worth. Law provides us with common rules. Multilateralism enables us to turn shared problems into concerted solutions, and democracy ensures that power comes from the people and is exercised for their wellbeing. I address this assembly on behalf of Guatemala, a country that knows from its own experience the value of these tools.

Our history has taught us that democracy, peace and respect for the law are not permanent achievements. They are built collectively and each generation must preserve them. A democracy rests on free elections, legitimate institutions, the separation of powers, freedom of expression, public participation, transparency and accountability But it also requires independent and effective institutions committed to the Constitution, the law and the popular mandate. Public institutions must not serve criminal networks, private agendas, personal loyalties, or political or economic interests that are at odds with the common good. They must serve the people, the constitutional order and society's democratic interests. When an institution strays from that purpose, it does more than simply lose legitimacy.

It weakens the democracy it is meant to protect. Democracy also earns its legitimacy in everyday life When a family is protected from poverty, when a child learns in a decent school, when a woman lives free from violence, when a community is no longer isolated, and when a young person can envision a future without being forced to leave their country. That is why in Guatemala, we are restoring the state's capacity to reach those who have been excluded from opportunities for far too long. The intersectional mano a mano strategy brings together health education, housing, nutrition and community development to address poverty at the local level following crop losses caused by climate related events. More than 450,000 families have received food assistance, while small scale producers have gained access to seeds, tools, inputs and insurance mechanisms. Public education is central to this effort.

More than 1 million students have participated in initiatives to strengthen reading comprehension. We have expanded educational opportunities, promoted scholarships, strengthened instruction in national languages, and accelerated the digital transformation of the school system. In healthcare, we have expanded and refurbished facilities, strengthened regional services, and made progress in the comprehensive treatment of chronic diseases and cancer. Alongside the revival of road projects and public works in historically underserved communities, the National Digital Connectivity Plan now provides internet service to 383 public entities. We have also strengthened early warning systems for earthquakes, tsunamis, floods and volcano hazards, restoring the legitimate presence of the state also means providing security in accordance with the law, strengthening prevention, protecting communities, and pursuing criminal networks rather than only their visible manifestations. It means improving investigations, institutional coordination, and the tracing of the financial flows that sustain illicit economies.

Guatemala maintains that the charter of the United Nations and international law must remain our common point of reference. The sovereignty and territorial integrity of states must be respected. Disputes must be settled by peaceful means. Human rights must be protected. International humanitarian law must be observed in all circumstances, and international obligations must be fulfilled. The law loses its ability to protect us when we accept its selective application.

National and international institutions lose legitimacy when they depart from their mandates in response to pressure, calculations or particular interests. Their authority rests on independence impartiality, transparency and respect for the law. There can be no there cannot be one rule for the powerful and another for the weak. Nor can there be victims whose suffering outrages us and others whose suffering we choose to ignore. For countries such as Guatemala international law does not constrain our sovereignty. It is one of its principal safeguards.

Guatemala believes in the peaceful settlement of disputes. We place our trust in dialogue, negotiation and the mechanisms provided for under international law. Because even the most complex historical differences can and must be resolved by peaceful means. We are deeply concerned by the persistence of armed conflicts in different regions of the world, and their devastating consequences for civilians. In every case, our position rests on the same principles respect for the charter and international law, the protection of civilians, safe humanitarian access and dialogue and diplomacy as indispensable paths towards a just, sustainable and lasting peace. We must not grow accustomed to war.

We must not accept violence as a permanent condition of our time, or allow entire generations to grow up believing that force is the only way to resolve our differences. Guatemala stands for peace. This December, we will mark 30 years since the signing of the agreement on a firm and lasting peace, which brought an end to 36 years of internal armed conflict. After years of negotiation, we chose to replace armed violence with the pursuit of dialogue. That is why we understand the value of international support and the role of the United Nations. Our experience allows us to share one conviction.

Negotiation is not a sign of weakness. Dialogue does not mean abandoning our principles. Seeking peace must never mean accepting injustice. We have also contributed to United Nations peacekeeping operations More than 6300 Guatemalan women and men have served under the United Nations flag in peacekeeping operations in different parts of the world. A country that knows the cost of war must also take responsibility for helping others preserve peace. Mr. president, we must strengthen the timely exchange of information, operational and judicial coordination, border security with respect for human rights, the protection of ports and transit routes, financial and asset investigations, and the recovery of assets derived from illicit activities.

We must also work together on prevention. Lasting security cannot be achieved through law enforcement alone. It requires education, decent work, resilient communities, accessible institutions and opportunities for young people. It requires us to reduce the social, territorial and economic spaces that criminal structures exploit to recruit, exert control and supplant the state. Our regional cooperation must be grounded in trust, shared responsibility and respect for sovereignty. It must not serve private agendas or become an instrument of interests alien to our peoples.

Climate change, pandemics, transnational organised crime, food insecurity, human mobility and technological transformation all demand cooperation. Guatemala, a country particularly vulnerable to the effects of climate change, knows that adaptation, risk management and the protection of rural livelihoods require national efforts, but also financing and cooperation commensurate with the needs capable of building capacity and delivering results. Defending multilateralism does not mean defending the status quo. The United Nations must become more effective, representative, transparent and responsive to people. It must make better use of its resources, reduce duplication and respond more swiftly without weakening the purposes for which it was created. Efficiency must strengthen, not erode, its three pillars peace and security, sustainable development and human rights.

Effectiveness cannot be measured solely in administrative terms, but rather by the ability to prevent a war, protect a population under threat, combat hunger, confront transnational criminal networks, or support a state in strengthening its institutions. We do not need a United Nations that is smaller in purpose. We need a United Nations that is stronger in results and firmer in defending democratic principles. That transformation must also reach the Security Council. Its composition must better reflect the realities of the 21st century and remedy the long standing underrepresentation of entire regions. When the veto causes paralysis in the face of serious threats to international peace and security, confidence in the entire system suffers.

We also face an important decision for the future of the organisation the selection of the next secretary general. Guatemala hopes that the process will be transparent and inclusive, and will identify an independent leader able to build bridges, defend the principles of the charter and lead the reform our organisation needs. The Latin American and Caribbean region stands ready and prepared to shoulder its responsibility to the international community. The time has come for a Latin American woman to serve as secretary general of the United Nations. Excellencies. Distinguished delegates.

The Republic of Guatemala reaffirms its commitment to the peaceful settlement of disputes and the observance of international law We welcome the fact that the International Court of Justice has set the date for the oral hearings concerning the territorial, insular and maritime dispute with Belize. For my country, this is more than a procedural milestone. With the notification of the hearings, the final procedural stage before the court delivers its judgment has begun. It marks the culmination of a legal dispute that has accompanied the people of Guatemala and successive governments since independence, and whose conclusion we eagerly await. We recognize that the court's judgment, once delivered, will bring the dispute to an end, and we trust that it will provide legal certainty to both parties and lay the foundations for a new chapter in relations between Guatemala and Belize. In closing, I wish to say that Guatemala will continue to do its part strengthening democratic institutions capable of meeting the needs of our people, resolutely confronting transnational organised crime, and those who seek to capture institutions defending international law, consistently promoting regional responses based on shared responsibility, and working for a United Nations capable of transforming itself to fulfil the promise contained in the opening words of our charter, we the Peoples.

Restoring trust will depend on our ability to show that even in times of uncertainty and division, we remain capable of building together solutions that none of us could achieve alone. Thank you very much.

Secretary-General,  His  Excellency  António  Guterres,  for  his

distinguished service to the United Nations and to the cause of

humanity. His place in the history of this institution is assured,

not merely by the office he has occupied, but by the principles he

has steadfastly upheld, the courage  and profundity with which

he has spoken when silence would have been easier, and his rare

ability to hold before the world a clear mirror of the perils that

confront  our  age  and  the  possibilities  that  still  beckon  beyond

them.

The challenges of our time

One  year  ago,  I  stood  at  this  very  podium  and  reminded  this

Assembly  that  if  the  United  Nations  is  to  remain  humanity’s

surest  hope  for  a  just  and  peaceful  world,  it  must  have  the

courage to confront aggression and the will to engage fully with

the defining questions of our age. I also argued that we must be

bold enough to undertake the institutional reforms necessary to

strengthen the Organization, enhance its credibility and enable

it to meet the challenges of a changing world.

Indeed,  I  am  pleased  that  the  theme  of  this  year’s  assembly,

“Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations

That  Delivers  for  All”  acknowledges  the  need  for  this

organization  to  be  made  fit  for  purpose  to  respond  to  the

challenges and to seize the possibilities of our time.

Today, we confront a climate catastrophe; an energy crisis; food

insecurity;  biodiversity  loss;  armed  conflicts  and  geopolitical

tensions; the horror of genocide; a spiralling cost-of-living crisis;

a mounting debt crisis; widening inequalities within and among

nations;  and,  perhaps  most  troubling  of  all,  a  weakening  of

multilateralism itself.

Yet  if  history  has  taught  us  anything,  it  is  that  even  when  the

world seemed to stand at the precipice, humanity has never been

entirely without the means to draw it back from the brink. We

have ended wars that seemed without end. We have confronted

economic calamities that threatened the foundations of societies.

We  have  overcome  dangers  that  presented  existential  threats.

Time and again, it has been our inventiveness, our courage and,

above all, our willingness to act together that have opened a path

where none seemed to exist.

The possibilities of our age

This is why I do not  wish to  linger or lament further upon the

difficulties before us. I wish instead to turn our gaze toward the

possibilities that lie beyond them. For within every crisis lies a

summons  to  solutions,  within  every  disruption  an  opportunity

for  renewal,  and  within  every  uncertainty  the  possibility  of

shaping a better future.

The possibilities before us are immense.

We  have  the  possibility of  silencing  the  guns  through  dialogue

and  diplomacy.  The  world  does  not  need  more  sophisticated

instruments  of  destruction;  it  needs  a  more  sophisticated

capacity for peace.

In  this  regard,  I  reiterate  Guyana’s  call  for  a  just  and  lasting

solution to the crisis in the Middle East, one that brings an end

to  the  suffering  of  innocent  civilians  and  recognises  the

Palestinian people’s legitimate right to self-determination and to

a secure homeland of their own. We reiterate our support for the

two-State solution.

We call as well for an end to the Russia-Ukraine war and the war

in Sudan, and for peaceful resolution of all conflicts that continue

to  consume  lives,  uproot  families  and  extinguish  the  hopes  of

millions in other parts of our world.

We reiterate our call for a viable solution for Cuba, one that is

peaceful, people centered, development-focused and allows for

the full aspirations of the Cuban people to be realized. Guyana

reiterates  CARICOM’s  offer  to  play  a  meaningful  role  in

achieving this objective.

In  Haiti,  resolving  the  multidimensional  challenges  remains

central  to  achieving  democracy,  stability,  peace  and  prosperity

for  the  Haitian  people.

The  sustained  support  of  the

international community through the provision of key financial

and  material  resources  is  critical  to  realizing  these  objectives.

Ultimately, the future of Haiti must be Haitian-led and Haitian-

owned.

Turning to my own country - Guyana has always advanced the

peaceful settlement of the controversy in relation to our border

with Venezuela. Despite the historical truth - clearly outlined in

the Arbitral Award of 1899 that determined the full, perfect and

final settlement of our border with Venezuela, we endured long

and repeated provocations and aggression.

The matter was referred to the International Court of Justice by

the Secretary General, acting pursuant to the Geneva Agreement,

and the Court twice pronounced on its jurisdiction to hear the

matter.  Recourse  to  the  ICJ  came  after  decades  of  efforts  to

resolve  the  controversy  bilaterally,  including  through  a  mixed

commission and the Good Offices of the UN Secretary General.

In  full  respect  for  international  law,  Guyana  participated  and

encouraged  Venezuela  to  participate  in  the  proceedings  of  the

ICJ.

Now that we have both participated in the hearings which were

completed  in  May  2026,  we  urge  Venezuela  to  abide  by  the

forthcoming ruling in accordance with their obligation under the

UN Charter, as Guyana will do.

We  look  forward  to  a  new  era  of  neighbourly  relations  in  the

interest of our peoples, the development of our countries and the

stability and prosperity of our region.

In pursuit of a stronger and safer region, Guyana is honoured to

be a founding member of the Shield of the Americas, launched

by President Trump in March 2026.

Since the founding of this initiative, Guyana has worked closely

with  the  United  States  and  thirteen  other  like-minded  nations

that  believe  in  building  a  Western  Hemisphere  that  values

freedom,  peace,  economic  prosperity  and  have  a  shared

responsibility and commitment to fighting transnational crime

and criminal networks.

It is our collective responsibility to never allow our region to be

overtaken by gangs or criminal networks.

We  understand  that  it  is  only  through  partnership,  shared

intelligence,  and  cooperation  that  we  can  effectively  tackle  the

threats  they  pose  to  our  economies  and  the  livelihoods  of  our

citizens.

This  week,  I  was  pleased  to  join  members  of  the  Shield  of

Americas  in  adopting  a  Joint  Communique  which  underscores

our collective resolve to strengthen the resilience of our region in

Economic, Security and Multilateral Coordination.

We  stand  at  the  threshold  of  a  new  era  of  technological

advancement.  Artificial

intelligence,  biotechnology,  digital

communications  and  other  extraordinary  breakthroughs  offer

the  prospect  of  transforming  health,  education,  agriculture,

productivity and public services on a scale scarcely imaginable a

generation ago. But the true measure of technological progress

will not be how powerful our machines become, but how much

more  empowered  our  people  become.  Technology  must  not

become the privilege of the few; it must become the servant of all

humanity.

We  have  before  us  a  new  opportunity  for  sustainable

development.  Development  must  not  merely  make  our

economies richer; it must  make our societies better.   We must

not  allow  further  slippage  in  our  pursuit  of  the  Sustainable

Development Goals. We must renew our commitment to them —

not  as  an  inventory  of  promises,  but  as  a  covenant  with  our

peoples and a practical blueprint for ensuring that development

reaches  every  citizen,  protects  generations  yet  unborn  and

creates lasting, inclusive prosperity.

One  way  to  arrest  this  slippage  is,  as  Guyana  is  doing,  to

mainstream the Goals into our national development strategies,

public  policies  and  budgets,  so  that  they  become  embedded  in

the priorities we set and the resources we commit, rather than

remaining  aspirations.    The  SDGs  must  not  only  guide  our

ambitions;  they  must  shape  our  choices  and  our  national

priorities.

In  Guyana,  we  have  made  significant  advances  including

universal  health  care,  free  education,  modern  infrastructure,

accelerated  access  to  affordable  housing,  opportunities  for  full

employment,  acceleration  of  financing  for  small  and  medium

sized enterprises, and digitizing service delivery.

Two  years  ago,  at  this  very  podium  I  committed  Guyana  to

provide  global  leadership  on  biodiversity.  In  July  2025,  under

Guyana’s  leadership,  the  Global  Biodiversity  Alliance  was

established  as  an  inclusive  platform.  In  just  over one  year,  the

Alliance  expanded  from  17  to  138  members,  bringing  together

governments,  international  organization,  including  the  UN,

development  banks,  Indigenous  Peoples,  local  communities,

scientists, universities and the private sector.

The  second  conference  of  the  Alliance,  to  be  held  on  October

2026,  will  begin  to  mobilize  the  resources  and  partnerships  to

deliver its ambitions.

At  the  same  time,  we  continue  to  advance  our  national  Low

Carbon  Development  Strategy  focused  on  turning  forest

stewardship and climate action into a new model for sustainable

development.

As  we  commence  this  81st  Session, we  have  the  opportunity  to

build a United Nations that is truly fit for purpose.

The  crisis  confronting  multilateralism  can  become  the  catalyst

for its renewal. The United Nations must not be a monument to

the past; it must become an instrument for the future. We need

a  Security  Council  that  reflects  the  geopolitical  realities  of  the

twenty-first century, not the power structures of 1945; a Council

that embraces the emerging multipolarity of our world, including

permanent  representation  from  Africa,  and  Latin  America  and

the Caribbean.

A new multilateralism

If  the  United  Nations  is  to  remain  humanity’s  best  hope,  then

this is not the hour to retreat from multilateralism. This is the

hour to reclaim and to renew it. For it is in times such as these—

when wars rage across borders, when the shadow of existential

threats falls across the future of human civilisation, when the old

certainties  are  dissolving  before  our  eyes—that  multilateralism

must rise.

Multilateralism rests upon the proposition that our destinies are

bound  together,  that  the  security  of  one  cannot  be  at  the

insecurity  of  another,  and  that  in  an  interdependent  world,

cooperation is a necessity; and where there can be no enduring

prosperity  where  inequality  deepens,  and  no  just  international

order where rules are applied selectively.

It  is  to  that  truth  that  this  eighty-first  session  of  the  General

Assembly must recommit itself. But recommitment cannot mean

merely  repeating  the  language  of  yesterday.  The  world  has

changed, and multilateralism must change with it.

We  need  a  new  and  invigorated  multilateralism—one  equal  to

the turbulence of our age, sufficiently courageous to confront its

trials,  sufficiently  imaginative  to  navigate  its  transformations,

and  sufficiently  principled  to  defend  the  rule  of  international

law.

To  make  the  United  Nations  fit  for  purpose  we  must  make  it

more  transparent,  accountable  and  responsive.  We  must

strengthen the General Assembly and give greater weight to its

deliberative and representative authority. We must bring greater

coherence to a system too often divided by institutional rivalries,

bureaucratic  silos  and  competing  mandates.  We  must  ensure

that the resources of the UN match the responsibilities we have

entrusted to it.

Leadership

But  institutions  do  not  reform  themselves.  They  require

leadership capable of seeing beyond the present and imagining

the institution the future demands.

The United Nations needs leadership that can bring its different

organs,  agencies  and  programmes  into  a  greater  unity  of

purpose.  Leadership  that  can  build  bridges  where  division  has

become habitual; leadership that can defend the principles of the

Charter without fear or favour.

The  United  Nations  needs  its  next  Secretary-General  to  work

with all member States to restore confidence in the Organization,

mobilise  its  energies,  and  turn  the  language  of  multilateralism

from aspiration into action. The reform of the United Nations,

the restoration of trust and the need to manage transformation

is,  therefore,  inseparable  from  the  question  of  leadership.  And

the  choice  of  its  next  Secretary-General  will  be,  in  no  small

measure, a choice about the kind of United Nations we wish to

leave to the generations that follow.

Guyana’s nominee for UN Secretary General

It is in this spirit that Guyana has put forward the candidature of

Her  Excellency  Carolyn  Rodrigues  Birkett  for  the  office  of

Secretary-General  of  the  United  Nations.  She  has  served  her

country,  represented  the  developing  world,  and  worked  within

the  multilateral  system  with  a  deep  understanding  of  both  its

promise and its imperfections.

We believe that her experience, her convictions and her record

of service speak directly to the kind of leadership this moment

demands.

Her  candidature,  therefore,  acquires  special  significance  amid

the profound challenges confronting the United Nations and the

international  order.  We  need  leadership  capable  of  restoring

trust  without  compromising  principle;  of  listening  without

surrendering conviction; of building bridges across the widening

chasms  between  North  and  South,  between  large  states  and

small, between the developed and developing worlds.

We  need  a  Secretary-General  who  will  defend  the  Charter  not

only  when  it  is  politically  convenient,  but  precisely  when  its

principles are under pressure.

The responsibility for recommending the next Secretary-General

rests,  in  the  first  instance,  with  the  Security  Council,  and  we

therefore respectfully place before its members the candidature

of  Carolyn  Rodrigues  Birkett.  Endorsed  by  the  Caribbean

Community (CARICOM), we invite all to consider her candidacy

on  its  merits  and  to  judge  whether  her  vision,    experience,

expertise and record can help restore confidence in the United

Nations at this critical moment.

Conclusion

The  United  Nations  was  conceived  in  hope—and  that  hope

remains  alive  in  the  pursuit  of  peace,  security  and  human

progress over the perpetuation of division and war. This is why

we must not abandon multilateralism because it is imperfect; we

must renew it because humanity still needs it.

Let  us  therefore  build  a  United  Nations  that  does  not  merely

reflect the world as it is, but helps create the world as it ought to

be—a world where law restrains power, cooperation overcomes

division,  and  every  human  being  can  look  to  the  future  with

hope.

Guyana believes that the choice remains ours as to whether the

divisions of our age will define the future, or whether nations can

summon the will to build a more peaceful, secure and prosperous

international order. The United Nations must be at the heart of

that endeavour—not as an institution looking back at the world

it was created to serve, but as one helping humanity shape the

world that is yet to come.

I thank you

President of the General Assembly, Secretary-General, Your Excellencies, Heads of State and Government, distinguished delegates. Honduras is coming to this Assembly today with the title of a founding nation, one of the 50 countries who, 81 years ago, signed the agreement in San Francisco, California, that was the United Nations Charter, the charter that today governs our work. Nine months ago the country went to the polls: our democracy and freedom were in peril. They were saved by the institutions that resisted, and the Honduran people that decided, at the polls, with their vote, decided to change the course of the country. And we—it's not just us saying that— international observers bore witness to elections that were flawless in terms of their conduct, flawless despite the challenging context. This was an effort waged by brave men and women, and we also enjoyed the support of international democracies who accompanied us in our attempts to rescue and restore our country's greatness.

As we began our work, we found ourselves faced with a people who never lost their dignity, neither did they lose hope. Today we are strengthening our institutions and our multi-party democracy. Mr. President, since the very first day in office, we decided to govern differently, with deeds. We are reducing expenditure so that we can invest in health care, education, infrastructure, and security. We're doing all of that whilst guaranteeing macroeconomic stability and with— and guaranteeing a great deal of fiscal responsibility. No national effort alone can suffice, in view of the global conditions that today determine the development of our nations.

Today the global economy is facing an energy crisis resulting from the high prices of oil. That crisis is having a direct impact on our people. This is the only forum in which the voice of a country of 11 million inhabitants is heard. Honduras exercises sovereignty over the full extent of its national territory. Moreover, it administers its natural resources in accordance with its constitution. The law applies to each and every individual, in all four corners of the country, because without legal security and certainty, and without respect for private property, there can be no peace, development, employment, or investment.

The right to development is something that it is the duty of the country's government to ensure for the millions of Honduran people. Honduras makes good on its promises. It honors its agreements and its treaties. These principles are neither selective nor biased. I visited Ukraine three months ago. There I saw a people defending its freedom and fighting for it, in full respect of its territorial integrity and its political independence.

I saw a country protecting civilians and working to achieve a lasting peace. Security cannot be imposed by decree. It is something that is built with resources, with training, and with political resolve. Today that is exactly what we're doing. We are equipping and strengthening our national police force and our armed forces. We're doing this because transnational organized crime does not respect borders.

Drug trafficking networks and gangs operate in several countries at the same time, and no country can vanquish them alone. It is a matter of shared responsibility. Every nation must do its part. Democracies whose interests are aligned must unite and act together, quickly and with resolve. It is only in so doing that we will enjoy security and prosperity in our hemisphere. Mr. President, there is another challenge that no country can face alone: natural phenomena.

Today we are weathering a severe drought, and we are taking tangible decisions to support our most vulnerable citizens. The hurricanes that have beset us in the past, and today's drought, have the same root cause: that is a climate which is operating at increasing extremes, and that will affect the entire world for decades. Our response is not simply to react to these disasters. Rather, we are taking action by preparing as best we can to mitigate the effects of climate change. We are investing our own resources in protecting lives, harvests, and access to drinking water. However, we want to go further.

Honduras is opening its doors to anyone developing new solutions for water, agriculture, early warning, and the infrastructure that our country requires. Addressing these challenges is allowing us to focus on the future. Honduras is a conscientious country, a country of law, a country in which we invite you to invest. Anyone who invests in Honduras will be offered opportunities, order, transparency, and clear rules. We are adhering to the International Monetary Fund guidelines. In the seven months that my country has been in office, we have increased our international reserves to the tune of $1.3 billion, and that is an increase of 13%.

We returned to the International Center of Arbitration, CIARI, on the 6th of March 2026. We'd been members of that center since 1989, and we returned to resolve our problems with a sense of solemn responsibility. With these steps, we sought to reiterate that in Honduras, rules apply to everyone, and rules are followed. On that basis, Honduras can offer concrete investment opportunities in logistics, industry, energy, infrastructure, agroindustry, mining, tourism, to name just a few sectors. We are the center of America. We stand between two oceans.

We are optimizing Puerto Cortés— that is a port in our Caribbean-Atlantic area— and it is the port with greatest potential for growth in the country, and one of the largest, most important ports in Central America. We are investing to strengthen our road infrastructure so that we can create a logistics corridor to join the Atlantic with the Pacific. This project and its location means that we can offer to the world safe, reliable, and efficient supply chains. Honduras is one of the world's key textile exporters. We manufacture the clothes of well-known brands. We also manufacture cable harnesses and automobile parts that are sold around the world.

They've come from Honduran factories. Around 200,000 Honduran people work in those industries. These factories, maquilas, and other forms of industry require stable energy at competitive prices. It is for that reason that the National Congress recently adopted a reform to our electrical energy law. That reform had been championed by the Presidency. In light of the above, we invite both national and foreign investment: investment in the development of Honduras's energy sector, investment in the generation, transmission, and distribution of energy.

Our land is fertile land. We are the largest coffee exporter in Central America and the fifth largest globally. Fifty percent—57%— of the coffee which Honduras exports is coffee recognized to be of extremely high quality, as well as accredited and specialized coffee. That is a reflection of the quality of our production and its standard of excellence. Honduras sees its agriculture, fisheries, and poultry industries as fundamental pillars for economic development, as well as for food security and job creation. Our commitment is to breathe momentum into these sectors sustainably.

We want to empower our producers and bring high-quality Honduran products to international markets. Our land harbors mineral wealth with vast potential that has yet to be harnessed. We have the opportunity to develop a modern, responsible, and sustainable mining industry so that we can create employment and transform these resources into development and prosperity for our people. We want to develop these resources with clear rules, in full respect of the environment and for the benefit of our communities. Our extraordinary biodiversity, natural riches, and cultural heritage make us a country with a vast wealth of potential for tourism. We have crystal-clear waters and reefs in the Bay Islands.

We have the Great Copan Ruins and the legacy of the Mayan civilization. And all of these things mean that we offer the world a unique combination of nature, history, and culture. And above all, we have the most valuable asset that any nation can hold: a young, hardworking, and capable population. A population who demands, and quite rightly so, the opportunity to use their talent on their own in their own country. We want to see investment. We want investment to arrive in the country and to stay.

We want investment that creates jobs and which brings knowledge to the table to train our young people. My commitment is to facilitate investment in Honduras. Honduras is in a period of renewal. It has once again begun to believe in its institutions. It is looking its allies straight in the face with pride and is working to build its future with a hardworking spirit. And it wants to see a future of order and hope.

Honduras reaffirms its commitment to peace, international law, sovereignty, and cooperation between states. Our country has understood that sovereignty does not mean isolation. Rather, it means the ability to establish bonds with the rest of the world on the basis of equality and respect. May God bless you. May God bless your nations. And may God bless Honduras.

Many thanks to you all.

Mr President, Mr Secretary-General, Excellencies,

It is a special honour to address this Assembly on behalf of Hungary. I speak here to the nations of the world, but also to my fellow citizens watching at home.

For much of my life, I served as a judge, in Hungary and at the European Court of Human Rights. That work taught me a simple lesson: The law must apply even to those in power.

Law does not weaken a state by placing limits on power. It gives citizens a reason to trust the state.

This belief will guide me as President. I will protect the Constitution, the freedom of our institutions and the dignity of every Hungarian citizen.

The state belongs to those who support the government, to those who oppose it and to those who have lost trust in politics altogether. A new political majority must not become the new owner of the state.

This April, the people of Hungary voted for democratic renewal. They expected more than a change of government. They expect public life to change: a state that serves rather than controls, courts that decide without pressure, a press that challenges power and public money that is used for the public good.

There must be accountability for corruption and abuse of power. But there must be no revenge. Justice cannot become a political weapon. A democratic state cannot repair past wrongs by repeating them with new people in charge. The same law must apply to those who

governed yesterday, those who govern today and those who may govern tomorrow.

A republic begins where power accepts its limits. That is the republic Hungary must now rebuild.

Trust from our partners will not return because of one election or one speech. Hungary asks to be judged by what we do.

We will be a reliable member of the European Union, a committed NATO ally and an active member of the United Nations. These partnerships do not take away our freedom. They protect it.

Hungary will defend its national interests, but it will do so as a partner. We believe that national interest and international cooperation do not have to stand against each other.

For Hungarians, the reasons are part of our own history.

Seventy years ago, the revolution of 1956 expressed our people's determination to govern themselves. Soviet tanks crushed that hope. Our appeals reached the United Nations, but the international community could not prevent our defeat.

Many countries represented here opened their doors to Hungarians who fled their country after the revolution. We remember both the cost of losing our independence and the help that allowed our people to start again.

Today, Ukraine is fighting to preserve its independence. Hungary condemns Russia's full-scale war of aggression as a violation of the United Nations Charter and international law.

We affirm Ukraine's right to self-defence, its sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders, and the right of its people to decide their own future.

The freedom Hungarians demanded for themselves in 1956 is a freedom we must uphold for Ukrainians today.

We remember those who have lost their lives in this war, and we want diplomacy to bring the killing to an end. But a lasting peace must respect Ukraine's sovereignty.

If taking territory by force becomes an accepted way of settling disputes, every smaller country will have reason to worry about its own future.

The principles of the Charter therefore matter to all of us.

Human suffering cannot wait for diplomacy to succeed. People in conflict need food, medicine and protection now. Hungary will continue to provide humanitarian aid to people in danger, especially the most vulnerable.

In the Middle East, we call for full respect for international humanitarian law and for aid to reach those who need it safely and without interruption.

Israelis and Palestinians must be able to live in security and dignity. A lasting peace must give their families reason to believe that their children can grow up without the fear that has marked so many lives.

For people forced from their homes by war or persecution, protection may first mean finding safety in another country. Hungary's own history gives us reason to understand that need.

At the same time, every state has the right to protect its borders. Hungary will do so in accordance with international law. We will fight illegal migration and the criminal networks that profit from it, while respecting human dignity and the protection given to refugees.

But security is not only about borders and wars.

People also need the chance to build a future where they live. They need homes, schools, health care and ways to earn a living. Poverty

and the lack of opportunity can drive people from their countries just as conflict can.

Hungary will continue to support development that helps communities build that future, based on their own needs and priorities.

We are ready to share our experience in education, health and digital development.

Water is another area where our interests meet. Drought can destroy crops, threaten food and energy supplies and take away people's income. Climate change is making these pressures greater.

Rivers also cross borders. What one country does can affect the water available to another. This makes cooperation essential.

Hungary has experience in water management, sustainable agriculture and climate adaptation, and we are ready to share it.

For many countries represented in this hall, food, energy, education, health and jobs are immediate concerns. We must give these issues the same serious attention that we ask others to give European security.

International cooperation works best when it responds to people's real needs and when every country has a voice.

Excellencies,

The United Nations faces a crisis of trust.

Too often, it fails to act when powerful states or their friends break the rules. No country should be above the law. We cannot have one rule for our friends and another for others.

But the answer is not to turn away from the United Nations.

We need it, and we need it to work.

It must be able to act, treat all its members fairly and apply the same principles to everyone.

Hungary is ready to do its part. We will stand for human rights, support peacekeeping and work with countries across the world to protect people and help diplomacy succeed.

We must also look beyond the problems of today.

Many of the decisions we make now will shape the lives of people who are not yet born. A school, a strong institution or a safe water system can benefit people for many years.

Future generations must therefore have a place in the decisions we make today.

Hungary supports stronger international action to protect their interests, including the appointment of a United Nations Special Envoy for Future Generations.

The United Nations cannot demand trust. It must earn it.

The same is true of every state and every public institution.

The Hungarian people have asked us to restore their confidence in the future. We will honour that choice by rebuilding trust at home and by becoming a country others can trust when their own future is at stake.

For Hungary, this is a new beginning. But the principle behind it is not new:

Power earns trust only when it accepts the law.

That is the responsibility Hungary accepts, and the work we are ready to undertake with you.

Thank you
