May peace be upon all of us.

Eighty-one years ago, from the ashes of the Second World War, Indonesia and the United Nations were born.

We emerged from a world devastated by war, with a shared conviction that never again should humanity leave its future to war and division, and we shared a founding promise: to build a future of peace.

For  eight  decades,  we  have  worked  to  turn  that  promise  into  progress:  nations  freed themselves from colonialism, globalization connected our economy, technology transformed our societies, and development improves the lives of billions.

But  progress  has  never  been  linear.  We  have  lived  through  financial  crises,  a  global pandemic, climate disasters, geopolitical rivalries, and conflicts around the world.

With every transformation and every crisis, one lesson remains clear: for peace and prosperity to endure, multilateralism must be resilient. It must be able to adapt, to respond, and most importantly to deliver.

Because  multilateralism  that  cannot  deliver  will  lose  people’s  trust.  And  without  trust, multilateralism will never endure.

Building  a  resilient  multilateralism  begins  with  resilient  nations.  It  starts  at  home.  And Indonesia has long understood this for decades.

In the 1960s, Indonesia developed the concept of national resilience: to safeguard our identity, to protect our sovereignty and unity, and to sustain our development in the face of challenges and obstacles.

At the heart of our resilience are our people. A nation is resilient when families can provide for  their  households,  when  farmers  can  produce,  when  workers  can  find  decent  jobs,  and when children can learn, grow, and dream about their future.

For  Indonesia,  this  means  building  greater  self-sufficiency  in  food  and  strengthening  our energy security.

Most importantly, this also means investing in the future of our people: ensuring our children receive quality education, and ensuring our people have access to essential healthcare.

At  the  same  time,  we  are  building  an  economy  that  can  withstand  shocks  and  create opportunities: more jobs, stronger industries, and greater productive capacity.

Central to our resilience is our ability to manage differences and preserve our unity.

As  a  nation  of  more  than  280  million  people,  Indonesia  has  learned  that  diversity  is  not something to overcome. It is something to manage, respect, and turn into strength, through democratic participation, dialogue and respect for differences, we preserve our unity.

From Aceh  to  Papua,  from  Mianggas  to  Rote,  Indonesia  is  one  people.  Indonesia  is  one nation.

We also continue to strengthen the promotion and protection of human rights, through our national mechanisms and our commitment to international human rights obligations.

This goes hand in hand with building our national resilience. Because human rights are not only the absence of violence. They are also about ensuring that people have food, education and healthcare.

To our neighbours, friends, and partners, let there be no doubt: Indonesia stands strong today, grounded  firmly  in  democracy,  human  rights,  and  the  rule  of  law. And  when  nations  are resilient at home, they have greater capacity to contribute beyond their borders.

A  food-secure  Indonesia  can  contribute  more  to  regional  and  global  food  security. A  more energy-resilient  Indonesia  can  contribute  more  to  the  global  energy  transition. A  stronger economy opens greater opportunities for cooperation and shared prosperity.

This is how national resilience becomes collective resilience. And this is how resilience helps us advance the SDGs.

A  resilient  nation  contributes  to  a  resilient  region.  Our  national  resilience  will  support  and complement a region that is stable, peaceful and predictable.

Southeast Asia is home to one of the world’s largest productive-age populations. It is now the world’s fifth largest economy, supported by a large and fast-growing digital economy.

At the center of this dynamic region is ASEAN. ASEAN brings together nations with different histories, political systems, levels of development, and national interests.

We do not always agree, but we have made a conscious choice: to stay together. And we choose to keep talking, even when agreement is difficult.

For almost six decades, ASEAN has managed differences, maintained communication, and continued seeking common ground.

This is the strength that comes from ASEAN unity and centrality. It enables us to engage all partners,  and  preserve  space  for  dialogue  and  cooperation,  even  as  strategic  competition intensifies around us.

At the same time, building a resilient region requires the ability to adapt. This is why ASEAN must continue to evolve, so that it remains fit for purpose and beneficial for its people and the wider region.

Excellencies,

Resilience  at  home  and  at  the  regional  level  must  be  matched,  by  a  multilateral  system capable of supporting and sustaining it.

This is where the United Nations remains indispensable. The United Nations gives nations the space to resolve differences without resorting to conflict.  It provides common rules, when interests  compete. And  it  allows  us  to  combine  our  capacities,  when  no  country  can  act effectively alone.

This is why Indonesia continues to believe in the United Nations. But believing in the United Nations also means believing that it must evolve with the world it serves.

Let  us  be  clear:  the  answer  to  imperfect  multilateralism  is  not  less  multilateralism.  It  is  a stronger and better multilateralism.

A multilateral system fit for the twenty-first century must be more representative, more agile, and better able to deliver.

Institutional transformation will not happen overnight. But the urgency of today’s challenges requires us to act now.

We  must  start  by  strengthening  our  collective  capacity  to  withstand  crises,  responding effectively to global crises and humanitarian situations, and sustaining peace, development, and cooperation.

At the same time, international financial architecture must also evolve: to respond better to the  needs  of  developing  countries,  and  to  give  them  greater  space  to  pursue  their  own development priorities and build their resilience.

But stronger institutions alone will not save multilateralism. Institutions are only as strong as the principles we are willing to uphold.

International law must be upheld consistently, sovereignty must be respected, and colonialism must be brought to an end.

This is where Palestine remains one of the clearest tests of these principles, and the test of our  conscience.  The  clear  violations  of  international  law  in  Gaza  and  the  West  Bank  are reminiscent of our world pre-1945. A world pre-the UN Charter, pre-the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and pre-the four 1949 Geneva Conventions.

A  world  where  a  certain  race  was  almost  annihilated.  Indonesia  knows  what  it  means  to struggle  against  colonialism,  to  struggle  in  a  world  where  international  law  was  weak  and might was right.

Our nation’s journey to independence has shaped our consistent support for the Palestinian people and their right to determine their own future.

Indonesia  will  continue  to  stand  with  the  Palestinian  people  until  their  right  to  self-determination is fulfilled and until an independent and sovereign State of Palestine is realized, based  on  the  Two-State  Solution,  in  accordance  with  international  law  and  internationally agreed parameters.

Palestine is not only a question for one region. It is a test of whether the multilateral system can uphold the very principles it was created to defend, and whether it can deliver when it matters most.

An  effective  multilateral  system  also  requires  effective  leadership.  Indonesia’s  leadership philosophy,  passed  down  through  generations,  teaches  us  that  leaders  must  possess  the capability  to  lead  by  example  from  the  front,  build  confidence  while  standing  among  the people, and empower from behind.

Leadership is not simply about commanding. It is about exercising wisdom and giving others the strength to move forward.

Secretary-General  António  Guterres  has  led  this  Organization  through  an  exceptionally challenging  period:  wars  and  geopolitical  tensions,  a  global  pandemic,  humanitarian emergencies, and rapid technological transformation.

Indonesia  expresses  its  appreciation  for  his  leadership  and  service  over  the  past  decade. Throughout these challenges, the UN continues to provide an important platform for dialogue and collective problem-solving.

The  next  Secretary-General  will  carry  an  equally  important  responsibility:  to  uphold  the Charter, strengthen the Organization, and to translate multilateralism into concrete results for people.

Effective leadership must also be accompanied with the full commitment of Member States to  make  multilateralism  work.  Indonesia  is  prepared  to  carry  its  share,  as  our  Constitution mandates us to contribute to a world based on freedom, lasting peace, and social  justice. Through  diplomacy  and  mediation,  Indonesia  has  contributed  to  resolving  conflicts  in  the region and beyond.

We  have  been  among  the  top  tier  contributors  to  UN  Peacekeeping  Missions,  deploying personnel  to  missions  around  the  world  since  1957.  For  nearly  two  decades,  Indonesian peacekeepers have served under the UN flag in Lebanon.

UNIFIL may be entering its final chapter, but Indonesia’s commitment does not end with the Mission. The experience, sacrifice, and dedication of our peacekeepers will continue to shape Indonesia’s contribution to international peace and security.

We will carry our diplomacy forward through humanitarian assistance, through peacebuilding, and through engagement across regions and institutions.

It is in this spirit that Indonesia present its candidature for a non-permanent seat on the UN Security Council for the 2029-2030 term. Our commitment is clear: Fostering Unity, Advancing Peace.

Fostering  unity  means  rebuilding  trust  in  the  multilateral  system  and  keeping  channels  of dialogue open. Advancing peace requires us to uphold international law and make effective use of the tools available to us.

Indonesia  will  work  to  keep  dialogue  open,  build  common  ground,  and  turn  shared responsibility  into  practical  cooperation.  We  will  uphold  the  UN  Charter  consistently  to maintain international peace and security.

We will bring the same principle that guides our foreign policy: to engage with all and to keep the space for cooperation open.

As  President  Prabowo  Subianto  mentioned  on  this  very  lectern  last  year:  one  thousand friends are too few and an enemy is too many.

The same approach guides Indonesia’s engagement with all partners. Through ASEAN, G20, D8,  BRICS,  MIKTA,  and  the  UN,  Indonesia  will  extend  the  friendship  to  deliver  practical cooperation.

Eighty-one years ago, Indonesia fought against colonialism so we could chart our own future. Today, we reaffirm our promise for a future of peace we all share.

One year ago, President Prabowo Subianto called upon us to draw closer, not drift apart.

Today, I carry that call forward.  And as we draw closer, let us also make each other stronger.

Strong enough for our nations to withstand crises. Strong enough for our regions to preserve cooperation. Strong enough for our institutions to deliver for people.

Because resilience is not simply about surviving the storms. It is about having the strength to keep moving forward together.

And only through our collective resilience, can the United Nations be strong enough to fulfil the promise we made 81 years ago, a future of peace, for generations to come.

I thank you.

Mr. President, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen,

Namaskar from 1.4 billion people of Bharat.

1. We are gathered at this General Assembly, when the United Nations enters its ninth decade. It was founded to maintain international peace and security, and take effective collective actions to that end. Members committed to develop friendly relations, and to strengthen universal peace.

2. Yet, even as we meet, conﬂicts and confrontations remain our primary preoccupation. The inability to maintain peace, is not just undermining security, but threatening progress, and retarding development. In a globalized world, the effects of war are felt worldwide. Countries far from conﬂicts, are being penalized for no fault of theirs. Those most impacted, often have the least say. This Assembly must face up to the true state of affairs.

3. This year, we are witnessing a conﬂict in the Gulf, one that is exacerbating an already difficult situation. We remain deeply concerned over continuing hostilities. The targeting of commercial shipping and seafarers, transiting international waterways, is simply unacceptable. India calls upon all parties to exercise restraint, de-escalate tensions, ensure protection of civilians, and uninterrupted ﬂow of energy and commerce.

4. The conﬂict in Ukraine, now in its ﬁfth year, is equally concerning. As Prime Minister Narendra Modi stated, endless war must give way now, to an end to war. India supports ongoing initiatives to bring peace. Even as this is underway, there is an urgent need to address the security of seafarers, and supply of food grains and energy. India is prepared to do everything possible, to ameliorate this situation, especially with regard to food and energy security.

5. Tensions and violence also regrettably continue in West Asia or the Middle East. We strongly believe, that a durable and lasting peace, requires a Two State solution. In the meanwhile, India is contributing to humanitarian assistance, and relief efforts for the Palestinian people.

6. Let us recognize that peace, is not just the absence of war. If the world is subjected to continuous threats and pressures, then we are really living on the edge of an abyss. All it takes is one more step to push us over. Therefore, it is imperative to strengthen stability, security and predictability. These are crucial elements, of the enabling environment for peace. If any of them are undermined, peace will inevitably be weakened. After eight decades of the UN, this should have become our second nature.

7. Instead, what we are actually seeing, is a weaponization of everything. A mindset of extreme competition has set in, undermining institutions, and establishing chokepoints. It extends from the world of ﬁnance, to constricting market access, disrupting supply chains and withholding technology. Resources and connectivity have become particularly subject to leveraging. As a result, nations are now more focused on de-risking and diversifying. While this may secure their interests to varying degrees, the overall atmosphere is no longer that of trust or goodwill.

8. The predicament of the Global South, is particularly acute. It faces a 4F crisis – of the security of food, fuel, fertilizer and ﬁnance. The combined impact of a Super El Nino, compounding fertilizer shortages and now impediments to grain movements, all these are cause for alarm. Moreover, SDG progress is under increasing pressure. The Global South’s right to industrialize, is also undermined by non-market practices and market denial. The march of technology, that was meant to instill hope, has now become a source of anxiety. Misuse of AI is sharpening bias, and diluting mutual respect. These directions bode ill for the aims and objectives of the United Nations.

9. A persistent threat to peace, has been the scourge of terrorism. That this could be state-sponsored, with cross-border purpose, makes it a direct affront to the global order. Governments indulging in such practices must be held accountable. There must be no dilution in our zero-tolerance approach towards terrorism. Its ﬁnancial aspects, in particular, should be exposed and should be countered.

10. Yesterday, a serial practitioner of terrorism, misrepresented facts before this Assembly. Arguments were invoked to normalize terrorism, and claim immunity from its consequences. That will not stand. Our right to defend ourselves against terrorism, will be exercised. Mr. President, friendship and goodwill cannot co-exist with terrorism. And understandings premised on that, will naturally be called into question. It is for the perpetrator of terrorism to mend its ways.

11. Given the state of the world, each member of the UN must ask themselves what they can do. Insofar as India is concerned, its inclusive growth and all-round progress, has advanced the prospects of one-sixth of humanity. When health, nutrition and education are effectively delivered, when drinking water, electricity, roads and housing are ensured, this veritably lifts the global SDG outcomes. But today, India has much more than that to offer. Our digital public infrastructure, is not only ensuring better governance, but is the backbone of delivering socio-economic beneﬁts. Rapid growth of infrastructure, is visible across all its dimensions. A continuously improving ease of doing business, ease of living, startup and innovation culture, and focused sectoral missions have all contributed to our economic story.

12. Even as India progresses, we are conscious of our global responsibilities. We know that many of our experiences and achievements, are replicable elsewhere. The deep solidarity of the Global South, has always encouraged us to share what we have. Therefore, we respond more actively, to the requirements of our partners. 600 major Indian development projects in 78 nations, testify to our commitment, a commitment that ranges from infrastructure, manufacturing and agriculture, to IT and to capacity building.

13. Climate action projects and initiatives, have been an important part of these endeavors. Whether it is clean energy and clean water projects, sustainable agriculture, or the dissemination of best practices and technology, our capabilities and experiences, have been reﬂected abroad. African nations and Small Island Developing States, have been our preferred partners in this journey. Initiatives like the International Solar Alliance, the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure, or the Global Biofuels Alliance are all making steady progress.

14. The turbulence of our times, also demands more from each of us. India has sent medical shipments to conﬂict zones, epidemic locations, and after natural disasters. As a ﬁrst responder, we were there early, be it the Nepal ﬂash ﬂoods or the Venezuela earthquake. Our limb ﬁtment camps, have given a new hope to many across the world. Whether to meet food and medicine shortages, energy and fertilizer needs, or creating livelihoods, India has contributed continuously and will do so. Our capacity-building and experience-sharing programs, have made a real difference across the Global South, especially in Africa.

15. The same international spirit, also inspires our contributions to safeguarding peace. India has always been at the forefront, of UN peacekeeping operations. Right now, our contingents are present in 9 out of 11 mandates. Our troops have stood their ground ﬁrmly, and professionally, even under pressure. We take pride, that an Indian woman combat helicopter pilot, was awarded the UN 2025 Military Gender Advocate of the year.

16. New challenges in the maritime domain, have added to longstanding ones on land. There have been attacks on commercial shipping, and seafarers in the Gulf, and from the Red Sea to the Black Sea. Indian seafarers have lost their lives, as indeed have others , from other nations. This is completely unacceptable. India has joined Liberia, and 23 other partners, in an initiative to rally global public opinion, against such unwarranted targeting. We must ensure, that the safety and security of shipping and seafarers, is never compromised. Scrupulously observing international law, is an integral element of that endeavour.

17. An issue central to current global conversations, is that of AI. India hosted the AI Impact Summit this February, gathering together the best minds on that subject. We view AI as a transformational driver, for human empowerment, economic prosperity and population-scale problem solving. We believe in the right of each nation, to shape its eco-system, with the development of its own models, and deployment strategies, consistent with its national goals and priorities. AI will be very much part of our partnership agenda, with the Global South.

18. As technology is democratized, this process is greatly facilitated, Mr. President, by an ethos of mutual respect. Indeed, care and consideration for the interests, and viewpoints

of others, reinforces even the prospects of peace. And that attitude is best fostered, by an appreciation of each other’s culture, heritage and traditions. In a globalized world, we must continuously and vigorously, promote international understanding. Economic rebalancing is well underway; the political one is also visible, and the third facet – cultural rebalancing – must now be taken forward.

19. We are now well on our way, towards a multi-polar world. The post-1945 order is giving way to new realities. This process of adjustment, accommodation and acceptance will not be easy. Much of the turbulence that we witness today, emanates from those very difficulties. Yet, the march of an intrinsically diverse world, towards a more democratic future, cannot be halted. Peace in a pluralistic order, requires civil conversations, it requires broad-based consultations, it requires transparent decision-making. Large sections of humanity, cannot be excluded from that process. The case for reformed multilateralism only gets stronger day after day.

20. After a decade of service and dedication, to the cause of multilateralism, we will soon bid farewell to Secretary General Antonio Guterres. India deeply values his many contributions, in particular, his personal support for Mission LiFE.

21. At the conclusion of this General Debate, we hope that all participating delegations, leave with a greater commitment to peace, to development and to prosperity. This cannot be an imposition, or even a negotiation; it must be a mindset, it must be an outlook, it must be a belief. In the lawns outside this building, are recorded the powerful words of Mahatma Gandhi, and that should serve as an inspiration for these times, and those words are that there is no way to peace; peace is the way.

I thank you.

President of the General Assembly, Distinguished Heads of State and Government, Secretary-General, Excellencies, A chairde, friends,

The United Nations is entering its ninth decade at a moment of great uncertainty and challenge for the global community.

Conflicts are having devastating effects on the most vulnerable.

The impacts of the climate crisis are felt in every corner of our world.

Hard won rights are being rolled back.

Narrow self-interest is breaking the bonds of solidarity which have so often lifted us to meaningful progress.

The international legal order is under tremendous strain.

New and emerging technologies that offer unlimited potential could also, without human intervention, create unprecedented dangers.

In such moments of uncertainty, it can be easy to question our foundations.

To retreat.

To turn inward.

To say that international cooperation is too difficult, that multilateralism does not work, that the problems of others are not our problems.

But that would be the wrong conclusion.

Because the answer to a world under strain is not less international cooperation. It is more.

The answer to the weakening of principles is not to abandon them.

It is to defend them.

And if our multilateral system is not working effectively, the answer is not to walk away from it.

It is to make it stronger, fairer and fit for the world we live in.

That is Ireland’s position.

And that is what all of us as members of the United Nations need to deliver on.

We should also remember what our collective commitment to the United Nations has achieved.

The multilateral system, anchored in the United Nations Charter, has been the foundation of many of humanity’s greatest achievements.

It has driven advances in poverty alleviation, healthcare, education, social protection, and food and nutrition security.

It has championed human rights and dignity and insisted that accountability matters.

It has given voice to the marginalised.

The people of Ireland understand that we live in an interdependent world; that the challenges we face are interconnected, cross borders, and require collective solutions.

Ireland currently holds the Presidency of the Council of the European Union.

Our stewardship of the EU’s agenda is deeply rooted in the principle of strength with unity. And this principle is at the heart of our vision for the United Nations.

As well as our unwavering commitment to the pillars which guide its work: peace and security, human rights, and development.

These pillars equally bear the weight of our shared ambition for a better, fairer and peaceful world.

Collectively, however, we are not delivering on their ambition. We are not staying the course.

At a time when global needs are increasing and becoming more complex, our responsibility to act does not diminish.

The denial of the fundamental human rights of millions of people around the world remains one of the defining challenges of our time. Renewed pressure on women's rights and gender equality is putting hard-won progress at risk.

Women and girls are being told that their ambitions, their education, their voices and their very presence in public life are unacceptable.

The situation in Afghanistan is one of the clearest examples.

The systematic exclusion of women and girls from education, employment and public life is not something that the international community can simply observe from a distance.

It is a profound human rights crisis. Girls are being denied the education that should shape their futures.

Women are being denied the ability to work, to participate fully in society and to contribute to the economic and social life of their country.

Their freedoms are being progressively erased.

And the world must not become inured to it.

We must not allow the absence of headlines to become an absence of action.

The women of Afghanistan have not disappeared.

And neither should our solidarity.

The same is true elsewhere.

Across the world, women and girls face conflict-related sexual violence, forced displacement, trafficking and discrimination.

Across the world, LGBTQI+ people face growing threats to their rights, safety and dignity.

Ireland remains firmly committed to the universality, indivisibility and equal application of human rights.

These principles are beyond question. That commitment is why Ireland is seeking election to the Human Rights Council for the 2027–2029 term.

And if elected, we will use that seat to defend the principle that human rights belong to everyone everywhere.

Today, Russia’s illegal war in Ukraine is more deadly for civilians than at any point since the start of their full-scale invasion.

Russia’s reckless drone and missile attacks, on Ukrainian towns and cities, continue to intensify. These are not the actions of a country interested in peace.

Russia could halt its brutal attacks at any time. Yet it refuses to do so.

Russia’s actions have already had direct global impact, in increased food and energy costs.

This time last year, a bushel of wheat was just over five dollars; this year it is more than seven dollars.

The fact that a permanent member of the Security Council is seeking to change borders by force, in clear violation of the UN Charter, is utterly unacceptable.

Sovereignty and territorial integrity apply equally to all States.

The international community must remain steadfast in our response, in support of the UN Charter and of a comprehensive, just and lasting peace.

Ireland stands in solidarity with Ukraine and will continue to do so.

We will continue to support efforts to hold Russia accountable for its actions.

There can be no impunity for war crimes, not in Ukraine, not anywhere.

That is why Ireland is a steadfast supporter of the International Criminal Court.

Ireland strongly opposes efforts to undermine the Court.  All measures against it should be immediately withdrawn.

The international legal order, founded on our agreements to make the world a safer and more secure place is being challenged.

International law represents the collective lessons drawn from conflict, suffering and atrocity.

The rules and institutions that we have built over generations exist to protect the rights, security and sovereignty of all states and all peoples.

When these principles are disregarded, the consequences extend far beyond any single conflict. We all become less secure.

Twenty years ago, the commission on war crimes and crimes against humanity in Darfur saw the international community come together to fulfil our collective responsibility to protect.

Despite the extraordinary efforts of the Sudanese people, the cycle of violence has continued.

The conflict has been inflamed and prolonged by harmful outside interference. All States and external actors must cease arming, financing and enabling the war in Sudan.

15 million Sudanese people are displaced from their homes.

Over 19.5 million face crisis levels of hunger. 33 million need urgent humanitarian assistance.

Violations of international law, including targeting on the basis of ethnicity, deliberate destruction of the means of survival, killing, torture, and sexual violence, are again being used as weapons of war.

We need to act decisively to support the people of Sudan to end this conflict.  We must support their aspirations for democracy, justice, and development.

Sudan has become a forgotten war, despite its devastating impact.

We must not allow the absence of daily headlines to become a licence for inaction. The people of Sudan deserve the same attention, urgency and solidarity that we rightly extend to crises elsewhere.

Despite its prevalence, we cannot ever allow ours to become indifferent to conflict and the human suffering it brings.

To do so would deny the shared humanity of its victims.

The peace plan on Gaza agreed last October was welcome, but it has not fundamentally changed the reality on the ground.

Israeli strikes continue. Humanitarian aid remains blocked. Civilians continue to suffer. We, the collected international community, have failed Palestine.

Ireland, like most gathered here, believes that the only viable solution to the decades of conflict, misery and wasted human lives, is a situation where a State of Palestine and a State of Isreal live side-by-side in peace, security and dignity.

There are modest signs of progress.

More countries have recognised the State of Palestine. An overwhelming majority of UN member states has endorsed the New York Declaration.

More of us have taken steps to push back against the illegal and violent settler occupation of Palestinian land in the West Bank.

But time is running out.

What we are witnessing on the ground is a deliberate attempt by some to make the prospect of a two-state solution impossible.

This is not some mad conspiracy theory – it is the stated intent of the Prime Minister of Israel who said clearly that “we are going to fulfil our promise that there will be no Palestinian state. This place belongs to us” as he permitted the E1 illegal development in East Jerusalem.

And the situation in Gaza remains an affront to all that is decent.

How can we tolerate a situation where civilians are so desperate for shelter that they have to make their homes in war-damaged and unsafe buildings?

Where eight children died because one of them collapsed?

Where the most basic humanitarian aid – food and shelter – is deliberately impeded?

When the full truth of what has happened - what is still happening - in Gaza is finally known, when the evidence is gathered, when the testimonies are heard, when the true horrors are finally and fully revealed, it will shame the world.

Nobody will be able to say that we did not know.

Let it not be said that we did not act.

In the West Bank, the relentless expansion of settlements has reached a scale without precedent, further eroding the prospects for a just and lasting peace.

Violent settlers continue to act with near-total impunity, while Palestinian communities face a sustained campaign of displacement and destruction – amounting to ethnic cleaning.

Entire villages have been razed, homes and vital infrastructure demolished, and thousands of Palestinian families driven from the places they have called home for generations and exposed to intimidation and violence.

The United Nations reports that this year there have been almost 200 attacks against Palestinians every month, a stark reminder of a reality that is deepening conflict, suffering, and despair.

The International Court of Justice has been clear: settlements in occupied Palestinian territory are illegal.

Ireland has acted, alongside others, to prohibit the import of settlement goods.

It is never too late to uphold international law.

The conflict in the Gulf remains deeply concerning and is having a serious impact around the world.

We need to get back to meaningful good faith negotiations by all sides.

Ireland has consistently stated that Iran must cease its attacks on its neighbours and also end its destabilising activities across the region; including strikes on ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

Vessels must be allowed to transit the Strait safely and without tolls, in line with international law.

If we are to build greater stability, Iran must never have a nuclear weapon.  Iran’s destabilising influence across the region must cease.

We need dialogue to achieve a negotiated settlement.

Since 1978 Irish soldiers have served with distinction in Lebanon in the UNIFIL peacekeeping operation. Ireland will continue to work with Lebanon, EU and international partners to support Lebanon’s future peace and security.

We have consistently condemned Hezbollah's attacks on Israel, which must cease immediately.

Israel must withdraw its military presence from southern Lebanon and bring an end to its military operations there. Israel's response has been wholly disproportionate.

We honour the courage, professionalism and dedication of all peacekeepers who have served under the UN.

We remember with particular respect those who lost their lives in the cause of peace.

We welcome the Secretary General’s report on the future of peacekeeping, and Ireland will work with others to ensure that this essential tool adapts to the twenty-first century.

Ireland also welcomes wider reform efforts in the UN system. These are necessary if we are to meet the challenges of our rapidly changing world.

But it is also necessary to point out that no reform process can succeed unless member states are prepared to support the United Nations politically, financially and through their actions.

We need the Security Council to live up to its mandate and respond to the crises around us.

Too long the veto has stymied the Council and eroded its legitimacy.

The Council’s membership must also finally be made representative of the world we live in; starting with the historic under-representation of African countries and ensuring that the voices of small and the most vulnerable states are heard.

I conclude by thanking Secretary-General António Guterres for his principled leadership and steadfast commitment to the United Nations over the past decade.

I especially commend his courage in tackling the climate crisis, the fundamental issue of our time.

From devastating floods in Nepal to wildfires across Europe, communities are increasingly experiencing the consequences of a changing climate.

The Paris Agreement remains a powerful example of what can be achieved when countries work together. Secretary Guterres has been a vital voice in calling Member States to action.

We look forward to working with the next Secretary-General in advancing the Charter's principles and strengthening this institution.

As the leader of a country that fought for its independence and its place among nations, I am deeply conscious of the inheritance we have received.

The United Nations, for all its imperfections, remains one of humanity's greatest achievements: a testament to the belief that peace, dignity and progress are best secured when nations work together.

At a time when that belief is under strain, it is our shared responsibility to renew it, strengthen it, and ensure it endures for generations to come.

Thank you.

Mr. President, Mr. Secretary-General, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. I had prepared a speech to present to you yesterday. The United States President described us as terrorists. We have been the victims of terrorism. I come from an Iran in which our esteemed Supreme Leader was assassinated without any legal framework or reason. I come from an Iran where, in truth, they bombed a school.

You see these children? These children perished under bombs, with weapons used by the United States and Israel. They were innocent, had committed no crimes. Lamerd, one of the small cities in a province in Iran, a sports hall where children were busy playing. The United States, by using weapons with multiple warheads, targeted that sports hall. They martyred, assassinated, our scientists, our men, women, and children.

Innocent children who, in truth, had committed no crimes, no sins. Those who are terrorists and train and protect terrorists describe us as such. We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists. Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country, and we defended ourselves with utmost strength. America and Israel attacked us, equipped with the latest technology and weapons systems, and our people stood steadfast.

Yes, they did hit us, but we did not bend the knee. We did not bow our head. We responded, but we did not hit civilian populations. They came into surrounding territories and targeted our universities, our healthcare centers, our schools, our hospitals, our infrastructures—all of it against international law. When I took over the responsibilities as President, they assassinated Ismail Haniyeh in Iran. On the day of my inauguration, Israel targets any neighborhood, in any city, in any province, commits assassinations like a true terrorist.

In Gaza, over 80,000 innocent civilians have been murdered, brutally murdered. Hundreds of thousands have been displaced. They are committing genocide by using the so-called technologies that they have at their disposal. Then they label others as terrorists. Are we the sources of instability? We only seek to live independently.

We are the ones who cause instability. Those who are committing terrorism and committing crimes, are they the protectors of peace and stability? None of the international laws have been adhered to by them. This is what we're facing. We don't want anything. We have received our response.

We need strength, because a people which is unable to defend itself will be trampled upon in today's world. We live in a world in which the powerful, instead of thinking about humanity, justice, fairness, and democracy, they seem to be the protectors and creators of instability and destruction. Whomever they wish to discredit, they label them as terrorists. Two hundred years—for the past two centuries— Iran has not attacked any country or any territory, but we've always defended ourselves steadfastly. But now we're being accused of being source of instability in the region? We're labeled terrorists?

And this has made it so that the path that we have chosen for ourselves requires power to defend ourselves. We do not seek power in order to attack or commit aggression. We seek energy for progress, not to threaten societies with weapons. And we wish to cooperate and collaborate for security. The people of Iran, in the past 7 months, our people, have been in the streets every night demonstrating in support of their land, of their homeland, so as to not allow those who were equipped and trained and armed by Israel and America to cause disruption in the security of their country. For 7 months, day and night, they've been present in the streets.

They are our source of power and our support. And that's why we stand fast. Iran must be powerful so as to avoid being threatened, to avoid its future being threatened. We do not wish to use our power for hegemony, and we do not seek our security in the insecurity of others. Vis-à-vis Iran's defense, our defensive systems have been built so that no one can think that bombing of Iranian cities will go unanswered. That is why we have the military power we do for defense.

But we say it clearly: in order to defend our country, we do not seek anyone's permission or approval. We seek energy for progress. For years, there have been—they have labeled centrifuges, international sanctions, other labels—when it comes to our nuclear technology. But for our country, peaceful nuclear technology is part of our inherent progress. For our sick people, it is cure and treatment. For the agricultural sector, it is food security.

For industry, it is advancement and progress and supply of electrical energy. Iran does not accept for nuclear technology to be at the exclusive disposal of some, of a handful. We will not— we will not bow our head and give up the right that is inherently ours. We say it clearly: no nuclear weapons, and no limitations to peaceful nuclear technology. Our peace will not come in the field of battle. But they must give the needed security to the people and nation of Iran.

We seek cooperation in order to have security. We live in a region in which warfare knows no borders. Crisis in one land will spill into the surrounding nations. That's why Iran does not see her neighbors as security rivals. We want to have strong neighbors. In waters in the Strait of Hormuz, we do not— we cannot let some have free access and gain their interests from a waterway while at the same time using that waterway to impose their aggressions upon us, to impose insecurity upon us, to forbid us access to our own waterways.

They close access for us to our own waterway, yet they keep supplying missiles and deadly military technologies to bring insecurity to all of the lands surrounding that waterway. We will not succumb to that. The expansion of warfare will not result in security. One cannot create chaos for the coastal countries seeking naval security. Excellencies, vis-à-vis Palestine, Palestine remains an open wound on the conscience of the international community, and Gaza remains a symbol of the failure of international mechanisms to prevent civilian suffering. For decades, resolutions have been adopted, yet occupation and violence have continued.

We cannot speak of peace while ignoring Palestine. Lasting peace in West Asia is impossible without justice for Palestine. As long as occupation, aggression, and injustice persist in the world, resistance will continue. If it is weakened in one form, it will reemerge in others, perhaps stronger still. Gaza, despite relentless killing and widespread devastation, has strengthened the people's faith in resistance. And resistance cannot be destroyed by bombs and siege.

This is human nature. If a human being is driven from his or her land, they will resist. If their homes are subjected to bombings and aggression and attacks, they will resist. What other choice do they have? Succome to bullying? To be driven from their homes, from their lands, and remain silent in the face of these threats and dangers?

And when they defend themselves, they're labeled as terrorists? The language makes it, unfortunately, clear the type of world that we're living in today. Our regional issues must be resolved in the region, at the hands of the countries in the region, without becoming a toy in the hands of outside aggressors. No relationship with a foreign power can become the tools of threatening neighboring countries in the region. And now, a few words with those who are responsible for having planned and carried out aggressions against our country and our people have experienced firsthand the result of their deadly aggression. And they have tested the strength and the steadfastness of Iran, and they have learned that Iran cannot be made to surrender.

Iran has never, ever been an aggressor, has never started a war, and has always shown her commitment to the negotiating table. They imposed the war on us, but we proved—we have proven—that we're not afraid of fighting, of war, a war that is defensive in nature. And we will stand in defense of our beloved Iran, our homeland, until our last breath. Ladies and gentlemen, the topic of this gathering is mutual trust. That cannot be achieved through words only, but by abstaining from using double standards. Atomic and nuclear bombs are in the hands of the Israeli regime, but the inspectors are requested to come to Iran.

Israel has murdered savagely over 70,000 innocents in Gaza, but Iran, while behind the table of negotiation, was bombed. Israel has the bombs, has weapons of mass destruction, not a member of the Non-Proliferation Treaty during her shameful life has not allowed a single inspection. But they are rewarded by all the means necessary for them to be able to bomb any capital in the region at will. I will repeat: the nuclear weapon is in Israel, but the inspectors in Iran. Israel kills, but Iran is subject to sanctions. This is a true tragedy, which would make anyone hearing it laugh, at best.

They kill, we are sanctioned, we are punished. Those who are ill, innocent people, the poor, the least privileged in our society, are the targets of these sanctions. And this is what the United States seeks to do with all countries: to sacrifice the population of a country in order to achieve her illegitimate goals. If we seek true peace and stability, we must apply a single standard for all. Iran does not seek special treatment. We seek equal rights.

Mr. President, Excellencies, dear friends,

The United Nations was born from a harsh lesson of history. The generation of  1945  had  learned,  at  terrible  cost,  that  while  states  can  choose  their actions, they cannot control all the consequences they set in motion.

That lesson is painfully relevant today.

We  are  living  through  a  period  of  profound  uncertainty.  Power  is  shifting. Conflicts are multiplying. And there is a growing tendency to treat the rules and  institutions  of  the  international  system  as  constraints  belonging  to another age.

But the United Nations was built precisely for times of uncertainty: to bring rules and restraint to an unpredictable world, and to prevent conflict from descending into catastrophe.

The task of our generation is both to preserve the institutions built by those that  came  before  us,  and  to  also  remember  the  hard-earned  wisdom  on which they rest.

Today,  that  wisdom  –  and  the  United  Nations  that  embodies  it  –  is  under enormous pressure.

This year marks eighty years since Iceland joined the United Nations.

For eight decades, Iceland has held that a small state should enjoy the same protection, rights and voice as a powerful one. That idea matters more today, not less.

Despite  its  shortcomings,  the  United  Nations  has  mattered.  And  it  has mattered a lot.

UN  peacekeeping  and  peacebuilding  operations  have  helped  prevent  and contain  conflict  around  the  world.  The  Universal  Declaration  of  Human Rights transformed our understanding of human dignity.

The Convention on the Law of the Sea became the Constitution of the Ocean, on which countries like mine depend, now strengthened further by the BBNJ Agreement.

The  International  Court  of  Justice  has  helped  states  settle  disputes  by peaceful means, through law rather than force.

And the International Criminal Court was created to ensure accountability for the most serious crimes.

The  United  Nations  has  advanced  gender  equality,  fought  racism  and discrimination,  delivered  humanitarian  assistance  and  helped  countries build more peaceful and prosperous societies.

But  loyalty  to  the  United  Nations  cannot  mean  pretending  that  everything works  perfectly.  Bureaucracy  can  be  cumbersome,  decisions  slow  and resources  fragmented.  The  Security  Council  -  entrusted  with  maintaining international peace and security - has too often been paralysed when action was needed most.

Too often, the veto has become a shield against action rather than a tool for preserving peace. So yes, the United Nations needs reform. And Iceland fully supports the UN80 reform process.

We  need  a  United  Nations  that  uses  resources  effectively  and  responds quickly when people need it. United Nations that delivers for all.

The  deeper  challenge,  however,  is  political.  The  strength  of  the  United Nations depends on our willingness to uphold the principles and wisdom on which they were founded.

The most basic rules of international relations are being tested. Not because we no longer know them. We do.

But because increasingly, governments apply them selectively. Meaning that international law applies - until it becomes inconvenient.

That  court  decisions  must  be  respected  -  unless  they  challenge  our  own actions or those of our friends.

That sovereignty is sacred - unless someone else's territory stands in the way of our ambitions.

We cannot build courts, celebrate them when they prosecute our enemies, and undermine them when they turn their attention to our friends.

When grave violations go unanswered, they are more likely to be repeated.

And for small states this is existential, not simply a matter of principle.

Russia's  brutal  war  against  Ukraine  is  a  clear  example.  Russia  invaded  a sovereign neighbour, seeking to change borders by force and deny another nation  the  freedom  to  determine  its  future.  Ukrainians  have  paid  an unimaginable price.

Behind every destroyed home is a family. Behind every casualty is someone who was loved.

Iceland's  position  remains  clear.  Ukraine  has  the  right  to  defend  itself,  to sovereignty  and  territorial  integrity,  and  to  a  just  and  lasting  peace  on  the basis of international law.

Our  support  for  Ukraine  defends  a  principle  on  which  all  our  countries’ security depends: That no nation gets to decide the future of another.

This principle must apply everywhere. Including in the Middle East.

In  Gaza,  we  continue  to  witness  repeated  violations  of  the  ceasefire  and continued  suffering  among  civilians,  despite  the  adoption  of  the  twenty-point Comprehensive Peace Plan and Security Council Resolution 2803.

The  suffering  of  Palestinian  civilians  cannot  become  background  noise. Children are still being killed. Families are still losing their homes. Parents are still trying to keep their children alive. Again. And again. And again.

We  cannot  accept  Gaza  being  repeatedly  destroyed  and  rebuilt  while  the underlying cause remains unresolved.

In the West Bank, illegal settlement activity continues to expand. Palestinian civilians face settler violence, too often enabled by impunity, inflammatory rhetoric and permissive policies.

Earlier  this  month,  Iceland  joined  eleven  other  states  in  addressing restrictions  on  trade  in  goods  from  settlements  that  are  illegal  under international law.

Our objective remains clear: A viable Palestinian state alongside Israel, with both peoples able to live in security, dignity and peace.

We have heard the words “moral cowards” from this podium. To me, moral cowards  are  those  leaders  around  the  world  who  refuse  to  sit  down  and negotiate a just and lasting peace. Those who deny access to humanitarian aid for people in desperate need. And moral cowards are those leaders who repeatedly go against and disrespect international law.

We must not allow the horrors in Ukraine and the Middle East to make other crises invisible.

In Sudan, years of civil war have brought atrocities, mass displacement and grave violations of international humanitarian law. As humanitarian leaders have reminded us, Sudan does not suffer from a lack of analysis. It suffers from a lack of action.

Acts that may constitute war crimes and crimes against humanity cannot be met with indifference. We created the International Criminal Court to ensure accountability for the most serious crimes. The freedoms codified in the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea  are  not  optional.  For  an  island  nation  dependent  on  open  maritime routes, freedom of navigation is fundamental.

We also must not forget how much progress has been driven by economic freedom.  Perhaps  humanity‘s  greatest  gift  is  our  capacity  to  create.  To imagine something that doesn‘t exist and then bring it into being.

Creativity  is  universal;  what  differs  is  whether  societies  give  it  room  to flourish.  Open,  free  markets  have  given  people  the  opportunity  to  create, exchange  ideas,  take  risks  and  build  better  lives  for  themselves  and  for others.

Another battle is taking place over what kind of societies we want to be.

Across  the  world,  authoritarianism  and  political  extremism  are  gaining ground.

We see attacks on democratic institutions, independent media, science and facts  in  public  debate.  Too  often,  these  movements  target  groups  whose rights supposedly matter less.

Women.  LGBTQI+  people.  Minorities.  Migrants.  People  who  look  different, love differently or live differently. These are not abstract groups. They are our daughters and sons. Our friends. Our neighbours. Our colleagues.

I am deeply concerned by the growing backlash against gender equality and LGBTQI+ rights - including within my own region, Europe.

We hear that equality has gone too far. That diversity has gone too far. That some  people  demanding  the  freedom  simply  to  be  themselves  somehow threaten the freedom of others.

I  reject  that  completely.  Human  rights  are  not  a  zero-sum  game.  Giving  a woman  equal  rights  does  not  take  rights  away  from  a  man.  Allowing  an LGBTQI+ person to live freely does not make anyone else less free. Quite the opposite.

We  should  be  very  careful  when  governments  begin  telling  us  that  some people's existence threatens society. History has taught us where that can lead.

And  let  me  be  clear:  Iceland  will  not  allow  others  to  define  our  values  or dictate the language we use to defend human rights.

Free societies are strongest when people are allowed to be themselves. But freedom  that  belongs  only  to  people  who  fit  someone  else’s  definition  of normal is not freedom.

A society that strips people of their dignity will eventually undermine its own democracy.

And  nowhere  is  this  backlash  more  extreme  than  in  Afghanistan,  where women and girls have been systematically erased from public life. Girls are denied education, women are denied basic freedoms. For me, this can only be described as gender apartheid.

On the Human Rights Council, we have sought to match words with deeds; from Iran and Afghanistan to accountability for violations in Sudan.

Throughout  our  Council  term,  Iceland  will  emphasize  gender  equality, LGBTQI+ rights, the rights of children and young people, and the relationship between human rights and the environment.

Human rights are not for some: They are for all.

The same commitment to facts and responsibility must guide us on climate change.

Leaders  who  deny  or  distort  science  should  explain  themselves  to  island communities watching the sea rise around them. To families losing land and livelihoods to drought and erosion - like in the Sahel.

In Iceland, we can see the changes taking place in our own region, the Arctic. Rising temperatures and receding ice are already changing ecosystems and the lives of communities across the region.

Nor  can  we  ignore  another  transformation  already  affecting  our  societies: artificial intelligence. This revolution is changing how we work, communicate and  receive  information.  It  is  also  making  it  easier  to  produce  convincing falsehoods and manipulate public debate.

Governments, businesses and scientists must cooperate internationally to harness the benefits of AI while confronting its risks.

And we need to move faster. Much faster.

In difficult times, nostalgia tempts us to imagine that the world used to be simpler and safer. It was not.

The decades after the Cold War saw genocide in Rwanda, horrific wars in the former  Yugoslavia  and  the  Congo,  the  rise  of  international  terrorism  and devastating civil wars.

Twenty-five  years  ago  this  month,  terrorist  attacks  in  the  United  States changed our world profoundly.

Thirty  years  ago,  the  Comprehensive  Nuclear-Test-Ban  Treaty  was established, yet the threat of nuclear proliferation remains with us.

What  distinguished  some  of  the  past's  best  moments  was  our  response: Countries  came  together,  built  institutions  and  negotiated  treaties.  They created  the  Human  Rights  Council,  OCHA,  ICC,  UN  Women  and  the UNFCCC.

They  placed  Women,  Peace  and  Security  on  the  agenda  of  the  Security Council and recognised sexual violence as a weapon and tactic of war. They adopted  the  Millennium  Development  Goals  and  later  the  Sustainable Development Goals.

To  put  it  simply:  None  of  this  happened  by  itself.  It  happened  because political leaders consciously chose cooperation over retreat.  That choice is before us again.

The  United  Nations'  next  Secretary  General  must  continue  reforming  this organisation, make difficult choices and direct resources where they make the greatest difference.

That will require courage from her.

And so will the choices made by every Member State represented in this Hall.

We must choose whether to uphold the law when it is inconvenient; whether to  defend  the  rights  of  people  who  are  not  our  citizens;  and  whether  to protect and respect a system even  when that system does not deliver the outcome we want.

That is the real test of our commitment to multilateralism. Not what we say when the rules favour us, but what we do when they do not.

For Iceland, the choice is clear. We choose international law over selective obedience. Accountability over impunity. Cooperation over isolation. Human dignity over division.

The  generation  that  founded  the  United  Nations  had  seen  first-hand  what could happen when restraints on power collapsed. The Charter, international law and the institutions that followed were their answer.

In that sense, the United Nations is a gift from a generation that learned that lesson at an extraordinary cost.

And now we need the courage to remember it.

Mr President,

Last year, from this very podium, Italy’s Prime Minister Giorgia  Meloni  recalled  that  56  conflicts  were  raging across the world - the highest number since World War II. Today, those same sources put that figure at 61. It is the stark truth of the numbers.

Pope Leo XIV issued a warning that Italy has made its own: we must never grow accustomed to war. Because first  we  become  accustomed  to  the  words,  then  to images, and finally to the victims. When war becomes something we  grow accustomed to – peace itself risks becoming a mirage.

We will not give up.

Against the law of the strongest, we choose the strength of the law. Against the politics of force, we choose the force of politics. This is the message Italy brings to the United Nations.

This  is  the  mission  of  Italian  diplomacy:  to  build bridges, open new paths, and keep dialogue alive even when it seems impossible. To work for peace, prosperity and  growth  -  because  growth  creates  prosperity,  and prosperity, in turn, consolidates peace.

Ukraine,  the  Middle  East,  the  Gulf,  Sudan  and  the Sahel  are  not  separate  crises.  Nor  are  trade  wars,  AI competition,  hybrid  attacks  and  their  economic  and social repercussions. Nor is terrorism in all of its many forms, which we continue to fight in every corner of the world.  These  are  all  different  fronts  of  a  single, profound transformation: the world order that emerged after World War II is coming apart. It was an imperfect order. It did not prevent wars, injustice or suffering.

But  today  the  world  balance  has  been  disrupted  and history,  which  someone  has  declared  that  it  has reached  its  final  chapter,  is  once  again  moving  at  a galloping pace.

But every race needs a finish line. Our task cannot be to stand and watch the fragmentation of our world, but it  must  be  to  build  a  new  framework  of  rules, responsibility  and  cooperation  capable  of  governing change.

Change  that  can  happen  only  through  political  will, the through  dialogue  among  nations, awareness  of  peoples  and  through  the  ability  of multilateral institutions to  rediscover a mission  equal to the challenges of our time.

through

The United Nations cannot simply record the divisions of  today.  It  must  have  the  ambition  to  imagine  the future.  It  must  recognize  its  limitations,  overcome  its paralysis  and instruments,  without its abandoning  its  deepest  raison  d’etre:  to  be  the  place

reform

where  conflict  gives  way  to  dialogue,  confrontation  to diplomacy, and fear to the search for shared solutions.

The  United  Nations  remains  the  most  universal place for pursuing this aspiration.

Not  because  it’s  perfect,  but  because  no  other institution can bring together, around the same table, such different interests, cultures, religions and visions of  the  world.  It  is  precisely  when  the  world  is  divided that  the  value  of  dialogue  grows  rather  than diminishes.

Italy believes in this institution, in its value and in its central  role.  We  believe  in  peace,  which  remains  our guiding  star—the  guiding  principle  of  Italy’s  foreign policy.  It  is  rooted  in  our  history,  enshrined  in  our Constitution, and integral to our identity.

Dialogue, however, is not a sign of weakness, nor does it  mean  neutrality.  Italy  knows  where  it  stands:  our home is Europe, our alliance is with the West, and our values are freedom, democracy and the dignity of every human being.

Yet  belonging  to  the  West  does  not  mean  retreating behind  fortress  walls.  It  requires  us  to  draw  on  the strength  of  our  values  to  engage  with  others,  build partnerships among equals, and mend the fabric of an international system that risks descending into chaos.

The European Union, the G7 and the West—of which we  are  proud  to  be  part—must  not  be  perceived  as walls.  They  must  be  bridges.  This  is  the  purpose  of IMEC, the economic and logistics corridor designed to connect  Europe  with  the  broader  Indo-Mediterranean region.

The same principle guides our relationship with Africa, a strategic priority for Italy and a major partner for our century.

The Mattei Plan now involves 18 countries and is built on a simple idea: not to decide for Africa, but to decide with Africa. It is not aid handed down from above, but a  partnership  among  equals—in  agriculture  and energy,  education  and  training,  infrastructure  and pharmaceuticals.

Producing  vaccines  in  Africa  saves  lives,  strengthens health  systems,  creates  jobs  and  supports  growth capable of generating stability.

It is in this spirit, and in defense of the right not to be forced to migrate, that we fight human traffickers who prey on poverty.

Agreements with countries of origin and transit help us combat  irregular  migration,  while  education,  training and  access  to  employment  support  safe  and  regular migration.

A world as complex as ours can be governed in only two ways: through shared rules, or through the law of the strongest.

Italy  has  made  its  choice.  Italy  stands  for  rules, dialogue and diplomacy.

That  is  why  we  have  condemned,  and  continue  to condemn, Russia’s aggression against Ukraine. We will continue to support Ukraine for as long as necessary, while  working  towards  a  just  peace  and  towards  a future in which Russia can once again be a partner in dialogue rather than a threat to Europe.

Russia,  as  a  permanent  member  of  the  Security Council, cannot evade its responsibilities. A ceasefire is not  a  concession  to  the  other  side;  it  is  the  first  step towards a European security architecture that protects everyone, including Russia.

This  is  why  we  view  with  grave  concern  the  growing hybrid  threats  posed  by  Russia  against  Europe,  and

why we have expressed our full solidarity with Germany following the attack on Leipzig Airport.

Peace  requires  openness,  but  it  also  requires  resolve. Dialogue  without  truth  is  weakness;  resolve  without dialogue leads to a dead end.

The same principle guides our approach to the Middle East.  Peace  can  come  only  through  a  two-State solution—two peoples, two States.

In Gaza, the truce has slowed the fighting, but it has not  yet  ended  the  suffering.  There  is  not  a  minute  to lose. The truce must be consolidated, humanitarian aid must be allowed to enter without obstruction, and the disarmament of Hamas must become a reality.

From the very beginning, Italy has mobilized the very best of its humanitarian capabilities. Through Food for Gaza,  we  have  delivered  food  and  essential  supplies provided by our farmers.

We  have  welcomed  and  cared  for  wounded  and vulnerable  children.  We  have  opened  our  universities and research centres to young Palestinians, because a future State also needs a future generation of leaders.

In Lebanon, the stakes extend far beyond the country itself and affect the entire region.

The Washington Agreement of 26 June opened a door. Italy is proud to continue hosting negotiating sessions in  Rome  that  have  helped  keep  that  door  open. (Reuters⁠￼)

For  decades,  Italian  troops  have  served  the  cause  of peace in southern Lebanon through UNIFIL and have helped train the Lebanese Armed Forces. We have also recently  approved  new  development  projects  for  the area, and we will continue to play our part even after the mission’s mandate comes to an end.

Dear colleagues,

Sixty-one  active  conflicts  mean  that  war is  advancing even far from the television cameras.

And as war advances, the principles on which we have built eighty years of international relations retreat: the international prohibition  of humanitarian  law,  and  freedom  and  security  of navigation.

the  use  of

force,

Defending  freedom  of  navigation  means  defending trade, jobs, growth and dialogue. Because where goods can move freely, weapons are less likely to do so.

The Strait of Hormuz must reopen. Dialogue must be revived  in  the  Gulf,  and  Iran  must  be  called  upon  to renounce any nuclear threat and any aggressive policy towards  other  countries  in  the  region.  Attacks  on shipping in the Red Sea must cease, as must Russia’s reckless  attacks  in  the  Black  Sea  on  shipments  of Ukrainian grain destined for Africa.

These crises may seem distant, but their effects reach into every household. They drive up the cost of energy, grain,  bread  and  fertilizers.  They  hurt  businesses, agriculture and families.

Food  security  concerns  us  all  and  demands  common solutions. Italy is working side by side with the United this Nations  Rome-based  agencies challenge,  making  available  the  best  of Italian expertise—from  agriculture  and  food  production  to satellite technologies that help reduce the use of land, water and pesticides.

to  address

Food security and water security are part of the same struggle. There can be no harvest without water. There

can  be  no  stability  without  a  harvest.  Where  water disappears, hunger, conflict and migration advance.

Mr President, dear colleagues,

The choice between force and politics is not confined to war.  It  extends  to  the  economy,  resources  and technology—to  every  sphere  in  which  unrestrained power risks prevailing over the human person. Politics must once again take the lead in shaping change.

We stand at the dawn of a technological revolution that is already reshaping the way we live, work, produce and make decisions: the artificial intelligence revolution.

The  great  inventions  of  the  past  took  centuries  to transform the world. Artificial intelligence is doing so in a matter of years. Those who control these technologies will enjoy an enormous advantage over those who are left behind.

The risk is that new inequalities, new dependencies and new  concentrations  of  power—or  even  new  forms  of domination—will emerge.

Entire  professions  may  disappear  or  be  transformed. Falsifying and manipulating reality will become easier.

systems  operating  without  human Automated oversight may produce extremely dangerous decisions.

Pope Leo XIV, in the encyclical Magnifica Humanitas, reminded  us  that  no  algorithm  can  take  the  place  of human conscience, and that any technology capable of striking  without  seeing  the  face  of  another  person lowers the moral threshold for conflict. Italy shares this vision.

But governing innovation does not mean demonizing it.

Artificial  intelligence  can  open  up  possibilities  that today  are  unimaginable—in  medicine,  research, environmental education,  manufacturing protection.  Every  major  technological  advance  has generated  fears,  but  it  has  also  created  opportunities and, over time, greater prosperity.

and

Turning  back  is  neither  possible  nor  desirable.  But neither  can  we  hand  over  our  future  to  technology without rules.

We  do  not  need  bureaucratic  cages  that  only  some would  respect.  What  we  need  is  a  balance  between transparency, oversight, security and the protection of intellectual property. We need to share the benefits of innovation and build mechanisms of mutual oversight.

This  is  precisely  the  task  of  the  United  Nations:  to establish common rules before events—or the strongest actors—impose their own.

The United Nations was born in 1945 out of a world in ruins, a world that had learned a simple truth: when each of us stands alone, we all lose.

Eighty-one  years  later,  that  lesson  is  more  relevant than ever. The United Nations was created to prevent violence  from  becoming  the  only  law.  But  to  remain faithful  to  that  mission,  it  must  regain  its  ability  to make decisions and, above all, to act.

With this conviction, Italy will continue to advocate for a universal moratorium on the death penalty—a cause rooted in civilization, in the defence of life and human dignity, which we have championed for years here, in this very building.

We  are  also  on  the  front  line  in  defending  individual freedom  and  women’s  rights,  and  in  fighting,  among other  things,  the  abhorrent  practice  of  female  genital mutilation.

We  must  have  the  courage  to  say  it:  too  often,  this Organization  appears  powerless.  For  far  too  long,  its reform has been held back by competing interests.

Italy wants a Security Council that is more legitimate, more  representative  and  more  accountable  to  all Member States.

Not an even more exclusive club, but one of the pillars of the far-reaching renewal of the United Nations that we  hope  the  new  Secretary-General  will  pursue— making  this  Organization  capable  of  deciding  and acting while there is still time to change the course of events.

Italy has always done its part, and it will continue to do so. We are among the leading contributors to the United Nations  budget  and  among  the  countries  with  the largest military presence in international missions. We place  our  men  and  women,  our  resources  and  our expertise  at  the  service  of  peace—in  UNIFIL  and  in every mission in which we participate.

To all our men and women in uniform go the gratitude of  the  Government,  our  institutions  and  the  Italian people.

Mr President, dear colleagues,

My  generation  was  born  on  a  continent  that  had endured two world wars and then went on to experience the longest period of peace in its history.

That was not a miracle. It was a choice—the result of political action.

Amid the ruins, men and women decided to pool coal and steel rather than use them to build new guns.

From that choice emerged an unprecedented endeavor: a  Union  founded  on  common  institutions,  peace, freedom, democracy, prosperity, human rights and the rule of law.

This  is  the  message  Italy  brings  to  New  York  today: peace is not an inheritance secured once and for all. It is a responsibility we must shoulder every day.

It must be defended with resolve. It must be built with patience. And it must be pursued without  ever giving up.
