PERMANENT MISSION OF JAMAICA TO THE UNITED NATIONS

NATIONAL STATEMENT BY

SENATOR THE HON KAMINA JOHNSON SMITH, JP

MINISTER OF FOREIGN AFFAIRS AND FOREIGN TRADE OF JAMAICA

AT THE

GENERAL DEBATE of the 81st SESSION OF THE UN GENERAL ASSEMBLY

26th September 2026

On  behalf  of  the  Government  and  people  of  Jamaica,  I

congratulate you on your election as President of this eighty-

first  session  of  the  General  Assembly  and  assure  you  of

Jamaica’s full support.

I also commend your predecessor, Her Excellency Annalena

Baerbock,  for  her  stewardship  of  the  Assembly  during  its

historic eightieth session.

And  to  Secretary-General  António  Guterres,

I  convey

Jamaica’s  profound  appreciation

for  your  committed

leadership  through  a  decade  of  extraordinary  global

uncertainty.

Your theme for this session could hardly be more timely.

Because today, trust is in short supply.

Wars  and  conflicts  are  devastating  communities  and

displacing  millions.  Geopolitical  tensions  are  deepening.

Climate change is destroying lives, livelihoods and decades

of  development  in  a  matter  of  hours.  New  technologies,

including  artificial  intelligence,  offer  extraordinary  promise,

while presenting risks we have not yet fully understood.

And  at  the  very  moment  when  collective  action  is  most

needed, confidence in multilateralism itself is being tested.

Jamaica’s position is clear.

The  shortcomings  of  multilateralism  cannot  be  solved  by

abandoning multilateralism.

For small states like ours, a rules-based international order is

not an abstract diplomatic preference. It is fundamental to

our sovereignty, our security and our development.

But  neither  can  we  safeguard  multilateralism  simply  by

defending it.

We must reform it.

We  must  make  it  more  representative,  more  accountable,

more  efficient  —  and  more  responsive  to  the  needs  and

realities of the people it was created to serve.

That is why Jamaica has chosen not merely to call for reform,

but to help lead it.

Our  Permanent  Representative  was  privileged  to  co-chair,

with  New  Zealand,  the  UN80  Initiative’s  Informal  Ad  Hoc

Working  Group  on  Mandate  Implementation  Review.  That

work culminated in General Assembly Resolution 80/251 — an

important  framework  for  improving  how  UN  mandates  are

created, implemented and reviewed.

Jamaica now continues that work alongside Norway.

Our objective is straightforward: a United Nations that spends

less time sustaining process for its own sake, and more time

fulfilling its purpose.

That is the multilateralism Jamaica believes in.

The selection of the next Secretary-General will be one of the

most  consequential  decisions  before  Member  States  this

year.

Jamaica proudly joins our CARICOM family in supporting the

candidacy of Her Excellency Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett of the

Cooperative Republic of Guyana.

Her candidacy also speaks to something larger.

Small  states  have  long  served  this  international  system  as

bridge-builders, consensus-makers and problem-solvers.

We learn very early that influence does not depend only on

size  or  power.  It  can  also  come  from  credibility,  dialogue,

principle and the capacity to bring people together.

These are  the strengths which our multilateral system needs

now, more than ever.

For Jamaica, the consequences of global challenges are not

theoretical.

On 28 October last year, Hurricane Melissa struck our island.

In a matter of hours, the most catastrophic hurricane in our

modern history inflicted damage and losses estimated at 56.7

per cent of our GDP.

Think about that.

More  than  half  the  value  of  an  entire  year  of  national

economic output, damaged or lost through a single event.

Jamaica had prepared.

Years of fiscal discipline had allowed us to build buffers. We

had  put

in  place  disaster-risk

financing,

including

catastrophe  insurance  and  an  independently  sponsored

catastrophe bond.

Those measures gave us immediate liquidity.

But no level of prudent national planning can fully insulate a

small  developing  state  from  a  climate  event  of  that

magnitude.

And  therein  lies  the  fundamental  inequity  faced  by  Small

Island Developing States.

We  can  do  everything  right.    In  fact,  Jamaica’s  reforms

balanced  economic  orthodoxy  with

innovation  and

expansion  of  support  for  the  most  vulnerable.  And  yet  one

hurricane can still erase decades of progress.

We  are  deeply  grateful  to  our  international  partners,  our

CARICOM family, our Jamaican diaspora and the thousands

of  individuals  and  organisations  which  stood  with  us  in  our

hour of need.

But Jamaica has not simply resolved to recover.

We have resolved to rebuild better and differently.

Our resilience must not be measured by how much suffering

we  can  withstand.  It  must  be  measured  by  how  well  we

prepare, how quickly we recover, how intelligently we adapt

— and whether we emerge stronger.

That is why the Government of Prime Minister Andrew Holness

established  the  National  Reconstruction  and  Resilience

Authority — NaRRA.

Its mandate is to drive reconstruction at speed and at scale;

to  coordinate  major

infrastructure  projects;  crowd

in

investment;  and  critically,  to  embed  resilience  into  the

Jamaica we are rebuilding.

We are not simply replacing what Melissa destroyed.

We are building the Jamaica that must withstand the storms

of tomorrow.

We have also submitted our updated Nationally Determined

Contribution,  completed  our  Long-Term  Strategy  for  a  low-

carbon, climate-resilient future, and advanced our National

Adaptation Plan.

But  national  ambition  must  be  matched  by  international

action.

Climate finance must become more accessible, affordable

and predictable.

And  the  international  financial  architecture  must  finally

recognise what SIDS have long said: income alone does not

and cannot measure vulnerability.

A country does not become less vulnerable to hurricanes and

other natural disasters because its per-capita income crosses

an arbitrary threshold.

We therefore continue to advocate for the use of measures

that go beyond GDP, including multidimensional vulnerability

indices,

in  determining  access

to  concessional  and

development finance.

Jamaica brings this message to the international community

from  a  position  not  only  of  vulnerability,  but  one  of

responsibility.

Over the past decade, we have undertaken difficult reforms

and made difficult choices.

Our  debt,  which  once  stood  at  more  than  140  per  cent  of

GDP, was brought down to 62 per cent before Melissa, with

unemployment then at a historic low of 3.4%.

We  built  macroeconomic  stability,  strengthened  investor

confidence  and  created  the  fiscal  space  that  ultimately

helped  us  respond  to  the  greatest  natural  disaster  in  our

modern  history.

We  are  proud  and  heartened  that

notwithstanding Melissa, Jamaica’s credit ratings have either

been stabilized or upgraded and unemployment still stands

at a low of 3.7%.

Those gains did not happen by accident.

They  required  discipline.  Partnership.  Sacrifice.  Consistency.

And long-term planning.

Our experience has taught us that the strongest response to

a crisis begins long before the crisis arrives — in the choices

we make, the institutions we build, and the buffers we create.

Jamaica  will  continue  to  take  responsibility  for  the  things

within our control.

But domestic responsibility must be matched by international

solidarity and cooperation.

Developing  countries  cannot  reasonably  be  expected  to

simultaneously

finance  climate  adaptation,  modernise

infrastructure,  strengthen  social  protection,  manage  debt,

absorb  external  shocks  and  achieve  the  Sustainable

Development Goals without an international financial system

responsive to their realities.

We do not ask to be relieved of responsibility. We ask for an

international  system  that  gives  responsible  countries  the

space to succeed.

That opportunity increasingly depends on technology.

Jamaica sees digital transformation and responsible artificial

intelligence  as  powerful

tools.

They  can  enhance

productivity, innovation and sustainable development for our

people.  Indeed,  they  can  be  an  equalizing  force  for  the

world.

We must therefore not allow AI to deepen old inequalities and

create an entirely new global divide.

Developing countries require investment in infrastructure, skills

and  capacity.  And  all  countries

require  governance

frameworks that safeguard privacy and intellectual property,

ensure  data

integrity  and  promote  the  ethical  and

responsible  use  of  emerging  technologies,  without  stifling

innovation.

The Pact for the Future, the Global Digital Compact and the

ABAS provide important foundations.

Our  task  now  as  a  global  community,  is  to  translate

commitments into action.

Development also requires peace and security.

For  Jamaica  and  our  Caribbean  region,  transnational

organised crime remains a serious threat.

Last  year,  from  this  podium,  Prime  Minister  Andrew  Holness

called  for  a  Global  War  on  Gangs  —  a  coordinated

international  effort  capable  of  matching

the

reach,

financing  and  sophistication  of

transnational  criminal

networks.

Jamaica reiterates that call today.

Illicit

firearms  do  not  manufacture  themselves

in  our

communities.  They  cross  borders.  Criminal  money  crosses

borders.  Criminal  networks  exploit  technology  and  operate

across borders.

Our response must therefore also cross borders.

We  call  for  stronger  cooperation  in  firearms  tracing  and

interdiction,  intelligence  and  information-sharing,  financial

investigations  and  law-enforcement  capacity-building.  We

also  urge  major  arms-exporting  states  to  strengthen  export

controls and post-delivery verification.

At home, Jamaica has invested heavily in our security forces,

strengthened  legislation,  enhanced  intelligence  gathering,

oversight and transformed policing.

The results are remarkable by any standard.

In 2025, Jamaica recorded its lowest number of homicides in

more  than  three  decades.  And  in  2026,  the  Global  Peace

Index  ranked  Jamaica  the  most  peaceful  country  in  the

Caribbean.

We  recognise  that  there  remains  work  to  be  done.  But  the

direction is clear.

Our objective is not merely fewer crimes.

It is a durable ecosystem of peace in which every Jamaican

can feel safe, raise a family,  do business and fulfil his or her

potential and retire in paradise.

Nowhere  in  our  region  is  the  challenge  of  criminal  gangs

more devastating than in our sister nation of Haiti.

Jamaica stands firmly with the Haitian people.

We  urge  sustained  international  support  for  the  Gang

Suppression  Force  and  for  the  Haitian  National  Police  and

armed  forces.  This  support  must  include  the  financial,

logistical  and  operational  resources  necessary  to  restore

security. We further call for the Security Council to renew the

mandate of the GSF at this imperfect but particularly critical

juncture. We are at a crossroads. We can lose gains, or we

can build on progress made.

The  international  community  must  send  an  unequivocal

message:  armed  gangs  cannot  be  allowed  to  determine

Haiti’s future nor that of the region.

Security  must  create  the  space  for  sustained  humanitarian

relief,  developmental  and  economic  progress.    But  even

more  foundationally,  security  must  create  the  space  for

political  stability,  democratic  governance  and  credible

elections, led and owned by the Haitian people.

Jamaica  remains  deeply  concerned  by  the terrible  human

suffering caused by armed conflicts across the world.

Wherever  conflict  occurs,  our  principles  must

remain

consistent.

International humanitarian law must be respected.

Civilians must be protected.

International law and the Charter of the United Nations must

be upheld.

And  diplomacy  must  remain  our  first  and  most  persistent

instrument for resolving disputes.

Respect for international law — including due regard for the

decisions  of  the

International  Court  of  Justice  —

is

indispensable  to  the  peaceful  international  order  on  which

small states depend.

Similarly,  with  respect  to  our  neighbour  Cuba,  Jamaica

continues

to  believe

in  dialogue  and  constructive

engagement.

We encourage  domestic  reform  and  greater  integration  of

Cuba into the international economic system, supported by

policies  that  create  pathways  for  progress  and  eliminating

the dire humanitarian crisis, rather than perpetuating isolation

under the blockade.  The suffering of the Cuban people is of

deep concern.

Jamaica believes that reparatory justice is, at its heart, about

truth,  acknowledgement,

justice,  repair,  compensation,

development  and

reconciliation.  Jamaica  not  only

supported  the  resolution  put  forward  by  Ghana  on  March

25th of this year, we also delivered to Buckingham Palace, a

petition

framing  critical  questions  on

the  matter  of

reparations.    The  petition  has  now  been  referred  to  the

Judicial Committee of the Privy Council.

Sixty-four years after Jamaica proudly raised our black, green

and gold flag as a politically independent nation, we remain

clear-eyed about the world around us.

We know its dangers.

But we also believe deeply in its possibilities.

The  United  Nations  must  change  if  it  is  to  remain  credible.

Jamaica supports the revitalisation of this General Assembly,

meaningful  reform  of  the  Security  Council,  and  greater

coherence, efficiency and accountability across the United

Nations system.

Reform is not an act of disloyalty to this institution.

Reform is how we preserve it.

Ultimately however, Mr. President, multilateralism must mean

something beyond these walls.

For a small state like Jamaica, its value is felt when our people

are safer; when opportunity is expanded; when vulnerability

does not become a barrier to development; when countries

that have acted responsibly are not penalised for shocks they

did not create; and when the voice of a small nation carries

the same dignity as that of a large one.

That is why Jamaica remains committed to this institution  —

not  because  it  is  perfect,  but  because  we  are  grateful  for

what is has achieved, and we believe in what it can become.

Small states can help lead that effort.

Our  own  journey  has  taught  us  that  vulnerability  need  not

mean  helplessness;  that  discipline  creates  resilience;  that

partnership multiplies possibility; and that even in moments of

profound crisis, nations can choose to build forward.

So let us restore trust through what we do.

Let us manage transformation with purpose.

Let us bring the same seriousness to preventing crises that we

bring to responding to them.

And  let us  never lose  sight  of  the  simple idea  on  which  this

institution was founded:

that nations working together, can achieve what none of us

can achieve alone.

That is the United Nations Jamaica believes in.

And  that  is  the  United  Nations  we  will  continue  working  to

reform and renew.

I thank you.

Mr. President,

Mr. Secretary General,

Every generation believes the challenges they face are unmatched.

Perhaps for us that is true.

We  are  at  a  unique  moment  in  history;  the  scale  of  knowledge  and  the

speed  of  change  are  unprecedented.  Every  day  brings  another  crisis,

another tragedy, another emergency, demanding our attention.

One  study  shows  that  average  screen  attention  has  fallen  from  2.5

minutes in 2004 to just 47 seconds today.

Of  course,  a  screen  is  not  the  world,  but  that  says  something  about  our

world  today:  that  attention  has  become  a  scarce  asset,  and  where  we

choose to direct it has never mattered more.

And  in  this  chamber,  attention  is  more  than  a  cognitive  resource.  It  is  a

geopolitical one.

It determines which conﬂicts receive sustained diplomacy and which fade

from the agenda.

Whether a ceaseﬁre holds after the cameras leave.

Whether humanitarian suﬀering remains intolerable, or becomes familiar.

And whether the world steps up, or scrolls and strolls away.

History  rarely  catches  us  entirely  by  surprise.  More  often,  it  catches  us

focused elsewhere.

Economic  disparity,  food  insecurity,  climate  change  disasters.  None  of

these challenges emerged overnight.

The warning signs have been there. The question is whether our attention

lasts long enough to act.

And what we neglect has a habit of shaping our future.

We see the cost of that neglect every day.

In  my  region,  from  Lebanon  to  Yemen,  to  Sudan,  protracted  conﬂict  is

deepening humanitarian suﬀering.

And  if  anyone  had  any  doubt  that  a  crisis  in  our  part  of  the  world  stays

there,  just  look  at  the  energy  and  grocery  bills  of  ordinary  families,  from

Mumbai to Madrid to Minnesota.

The  Iran  war  has  shown  how  quickly  instability  can  disrupt  trade,

investment, and lives beyond the region.

Then there is Gaza.

For decades, I have stood before this Assembly and warned of the dangers

of leaving the Palestinian-Israeli conﬂict unresolved.

But  the  international  community  chose  to  manage  the  conﬂict,  not

confront it.

And  every  new  Israeli  violation  was  treated  as  “temporary”,  diverting

attention  from  the  reality  being  created  on  the  ground.  Until  temporary

became permanent, and permanent became policy.

Of  course,  this  is  not  the  world’s  only  injustice.  But  one  of  the  world’s

longest-running  occupations  forces  a  basic  question:  If  international  law

can be ignored for decades, then what exactly is that law worth?

And how can we enforce it if we won’t even call out its violations?

In  Gaza,  the  evidence  is  overwhelming:  In  the  ﬁrst  300  days  of  the  so-

called ceaseﬁre, at least 300 Palestinian children were killed. Jordan’s ﬁeld

hospitals  have  also  been  targeted.  President  Trump  has  pushed  hard  for

moving  the  goalposts,  continuing  its  attacks  and  destruction  of  civilian

infrastructure,  refusing  to  withdraw,  and  squeezing  Palestinians  into

barely a third of Gaza.

This  can  no  longer  be  dismissed  as  temporary  military  measures,  or  a

consequence of war. Accountability begins when we call things what they

are:  an  attempt  to  erase  Palestinian  life  and  impose  a  new  territorial

reality in Gaza.

And while the world has been focused on Gaza, something extraordinarily

dangerous is unfolding in the West Bank.

Some may think we have seen this before.

Settlements. Violence. Displacement. More of the same.

But it is not. Nor is it simply an escalation. This is a fundamental shift.

What was once a creeping process has exploded into something far more

aggressive.

Settler  violence  is  rampant.  Palestinians  are  being  beaten,  shot  and

terrorised. Homes torched. Property destroyed. Families driven from their

land.

And  Israel  is  tightening  its  grip  on  more  of  the  West  Bank,  seizing  land,

expanding settlements and pushing Palestinians out.

It is time to see what is happening for what it really is. Because when the

language is sanitised, the actions become normalised.

Demolishing  Palestinian  homes  to  expand  illegal  settlements  is  not  “law

enforcement.” It is forcible transfer.

Appropriating  occupied  land  is  not  “land  registration.”  It  is  de-facto

annexation.

A  choking  network  of  checkpoints  and  barriers

is  not  “security”

infrastructure. It is a system of subjugation.

Systematic attacks on Palestinian communities are not “settler unrest.”

The  Israeli  government

‘criticises’  the  violence  before

international

audiences.  They  call  those  responsible  a  “handful  of  rioters.”  They  assure

us that Israel is a country governed by law.

Yet, what’s happening on the ground says otherwise: Israeli soldiers stand

by as settlers attack Palestinians, often protecting the attackers or joining

them.  They  have  blocked  ambulances  from  reaching  the  injured.  They

have targeted international journalists who are trying to say the truth.

And  when  soldiers  watch,  enable,  and  sometime  even  participate  in

violence against civilians, this is no longer about “a handful of rioters.”

And the question is no longer whether a few extremists are breaking the

law. The question is, is this the behaviour of a democratic state governed

by law?

What is unfolding across the West Bank is not a series of isolated acts. It is

elements  of  a  single  policy  to  compel  an  entire  population  to  leave  their

land.

And there is a name for that: forced displacement.

And that is a war crime.

If  we  are  to  resolve  the  Palestinian-Israeli  conﬂict,  the  world  must

abandon some illusions:

The ﬁrst is that Gaza and the West Bank are separate stories. They are not.

They are two fronts of the same Israeli strategy. In both, Palestinians are

being  killed.  In  both,  the  reality  on  the  ground  is  being  remade.  Gaza

through destruction. The West Bank through de-facto annexation.

The objective is the same: To make a viable Palestinian state impossible.

Another  illusion  is  that  this  Israeli  leadership’s  rejection  of  Palestinian

This government has been accelerating settlements and land seizures.

But  it  began  long  before.  Since  Oslo,  the  map  has  changed—piece  by

And the most dangerous illusion:

That the Arab world never sought peace.

The Arab Peace Initiative in 2002 oﬀered Israel normalisation with 57 Arab

and  Muslim  states,  including  Iran  and  Iraq  at  the  time,  in  exchange  for

For  over  twenty  years,  that  oﬀer  has  stood.  The  obstacle  hasn’t  been  the

willing to accept it.

This Israeli government understands the power of attention. And lately, it

has not liked the attention it’s been getting.

And  the  question  here  is:  If  Israel  continues  its  antagonistic  approach  in

My friends,

Whether  in  Gaza,  Sudan,  Ukraine,  or  anywhere  people  live  with  war,

King delivers Jordan’s address at 81st UNGA - King Abdullah II Official Website

Mr. President, Excellencies,

The international order is experiencing a period of great instability. The free and open international order based on the rule of law that we  have  fostered  is  facing  difficult  challenges  on  multiple  fronts. Amid  a  shifting  balance  of  power  and  intensifying  geopolitical competition, innocent civilian lives are being lost around the world every day.

The  “stable  post-Cold  War  era”  is  now  a  thing  of  the  past.  The distribution  of  goods  is  stagnating,  people  across  the  world  are suffering  from  high  cost  of  living,  progress  towards  development goals is not on track, and human rights issues are arising in various places around the world.

Against this backdrop, has the United Nations, now eighty years on since its foundation, been failing to fulfill its role in promoting peace and stability around the world? We are even hearing such concerns today.

Despite  these  concerns,  the  United  Nations  has  never  been  more important than it is today in bringing about peace and stability to the world, and enabling the international community to overcome new challenges and prosper. Japan will continue to fulfill its significant responsibilities towards the United Nations. And I am here today to express that resolve.

This  year  marks  the  70th  anniversary  of  Japan’s  accession  to  the United Nations. In this milestone year, I would first like to address how Japan has been tackling the challenges facing the international community, working hand-in-hand with the United Nations. Then, together with you all, I would like to take this opportunity to revisit the role of the United Nations in the international community.

2.  Challenges  facing  the  International  Community  in  light  of Escalating International Tensions

First, let us turn our attention to escalating international tensions.

The situation in the Middle East has been growing increasingly tense, and free and safe navigation is increasingly under challenge in the Strait  of  Hormuz,  which  is an  international  public  good.  Japan,  in cooperation with the international community, has been continuing to engage in diplomatic efforts with a view to achieving an early de-escalation of the situation across the Middle East.

Furthermore,  supply  concerns  regarding  fuel,  chemical  products, and medical supplies, are causing significant impact on people’s lives and  business  operations.  Due  to  disruptions  in  the  supply  of fertilizers, the risk of a food crisis is mounting, with Africa and Asia being hit particularly hard.

For many years, we have engaged in dynamic trade in the free and open  seas  spanning  the  Pacific  Ocean  to  the  Indian  Ocean,  and together, we have built a strong and prosperous region. This holds true also in the Atlantic Ocean and Mediterranean Sea. We wish to extend this to Africa as well, to turn it into a main artery for growth and  prosperity.  To  that  end,  exactly  ten  years  ago,  former  Prime Minister  ABE  Shinzo  advocated  a  “Free  and  Open  Indo-Pacific (FOIP)”  at  the  Tokyo  International  Conference  on  African Development (TICAD) held in Kenya.

However, due to the recent intensification of geopolitical tensions, free trade has been hampered, and stable energy supplies, and supply chains in general, have been disrupted.

Amid this situation, in May this year, I announced the ”Updated Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP)”. There I appealed that it is essential for countries to acquire the capabilities to freely determine their own futures and resilience across economic, social, and security domains.

Japan places particular emphasis on the following three pillars that embody this idea.

First,  Japan  is  engaged  in  strengthening  the  resilience  of  supply chains for energy and critical materials.

For global energy security, it is crucial to ensure free and transparent energy trade, engage in international coordination on strengthening oil  stockpiling, and  enhance  collaboration  between  producing  and consuming countries. Japan has also launched the “Partnership On Wide  Energy  and  Resources  Resilience  Asia  (POWERR  Asia)”  to strengthen  energy  and  resource  supply  resilience  in  Asia,  and  has been  promoting  cooperation  in  areas  such  as  stockpiling  capacity development and credit provision.

Furthermore,  Japan  is  currently  formulating  a  comprehensive cooperation plan aimed at strengthening the economic and energy resilience  of  the  Gulf  countries  in  the  Middle  East.  Through  this initiative,  we  will  work  to  further  strengthen  the  collaboration between  the  Asia-Pacific  region,  including  Japan,  and  the  Gulf countries to ensure a stable global energy supply.

Moreover, concerns about arbitrary export restrictions are growing throughout the international community. Japan is proposing a vision for  strengthening  supply  chains,  which  encompasses  not  only  the development  of  alternative the enhancement of countries’ ability to respond to supply disruptions, in particular in the field of critical minerals.

Under  this  initiative,  we  are cooperating with countries that produce critical minerals to enable them to  play a greater role in mining,  refining, and  processing. In June,  we  established  “RISE+”  under  the  World  Bank  Group  and pledged a contribution of 20 million US dollars to help develop the infrastructure essential for critical minerals production.

Second,  Japan  is  devoted  to  enhancing  cooperation  towards  peace and stability.

Since the end of the Second World War, Japan has consistently and seriously  pursued  efforts  towards  nuclear  disarmament  and  non-proliferation. At the very heart of our aspiration for “a world without nuclear  weapons”  lies  the  earnest  plea  of  the  hibakusha:  the catastrophic  consequences  of  nuclear  weapons  must  never  be repeated.

It is Japan’s mission, as the only country to have ever suffered atomic bombings  during  war,  to  lead  the  efforts  of  the  international community  towards  a  “world  without  nuclear  weapons”.  Japan strongly calls for solidarity within the international community to maintain  and  strengthen  the  Nuclear  Non-Proliferation  Treaty (NPT)  regime,  to  which  both  nuclear-weapon  states  and  non-nuclear-weapon  states  are  parties.  Furthermore, Japan  will persistently  advance  realistic  and  practical  efforts,  including enhancing  the  transparency  of  nuclear  forces, and  promoting  a deeper understanding of the realities of atomic bombings.

The situations in Ukraine and North Korea have reminded the world of  growing  risks  and  threats  posed  by  nuclear  weapons.  There  are also  concerns  regarding  the  proliferation  of  nuclear-  and  missile-related  technologies the  strengthening  of  military cooperation  between  Russia  and  North  Korea.  The  security  of  the Indo-Pacific and the Euro-Atlantic is inseparable.

The advancement of North Korea’s nuclear and missile programs, as well as its use of malicious cyber activities, including cryptocurrency thefts as a source of funding, are clear violations of relevant Security Council resolutions and pose a serious threat to international peace and  security.  The  full implementation  of  Security  Council resolutions, under the principle of the complete denuclearization of North Korea, is essential.

Moreover,  the  issue  of  abductions  by  North  Korea  is  an  ongoing matter  with  lives  at  stake.  The  abductees  are  still  denied  their freedoms, and their families continue to suffer. This  is a matter of grave  concern  not  only  for  Japan,  but  for  the  international community.  As  the  abductees  and  their  families  are  aging,  the abductions issue must be resolved immediately.

For  the  sake  of  the  future  of  both  Japan  and  North  Korea,  I  am prepared to engage in dialogue and take concrete action to establish a mutually fruitful relationship in accordance with the Japan–DPRK Pyongyang Declaration.

Third,  Japan  will  continue  to  contribute  to  the  maintenance  and development of a free and open international order based on the rule of law.

Any  attempts  to  unilaterally  change  the  status  quo  by  force  or coercion are contrary to the principles enshrined in the Charter of the  United  Nations  and  must  never  be  tolerated  anywhere  in  the world.

Russia’s aggression against Ukraine is the most obvious example. A permanent  member  of  the  Security  Council,  with  a  special responsibility for international peace and security, has initiated an act of aggression against  another country, and has vetoed Security Council  resolutions  concerning  its  own  actions.  In  this  current situation, it must be said that the Security Council is not functioning for international peace.

Since  the  end  of  the  Second  World  War,  Japan,  as  a  peace-loving nation,  has  attached  great  importance  to  the  rule  of  law  in  the settlement  of  any  disputes.  This  is  demonstrated  by  Japan’s consistent  support  for,  and  its  contributions  of  judges  to,  various international  judicial  organs,  such  as  the  International  Court  of Justice  (ICJ),  the  International  Criminal  Court  (ICC)  and  the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS).

We established a unit for peace mediation within the Government of Japan in March of this year. Japan will play a more proactive role in the peaceful settlement of disputes.

Furthermore,  the  maritime  order  based  on  the  rule  of  law  is currently being greatly shaken in the Strait of Hormuz. Ensuring free and  safe  navigation  through  the  Strait  of  Hormuz  for  all  vessels without additional costs, as has been the case, is extremely important not only for the security of the Middle East, but also for the stability of the global economy as a whole. Similarly, it is essential to ensure stability in the Bab el-Mandeb  Strait.  Japan  will  continue to work closely  with  relevant  countries  and  the  International  Maritime Organization (IMO) towards the maintenance of the maritime order in the Middle East.

3. Japan’s Commitment to the United Nations and Multilateralism

Next,  I  would  like  to  set  out  Japan’s  efforts  and  commitments towards the United Nations and multilateralism.

Since becoming a Member State of the United Nations in 1956, Japan has  acted  decisively  to  address  global  challenges,  such  as  the eradication of poverty, economic and social development, women’s empowerment, climate change, and global health. We have done so through  our  Official  Development  Assistance  (ODA),  channeled international  organizations,  and  have bilaterally  or  through deepened our solidarity with the Global South.

To  date,  Japan  has  provided  ODA  totaling  over  670  billion  US dollars  to  developing  countries  and  regions,  and  has  dispatched almost  60,000  Japan  Overseas  Cooperation  Volunteers  to  99 countries.  Additionally,  Japan  has  been  promoting  initiatives towards achieving universal health coverage (UHC) across the globe.

Since  1993,  Japan  has  co-organized  the  TICAD  together  with  the United  Nations.  TICAD  has  served  as  a  platform  for  reflecting Africa’s voice in the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), and for Japan to first put  forward  the concept of  FOIP.  Africa  is endowed with a dynamic young population and possesses enormous economic potential.  Japan  will  continue  to  promote  its  diplomacy  towards Africa  so  that  Japan  and  Africa  can  become  more  resilient  and prosperous  together.  For  example,  we  will  promote  industrial development, job creation, and enhanced connectivity in Africa.

Furthermore,  next  year,  I  will  host  the  Pacific  Islands  Leaders Meeting  (PALM)  in  Yokohama,  Japan,  which  Japan  has  convened together  with  the  Pacific  Islands  region  since  1997.  Japan  aims  to further deepen our collaboration with the Pacific Island Countries region  and  promote  the  stability  and  prosperity  of  the  region, including addressing common challenges such as maritime security and climate change.

Several large-scale disasters have occurred and continuously caused extreme  damage  around  the  world  this  year,  including  in  Japan. Natural disasters  are becoming more severe  and  frequent. Japan is striving  to  become  the  world’s  leading  nation  in  disaster  risk reduction. To share Japan’s expertise and technology in disaster risk reduction and contribute to global efforts in this field, I appointed a new  Minister  of  State  for  International  Disaster  Risk  Reduction Cooperation in my Cabinet reshuffle last week. I myself, in 2015, as Minister  for  Internal  Affairs  and  Communications,  attended  the United Nations World Conference on Disaster Reduction, where the Sendai  Framework  for  Disaster  Risk  Reduction  was  adopted. Promoting this framework remains one of our top priorities to this day. It is in Sendai that Japan will host the Asia-Pacific Ministerial Conference on Disaster Risk Reduction in October next year.

To protect the lives of present and future generations, all States must take serious action to tackle global warming. I believe that climate action and economic growth can go hand-in-hand.

Japan has been advancing Green Transformation (GX) efforts with the  goal  of  achieving  net-zero  by  2050  by  harnessing  Japan’s technological capabilities. Such capabilities include establishing the basis for the production and engineering of materials such as green steel, utilizing the world’s most efficient gas-fired power generation, and popularizing the adoption of energy-efficient data centers.

We  will  enhance  these  efforts  with  a  view  to  strengthening  the resilience  of  the  energy  supply-demand  structure  and  vigorously advance  the  Policy  Package  for  Wide  Energy  and  Resources Resilience (POWERR  GX). Furthermore,  Japan  will  contribute  to  global  climate  action, including through GX-related efforts, such as the Asia Zero Emission Community  (AZEC)  that  simultaneously  achieve  decarbonization, energy security and economic growth.

through  Green  Transformation

Next year, Japan will host the World Horticultural Exposition 2027 in  Yokohama,  which  is  an  industrial  trade  fair  showcasing  green technologies  and  approaches  to  sustainable  development.  We sincerely hope that many of you will come to join this expo.

There  are  also  challenges  arising  from  technological  innovation. Whilst advances in AI bring tremendous opportunities for humanity, they also pose challenges, including those related to national security. We also urgently need measures to tackle the spread of information not based on facts, as well as the spread of propaganda. Japan took the initiative to launch the “Hiroshima AI Process”, establishing the world’s first international principles and code of conduct to govern generative AI. In parallel, Japan has been working with like-minded partners and Global South partners to co-create a “safe, secure and trustworthy AI” ecosystem, and will enhance cooperation on safety to respond to the risks of highly capable frontier AI. To accelerate these efforts, we intend to host an AI Summit in Japan at the earliest opportunity.

Since the end of the Second World War, Japan has built the peace and  prosperity  it  has  today  through  the  tireless  efforts  of  our predecessors and the goodwill of a large number of countries. In the course of these efforts, Japan itself has consistently acted in the spirit of  multilateralism  towards  addressing  challenges  facing  the international community.

However, these challenges cannot be solved by any single country acting alone. Now, more than ever, the flag of the United Nations must  be  held  high,  and  under  that  banner,  Member  States  must mobilize the collective strength of the membership to elaborate new rules and build a framework for cooperation. I am convinced that the United Nations is the only organization capable of taking the helm on a global scale.

To this end as well, reform of the United Nations is essential.  The United Nations is a “vessel”, and the responsibility for determining its  contents  lies  with  us,  namely  the  Member  States.  Rather  than lamenting the institutional fatigue of the United Nations, Member States should unite with one heart, vigorously advance reform of the United Nations and transform the organization into a more resilient and effective United Nations. Let us move forward, building on the achievements of the current Secretary-General António Guterres.

At the same time, the Charter of the United Nations, which is now 81  years  old,  should  also  be  reviewed.  Regarding  the  so-called “enemy  States”  clauses,  a  United  Nations  General  Assembly resolution was adopted in 2005 to delete references to ‘enemy States’ from the Charter of the United Nations, expressing the resolve of the Heads of State and Government of all Member States. In accordance with this resolution, these clauses must be deleted. I would like to strongly emphasize this position as Japan takes pride and honor in its significant contributions to the efforts of the United Nations for the last 70 years.

Furthermore,  as  a  matter  of  utmost  importance,  reform  of  the Security  Council  is  urgently  needed.  The  current  structure  of  the Security Council, whose mandate is to maintain international peace and security, reflects the international situation as it stood in 1945. We  need  to  transform  it  without  delay  into  a  structure  that  truly reflects the current realities of the international community. To this end, it is essential to expand the number of both permanent and non-permanent  members  in  order  to  ensure  the  legitimacy  and representativeness  of  the  Security  Council.  A majority  of Member States support the expansion of both categories.

Japan is determined to fulfill its solemn responsibility in these UN reforms.

4. Concluding Remarks

In  the  70  years  since  we  became  a  UN  Member  State,  Japan  has consistently  contributed  to  the  peace  and  prosperity  of  the international  community  as  a  peace-loving  nation,  under  its exclusively defense-oriented policy. Furthermore, we have worked hand-in-hand  with  the  United  Nations  on  the  two  indispensable tasks of establishing rules and institutions and providing support on the ground. This policy will remain unchanged in the future. In light of this history, Japan feels a sense of responsibility to safeguard the ideals of the United Nations as our beacon of hope, and to carry that light forward into the future.

To  that end, with  its  renewed  commitment to  the United Nations and  multilateralism,  Japan  will  continue  to  steadily  take  actions. Now,  at  a  time  when  the  world  is  in  turmoil,  the  United  Nations itself  must  be  reborn  as  a  “more  resilient  and  effective  United Nations”  and  regain  the  trust  of  the  international  community. Together with this more resilient and effective United Nations, Japan is  determined  to  create  peace  and  prosperity  by  making  the  Indo-Pacific  and  the  international  community  more  resilient  and prosperous.

Thank you very much.

In this regard, we propose to redevelop the United Nations mechanism for the

First  and foremost, it is  necessary to  establish, within  the framework of the General  Assembly,  the  permanent  public  registry  of  the  implementation  of resolutions and obligations by Member States.

This  Registry  could  include  the  following  information  and  ensure  the

The  first  —  systematically  record  and  verify  the  level  of  implementation  of

adopted decisions.

The second — establish the obligation for Member States to regularly submit

The third — provide analytical reviews on sectors and regions.

States.

The Registry could  be administered  by  the United Nations Secretariat, with

the support of independent experts.

If decisions of the Organization are systematically not implemented, I propose

the gradual response mechanism.

The first stage — an official notification to the concerned State, followed by

consultations with the relevant bodies of the Organization.

The second stage — the deployment of a monitoring mission to the country concerned to assess the objective obstacles preventing the implementation of the decisions and to prepare recommendations.

The  third  stage  —  consideration  of  the  case  —  right  here  —  at  a  plenary meeting of the General Assembly to determine the status of the concerned State in terms of its systematic implementation or non-implementation of United Nations decisions.

The fourth stage — the initiation of appropriate procedures under the Charter of the United Nations with regard to States that fail to comply with the requirements.

In  particular,  the  matter  could  be  referred  to  the  United  Nations  Security Council for consideration of restrictive measures provided for under international law, including:

The first - temporary restrictions on participation in United Nations programs.

The second - recommendations to review existing formats of cooperation.

And other diplomatic measures, where appropriate.

I believe that when cases of systematic non-implementation of United Nations’ decisions are considered, the permanent members of the Security Council should voluntarily refrain from using the veto.

If a mechanism designed to ensure the implementation of the Organization's decisions is systematically blocked by permanent members through the use of the veto, such practice would no longer be consistent with the spirit of the UN Charter and the principle of equal responsibility of Member States.

Therefore,  we  should  once  again  consider  the  possibility  of  voluntarily restraining  the  use  of  the  veto  in  matters  related  to  the  implementation  of  the Organization’s decisions.

This approach could promote universality, the equality of all states regardless

of their size, the primacy of diplomacy and avoid the double standards.

In order to implement this initiative, I propose establishing the open working group within the General Assembly with the participation of the interested Member States.

The  working  group  could  conduct  intergovernmental  consultations  and

prepare a report on possible models for the proposed mechanism.

Following these consultations, the General Assembly and the Security Council

should consider adopting the relevant resolutions and decisions.

The strategic objective of this initiative is to ensure that the decisions of the Organization are treated not merely as political recommendations, but as genuine international obligations.

Improvement of their implementation would strengthen the rule of international

law and reinforce confidence in the United Nations.

Kyrgyzstan is  ready to initiate  interstate discussions on the development of

The prior review of sanctions initiatives would help ensure that their potential

humanitarian, economic and social consequences are taken into account.

An important element of the proposed mechanism should be  the  enhanced

transparency and accountability.

States  initiating  sanctions  should  clearly  indicate  the  legal  basis  for  such measures,  explain  their  necessity  and  objectives,  and  define  clear  criteria  and conditions for their eventual removal.

I believe it would be appropriate to establish, under the auspices of the United Nations,  the  unified  international  mechanism  for  monitoring  sanctions  and reviewing them on a regular basis.

Only  then  can  the  central  role  of  the  United  Nations  in  maintaining

international peace and security be strengthened and its mandate enhanced.

This would also help eliminate the risk of sanctions being used arbitrarily by

one country against another for political or economic gain.

No state should act arbitrarily.

The United Nations must be strong.

Every  country  should  tremble  when  the  United  Nations  intends  to  impose sanctions. Only then the strict international order can be established in the world.

Otherwise,  some  decisions  of  the  United  Nations  may  no  longer  be  taken

seriously, while states simply act according to their own discretion.

Every decision of the United Nations should be implemented without delay.

If  a  state  fails  to  implement  such  decision  and  other  countries  cease

cooperation with it, the effectiveness of sanctions will increase.

Only then will decisions can be implemented promptly, and the United Nations

Otherwise, existing sanctions will become a sort of children's toy.

Kyrgyzstan is a mountainous country.

We are particularly vulnerable to the effects of melting glaciers.

This is not an abstract threat.

It is an environmental challenge of regional significance.

I believe it is extremely important and necessary to unite international efforts

in addressing climate challenges and the problems facing mountainous regions.

Therefore, Kyrgyzstan stands fully ready to serve within the United Nations as the  voice  of  small  and  developing  countries  in  addressing  the  climate-related challenges affecting mountainous regions.

Continuing the topic of climate change, I would like to draw your attention to

another environmental challenge.

As we all know, global problems and disasters often have their origins at the

local level.

This issue concerns the unique high-altitude Lake Issyk-Kul, which is part of the UNESCO Biosphere Reserve and is included among wetlands of international importance under the Ramsar framework.

Today, this invaluable natural water reservoir is under severe climatic stress.

Over the past 170 years, the water level has fallen by almost 14 meters, while over  the  past  five  years  the  rate  of  decline  has  reached  approximately  seven centimeters per year.

101  rivers  historically  flowed  into  the  lake,  but  today  only  around  30  flow

throughout the entire year.

The main source of water for Lake Issyk-Kul is the glaciers of the Tien Shan

mountains.

Over the past 70 years, more than 30 % of the region's mountain glaciers have

melted.

Nearly 20 % of this reduction has occurred within just the past seven to ten

years.

This  process  poses  a  direct  threat  to  the  biodiversity  of  the  region  and

economic stability of hundreds of thousands of people.

As part of our efforts to preserve Lake Issyk-Kul, Kyrgyzstan is mobilizing all

available domestic resources.

In particular, the State Concept for the Sustainable Development of the Issyk-

Kul Ecological and Economic System until 2030 is being implemented.

Strict environmental restrictions have been introduced, and pilot projects have been  launched  to  monitor  the  depth  of  the  lake  using  underwater  robotic technologies.

Large-scale efforts to clean the lakebed  and its waters are continuing  on  a

regular basis.

The scale and speed of climate change exceed the capacities of any individual

mountain country and require consolidated international action.

The loss of Lake Issyk-Kul would not be merely a local tragedy.

It would become an irreversible environmental loss for the entire region.

In order to understand the potential scale of this environmental challenge and the costs associated with preventing it, it is important to look at the fate of the Aral Sea and Lake Chad, both of which have suffered severely over recent decades.

(Pictures)

Please take a look.

Not so long ago, the Aral Sea and Lake Chad, just like Issyk-Kul today, were

full and reservoir with full of water.

Today, they have largely dried up.

For us, these examples must serve as a clear warning.

Taking this opportunity, I officially call upon the United Nations, international financial institutions and donor countries to support our initiative to establish, under the auspices of the Organization, the Special joint trust fund for the preservation of Lake Issyk-Kul.

In  order  to  demonstrate  our  commitment  through  concrete  action,  we  are

prepared to contribute 10 million US dollars from the state budget to this fund.

In our culture, there is a concept known as “Amanat.”

It means the duty to carefully preserve what our ancestors have entrusted to

us and to pass it on to future generations.

In this sense, it would be fair to state that Lake Issyk-Kul is our shared climate

Amanat.

We are not asking for help.

We are proposing  a joint global partnership to preserve  this unique  natural

resource of the Earth.

Before it is too late, let us unite our efforts and resources within the framework

of this trust fund.

Ladies and Gentlemen,

The challenges before us are shared. Therefore, our response to them must

We stand at the threshold of a new era of change.

Safe, just and sustainable future can be built only through collective action.

The destiny of our planet and future generations is the responsibility of each

and every one of us.

This year, Kyrgyzstan celebrates the 35th anniversary of its independence.

Throughout  this  period,  our  country  has  faced  many  different  challenges. Since  then  we  chose  cooperation  over  confrontation,  creation  over  destruction, and embarked upon the path of sustainable development.

There  is  one  thing  we  must  all  remember:  peace  does  not  come  about  by

Therefore,  let  us  turn  our  words  into  action  -  concrete  steps  that  improve

Let  us  build  together  a  world  in  which  dialogue  is  stronger  than  weapons, mutual  respect  is  stronger  than  fear,  and  cooperation  among  nations  delivers tangible results for all humanity.
