Climate Change

Yet even as we advance, the climate crisis is moving the goalposts. This year, our Federation and the wider Caribbean face severe drought; by the end of May,

rainfall was 44 percent below the long-term average. We are investing in resilient infrastructure, but no Small Island Developing State can adapt indefinitely to a crisis  the  world  continues  to  intensify.  Adaptation  cannot  excuse  inaction elsewhere.

Distinguished  colleagues,  the  science  is  unequivocal.  The  years  2015 to  2025 were the warmest on record, and in 2025 global average temperature remained about 1.43 degrees Celsius above the pre-industrial baseline, while global mean sea level stood approximately eleven centimetres higher than in 1993. For island nations, this is a question of sovereignty and statehood. If our coastlines retreat, our sovereignty must not.

Climate-induced  sea-level  rise  must  never  erase  a  State's  international  legal personality, extinguish its UN membership, deprive its people of nationality, or diminish  lawfully  established  maritime  zones  and  sovereign  rights.  The International Law Commission has laid foundations for continuity of statehood, sovereignty and maritime entitlements. This Assembly must turn them into firm guarantees.

International  law  has  spoken  with  increasing  clarity.  Saint  Kitts  and  Nevis welcomed the International Court of Justice Advisory Opinion on States' climate obligations.  Clarification  must  now  become  compliance,  commitments  must become conduct, and promises must become performance. States must reduce emissions,  strengthen  adaptation,  honour  climate-finance  responsibilities  and cooperate with countries bearing consequences vastly disproportionate to their contribution to this crisis.

Those who contributed least must not pay the greatest price.

Our oceans must also move from promises to protection. Saint Kitts and Nevis ratified the BBNJ in 2025. Implementation now matters: large ocean states need access  to  capacity-building,  marine  technology,  scientific  knowledge  and financing, while benefits from marine genetic resources must be shared fairly.

For island nations, the ocean is not the space between us and the world; it is our highway, heritage, livelihood and lifeline.

MVI - From Recognition to Application

Across climate action, sea-level rise and ocean governance, one reality remains: resilience has a cost. For decades, Small Island Developing States have argued that income is not the same as resilience. Per capita income cannot show exposure to hurricanes, drought, pandemics, shipping disruption, energy shocks, conflict or tourism collapse, nor how quickly one shock can erase years of investment.

This year, Saint Kitts and Nevis stood before the United Nations and completed a pilot Vulnerability and Resilience Country Profile under the Multidimensional Vulnerability  Index  Framework.  And  what  did  we  learn?  We  learnt  what  our grandparents always knew. A house can look strong from the road and still have rot in the rafters. Vulnerability is not a statistic, it is a roof that was destroyed in hurricane Beryl. It is the school that became a shelter. It is the family rebuilding for the 3rd time in a decade because storms have no patience for GNI per capita. We are not asking that Gross National Income be discarded; we are asking that it stop being expected to tell a story it was never designed to tell. GNI can count our coconuts and our cruise ships. It cannot count our courage and it cannot count the price we pay to simply remain. It cannot capture the cost of rebuilding the same bridge, clinic or seawall again and again, while nations twice our size and half our vulnerability borrow cheaper than we do.

We therefore call on the World Bank, the IMF, development banks, climate funds and every partner here to incorporate MVI into the architecture of financing. Not as  charity,  but  as  arithmetic  and  justice  made  real.  If  vulnerability  can  be measured, it must be considered.

Artificial Intelligence and the Emerging Digital Divide

Mr. President, the next great divide between nations must not be digital. Artificial intelligence offers extraordinary possibilities. Saint Kitts and  Nevis intends to participate. But we must ask who will shape this new age and who will live with decisions made elsewhere.

At the end of 2025, some 2.2 billion people remained offline. But the AI divide also concerns computing power, data, research, skills, energy, cybersecurity and capital. With the global AI market projected to reach about US 4.8 trillion dollars by 2033, developing countries cannot simply consume technologies designed and governed elsewhere. We must have a place where AI's future is decided.

Saint Kitts and Nevis welcomes the Independent International Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence and the Global Dialogue on AI Governance. Inclusion must lead to capability. Developing countries need affordable computing power, infrastructure, skills and safeguards for privacy, data sovereignty, cybersecurity and  rights.  At  home,  we  are  advancing  a  Whole-of-Government  Technology Strategy,  securing  digital  identity  and  digital  public  services.  Regionally,  the Caribbean AI Task Force supports cooperation on governance, innovation and responsible adoption.

Artificial intelligence is already transforming the world.

Saint Kitts and Nevis chooses to help shape that transformation!

CARICOM, Diplomacy and Global Peace

As small states, we know a simple truth: alone, we are small; together, we are formidable. The Caribbean's declaration as a Zone of Peace must retain its force as geopolitical competition moves closer to our shores. Our response must remain anchored  in  sovereignty,  territorial  integrity,  international  law,  peaceful settlement  of  disputes  and  diplomacy.  CARICOM  supports  the  International Court of Justice as the lawful path for resolving the Guyana-Venezuela dispute and the judicial process concerning Belize and Guatemala.

We defend international law because, for small states especially, the alternative is a world where power becomes the rule. Across Gaza, Ukraine, Sudan, Yemen, Chad and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, civilians continue to bear an unconscionable burden. Saint Kitts and Nevis affirms one standard: international law  applied  consistently,  not  selectively;  and  conscience  applied  evenly,  not conveniently.

There can be no hierarchy of human suffering.

Mr. President, the future of multilateralism also depends on its leadership.

Saint  Kitts  and  Nevis  proudly  joins  CARICOM  in  endorsing  Her  Excellency Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett of Guyana for the office of United Nations Secretary-General. Her distinguished record of service, commitment to multilateralism and understanding of the challenges facing developing nations reflect the leadership this moment demands. Her candidature, as an Indigenous woman from a small developing state, also reaffirms that global leadership must be defined not by the size of a nation, but by the vision, integrity and capacity of those called to serve.

Africa - Caribbean Cooperation

Mr. President, few bridges carry greater historical meaning or future potential than  that  between  Africa  and  the  Caribbean.  The  Atlantic,  once  a  passage  of forced  displacement  and  separation,  is  becoming  a  pathway  of  return  and reconnection. Africa-Caribbean cooperation must move beyond sentiment; our shared history must help build a shared future through capital, trade, technology, knowledge, culture and coordinated diplomacy.

South-South cooperation must be felt in jobs, businesses, knowledge transfer and opportunity.  It  complements,  not  replaces,  North-South  cooperation  and  the obligations of developed countries.

Greater  agency  must  also  include  justice.  At  the  Second  Africa-CARICOM Summit,  our  leaders  signed  the  Addis  Ababa  Declaration,  and  this  year,  the

African  Union's  reparations  mechanisms  and  the  CARICOM  Reparations Commission held their first joint meeting, establishing permanent coordination. On 25 March 2026, this General Assembly adopted Resolution 80/250, declaring the  trafficking  of  enslaved  Africans  and  racialised  chattel  enslavement  of Africans as the gravest crime against humanity. Saint Kitts and Nevis welcomed this historic recognition, but recognition cannot be the destination. Reparatory justice must move from recognition to remedy and from words to action.

Haiti, Cuba & Taiwan

Distinguished colleagues, when we speak of reparatory justice, sovereignty and solidarity, Haiti cannot be an afterthought. Approximately 1.47 million people are  internally  displaced,  while  nearly  half  the  population  faces  acute  food insecurity. In the very near future, the first round of presidential and legislative elections will take place. The Haitian people must choose their leaders freely, credibly and safely. Saint Kitts and Nevis joins CARICOM in calling for the full deployment of the United Nations-authorised Gang Suppression Force and the timely renewal of its mandate, alongside Haitian-led recovery and governance.

Mr. President, we remain deeply concerned about the humanitarian situation in Cuba.  St.  Kitts  and  Nevis  has  contributed  humanitarian  relief  to  the  Cuban people,  and  our  very  own  Nationals  studying  there.  We  welcome  the  recent measures undertaken by the Cuban Government to improve the well-being of its people and encourage further meaningful action. We urge constructive dialogue between the Governments of Cuba and the United States. Engagement, mutual respect and cooperation offer the best path towards improving the lives of the Cuban people and advancing peace and stability throughout our region.

Saint  Kitts  and  Nevis  remains  steadfast  in  its  friendship  with  the  Republic  of China (Taiwan) and support for its meaningful international participation. Earlier this  year,  we  joined  other  Member  States  in  requesting  Taiwan's  observer participation  in  the  Seventy-ninth  World  Health  Assembly.  We  continue  to support  its  meaningful  participation  in  the  World  Health  Organization,  the

International  Civil  Aviation  Organization  and  other relevant mechanisms,  and reiterate that differences across the Taiwan Strait must be resolved peacefully.

To The Young People, The Unseen Majority

Mr.  President,  no  generation  has  a  greater  stake  in  our  decisions  than  young people. Half of the world's population is under thirty, yet 67 million young people were unemployed last year and more than a quarter of a billion were neither in employment, education nor training. AI, the green transition and climate change are reshaping their future jobs. We must prepare them.

Last  year,  our  Prime  Minister  introduced  this  Assembly  to  our  ASPIRE Programme  -  Achieving  Success  through  Personal  Investment,  Resources  and Education - for citizens aged 5 to 18. Built on savings, investment and financial education, ASPIRE has opened more than four thousand savings accounts, with our Government committing more than US 2 million dollars to give children a financial foundation for adulthood. We are now piloting our financial education curriculum  in  schools  and  training  teachers  for  national  rollout.  We  are  not simply giving children money; we are giving them the knowledge to make money work for them. Financial independence must not be reserved for those born into wealth.

Conclusion

Mr. President, distinguished colleagues, for eighty-one years this institution has represented  a  bold  conviction:  that  despite  our  differences,  nations  can  come together  around  common  rules,  responsibilities  and  human  dignity.  That conviction is worth defending. But institutions cannot live indefinitely on their founding promises. They must be judged by what those promises produce.

Saint Kitts and Nevis remains ready to do its part and to work with every nation here towards a more peaceful, sustainable, equitable and humane world.

Trust is not  something we  can  demand.  It must be earned:  by  promising less, delivering more, and letting the proof speak where our words once stood alone.

Let this Assembly be remembered not for what was said here, but for what was done after.

The tide is rising. Let our resolve rise faster still.

Thank you.

I would like to begin by expressing my gratitude and respect to all Member

States of the United Nations and the staff of the UN Secretariat for their

dedication to a prosperous future for all of humanity.

I extend my sincere congratulations to His Excellency Dr. Khalilur Rahman on

assuming the Presidency of the 81st Session of the UN General Assembly. I also

express my gratitude and pay tribute to Secretary-General António Guterres for

his tireless service over the past decade.

The United Nations, which has a history of upholding human dignity and

pioneering the way for future generations, now stands at a grave crossroads.

The glacial flooding in Nepal that claimed many lives and destroyed the

foundations of people’s livelihoods evidences that the climate crisis is a reality

of today, not tomorrow.

Persistent armed conflicts around the world, including those in Ukraine and the

Middle East, continue to threaten the survival of humanity.

Emerging technologies such as drones are rapidly transforming warfare and

posing serious challenges to human rights and the international law-based order.

Tensions surrounding the Strait of Hormuz are undermining the fundamental

principles of ‘free and safe navigation’ and heightening the vulnerability of

energy supply chains.

“The United Nations was not created in order to bring us to heaven, but in order

to save us from hell.”

These words of the second Secretary-General of the UN, Dag Hammarskjöld,

compel us to ask ourselves:

Is the United Nations today capable of saving humanity from war, poverty, and

disaster?

Is the United Nations living up to its promise of restoring peace and achieving

sustainable development?

Ironically, the geopolitical crisis brought on by the turbulence in international

order has reminded us of the cherished value of multilateral cooperation and

international norms.

In an era of fragmentation marked by fierce competition for immediate survival,

values such as cooperation, mutual prosperity, and solidarity can sound like

hollow outcries.

However, like the founders who, having witnessed the ravages of war,

conceived the United Nations, the deeper the crisis, the more we need to return

to the basic principles of the UN.

Last year, I proudly announced from this podium that the Republic of Korea,

which will be a beacon of light for global citizens, has returned to the

international community.

Today, I stand here to make clear the Republic of Korea’s bold resolve to lead

the effort to restore the spirit of the United Nations and reconnect the world, as

a nation that has risen through the solidarity of the international community.

The worldwide popularity of K-culture serves as an example demonstrating that

universal empathy is possible, showcasing the potential of global connection.

The stories and content that grew out of Korea’s unique experience have

become a ‘language of solidarity’ that crosses borders.

Just as culture has connected people across borders, so too can nations reunite in

the face of common problems.

The Republic of Korea will build on the power of empathy and solidarity that

culture has brought to light. We will harness that power to address the common

challenges facing all of humanity.

To that end, allow me to set out the three visions of the ‘K-Initiative’ toward

fulfilling this commitment.

First, the ‘Global AI Universal Basic Society.’

The Artificial Intelligence revolution is both a massive opportunity and a crisis

for humanity. While it can be a core driver of new prosperity and sustainable

development, it will only deepen inequality and imbalance unless we are

properly prepared for it.

Young people around the world, in particular, are facing growing anxiety about

their employment and their future as the pace of change becomes increasingly

difficult to keep up with.

This boils down to a clear direction for the new era we seek to build. It is the

‘AI Universal Basic Society’ where everyone can benefit from technological

progress.

The Republic of Korea is pursuing an AI transformation that will ensure

stronger protection of fundamental rights across fields such as social security,

labor, housing, and culture, beginning with our ‘AI Universal Basic Health’

program.

I believe this resonates with the core spirit of the UN Sustainable Development

Goals, which prioritizes the guiding principle of “leaving no one behind.”

It also harnesses the AI revolution as a new driver to accelerate the realization

of ‘economic, social and cultural rights.’

The Republic of Korea will build the ‘Global AI Hub’ platform to share this

vision with the international community, in collaboration with international

organizations, multilateral development banks, the business sector, and

academia.

The Republic of Korea envisions a ‘Global AI Universal Basic Society’ where

no country or individual is left out from access to the basic benefits of AI

development. We will take the lead in shaping AI into a tool for solving the

shared challenges we face, such as the climate crisis, public health, food

insecurity, and refugee issues.

Second, the ‘green transformation.’

The climate crisis is often referred to as a ‘global group project shared by all 8

billion people on Earth.’

A single country cannot tackle this challenge alone. At the same time,

abandoning growth cannot bring everyone on board.

The Republic of Korea announced its ‘2035 Nationally Determined

Contributions’ as part of its active participation in the Paris Agreement and UN-

centered climate action.

The ‘Korea Green Transformation’ strategy aims to convert our industrial

structure, creating a virtuous cycle in which carbon neutrality leads to new

growth engines and decent jobs.

We are ready to share our experience and best practices with the international

community. Co-hosting the ‘4th UN Ocean Conference’ with Chile in 2028

reflects our commitment to leading discussions on the sustainable development

of our oceans.

Third, the coalition for global energy supply chains.

Recently, there have been repeated blockades of sea routes in the Strait of

Hormuz and the Red Sea. This has underscored the stark reality that the

weaponization of key energy and logistics supply routes can send severe

shockwaves to the lives of ordinary people around the world.

Freedom of navigation and safe passage through international straits is a right

grounded in international law and serves as a bedrock of the global economy.

Attacks on merchant vessels and threats to the lives and safety of crew members

cannot be justified under any circumstances.

While making greater use of existing frameworks such as the International

Energy Agency, the Republic of Korea will build a more robust framework of

cooperation for energy supply chains to prevent the supply chain crisis from

escalating into a broader threat to the global economy and people’s livelihoods.

By nature, these problems cannot be resolved by any one of us alone. At the

same time, we cannot afford to sit idly by and wait for all nations to arrive at a

single solution.

The most urgent and realistic path is for countries with the capacity and

willingness to supply global public goods to join hands and broaden the scope

of cooperation.

I would like to call this a ‘Partnership of Constructive Contributors.’

I am not seeking to propose a new organization, nor an exclusive grouping. The

idea is to respect the functions of the existing international order and the UN,

work together in a flexible and open manner in areas where each country has

particular strength, and expand our ties of cooperation into new areas.

By continuing to build on the achievements of collaborating ‘separately yet

together,’ we can move beyond geopolitical rivalry, deadlock, and

fragmentation, and rebuild trust in multilateralism.

The United Nations must evolve with the times.

Agreements reached at the negotiating table must translate into real change on

the ground, so that people around the world can feel their impact in their daily

lives.

We must reduce duplication across organizations and programs, accelerate

decision making, and direct limited resources where they are needed most.

In this spirit, the Republic of Korea supports the ‘UN 80 Initiative,’ which will

improve efficiency, prioritize field operations, and deliver greater results.

We also support the reform of the UN Security Council, so that it operates in a

more effective, democratic, and accountable manner.

The Republic of Korea will live up to its responsibility and position to deliver

results that can be vividly felt by people around the world across the UN's three

pillars of peace, development and human rights.

Through the ‘Busan Global Partnership Forum,’ we will continue to support

inclusive growth, share Korea’s development experiences such as the Saemaul

Undong, and continue to make sustainable and innovative investments.

When it comes to peace on the Korean Peninsula, the Republic of Korea knows

firsthand the change that the United Nations has brought about.

Thirty-five years ago, the two Koreas were admitted to the UN as members on

this very stage. It was a crucial turning point that laid the foundation for

peaceful coexistence, freeing us from the relentless rivalry and confrontation

that followed our division.

One year ago, I stated from this stage that the Republic of Korea would begin a

new journey toward ‘peaceful coexistence and shared growth on the Korean

Peninsula.’

Today, as we set out on this new journey, I would like to present to the

international community the three blueprints for the road to peaceful

coexistence on the Korean Peninsula.

First is inclusive peaceful coexistence built on mutual respect. Based on the

respect for each other’s systems and acknowledgement of our differences, we

will explore ways for shared growth through cooperation.

We will continue to respect the North on the international stage and seek

cooperation wherever possible. We hope that opportunities will emerge for us to

work together in the international community, in areas such as public health,

disaster response, and the climate crisis.

Second is stable peaceful coexistence that renders conflict unnecessary. We will

work to institute mechanisms for preventing crisis and managing conflicts.

Reestablishing basic channels of communication and building trust will be the

first step toward a stable peaceful coexistence.

Third is responsible peaceful coexistence contributing to world peace.

We will go beyond building a Korean Peninsula free from war and nuclear

weapons to promoting stability and cooperation in Northeast Asia, while

actively contributing to global efforts to build a world free from war and

conflict.

The most critical task is to bring an end to this decades-old war on the Korean

Peninsula and establish a lasting peace regime.

For decades, the two Koreas, along with key countries such as the U.S. and

China, have recognized the need for a peace regime on the Korean Peninsula

and discussed ways to achieve it.

Fortunately, President Trump’s resolve has recently created a hard-won

opportunity for change.

I hope the long-suspended dialogue between North Korea and the U.S. can

resume without delay. We will lay the groundwork for this to develop into a

dialogue among the parties aimed at ending the war on the Korean Peninsula

and transitioning to a peace regime.

I am confident that the dialogue for establishing a peace regime on the Korean

Peninsula can provide a valuable framework not only for normalizing relations

among the parties concerned, but also for fostering shared growth through

multilateral cooperation and promoting stability and cooperation in Northeast

Asia.

In this process, we will begin with a stop to further advances in North Korea’s

nuclear and missile capabilities, followed by their reductions in the medium

term, moving toward a Korean Peninsula free from nuclear weapons over the

long term.

I hope that the United Nations, which created a pivotal moment for peaceful

coexistence on the Korean Peninsula thirty-five years ago, and the Security

Council, which has safeguarded the peace and stability of the international

community, will once again play a responsible and constructive role.

As a direct party to peace on the Korean Peninsula, and as a pacemaker, my

government will exert every effort to open and sustain the path toward dialogue.

The true performance of UN does not lie solely in the figures and charts of

reports, or in the declarations made in conference rooms.

The raison d'etre of UN will be proven only when children's laughter replaces

gunfire, when young people can enjoy the opportunity to learn, work, and take

on new challenges, and when anyone, anywhere, can choose to live the life they

want.

In 2015, the international community adopted the Sustainable Development

Goals as our shared commitments for a bright future.

As we approach the 2030 deadline, now is the time to chart a new path forward

for the next generation.

It is imperative for young people, our future generation, to define problems

together, formulate solutions, and become co-designers who can lead the action.

We need to bring more youth voices into international decision-making by

widening opportunities for participation and communication, as well as making

bold investments in the potential of the next generation.

The Republic of Korea can testify more vividly than anyone else, to the noble

power of solidarity embodied by the United Nations.

Our own experience of achieving industrialization and democratization in the

wake of war stands as proof of how the world can bring about miraculous

changes with one mind and one heart of the international community.

We are ready to repay that solidarity with greater responsibility and

contribution.

We will reconnect a divided world, build a future that leaves no one behind, and

chart a course for the next generation to dream of a better tomorrow.

The Republic of Korea stands ready to lead the way toward a peaceful

coexistence on the Korean Peninsula, and toward “a United Nations that

delivers for all.”

Thank you

speaker_name: Sheikh Sabah Al-Khaled Al-Hamad Al-Mubarak Al-Sabah
text:
Thank you, Mr. President. In the name of God, most compassionate, most merciful. Your Excellency, president of the General Assembly, your Excellency, Secretary General, your Majesties, excellencies Highnesses, ladies and gentlemen, may the peace and blessings of God be upon you. At the outset, I am pleased to convey to you the greetings of His Highness, the Emir of the State of Kuwait, Sheikh Meshal Al-Ahmed Al-Jaber Al-Sabah, along with his wishes for the success of this session. We would also like to congratulate His Excellency, Doctor Khalilur Rahman and the Friendly People, People's Republic of Bangladesh on his election as president of the General Assembly. We affirm our support for His Excellency and we salute his wise choice of theme for this session Restoring Trust and Managing Transformation.

A United Nations that delivers for all. We would also like to express our gratitude to Her Excellency Miss Annalena Baerbock, for her valued efforts during her presidency of the previous session. We would be remiss not to applaud the efforts, good offices and initiatives of the Secretary General aimed at strengthening multilateralism and that include initiatives such as UN 80 and the pact for the future, as well as the ongoing efforts to address global challenges, crises, conflicts, wars, climate change and terrorism, as well as the efforts to assist member states in order to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals and to strengthen international cooperation on artificial intelligence. We hope that these efforts will continue beyond the conclusion of the Secretary General's term in an in a manner to guarantee the continuity of work to reform and develop the organizations bodies to enhance its effectiveness and performance in discharging its responsibilities. In this context, we emphasize that Security Council reform and the Security Council is the body charged with maintaining international peace and security has become essential to keep pace with the significant increase in the number of member states and the changes in international relations since the establishment of the organization. There is an urgent need for the Council to become more representative, effective and transparent in carrying out its responsibilities.

Mr. president since last February, the state of Kuwait, the countries of the Gulf Cooperation Council and the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan have been subjected to illegal Iranian aggression involving ballistic, ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones. All while we are not a party to the conflict in the region. These attacks are a flagrant violation of the international law, international humanitarian law and the UN charter. These brutal attacks have systematically and repeatedly targeted civilian objects and critical infrastructure, including Kuwait International Airport, power and water stations, oil facilities as well, revealing a hostile approach aimed at disrupting the foundations of life and critical infrastructure. These heinous attacks have claimed the lives of several martyrs and innocent civilians. They have also resulted in numerous injuries and have inflicted material and economic damage.

And furthermore, to inflict harm on the economies of the region and the world, and to disrupt global trade and oil markets, Iran is obstructing maritime navigation and closing the Strait of Hormuz to use it as a bargaining chip in the war in violation of international law and the relevant Security Council resolutions. In this regard, the State of Kuwait expresses its deep appreciation to the brotherly and friendly nations who have stood by Kuwait and demonstrated solidarity. We also salute the countries that have sponsored Security Council Resolution 2017 and the other resolutions issued by the Human Rights Council and the International Maritime Organization, which have condemned the Iranian aggression as a threat to international peace and security. Demanding its cessation and affirming the inherent rights of states to self-defence, as per article 51 of the UN charter. They have also stressed the importance of guaranteeing freedom of navigation without restrictions or conditions and based on. Kuwait's belief that the security and stability of the Arabian Gulf region constitutes a fundamental pillar of regional and international security and stability, as demonstrated by the repercussions of the war and Iranian aggressions.

We reiterate the support for all diplomatic efforts aimed at de-escalation and a peaceful resolution to the existing dispute, and we applaud the mediation efforts led by Qatar and Pakistan, while emphasizing the need to reach a sustainable regional understanding based on a firm commitment to the principles of good neighbourliness, respect for state sovereignty and non-interference in internal affairs, as well as refraining from the use or threat of use of force. In addition to ceasing support for proxies and militias and addressing the security concerns of all countries in the region, including. The Iranian nuclear file, ballistic missiles and drones, while stressing the guarantee of freedom and safety of navigation and the right of passage through the Straits of Hormuz and Bab el Mandeb. In accordance with the international law and the 1982 UN convention on the law of the sea. Mr. president, the State of Kuwait is committed in its foreign policy to the principles of the UN charter, in particular, respect for the principle of good neighbourliness, respect for state sovereignty and non-interference in internal affairs. Accordingly, the State of Kuwait views the brotherly Republic of Iraq as a neighbour with whom we share close ties as a and our partners in security and stability.

Since the fall of the former regime in 2003, Kuwait has supported and stood by Iraq in facing security, political and economic challenges in order to help Iraq restore its regional and international role and standing. Kuwait believes that a stable, secure and prosperous Iraq serves the shared interests of Kuwait and the entire region. In this context, the State of Kuwait commends the measures taken by the Iraqi Prime Minister, Mr. Ali al-Zaidi, to consolidate arms under state control and to strengthen Iraq's bilateral relations with neighbouring countries. We look forward to enhancing confidence building measures between the two countries and to elevate our bilateral relations to broader horizons, as well as to resolve all outstanding issues. Most important of these issues are the maritime border demarcation beyond marker 162, as per the rules of International law and the 1982 UN Convention on Law of the sea. We also emphasize the need to adhere to bilateral security and technical agreements and arrangements signed between the two countries.

Very important among these agreements is the Abdullah Agreement and the 2008 Security Exchange Protocol. These agreements serve as vital legal and practical instruments for regulating navigation, protecting the environment, combating terrorism, as well as combating the illicit trafficking of arms and narcotics, and enhancing shared security. The State of Kuwait calls upon Iraq to cooperate with the high level representative of the Secretary-General pursuant to Security Council Resolution 2792, in order to achieve the progress and desired outcomes regarding Kuwaiti prisoners and missing persons, as well as nationals of third countries and the recovery of Kuwaiti property, including the National Archives. Mr. president, the State of Kuwait reiterates its principled and firm position, condemning the ongoing violations by the Israeli occupation forces against the brotherly Palestinian people. The Palestinian people continue to suffer under difficult living conditions caused by policies of displacement, arrests and settlement. We call for the full implementation of the Comprehensive Peace Plan and its subsequent phase adopted by Security Council Resolution 2803.

This includes the complete withdrawal of Israeli occupation forces from Gaza, the assurance of humanitarian aid, access, and the return of the Palestinian Authority to the Gaza Strip. We affirm that the Gaza Strip is an integral part of the occupied Palestinian territory. In this regard, we welcome the measures and decisions taken by the United Kingdom, France and several other nations to condemn settlement activities and to impose sanctions against settlers involved in acts of violence and terrorism against Palestinians, as well as banning the import of goods and products originating from the settlements. The State of Kuwait reiterates that a just, comprehensive and lasting peace in the region remains contingent upon an end to the Israeli occupation of all Arab territories, as well as enabling the Palestinian people to exercise their legitimate and inalienable rights. It also rests upon the establishment of an independent Palestinian state on the borders of June 4th, 1967, with East Jerusalem as its capital. Mr. president, the sisterly Republic of Yemen is witnessing a serious military escalation as a result of the attacks by Houthi militias against several governorates and areas along the West Coast aimed at threatening navigation in the Bab el Mandeb Strait.

In this regard, the state of Kuwait reiterates its full support for UN led efforts aimed at a comprehensive, sustainable and Yemeni led settlement. In accordance with the three agreed references and the relevant Security Council resolutions, in particular resolution 2216. The State of Kuwait affirms that any political settlement must safeguard Yemen's unity, sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity. A settlement must end the suffering of the Yemeni people and must open prospects for security, stability and economic development. We also stress the need to preserve the security and safety of maritime navigation in the Red sea and the Bab el Mandeb Strait. We also condemn in the strongest terms the attacks by the Houthis against the sisterly kingdom of Saudi Arabia, targeting civilian and economic facilities in several cities.

In this context, we affirm that the security of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia is an integral part of the security of the State of Kuwait and the security of the GCC states. Mr. president, the State of Kuwait reiterates its solidarity with the sisterly Syrian Arab Republic. We welcome the measures taken by the international community to lift the sanctions against Syria and to remove Syria's name from the list of state sponsors of terrorism. We also affirm our support for all efforts aimed at rebuilding state institutions and aimed at advancing a Syrian led, comprehensive, inclusive political process led by the Syrians. With the active participation of all segments of society in Syria and aimed at fulfilling their aspirations for security, stability and a life of dignity. In this context, we stress the need to respect Syria's sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity We condemn and reject the attacks and incursions by Israeli occupation forces into Syrian territory.

These acts are a serious escalation and a violation of the 1974 Disengagement of Forces agreement. They undermine security and stability in the region. With regards to the sisterly Lebanese Republic, the state of Kuwait affirms the importance of Lebanese state institutions and the need to extend their full authority over the entire territory of Lebanon, and to restrict the possession of arms exclusively to the state, thereby reinforcing Lebanon's sovereignty and preserving its security and stability. Here, we also emphasize the importance of maintaining an international presence along the blue line to ensure the full implementation of UN resolution 1701, and we reiterate our demand for Israel's withdrawal from all occupied Lebanese territories. And with regards to developments in the Republic of Sudan, the Federal Republic of Somalia and the state of Libya, we affirm the need to adhere to peaceful resolution and to engage in political dialogue to resolve disputes as per the relevant Security Council resolutions and the principles of international law, so as to protect the unity, territorial integrity and sovereignty of these sisterly nations. Mr. president, since Kuwait's independence, our foreign policy was based on firm principles, namely moderation and balance, and a firm commitment to the charter of the United Nations and International law, and on support for multilateralism and the belief that dialogue and the peaceful settlement of disputes are the best means to maintain international peace and security.

The State of Kuwait also believes in a complementary relationship between security and development. There can be no security without development and no development without security. Accordingly, Kuwait has based its development in humanitarian diplomacy on a pioneering role for the Kuwait Fund for Arab Economic Development. Since 1961, the fund has contributed to financing development projects in 107 countries. This stems from a belief that addressing the root causes of crises is not limited to security measures, but requires supporting development, providing the foundations for a life of dignity, and building more resilient and stable societies. At the national level, Kuwait is confidently progressing towards its Kuwait Vision 2035 by accelerating the implementation of development projects, diversifying its economy and sources of income, continuing its digital transformation, empowering women and youth, developing its legislation and consolidating governance and transparency.

These efforts should enhance the efficiency of institutions and the competitiveness of the economy, and will establish Kuwait as a leading financial, commercial and control centre in the region. In conclusion, Mr. President, my country has known the cruelty of occupation and the bitterness of aggression and has suffered from wars that have ravaged and continue to ravage our region for four decades. From this experience, we have realised that they are the people who pay the price of conflicts. We have recognised the need for the world to stand together, united in support of justice and in adherence to the UN charter and international law. Out of our experience, we became firmly convinced that peace is the choice of wisdom and is protected by ability and dialogue does not diminish rights, but preserves them, and that security is not protected by force alone. But it is anchored in justice, the rule of law, and the principles of international legitimacy.

The message of the state of Kuwait is one that has embraced in both word and deed, and to which it remains committed, that a just peace is the path to stability, and that respect for state sovereignty, the preservation of the rights of people, and recourse to international law for resolving disputes are indispensable pillars for security and stability of all states. The state of Kuwait shall remain, as the world has known it, to be a voice of wisdom and moderation, a proponent of dialogue, cooperation, and openness to partnerships that serve mutual interests. A champion of justice and a partner in consolidating international peace and security. We believe that peace is the path to a future where rights are protected, nations are stable, and generations enjoy security and prosperity, and may the peace and blessings of God be upon you. On behalf of the Assembly. I wish to thank the Crown Prince of the State of Kuwait.

Lao People’s Democratic Republic

Statement by

H.E. Mr. Thongsavan PHOMVIHANE,

Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Lao PDR

The General Debate of the 81st Session of the United Nations

General Assembly

New York, 26 September 2026 (As delivered)

1. At the outset, allow me to express my warmest congratulations to His Excellency Dr. Khalilur Rahman on his election as President of  the  81st  Session  of  the  United  Nations  General  Assembly.  My delegation  assures  you  of  our  full  support  and  cooperation throughout your Presidency. I also express our deep appreciation to Her  Excellency  Annalena  Baerbock  for  her  dedicated  leadership during the 80th Session.

2. The

theme  for

this  session,  “Restoring  Trust,  Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All,” arrives at  a  pivotal  juncture.  For  developing  and  vulnerable  countries,  a well-resourced  and  responsive  United  Nations  is  an  indispensable anchor.  Restoring  trust  in  our  international  system  requires  us  to uphold predictable support, honour commitments, and reaffirm our fidelity to the UN Charter.

3. For  the  Lao  PDR,  restoring  and  deepening  trust  begins  with  a renewed commitment to inclusive multilateralism, with the United Nations  at  its  core.  When  dialogue  is  guided  by  mutual  respect, transparency,  and  genuine  cooperation,  multilateralism  yields tangible benefits for all people.

4. Our  world  continues  to  confront  severe,  multifaceted  crises: geopolitical  tensions,  macroeconomic  instability,  supply  chain disruptions, and accelerating climate emergencies. These headwinds place  immense  strain  on  the  most  vulnerable  economies,  where rising energy and food prices jeopardize the livelihoods of millions of people in countries in special situations.

5. The ongoing conflicts in the Middle East demonstrate how rapidly confrontation  can  destabilize  global  stability.  Sustainable  peace cannot  be  forged  through  force  or  unilateral  action;  it  requires diplomacy,  respect  for  sovereign  equality  and  territorial  integrity, and strict adherence to international law.

6. The question of Palestine remains an enduring test of multilateral credibility.  We  remain  deeply  concerned  by  the  humanitarian catastrophe  and  immense  reconstruction  requirements  in  Gaza,  as well as mounting challenges in the West Bank. To prevent the two-state  solution  from  slipping  beyond  reach,  the  international community  must  secure  a  just,  comprehensive,  and  lasting  peace, one that fulfils the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people to self-determination  through  an  independent  State  of  Palestine  with  full membership in the United Nations.

7. In  the  same  vein,  the  Lao  PDR  reiterates  its  principled  position against  Unilateral  Coercive  Measures.  The  prolonged  economic, commercial,  and  financial  embargo  against  the  Republic  of  Cuba continues to inflict hardship on its people. We call for the immediate and unconditional lifting of these sanctions, including logistics and energy blockades, and the removal of Cuba from the list of “State Sponsors of Terrorism.” Such steps are essential first humanitarian measures  toward  restoring  trust  and  reaffirming  the  primacy  of international law.

8. The  gap  between  commitments  and  delivery  on  climate  change equally  tests  the  credibility  of  multilateralism. Although  the  Lao PDR has contributed only a small share of global greenhouse gas

emissions, our people are increasingly affected by floods, droughts and extreme weather conditions.

9.  The Lao PDR remains fully committed to the Paris Agreement and its  Nationally  Determined  Contributions.  However,  climate ambition must be matched by adequate, predictable, and accessible climate finance, technology transfer, and capacity-building to enable vulnerable  developing  states  to  adapt,  build  long-term  resilience, and pursue low-carbon growth pathways.

10.  The  Lao  PDR  welcomes  the  UN80  Initiative  to  enhance  the coherence,  transparency,  and  effectiveness  of  the  UN  System. Systemic reform must ensure a balanced approach across all three pillars  of  the  Organization:  peace  and  security,  sustainable development, and human rights.

11.  The  implementation  of  the  Pact  for  the  Future  and  the  Global Digital  Compact  must  focus  on  narrowing  the  digital  divide. Artificial intelligence and digital technologies must serve human development,  strengthen  local  technical  capacities,  and  respect national development priorities.

12.  As  an  active  member  of  the  Association  of  Southeast  Asian Nations (ASEAN), the Lao PDR reaffirms that a united, integrated ASEAN serves as a cornerstone of regional peace and multilateral stability.  We  remain  steadfast  in  supporting  ASEAN  centrality within  the  evolving  regional  architecture,  where  ASEAN-led mechanisms foster trust and practical cooperation.

13.  This  year  carries  special  significance  as  we  begin  implementing the ASEAN Community Vision 2045 alongside its Strategic Plans across  all  three  community  pillars.  It  also  marks  the  50th Anniversary of the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation in Southeast Asia (TAC)—a foundational framework whose core principles of peaceful  coexistence  and  mutual  respect  remain  fully  relevant today.  ASEAN  remains  the  bedrock  of  Lao  PDR’s  regional engagement.

14. Despite severe external economic shocks and natural disasters, the Lao economy continues its steady recovery through strong national ownership and strategic international partnerships. Guided by our Sovereign and Self-Reliant Economic Policy, the Lao PDR has adopted the 10th National Socio-Economic Development Plan (2026–2030).

15. The 10th NSEDP focuses on six core national outcomes:

o  First: Executing a sovereign and self-reliant economic policy

aiming for steady annual GDP growth of 6% or higher;

o  Second: Developing high-quality human resources capable of

driving technological transition;

o  Third: Improving living standards, ensuring balanced urban-

rural development, and alleviating poverty;

o  Fourth:  Protecting  natural  resources,  building  climate

resilience, and mitigating disaster risks;

o  Fifth:  Enhancing  regional  and  global  economic  integration

and connectivity; and

o  Sixth: Strengthening the efficiency and transparency of public

administration and governance.

16. Central to this strategy is transforming the Lao PDR from a land-locked  country  into  a  land-linked  regional  gateway.  Strategic infrastructure, including the Laos–China Railway, the Laos–Viet Nam Railway project, expanded transit corridors, and access to the sea via Vung Ang International Port are actively driving regional trade and integration. Our long-term vision towards 2055 aims to firmly establish the Lao PDR as an upper-middle-income nation with sustainable, inclusive growth at its core.

17.   This  year  marks  a

landmark  milestone

in  our  national development. The Lao PDR remains fully committed to its formal graduation  from  Least  Developed  Country  (LDC)  status,  in accordance with relevant General Assembly resolutions.

18.  As  the  UN  Secretary-General  António  Guterres  rightly  stated, LDC  graduation  must  be  “a  reward,  never  a  punishment.”  To safeguard our hard-won development gains and prevent structural setbacks, we are executing a robust Smooth Transition Strategy (2026–2029).  We  call  on  our  international  partners  to  provide transition  support,  extend  smooth  adjustments predictable regarding  International  Support  Measures  (ISMs),  and  expand concessional financing to build enduring economic resilience.

19.   The  2030  Agenda  for  Sustainable  Development  remains  fully embedded within our national planning. As we prepare to present our Fourth Voluntary National Review (VNR4) at the 2027 High-Level Political Forum, we remain dedicated to an open, transparent assessment of our progress.

20.  For the Lao PDR, the nexus between peace and development is a lived experience. As a country heavily impacted by wartime cluster

munitions  for  over  five  decades,  we  have  placed  unexploded ordnance (UXO) clearance at the heart of our development agenda through  the  national  SDG  18:  "Lives  Safe  from  UXO." Removing UXO is not merely a technical task. It is about restoring fundamental  safety,  securing  agricultural  land,  and  reclaiming development opportunities for our communities.

21.  Building on this commitment, the Lao PDR proudly hosted the 3rd Review  Conference  of  the  Convention  on  Cluster  Munitions (CCM)  early theme: “Accelerating Progress Towards a World Free from the Threat of Cluster Munitions.” Our Presidency demonstrated that mine action is  an  indispensable  foundation  for  poverty  reduction,  human dignity, and sustainable development.

in  Vientiane  under

this  month

22.   As Secretary-General António Guterres prepares to complete his distinguished  tenure  at  the  helm  of  our  Organization,  the Government  and  people  of  the  Lao  PDR  wish  to  express  our profound  appreciation  and  heartfelt  gratitude  for  his  principled leadership, moral clarity, and unwavering dedication to the United Nations.  A  true  and  trusted  friend  of  the  Lao  PDR  and  fellow the  Global  South, peace-loving  developing  nations  across Secretary-General  Guterres  will  be  warmly  remembered  for  his tireless  advocacy  for  international  financial  architecture  reform, climate justice, sustainable development financing, and the dignity of countries in special situations. His legacy of solidarity and bold championing  of  equity  will  continue  to  inspire  our  collective multilateral efforts for years to come.

23.  In conclusion, the Lao PDR firmly believes that the United Nations remains the essential home of global cooperation. No single nation can  overcome  today's  complex  global  challenges  alone.  Let  us unite  our  collective  strength,  renew  our  trust  in  multilateralism, and  work  together  to  build  a  peaceful,  resilient,  and  prosperous world where no nation and no person is left behind.

I thank you.

text:
Mr. President. Mr. Secretary General, the more I reflect on the theme of this session of the General Assembly Restoring Trust and Managing transformation, a United Nations that delivers for all the more convinced I become of the wisdom of that choice. Without mutual trust, peace and security cannot take root among states, nor can cooperation among them flourish. More than 80 years ago, the United Nations was founded on the promise that the force of law would replace the law of force. Yet we still live in a world of multiplying wars and conflicts, a world that spends more on armaments than on development. Civilians remain the primary victims, while millions face displacement, hunger and deprivation.

The problem is not the absence of rules. It is their selective application, if not their outright non-application. The sovereignty of states cannot be untouchable in one place and negotiable in another. Nor can the rules of international law apply to some, but not to others. Restoring trust requires respect for international law. It requires investment in preventing conflicts before they erupt, and in development before poverty and deprivation become a source of violence, extremism and terrorism.

Development two is a matter of peace. There can be no sustainable peace in a world of widening economic disparities, where some states spend more on servicing their debt than on the health of their citizens and education of their children. This does not absolve developing countries of their responsibility to undertake reform, combat corruption and build institutions. But those efforts require a fairer and more equitable international economic order, one that offers them genuine opportunities to advance. Mr. president, our shared responsibility is equally evident in the face of the profound transformations our world is undergoing. Climate change threatens the lives and livelihoods of millions.

Those countries that have contributed least to it bear its gravest consequences. This calls for equitable adaptation, finance and technology transfer. At the same time, the artificial intelligence revolution is opening unprecedented horizons for progress across every sphere of life. Yet it also raises challenges for the future of work and for human rights and fundamental freedoms This calls for international governance that places the human being with his or her freedom and privacy at the heart of this transformation. Above all, we must not allow an artificial intelligence divide to emerge on top of the existing gaps in wealth and development. Restoring trust requires that every individual feel that the law protects them their development do not exclude them, and that progress leaves no one behind.

Mr. president, if restoring trust is a challenge facing our world today for Lebanon, it is not a mere slogan. Just as managing transformation is not an option up for debate. Together they constitute the very essence of the mission. We pledged before our people, before our Arab brothers, and before the entire world. On the day I was entrusted with leading the government of Lebanon, we assumed this responsibility at a time when our country faced three existential challenges. The first was to regain the trust of its people.

After the financial collapse and the Beirut port explosion and the tragedies and wounds they left behind. The second was to reclaim its national decision making so that no authority stands above that of the state. No weapons exist outside its armed forces, and no decision on war and peace is taken outside its constitutional institutions. The third was to recover all of its territory from Israeli occupation, and to extend its sovereignty over the entirety of its national soil through its own forces. In implementation of the Taif Agreement and insincere respect for the relevant international resolutions on Lebanon. Foremost among these is resolution 1701, which remains to this day a fundamental point of reference governing relations between Lebanon and Israel.

Trust rebuilt decision making. Reclaimed. Land liberated. That is the equation for Lebanon's recovery. These are not three separate challenges. They are three facets of a single cause.

Restoring a state that its citizens trust that is master of its own decisions, and that exercises sovereignty over the whole of its territory. Mr. president, first, the trust we seek to restore is not trust in words. It is trust in institutions that protect rights in a judiciary that guarantees justice, in an economy that restores prosperity to the people and gives young people the opportunity of a better future. We cannot speak of restoring trust without recalling the Beirut port explosion. The wound of the 4th of August remains open. It cannot heal without truth, justice and accountability, and these will inevitably come.

Some might feel, may feel that our government has not yet fulfilled all of its commitments. We do not claim that the task is complete, but fairness demands that we not overlook the scale of legacy we inherited paralysed institutions, a public administration of diminished effectiveness, an economy stripped of the foundations of growth, and a state weakened by compounding crises and by decades of external interference. Even though we have not used the difficulty of our circumstances as a pretext to retreat from our commitments and we will not retreat. Lebanon has launched reforms on several fronts, namely revitalizing the public administration, strengthening the independence of the judiciary, modernizing the media law and abolishing the death penalty. It is also advancing towards the completion of financial reforms aimed at restoring order to the financial system and recovering depositors funds. These reforms should pave the way for an agreement with the IMF.

Such an agreement is an indispensable tool for restoring international confidence in Lebanon, and a gateway to securing the financing needed from all our regional and international partners for economic recovery and reconstruction. Our aim in pursuing reform is not to ask our people to renew their trust in the state. Rather, through reform, we seek to rebuild a state worthy of its people's trust. Second, a state does not regain the trust of its citizens through reform alone, but also by reclaiming its national decision making. In that spirit, we did not merely affirm the principle that weapons must be exclusively in the hands of the state, and that decisions on war and peace rest solely with its constitutional institutions. We translate that commitment into decisions taken by the Council of Ministers, notably in August and September of last year and again in March of this year.

That was after Lebanon found itself in a war that it did not choose. It was imposed upon us despite our repeated warnings. Again repeated warnings of the dangers of being drawn into it. As the war in the region widened and initiatives to end it multiplied, we held fast to a non-negotiable principle. No one speaks for Lebanon and no one negotiates on its behalf except the Lebanese state through its constitutional institutions. It is true that Lebanon is affected by developments in its surroundings.

Lebanon. It is true that Lebanon is affected by developments in its surroundings. That does not mean, however, that we accept its becoming once again an arena for the conflicts of others or a burning bargaining chip in their hands. Lebanon's future. Will not be decided on its behalf, nor may it. Security and stability become the price of settlements concluded in its absence.

Third our position on the war has been clear from the outset. We wanted to end. We want the cease fire consolidated. We want Israel to withdraw from all Lebanese territory up to our internationally recognised borders, in accordance with the 1990. With the 1949 General Armistice Agreement and as affirmed by resolution 1701. We want the release of all our detainees, the safe and dignified return of our people to their villages and towns, and the reconstruction of what the war has destroyed.

It was in that spirit that the Lebanese state entered into negotiations with Israel under the kind auspices of the United States of America and its president, for which we are grateful. With a view to reaching arrangements that ensure an end to the war and the restoration of Lebanon's full sovereignty. The sovereignty to which we are committed is indivisible. It requires Israel's withdrawal from all Lebanese territory. It equally requires the extension of the authority of the Lebanese state through its own forces, over the entirety of its territory, with weapons held by the state alone. It is on these two principles, and on the basis of reciprocity and phased implementation, that the tripartite framework reached in the negotiations rest.

However, the success of any agreement is measured not by declared intentions but by fulfilment of commitments. What is required today, therefore, is to complete the translation of this framework into practical steps within a clear timetable and with a verification mechanism that ensures the implementation of all its provisions. Mr. president, in this context, I must pay tribute to the role played by the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon, Unifil, and to the courage of its leadership, personnel and staff and their sacrifices in preserving stability, supporting the Lebanese Armed forces and implementing resolution 1701. Two. All the countries that have contributed troops to this force, Lebanon extends its profound thanks and appreciation. We have taken note of Security Council Resolution 27, 90 of 2025 of 2025, which decided to terminate Unifil's operations at the end of this year and to begin its gradual withdrawal, and requested the Secretary general to explore available options for the continued implementation of resolution 1701.

What we wish to stress here and today is the need to avert the vacuum that Unifil's withdrawal could create, where it to take place without agreement on a new international force to replace it. Such a force should ensure the continuation of monitoring, reporting and liaison functions and its role should complement the requirements for implementing the tripartite framework. Mr. president, recovering the. Mr. president, recovering the land does not mean only the withdrawal of occupying forces. It also means the return of its inhabitants and the revival of life in their villages and towns. The war has left behind a vast humanitarian crisis in Lebanon.

It has caused extensive destruction to housing, public facilities, infrastructure and productive sectors, and has deprived large numbers of Lebanese of their homes and livelihoods. While we thank the United Nations entities and our international partners for him for their humanitarian contributions, we call at the same time for continued funding to meet the basic needs of those affected, particularly the displaced. In parallel with the requirements of early recovery as well as reconstruction and development. The reconstruction of the South is not merely the rebuilding of stone. It is the rebuilding of people's lives, the restoration of their livelihoods, and the affirmation of their right to live in safety and dignity on their land. Mr. president, the Lebanon that stands before you today does not shirk its responsibilities, nor does it ask others to do what it is duty bound to do itself.

We are shouldering our responsibility for reform and for extending the authority of the state over the entirety of our territory. But we are entitled to ask the international community to shoulder, in turn, its responsibility to ensure respect for Lebanon's sovereignty and the implementation of resolutions of international legitimacy. Mr. president. There can be no lasting stability in Lebanon without lasting stability in our region. And there can be no stability in the region as long as this organisation remains unable to enable the Palestinian people to exercise their inalienable right to self-determination. Like all other peoples of the world, no less and no more.

This is despite the dozens of resolutions adopted by this Assembly and by the Security Council that lay clear foundations for that right. Not to mention the Arab Peace Initiative. As for the tragedy of wounded Gaza, it has put the conscience of the world and the important inability of its institutions to a test from which there can be no escape. I must stress here that cutting off funding to Unrra or undermining its mandate does not, uh, end the rights of Palestinian refugees. Even if that's what some seek. On the contrary, it compounds their suffering, jeopardizes the prospects for a just and lasting solution to their cause and increases the burden on host countries, foremost among them Lebanon.

With regard to the security situation of region, Lebanon wishes to renew its solidarity with the states of the Arab Gulf and with Jordan in the face of Iranian attacks that threaten regional security and the freedom and safety of maritime navigation. The effects of these attacks are not confined to theatres of confrontation. They extend to supply chains to the prices of goods, particularly food and energy, and to inflation rates. Mr. president, allow me to conclude by returning once more to the theme of this session of the General Assembly, Restoring Trust and Managing Transformation for a United Nations that delivers for all. The truth is that we cannot call on the states of the world to change their conduct, while failing to make the necessary changes within our own organization so that it delivers the results expected of it and regains the trust of the peoples of the world. The reality is that the world has changed profoundly since 1945.

The membership of the United Nations has grown nearly fourfold. Colonialism has ended Africa has risen. Asia has been transformed and new powers have emerged. The balance of the global economy has shifted. Yet the basic composition of the Security Council remains captive to a historical moment dating back to the end of the Second World War. Africa and the Arab world cannot remain without permanent representation on the Council, nor can small and medium sized states remain mere spectators to decisions that concern their security and the and their future.

We know that Security Council reform is a complex matter, but the difficulty of reform is no argument against its necessity. Indeed, reform of the United Nations must begin here with the Security Council. For it is the Security Council that bears primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security are therefore once again add Lebanon's voice to that of the majority of the members of our. Of our organisation in calling for an expansion of the Security Council that achieves more inclusive and equitable representation. Being realists, we do not call for the abolition of the veto. Rather, we call for strained in its use in cases of genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity and serious violations of international humanitarian law.

We insist on reform of the United Nations only because we want it to be more representative, more democratic and more effective organization We want an organisation true to the purposes and principles of its charter, yet ever renewed, so that it may rise to the challenges of our rapidly changing world and meet the aspirations of our peoples and their new generations. I thank you. On behalf of the Assembly. I wish to thank the president of the Council of Ministers of the Lebanese Republic.
