The imbalance is no, not a favour for Africa. It is necessary to restore United Nations trust, credibility and legitimacy. Mr. president. The choices before the 83rd General Assembly is stark. We cannot allow multilateralism to drift towards irrelevance, or we can change course and act boldly to restore trust, credibility and legitimacy.

Liberia's journey for civil conflict to constitutional democracy, and from broken institutions to accountable governance, shows what is possible when nations commit deliberately and consistently to restoring trust and managing transformation. As we did in San Francisco in 1945 Liberia is ready. Together with all member States to save mankind from the scourge of war guarantee human dignity and leave no one behind. Let us leave this assembly committed to a United Nations that is not deliberate on crisis, but also resolve them and restore trust through results. Protect the vulnerable, honour the right of all nations, and secure a peaceful planet for generations to come. Thank you.

On behalf of the Assembly.

Your Excellency Dr. Khalilur Rahman, President of the General Assembly of the United Nations. Your Excellency Mr. António Guterres, Secretary-General of the United Nations. Ladies and gentlemen. We meet today as the world undergoes a profound transformation, not only in the balance of power but in the very concept of power, and the ethics of its use. This transformation is reshaping the meaning of security, the nature of alliances, and the capacity of the international order to uphold the foundations and principles upon which and for which it was established. At the heart of these transformations lies a question that transcends the borders of states and continents: how can we build an international order in which the rule of law is an equal right, not a privilege of the most powerful?

And how can we make cooperation a genuine partnership among nations, rather than a carving-up of spheres of influence? We, in the Arab and Islamic world, and on our African continent, do not approach this question as observers, for we live its consequences every day. That reality unfolds before us at every moment in Palestine, whose delegation, we regret, has not been able to participate with us in this session. There, the plight of the Palestinian people continues to worsen after decades of occupation, repression, and alteration of their identity, yet they remain steadfast in their adherence to their right to life and to self-determination. These are rights guaranteed without discrimination by international law and international humanitarian law. All of humanity yearns for international instruments and resolutions to move from texts and promises to a reality, and for the right of the Palestinian people to their state to be realized in accordance with international law.

The continued undermining of these prospects for its establishment not only squanders opportunities for peace; it also drives the region toward a widening cycle of conflict, the spread of extremism, and a search for alternatives amid major expansionist projects that extend beyond occupied Palestine to Syria and Lebanon. Neither the Islamic and Christian holy sites, nor civilians, nor civilian infrastructure in Palestine have been spared the ravages of this conflict. Its repercussions have extended to the Arabian Gulf, most recently in the attack against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. We affirm our full solidarity with the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in safeguarding its security, its territorial integrity, its citizens, and its holy sites. We reject any targeting that threatens it or endangers Islamic holy sites. The security of the Kingdom and the Gulf, given their Arab and Islamic weight, is not a national matter, but it is a pillar of the security and stability of our region.

The ongoing armed conflict in the Sudan, our brotherly neighbor, has made its people the victims of a devastating war for which they are paying a hefty price. In that war, interests and interventions collide, and its effects extend beyond the borders of Sudan, endangering the security and stability of the region and the unity of its states. The instability in the Sahel region represents an existential threat to the integrity of its states. That threat stems from the nexus of terrorism, organized crime, poverty, climate change, displacement, and migration, and from the widening of the cycle of armed conflict in the region. It is no longer acceptable for the world to regard the Sahel merely as a source of resources, an arena for international competition, or a footnote in global decision-making. Africa, whose journey we have followed since the founding of the African Union, is not the margin of the world; it is one of the centers of the world to come.

Libya does not lie on the edge of Africa; Libya is of Africa, of its history, of its security, and of its future. Decades ago, an African will emerged from the Libyan city of Sirte that contributed to the establishment of the African Union. That fact reminds us that Libya has never been merely a bridge between Africa and the Mediterranean, but a partner in shaping the African project itself. We, therefore, view the security of the Sahel region as part of Libya's own security and stability. We view the security and stability of the states of the region and all our African neighbors, near and far, together with developing Africa, all as investment in the common security of Africa and its European neighborhood. This is not assistance provided by one party to another, nor is it a responsibility borne by one party alone.

Likewise, we view the Mediterranean basin not as a barrier between Africa and Europe, but as a shared space of connection. Relations among its countries should move from beyond merely managing migration and crises toward making the Mediterranean a bridge for development, trade, energy transition, investment, and common security. Ladies and gentlemen. Geographically and politically, Libya stands at the meeting point of these worlds. It is Arab in its identity and language, African in its geography, destiny, and belonging, Mediterranean in an intrinsic part of its culture, interests, and partnerships, and Islamic in its civilizational values, which incline toward peace, security, and building bridges with its neighbors. The multiplicity of these circles is not a contradiction but a source of strength, responsibility, and opportunity.

From this geopolitical vantage point in particular, we have learned a harsh lesson in recent years. When the state weakens, the vacuum does not remain empty; competing interests fill it, armed groups become active within it, criminal and smuggling networks spread, illicit funds seep in, and institutions themselves become arenas of struggle for influence. At that point, the state does not merely lose part of its security. Its national decision-making begins to lose its independence. This brings us to the essence of what sovereignty means to us. Sovereignty is not merely a flag raised or borders drawn on maps, nor is it slogans repeated while judicial and oversight institutions fail to exercise their roles independently and responsibly.

Sovereignty means that national decision-making is free. It also means that our cooperation and integration with United Nations bodies are based on transparency, seriousness, and impartiality, free from selectivity and double standards. Sovereignty means protecting the rights and dignity of the Libyan people from violations, whoever the perpetrator, and ensuring that no one is above the law and no one escapes accountability. Sovereignty means that state institutions are stronger than individuals and groups, and that weapons are subject to the law. It also means that the country's wealth remains the property of the people, not spoiled to be divided among parties, networks of interest, or dubious partnerships that exercise some sort of custodianship over the state. Sovereignty means preventing corrupt money from buying influence.

It means preventing influence from becoming an immunity that shields corrupt money. If that cycle becomes entrenched, it weakens the state from within and threatens the survival of its institutions. In this context, we call upon the Security Council to discharge its responsibilities and to follow up on the United Nations reports submitted to it. This includes the report of the panel of experts on violations and cases of noncompliance. We call upon the Council to give serious consideration to the panel's recommendations and to take the necessary action within its established mandates. The purpose is to ensure the effective implementation of the Council resolutions and the relevant sanctions measures without selectivity or double standards.

Documented violations should not become mere recurring facts in reports, nor should accountability end at documentation. The authority of international law and the credibility of its institutions are measured by their ability to move from monitoring violations to holding perpetrators accountable, and from resolution to implementation for all without exception. Sovereignty also means that the state's foreign relations are an extension of its national interests, not an extension of others' conflicts within it. Mr. President. Libya paid a heavy price when regional and international balances of power were transformed into balances within its own territory. Accordingly, our vision for Libya's external relations is clear.

We do not seek to replace one influence with another, one axis with another, or one dependency with another. We want strong relations with our Arab surroundings, especially our neighboring countries. We want Libya to regain its natural role within its African continent. We want balanced strategic partnerships with our Mediterranean neighbors and our regional international sphere based on a single principle, namely common interests, mutual respect, non-interference, and respect for national sovereignty. Libya's true ally is not one who seeks out the strongest party within it. The true ally is one who wants a strong Libyan state.

The true partner is not one whose interests are tied to the continuation of division. The true partner is one whose shared interest with us grows as Libya becomes more united, stable, and prosperous. We want states to compete in Libya on investment, reconstruction, energy, technology, and development, not for influence within its institutions. Ladies and gentlemen. After years of political division and polarization that have drained the state and society, Libya no longer needs more crisis management, but rather the will to end the crisis. Our goal is clear: a unified sovereign state whose institutions derive their legitimacy from the will of its people.

The path to that goal is a return to the people through constitutional and legal mechanisms, referendums, and free and fair elections. The people are the source of legitimacy, and it is they who can give institutions their unity and stability. Temporary deals cannot do so, nor can fragile settlements that collapse whenever the balance of power shifts or loyalties change. Here, we welcome the effort and intention of every state sincerely seeking to end the political and institutional division. We also appreciate the role entrusted to the United Nations support mission in Libya and its responsibility for facilitating the political process. Nevertheless, past experience obliges us to be clear.

Any sustainable political process must not violate four governing principles. First, respect for legitimacy and for the constitutional and legal frameworks enforced, without circumventing them or creating political arrangements outside established frameworks and procedures. Second, the principle of national ownership is a red line. International mediation must not turn into custodianship or into solutions crafted from abroad. The will of Libyans is the foundation, and the inclusion of all the different parties without exclusion or imposition is the true guarantee of the sustainability of any solution. Third, ensuring equal opportunities for all parties, as well as rejecting the use of force, influence, or effet accompli to impose predetermined political outcomes.

Fourth, commitment to transparency in understandings and agreements. This requires defining the phases of implementation, their timelines, and the entities responsible for them. It also requires establishing clear mechanisms for oversight and accountability so as to ensure outcomes that are implementable, legally sound, and capable of producing legitimate and stable institutions. Experience has taught us that fragile settlements can begin to unravel as soon as the balance of power shifts or their outcomes emerge. Any arrangements that disregard national legal frameworks expose themselves to challenge and dispute. They reproduce the crisis rather than end it.

Sustainable legitimacy and legality are not created by effet accompli, nor are they protected by shifting balances of power. They are created by the will of the people and protected by the law. In translating these principles into national responsibility and concrete action, we announce from this rostrum the launch of work on a national committee for de-escalation and confidence building. The committee will draw on national and local initiatives. It will aim to prevent conflicts, contain escalation, and prevent its recurrence. This is in addition to supporting reconciliation and creating a safe environment for the political and electoral process.

Here, we call upon all Libyan parties to engage in this framework. We also call upon the UN and Libya's partners to support and facilitate it with full respect for sovereignty and national ownership. Ladies and gentlemen. A Libya that regains its sovereignty and the unity of its institutions will not be a gain for Libyans alone. It will be a force for stability in the Arab world, a source of strategic depth for security and development in Africa, a responsible partner in the Mediterranean, and a bridge for cooperation between North and South. From this rostrum, Libya announces its candidacy for the membership of the Security Council for the term 2028-2029 for the African seat.

Its campaign is conducted under the slogan "Consolidating Justice for Security and Peace: Libya, a Bridge Among Nations." Libya looks forward to the confidence and support of the member states in this endeavor. This candidacy is not merely a diplomatic ambition. It embodies a national will for Libya to regain its natural role in the international arena and to shoulder its responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security. It stems from a firm conviction that peace is built not merely on the absence of conflict, but on establishing justice and addressing the causes of injustice and instability. Libya does not seek the seat merely to occupy a position.

Rather, it seeks to contribute to building a more equitable international order and to serve as a bridge among nations, a voice for consensus, and an active partner in peacemaking. Hence, our message to our friends and partners is not that they should abandon their interests in Libya, but that they should build those interests with us on a firmer foundation, namely that their interests lie in Libya's stability, not in the fragility of its institutions, and in partnership with Libya, not in influence within it. We, Libyanes, bear the responsibility, the primary responsibility. Patriotism is not only the defense of sovereignty against negative foreign interference. It also is the protection of the state from corruption within, the safeguarding of public funds, the upholding of the rule of law, and the placing the nation above power and self-interest. Libya today has an opportunity to leave behind the cycle of transitional phases and to enter the era of the state.

It has an opportunity to regain the role befitting its history, its position, and its standing among nations. Libya does not want to be an arena on whose soil the interests of others are balanced, but a state that shapes its own balance by its own will. It does not want others to compete for influence within it, but to compete for partnership with it. That is the path we choose for Libya: a state sovereign in its decisions, unified in its institutions, just among its citizens, and a partner for peace and stability in its region and the world. That is the right of our people, our responsibility towards them, and our trust to future generations. May the peace and mercy and blessings of Allah be upon you.

En nombre de la Asamblea General.

Mr. Secretary-General,

Excellencies,

Distinguished Delegates,

In 1979, thirty-four (34) years after the creation of this United Nations,  my country, Saint

Lucia, though small in geography, but large in courage, dignity and conviction, took its seat

among the community of nations brimming with hope, optimism and trust in the promise and

goals of this body.

Today we meet at a moment of profound international uncertainty. Conflict is spreading, trust

is eroding, development gains are being reversed, and the rules intended to protect humanity

are too often applied selectively.

For  small  island  developing  states,  these  crises  are  not  abstract.  They  are  lived  realities.

Climate change threatens our homes, livelihoods, and very existence. Debt limits our ability

to  invest  in  people.  Digital  technologies  are  transforming  our  societies,  but  without

safeguards, they can reproduce old patterns of domination in a new form. And in our own

Caribbean neighbourhood, the people of Haiti continue to endure a humanitarian and security

catastrophe that demands more than statements of concern.

The  theme  before  us,  “Restoring  trust,  managing  transformation:  a  United  Nations  that

delivers for all,” must not remain a slogan. Trust will be restored only when promises are

matched by action, when commitments are honoured, and when the United Nations delivers

meaningful results for every nation, and when there is due regard for multilateral principles

not only for the most powerful, but also for the weakest of us as well.

This Assembly should not be a place where the world expresses sympathy without accepting

responsibility.

We need action. We need justice. And we need a renewed international compact based not on

power, but on principle; we need multilateralism, not unilateralism. In the words of a former

UN Secretary General, “The United Nations was not created in order to bring us to heaven,

but in order to save us from hell.”

Climate Change and Climate Finance

For Saint Lucia, climate change is not a distant environmental issue. It is a direct threat to

national security, economic stability, food and water security, and human survival.

Whilst  the  world  focuses  on  headline-grabbing  events  like  monster  hurricanes,  melting

glaciers and tidal waves, climate change is affecting Saint Lucia daily in small but significant

ways, such as the unusual bouts of drought in the rainy season, unprecedented floods in the

dry season, and the stifling of our beaches and coastlines by sargassum.

Our  people  contribute  little  to  global  emissions,  yet  these  events  constantly  set  back  our

people’s development and livelihoods and demand that we find the resources to reverse the

damage.

Saint Lucia calls for climate finance that matches the scale of the crisis: expanded grants and

concessional funding, faster and simpler access, full support for loss and damage, meaningful

debt relief, and financing that reaches vulnerable communities directly.

Eligibility for finance must reflect not only income, but climate vulnerability.

Climate finance is not charity. It is about justice, responsibility, and survival.

We must stop confusing loans with solidarity. A loan is not justice when a small vulnerable

nation is forced to borrow to repair damage it did not cause.

A  United  Nations  that  delivers  for  all  must  deliver  for  those  on  the  front  lines  of  climate

change  through  accessible  finance,  concrete  support  and  measurable  results,  not  merely

through declarations.

International Crises

Saint Lucia laments the continued conflicts and human suffering across the globe, including

Ukraine,  Sudan  and  the  wider  Middle  East,  including  Gaza,  and  calls  for  renewed  efforts

towards peace, stability and respect for international law.

In  accordance  with  their  right  to  self-determination  and  UN  resolutions,  in  particular

Resolution 3236 of 1974, the People of Palestine should be allowed their own State and full

membership of the UN, alongside the state of Israel.

Haiti: Responsibility to a Sister Nation

We also speak today about Haiti.

Member states of this organisation must act in a manner that will restore the trust of the people

of Haiti in the United Nations. Some member states have failed to meet their commitments

and pledges to the Gang Suppression Force in Haiti, whose one-year mandate ends this month.

The Security Council is urged to renew the Force's mandate, and member states to provide

the necessary resources to operate effectively and successfully.

While gang violence is the main factor to be resolved in Haiti, the crisis in this country is

multidimensional.  The  international  response  must  include  long-term  social  and  economic

assistance that will help restore an acceptable quality of life for the people of Haiti.

That  is  why  the  Caribbean  Community  has  been  actively  engaged  in  Haiti,  a  Caribbean

Community member state, to assist with a solution to the political and governance dimensions

of the crisis. Through its Eminent Persons Group, comprising three former Prime Ministers,

it will continue to facilitate dialogue amongst Haiti’s political and civil society stakeholders

as they work towards holding the first round of General Elections this year.

Trust  in  the  United  Nations  will  be  restored  if  the  daily  lives  of  the  people  of  Haiti  are

transformed and enhanced.

CUBA

It is in a similar quest for trust and transformation that Saint Lucia believes there should be

dialogue and the removal of all obstacles that hinder the true development of the people of

Cuba.

Cuba  has  long  been  celebrated  for  its  continued  contribution  to  health,  education  and

development across our region and beyond. Saint Lucia stands with the Cuban people in their

hope  for  a  better  future,  supported  by  the  friendship  and  solidarity  of  the  international

community.

Republic of China (Taiwan)

In the same spirit of transformation and consistent with our commitment to the right of all

people to self-determination, Saint Lucia supports Taiwan’s full membership in the United

Nations.

Reform of the Security Council

Saint Lucia believes that a truly inclusive United Nations must ensure that its decision-making

bodies reflect the world that they serve.

Saint  Lucia  advocates  for  a  comprehensive  reform  of  the  Security  Council  to  enhance  its

legitimacy and effectiveness in addressing contemporary global challenges, thereby restoring

trust and a more inclusive multilateral system.

Mr. President

A  21st-century  United  Nations  Security  Council  could  have  been  more  successful  in  its

responsibility for international peace and security had it not been anchored in the world of

1945.

The prolonged reform process must be concluded quickly to include expanded permanent and

non-permanent  membership  for  Africa,  the  Asia-Pacific,  and  Latin  America  and  the

Caribbean regions. This reform is essential to restore trust in the United Nations and ensure it

delivers peace and security for all. Saint Lucia pledges its commitment and dedication to work

with like-minded nations to achieve the stated reforms.

Secretary General

I wish to take this opportunity to thank the outgoing Secretary General, Antonio Guterres, for

his sterling service, especially his steadfast solidarity with the Caribbean through the many

challenges and disasters our region has faced. We commend him for his sincere and positive

leadership of this organisation. Saint Lucia wishes to express its endorsement of the candidate

of the Republic of Guyana, Ms. Caroline Rodrigues-Birkett, for the post of Secretary General.

Her  distinguished  record  of  public  and  international  service  speaks  directly  to  the  kind  of

leadership this moment demands.

Reparations and Historical Justice

On  the  25th  of  March,  2026,  the  General  Assembly  approved  one  of  its  most  historic  and

consequential  resolutions  that  declared  the  trafficking  of  enslaved  Africans  and  racialised

chattel enslavement of Africans as the greatest crime against humanity. This resolution and

the  subsequent  establishment  of  the  High  Level  Global  Advisory  Council  on  Reparatory

Justice is a very significant step in the search for reparations for the transatlantic slave trade

and the enslavement of Africans in the Americas and the Caribbean.

I want to thank the President of Ghana for spearheading and championing the resolution.

Saint Lucia congratulates the Government of Jamaica on its successful petition to the British

monarch for him to refer three questions to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council over

the legality of the enslavement of Africans in Jamaica.

Reparations  are  not  about  vengeance.  They  are  about  truth,  acknowledgement,  repair  and

transformation.

Reparations are not about seeking charity or revisiting history for its own sake. History is not

behind  us  when  its  consequences  remain  embedded  in  wealth,  power,  institutions  and

opportunity.

Reparations are about addressing the continuing effects of slavery and colonial exploitation,

restoring dignity, advancing development and building more equitable relationships with the

states and institutions that benefited from these systems.

Digital Colonisation and Digital Sovereignty

Digital technology is a new form of power that is rapidly transforming the world, and while

it offers enormous opportunities for mankind, it can also create a new hierarchy in which a

small number of corporations and powerful states control the systems on  which the rest of

humanity depends.

We must ensure that artificial intelligence does not widen the gap between the powerful and

the vulnerable. Technology must strengthen aspirations, not quietly erode them.

Saint Lucia therefore calls for strong global standards on data protection, privacy and artificial

intelligence;  equitable  access  to  digital  infrastructure,  cybersecurity  and  affordable

connectivity; fair technology transfer; transparent algorithms; protection from surveillance,

disinformation and cyber exploitation; and meaningful participation by small states in shaping

global digital rules.

The digital future must not be owned by a few. It must be governed for  the benefit of all.

Managing  transformation  means  ensuring  that  no  nation  is  left  powerless  in  the  face  of

technological change.

A United Nations That Delivers for All

Mr. President, my country, Saint Lucia, is small, open, and vulnerable, but our people refuse

to impose limits on their aspirations. History has blessed us with unimaginable natural beauty,

ambitious,  friendly  people,  and  two  Nobel  Laureates.  However,  an  unfair  international

financial system threatens the very existence of small island states like Saint Lucia. The rules

governing global finance affect our development, and our attempt at economic diversification

is hindered by unfair and unequally applied rules.

Oceans of water separate us from the global powers, but our challenges are mainly connected

to decisions made in their capitals. Emissions released from these countries affect our climate.

Weapons  and  drugs  trafficked  through  international  networks  instigate  violence  and  gang

warfare in our region.

Lack of access to affordable technology slows our development. Mr. President, Saint Lucia

refuses to give up. We are educating our people to ensure that their skills are relevant. We are

modernising agriculture to ensure our food security. We are dealing with the scarcity of water

due to climate change by exploring new sources of groundwater supply and encouraging the

harvesting of rainwater. We are reducing youth unemployment through the creation of the

successful  Youth  Economy  Agency.  We  are  encouraging  the  spirit  of  entrepreneurship  by

supporting  small  and  micro  enterprises,  especially  women-owned  businesses.  We  are

promoting healthy lifestyles and universal healthcare for the provision of equitable, accessible

and affordable healthcare for our citizens.

Mr President, Saint Lucia continues to insist that governance must be about the improvement

of the lives of the people. We have maintained fiscal discipline, reduced unemployment as we

continue to create new opportunities and an enabling environment for investment in tourism

and other productive sectors.

Saint Lucia believes that a better world is within our reach if we choose cooperation over

coercion and ensure that justice and fairness prevail for all.

The 81st Session of the UN General Assembly must be remembered for turning its laudable

theme  into  actionable  commitments  and  those  commitments  into  meaningful  change.  As

Mahatma Gandhi says, “In a gentle way you can shape the world.”

The  people  of  Saint  Lucia  remain  confident  in  our  collective  capacity  to  shape  that  better

world, even as Saint Lucian Nobel Laureate, Sir Derek Walcott reminds us that  “the future

happens no matter how much we scream.”

Our task is to meet that future with courage and purpose. Our other Nobel Laureate Sir Arthur

Lewis said, “Economic development requires taking risks and embracing change.” And with

the speed of Julien Alfred, let us embrace that responsibility together and act with the resolve

this moment demands.

I thank you.

GENERAL DEBATE 81ST SESSION OF THE UNITED NATIONS GENERAL ASSEMBLY

STATEMENT BY H.E. SABINE MONAUNI DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER, MINISTER OF FOREIGN AFFAIRS, ENVIRONMENT AND CULTURE OF THE PRINCIPALITY OF LIECHTENSTEIN

Liechtenstein  joined  the  United  Nations  36  years  ago  as  its  160th

member.  We  did  so  driven  by  the  conviction  that  we,  as  one  of  the

smallest members of the international community, should be part of the

most

important  conversation  on  global  governance,  with  the

participation of all States, big or small, in developing international norms

and standards – and also in upholding respect for them. Sovereignty was

a  key  theme  of  our  domestic  discussions  resulting

in  our  UN

membership. We joined out of enlightened self-interest - the belief that

we need the UN to secure respect for our sovereignty, through upholding

international  law,  as  the  basis  for  our  security  and  prosperity.  To  this

end, we also decided to make our own contribution, to make best use of

the opportunity offered to us as a small State, to be an active part of the

biggest peace project in the history of humankind.

Our  belief  in  the  United  Nations  remains  steadfast.  This  is  the  place

where we can make our voice heard, where we can put ideas forward,

and where we can gather to try to solve the issues that affect us all. We

have  greatly  benefitted  from  our  membership,  and  the  UN  has

consistently been a key platform for our foreign policy. Our membership

has consistently enjoyed high levels of support in our population.

But  today  we  also  find  ourselves  in  a  moment  where  instability  and

uncertainty  dominate  the  conversation.  Our  organization  no  longer

seems able to deliver on the key promise of the UN Charter  – to save

future generations from the scourge of war. It can no  longer count on

the unconditional support of its most powerful Members for the guiding

rules of international law. It is increasingly ignored or sidelined in efforts

to  address  both  the  traditional  and  new  challenges,  such  as  the

regulation  of  Artificial

Intelligence.

It

is  permanently  squeezed

financially.  Legal  obligations  to  pay  are  turned  into  tools  to  exercise

political leverage. As a result, the United Nations has moved down the

foreign  policy  agenda  even  of  States  who  have  a  strong  history  of

supporting it. We can no longer take it for granted that our people will

continue their strongly positive views of our organization.

This is the difficult moment in which we find ourselves. But rather than

engaging  in  doomsday  scenarios,  we  have  to  find  the  opportunities

hidden  in  the  challenge.  The  overwhelming  majority  of  the  States

present  in  this  room  believe  in  the  United  Nations.  They  want  to  see

positive change, for the UN to emerge stronger,  more effective, more

relevant. But we all have to be prepared to be part of the change that we

want to see. Resisting the temptation of collective inertia and of waiting

for positive change to happen on its own will require our active political

investment.

We  are  grateful  to  Secretary-General  Guterres  for  his  service  to  the

organization and for his proposals to adapt the organization to the needs

of today. On the basis of his ideas, our delegations here have done good

work that will show positive results over time. This is important. It shows

that we can come together also during times of deep political division. It

is also not enough. The steps we have taken are just the  beginning of

what we need - a political agreement that combines significant structural

change with a reliable financial commitment and firm support for the UN

Charter from all. This is also the vision we are looking for in the person

that will be appointed as the next Secretary-General. We hope that this

decision will come very soon, in order to give the new Secretary-General

the  time  she  needs  to  prepare  for  this  most  unique  of  jobs.  And  we

remain convinced that having a woman at the helm of the United Nations

is long overdue for an organization that prides itself on its role in gender

equality.

At its core, the United Nations is a peace organization. This is the promise

of the UN Charter, and this is what our people expect from the UN – and

the reason why they hold it in high esteem. Over the past year, we have

seen  a  record  number  of  armed  conflicts  around  the  world  –  and  a

rapidly  diminishing  role  of  the  United  Nations  in  ending  them.  In  the

Middle East, the UN’s role has been further reduced, in contrast to the

central position it has taken up over the years.  In Ukraine, there are few

prospects for a peace process even though the aggression has now lasted

longer  than  World  War  I,  without  even  a  nominal  role  for  the  United

Nations.  In  Sudan,  the  role  of  the  UN  is  limited  to  alleviating  the

enormous  suffering  of  the  civilian  population,  with  no  prospect  of  a

political solution and an end to the conflict.

We  are  well  aware  of  the  political  dynamic  in  the  Security  Council,

primarily  tasked  with  matters  of  peace  and  security  –  which  severely

limits  the  options  for  UN  action.  But  the  conversation  must  not  end

there. There are alternatives for action. This Assembly in particular has

wide authority over matters of peace and security – and it is universal in

composition.  A  glance  at  its  history  demonstrates  its  authority  in

peacekeeping, conflict termination and accountability. It is time that we

make  better  use  of  this  authority.  The  Veto  Initiative,  which  we  were

proud  to  spearhead,  provides  a  platform  for  such  action.  What  is

required is the will to spend our political capital here in this room – on

peace  rather  than  force,  by  dealing  with  conflict  through  diplomacy

rather than through war.

The United Nations must not accept being reduced to a crisis mitigation

organization  that  distributes  States’  contributions  to  a  skyrocketing

humanitarian assistance bill. Instead, we need to see a return to the UN

doing  political  work  to  prevent,  contain  and  end  conflict,  through  the

wide range of peace operations available, and through a strong interplay

between  a  Secretary-General  who  is  proactive  and  offers  creative

solutions, backed by the UN membership.

Any successful community must be grounded in the rule of law. And so

it is with the international community: our commitment to the law as the

foundation for the conduct of international affairs is grounded both in

principle and pragmatism. The biggest strength of the United Nations is

that it is firmly grounded in rules we have all agreed on  – and that we

have  all  agreed  apply  to  all  of  us.  This  foundational  agreement  is

increasingly  challenged,  with  alarming  trends  to  dismiss  and  ignore

international law altogether which can only result in a world where might

makes  right.  This  would  result  in  catastrophic  human  cost,  a  further

proliferation  of  conflict  and  have  devastating  effects  on  development

and  on  human  security.  We  hope  that  both  small  and  medium-sized

States  will  come  together  in  our  common  interest  for  a  strong

multilateral system, on the basis of respect for international law. This is

the moment for us to unify in support of what the United Nations is built

on.

Naturally,  we  are  also  strong  supporters  of  international  courts,  the

indispensable  enforcement  mechanisms  of

international

law.

Liechtenstein joined the jurisdiction of the International Court of Justice

four decades before we joined the UN. We have made more submissions

to the Court over the past decade than in its entire history before. We

strongly  support  its  work  and  its  competence  in  both  its  advisory  and

dispute settlement functions. We encourage all to join us in submitting

to the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court.

Liechtenstein  is  also  strongly  committed  to  the  International  Criminal

Court, the first permanent international court with jurisdiction over the

most serious crimes under international law – genocide, crimes against

humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression. We will continue to

support  the  Court  and  its  mandate  to  ensure  accountability  and  its

central message - that nobody is above the law. In joining the ICC, we

have exercised our sovereignty and delegated the jurisdiction we have

ourselves to an international Court which we have helped create. We are

proud of the way the Court has addressed the challenges to its resilience

over  the  past  year,  in  the  face  of  relentless  political  attacks  and

unprecedented  sanctions.  We  hope  that  more  States  will  join  this

project,  which  is  one  of  the  landmark  achievements  in  the  history  of

international treaty-making.

The  Rome  Statute  also  criminalizes  the  supreme  international  crime  –

the crime of aggression, which complements the prohibition of the illegal

use of force, the core piece of the UN Charter. At the international level,

by signing the UN Charter we have all agreed to refrain from the threat

or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence

of another State. This is the most ambitious collective commitment to

end war that has ever existed. Amidst accelerating human suffering the

world over, it has never been more important for us to implement this

commitment.

It  has  now  been  many  decades  since  scientists  first  warned  us  of  the

dangers of Climate Change. Nevertheless, we have continued to run into

the climate abyss, leaving the coming chaos for our children and their

children. It is almost impossible to believe that we need to reiterate the

facts: the climate crisis is real. We are seeing its effects every day, from

heatwaves  that  bake  the  soil,  to  heavy  rains  that  turned  the  parched

ground into mud. People are starving in the heat and drowning in the

floods.  Crops  can  no  longer  be  sustainably  harvested;  animals  and

pollinators  are  dying  out.  Liechtenstein  commits  to  working  with  all

States to address these harms and to reverse these trends as much as

we still can.

We support the Advisory Opinion of the International Court of Justice on

Climate Change. And this week we were proud to join the adoption of a

High-Level Declaration on Sea-Level Rise, including a commitment to the

continuity of Statehood for all UN Member States. Only a few years ago,

Member States in this debate wondered aloud if their nameplates would

be ‘switched off’. The commitment we made this week is to guarantee

that  this  will  not  happen.  In  the  face  of  seas  which  inundate  whole

territories, standing up for self-determination is the least we can do for

those most affected.

This week has also seen an intense debate on harnessing the potential of

Artificial  Intelligence.  But  perhaps  what  we  are  discovering  in  these

conversations are our own limits to understanding what that potential

might  be.  Reporting  from  the  most  powerful  and  well-capitalized  AI

companies tell us that we are on a precipice either of a technology-fueled

utopia  or  an  apocalypse.  Whether  we  achieve  one  or  the  other,

unfortunately, has been treated as a secondary priority to the ‘AI race’ –

one that has no clear finish line – and, for that matter, a dubious prize.

Liechtenstein supports the regulation of Artificial Intelligence. Unless we

have a clear understanding of the methods, processes, and purposes of

the  huge  variety  of  AI  systems,  how  can  we  risk  the  consequences  to

human rights, to our environment,  to the long-term capacities for our

critical thinking and ultimately to the future of the human species? We

are already seeing the impacts on civilians as armed forces increasingly

integrate AI capabilities into their targeting systems in warfare. AI tools

have to be made for humanity, lest we become the source material for

AI systems to use - or merely the victims in its crosshairs.

Many  of  us  standing  here  this  week  have  mused  about  the  UN’s

imperfections or expressed our concerns about its diminished relevance.

The UN is, indeed, in a fragile place. But very few of us want to live in a

world in which the United Nations is rendered obsolete. On the contrary,

we realize how much we need the UN. In the often-repeated quote, the

UN was not built to take us to heaven. But in an era where it may not

even be able to save us from hell, this universal organization retains the

unparalleled ability to meet us where we are. It is up to us to do what we

can to bring it closer to carrying out its mission under the UN Charter.

Liechtenstein  commits  to  doing  our  part  with  you  all  in  service  of

multilateralism and of the peoples we serve. I thank you.

Mr. Secretary-General,

Excellencies,

Ladies and Gentlemen,

Allow me, at the outset, to congratulate you, Dr. Khalilur Rahman, on your

election as President of the Eighty-first session of the General Assembly.

On behalf of the Government of Sri Lanka, I wish you every success and

assure you of our fullest support in the discharge of your mandate.

We  also  convey  our  deep  appreciation  to  your  predecessor,  Madam

Annalena Baerbock, for her able stewardship of the Eightieth session.

Let  me  also  take  this  opportunity  to  acknowledge  the  leadership  of

Secretary-General António Guterres as he concludes his term.

Seminal changes are taking place across the world at a pace faster than

many institutions are able to adapt or respond. People across the globe

are demanding greater clarity, honesty and action from their leaders and

institutions.

The  theme  of  this  year’s  General  Debate  —  “Restoring  trust,

managing transformation: a United Nations that delivers for all”

— goes to the heart of this challenge.

The  erosion  of  trust  is  reflected  in  unresolved  conflicts,  humanitarian

crises  that  outpace  available  resources,  increasingly  frequent  climate

disasters,  widening  inequalities,  and  technological  advances  that  are

moving  faster  than  governance.  Together,  these  developments  have

contributed  to  a  growing  perception  that  global  institutions  are  distant

from the people they are meant to serve.

Sri  Lanka  understands  this  reality  deeply.  My  country  has,  on  many

occasions in the past, experienced the consequences of deficits in trust

and breaches of the social contract. Two years ago, marking a watershed

moment  in  our  history,  the  people  of  Sri  Lanka,  representing  all

communities  and  walks  of  life,  gave  a  resounding  mandate  to  the

Government  of  President  Anura  Kumara  Dissanayaka  to  address  these

challenges and institute meaningful change. Since then, our Government

has been working with determination to rebuild trust from the ground up.

We  are  building  trust  through  action  —  not  rhetoric;  through  delivery,

discipline  and  the  courage  to  confront  wrongdoing.  Sri  Lanka,  too,  is

therefore undergoing a historic transformation and rejuvenation.

Despite conflicts in several parts of the world, including in West Asia, and

climate calamities, including the cyclone that struck Sri Lanka, my country

has  restored  macroeconomic  stability  following  the  economic  crisis  of

2022.  Today,  Sri  Lanka  has  been  reclassified  by  the  World  Bank  as  an

upper-middle-income economy, and ratings agencies have recognised this

positive trajectory.

However,  these  developments  do  not  fully  reflect  the  vulnerabilities  of

countries exposed to debt and external shocks. While we work with our

global partners to consolidate this hard-won stability, we remain conscious

of  the  critical  need  to  address  the  hardships  faced  by  vulnerable

communities.

Cyclone  Ditwah  was  one  of  the  worst  natural  disasters  in  Sri  Lanka’s

recent history and devastated several parts of our country.                The

calamity resulted in the loss of hundreds of lives and affected more than

two million people. Livelihoods were disrupted and critical infrastructure

was destroyed.

Having  experienced  this  tragedy,  we  understand  deeply  the  challenge

posed by the Himalayan floods to the people of Nepal and China.        We

extend our deepest sympathies to the victims.

These  tragic  events  demonstrate  the  enormous  human  and  economic

costs of climate change. Sadly, its harshest consequences continue to be

borne by countries that have contributed least to global emissions.

The call for action on climate impact is not merely immediate.                  It

is overdue. Climate justice must become an urgent reality.                    For

our part, Sri Lanka is on track towards achieving 70 per cent renewable

energy by 2030 and carbon neutrality by 2050.

For  three  decades,  Sri  Lanka  suffered  a  protracted  conflict  that  caused

enormous

loss

and

suffering

to

all

our

communities.

Although the guns fell silent 17 years ago, the deep wounds of that conflict

remain, and much remains to be done to heal them.                  We are

determined to  prevent  a  recurrence  of  such  a  tragedy  and to  pursue  a

path  towards  national  unity  and  reconciliation.  In  this  regard,  our

Government is strengthening national institutions to address outstanding

issues.  Throughout  these  two  years,  we  have  remained  firm  in  our

rejection  of  racism  and  religious  extremism  in  all  its  forms  and

manifestations. We will continue to work tirelessly to build a nation that

is more secure, inclusive and united — a nation made stronger by the full

richness of its diversity.

In addition to the consequences of natural calamity, Sri Lanka, like many

other countries, is experiencing the severe impact of conflicts in West Asia

and elsewhere.

As an island nation situated at the crossroads of the Indian Ocean, and

as a country with a large number of migrant workers in West Asia, these

developments have direct security, economic and social implications for

us.

I am pleased to note that, even during these challenging times,           Sri

Lanka has continued to uphold its commitments to international law and

to ensure sanctity of human life and human dignity.

Mr. President

In March this year, amidst a highly volatile geopolitical landscape,        Sri

Lanka found a ship of a party to a conflict in distress close to our territorial

waters  with  many  sailors’  life  in  peril.  We  took  the  difficult  path  of

navigating  a  wilderness  of  sensitivities  and  marshalling  our  limited

national resources to rescue and look after the wounded and sick. Hard

as it was, we went on to rescue hundreds more.                 We saw

human lives in danger, and we acted - founding ourselves on international

law  and  on  humanity.  While  safeguarding  our  neutrality,  we  placed

humanity above all else. As President Disanayaka has reiterated, “we will

never hesitate to protect humanity.                              If there are

actions that must be taken to protect human lives, we will not hesitate to

take them under any circumstance”.

This,  Mr.  President,  is  the  Sri  Lanka  we  wish  to  bring  before  the

world - a small island nation with a big heart which believes that even in

times of conflict and profound division, there remains space for humanity.

And that is also what we wish to see reflected in the world. We need a

world  where  our  capacity  to  uphold  humanity  grows  faster  than  our

capacity to destroy it. That is the transformation we should seek.

It is for these reasons that we are pained by the developments in Gaza

and the Occupied Palestinian territories.

The  global  security environment  has  deteriorated  significantly  in  recent

years. It is difficult to accept that, in a world with so much wealth and

knowledge,  vast  resources  continue  to  be  spent  on  weapons  while

children face starvation and are deprived of medicine and education.

Sri Lanka remains deeply concerned by the conflicts in West Asia and by

the

heavy

cost

being

borne

far

beyond

the

region.

International  law,  including  International  Humanitarian  Law,  must  be

adhered  to  and  respected  by  all  parties.  We  reaffirm  our  position  that

dialogue is the only viable way forward.

Sri  Lanka  continues  to  support  the  inalienable  rights  of  the  Palestinian

people,

including

their

right

to

self-determination.

We are among the countries that first recognised Palestine as a distinct

State in the 1980s. We stand in solidarity with the international community

in  calling  for  an  independent  and  sovereign  State  of  Palestine, existing

side by side with Israel, in peace, within the pre-1967 borders.

We welcome the resolution of the Security Council on a ceasefire in Gaza

and  urge  all  parties  to  uphold  it.  Humanitarian  assistance  must  reach

civilians  without  obstruction.  The  recovery  and  reconstruction  of  Gaza

must be an urgent priority.

Sri  Lanka  is  proud  of  its  longstanding  contribution  to  United  Nations

peacekeeping,  in  pursuit  of  global  peace  and  security,  having  deployed

more than 21,000 personnel on numerous missions since 1957.

Our Blue Helmets, through their dedication and service over many years,

have earned the trust of local communities and the commendation of UN

field missions.

Today,  they  continue  to  serve  with  distinction  in  some  of  the  most

challenging  environments  under  the  UN  flag  —  protecting  vulnerable

civilians, deterring violence and helping war-torn communities transition

from conflict to stability.

Sri Lanka has also long championed multilateral disarmament — from our

early call for an Indian Ocean Zone of Peace to our leadership at the 1995

NPT Review and Extension Conference.

At a time of rising geopolitical tensions and rhetoric of nuclear escalation,

we  remain  firmly  convinced  that  the  only  real  guarantee  against  these

weapons is their total and verifiable elimination.

As we approach 2030, we must deliver on the Sustainable Development

Goals, which remain our collective blueprint for sustainable development.

Sri Lanka once again calls for reform of the international financial system

and  for  fairer  rules  governing  debt  and  development  finance.  We

welcomed the Seville Commitment last year, including its call for urgent

action  to  close  the  four  -trillion-dollar  financing  gap  for  sustainable

development  in  developing  countries.  It  is  now  time  to  translate  those

commitments into concrete action.

We  remain  steadfast  in  recognising  poverty  and  inequality  as  factors

requiring our urgent attention.

Our national budget last year made historic allocations to the healthcare

and education sectors. We take pride in our longstanding policy of free

and  universal  healthcare  and  education,  and  remain  committed  to

strengthening these important pillars of social justice.

While  actively  implementing  all  SDGs  without  discrimination,  we  fully

subscribe to and proactively engage with SDG 16, which underscores the

importance of just and inclusive institutions that build and restore public

trust and treat all people equally.

Sri  Lanka  has  long  championed  and  contributed  towards  a  fair  and

peaceful order at sea under the United Nations Convention on the Law of

the Sea — a legal regime which we have helped shape.                 We

also support the work of the Commission on the Limits of the Continental

Shelf. We remain committed to preserving the oceans as a shared space

for peaceful and sustainable use, and for international cooperation. Our

nation’s prosperity is closely linked to the Indian Ocean.

As a founding Member of the Agreement on Marine Biological Diversity of

Areas Beyond National Jurisdiction, the BBNJ Agreement, we reaffirm our

commitment  to  safeguarding  the  oceans  as  a  common  heritage  of

humankind for present and future generations.

We  look  forward  to  the  further  operationalisation  of  the  Agreement,

complementing the processes of the International Seabed Authority.

One of the key pillars of the decisive mandate given to us by the people

of Sri Lanka was to build a transparent and ethical nation. In delivering

on this mandate, we have placed good governance, anti-corruption and

institutional transparency at the core of a comprehensive national integrity

drive that is being vigorously pursued.

We  have  seen  all  too  clearly  how  corruption  weakens  democracy  and

destroys trust. We continue to enforce the law against corruption without

fear or favour, irrespective of a person’s background or social standing.

Investigations  and  prosecutions  continue  to  progress  without  political

interference.

Substantial progress has been made in strengthening the independence

of  institutions  responsible  for  investigating  and  prosecuting  bribery  and

corruption.

My  President,  who  addressed  this  Assembly  last  year,  also  highlighted

how  narcotics  and  related  organised  crime  have  become  a  menace  for

many  countries,  as  well  as  our  Government’s  comprehensive  efforts  to

address this menace.

One year on, our “United as a Nation” Anti-Narcotics National Programme

has made significant progress, including through the arrest of key figures

in the narcotics supply chain.

We  reiterate  our  call  on  the  global  community  to  promote  meaningful

technology  transfers,  ensure  equitable  access  for  developing  nations,

bridge the digital divide, and build safe, secure and trustworthy systems

that leave no one behind.

Sri  Lanka  is  in  the  process  of  building  a  digital  future  that  includes

everyone. We have developed national AI ethical guidelines in line with

international frameworks.

We must ensure that emerging technologies and artificial intelligence are

developed and used responsibly and consistently with international law,

including the well-established principles of international humanitarian law.

Their  development  and  use  must  contribute  to  international  peace  and

security while advancing humanity's collective interests.

The interests of humanity must always guide the development and use of

these technologies.

For Sri Lanka, the United Nations is an indispensable partner. The UN has

stood with us in challenging times and supported our development.

For  many  of  us  in  the  developing  world,  the  United  Nations  is  also  an

expression of a fundamental promise: that every nation, large or small,

has a voice; that every people has a right to dignity and development;

and that, in an interdependent world, no country should be left to confront

global challenges alone.

For more than eight decades, amidst its flaws and with much room for

improvement,  the  United  Nations  has  given  practical  meaning  to  that

promise.

However,  genuine  faith  in  multilateralism  requires  the  courage  to

acknowledge where the system has fallen short, the humility to listen to

those who feel unheard, and the determination to make our institutions

more effective, more representative and more responsive.

In this regard, Sri Lanka supports the UN80 Initiative as an opportunity to

renew and strengthen the United Nations and advance meaningful reform.

Managing transformation cannot mean managing change for some while

asking others merely to adapt to its consequences.

The transformation taking place in our world must be inclusive.

It  must  narrow,  rather  than  deepen,  the  divides  between  North  and

South; between those who shape new technologies and those who merely

receive them; and between those who possess resilience and those who

are most exposed to global shocks.

My  country  comes  to  this  Assembly  not  with  the  expectation  that  the

United Nations can solve every problem, but with the conviction that there

are problems which no country can solve alone.

Our answer must therefore be a renewed faith in multilateralism and a

United  Nations  that  listens  more  closely,  represents  more  fairly  and

delivers for all.

preventive diplomacy remains the most effective means

To create an environment conducive to inclusive growth

law.  We  remain  committed  to

We must acknowledge that climate change is no longer a

future  threat  but  a  present  reality.  Lesotho  is

increasingly  experiencing  severe  floods  and  droughts,

resulting in unparalleled land degradation and extensive

damage  to  critical  infrastructure.  Despite  contributing

minimally  to  global  greenhouse  gas  emissions,  Least

Developed Countries like Lesotho bear a disproportionate

brunt  of  climate  impact.  Global  warming  and  rising  sea

levels pose existential threats, particularly to small island

developing  states.  We  stand  in  solidarity  with  these

nations and call for greater global action.

To  cope  with  these  climate-related  challenges,  we  call

strengthen capacity of developing countries to effectively
