Thirty-five years ago, Lithuania  returned to its rightful place  in the global community of sovereign states. By joining the United Nations, we reaffirmed our  strong  commitment  to  the  global  order  based  on  international  law, territorial integrity, state sovereignty, and human dignity.

It was a glorious moment for a nation  well taught by historical experience that freedom and independence cannot be taken for granted. They must be constantly – and consistently – defended.

Today, I am standing here to speak for the same dream that inspired Lithuania in 1991. The vision of a more just, secure, and peaceful world.

Today, I am backing up the principles of the United Nations which, sadly, are being put under increasing pressure.

Recent  years  have  brought  us  numerous  high-intensity  and  far-reaching conflicts that dominate the global affairs on a scale not seen in decades.

We  witness  geopolitical  instability  in  Europe,  the  Middle  East,  and elsewhere. It is made worse by growing nuclear ambitions in the Middle East and Asia, as well as the irresponsible transfer of military-related goods, dual-use items, and sensitive technologies.

In recent months, Iran has continued attacking neighbouring countries, often through its proxies, while actively impairing the freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz. These  actions constitute a serious threat to regional and international peace and security. We reaffirm our full solidarity with the Gulf

Cooperation Council states and Jordan. We call on Iran to halt its nuclear and missile programs, as well as its collaboration with armed groups across the Middle East.

Lithuania commends all efforts to find a solution ensuring the  freedom of navigation.  We  will  contribute  with  our  demining  capabilities  to  the international maritime missions in the Strait of Hormuz.

As regards the situation in the Gaza Strip, my country supports international efforts to maintain and consolidate the ceasefire. The Comprehensive Plan to End  the  Gaza  Conflict,  including  the  deployment  of  the  temporary International Stabilisation Force, provides the guidelines to follow.

Lithuania  reiterates  the  importance  of  full  demilitarisation  and  calls  on Hamas  and  other  non-state  armed  groups  to  disarm  and  permanently decommission  their  weapons.  Humanitarian  aid  must  also  be  allowed  to reach those in need safely, and without obstruction.

To  this  day,  the  two-state  solution  remains  the  only  way  towards  a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace. In this light, it is crucially important to  abstain  from  any  further  actions  incompatible  with  a  credible  political process.

The one conflict that poses the greatest threat to the world order is Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, supported by its proxies.

In  the  twelve  years  since  the  illegal  occupation  of  Crimea,  Russia  has escalated from clandestine operations and limited warfare in Eastern Ukraine to  massive  military  operations,  mass  killings,  and,  ultimately,  the  largest drone attacks against civilian infrastructure the world has ever seen.

The  current  stage  of  the  war,  which  began  with  the  full-scale  invasion  in February 2022, has already lasted longer than the First World War.

In the last 55 months, Russia has suffered 1.5 million military casualties. In the last year, it  has gained 0.3 percent of  Ukraine’s territory at the cost of over 400 thousand soldiers killed and wounded.

Yet  all  these  enormous  efforts,  all  that  blood  and  tears,  basically  came  to nothing.  Ukraine  is  still  standing  proudly  as  an  independent  state.  The Ukrainian language, culture, and national identity are alive and thriving.

In all but name, Russia has already lost the war. Yet its leadership does not allow  itself  to  admit  defeat,  fearing  international  legal  accountability  and possible  revenge  from  its  own  people. As  the  inevitable  approaches,  the stakes get higher, and the Kremlin regime increasingly finds itself cornered.

How much more Ukrainian civilian lives will be sacrificed on Russia’s war altar? How many people will be tortured, sexually assaulted, thrown into dark dungeons,  never  to  see  the  sunlight  again?  How  many  children  will  be illegally  separated  from  their  parents  and  sent  to  Russia  to  suffer indoctrination?

We do not know the answers, yet we must all feel the deep pain brought by this  brutal  and  pointless  war. And  we  all  should  join  our  forces  to  draw Ukraine’s victory closer.

For  it  is  only  Ukraine’s  final  victory,  safeguarding  its  sovereignty, independence,  and  territorial  integrity,  that  could  ensure  the  global  peace, security, and the credibility of the United Nations charter.

What we cannot allow is a brute force prevailing over international law. We cannot tolerate any longer Moscow’s colonial aspirations, which undermine global food security and driving up food prices.

Russia’s  imperial  ambitions  reach  far  into  Europe,  Africa,  and  Asia.  No country should consider itself immune from this threat.

Naturally,  Lithuania  witnesses  many  dangers  up  close.  In  recent  months, Russia’s war of aggression has led to numerous violations of our air space by

combat  drones.  Russia  has  also  intensified  hybrid  attacks,  disinformation, and sabotage efforts.

Where  Russia  advances,  opening  Pandora’s  box  of  new  techniques  for destabilization, other hostile actors follow, learning new skills and ideas.

Attacks  on  information  integrity  pose  an  especially  troubling  challenge  to every  society.  Disinformation,  foreign  information  manipulation  and interference, and the falsification of history erode trust, restrict civic space, and target journalists and human rights defenders. As a result, human rights, democracy, and security suffer.

This risk is further enhanced by the development of artificial intelligence. As we  all  know,  AI  has  a  huge  potential for  transformation,  especially  in  the field  of  economy.  Whole  sectors,  including  those  related  to  defence  and security, might get radically changed or destroyed almost overnight. As any instrument, AI is also increasingly used by those seeking to cause harm and destruction.

Lithuania strongly believes that the future of AI must not be determined by authoritarian  control, technological  coercion, or the malicious use of data. We are therefore investing in trusted AI capabilities, promoting responsible AI  deployment,  and  advancing  the  Vilnius  Convention  –  the  world’s  first legally binding international treaty on artificial intelligence.

By demonstrating how shared principles can be translated into concrete legal commitments,  we  hope  to  contribute  significantly  to  the  United  Nations Global Dialogue on AI Governance.

Lithuania  invites  the  international  community  to  unite  in  addressing significant  legal,  ethical,  and  strategic  challenges  posed  by  artificial intelligence.  With  even  major  technology  companies  sending  warning signals that control of AI might slip out of humanity’s hands, the time is ripe for collective action.

Together,  we  must  ensure  that  AI  serves  human  dignity,  sustainable development,  and  international  security,  rather  than  becoming  a  new instrument  of  inequality,  manipulation,  or  conflict.  At  any  cost,  human accountability, law,  and  peace  and  security  must  be safeguarded.

international

The credibility of the United Nations depends on its ability to respond firmly to  aggression,  unlawful  conquest,  forced  deportations,  and  crimes  against humanity, and also to coordinate the global response to the growth of AI.

If we are serious about preserving peace, we must defend justice and strongly support those fighting for their freedom.

I am grateful to the Secretary General, His Excellency António Guterres, for his long-lasting service and his focus on reforming the United Nations into a more effective, modern, and responsive organization.

This  is  the  correct  path  to  follow.  There  is  no  other  way.  No  nation  can confront today’s challenges alone. Aggression cannot win. It is only through multilateralism, solidarity, and the unity of all Member States that we can uphold peace, security, and the rules-based international order.

It  is  also  important  to  learn  from  the  many  lessons  of  history.  Today,  too many seem unwilling to recognize and confront the past crimes committed by totalitarian regimes, including Soviet crimes.

This is a fundamental flaw. We must remember the past so as not to repeat it!

That is why Lithuania is promoting the concept of historical remembrance. My personal wish is to see the Pan-European Memorial to all victims of the 20th century totalitarian regimes unveiled in Brussels as soon as possible.

There  is  one  lesson  Lithuania,  having  survived  and  overcome  numerous occupations  and  waves  of  repression,  can  share  with  the  international

community. Freedom can be delayed, but it cannot be extinguished; justice can be challenged, but it cannot be defeated.

This, I believe, is a message that goes far beyond an experience of a single person, or a nation. It speaks to the whole humankind, united in our shared dignity.

At a time of growing global uncertainty and power politics, we need even more  multilateralism  grounded  in  international  law,  the  UN  Charter,  and universal human rights. We need to resist the law of the strongest collectively, in order not to fall under the yoke separately.

The time to act is now. And I believe – I want to believe – that we have what it takes to make the world a more just, secure, and peaceful place to live!

Thank you.

Madam president, excellencies, first and foremost, allow me to extend my warmest congratulations to His Excellency Doctor Khalilur Rahman on his election as president of the General Assembly. He can certainly count on Luxembourg's full support throughout his tenure. Madam president, the theme that has been chosen for this general debate can hardly be more timely. When I try to paint an honest picture of the world we live in, one thing strikes me in particular trust is under growing strain. Trust between nations, trust between people, and, perhaps most importantly, trust in our ability to work together. And yet, I believe that trust is precisely where we should begin Not because trust is easy, but because every lasting achievement of the international community has begun with a decision to trust.

This is my first address to this Assembly as Head of State of the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg, I assumed office less than a year ago. It is therefore a particular honor to stand before you today and to reaffirm from this podium the importance Luxembourg attaches to the United Nations and to a rule based international order grounded in the rule of law. But this moment also makes me reflect on what the United Nations means from the perspective of my own generation. As a relatively young man who has had the privilege of traveling the world, I have been fortunate to meet people from very different cultures, backgrounds, and traditions. These experiences have left me with a simple and lasting conviction. We can learn a lot from each other, and I remain convinced that it is only by working together that we can overcome the many challenges our world is facing today.

This conviction is not naive. I am fully aware of the difficulties confronting us, but precisely because the world is becoming more difficult, I believe we must resist the temptation to give up on cooperation. There has never been a time when communication between people in different parts of the world was so easy. Millions of young people have virtual friends and acquaintances across continents through social media, gaming, and countless other forms of connection. We have never been so connected, and yet we seem increasingly unable to trust one another. This should make us reflect.

Is it still possible to build a world order in which respect and the willingness to work towards common goals can prevail over the pursuit of self-interest and power? I believe it is, but it will require determination, dialogue and a willingness to look beyond immediate interest. And this is why the United Nations matters. Madam Presidents. Luxembourg has believed in this principle from the very beginning. 81 years ago, still deeply marked by the horrors of the Second World War Luxembourg was among the 51 founding members that came together in San Francisco to lay the foundations of a new international order.

At the time, we were the smallest country represented. We have prospered in the peace that Europe enjoyed for decades after 1945, and we have never forgotten that the peace could not be taken for granted. It was built generation after generation by those who chose cooperation over confrontation. Today, that peace is being challenged once again. Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine has brought war back to our continent. It is a stark reminder that peace requires constant commitment, and that the principles on which our international order was built must be defended.

The United Nations itself was born from that choice. Its charter called upon us to unite our strength to maintain international peace and security, and above all, to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war. 81 years later, that promise is under considerable pressure, but it has not failed. Multilateralism may be imperfect, but disenchantment should lead us to reform, not to dismissal. The question is, therefore, not whether we still need multilateralism. The question is whether we have the courage to make it better.

Madam president. Madam president, this brings me to a question that is very dear to my heart. What kind of world do we want to bequeath to future generations? We often talk about young people as if they came from the future. Truth be told, they are already shaping the present. Therefore, it is incumbent upon us to ask ourselves if we're really preparing a future that is going to earn their trust.

My personal experience has done nothing but reinforce this conviction. This year I had the privilege of succeeding His Majesty King Carl Gustaf of Sweden as honorary chair of the World Scout Foundation. My long standing commitment to the Scout movement has taught me a great deal about the power of intergenerational dialogue, solidarity, and the values of the Scout movement. It's also taught me something absolutely fundamental. Placing our trust in young people means giving them responsibilities, allowing them to take action. They are growing up in a world in which there are extraordinary possibilities.

But it's also a world where uncertainty runs deep. Artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies are already transforming our way of life and the way in which we work. The enthusiasm they give rise to also goes hand in hand with the very real concerns, the current debates about the most extreme risks of AI remind us that technological progress cannot be divorced from responsibility. As we confront these transformations, we should endow our young people with the means to develop their critical thinking skills and their creativity. And this is exactly what education is supposed to do transmit knowledge and competencies, but also to teach young people to call things into question, to open up to others and to shoulder your responsibilities. Against this backdrop, I believe that we should have one guiding principle.

Human beings should be at the heart of all of our decision making. We must protect the rights, security, and the well-being of all. We should also listen to young people, ask them what we can build, working hand in hand through different cultures and generations. I saw for myself everything that young people are capable of accomplishing. When we give them our trust, we give them responsibilities and the necessary space to take action, as well as when we encourage them to work together This is why Luxembourg supports the UN's youth delegate programme, as well as the United Nations Youth Office. It is also why our commitment to education, science and culture remains so important, in particular through our term on the Executive Board of Unesco for the period 2025 2029.

It is precisely these qualities which allow trust to flourish. Madam president, Luxembourg's commitment to the United Nations is underpinned by all three pillars peace and security, human rights and development. Solidarity must be translated into deeds. We continue to allocate 1% of our national income to development cooperation. We're also building long term partnerships with vulnerable countries. We remain committed to the multilateral humanitarian system, as well as to all those who are providing assistance where it is most needed.

The same level of responsibility applies to peace and security. Conflicts affect all human beings women, children, older persons, persons with disabilities, as well as people who are already vulnerable. Protecting civilians and defending human rights cannot take a back seat to other considerations. Luxembourg has Unstintingly worked to contribute to this effort through peacekeeping operations humanitarian interventions protecting children affected by armed conflict, the women peace and security agenda, as well as the mine clearance humanitarian activities in Ukraine. The experience we gained as an elected member of the Security Council in 2013 and 2014 showed us that elected members can make a real difference, especially when the permanent members of the Security Council are divided. It is for this reason that Luxembourg is asking for member states to place their trust in it, as it seeks a Security Council seat for the 2031 2032 period.

We do this humbly, but firm in our conviction, our conviction that a small country can offer up a different perspective, can bring different positions closer together and help find common ground. When this is particularly difficult, it is the same conviction which guides our commitment to human rights at a time when respect for human rights is being subjected to growing pressures, we must resist the temptation to see it as something that's up for discussion. Human rights are neither a privilege reserved for the few, nor the expression of one culture, of one political system. They are the very bedrock of human dignity. Our commitment is also concrete. As a member of the Human Rights Council for the period 2022 2024, Luxembourg took the full measure of just how important it is to defend human rights through multilateralism.

We continue to support the office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, as well as efforts aimed at clarifying the fate of persons who were disappeared in Syria. Madam president. Restoring trust also means making our institutions worthy of that trust. The Security Council must become more representative, more effective, and more accountable to the entire membership of the United Nations. Africa in particular, and it was said many times today, should have a stronger voice. And when the Security Council is paralysed.

The General Assembly must be able to play its rightful role. The United Nations must reform so that it can deliver more effectively, particularly when resources are constrained. But reform must never become an end in itself. The purpose of institutions is to serve people Ultimately, the test of multilateralism is not how many resolutions we adopt or how many meetings we hold. It's whether a child is safer because of our decisions. Whether a young person can receive an education, whether a family can live in dignity, whether a small country can believe that international law will protect it when power alone cannot.

This is why trust matters, and this is why Luxembourg will continue to defend multilateralism. Because we know what happens when it fails. Madam president, climate change reminds us, perhaps more clearly than any other challenge, that we cannot solve global problems by acting alone. It transcends borders and generations. Small island developing states are already experiencing consequences that threaten their very existence. Luxembourg may be landlocked, but we are deeply committed to this common effort, including by drawing on the expertise of our financial centre in green finance.

Our interests may differ, but our future is shared. Madam president, the world is becoming more fragmented. The international order is under strain. We need to recognise this reality. But we should not mistake a world of competing centres of power for a more just or stable international order. For Luxembourg, the answer is clear Our experience has taught us that international law and multilateral institutions give countries, whatever their size, a voice and place at the table.

It is not about resisting a changing world, but to make multilateralism fit for that world. I believe this is ultimately what the United Nations asks of us, not that we agree on everything, not that we abandon our national interests, but that we recognise that there are challenges for which no nation, however powerful, can find lasting solutions alone. We can look at the imperfections of multilateralism and conclude that it no longer works, or we can reform it fairly, strengthen it, and make it worthy of the trust that future generations will place in us. I know which choice I want to make, because this is the world I want to leave to my children. A world where dialogue is stronger than confrontation, where respect between nations allows differences to become sources of strength rather than division. Where international law protects weeks, protects the weak as well as the strong.

If we restore trust, if we listen to the next generation, and if we have the courage to act together, the United Nations can continue to be more than a reflection of the world as it is. It can remain an instrument for building the world we want to leave behind a world worthy of the trust of those who will inherit it. Young people do not expect us to solve every challenge, but they do expect us to try. They expect us to act with responsibility. And above all, they expect us not to lose faith in our ability to shape a better future. And that is the promise we should make to the next generation.

Thank you.

Allow me to begin by congratulating you, Dr. Khalilur Rahman, on your election as President of the

General Assembly. You can count on Latvia’s support.

I am looking forward to working together for a stronger United Nations and a safer world.

For  the  past  year,  we  have  heard  it  again  and  again:  the  world  order  is  breaking  down.  The  rules-based  order  that  brought  stability  is  under  growing  strain.  Something  new  is  taking  shape.  What comes next is not certain.

But  one  thing  is  certain.  The  world  has  changed.  International  trade.  Mobility.  Technology.  What happens far away is no longer far away.

Instability travels. Conﬂicts cross borders. What happens in Ukraine does not stay in Ukraine. What happens in the Middle East, in the Red Sea, and in Sudan does not stay there.

The  same  is  true  of  other  global  threats. Technology  has  made  distance  matter  even  less. Artiﬁcial intelligence oﬀers enormous opportunities. But in the wrong hands, it can also become a powerful

tool for deception, disruption and conﬂict.

And nature respects no borders either. Heatwaves do not stop at checkpoints. Rising seas threaten to erase entire island nations from the face of the Earth. And far from the ocean, the danger is just as real. In the mountains, a river can turn into a deadly ﬂood in seconds, sweeping away homes, roads

and  lives.  We  just  witnessed  catastrophic  ﬂood  wave  in  Nepal  where  also  33  Latvian  citizens disappeared. Global climate change does not have borders or citizenships.

Diﬀerent threats. The same lesson: none of us can face them alone.

We  are  in  the  same  boat.  Perhaps  Noah’s  Ark  is  no  longer  just  a  biblical  story.  Diﬀerent  nations. Diﬀerent realities. But increasingly, a shared fate.

And when we share the same boat, we need something that holds us together.

We already have it – the United Nations Charter and its principles. Sovereignty. Territorial integrity.

The peaceful settlement of disputes. Respect for human rights. The rejection of aggression.
