Ladies and gentlemen,

For Latvia, these principles are written into our history.

Latvia  and  its  people  know  what  it  means  to  lose  sovereignty  and  freedom.  For  50  years,  our independence was denied. But Latvia’s right to sovereignty endured.

We  restored  our  independence  through  the  courage  and  determination  of  our  people. And we  did not stand alone. We had friends who never accepted Soviet occupation as legitimate.

That history stays with us. Sovereignty and territorial integrity are the foundation of our freedom and our security.

And  the  same  is  true  for  every  country  represented  in  this  Hall.  When  one  state  believes  it  can redraw the borders of another by force, every border on every continent becomes negotiable.

These principles now are being tested in Ukraine.

Russia’s war against Ukraine strikes at the very heart of the United Nations Charter. Borders changed by force. Territory seized by force. Children taken by force. Ukrainian civilians targeted by Russia.

Schools.  Hospitals.  Homes.  Markets.  Energy  infrastructure.  Russia’s  attacks  reach  far  beyond  the battleﬁeld. They are directed against the people of Ukraine and the foundations of their daily lives. Drones are used to hunt civilians - human lives are threated by targets in a safari.

These  are  not  policy  disagreements.  These  are  grave  violations  of  international  law.  And  where crimes are committed, there must be accountability. Let us not look away.

Russia is a permanent member of the Security Council. With that comes a special responsibility for international  peace  and  security.  Instead,  Russia  is  violating  the  very  principles  it  is  entrusted  to uphold.

Russia started this brutal war. Russia can end it. It can stop its attacks. It can withdraw its forces. It can  leave  Ukraine’s  sovereign  territory.  Latvia  continues  to  call  for  an  immediate  and  full  ceaseﬁre.

Ukraine deserves just peace.

Members of the United Nations,

Not  every  attack  on  the  international  order  looks  like war.  Drones  carrying  explosives  at  airports. Drones  crashing  into  homes.  Airspace  violated.  Critical  infrastructure  damaged.  Power  stations

suddenly in ﬂames. Cyberattacks.

https://www2.mfa.gov.lv/en/newyork/news/74028-statement-by-h-e-mr-edgars-rinkevics-president-of-the-republic-of-latvia-at-the-81st-session-of-the-u… 3/6

News | Permanent Mission of the Republic of Latvia to the United Nations

We  sometimes  call  them  hybrid  threats.  But  it  sounds  as  innocent  as  hybrid  cars.  In  reality  those

threats to international peace and security are as dangerous as conventional wars.

Guarding the eastern border of NATO and the European Union, Latvia faces these threats every day.

Illegal migrants are deliberately exploited and pushed towards our border with Belarus. Cyberattacks

target  our  critical  networks.  Acts  of  sabotage  seek  to  create  fear  and  instability  in  our  societies.

Russia’s shadow ﬂeet exploits legal grey zones and puts our security and environment at risk.

Even in this very building, at the Security Council table, we have heard Russia spread blatant lies and

make threats against Latvia and other free and democratic countries.

Distinguished Delegates,

That brings us back to a fundamental question.

What is the United Nations role if its members are threatened and its principles violated?

The United Nations cannot take its relevance for granted. It must earn it — day by day. Not through

the number of meetings we hold. Not through the number of resolutions we adopt. But through real and tangible results.

The United Nations must prove that it can still make a diﬀerence when it matters most.

That requires institutions that work. Latvia supports the Secretary-General’s UN80 initiative. Reform

is not about weakening the United Nations. It is about making it stronger, more focused and better able to deliver on its mandate.

That must include also the Security Council. Its composition must better reﬂect the world of today,

not the world of 1945. Latvia supports an expanded and more representative Security Council.

Reform is also about leadership.

This year, we will select the next Secretary-General.

The  choice  matters.  The  next  Secretary-General  must  defend  the  Charter  with  conviction.  Must uphold international law.

That  is  what  true  leadership  means. To  speak  up  for  the  weak  against  the  powerful. That  the  true

leadership means.

Dear Colleagues,

Latvia  now  serves  as  an  elected  member  of  the  Security  Council  and  will  hold  its  presidency  in

November.

https://www2.mfa.gov.lv/en/newyork/news/74028-statement-by-h-e-mr-edgars-rinkevics-president-of-the-republic-of-latvia-at-the-81st-session-of-the-u… 4/6

News | Permanent Mission of the Republic of Latvia to the United Nations

Latvia came to the Council with a simple promise: to stand up for international order, to speak clearly

when it is violated, and to make the voices of smaller nations heard. That reﬂects who Latvia is and

what Latvia believes in.

At the core are real people. That is why Latvia will continue to do everything possible to help return

Ukrainian  children  deported  to  Russia.  Children  have  been  taken  from  their  families,  their communities  and  their  country. We  know  such  stories  from  the  darkest  chapters  of  history. Today,

those things are happening again.

We support every genuine eﬀort to secure the return of the Ukrainian children. We are grateful for First Lady Melania Trump’s eﬀorts to help bring them home. These children need to come home now.

The most vulnerable must be protected. This includes conﬂict-related sexual violence. Survivors need

justice, not silence.

These priorities underpin Latvia’s bid for a seat on the Human Rights Council at 2028 elections.

Mister President, Excellencies,

We  need  a  place  where  every  state,  large  or  small,  has  a  voice.  Where  threats  to  peace  can  be

confronted  together.  Where  disputes  can  be  resolved  through  dialogue,  not  force.  Where international law protects the strong and the weak alike.

That was the promise of the United Nations 81 years ago. It remains our responsibility today. It is not

a Christmas wish for this year. We must stand by our principles always.

The world has changed. The threats have changed. But our fundamental purpose has not: to maintain international peace and security.

That purpose is worth defending. And this Organisation is worth reforming so that it can deliver.

Let us make the United Nations work — for peace, for security, and for all of us.

Thank you!

speaker_post: Minister of Foreign Affairs, African Cooperation and Moroccans Abroad
text:
Your Excellency, president of the General Assembly. Mr. Secretary General, your excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. I extend my sincere congratulations on behalf of the delegation of the Kingdom of Morocco to His Excellency, Mr. Khalil al-Rahman, on his election as president of the General Assembly at its 81st session, and I wish him every success in his lofty mission. I also commend the tireless efforts of Secretary General Antonio Guterres, since he assumed the leadership of our organization amid the major divisions the world has experienced over the past decade, he has emerged as a voice of wisdom, consensus and pragmatism, defending tirelessly and courageously the United Nations system and international law as the two fundamental pillars for the maintenance of international peace and security. Mr. Guterres has remained a symbol of multilateral diplomacy and of international cooperation in overcoming the turmoil and obstacles facing our world today. Mr. president, the most apt description of our international reality is the one expressed by His Majesty King Mohammed the Sixth.

May God assist him when His Majesty said, and I quote, the world is changing at an unprecedented pace and certainties are steadily receding. This has led to a blurring of standards and concepts. Alliances have become open to question. International law is frequently violated. And its capacity to regulate international relations faces numerous challenges. End of quote from His Majesty the King We are therefore facing a world whose fundamental features are the following.

First, the escalation of acute and diverse international crises military, economic, energy related and environmental. Second, the spread of confrontational tendencies as a key determinant of relations between states. Third, the difficulty of predicting the outcome of crises. We know when they begin but not when they will end. Fourth, the diminishing capacity of existing regulatory structures to play the role in preventing and managing crises in this complex international context. Mr. president, I wish to focus on three areas to which the international community must accord priority.

First, confronting non-state armed groups as a threat to international security and stability. Second, addressing climate change and its effects. Third, tackling regional challenges, particularly in the Middle East and Africa. The role of non-state armed groups that threaten the security and stability of states has grown considerably. Indeed, they now seek to control maritime corridors and straits and to threaten freedom of navigation. They also target facilities in a number of countries.

At the global level, more than 200 million people live in areas under the control of armed groups or in contested areas. Moreover, more than 130 non-state armed groups have been identified as legally classified parties to armed conflicts. These figures clearly reflect the scale of the spread and proliferation of these groups. In a world that, over the past two decades has become less secure and less stable. Further, the close links between these armed groups and separatist militias on the one hand, and terrorist organizations and criminal networks, as well as mercenary elements, on the other hand, are evident to all. It is therefore a mistake to believe that some of these groups are peaceful or constructive, or that they can engage in the settlement of conflicts.

All these groups use violence to impose a fait accompli and to serve the agenda of those who control them. They must therefore be dealt with firmly, and responsibility must be assigned to the states that sponsor Harbour Finance and armed them, and provide them with safe haven and support. The responsibility of these sponsoring states is not merely political, it is also legal, moral and historical. These groups and their sponsors alike cannot be allowed to become a means of evading responsibility or a tool for carrying out what states cannot do directly. Hence, deterrent sanctions must be imposed on these groups and their sponsors. All those who provide them with support, financing or arms must be held accountable.

Mr. president, there can be no way to sustain peace and development without effectively addressing the challenge of climate change, which is no longer a future threat. It is already affecting water and food security, as well as the stability of territories, economies and the living conditions of populations. Despite its limited contribution to greenhouse gas emissions, Morocco remains among the countries most vulnerable to the impacts of climate change. Accordingly, in line with the vision of His Majesty King Mohammed VI, may God assist him The Kingdom has adopted a proactive policy based on the continued construction of dams, the interconnection of water basins, seawater desalination, the reuse of treated wastewater and the rationalization of water resource management, particularly in the agricultural sector. This national effort forms part of an international commitment to climate action. On that basis, the Kingdom has set for the period 2026 2035, a target of reducing greenhouse gas emissions by up to 53% by 2035, while placing adaptation and the strengthening of territorial resilience at the top of its priorities.

This effort has extended to the African continent, which suffers from the devastating effects of climate change. The Royal Initiative to establish three African climate commissions for the Congo Basin the Sahel region and the African island states, has generated promising momentum to strengthen African climate action and coordination among the states of the continent in addressing these challenges. However, addressing climate change cannot rely on national efforts alone. It requires the provision of affordable and accessible financing, technology transfer and genuine international solidarity, enabling developing countries to fulfill their responsibilities towards present and future generations alike. Mr. president, Madam President, the Palestinian question remains a constant priority in the foreign policy of the Kingdom of Morocco, based on its belief in the justice of this, that this is a just cause and its central to achieving peace and stability in the Middle East region. Building on this conviction, the Kingdom of Morocco, under the leadership of His Majesty King Mohammed VI, believes that the establishment of a lasting peace in the Middle East depends on the establishment of an independent, sovereign and viable Palestinian state.

On the borders of the 4th of June 1967, with East Jerusalem as its capital, living side by side with the State of Israel in peace and security. In the face of the tragedy that the brotherly Palestinian people continue to endure, the Kingdom renews its call for respect for the ceasefire in Gaza and for the entry of humanitarian assistance into the strip in sufficient quantities without impediment or interruption. At the same time, Morocco stresses the need to support the Palestinian Authority, particularly in the financial, technical, structural, humanitarian and training fields and to accompany the reforms it is undertaking within its various institutions Morocco also renews its support for the pivotal role of the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East. In keeping with its approach of supporting initiatives aimed at achieving peace in the Middle East, Morocco has decided to participate in the international stabilisation force in Gaza and to contribute through humanitarian and security initiatives to establishing a climate of peace and security in the region by contributing to the training of the Palestinian police, deploying high ranking military officers to the internal security forces, and setting up a military field hospital. In addition to its readiness to lead a programme to counter extremism, developments in the West Bank are deeply alarming, including the adoption of certain laws that affect the legal status of Palestinian territory and pave the way for their seizure for the purpose of settlement expansion, as well as the systematic violence perpetrated by Israeli settlers against Palestinian citizens. All these measures point in one direction the displacement of the population and the undermining of the material basis for the establishment of an independent Palestinian state.

With regard to the city of Jerusalem, Morocco expresses its deep concern about unilateral Israeli measures and the repeated violations of the sanctity of Al-Aqsa mosque, which constitutes serious transgressions that contribute to fuelling the discourse of extremism and hatred at the expense of the voice of wisdom and moderation. As the chair of Al-Quds Committee, His Majesty King Mohammed VI, may God assist him, continues his work to preserve the historical, cultural and spiritual identity of the holy City and its legal status, as well as to improve the living conditions of the inhabitants. Combining political and diplomatic action with programmes implemented on the ground by Byte Mal Al-Quds al-Sharif Agency, the executive arm of Al-Quds Committee. Mr. president, despite its significant human, natural and civilizational assets, the African continent faces a gap between the scale of the commitments announced for its benefit by the international community and the value of what has actually been achieved on the ground. Contrary to the stereotypical image held by some, Africa is not a continent of conflicts and a hotbed of problems. Rather, it is a land of opportunity and potential, capable of devising solutions and putting forward initiatives That is the idea summed up by His Majesty King Mohammed VI.

May God assist him in his eloquent words. Africa must trust Africa, end of quote. The enlightened royal vision for Africa, which has materialised through a significant number of projects, stems from a firm conviction that the continent has attained a level of maturity that qualifies it to participate effectively in all decisions relating to its affairs. Indeed, it is capable of contributing to formulating proposals and solutions to the challenges facing the world as a whole. Morocco has translated this vision into practical and tangible royal initiatives, the most prominent of which are perhaps the royal initiative to enable Sahel states to access the Atlantic Ocean, as well as the African Atlantic states process. The African Atlantic Gas pipeline project, as well as investments in regional infrastructure cooperation in the areas of food security, fertiliser production and training programmes for African executives.

This is in addition to partnerships in the areas of health, renewable energy and water resource management. Madam president, with regard to The North African region. Thanks to the momentum initiated by His Majesty King Mohammed VI. May God assist him The question of the Moroccan Sahara reached a historic turning point with the adoption by Security Council of Resolution 2797 last October. Since then, this regional dispute has embarked on an irreversible course, breaking with the past and looking to the future with a view to its final settlement. This track rests on principles and parameters that admit no interpretation, nor any reading between the lines or in the margins, as some are vainly attempting deluding themselves in flagrant denial of reality and total disregard for established truth.

These principles, as set forth in the Security Council resolution, are as follows. First, there is no solution outside the framework of the autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty. Second, there is no approach or mechanism other than the political negotiation process under the auspices of the United Nations and on a sole basis, namely the Autonomy Initiative presented by the Kingdom of Morocco. Third, there can be no discussion or dispute regarding the responsibility and obligations of the four parties clearly identified by Security Council. Resolution 2797. Fourth, there will be no maintaining of the status quo preferred by the other parties.

The train of political solution has already departed. Fifth, there is no credibility for interlocutors who violate the ceasefire and refuse to respect Security Council resolutions. Sixth and last. There can be no tolerance for the continued holding of the population of the camps as hostages for half a century, in flagrant violation of international law and international humanitarian law. Alongside with its firm commitment to the final settlement of this regional dispute. Affected regional dispute.

The Kingdom of Morocco steadfastly continues to drive social and economic development in its southern provinces, particularly in the areas of infrastructure, university, education, health sector and airports, among others. It is a fortunate coincidence that tomorrow, God willing, the inhabitants of these Saharan provinces will fulfill their national and political duty by participating, as they have always done in the past in the legislative elections of the Kingdom. In so doing, they will strengthen democratic representation and contribute to the day to day management of the needs of the inhabitants of the Moroccan provinces. Madam president, the Kingdom of Morocco. True to its constant approach, is determined to contribute effectively and responsibly to the maintenance of international peace and security. This is done in accordance with a realistic vision of international cooperation, grounded in solidarity and with full respect for international law, national sovereignty, and territorial integrity.

It is in this context that the Kingdom of Morocco has presented its candidacy for a non-permanent seat on the Security Council for the term 2028 2029, so that it may continue to serve peace, collective security and multilateralism with full respect for the purposes and principles enshrined in the charter of the United Nations. It is the candidacy of a kingdom with a diplomatic heritage spanning several centuries, which carries the vision of His Majesty King Mohammed VI. May God assist him as an actor for stability, as an anchor for stability and sustainable development in the world. This candidacy also reflects the continued contribution of the Kingdom of Morocco to the three pillars of the United Nations, namely peace, development and the rule of law. I thank you.

President of the General Assembly. Secretary general. Heads of state, heads of government. Delegates. Your excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, I am addressing you as the representative of the smallest member state of this organisation in terms of its landmass and one of the smallest in terms of its population, barely two square kilometers bordering the Mediterranean. And yet, in this forum, there are no small or large states.

Here, every one of the 193 members has a voice, one alone and of the same weight. Here the charter only recognizes states equal in sovereignty, equal in rights, but also. And I wish to stress this point equal in terms of responsibility, because the equality that our organization bestows upon us is not a privilege that we enjoy. It is a responsibility that we bear. This responsibility is our shared, unique duty to uphold the law and multilateralism shared. Because no state, regardless of how powerful it is, can preserve peace alone or address global threats alone.

Unique because everybody must shoulder it without leaving it to others to honor the promise of San Francisco. It is this message that His Serene Highness Prince Albert the Second, the Prince of Monaco, charged me with bringing to this rostrum with his greetings of trust and friendship. President, the Principality of Monaco wishes sincerely to congratulate you upon your election to the presidency of this 81st session, for which you have chosen the topic Restoring Trust, Managing transformation. A UN that delivers for all. You can count on the full support of my country, and I also wish to warmly thank the Secretary General, Antonio Guterres, who is finishing his second mandate amidst particularly grave circumstances. Why does a state such as mine believe so strongly in international law?

The answer goes for all. When might makes right. It is the smallest states who are the first to be threatened when force is regulated by the law. All of humanity is protected. Sovereign equality between states, honoring commitments, peacefully settling disputes are therefore not abstract concepts. They are our front line of protection.

And yours too. With the balance as is set out by the charter between the three pillars peace and security, development and human rights. Nevertheless, this protection is today under assault. Rearmament is accelerating throughout the world. We are seeing the use of force once again as being another political tool for some Trade is breaking down and we are seeing a race to capture critical resources. The private sector is also part of this.

Of these power relations. We are now in the era of the geo economy, and this is fertile ground for disinformation, which undermines people's trust in their institutions and leads them to question verifiable facts. Our belief has never been tried to such an extent since 1945 in Ukraine, the Middle East, Sudan, the Sahel in many other places out of the media spotlight. Civilians are paying the price for conflicts which have discarded the most basic rules of humanity. And never, since 1945 has the very legitimacy of states and multilateral bodies such as the UN, been called into question to such an extent. Given this danger, let us recall our mission.

In the words of Dag Hammarskjöld, the second Secretary general of the UN. The UN was not created to take mankind to heaven, but to save humanity from hell. That is the exact scope of our task, and that is why we do not have the right to give up. First in Ukraine for almost five years, a permanent member of the Security Council has been waging a war of aggression against a sovereign state in flagrant violation of the charter. From the very outset, Monaco condemned this aggression unambiguously and unreservedly. We voted in favour of all of the General Assembly's resolutions calling and demanding for Russian forces to withdraw.

We took all restrictive measures aligned with EU measures, and we also provided our humanitarian support to the Ukrainian people and hosted people displaced by the war. Our support is unwavering and it will remain so. Monaco will never recognize any annexation of territory obtained through force. Allowing this for one state would be tantamount to allowing it for all. The principality welcomes the ongoing diplomatic efforts and hopes that they will lead to fair, comprehensive, lasting peace, respecting Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity. Next to the Middle East, Monaco was greatly relieved by the cease fire, which entered into force in Gaza, and the fact that the hostages were freed.

Nothing can ever justify the acts of terror of the 7th of October, but nor can anything justify the price paid by the civilians in Gaza. The principality calls on all parties to strengthen the fragile ceasefire and to respect every stage of it, ensuring full, safe, unhindered humanitarian access. We support efforts to rebuild Gaza, and we are concerned about the ongoing violence in the West Bank, in the occupied territories which ride roughshod over human rights and dishonor democratic values. Our our belief remains the same. The only viable option is the two state solution Israel and Palestine, living side by side in peace and security. Within safe and recognized borders.

Any policy that makes that scenario less likely through settlement, building, or sowing terror makes peace less likely to. In Lebanon, two. Monaco supports de-escalation efforts and calls on all parties to fulfil their commitments. First and foremost Security Council Resolution 1701. The people of Lebanon. Lebanon have the right to a fully sovereign state in peace throughout its territory in the Persian Gulf.

Finally, tensions around Iran remain a source of deep concern. Monaco pays tribute to all the civilian victims of the conflict and reiterates its solidarity with the countries of the Gulf who have been affected by the attacks. Here again, only negotiations can lead to a global agreement on the Iranian nuclear program and will prevent further escalation above and beyond these crises, Monaco will continue to contribute to international cooperation focused on the least developed countries through its support to the International Committee for the Red cross. The High Commissioner for refugees and the World Food Programme, through development Aid geared towards the health, education and empowerment of women and girls. Restoring trust also means changing the organisation itself. Monaco supports the UN 80 initiative to make the organisation more streamlined, more understandable, more efficient and closer to people on the ground.

Still, the UN needs resources to function. My country fulfils its financial contributions in full and on time, and we call on all other states to do likewise. But this necessary step is not enough. In the light of the changes that have to be undertaken, that is why Monaco calls on the real leaders of the United Nations to rethink the architecture of our system from 2030. Bringing on board the public and private sector, civil society and educational and cultural hubs, streamlining processes, preventing mandate duplication, consolidating specialized agencies, regional centres and the secretariat, and guaranteeing small states genuine inclusivity. There is plenty of work to do.

The time of the law is patient, but this patients should not be confused with inertia. In the same vein, the principality is in favour of a reform of the Security Council to make it more representative to today's realities. While also preserving its ability to act. And we are also in favour of the revitalisation of this General Assembly, the House of Equality between States. This session will also see the election of the next Secretary General of the organisation. Monaco calls for a transparent, inclusive and rigorous process.

After 80 years, the Principality hopes that women candidates will be seriously considered. The organisation would do well to demonstrate at its helm the equality for which it stands. Ladies and gentlemen there is one area where multilateral trust has recently produced tangible results, and it is dear to the heart of His Serene Highness Prince Albert II, and that is to say, the ocean. The entry into force of the Agreement on Marine biodiversity of areas beyond national jurisdiction, which Monaco was one of the first countries to sign and ratify, is a victory of the law over seizure of cooperation over predation. We now need to translate these commitments into acts to protect 30% of the ocean by 2030. To finally agree on an ambitious and binding agreement on plastics pollution and exercise extreme caution with regards to deep seabed mining.

The ocean is nobody's property. It is everyone's responsibility. Monaco will continue to do its part in this vital task, relying on science, which is the only universal compass. And what goes for the ocean also goes for the climate The Paris Agreement remains our common framework. Monaco will honour its commitments by reducing greenhouse gas emissions by 67.5% by 2030, and by achieving carbon neutrality by 2050. The principality calls on all countries to show more ambition in their national contributions, and not to abandon island and coastal states, which are the most vulnerable, because the climate crisis is no longer a distant threat.

Heatwaves, fires and floods are multiplying, and the Mediterranean, which my country borders experienced last year, its second highest surface temperature ever recorded. And because science is being questioned, let us recall, as the prince did in Cop 30 in Belgium, that science has never been as certain, as accessible and as clear. Four years before the 2030 deadline, the Sustainable Development agenda must not become the symbol of our broken promises. Let us be candid as we take stock. States alone cannot make progress. We need to have a renewed framework for cooperation with those who create wealth and shape innovation.

Businesses, first and foremost, and civil society. Lastly, preparing for the future and ensuring it benefits everyone means mastering technological changes Artificial intelligence is creating enormous opportunities for human development, but it also entails genuine risks. The Global dialogue on AI governance, which was held this year in Geneva, confirmed this. These technologies must remain at the service of humanity, and the United Nations cannot remain a spectator. Monaco supports the implementation of the Global Digital Compact and a new normative framework on AI based on law and shared ethical principles, respecting human rights and being accessible to all states. Finally, the principality calls for strengthened cooperation to deal with cyber threats and for inclusive transitions both within states and within societies.

President. When he received the Nobel Prize in Literature, the great French writer Albert Camus defined the task of his generation thus not to reform the world, but perhaps even greater to prevent the world from destroying itself. Today, that is our task preventing the world from destroying itself, preventing LA for being destroyed, destroyed by force, preventing trust, being destroyed by mistrust, and preventing the planet from being destroyed under the weight of our negligence. Trust is not decreed. It is won through deeds and through promises kept That is the overarching principle that a state such as mine aims to fulfil. Being consistent.

Keeping our word. Ladies and gentlemen, on behalf of His Serene Highness Prince Albert II, I wish to reiterate the commitment of Monaco to the United Nations, to its charter, and to the ideal that led to its establishment, saving future generations from the scourge of war and building together a common house where even the smallest states can take their rightful place. Because here the law protects them all. This pledge will only be fulfilled through the might of the law and not through might makes right. Thank you.

Madam Vice President of the General Assembly,

Deputy Secretary General,

Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen,

This  summer,  the  Republic  of  Moldova  turned  thirty-five.  For much of that time, the world described us as a country caught between East and West - a place where others decided. I stand here as the new Prime Minister of a country that has decided.

Small countries do not choose their geography or their size. But small,  does  not  mean  powerless.  Nations,  like  people,  are shaped by the choices they make - whom they trust, whom they elect,  whom  they  call  friends,  and  how  they  respond  when things turn against them.

For  a  long  time,  others  made  many  of  those  choices  for  us. Soviet  authorities  deported  our  families  to  Siberia,  forced  our Romanian  language  into  another  alphabet  and  told  us  it  had another name. After independence, Moscow used gas and trade restrictions as leverage over our country.

Step  by  step,  we  began  choosing  for  ourselves.  Romanian  is in  the  Latin  alphabet  and  spoken  freely. again  written Governments change peacefully at the ballot box. And when our democracy  was  threatened,  Moldovans  have  defended  it through elections and civic action.

We  also  reduced  Russia's  economic  leverage  on  us.  We diversified  our  gas  purchases.  In  just  five  years,  renewables grew from almost nothing to around 30%. Our electricity system is increasingly integrated with Romania and the European grid, and our companies sell on some of the most demanding markets in Europe and the world.

But  the  Kremlin  kept  trying.  Moldova  faced  illicit  financing, disinformation, cyberattacks and vote buying. Russia spent the equivalent of roughly two percent of our GDP trying to influence last year's election.

Moldovans answered that their home is not for sale.

Each  of  these  choices  carried  a  cost.  But  each  taught  us  the same lesson: we cannot control everything around us, but what we do still matters.

That is the source of our optimism. Our future remains in our own hands.

And nowhere is that choice clearer today than in our European path.

European integration has become our national project. Moldova has  been  a  candidate  country  since  2022,  accession

negotiations  are  underway,  and  we  are  moving  quickly.  Our ambition  is  clear  -  to  anchor  Moldova  firmly  in  the  European family.

For  us,  joining  the  European  Union  is  not  about  replacing  one sphere  of  influence  with  another.  It  is  the  opposite.  It  is  our citizens  exercising  their  right  to  choose.  Choose  democracy. Choose prosperity. Choose peace.

That  European  choice  goes  hand  in  hand  with  a  strong transatlantic partnership. For Moldova, these are not competing directions. The United States has been an important partner in independence  and strengthening  our  security,  energy resilience. We want the next chapter of that relationship to be increasingly  about  trade,  investment,  technology  and  building things together.

But  membership  is  not  only  about  what  Europe  can  give Moldova. It is also about what Moldova can bring - a democracy that has learned to resist interference, an emerging economy, a country  contributing  to  stability  on  Europe's  eastern  frontier, and a small state willing to experiment, reform and move quickly.

Being  small  imposes  constraints.  But  it  can  also  be  an advantage.

Moldova  is  not  a  huge  domestic  market.  We  cannot  outspend the largest economies. So we have to compete differently - with permits  in  days  rather  than  months,  clear  regulation,  digital public services and rules that change when they no longer make sense.

Technology is moving faster than regulation almost everywhere, and  artificial  intelligence  is  widening  that  gap.  Small  countries can have a natural edge here.

We want Moldova to become a place where emerging tech can be  tested  responsibly  through  regulatory  sandboxes  -  where regulators learn  alongside  companies,  rules  adjust  with evidence,  and  good  ideas  do  not  wait  years  to  reach  the  real economy.

When an entrepreneur arrives with a technology for which the law has not caught up, the answer should not simply be: "There is no rule for this." It should be: "Let us find a safe way to test it."

We may never have the deepest pools of capital or the largest GPU clusters. But we can build better rules and be more agile. Smallness  does  not  have  to  mean  weakness.  Sometimes  it means  turning  faster  and  delivering  when  larger  countries cannot.

And that leads to a broader point about small nations.

Power has never been equal. It never will be. But inequality of power must never become inequality of sovereignty. Countries are not buffers. Nations are not bargaining chips.

Nowhere is that principle being tested more brutally today than next door to us.

Safety is not abstract for me. Kyiv was home for nearly fifteen years, including on 24 February 2022. That morning, as parents,

we struggled to explain to our 3 boys - one, ten and twelve at the time - what war actually meant.

Perhaps  nothing  captures  the  normalization  of  this  war  better than the arithmetic children have learned.

Think of a typical night. A jet-powered Shahed drone is reported heading toward Kyiv. A twelve-year-old checks the map, knows roughly how fast it is travelling, and does the math in his head — ---  perhaps  forty  more  minutes.  Forty  more  minutes  of  sleep before the approaching drone sends him to the bomb shelter.

Children  have  become  frighteningly  good  at  this  -  the  nightly arithmetic of war.

In  Moldova,  we  cannot  begin  to  compare  our  suffering  with Ukraine's.  Yet  Russian  drones  have  repeatedly  violated  our airspace  and  fallen  on  our  territory.  The  danger  is  that  the unacceptable starts to feel normal.

For us, too, this is about the safety of our families. We must not grow  accustomed  to  it.  Repetition  does  not  make  a  violation acceptable.

And  because  these  are  not  abstract  questions  for  Moldovans watching  at  home,  allow  me  to  speak  to  them  directly  for  a moment.

{In Romanian}

Dragi moldoveni,

Știu că mulți dintre voi urmăriți cu neliniște știrile despre războiul de alături, despre dronele rusești care s-au întețit, și vă gândiți deja  la  iarna  care  vine.  Da,  ne  așteaptă  o  iarnă  grea.  Datoria noastră, a Guvernului, este să ne pregătim și să-i ajutăm mai ales pe cei care au cel mai puțin. Pentru asta muncim și despre asta vorbim cu partenerii noștri aici.

Dar vreau să vă rog un lucru important: să ne ținem grămăjoară. În momentele grele, asta ne-a ajutat de fiecare dată - să nu ne lăsăm singuri unii pe alții, să ne ajutăm vecinii, părinții, oamenii care o duc cel mai greu. Putem avea păreri diferite, putem vota diferit. E firesc într-o țară în care oamenii gândesc liber. Dar grija pentru  cei  de  lângă  noi  trebuie  să  ne  unească.  Suntem  o  țară mică.  Tocmai  de  aceea  e  cu  atât  mai  important  să  știm  că  nu suntem singuri și că ne putem sprijini unii pe alții.

__

(Translation in to English: My fellow Moldovans,

I know many of you are anxiously following the news about the war next door and the growing threat from Russian drones, and are  already  thinking  about  the  winter  ahead.  Yes,  a  difficult winter awaits us. Our duty as a government is to prepare and to help those who need it most. That is what we are working on, and that is what we are discussing with our partners here.

But  I  want  to  ask  something  important  of  you:  let  us  stick together.  In  difficult  times,  this  is  what  has  always  helped  us through:  being  there  for  one  another,  helping  our  neighbours, our  parents  and  those  struggling  the  most.  We  may  hold

different  views.  We  may  vote  differently.  That  is  natural  in  a country where people think freely. But caring for those around us must unite us. We are a small country. That makes it all the more important to know that we are not alone and that we can count on one another.)

___

That solidarity at home must go hand in hand with clarity about the danger around us.

This is not a tragedy without an author. Russia launched a war of  aggression  against  a  sovereign  neighbour.  It  occupied territory  and  continued  to  attack  Ukrainian  cities.  Ukraine  did not choose this war. Russia did.

We  often  speak  about is "war understandable. Governments have other crises. Families have their own worries. Attention moves on.

fatigue".  The  phrase

But  being  tired  of  a  war  you  can  switch  off  is  different  from being  tired  because  an  air-raid  wakes  your  children  again tonight  -  and  different  still  from  the  exhaustion  of  Ukrainian soldiers spending another cold night in the mud.

Moldova could not choose that this war began next to us. But we could choose our response.

We welcomed people fleeing the war. We kept transport routes open. We reduced the cost of rail transit for Ukrainian cargo with grain.

These decisions were not always cost-free or politically easy at home. We made them because the way this war ends matters far beyond our region.

If  aggression  is  rewarded,  it  becomes  a  precedent  -  for  the aggressor  and  for  everyone  watching.  Peace  must  protect sovereignty and create the conditions for lasting security.

The same principle applies within our own borders.

Russian military forces remain, illegally and without our consent, in the Transnistrian region of Moldova. We will continue to seek their unconditional withdrawal and the peaceful reintegration of our  country,  with  full  respect  for  Moldova's  sovereignty  and territorial integrity.

We want people on both banks of the Nistru to live together in a peaceful, democratic and prosperous Moldova.

And  because  we  believe  small  states  should  help  shape  the international  system,  not  simply  depend  on  it,  Moldova  is honored to present its candidacy for the Presidency of the 82nd session  of  the  United  Nations  General  Assembly.  We  want  to contribute  to  a  UN  that  is  more  effective,  more  inclusive  and focused on results.

Excellencies,

We live in a world with plenty of reasons for pessimism. Moldova chooses something else.

Not naïve optimism. Not the belief that problems disappear if we refuse to see them. The optimism that comes from knowing that our future is still in our own hands.

For  too  long,  Moldovans  were  told  that  our  country  was  too small,  too  exposed,  too  divided  to  choose  its  own  future.  We have spent enough time believing that. We know our problems. But we should also know our strength.

We are a free country. Our people are humble, work hard, and put  family  first.  Our  diaspora  is  spread  across  the  world,  but stays  close  to  one  another  and  deeply  cares  about  what happens  at  home.  Only  when  it  comes  to  vineyards  does modesty become a little harder for us - we quietly suspect our wines might just be the best in the world.

We  have  friends  across  Europe,  across  the  Atlantic  and  far beyond. And we finally have a realistic path to build a country our children should not need to leave in search of opportunity.

Moldova may never be a great power. But we have everything it takes to be a great country.

I thank you.

speaker_post: President of the Refoundation of the Republic
text:
Excellencies, president of the United Nations General Assembly. Excellencies, heads of state and government. Your Excellency, Secretary General of the United Nations, distinguished delegates. Ladies and gentlemen, I am particularly proud and honored to address this August Assembly today on behalf. Of the Republic of Madagascar. At this 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly For the rest of my speech, allow me to now speak to you in the Malagasy language.

My mother tongue, in honor of my country and the Malagasy people I would like. First of all, on behalf of the Malagasy people and in my own name, to extend my sincere congratulations to Mr. Khalilur Rahman on his election as president of the 81st General Assembly, as well as to the Vice Presidents. In this regard, I wish to reaffirm Madagascar's support and its full readiness to work in a genuine spirit of cooperation to ensure the success of all of our work throughout this session. Mr. President. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. We must acknowledge that the challenges that we have faced for decades, namely food insecurity, disease armed conflict, or natural disasters are still with us.

Thus for Madagascar. As for many other nations, the new emerging challenges must not overshadow the priorities that still require our attention. The theme of this 81st session calls upon us to assume our shared responsibility for our destiny, and for that of future generations, with clear vision placing collective action, the common good, and the welfare of humanity at the center of our responses to the profound transformations shaping our world. In light of these intersecting transformations and challenges, the question of trust in our collective action arises with renewed urgency. Indeed, we must admit, taking into account. All the hopes and expectations that we, the peoples of the United Nations, have placed in our organization.

That trust has gradually eroded over time. The most vulnerable populations affected repeatedly or continuously by health crises, food insecurity and hunger, the impacts of climate change and conflicts exacerbated by current geopolitical tensions sometimes come to feel a certain skepticism regarding our collective capacity within the United Nations system to respond to the scourges of our age. Mr. President. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, in this regard, the realities on the ground in my country speak for themselves. In southern Madagascar, mothers walk dozens of kilometers under scorching heat. In search of water.

From the bed of a dried up river. In the east. Every year, increasingly violent and destructive tropical cyclones devastate crops, infrastructure and human lives. In other regions, floods engulf rice granaries, affecting entire communities. These images illustrate the daily vulnerability of our people, our Malagasy population Faced with these recurring humanitarian emergencies amplified by climate change, considerable investments are made, reflecting the unwavering commitment of our development partners working every year towards the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals. The SDGs, whether that be fighting hunger, providing education or providing access to basic services for vulnerable populations.

And we hope to mobilize $1.5 billion over five years for the implementation of the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework for the period 2024 2028. Yet, beyond commitments and resources mobilized. What matters to us is their tangible impact on the daily lives of our people. Faced with the challenges of a constantly changing world, the Refoundation government that I lead places food sovereignty, health and education at the heart of its action. This priority commitment serves the entire population, particularly women and children, while providing our youth with a means to build their future with confidence and contribute to national development. With more than 55% of its population under the age of 25, Madagascar enjoys a tremendous demographic dividend, driven by a firm political determination to build a brighter future for this dynamic youth.

We recognize the importance of an education system which is fully aligned with labour market realities, an essential condition for sustainable development, and we hope that cooperation in this area will move beyond a strictly quantitative approach, measured only by the volume of infrastructure built or the number of students enrolled, and instead adapt fully to economic realities on the ground. Our aim is to focus on future oriented sectors. While redefining our indicators of success. To prioritize the practical acquisition of skills and medium term employment outcomes. Mr. president, excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. Madagascar's foreign policy is guided above all by the imperatives of economic and social development for the well-being of its people.

Madagascar has chosen a policy of engagement in all directions We are open to all international partnerships, capable of meeting the aspirations of our people and supporting the general policy of the state of the refoundation. Madagascar's position of neutrality with regard to global conflicts is consistent with its diplomatic tradition and its desire to preserve constructive relations with all its partners. This idea is not ideological, but is based on international partnership that can meet the aspirations of our people in an open spirit, without exclusivity, in full respect for national sovereignty, the achievement of our ambitions cannot be separated from the international context in which they are pursued. Excellencies, Mr. President, ladies and gentlemen, can we speak of development when international peace and security are being tested by multiplying crises around the world and persistent tensions? Restoring trust requires the United Nations to maintain and to restore peace. We must be concerned that the multilateral system is struggling to contain escalating tensions fueled by geopolitical rivalries.

These crises now affecting different regions of the planet. Have consequences for our states. They directly impact our economies and the daily lives of our populations through disruptions in energy supply chains. And difficulties in the delivery of essential goods. These are all factors which further aggravate the vulnerabilities that we already face. Confronted with this reality, we must have the courage to recognize and to accept the limitations of the multilateral system in its current form and functioning.

It is urgent to initiate concerted and lasting action to guarantee every people the right to pursue their development in dignity and in stability. Mr. president, excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, far from observing the world as a passive spectator, Madagascar positions itself as an actor fully aware of its strategic place and responsibilities. Our country remains a committed and operational partner in the service of peace, development and security, maritime security and the Mozambique Channel and the Western Indian Ocean remains at the heart of the regional initiatives in which Madagascar actively participates. We are determined to strengthen regional and multilateral cooperation founded on respect for national sovereignty. Whilst also welcoming partnerships that align with our priorities and serve as genuine drivers of development. We also want to be part of strengthened regional cooperation in order to guarantee the security of maritime areas.

This approach will make it possible to ensure the sustainability of our energy supply chains. Mr. president, excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, what form of United Nations cooperation should we establish to support the contemporary transformation of our world? How can we restore trust? Mr. president, ladies and gentlemen, we must look to the future with greater ambition. To ensure lasting and measurable impact over the medium and long term. And to do this, we must move on to a new stage, one of increased solidarity.

That is more integrated and better coordinated. Madagascar advocates for a multilateral system that is not only capable of acting, but that is also capable of supporting member states in their efforts to break the cycles of poverty and insecurity. My country aspires to an international order founded on the primacy of international law. And trusts in the virtues of dialogue and diplomatic action. Our commitment to multilateral cooperation remains unwavering. Multilateralism is a privileged forum where states unite in a shared responsibility.

Enabling them to define common and appropriate solutions in the face of challenges such as epidemics and climate disasters or armed conflicts arising from contemporary geopolitical rivalries and latent multidimensional tensions. History and future generations will judge our organization according to a single criterion namely our ability to fulfil our original mission, serving all peoples without exclusion or privilege, and in full respect for the sovereignty of nations. It is imperative to restore to the United Nations fully its central role as a guardian of peace, as a strengthened institution capable of restoring order and challenge, and addressing the challenges of our time. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, our challenge today is therefore, to rethink our mechanisms of cooperation through greater synergy between UN agencies and governmental structures in order to optimize the effectiveness of our actions on the ground, but also to provide better visibility of tangible results achieved for the benefit of populations. In this regard, the success of our agenda largely depends on strengthening governance and strengthening institutions priorities that are fully integrated into Madagascar's process of refoundation. We recognize also the absolute necessity of reforming the United Nations so that it may serve all peoples.

And in this spirit, we would like to propose the following first. More inclusive global governance. This must begin with a rebalancing of decision making power. First and foremost, by restoring the General Assembly's full political weight and central place in global governance, it remains indeed the only organ where every nation, regardless of power, enjoys an equal and sovereign voice. We must also correct the historical imbalance affecting Africa's representation on the Security Council. Indeed.

Africa cannot remain on the margins of decisions. We have 1.4 billion inhabitants. Decisions concerning international peace and security. Africa should be granted permanent representation on the Security Council in accordance with the Ezzelini consensus and the Sirte Declaration, which expresses which express a common position grounded in justice, equity and representation. Representativeness within the African Union. We must also strengthen coherence between programmes implemented by the UN Resident Coordinator offices and national priorities.

UN country teams on the ground must listen carefully and respond effectively to priorities defined by host governments. Avoiding one size fits all approaches. Secondly, we need a more accessible international financial architecture for effective development support. We must not neglect the reform of the international financial architecture. This means we need to rebalance access to financing. Current aid and lending criteria often rely solely on GDP per capita, excluding many vulnerable countries.

The United Nations should therefore take into account the Multidimensional Vulnerability Index. So that access to concessional financing. Reflects climate shocks and external debt burdens. It would also be wise to support durable debt relief. This means advocating a for a faster, more predictable, and more inclusive sovereign debt restructuring mechanism. That would allow vulnerable countries to invest in the Sustainable Development Goals, rather than servicing unsustainable interest payments The procedures for accessing UN funds should also be drastically simplified in order to reduce disbursement delays for a vulnerable state facing crisis.

Administrative slowness undermines confidence in the effectiveness of multilateralism. Third. Greater effectiveness in responding to climate and humanitarian emergencies. The multilateral system we seek should guarantee the fulfilment of climate climate finance commitments. It should serve both as a catalyst and a guarantor to ensure that developed countries in the North are honour their commitments on climate finance, but particularly for the most exposed nations. It's also important to link emergency assistance with long term structural investments.

Mr. president. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, by embracing this theme, we are undertaking a commitment, namely to not postpone the reforms that are essential for enabling our organisation to act with the integrity required by the challenges of our age. Building upon the achievements of the United Nations over 81 years. Our predecessors were able to build an organisation suited to their time. It is now our responsibility to refound it so that it can address the challenges of today and tomorrow. Let us pass on to future generations an organisation that unites, protects and acts.

For its part Madagascar is preparing at the national level. A framework for the effective implementation of this transformation within our means Indeed, the process of refoundation initiated following the mobilisation of Malagasy youth just one year ago, serves as the foundation for responsible governance, supported by strong institutions devoted to the public interest and having restored citizens trust in the state. This represents a genuine patriotic awakening, driven by the deep conviction that sustainable development requires every citizen to find a full and meaningful place within the nation. To give substance to this vision, we have launched a historic process of inclusive national dialogue, bringing together all the vital forces of the nation young people, women, persons with disabilities, political parties, civil society, the armed forces and the private sector. We have established a clear timetable. Our goal is to hold free, transparent and universally accepted elections before the end of 2027.

Mr. president, excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, this platform speaking here at this rostrum also gives me the opportunity to express our gratitude to all our partners for the trust and support that they have provided and for the fraternal support of the Southern African Development Community, Sadc and the United Nations are going with standing with us hand in hand since the beginning of the refoundation process. Long live international cooperation and solidarity. Long live the United Nations. I thank you for your kind attention.

Mr President,

Mr Secretary-General,

Excellencies,

Ladies and Gentlemen.

Assalamu Alaikum Warahmatullahi Wabarakaatuh, And a very good morning.

I congratulate you, Mr. President, on your election as President

of the eighty-first Session. You can count on the full support of

the Maldives as you lead this Assembly.

I also thank the former President of the General Assembly, Her

Excellency Annalena Baerbock, for her leadership of the eightieth

Session.

This year’s theme, “Restoring trust, managing transformation: a

United Nations that delivers for all”, captures the task before us.

Trust will not be restored by words alone. It will be restored by

what this Organization delivers for every country, large or small.

Thirty-seven years ago, the Maldives asked this Assembly    to

face a simple truth:

That “Small States can be highly vulnerable to external threats

and acts of influence.”

In response, this Assembly adopted Resolution forty-four, fifty-

one an initiative led by the Maldives, affirming the importance of

protecting  the  sovereignty  and  territorial  integrity  of  small

States.

That  was  true  then  and  it  is  true  even  today.  But  the  threats

have evolved.

Insecurity now travels through sea lanes, supply chains, financial

markets, digital networks and new technologies.

Today,  sovereignty  can  be  weakened  without  a  single  border

being crossed. It can be undermined when external powers limit

a State’s freedom to choose.

This is why   the Maldives comes before this Assembly   with a

clear message:

“Every State, large or small must have the freedom and capacity

to shape its own future.”

A sovereign future.

And that future begins with peace.

The  Indian  Ocean  must  remain  peaceful.  It  must  remain  as  a

region  where  trade  can  flow  and  where  States  can  prosper.

Regional  competition  among  major  powers  must  not  limit  the

choices of smaller States.

Conflict does not have to reach our shores to affect us.

In  today’s  interconnected  world,  a  crisis  far  away  can  quickly

become a crisis at home.

Interruption  to  maritime  traffic  through  the  Strait  of  Hormuz

raises  fuel  prices.  It  affects  food  supplies  and  air  travel.  The

consequences of this are felt across tourism and public finances

in the Maldives.

The Maldives condemns the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

The Strait must remain open and safe.

The  Maldives  further  condemns  the  attacks  on  Saudi  Arabia,

United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Qatar, Kuwait, Oman and Jordan.

The  Maldives  appreciates  the  diplomatic  efforts  of  Oman,

Pakistan and Qatar to de-escalate the crisis and bring the parties

to dialogue.

The right to a sovereign future must belong to all.

And nowhere is that right more brutally denied than in Palestine.

Israel's genocide and war crimes against Palestinians continue.

And their actions are not confined to Gaza.

Its  military  attacks  across  the  region  have  violated  the

sovereignty of other States.

Security cannot be built by exporting insecurity.

Nor  can  any  country  demand  respect  for  its  sovereignty  while

violating the sovereignty of others.

No State should be shielded from accountability by its power or

political alliances.

But condemnation alone is not enough.

Every Member State must ask: What have we done to end this

violence?

The United Nations must ask itself the same question.

The problem is not a lack of law. The rules are clear. What is

absent, is equal application.

International  law  cannot  bind  the  weak  and  bend  for  the

powerful. The same rules. The same standard. No exceptions.

Israel’s genocide in Gaza must end.

Israel’s illegal occupation of Palestine and other Arab lands  must

end.

Illegal settlements must end.

Humanitarian assistance must reach Palestinians safely, rapidly

and at scale.

And the decisions of international courts and the resolutions of

this Organization must be respected and implemented.

For  the  Palestinian  people,  a  sovereign  future  means  freedom

dignity.

Self-determination.

And the right to live with security in their own State.

The Maldives will always stand with the Palestinian people and

their undeniable right for that future.

That  is  why  I  reiterate  our  call  for  the  recognition  of  an

independent and sovereign State of Palestine, based on the pre-

1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital.

And  if  this  Organisation  is  to  restore  trust  and  deliver  for  all,

Palestine must become a full Member of the United Nations.

Conflict is not the only threat to sovereignty. Forces beyond our

borders can also limit a State’s freedom to shape its own future.

For  SIDS  like  the  Maldives,  none  is  more  consequential  than

climate change.

For  SIDS,  climate  change  is  altering  the  very  physical

foundations of our nations.

Sea level rise is therefore not simply an environmental concern.

It is a matter of national planning and national security.

It is a matter of sovereignty.

Let there be no doubt.

Rising seas may alter our shores.

But they will not erase our statehood.

They will not reduce our rights.

They will not weaken our maritime entitlements.

And they will not diminish our national agency.

Our response must be to adapt innovate and build.

But resilience demands the means to act.

That means finance must reach those who need it.

At the scale.

At the speed.

And on the terms needed to build resilience.

That is why COP31 in Antalya must be a COP of delivery.

Implementation must be the measure of commitment.

We must move faster. We must speed up the 2030 Agenda. And

we must turn ABAS into measurable progress for SIDS.

For  island  nations,  that  progress  cannot  be  separated  from  a

healthy  and  sustainably  managed  ocean.  Therefore,  the  first

Conference of the Parties to the BBNJ Agreement must deliver

from day one.

Ultimately,  global  commitments  matter  only  when  they  enable

progress at home.

His  Excellency  President  Dr  Mohamed  Muizzu  has  set  a  clear

ambition:  for  the  Maldives  to  become  a  developed  country  by

2040.

We  are  pursuing  that  goal  by  raising  productivity,  diversifying

our  economy,  building  resilient

infrastructure,  expanding

renewable energy and investing in our people.

Our future will be built by Maldivians.

But the international system can widen or narrow our choices.

Technology  transfer,  resilient  supply  chains  and  accessible

finance  expand  choice.  Technological  dependence,  external

shocks and unsustainable debt limits it.

This  is  why  reform  of  the  international  financial  architecture

matters.

We must implement the Sevilla Commitment and deliver on its

promises on finance, debt, and reform.

Earlier this year, the Maldives joined other developing countries

in launching the Borrowers’ Platform.

It  must  become  a  lasting  mechanism  that  gives  developing

countries not just a place in the financial system, but a voice in

shaping it.

But for SIDS, greater agency also depends on progress at home.

We  must  build  our  institutions,  improve  stability,  and  attract

responsible investment and meaningful partnerships.

And these partnerships must build national capacity and support

national ambitions.

Partnerships  must  serve  national  needs  strengthen  what  we

have and leave us more capable than before.

Our shared challenges can become shared opportunities.

This is the spirit of President Dr Muizzu’s Maldives First policy.

Partnerships built around respect national interests and mutual

contribution.

And

the  same  principle  must  guide

the

technological

transformation before us.

Artificial intelligence offers significant opportunities.

For  small  States,  AI  can  close  distance.  It  can  help  overcome

scale.

And it can put better health care, education, and public services

within reach.

But these opportunities must be shared.

Every country must have a voice in shaping the global rules for

AI.  The digital future should strengthen our ability to serve our

people better. Not create new forms of dependence.

And as the world transforms, so must the United Nations.

The  UN80  Initiative  is  an  opportunity  to  reduce  duplication,

improve accountability, and focus resources on results.

But efficiency must not be measured simply by what we cut. It

must be measured by what we deliver.

And the United Nations must not retreat from the countries that

need it most, in the name of efficiency.

Reform must preserve a meaningful UN presence on the ground,

particularly in SIDS.

The  UN  Development  System  must  respond  to  the  needs  of

programme  countries  and

remain  guided  by

relevant

international frameworks. The reform process must be Member-

State-led. It must be inclusive and transparent.

This  is  how  reform  will  restore  trust.  By  bringing  the  United

Nations closer to the people and the countries it serves.

Reform  must  also  confront  one  of  this  Organization’s  oldest

weaknesses: Unequal representation.

The  Security  Council  cannot  reflect  the  world  of  1945  while

deciding for the world of today.

It  must  be  expanded  in  both  permanent  and  non-permanent

categories.

SIDS must have a rotating seat.

Africa must receive the representation long denied to it.

And the veto must be abolished.

After all, representation is not merely symbolic. Who sits at the

table shapes what the table sees.

Small  States  understand  how  closely  climate,  finance,  trade

supply chains and security are connected.

We also know that international law is our strongest safeguard

against unequal power. That principle must remain at the heart

of the international system.

The  Maldives  will  take  its  seat  on  the  Economic  and  Social

Council for the 2027 to 2029 term.

We  are  seeking  election  to  the  Human  Rights  Council  for  the

2028 to 2030 term.

And we seek the support of Member States for a seat on the UN

Security Council for the 2033 to 2034 term.

We  do  so  because  small  States  must  be  decision-makers,  not

decision-takers.

Representation  matters  not  only  within  the  bodies  of  this

Organization. But also, in its leadership.

As Secretary-General Guterres approaches the end of a decade

of  service,  The  Maldives  thanks  him  for  his  leadership  and

commitment to international cooperation. Thank you Secretary

General Guterres.

The  process  to  choose  his  successor  must  be  transparent  and

based  on  merit.  It  must  draw  from  the  full  breadth  of  talent

available to this Organization.

For more than eight decades, every Secretary-General has been

a man. It is time for a woman to lead this Organisation.

A  leader who will  defend  the  Charter,  without exception.  Who

can turn reform into delivery. And who will listen to all Member

States, including the smallest.

The task ahead is immense. The choice we make must meet it.

So, what should this Assembly do?

The Maldives proposes a simple test for a sovereign future.

When  we  act  on  conflict,  climate,  finance,  technology,  or

institutional reform, let us ask:

Does this decision expand a State’s freedom to choose?

Does it build national capacity and reduce dependence?

Does it protect sovereignty and independent decision-making?

If the answer is no, we must change course.

And we must hold every State to the same standard.

Let this be the measure of international cooperation. Not what

we promise, but what we make possible. That is the measure of

a United Nations that delivers for all.

In 1989, the Maldives asked this Assembly to protect small States

from external threats. Today, we ask it to protect something just

as fundamental: Every State’s freedom to choose its own future.

A future chosen by its people.

A future grounded in international law.

A sovereign future for every State.

I thank you.

Mr. president, excellencies, I am appearing addressing this assembly representing the first female president of my country, doctor Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo whose government places people at the heart of the actions of the state and works on a daily basis to achieve freedom, democracy, social justice and substantive equality. Mexico conducts its public life according to a conviction that I'm bringing to you today, from this rostrum, to make shared prosperity a reality for all people. Mr. President, Mr. Secretary-General, Excellencies,

I ask every nation here - are we still willing to work together?

The principles in the UN Charter, affirmed by each one of us taking our seat in this hall, are now tested not by argument - but by neglect or ill intention.

The  credibility  and  effectiveness  of  multilateral  institutions  is  imperative  for  small nations.  It is past time to better turn the urgency expressed in political declarations and resolutions into results, not repetition.

We speak from our own experience when we underscore the importance of acting together.   An institution that takes decisions collectively must also be accountable, collectively.

The United Nations is long overdue to reflect and renew the same spirit with which our  Marshallese  people  first  came  to  the  UN,  by  delivering  an  apology  and acknowledgement  of  the  harm  caused  by  impacts  from  the  67  nuclear  weapons tested  on  our  islands  during  our  time  as  a  UN  Strategic Trust Territory  -  between 1946  and  1958. The  sacred  trust  of  the  UN Trusteeship  to  ensure  our  well-being was  jeopardized  by  these  tests  and  the  lack  of  due  acknowledgement  remains  a moral failing.

For generations, our families have testified to displacement, illness, contamination and loss, all of them impacts to our core human rights. As our survivors would say, “this is a song that has been sung far too many times”.

It  was  in  this  same  building  that  the  UN  Trusteeship  Council  sat  in  session  and voted on Resolutions 1082 and 1493, in 1954 and 1956 respectively, to effectively authorize further nuclear testing over the demands of our local leaders and many citizens.

The  United  Nations  ultimately  allowed  the  testing  to  continue,  but  the  shock  and tragedy  of  nuclear  exposure  in  the  Marshall  Islands  was  a  profound  driver  of  the 1963 global ban on atmospheric testing of nuclear weapons.

We  acknowledge  the  ongoing  actions,  dialogue  and  complex  legacy  of  the  UN’s administering  authority,  the  United  States.    But  the  role  of  the  United  Nations cannot  pass  without  comment    For  us  –  and  for  fellow  member  states    –  this apology is an opportunity to reflect upon the past, to bring healing and closure to the Marshallese people.

We carry no larger agenda – other than to ensure that the United Nations will do better.

As  we  face  a  world  in  which  scientists  tell  us  overshooting  the  1.5  degree temperature  limit  that  we  agreed  in  Paris  is  increasingly  likely,  we  all  need  to  to wake up and act.

Our focus now must be on preventing or minimizing the overshoot, shortening the time we spend above 1.5, and doing everything possible to fight our way back.

As we gather in Tuvalu, Fiji and Turkiye for this year’s climate pre-COP and COP, our response to the threat of overshoot must be overwhelming. A much accelerated transition away from fossil fuels is the only logical response. Continued investment in fossil fuels is not only immoral but irrational. Technologies exist which   provide secure, stable, zero-emissions energy. We are employing them in my own country, where,  in  the  next  18  months,  renewable  energy  will  cut  fossil  fuel  use  in  our remote outer atolls by 88%, giving many access to electricity for the first time. We must do everything in our power to accelerate the deployment of renewables, and to reduce fossil fuel production and consumption with equal speed.

This includes shipping, where we have the opportunity at the International Maritime Organisation to adopt binding regulations that will place international shipping on a clear path to net zero by 2050 and generate the revenue required to ensure a just and equitable transition.

Mr President,

Mr. President

This  crisis  has  the  power  to  divide  us,  or  to  prove  that  we  all  remain  willing  to achieve common goals.

As  a  low-lying  atoll  nation  with  no  higher  ground,  sea-level  rise  is  an  immediate and  stark  reality.    This  week’s  UN  High  Level  Meeting  on  Sea-Level  Rise  has helped achieve new understandings in international law.

It is the seas that are rising around us, and not our islands which are sinking.  Our boundaries and baselines of today - the political footprint on the map - will endure in  the  face  of  aggressive  sea-level  rise  scenarios. As an atoll nation - our tide gauge is proof enough that far more action is needed. And we are acting. Confronted with rising seas on our most vulnerable shorelines, we completed the Ebeye Seawall and Footpath last week, 1.8 kilometers of ocean-side  protection  built  with  support  from  the  World  Bank,  the  Green  Climate  Fund, and our own resources.   Engineered for rising seas, it now protects 8,400 people and  critical  energy  infrastructure,  reduces  annual  coastal-flooding  losses,  and anchors resilient future development on Ebeye, including schools, housing, and the proposed  new  hospital,  while  providing  a  safe  public  space  that  strengthens community wellbeing. It cost $75 million dollars, took 70,000 tonnes of rocks, took more  than  a  decade  to  do  -  and  it  is  just  one  island  of  over  a  thousand.
