Mr. President, Mr. Secretary-General, Ladies and Gentlemen,

A child who will sit at a school desk for the first time this autumn will, in 2040, be a young person just entering adulthood. We do not know exactly what the world in which that young person will live will look like. But we already know that it will be different from our own.

Artificial intelligence will transform professions, industries and the ways in which decisions are made. Energy will be governed by a new configuration and a new logic of operation. Climate change will affect economies, agriculture, cities and the movement of people. Demographic change will reshape labour markets and social protection systems. Security will no longer depend on armies and borders, but also on power grids, data centres, cables, satellites, algorithms and trust in the information we receive every day.

And yet today, as we prepare for that future, millions of people are living through war or under the threat of war. More than one hundred million people have been forcibly displaced. More than 270 million children and young people are not in school.

This is the paradox of our time. Humanity has never possessed such immense scientific and technological capabilities. And yet, it has never been more evident that technological capability does not automatically produce political wisdom.

That is why the real question before this Assembly is not simply how we will manage the crises of 2026. The real question is this: what kind of international order will we leave to the generation that is entering school today?

For a small country like mine, this is not an academic question. It is a question of survival.

Thirty-three years ago since we became part of the United Nations the world looked very different. The Cold War had ended. There was hope that a new era was beginning; an era in which cooperation would gradually replace confrontation.

Our region, however, was living through a very different reality. Yugoslavia was disintegrating in bloodshed. Wars were being fought just beyond our borders. The fear that the violence might spread was real.

And yet, my country chose peace. It chose stability. It was in those circumstances, on our territory, that the United Nations did something it had never done before: it established the first preventive peacekeeping mission in the history of the Organization.

That experience left a profound lesson in our national memory, a lesson to which I will return towards the end of my address.

Peace does not begin when war ends. Peace begins when politics is wise enough to prevent war from beginning.

Perhaps that is why small countries sometimes see international politics differently.

Great powers have room for strategic shifts that small sized states simply do not have. For a great power, a mistaken geopolitical calculation may mean a change of strategy. For a small sized country, the same mistake can mean a lost decade.

That is why we cannot afford to be indifferent to the rules. Nor can we afford to believe that the rules will defend themselves.

The world taking shape before us is a world of sharper competition. Power is being redistributed. Relations among the major powers increasingly shape trade, technology, energy, critical raw materials, transport routes and digital infrastructure.

What we called economic interdependence only yesterday, we increasingly see today also as a matter of national security. Globalization is not disappearing. It is being reshaped. Supply chains are changing. Production is once again becoming a geopolitical question.

States are asking not only where something can be produced most cheaply, but who can be trusted; not only where energy comes from, but whether it will be available when a crisis strikes; not only who develops the next generation of technology, but who will set the rules under which it will operate.

Alliances, too, are changing under the pressure of this same world.

Macedonian citizens know where they belong. We are a NATO Ally. The United States is our strategic partner. Full membership in the European Union is our strategic commitment.

These are not three separate policies. They are one geopolitical orientation, an orientation grounded in democracy, collective security, the rule of law and an open economy.

In a time of uncertainty, our response is not strategic ambiguity. Our response is clarity.

But clarity in our alliances does not mean turning away from the world. Quite the opposite. It is precisely a state that is confident in its democratic and strategic choices that can engage and cooperate with greater confidence with countries that have different histories, different interests and different political perspectives.

The world does not need yet another division into permanent camps. It needs competition with limits and rules that all must respect. Alliances that take responsibility. And international institutions that remain a space for dialogue precisely when dialogue is most difficult.

That is why the United Nations matter.

Not because they can resolve every conflict. Clearly, they cannot. Not because every resolution is given effect. Clearly, that is not always the case.

And that should not discourage us; it should strengthen our determination to protect these United Nations and the rules upon which they are founded, and to stand for multilateralism grounded in values, mutual respect and rules.

Because a world without a place where all states, regardless of their size, can sit under the same roof and invoke the same principles would be even more dangerous than the world we see today.

In 1954, Dag Hammarskjöld reminded us of a thought: The United Nations were not created to take us to heaven, but to save us from hell.

Seven decades later, it is worth understanding the essence of that statement. We should not demand perfection from the United Nations. We should demand relevance.

The capacity to prevent and to mediate. The capacity to protect human dignity. And, ultimately, the capacity to uphold principles even when applying them is politically inconvenient.

Today, trust in the international system is being jeopardized precisely because too many people have a justified sense that the rules do not apply equally. That power sometimes takes precedence over principle. That commitments are conditional. That agreements last only as long as interests remain unchanged.

For small sized states, this is an especially dangerous world.

Our own history has taught us that international compromises are very difficult, and that peace, stability and integration require political courage and hard sacrifices.

And without wishing to sound patronising, if anyone wants to see an example of a country that has repeatedly given up something that naturally belongs to it as a fundamental right—something that many take for granted—all they need is to look at the recent history of my country.

A history marked by challenges, by security risks of regional proportions, by constant compromises and concessions made in the name of peace and cooperation and the higher goals of integration—often at the expense of our most basic understanding of dignity and justice.

We have taken truly difficult decisions. We have continued forward even when processes lasted longer than one generation of citizens could reasonably have expected.

But precisely for that reason, with the benefit of distance from those decisions and with a clear awareness of reality, I can responsibly say today that trust cannot be a one-way obligation indefinitely.

If small sized states are expected to comply with the rules, then the rules must also provide them with predictability. If candidates for membership in an organization are required to meet certain criteria, then meeting those criteria must lead to progress. If we ask citizens to trust institutions, then institutions must demonstrate that their word has value and that their commitments endure.

The rule that applies today cannot be different tomorrow simply because the balance of power has changed. And a commitment undertaken cannot be a temporary political convenience. It must be a foundation on which people can plan their future.

We ask our citizens to believe in cooperation, in good neighbourly relations, in compromise, and in mutual respect.

We tell them that lasting peace is worth more than a short-term political victory; that respecting agreements is a sign of strength and wisdom, and that it is the right thing to do, not a sign of weakness; that European and Euro-Atlantic integration means accepting rules that apply equally to all.

But that argument becomes much harder to sustain when citizens see that, in international relations, principle sometimes gives way to power; that criteria can change while the process is already under way; or that some are expected to demonstrate consistency that others do not always demand of themselves.

We cannot tell people, “Trust the rules,” when they can see that the rules do not apply equally. We cannot convince them that compromise is a virtue, if every compromise produces a new demand. And we cannot expect trust in international institutions if citizens come to believe that their fate is created more often by the political weight of their state than by the strength of an agreed principle.

This is a question of legitimacy.

Because our authority as elected leaders does not derive from the office itself. It derives from the people who elect us, who hold us to account, and who every day compare what we tell them with what they see.

And today, they see more than ever before.

We live in an age in which information travels around the world in seconds. Never before has humanity had access to so much knowledge. But never before has it been exposed to so much manipulation, half-truths, fabricated images, propaganda and organized disinformation.

That is precisely why politics is entering a new, more difficult and more complex era.

Our task is no longer simply to inform our citizens. We must earn their trust.

It is not enough to tell them what is true. We must build institutions they can trust when the truth is uncomfortable for everyone. It is not enough to speak to them about values. We must show that those values have meaning and carry a cost—even when defending them requires patience, political capital, or choosing the more difficult path.

We are called upon to convince our societies that cooperation is better than isolation, that the rule of law is better than unilateral behavior, that compromise is better than conflict, and that institutions are better than the rule of sheer force.

But for that conviction to carry weight, we ourselves must be consistent.

Values are not sustained by speeches. They are sustained when they are upheld precisely at the moment when it is easiest to abandon them.

And this may be the greatest challenge of our time.

The world is changing at extraordinary speed. The centres of power are shifting. Technology is changing. Economic relations are changing. Security doctrines are changing. Alliances are changing. History is accelerating once again.

In such periods, there is always a temptation to declare that old principles are no longer practical; that the law must adapt to power; that values are a luxury that can wait until the crisis has passed.

But that is precisely when we need them most.

Because if, in times of change, we abandon the rules that protected us in times of stability, we will not gain greater freedom. We will inherit a world in which every subsequent decision depends on who has more power at that particular moment.

And such a world is especially dangerous for small sized states.

That is why our duty as leaders is not to promise our people a world without injustice, without disappointment, and without conflicting interests. Such a world does not exist.

Our duty is far more demanding.

To preserve faith in the rules even when it is clear that the rules are being broken. To defend cooperation even when confrontation appears more popular. To sustain trust in institutions not by asking people to look less closely and ask fewer questions, but by making institutions more worthy of their trust.

And not to allow disappointment with the imperfections of the international order to lead us towards something far worse: a world in which there is no order at all.

That, in my view, is one of the greatest political and moral responsibilities of our generation.

It applies to the international system. And it applies to Europe.

We will not abandon the European idea because the European path has been difficult. The European Union remains, for us, our natural political, economic and institutional home.

And we have work to do at home. We must strengthen the rule of law. Build more effective institutions. Build a more competitive economy. And strengthen our citizens ’confidence in their own state.

That is our responsibility, and we will not shift it to Brussels.

At the same time, we expect European integration to remain a merit based-process based on measurable criteria—not a process in which bilateral issues can continually move the goalposts.

We are not asking for an easier path. We are asking for a path governed by rules. We are not asking for lower standards. We are asking for standards to remain standards.

This is equally important for Europe’s credibility at a time when its geopolitical weight will increasingly depend on its ability to translate its commitments into tangible political outcomes, and on its resolve to uphold the values it espouses and to remain steadfast in advancing them, despite the many challenges it faces.

The future international order will not be shaped only on battlefields or in diplomatic halls. It will also be shaped in laboratories. In schools. In factories. In energy grids. In data centres. And in the ability of societies to make sense of the changes that technology is bringing.

Artificial intelligence is no longer a subject of the future. It is infrastructure for the present.

Today, the world is once again recognizing the value of resilience. Of reliable energy. Of infrastructure. Of diversified transport routes. Of nearby and trusted supply chains.

For us, the intensive development of Corridors VIII and X is part of a broader European vision: to better connect the Adriatic, the Black Sea, the Aegean and Central Europe; to provide goods, energy and people with more routes and greater connectivity; and to ensure that the region becomes interconnected in infrastructure rather than remaining on the geopolitical periphery.

Our geography does not have to be our destiny. It can become our advantage if we build the institutions and infrastructure that transform our geographical position into connectivity.

At the same time, we must also approach migration differently.

Migration begins where there is no security, no employment, no education, no access to water, no prospects, or no confidence that tomorrow will be better than today. It is not simply a matter of borders. Responsible policy must bring together security, human dignity, development and the real needs of labour markets.

Climate policy, too, will have to become more grounded in reality.

The green transition is essential. But if we make it socially unsustainable, we will lose the political support that is necessary to implement it. If we make it technologically dependent on a handful of sources, we will create new challenges while addressing old ones. If we expect poorer countries to move at the same pace without providing them with equal access to capital and technology, we will create injustice instead of a transition.

That is why future climate policy must, at the same time, be environmental policy, economic policy and social policy.

Mr. President,

All of this brings us back to the central theme of this session: trust.

Trust is not a sentiment that can be created by adopting a resolution. It is an outcome. It is built when an institution delivers on the purpose for which it was established.

That is why reform of the United Nations is necessary. So that the Organization can become more capable. So that it can deliver greater results. And certainly not to replace the responsibility of national states. But to act where collective action is needed.

Multilateralism does not begin in New York. It begins with the quality of the states that come to New York.

We are a small sized country. But we refuse to let the smallness of our territory define the scale of our ambition.

Our ambition is to become a serious state. A state that its allies can trust. A state in which young people can plan their future. A state that respects the diversity and multicultural character of its society. A state confident enough to defend its own identity without denying the identity of others. A state that knows its history but is not imprisoned by it. And a state that does not expect others to build it in its place.

That, to me, is modern sovereignty. Not isolation. Capability.

This year, Secretary-General António Guterres reminded us that the Charter begins with the words: “We, the peoples.” And he added: “Not we, the powerful. Not we, the victors.”

In those few words lies the reason why a small sized European country continues to believe in this Organization, even when it is disappointed by it.

Because the alternative to a world governed by rules is not a world in which everyone is free. It is a world in which the strongest are the freest. And everyone else depends on their goodwill.

Such a world may appear effective for a moment. But it is never stable.

Some three decades ago, the United Nations came to our country with a new idea: that the international community does not have to wait for violence to begin before it acts.

Today, we once again need that same political wisdom.

We must not wait for technology to create new inequalities before we establish rules. We must not wait for young people to leave before we build societies in which they see a future worth staying for. We must not wait for institutions to lose all public trust before we reform them. And we must not wait for the world to become fully divided into opposing blocs before we rediscover the value of dialogue.

That child with whom I began will be fourteen years older when the world enters 2040.

None of us today can promise that child a peaceful world. Nor a world without crises. Nor a world without competition.

But we can leave that child something else.

A world in which power is not the only argument. A world in which knowledge is not the privilege of the few. A world in which alliances create security, rather than new lines of fear. A world in which technology serves humanity. And a world in which a small state has the right to the same dignity, the same rules and the same voice as a great power.

That is the promise worth renewing.

Not because we are naive about the world as it is. But because we are realistic enough to understand what happens when the world is left to power alone.

Macedonians and the Macedonian citizens will share their burden of responsibility.

Thank you.

Mr. president of the General Assembly, your Excellencies, heads of State and Government. Mr. Secretary General, ladies and gentlemen, it is a great honor for me to address this August Assembly on behalf of His Excellency General Assimi Goïta, president of the Transition and Head of State, and to deliver the statement of the Republic of Mali. Mr. president, please allow me to warmly congratulate you on your election as a president of the 81st session of the General Assembly. And from the outset, I assure you, of Mali's full cooperation throughout your mandate. I also would like to take this opportunity to pay tribute to your predecessor for the remarkable conduct of the work of the 80th session. And finally, I wish to express our sincere appreciation to Mr. Antonio Guterres, Secretary general of the United Nations, for his commitment over the past ten years in the service of our organization and in the service of peace, development and human rights throughout the world.

Your excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. On exactly 66 years ago, six days only after becoming independent and sovereign Mali, under the leadership of President Modibo Keïta, was admitted to the UN with the support of the Republic of Tunisia and of the salon, currently Sri Lanka. We welcome the theme of the 81st session of the General Assembly, namely restoring trust, supporting Transformation, a United Nations organization that delivers for all. This theme is very timely and relevant because beyond encouraging reflection on how our organization can regain credibility and effectiveness amid multiple crises and challenges to multilateralism, it especially calls on member states to restore trust and seek common solutions to the many challenges of our time. And how can this be achieved? For its part, Mali reaffirms its unwavering commitment to reformed multilateralism founded on strict respect respect for the purposes and principles of the United Nations Charter, um particularly sovereign equality Territorial integrity.

Non-use of force, mutual respect, and non-interference in the internal affairs of a state. The further we move away from these principles, the closer we come to cycles of conflict. And we all know that the blatant violations of international law its selective application, double standards in the management of crises throughout the world, abusive recourse to force and threats and policies of hegemony and domination in violation of the charter of this organization have seriously undermined public confidence throughout the world In international institutions, especially the United Nations. We therefore call for the lifting of unilateral coercive measures, which undermine state sovereignty and endanger the well-being of populations in approximately 30 countries throughout the world, which are affected by such sanctions. To these practices, which undermine the current governance, we need to add the slowness of anticipation within the United Nations, which too often leaves the organization reduced to observing crisis after they have erupted. That's the case in Israel, where for several decades we had a security crisis for.

Also the crisis in Libya provoked by the NATO interference in 2011. Uh, the NATO action in Libya significantly worsened the security, political, humanitarian and human rights situation in our region through in particular, the spread of terrorism and violent extremism Now, faced with this reality, it is legitimate to question the effectiveness of the tools available to our organization. It is for this reason that we welcome the Strategic review of the United Nations Regional Office for West Africa and the Sahel, which should lead to an approach better aligned with the realities and concerns of the people impacted. The government of Mali reiterates its strong condemnation of international terrorism and its foreign state. Sponsors, who finance arm, provide logistical support and intelligence to this organized transnational crime. Other independent sources also corroborate these unacceptable actions by Ukraine. Here we have a country which claims to be protecting its territorial integrity, where, as in Africa, in the Sahel, it provides clear support to terrorist groups and other harmful groups which undermine the territorial integrity of our countries. Given our history, the international community in particular Africa, cannot just remain silent in the face of what it was being done by Ukraine. It has enormous consequences for African countries, and it goes beyond that. We understand very well that Ukraine is just a visible part of the iceberg, which is trying to destabilize our country, to break our determination to throw off the colonial yoke terrorism, which is nurtured and supported from outside, does it in three ways. First, in the armed way.

We know that it's attacking civilian populations. It's a security crisis in the economic way, which impacts our countries and through the media notably through us, organized and systematic disinformation campaigns and certain media outlets nostalgic for colonial past play a role in these. The coordinated attacks of 25th April and 4th of July 2026, and several uh locations in Mali caused numerous casualties, and they demonstrate the existence of the dangerous connection that we're becoming increasingly aware of. So the scenario we witnessed in 12 in 2012 is repeating itself now with terrorist groups and so-called separatist armed groups now forming openly terrorist coalition against Mali institutions and populations. Regional and international responses, including the deployment of international forces, have failed to halt these complex security crises and massacres affecting Sahelian populations. And that is why His Excellency Ibrahim Tower of Burkina Faso.

And president of the Confederation of Sahel states. Um General Assimi Goita, president of transition and head of State of Mali. General Abdul Rahman Tijani, president of the Republic of Niger and head of state. Our three heads of state took the historic decision on 6th July 2024. Niamey, to create the Confederation of Sahel states so that to take responsibility for the fate of our nations and citizens establishment. To date the AES Confederation has achieved real and encouraging progress in various areas.

I reaffirm here the determination of our three heads of state to pursue and intensify the fight against terrorism in all of its forms and manifestations. The Malian delegation fully endorses that statement that will be delivered by His Excellency Mr. Traore, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Burkina Faso, on behalf of the Confederation of Sahel States, which brings together Burkina Faso, the Republic of Mali and the Republic of Niger. Malian forces on their own and also within the as unified force and with the support of the Russian Federation, are today on the front line against imposed terrorism. I would even go so far as to say, as a hybrid war by oxy, whose implications extend beyond our region. I also salute all partners who continue to support Mali and the countries of the Sahel in this difficult context, victory against terrorism this global existential threat requires pooling efforts and resources, but above all, it requires a shared understanding of the phenomenon of terrorism itself. Because contrary to what some would have us believe, there is no such a such thing as a good terrorist and a bad terrorist.

The three, as member countries remain open to cooperation with all partners who respect, uh, our main principles governing our countries, namely respect for our sovereignty, territorial integrity. The respect for our strategic choices, including our choices for partnership, and also taking into account the interests of our populations. And we do not accept dictates here, rather. Rather, we seek sincere and healthy cooperation and partnership conducted in mutual respect. And in this spirit, Mali, in line with the principles and goals of its print of its policy, will continue to conduct its diplomacy on the basis of good neighborly relations. Mutual respect.

Non-interference in the domestic affairs of other states, and the peaceful settlement of disputes. I would like to use this opportunity to pay tribute to all victims of the cowardly barbarism of terrorism who have sacrificed their lives. I also would like to pay tribute to our defense and security forces for their courage, their professionalism and their unwavering dedication in defending sovereignty, territorial integrity of our countries and protecting our people. I pay special tribute to the memory of the General Sadio Camara, Minister of Defense and Veterans Affairs, whose legacy of patriotism, courage and sacrifice will continue to inspire future generations of Malians and people in the Sahel Mr. president, to reinforce security. And ensure the sustainable the return of peace the government is implementing a comprehensive and integrated strategy for stability and prosperity of our country, and for this, the state continues to extend a hand to all those willing to lay down their arms and return to the Republic, in line with the conclusions of Inter Malian dialogue and the National Charter for Peace and Reconciliation. Already, thousands of former combatants who meet the conditions have, uh, either joined the defense of security forces or entered civilian employment.

Mali's sovereignty is very precious to us, and it is not negotiable. Sovereignty is not limited to defending our territory. It also means we are controlling our economic choices, that we are managing and developing our natural resources and mining resources, our gold and lithium strengthening our productive sectors, and also creating greater opportunities for our youth. And in this spirit, the government remains committed to implementing the 2063 vision and the National Strategy for Emergence and Sustainable Development 2024 2033. These two ambitious programs are designed to meet the legitimate aspirations of the Malian people, and they constitute a generational pact. And it shows our determination to build a sovereign state, a competitive economy, a just society, a country in which every citizen can thrive with dignity.

The government placed at the heart of its action, economic recovery and public welfare because they're essential to lasting peace and stability. Thus, through appropriate reforms, the government, in addition to improving political um situation, we've improved economic governance, including better management of public affairs and greater domestic resource mobilisation. Me and my country today, I must say, works very hard to. Mobilize the resources that we need, because the international assistance on its own, however great it is, never developed a country. If we looked today, the level of international assistance and we compare that with the needs for financing in our countries, the places where millions of young people arrive at the labour market in Mali and Burkina Faso and Niger and in Africa, we can see that the international assistance will never be enough, and we need to mobilize our own resources, and we need to have confidence that we will be able to have other sources of funding so that our country can move forward, so our countries will continue counting on their own whilst leaving the door open. Who want to work with us?

Public spending is increasingly directed today towards a structuring productive investment, better access to basic services and training and employment for young people and women in particular. And this ambition requires greater local processing of our natural and mining resources, stronger national production capacities and an active role for youth in Mali's economic and social transformation. Mali intends to continue its national refoundation to guarantee security, justice, wellbeing and prosperity for all of its citizens. And once again, we we count first and foremost on ourselves in this. Mr. president. Now regional international issues.

A government remains attentive to developments across Africa and around the world, and we encourage, therefore, efforts aimed at the rapid and lasting resolution of conflicts on the African continent. Um, regarding the situation in the Middle East, Mali reaffirms its full support for the for the brotherly Palestinian people and their legitimate struggle to exist as a fully recognised state. Mr. president, the. International situation in such that we have to acknowledge the international order is undergoing profound change. And the longer we ignore it, the less we will we will be able to adjust to it. The question is no longer whether the world is moving towards multipolarity, but rather which actors will shape this new order, and how will they cooperate to meet the aspirations of people throughout the planet?

We share And here we are talking about cooperation, not confrontation. And not the law of the strongest to govern the world in this changing environment. Mali will pursue a foreign policy based on sovereign equality of states, on diversified partnerships, on defence of national interests and constructive engagement for peace and prosperity throughout the world. Our objective here is strategic autonomy for Mali, strategic autonomy for the Confederation of the Sahel states. The strategic autonomy for Africa in both security and development areas, and this autonomy does not mean a rupture. Rather, it seeks to make Africa into a credible and indispensable partner for global stability and prosperity climate change and desertification.

For Mali and the Sahel remain a major source of economic, social and environmental vulnerability. They affect agriculture and livelihoods. They also. We have to acknowledge it, threatening peace and security. We therefore call on member states to focus on adaptation, on access to climate finance, on indigenous technologies and solutions tailored to Sahelian realities. We advocate stronger links between efforts to combat desertification, food security initiatives, water management, conflict prevention, and resilience building.

Mr. president, the world is experiencing extraordinary technological advances, including generative artificial intelligence. It is something that comes up in debate after debate. AI offers enormous opportunities, and we acknowledge that, but also significant risks. We must be lucid here. We must not simply consume AI technology. We must master it, adapt it to our realities, and contribute to its development.

This requires, uh, defining and creating appropriate legal and ethical frameworks for us. Digital and technological sovereignty has become an essential dimension of national sovereignty. We must invest in skills, in research, in, in, in innovation in infrastructure, so that young people can participate fully in this transformation. For this reason, the head of state of the Republic of Mali, Assimi Goita um, has established Mali's Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Robotics to promote our country's digital sovereignty. On the issue of international migration, Mali, which is a country of origin, transit and destination at the same time, Mali therefore reaffirms its attachment to international cooperation and considers human mobility is a benefit for humanity. It is important in this room to say it, to repeat it, that for us, human mobility is not a threat.

It is a benefit. And all of the countries in this assembly have benefited from migration, even though other aspects need to be managed. So migration, mobility is a benefit for humanity. We call therefore, for respect of the rights of the migrants in in accordance with international conventions. Mr. president, by way of conclusion Mali recalls that the multilateral framework, which is embodied by the United Nations, stands at a crossroads The time has come for us to assume our shared responsibility for a reformed United Nations refounded. I was going to say that's how vast the scope of work is a United Nations that is more just, more representative and truly the service of all of the people in the world without distinction.

This is an essential condition to restoring the trust of member states and people in the organisation. It requires strengthening representation within multilateral institutions, including multilateral financial institutions, and ensuring that Africa's voice is heard more clearly in decision making bodies which affect the future of our world, the future of humankind. Mali reaffirms its readiness to contribute to common efforts of the international community. For a world which is more peaceful, more secure, more just, more prosperous, and finally, more united, I thank you.

Mr. president, excellencies, distinguished delegates. Dear friends, the chosen theme for this year's General Assembly is restoring trust, managing transformation. I don't think that there could be a more appropriate framing for our discussions of this week. Trust Or more properly. Properly, the lack thereof is the greatest challenge currently facing our world. The erosion of trust that has gripped our societies runs deep.

Where once people embraced trust, now people are gripped by suspicion, suspicion of governments, suspicion of institutions, suspicion of businesses, even. All too often suspicion of each other. I am talking about suspicion, not skepticism. Skepticism. The legitimate questioning of those who hold power over people's lives is the lifeblood of a democratic society. Suspicion.

However, the assumption that others are automatically looking out for their interests and not those of the common good is poison to any democratic society. No community can succeed if we blindly believe that our neighbors are out to do us down just as no country can succeed if it blindly believes that its neighbors, even those it may long have considered and seen as friends, are out to get it. Which means restoring trust, rebuilding alliances, remaking friendships must be the central mission for all of us here at home and abroad. It must also be the central mission of the remaking of this United Nations To change. You have to believe. We know we need to change how the United Nations works, how it takes decisions, and how it delivers on the ground.

But we can only make that change, achieve that transformation if we believe that change is possible. Nobody ever successfully renovated the House without the faith that however hard the work, however many setbacks faced along the way, the end result would be a real improvement on what went before. So we need to show faith that however hard the work, however many setbacks faced along the way, the end result of transforming this house, this home of all the nations, will be a real step forward. And as this United Nations embarks on its ninth decade of service, the need for a step change in how the international community works together solves problems together is arguably needed more acutely now than ever before. That erosion of trust is leading to the corrosion of the international order, not the improvement of the international order, but the destruction of the international order. An international order that, for all its flaws and failures, has seen more children escape hunger, more families live in peace, and more children grow into old age than any era before it.

To destroy the international settlement, without any idea of what comes next would be an act of wanton destruction that would rightly never be forgiven or forgotten by the tens of millions whose future it would betray. So let us be bold and let us say it loud and clear. Let us be utterly unequivocal. Now more than ever, is a moment for more cooperation, not less. More dialogue, not less. More trust, not less.

That is the only way that we will manage to find paths to progress on the all too many, all true, all too intractable conflicts blighting our world today. In Malta, the smallest member state of the European Union, we have always been a bridge between Europe and the Middle East. So allow me to focus on two of those conflicts on our doorstep. Firstly, Ukraine. It is all too easy and all too great a mistake for us to fall in the trap that repelling the invasion of Ukraine becomes another never ending conflict, a grinding tragedy on the corner of our continent about which we can do nothing. Malta will never accept that despair.

Europe must never accept that despair. The world must never turn its head away in despair. Malta remains as adamant in our condemnation of that invasion today as we were on day one in February 2022. And Malta is equally as adamant that a just and lasting peace must guarantee Ukraine's sovereignty within its internationally recognised borders. That will only come about through a diplomatic process that the Ukrainian people can have full trust in. They will only have such trust if the process follows a full and unconditional cease fire and the full participation of Ukraine and its people in the subsequent peace talks.

Rightly the Ukrainian people will never have trust in any search for a settlement which involves their government being frogmarched to the table, one arm tied behind its back, whilst the guns still blaze. The issue of trust is clearly also central to the very worrying situation in Gaza The people of Israel need to have trust that Hamas will be disarmed, and that they will play no future role in the governance or security structures of Gaza. But the people of Gaza need to have trust that there is a path to a just peace. It is impossible to build that trust with a humanitarian situation as acute as that being experienced in Gaza right now. Malta's voice remains unwaveringly with the global calls for safe, sustained and unhindered humanitarian access throughout Gaza in accordance with international law. We firmly believe that the Gaza peace plan provides the best path towards ending the conflict and advancing credible political progress.

To achieve that progress, all parties and I emphasize all parties must fully respect and implement the objectives and commitments set out in the plan. And naturally, no progress can be made. If there is any question of the forced displacement of any of the Palestinian population. Indeed, it is incumbent on each and every one of us in the international community to rebuild the trust needed to underpin the conditions where genuine progress can be made towards a negotiated and lasting two state solution. That is the only solution. Nobody, however, is under any illusion how out of reach?

Unfortunately, that seems at the moment. But nor is this the moment to shy away or run away from the only goal that will guarantee the people of Israel and Palestine living side by side with the peace, prosperity and stability that they both deserve. Sadly, any progress towards a long term solution is being endangered by the situation in the West Bank settlement expansion, running directly counter to the resolutions of this General Assembly and designed to undermine the Palestinian territorial integrity, must stop and stop now. So too, must the violent settler attacks on Palestinian communities increasing at an alarming rate. Behold, they must be halted. These are all essential preconditions to a just and lasting peace, as is a credible and reformed Palestinian Authority that can demonstrate to citizens of both Palestine and Israel that it has the transparency, the accountability, the institutional effectiveness, and, above all, the democratic legitimacy to be a truly effective partner for peace.

Malta stands ready to play its part in building the capacity of both a renewed Democratic Palestinian Authority and the robust civil society that must underpin it, not just in Ukraine, Gaza and Israel, but across the world. Be it the conflict in Sudan, the ongoing violence in Myanmar or the instability across the Sahel. It is evident that diminished trust means diminished chances of finding solutions. You could put it as starkly as no trust equals no peace. Of course, no matter the conflict, each with its own individual and particular circumstances, there is no easy way of building trust. But equally, there is no easy way of avoiding the need to build trust.

We all know from our lives as much as from the experiences of our own countries, just how hard it is to rebuild trust when it has evaporated. Yet we also know the consequences if we give up trying, and the rewards that can come. If, however, slowly and however tentatively, we can start. If it is hard enough to build trust human to human face to face, it can be, of course, infinitely harder to build trust. Of machines, of the technology shaping all our lives. Yet the challenge of how we can manage to trust that technology and the organisations behind it is rapidly becoming the most pressing challenge of our age.

The sheer spread and the sheer power, the sheer speed of artificial intelligence is mind blowing. It appears to be moving far too fast for anybody let alone governments, to manage to keep pace. It can seem, whether from the perspective of a leader, consumer or parent, to be overwhelming. There is no escaping that. This is the biggest change and the biggest challenge that any of us will experience in our lifetime. So much so that we barely have the words to describe how monumental a disruption it is proving to be.

The usual phrases step change, paradigm shift just don't seem to capture the scale. And we should also be under no illusion that the currently existing rules, the traditional models of governance are in any way or manner up to grappling with the revolution that we are living through. Which is why, if we stand any chance of helping to build citizens trust in these advanced technologies, we need to begin by being honest and transparent that governments, just as individuals, we are still finding our way, that we don't have all the answers. What we do have, what we must have, is the will and determination to act and the right values to underpin those actions. And of course, it almost goes without saying that no state, however micro or mighty, has any chance of getting a grip if they try to go it alone. We only stand a chance as humanity.

On getting a grip on technology that seeks to ape our humanity. If we collectively work together. Acknowledging that the rules need to be set globally and they need to be stuck to. Even as they develop, as the tech develops. If we are to stand any chance of securing public confidence that AI can enhance and not destroy humanity, we need a set of international rules that reflect international law. So Malta, my country, wholeheartedly supports the implementation of the global Digital Compact and wider UN efforts to strengthen international digital cooperation.

To fragment is to fail, and that applies equally to fighting the new threats from the new frontline in global conflict and disruption. Cyber attacks, attacks on critical infrastructure, disinformation, the cutting of the underwater cables that connect us all to each other. These are not theoretical threats. They are constant and existential threats. For a small nation like Malta, a small island in the Mediterranean that relies on our connections to the rest of the world. They are, yes, existential threats.

Tackling them must be a priority. The priority for this United Nations. We need to embrace every emerging technology that can help us fend off those threats and build our digital resilience today. The guardians of our democracy, of our freedoms are just as likely to be found coding at a keyboard as marching in uniform. Both must work in lockstep together. Security will always, of course be physical.

Yes, but now it must also be digital. The change must then be reflected in the way we work together to achieve our different and common goals. I know that I am preaching to true believers, Mr. President and Mr. Secretary General, when I say that there must be no letup, no slowing down in the relentless, relentless drive for reform of how disunited nations and its agencies does its business and delivers its services, to take our foot off the gas would be to let down the millions who need this United Nations to do better, be better at tackling the problems that blight their lives. That is why the goal of this General Assembly, a United Nations that delivers for all, is so important and so urgent. If we are to have any hope of renewing the trust of the citizens with serving global institutions and the global order. We have to show that those institutions, this institution, can indeed deliver deliver in ways that change tangibly lives for the better.

We must never lose sight and never lose faith in the values that brought us together in the first place. As nations united. Malta is and always, of course, will be a passionate advocate and promoter of and passionately committed to multilateralism. At the core of all we do must be the code and conscience of the founding charter of this United Nations. But the implementation of those values, the way we turn those fine words into fine actions, must always be a process of constant evolution. We can never stand still if we are to keep cooperation alive.

So Malta remains thoroughly committed to the implementation of the pact for the future and all of its associated actions. Reforms must, yes, remain Member State driven and firmly anchored in the intergovernmental process, and efficiency must not come at the expense of effectiveness on the ground. Malta solidly backs a strong and effective resident coordinator system as the key anchor of UN action at a country level, and I can't reiterate often enough or restate strongly enough, that the only effective antidote to the cancer of cynicism and suspicion is effective and concerted action to tackle the greatest threat to our people and our planet. And alongside spreading conflict and the dangers of uncontrolled technology, the greatest threat to us all, and especially island nations like Malta, is man made climate change. I say, and I express this to all of you. Just look at the weather extremes we have been experiencing in Europe, particularly during these last weeks, to do nothing, to stand by and just wash our hands of it would be a moral and practical betrayal of the citizens, of the millions of citizens who put their faith in us, that we won't flinch from the biggest problems and the toughest solutions and decisions needed to tackle them So we must not stand by.

We must stand firm. Stand firm against the torrent of disinformation that fuels the deniers. Stand firm against the vested interests that seek to block effective action. Stand firm against the naysayers who say that. Because all don't choose to act. Nobody should.

To those cynics, I want to point out an instance that shows how hope can triumph over defeatism. And I go back to 1967 when representing the then geographically smallest member state of the Europe of the United Nations, a member state that had been a member of the United Nations for less than three years, Arvid Pardo spoke up in this General Assembly in a stirring speech, Malta's permanent representative made a passionate plea to the world's common humanity. He may have been speaking on behalf of a very small nation, but he had a very ambitious vision. Pardo Pardo called for the world to treat the resources of the oceans beyond their own borders as the common heritage of mankind. His demand for a law of the sea was prescient, but to achieve it took persistence. In fact, it took 27 years before it came into being.

What motivated Malta's action, then, is what motivates Malta's demands now? Doing nothing meant leaving the world's oceans to the mercy of the world's biggest, strongest and richest nations. Taking action showed that, and I quote, they belonged to all of humanity. Those living and those who still had to be born. That spirit was evident was evident when, in 1988, right at the start of the concern about global warming, Malta proposed the United Nations General Assembly resolution that recognized climate change as a global problem, requiring collective and global solutions suspicion of collective action won't be counteracted by retreat. It will only be overcome by the strength to turn convictions into action.

The phrase dare to dream has become perhaps the world's most common motivational phrase, imploring us that all we have to do is have the courage to dream, and those dreams will almost automatically become reality. And yes, we should all indeed dare to dream, to inspire ourselves, to turn hope into achievement, but to turn initial aspirations into sustainable attainment takes something more than just dreams It takes trust. Trust that by working together, we achieve more than we could ever achieve alone. It is that belief in the power of trust which underpins the values that brought me into public life. It is that belief in the power of trust, even now when it can seem a commodity in all too short supply, that convinces me that ultimately it trust will prevail. That ultimately, we as a world will find the courage to dial down the disbelief and crank up the confidence.

If we don't. If we don't realise that mutual suspicion can only lead to mutual destruction, if we don't realise that closing our minds to those who don't share our worldview limits our chances of solving the world's biggest problems. If we don't realise that limiting dialogue only to those who are like minded in reality can only drive us further apart, we face a very bleak future indeed. I refuse Malta refuses to believe that such a future is any more inevitable than it is desirable There is only one simple antidote to the destructive power of suspicion. It is one that may not, as of yet, have appeared on many motivational bumper stickers, but it is one that must be our lodestar. So I say to my fellow leaders, as much as I say to my fellow citizens of this planet, let us dare to trust, dare to realize that even those who we disagree with the most must become a part of the solution, and not a prolonger of pain.

Thank you very much.

Distinguished Mr. President,

Distinguished Mr. Secretary-General,

I  do  want  to  congratulate  Dr  Rahman,  on  his  election  as  President  of  the United Nations General Assembly, and I also wish to thank Ms Baerbock for her leadership of the 80th session of the General Assembly.

Let me also make a special thanks to Secretary-General Guterres, whose stewardship of this Organization and partnership with Montenegro over the past decade we deeply value. It is my honor to address you today as President of Montenegro, a Balkan and  Mediterranean  country,  a  credible  NATO  Ally,  steadily  advancing towards  membership  in  the  European  Union,  and  deeply  committed  to regional cooperation and effective multilateralism.

In Montenegro, we have an old and simple saying: a person’s word carries weight. This implies that a promise creates responsibility. And what is true between people should also be true between nations.

In  the  opening  words  of  the  UN  Charter,  the  nations  of  the  world  made perhaps the most important promise of all: “to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war.”

Eight decades later, as conflicts take lives and displace millions, geopolitical rivalries  place  the  international  system  under  growing  pressure,  and  new challenges test our collective capacity to respond.

So, how well have we kept our pledge? This is best told in numbers: In  2025,  the  world  witnessed  more  armed  conflicts than  in  any  year  since 1946. Sixty-five active conflicts, 8 of which between states. More than 240 thousand lives lost to organized violence, the deadliest toll in three decades.

About 120 million people driven from their homes, roughly 1 in 70 people. So,  are  we  leaving  a  better  world  to  the  generations  after  us,  or  have  we eroded  trust  in  our  collective  capacity  to  evade  conflicts  and  confront  the challenges that face the world.

Trust is not built through declarations. Trust is built when commitments are honored,  when  rules  are  applied  consistently,  when  institutions  act  with

responsibility,  and  when  people  can  see  that  international  cooperation produces tangible results in their lives.

Twenty  years  ago,  shortly  after  peacefully  restoring  our  independence, Montenegro  took  its  seat  in  this  Assembly  as  a  full  member  of  the  United Nations. This year therefore holds special significance for us. We celebrate twenty years of our UN membership as a sovereign country.

A child born in Montenegro that year is now twenty years old. A generation has come of age witnessing Montenegro’s transformation from a newly independent state into a country helping shape the Balkans defined not by the conflicts of the past, but by the opportunities of the future.

On the geostrategic front, Montenegro has paved the path towards our future in  the  EU,  which  is  now  within  reach.  Our  goal  is  clear:  by  2028,  to  see Montenegro’s flag stand among the member states of the European Union. In 2017, Montenegro joined NATO, strengthening not only our own security but also contributing to the stability of our entire region. We have kept good relations  with  our  neighbors  and  demonstrated  that  a  multi-ethnic,  multi-religious  and  multicultural  society  can  turn  diversity  into  confidence, belonging and common purpose.

At  home,  we  have  transformed  our  economy  and  strengthened  the democratic  institutions  on  which  lasting  prosperity  depends.  Much  work remains  ahead  of  us,  but  the  foundations  have  been  laid  for  a  society  in which talent and effort open doors; and a country where young people can imagine their future at home.

For us, the European Union is not simply a destination we wish to reach, but a value-based journey that we have embarked on. When  the  European  perspective  of  the  Balkans  was  reaffirmed  at  the Thessaloniki Summit in 2003, the world looked very different.

Multilateralism and international cooperation were expanding. The European Union was one of the most attractive political projects in the world and would welcome thirteen new member states over the following decade. At the same time, the Balkans was still  emerging from the devastation and divisions of the 1990s.

More than two decades later, we live in a profoundly different international environment.

The international order is entering a new and uncertain phase. This is why enlargement of the European Union is an act of strategic foresight. It is one of the best investments Europe can make in peace, security and long-term stability.

Montenegro is proud to stand today at the forefront of that process, ready to serve as an example for other candidate countries.

Not  because  our  journey  has  been  without  difficulties.  But  because  our journey  demonstrates  something  essential:  progress  is  possible.  Reforms matter. And democratic political culture pays off.

Earlier this year, leaders from across Europe gathered in Montenegro for the European Union–Balkans Summit. For  Montenegro,  that  gathering  carried  a  meaning  far  beyond  protocol.  It demonstrated how far our country has travelled and how close our European future has become. It also sent an important message about our region:

The future of the entire Balkan region lies within the European Union.

Our region has carried the weight of division for too long. A new chapter is being  written  through  cooperation,  connectivity,  economic  opportunity  and European integration.

My generation has a responsibility to help complete that chapter. These responsibilities are not important because of the titles they carry. They are important because of what they allow us to contribute — to reconciliation, connectivity, democratic resilience and the European future of our region.

And lasting reconciliation cannot be built on denial, selective approaches to justice or the glorification of those convicted of war crimes. It requires respect for the judgments of international courts and equal dignity for every victim, regardless of their identity or background. And in a world searching for proof that cooperation still works, Montenegro is contributing to the vision that the Balkans become that proof.

The principles that guide us at home guide us here, in this very organization. Our  engagement  within  the  United  Nations  system  is  guided  by  the  same principles.  Montenegro  is  a  reliable,  credible  and  predictable  partner, committed to an effective multilateral system with the UN Charter at its core, aligned with the European Union’s Common Foreign and Security Policy and

working  closely  with  our  NATO  Allies  and  EU  partners  in  support  of international peace and security.

This commitment comes at a time when the United Nations itself is facing a profound test.

Climate  change  is  testing  the resilience of states and societies. The answer cannot be less multilateralism.

It must be more effective multilateralism.

Montenegro  therefore  strongly  supports  the  UN  reform  agenda  and  the ambition to build a United Nations that is more effective, more agile, more accessible, financially sustainable and fit for the challenges of our time.

This reform must strengthen the UN’s ability to deliver where it matters most: in  preventing  conflict,  protecting  human  rights  and  freedoms,  advancing sustainable development and responding effectively to humanitarian crises. This responsibility extends to the Security Council itself, which must become more  effective,  representative,  accountable  and  transparent.  And  the exercise of the veto must carry the weight of conscience, above all when the world is confronted with mass atrocities and the large-scale loss of civilian life.
