Your Excellency, Mr. president. Excellencies, Mr. António Guterres, Secretary general of the United Nations. Honorable ministers, ambassadors, ladies and gentlemen, peace and blessings be upon you. At the outset, I would like to express my sincere congratulations to Doctor Khalilur Rahman on assuming the presidency of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly. I am convinced that his great experience and acumen will contribute in the successful conduct of the work of this session. I would also like to express my sincere thanks to Her Excellency Annalena Baerbock, for the excellent stewardship of the 80th session of the United Nations General Assembly.

I would like to thank His Excellency Mr. Antonio Guterres, the Secretary General of the United Nations, for his concerted effort to develop the United Nations and promote its role. Mr. president. It is my honor to convey to this distinguished gathering the greetings of His Excellency, uh, the President of Mauritania. Mohamed Rozani. And he wishes all the success for this session. His Excellency honored me to address the General Assembly on his behalf.

The theme of this session, Restoring Trust, Managing transformation. A United Nations that delivers for all, reflects the core of our responsibilities towards the common goal of this organization that was established after the horrors of the 20th century. They decided to rely on the strength of law and not that of the might. They decided to choose dialogue instead of confrontation. Our responsibility today is to maintain the scores, and we have to counter the selectivity in applying international law, especially when there is a systematic avoidance of collective commitments. Some countries do not want to uphold the same rules that they call on others to uphold.

This leads to weakened collective cooperation mechanisms. We no longer can prevent conflicts or settle them. This danger extends to institutions that might falter and fail. Multilateralism is not limited to the interests and sovereignty of states. It is not a a an example of weakness. It.

Instead, it is a necessity to ensure human dignity, bring peace, and confront challenges. Defending the United Nations is a defense of the right of all peoples to determine their future and participate in decision making. Those decisions that define their destiny. We want a more just United Nations. A United Nations capable of confronting the current challenges. Challenges.

After more than eight decades since the establishment of the UN, the Security Council reform has become a necessity to ensure. A fair representation of Africa, including permanent and non-permanent. Membership. While reviewing the financial architecture, this will ensure a participant cooperation on equal footing and open greater opportunities for development. The reform of this organization cannot be complete without promoting its ability to meet the promises of development. As 2030 approaches, we call for accelerating the implementation of the SDGs, and we support the UN 80 initiative as well as the pact of the future.

Mr. president, ladies and gentlemen the Islamic Republic of Mauritania renews its commitment to the principles and purposes of the UN charter and the norms of international law, as well as the resolutions of international legitimacy. Our foreign policy is based on good neighbourliness, the respect of states sovereignty, independence and non-interference in their internal affairs, as well as the peaceful settlement of disputes and ensuring the just causes proceeding from such principles. My country, under the leadership of His Excellency, the President of the state, Mohammed, will continue to build a modern state that is coexistent in synergy with its neighbours and open to the entire world. On the national level, we have adopted a comprehensive strategy with its political, economic, social and security dimensions. We made dialogue, consul and consultation. The pattern for public offices.

Thus, His Excellency the President launched a comprehensive national dialogue that is all inclusive. It does not exclude any strata of society to ensure consensus on the development of our institutions and entrench a state of law, a democratic state that protects rights and freedoms. Turning to the social context, we promote social cohesion and community unification through fighting discrimination and vulnerability while addressing any weakness inherited. We try to promote the synergies and develop our economies to limit poverty and provide the basic services to the most needy. We have also expanded the medical services through establishing a Medicare fund for all those who are not currently covered with medical insurance. We provide certain basic medical services to the most in need, especially mothers, the the mothers, the elderly, and those with disabilities.

Turning to education, reforming this sector is the basis of our effort to provide high quality education that provides equal opportunities and ensure equity Turning to good governance, we focus on transparency, the independence of the judiciary, and combating corruption while reforming public offices and promoting investment. Our approach. Addresses the hike in prices, confronting any threats to the security or terrorism while tackling also vulnerability and poverty. The complementarity between all those dimensions ensured our country's security and stability in an environment full with disruptions. Mr. president, Mauritania Mauritania adopts a balanced approach that covers all our inheritances, be it African, Islamic, Arab and others. We are guided by our foreign policy, underpinned on cooperation, solidarity and the respect of sovereignty and good neighbourliness.

Proceeding from the above, we believe that confronting the common challenges necessitates promoting multilateralism. We need concert. The concerted effort of the international community. In a practical translation of such effort. My country, through its participation in the different events and peacekeeping missions, contributes in the peaceful settlement of disputes and promoting cooperation and coordination, both regionally and internationally. This contribution is based in our belief in the need to have durable and just cooperation because no one country, no matter how powerful it was, can stand alone to confront the challenges of such an interconnected world.

Covid 19 and the subsequent disruptions in the supply chains of food and energy, as well as the conflicts and wars, demonstrated how the interests of states are interconnected along with their peace and security. Migration is at the core of such common challenges. People's mobility strives for a better future, better job opportunities, better, better development. However, the high influx of migration and their complexity reveals the reality that should be analyzed without any exaggeration, exaggerations, and it should also preserve the unity of societies. We need an effective response to this challenge through cooperation between the countries of origin transit and destination. We have to ensure a fair share of the responsibilities and burdens and address the root causes of irregular migration, while combating human trafficking and smuggling.

To contain such influxes and ensure at the same time the dignity of migrants and their rights. The solution is in our common responsibility and solidarity. Mr. president. The expanded theatre of conflicts and the escalating humanitarian cost of such conflicts requires greater protection of civilians, while ensuring the peaceful settlement of such disputes for the sake and benefit of communities. The systematic destruction witnessed in the Palestinian territory and the ensuing fall of victims and displacement are of the responsibility of the international community, especially the United Nations. We have to protect the Palestinian people and end their suffering.

In this vein, we renew our support for a just and lasting solution to the Palestinian cause based on the peace, the Arab Peace Initiative and the UN resolutions. To establish the state of Palestine that is independent, viable. Along the lines of the 4th of June 1967, with East Jerusalem as its capital. We appreciate the mediation effort undertaken by the United States of America, Egypt, Qatar to Turkey or Turkey, and we stress the need to implement the Security Council Resolution 2803 issued on the 17th of November 2025 on the peace plan in Gaza. This will bring about peace and ensure reconstruction in the Gaza Strip. We would like to recall the historic step.

Taken by a number of European countries over the past year, when they recognised the state of Palestine. We do welcome and commend the recent measures undertaken by a number of European countries to impose sanctions on Israeli settlers who have been implicated in violent acts against the Palestinian people. However, even though they are important. But such initiatives should not be isolated. Instead, they should be a driver for more firm international action to put an end to the settlement activity. While opening the horizon for the two state solution.

Paradoxically. That we have denied the Palestinian people from participating in this international forum at a time when the Palestinian question is at the forefront of our agenda. At a time when the Palestinian cause comes at the forefront of the international agenda. They were not able to attend. This go contravenes the spirit of dialogue and pluralism that the United Nations is underpinned upon in this domain. We stress that the State of Palestine has gained the recognition of most of the Member States of the United Nations.

This reflects a wide range, uh, support international support of the Palestinian people and their establishment of an independent statehood. Therefore, we call for the, um, the participation of the Palestinian the Palestinians in the UN forums so that they can achieve their aspirations and defend their just cause before the international community. We renew our support to the people of Lebanon in the face of the violations that they have endured. We have to end their suffering and ensure their sovereignty. We are also standing in solidarity with Sudan. We are committed to Sudan's unity, sovereignty and territorial integrity.

We call for an immediate end to this war, giving priority to dialogue while protecting civilians and ending their suffering. Turning to Libya, we support the UN efforts and the African Union's effort to reach a permanent settlement that would maintain the country's unity and sovereignty, sovereignty, while ensuring peace and stability to the people of Libya. We renew our support. To the efforts made. Um in the. Al-Arabiya in Yemen and the initiatives taken by the Arab, uh, countries, as well as the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia to support that country.

We stress our principled position on the conflict of the Western Sahara and hope to reach a just and sustainable solution that will be accepted to all parties. We express our deep concern towards the military escalation in the Middle East and the resulting threat to the entire region and its stability. The repercussions of which would also reach the Strait of Hormuz and the. Regional and international navigation in this important waterway. We support the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, the State of Qatar and the Kingdom of Bahrain and Kuwait, as well as the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan. Uh in the face of the attacks against their stability and security.

We have to preserve states, territories and call upon all countries to de-escalate and ensure self-restraint, ensure dialogue, and save the region and its peoples from more crises and sufferings. Mr. president, ladies and gentlemen The world today faces. An important moment that goes beyond political challenges. It. There are acute humanitarian, environmental and economic challenges. My country Mauritania.

Knows full well the importance and sensitivity of this moment. We would like to stress with humility from this common home that brings us together from the United Nations, that we all shoulder this responsibility before history. We have to leave to the future generations a better world than the one we've inherited. We are capable of that. Once we redirect ourselves to the path of peace through renewing our common and joint effort. The United Nations must regain its effectiveness to serve peace and security, especially common security.

We can do that if we rightfully address the deep transformations that are reshaping the entire international landscape. The. These are the provisions of the 2030 agenda, its goals and objectives, and the expanded scope of knowledge, the accelerated technology, and their subsequent results and impacts. We can do that if we return with wisdom to what our Founding Fathers have been guided upon the common principles and purposes that gather us under the umbrella of the United Nations for more than eight decades. By bringing hope that good governance, technological development and the advancement will be an addition that will be in all our benefits, that will save the entire humanity from the current challenges. Thank you, and peace and blessings of God be upon you.

I thank. The. Minister of Foreign Affairs, African Cooperation and Mauritanians abroad of Mauritania.

speaker_post: Minister of Foreign Affairs, Regional Integration and International Trade
text:
Allow me to congratulate you on your election to the Presidency of the General

Assembly and assure you of the support of my delegation.

I also wish to pay tribute to His Excellency António Guterres for his outstanding

dedication  and  commitment  to  this  Organisation  during  his  two  terms  as

Secretary General. He will be remembered as a leader with a steady hand always

guided by principles of fairness, compassion, and dignity for all.

The United Nations has now completed the first eight decades of its existence.

Eight  decades

replete  with

resolutions,  declarations  and  action  on

decolonization, development, new international order, the new constitution for

the oceans, as well as climate and the environment, technology, human rights,

international law and peacekeeping.

Created  in  the  aftermath  of  the  Second  World  War,  the  immediate  focus  was

obviously  on  peace  and  security.  But  the  UN  system  has  evolved  significantly

over the decades to expand its scope and sphere of influence, within the confines

of its Charter.

However,  the  UN  must  now  look  to  the  future,  building  on  its  record  of

achievements as well as from lessons learned from what it could not achieve.

UN Reform

As we look to the next eighty years, we must ask ourselves a searching question:

is the UN fit for the purpose for the 21st century— not the world of 1945, but the

world of today and beyond?

We are entering a new era of international relations defined by unprecedented

technological developments.

Often  absent  from  the  table  where  the  rules  of  tomorrow  are  being  adopted,

developing countries risk being left further behind.

The  same  exclusion  afflicts  the  international  financial  architecture,  which

remains skewed against the Global South.

Developing nations must have a seat at the table as equal stakeholders.

We  all  acknowledge  that  the  three  pillars  of  the  UN  Charter  are:  Peace  and

Security; Development and Human Rights. The twin institutional pillars provided

in the Charter were, and still are, the Security Council and ECOSOC as the apex

bodies for achieving these purposes. However, over the years, optimal use has

been made primarily of only one of these organs.

We need to enhance and accelerate the revitalisation of the General Assembly

and that of ECOSOC so that they are not merely forums for debate, but engines

of action.

This must be done as we bring about the reform of the Security Council.

The  historical

injustice  regarding  the  composition  of  the  Council  was

acknowledged in Action 39 of the Pact for the Future but the process for reform is

still stalled.  Mauritius fully supports the Common African Position — the Ezulwini

Consensus and the Sirte Declaration — calling for no fewer than two permanent

and five non-permanent African seats on the Council.  Mauritius also supports

the call for SIDS to have a seat on a reformed Council.

On the question of the veto, Mauritius aligns itself with the position of a growing

number  of  States  that  in  the  event  the  veto  is  retained,  any  new  permanent

member must have the same rights as the original permanent members.

Mauritius also supports the Franco-Mexican Initiative on the suspension of the

veto in cases of mass atrocities.

We support the positions of the G4 and of L69 on Council reform, and we reiterate

our support for India's candidature for a permanent seat, commensurate with its

constructive role in global affairs.

Mauritius welcomes the increasing recourse to the International Court of Justice

as a mechanism for the peaceful  settlement  of disputes and  determination of

issues of international law. We call upon Member States which have not yet done

so to accept the compulsory jurisdiction of the ICJ.

We  welcome  the  landmark,  unanimous  Advisory  Opinion  of  the  ICJ  on  the

obligations of States in respect of climate change. This was a vindication of the

tireless advocacy of Vanuatu and the Core Group of States. Mauritius was proud

to stand among them.

We call for the full operationalization of this Advisory Opinion, including through

the  follow-up  action  requested  by  this  Assembly,  in  accordance  with  the  UN

General Assembly landmark resolution of 20 May 2026, welcoming the Advisory

Opinion  of  the  International  Court  of  Justice  on  the  obligations  of  States  in

respect of climate change.

We also support the legal principle — affirmed by the ICJ- that States are under

no obligation to update their maritime baselines or zones to account for climate-

induced  sea  level  rise.  Mauritius  calls  for  the  principle  that  statehood  and

sovereignty are not impacted by sea level rise, to be formally codified.

Mr President,

Water  stands  at  the  frontline  of  the  climate  crisis.  Water  is  a  major  concern

globally,  and  Mauritius  welcomes  the  holding  of  the  UN  Water  Conference  in

December this year. We look forward to this crucial global issue being addressed

by the international community as a matter of urgency.

We  also  call  for  enhanced,  accessible,  and  predictable  climate  finance

accompanied  by

comprehensive  capacity-building  and  disaster-risk

management for the most vulnerable.

I  also  wish  to  highlight  that  Mauritius  is  currently  conducting  a  constitutional

review exercise which will include giving constitutional protection to the Rights of

Nature.

Development Financing

The  crisis  in  development  financing  is  deepening.  Concessional  financing  for

developing countries is declining precisely when the need is greatest.

The graduation of countries, including Small Island Developing States, should be

encouraged and supported and not prejudice access to affordable finance.

Mauritius calls for a review of the criteria for access to concessional financing,

that reflect vulnerability rather than income per capita alone.

We also call for the strengthening of the rules-based multilateral trading system

and for fair, transparent, and equitable mechanisms for resolving trade disputes.

New Technologies

The  rapid  evolution  of  digital  and  emerging  technologies,  including  artificial

intelligence, is already shaping economic, social, and institutional developments

across the globe. We support the GA resolution establishing the Global Dialogue

on  AI  Governance and  welcome  the  work  being  done  by  the  Independent

International Scientific Panel on AI.

For  Mauritius,  digital  innovation  is  a  developmental  imperative.  We  have

launched, with UN support, a National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025–2029

and a National Fintech Strategy 2026–2030.

We need an open, transparent and inclusive dialogue on governance of the new

technologies  which  ensures  that  the  benefits  of  technological  progress  are

shared equitably and that the risks are managed collectively.

Oceans

As a coastal state with an EEZ of 2.2 million square kilometres — that is, more

than one thousand times our land mass — Mauritius is profoundly connected to

the ocean.

We  reaffirm  our  unwavering  commitment  to  UNCLOS  as  the  legal  framework

governing all activities in the oceans  including  the  seabed  and  subsoil  beyond

national jurisdiction.

We  welcome  the  decisions  of  the  UN  Commission  on  the  Limits  of  the

Continental  Shelf  approving  the  submission  lodged  by  Mauritius  in  December

2008 and approved in March 2011 as well as the second one filed in May 2009 and

approved in July 2026.

We welcome the 100th ratification of the BBNJ Agreement and calls for its prompt

and  effective  implementation.    We  look  forward  to  its  first  Conference  of  the

Parties  advancing  the  institutional,  financial,  and  procedural  arrangements

necessary for the effective implementation of the Agreement.

Collaboration  is  key  to  effective  maritime  security,  maritime  surveillance  and

Domain Awareness. We call on the international community to support regional

and sub-regional initiatives in this regard.  I am pleased to inform that Mauritius,

with the support of the European Union and the Commission de l’Océan Indien,

will host a Ministerial Conference on Cybercrime and Sea Cables security in the

Western Indian Ocean in the first quarter of 2027.

Mauritius  welcomes  the  major  developments  taking  place  across  Africa  with

regard to greater integration and pooling of resources particularly  in relation to

capacity  building.  In  this  regard,  Mauritius  has  initiated  action  at  the  UN  for

promoting  enhanced  regulatory  frameworks  in  developing  countries  namely

through pooling of resources.

Mauritius  attaches  great  importance  to  the  elimination  of  all  forms  of  racism,

racial discrimination, and xenophobia. We welcome the High-Level Meeting on

this subject and reaffirm our commitment to the International Decade for People

of African Descent.

Mauritius is fully committed to supporting the Convention on the Elimination of

All  Forms  of  Discrimination  against  Women  and  the  Beijing  Declaration  and

Platform for Action. Earlier this year, Mauritius adopted new legislation to further

enhance the protection of women’s rights.

SDGs

We are deeply concerned by the  effects  of regional conflicts and instability on

development, economic growth, food security and the achievement of SDGs.

The crisis in the Gulf and threats to freedom of navigation have sent shockwaves

across the global economy. For a small, open economy such as Mauritius, which

depends on maritime trade routes for over 90% of its primary energy imports and

more than 70% of its food supply, these effects are felt acutely.

We call for restraint, for dialogue, and for a durable diplomatic resolution.

Palestine

Mauritius reaffirms its longstanding position in support of the inalienable right of

the Palestinian  people to self-determination  and  to  an  independent,  sovereign

state, with East Jerusalem as its capital, living in peace and security alongside its

neighbours. The cycle of violence must end. Too many people have suffered for

far  too  long.  We  note  with  deep  concern  that  the  establishment  of  unlawful

settlements may be a major obstacle to peace.

Chagos Archipelago

I  now  come  to  an  issue  which  for  Mauritius  is  non-negotiable,  it  concerns  our

sovereignty over the Chagos Islands. The agreement on the Chagos Archipelago,

signed by Mauritius and the United Kingdom in May 2025, stands as living proof

that  trust  in  multilateralism  and  UN  judicial  organs  can  achieve  the  peaceful

settlement  of  disputes  and  the  completion  of  our  nation's  decolonisation  and

restore the rights of Mauritians of Chagossians origin by force of law.

Trust especially amongst neighbours and in the region is reinforced when there is

the respect for the rule of law, for the resolutions of the United Nations General

Assembly, the ruling of the International Tribunal on the Law of the Sea, and the

ICJ’s  Advisory  Opinion  on  the  Chagos  Archipelago,  which  carries  authoritative

obligations.

We trust that States which laid the foundation of the new post war legal order will

recommit to full respect and compliance with international law and correct this

historical injustice without delay, as William Ewart Gladstone, four-term British

Prime  Minister  and  great  campaigner  for  peace  and  freedom  put  it,  “Justice

delayed is justice denied.”

Monsieur le Président,

Tromelin

L’île de Tromelin fait partie intégrante du territoire de la République de Maurice.

Nous avons constamment maintenu notre position concernant la souveraineté

de la République de Maurice sur cette île.

Nous réitérons notre appel à la France à s’engager de manière constructive en vue

du  règlement  du  différend  relatif  à  l’île  de  Tromelin,  dans  l’esprit  d’amitié  qui

caractérise les relations entre nos deux pays.

Social Development

Mauritius is committed to upholding the pledges made at the Social Summit in

Doha last year.

Nowhere is that promise to universal social protection more concrete than in our

health  services.  As  Non-Communicable  Diseases  and  a  rapidly  ageing

population place growing pressure on our health system, we are strengthening

public  healthcare  through  major  investments,

improved  service  delivery,

expanded  specialised  care  and  a  greater  focus  on  prevention.  Mauritius  will

continue to offer free and quality public healthcare to each and every citizen.  We

thus  welcome the  holding of  the  2027  High-Level  Meeting  on  Universal  Health

Coverage, and Mauritius stands ready to contribute to that global effort.

High-Level Meeting on Pandemic Prevention, Preparedness, and Response

Today,  the  High-Level  Meeting  on  Pandemic  Prevention,  Preparedness,  and

Response met at a decisive moment, and decisive moments demand more than

mere  intentions.    Mauritius  supports  the  conclusion  of  the  terms  of  Benefit-

Sharing  guaranteeing  vulnerable  countries,  real  access  to  affordable,  safe,

effective  and  quality  medicines,  including  generics,  vaccines,  diagnostics  and

health  technologies.  It  is  of  crucial  importance  to  widen  pandemic  financing

eligibility,  including  with  the  Pandemic  Fund,  to  formally  incorporate  the

Multidimensional Vulnerability Index.

Road Safety

Mauritius also  welcomes UN  initiatives  on  Road  safety  – an  issue  to which  we

attach  the  highest  importance,  and  which  acts  as  a  silent  epidemic  that

continues to claim far too many lives, disproportionately in developing countries.

We call for greater international attention and resources for this critical issue.

Monsieur le Président,

Nous  nous  trouvons  à  un  tournant  décisif  dans  l’histoire  des  Nations  Unies.

L’organisation fait face à des défis majeurs, tant sur le plan interne que sur le plan

externe.

En  interne,  le  processus  engagé  par  le  Secrétaire  général  pour  réactualiser  la

structure administrative et financière de l’organisation pourra permettre à notre

organisation d’être mieux équipée pour relever les défis futurs.

Sur  le  plan  externe  le  rôle  et  les  fonctions  de  l’organisation  ainsi  que  la

composition de ses principaux organes sont remis en question et sont appelés à

être redéfinis.

La volonté affichée par la communauté internationale après la guerre, de se doter

d’un instrument de collaboration en vue d’instaurer un nouvel ordre mondial est

toujours présente. Le fait que le nombre d’acteurs ait plus que triplé durant les

huit  dernières  décennies,  reflète  un  engagement  encore  plus  grand  et  plus

diversifié qu’au moment de la création de l’ONU.

Nous  sommes  confiants  que  la  communauté  internationale,  dont  environ  la

moitié  est  composée  de  jeunes  qui  aspirent  à  protéger  la  planète,  à  mieux

partager les richesses et à utiliser les nouvelles technologies à bon escient, saura

relever les nouveaux défis.

Nous renouvelons notre attachement au multilatéralisme  aussi bien que notre

confiance dans sa capacité à répondre aux attentes des peuples.

Je vous remercie, Monsieur le Président.

HONOURABLE DR. GEORGE T. CHAPONDA, M.P., MINISTER OF FOREIGN AFFAIRS  AND INTERNATIONAL COOPERATION,

DURING THE GENERAL DEBATE OF THE 81ST  SESSION OF THE UNITED NATIONS GENERAL ASSEMBLY,

28 SEPTEMBER, 2026

Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Lilongwe 3.

September, 2026

Mr. President;

Your Excellencies;

Distinguished Delegates,

I have the honour and priviledge to deliver this statement on behalf of

His  Excellency  Professor  Arthur  Peter  Mutharika,  President  of  the

Republic of Malawi, and the people of Malawi.

I  congratulate  you,  Mr.  President,  and  all  Vice  Presidents,  on  your

election  to  lead  this  81st  Session  of  the  United  Nations  General

Assembly.  Malawi  pledges  its  full  support  to  your  leadership.  We  also

extend  our  profound  appreciation  to  the  Secretary-General  for  his

unwavering dedication to our shared global values.

The

theme

for

this  session,

"Restoring  Trust,  Managing

Tansformation:  a  United  Nations  that  Delivers  for  All,"  strikes  at

the  heart  of  our  current  global  reality.  We  live  in  an  era  of  deep

fractures. Trust between nations has eroded. Global systems are failing

to  manage  rapid  technological,  economic,  and  environmental  shifts

equitably. For the United Nations to remain relevant, it must transform

into  an  institution  that  delivers  tangible  progress  for  the  most

vulnerable,  leaving  no  nation  behind.  I  would,  therefore,  like  to

highlight six opportunities for restoring trust, managing transformation

and, thereby ensuring a United Nations that delivers for all.

The first opportunity is accelerating sustainable development and

economic transformation:

Mr.  President,  the  timeline  for  the  2030  Agenda  for  Sustainable

Development  is  rapidly  drawing  to  a  close,  yet  the  promises  of  the

Sustainable  Development  Goals  (SDGs)  remain  dangerously  out  of

reach  for  millions.  For  Malawi,  the  pursuit  of  wealth  creation,  self-

reliance  and  economic  transformation  is  not  merely  a  political

aspiration;  it  is  an  urgent  survival  strategy.  Because  of  this,  we  have

remained  steadfast  in  implementing  the  SDGs,  in  alignment  with  our

long-term  development  vision,  the  Malawi  2063.  On  this  note,  Mr.

President, I am happy to report that Malawi successfully presented our

third  Voluntary  National  Review  during  the  2026  ECOSOC  High-Level

Political  Forum,  thereby  reaffirming  our  commitment  to  the  2030

Agenda for Sustainable Development and the  Malawi 2063, as well as

our  desire  to  accelerate  sustainable  development  and  economic

transformation.  The  review  revealed  that  even  though  we  face

numerous  structural  challenges,  we  have  made  some  progress  on

many of the SDGs.

Mr. President, our goal is to systematically transform our economy by

modernizing  agriculture,

expanding  mining  and  accelerating

digitalization.  However,  national  efforts  alone  cannot  dismantle  the

structural  barriers  built

into  the  global  economic  architecture.

Developing  nations

require  deliberate,  scaled

investment

in

industrialization,  sustainable  infrastructure  and regional  value  chains

to  transition

from  primary  commodity  exporters  to  diversified,

industrialized economies.

In  addition,  we  cannot  achieve  sustainable  development  while

drowning

in  debt.  Malawi,

therefore,

calls

for

immediate,

comprehensive debt relief and restructuring. The current international

financial  architecture  forces  developing  nations  to  choose  between

servicing  predatory  debts  and  investing  in  health,  education  and

climate resilience. This is a moral failure.

We  also  call  for  a  massive  scaling-up  of  concessional  development

financing. We need targeted investments in our key productive sectors,

namely  agriculture,  industrialization  and  infrastructure  development

as follows:-

(a)   Agricultural  modernization

through  mechanization

and

commercialization to guarantee food security;

(b)   Building local industry so that we stop exporting raw materials,

and  create  decent  jobs  for  our  youth,  who  make  up  nearly  40

percent of the Malawi population; and

(c)   Developing robust transport, energy and digital infrastructure to

connect Malawi to regional and global markets.

We,  therefore,  call  upon  our  international  partners  to  align  their

support  with  national  blueprints  like  the  Malawi  2063  in  order  to

generate meaningful job creation and shared prosperity.

The  second  opportunity  is  strengthening  climate  action  and

resilience:

Mr. President, Malawi contributes negligibly to global greenhouse gas

emissions,  yet  we  remain  on  the  frontline  of  the  climate  crisis.  In

recent  years,  devastating  cyclones,  prolonged  droughts  and

increasingly  erratic  weather  patterns  have  destroyed  infrastructure,

devastated  crops,  displaced  thousands  of  our  citizens  and  inflicted

severe damage on our economy. This year, we face the added threat of

El  Niño-related  extreme  weather,  which  risks  further  undermining

livelihoods, food security and economic stability.

As such, we are fighting back by embedding climate resilience into our

national  development  planning  and  strengthening

locally  driven

adaptation measures. However, our efforts are continually outpaced by

the  scale  and  speed  of  climate  change.  Climate  shocks  repeatedly

destroy  infrastructure,  decimate  agricultural  production,  exacerbate

food insecurity, and erode hard-won development gains.

The  global  community  must  therefore  move  beyond  rhetoric  and

translate commitments into meaningful action. We call for the full and

effective  operationalization  and  capitalization  of  the  Loss  and  Damage

Fund. Major historical and current emitters must honour their climate-

finance commitments by providing accessible, predictable, grant-based

and highly concessional financing, rather than relying on debt-creating

instruments

further  burden  vulnerable  countries  already

struggling  to  cope  with  the  consequences  of  a  crisis  they  did  little  to

cause.

Malawi, therefore, calls for enhanced, predictable and easily accessible

climate finance, with greater emphasis on adaptation and disaster-risk

reduction.  We  need  sustainable  investment  in  early-warning  systems,

climate-resilient

infrastructure,

sustainable

land  management,

climate-smart agriculture and locally led adaptation.

Climate change is an existential threat to Malawi's development and to

the hard-won gains we have made.

Mr.  President,  the  third  opportunity

is  to  reform  global

governance and strengthen multilateralism:

The  current  global  challenges  underscore  a  fundamental  truth:  our

multilateral

framework

is

fractured  because

its

foundational

architecture  is  obsolete.  The  institutions  designed  in  1945  no  longer

reflect the geopolitical and economic realities of 2026.

Malawi reaffirms its unwavering commitment to multilateralism, but it

must  be  a  multilateralism  that  is  inclusive,  fair,  and  democratic.  We

call for an urgent comprehensive reform of the United Nations Security

Council  to  correct  the  historical  injustice  done  to  Africa.  Africa

deserves  permanent  representation  with

full  veto  privileges,  as

articulated in the Ezulwini Consensus. Furthermore, the international

financial  architecture,  specifically  the  IMF  and  the  World  Bank,  must

be  radically  overhauled.  The  current  system  traps  developing  nations

in cycles of unsustainable debt, forcing governments to choose between

servicing  foreign  loans  or  funding  basic  education  and  healthcare  for

their citizens.

Mr. President, because Malawi strongly believes in multilateralism, we

take  responsibility  when  called  upon  by  the  international  community

to  participate  in  causes  that  further  the  aims  of  this  organisation.

Malawi remains firmly committed to the rule of law, accountability and

the peaceful resolution of disputes as indispensable foundations of an

effective  multilateral  system.  It  is  in  this  spirit  that  Malawi  has

presented  the  candidature  of  Lady  Justice  Tujilane  Chizumila  for

election  as  a  Judge  of  the  International  Criminal  Court  for  the  term

2027–2036.  Justice  Chizumila  is  a  distinguished  jurist  with  extensive

judicial and legal experience at the national, regional and international

levels, including her service as a Judge of the African Court on Human

and  Peoples’  Rights.  Her  candidature  reflects  Malawi’s  commitment  to

strengthening  international  justice  through  experienced,  independent

and highly qualified judicial leadership.

As  States  Parties  prepare  to  elect  six  judges  to  the  International

Criminal  Court  in  December  2026,  Malawi  respectfully  seeks  the

valued  support  of  States  Parties  for  the  candidature  of  Lady  Justice

Tujilane  Chizumila.  We  are  confident  that  her  extensive  judicial

experience, commitment to the rule of law and demonstrated service to

justice  and  human  rights  would  enable  her  to  make  a  meaningful

contribution  to  the  work  of  the  Court.  Malawi  looks  forward  to  the

support  of  fellow  States  Parties  for her  election  and  to  continuing  our

collective efforts to strengthen the institutions of international justice.

Mr.  President,  the  fourth  opportunity  for  restoring  trust,  managing

transformation, and thereby ensuring a United Nations that delivers for

all,

lies

in  strengthening  global  health  security.  Economic

transformation and  sustainable  development  are  impossible  without  a

healthy  population.  The  vulnerabilities  exposed  by  recent  global

pandemics continue to linger, reminding us that global health security

is only as strong as its weakest link.

Malawi  is  making  strides  toward  achieving  Universal  Health  Coverage

and strengthening our primary healthcare systems. However, systemic

global  inequities  in  healthcare  access,  medical  manufacturing  and

vaccine  distribution  remain  glaringly  unresolved.  True  global  health

security  demands  decentralized  pharmaceutical  manufacturing

capabilities, unrestricted technology transfers and intellectual property

waivers  during  health  emergencies.  My  delegation  appeals  to  all  of  us

here  to  finalize  a  robust,  legally  binding  Pandemic  Treaty  that

guarantees  equity,  solidarity  and  immediate  resource  sharing  for  the

Global South.

We  also  call  for  collaboration  in  efforts  to  build  long-term  resilience

against  pandemics,

through

investments

in

our  domestic

pharmaceutical  manufacturing  capacity.  By  producing  essential

medicines within Africa, the entire world gains through stronger health

security  and  stable  supply  chains,  especially  through  faster  outbreak

response.

Mr.  President,  the  fifth  opportunity  is  to  promote  human  rights,

peace and international security:

Malawi  firmly  believes  that  development,  peace  and  human  rights  are

inextricably  linked.  We  remain  deeply  committed  to  upholding  the

constitutional  rights  of  all  our  citizens,  strengthening  our  democratic

institutions  and  maintaining  an  uncompromising  stance  against

corruption. Further, we strongly defend the right to development as an

inalienable  human  right.  True  freedom  cannot  exist  in  conditions  of

extreme poverty and systemic economic exclusion.

On  the  global  stage,  we  view,  with  great  alarm,  the  proliferation  of

violent conflicts, unconstitutional changes of government, geo-political

fragmentation  and  acts  of  racism,  racial  discrimination,  xenophobia,

and  related  intolerance.  Mr.  President,  the  Malawi  nation  is  not

standing  aloof  as  all  these  alarming  developments  occur.  Malawi

continues  to  play  its  part  in  global  peace  operations,  deploying  our

brave  men  and  women  to  United  Nations  peacekeeping  missions  to

safeguard stability on our continent. In this regard, let me reiterate the

calls  for  immediate  cessation  of  hostilities  in  all  active  conflict  zones

worldwide.  Global  resources  currently  being  funneled  into  destructive

warfare  should,  instead,  be  redirected  towards  eradicating  poverty,

building schools and financing sustainable development.

We  also  reaffirm  our  solidarity  with  global  efforts  to  combat  racism,

racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance.

The  last,  but  not  least,  opportunity  is  in  advancing  economic

diplomacy and strategic partnerships:

Mr.  President,  in  alignment  with  the  Malawi  2063,  our  foreign  policy

prioritizes  robust  economic  diplomacy.  Malawi  recognizes

navigating  the  complexities  of  the  2020s  requires  a  paradigm  shift

away  from  traditional,  paternalistic  foreign  aid,  toward  genuine

reciprocal  economic  diplomacy.  For  this  reason,  we  are  actively

strengthening bilateral and multilateral partnerships to attract foreign

direct

investment,  enhance

international

trade,  and  mobilize

development assistance. Malawi is open for business.

Further  to  this,  Malawi  highly  values  South-South  and  triangular

cooperation.  Collaborative  initiatives  with  fellow  developing  nations

allow us to share cost-effective technologies, best practices, and home-

grown  solutions  in  climate-smart  agriculture,  renewable  energy,  and

digital  governance.  We  will  continue  to  deepen  these  alliances  to

accelerate our national development priorities.

Mr. President, as we take steps to grasp these opportunities, we must

also  recognize  the  emergence  of  Artificial  Intelligence,  which  presents

both  opportunities  and  threats  to  humanity.  Malawi  welcomes  the

transformative potential of AI as an expression of human ingenuity and

as  an

increasingly

important  tool

for  accelerating  sustainable

development.  For  developing  countries,  including  Malawi,  AI  offers

opportunities to strengthen agricultural productivity and food security,

improve  healthcare  and  education,  enhance  climate  resilience  and

disaster  preparedness,  expand  financial  inclusion,  and  improve  the

efficiency  of  public  services.  Malawi  believes,  however,

technological  advancement  must  remain  human-centred:  Artificial

Intelligence  should  complement  and  enhance  human  capabilities

rather than diminish the indispensable role of people in shaping their

own development.

At  the  same  time,  Malawi  recognises  that  the  rapid  expansion  of

Artificial  Intelligence  presents  significant  challenges,  particularly  for

developing  economies  with

fragile

labour  markets  and

limited

technological  infrastructure.  Automation  could  disrupt  employment

and  widen  existing  inequalities,  while  unequal  access  to  computing

capacity, data, digital infrastructure, skills and financing risks creating

a  new  technological  divide  between  and  within  countries.  Malawi

therefore  calls  upon  the  United  Nations  to  continue  promoting  an

inclusive,  ethical  and  development-oriented  global  framework  for  AI

governance—one  that  safeguards  human  dignity  and  employment,

builds  the  technological  capacities  of  developing  countries,  facilitates

equitable  access  to  AI  technologies  and  ensures  that  the  benefits  of

innovation  contribute  directly  to  the  achievement  of  the  Sustainable

Development Goals. No  country should be left behind in the emerging

AI-driven global economy.

Mr.  President,  in  conclusion,  restoring  trust  requires  honesty,

accountability  and  action.  Managing  transformation  requires  courage,

vision  and  solidarity.  The  choices  we  make  today  will  reverberate  for

generations  to  come.  We  can  choose  to  retreat  into  isolationism  and

protectionism,  or  we  can  choose  to  summon  the  political  courage

required to build a fairer, more resilient and inclusive world.

Malawi  stands  ready  to  play  its  part.  We  are  transforming  our

economy,  reforming  our  institutions  and  investing  in  our  people.  But

we cannot do it alone in an unfair global environment. We stand ready

to  work  hand-in-hand  with  all  member  states  to  bridge  the  divides,

restore  trust  in  multilateralism  and  deliver  a  sustainable  dignified

future for all humanity

Let  this  81st  Session  of  the  General  Assembly  mark  the  turning  point

where  the  United  Nations  transitions  from  a  forum  of  speeches  to  an

engine  of  delivery.  Let  us  build  a  United  Nations  that  delivers  wealth

instead of poverty, resilience instead of vulnerability, and peace instead

of conflict. A United Nations that truly delivers for all.

Thank you very much

Distinguished Delegates, Ladies and Gentlemen,

1. I join others in congratulating my friend, His Excellency Dr. Khalilur Rahman, on his election as President of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly.

2. You have Malaysia’s full support as you lead this Assembly through a period of profound global uncertainty.

3. Indeed, we are meeting at the most challenging time for the UN in many years.

4. The world has become accustomed to crisis. Wars are escalating. Major-power rivalry is sharpening. The international arms-control architecture is under strain. New technologies are transforming societies faster than our institutions can adapt.

5. But perhaps the greatest danger is not any one crisis. It is the growing belief that the international system cannot solve them.

6. That is the trust deﬁcit confronting the UN today.

7. And Malaysia believes we must confront it openly and honestly. Trust can only be restored through concrete action.

8. When international law means what it says. And when the

people of the world can look to this Hall, and believe that their voices still matter.

9. We must remember that the UN is not merely here for the aftermath of war, but to prevent war from taking place.

10. Yet too often, we respond only after disaster has arrived.

11. We count the dead. We deliver supplies. We rebuild what has been destroyed. And then we wait for the next crisis.

12. This cannot be the future of multilateralism. We must move from reaction to prevention.

13. And nowhere is that task more urgent than in Gaza.

14. Malaysia will not stand here and recite statistics that everyone in this Hall already knows. We all know the scale of death in Gaza.

15. We know how many children, families, medics, aid workers, and journalists have been slaughtered.

16. We also know that Gaza represents the highest number of children made orphans, in a single conﬂict.

17. Malaysia, and many other Member States, have exhausted every eﬀort in the pursuit of justice for Gaza.

18. We have consistently called for immediate ceaseﬁre and unrestricted supply of aid.

19. We have supported humanitarian works in Palestine.

20. We have pushed for punitive action towards Israel.

21. And we have advocated for full Palestinian membership in this Hall.

22. And yet, again and again, the collective will of this Assembly has encountered the silencing eﬀect of the veto.

23. Malaysia will speak plainly:

24. We are sick of it.

25. Nowhere is the need for reform more critical than in the Security Council. Nowhere are the shortcomings of the UN more glaring than in the Security Council.

26. The exercise of the veto must be questioned and strongly challenged by every single member of this General Assembly. Particularly in cases of crimes against humanity.

27. Resolution 76/262 has already created an accountability channel between the Council and this Assembly.

28. We must make full use of this Resolution as a launchpad for

greater accountability regarding the use of the veto.

29. Expanding the Council's membership alone will not be enough to resolve its failures. It is the veto that must be challenged, and it is the veto that must be abolished. We must begin the work now.

30. There is still time to save the global order. The paralysis of the Security Council will not be the paralysis of the UN.

31.It is fair to say that global trust in the UN's ability to deliver is at an all-time low.

32. This, in turn, demolishes trust in the very idea of the multilateral order.

33. The citizens we serve and represent are afraid, Excellencies.

34. They are watching the world order fragment.

35. They are witnessing the re-emergence of an arms race.

36. They have heard overt threats to use nuclear weapons.

37. And they are seeing their governments choose not to regulate A.I., and the many ways it is being abused, but instead give it more power.

38. In such chaotic times, the only way to course-correct is to rebuild trust in the power of pro-active governance and

multilateralism.

39. Trust comes from the way in which we, as world leaders, can manage transformative forces.

40. For centuries, global power was concentrated in states. But today, a new source of power has emerged.

41. A handful of private actors now control how billions of people communicate, work, transact, and consume information.

42. Artiﬁcial intelligence is changing how economies operate, how societies function, and how governments make decisions.

43. The opportunities are enormous. But so are the risks.

44. We must therefore ask a simple question: Who governs the transformation?

45. Technology must serve humanity. Never the reverse.

46. And the answer cannot be that a small number of companies or countries decide the rules for everyone else.

47. The UN must continue to empower Global South countries, who are likely to be more greatly aﬀected by unequitable A.I. development, to participate in global discussions on A.I.

48. The Global South cannot simply become a destination for data

centres, while decisions about A.I. are made elsewhere.

49. We must be partners in innovation. Not merely customers and markets. And not merely destinations for investment.

50. Partners, involved in the decisions that will shape our future.

51. Equitable decision-making, and equitable development.

52. That means managing the enormous demands that tech infrastructure places on water, energy, land, and other resources, so that the beneﬁts of A.I. can be shared more broadly, across borders.

53. In our hyper-connected world today, indeed, very few things stay where they begin. Technologies are rapidly shared, and they can just as rapidly disrupt. Similarly, war can also travel beyond borders.

54. Across West Asia, escalating conﬂict threatens some of the world's most important routes for energy and trade, including the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandab.

55. The consequences of conﬂict do not stop at these shores. A family in Southeast Asia has no part in these disputes. Yet that family still pays the price, when food, fuel, and cost of living rise.

56. Malaysia therefore urges all parties to step back from escalation.

57. Diplomacy has shown that dialogue is possible. That path must not be abandoned.

58. Or we risk sending further shockwaves through global markets, and needlessly bringing suﬀering to innocent families around the world.

59. Most nations in this Hall are not great powers. Yet decisions taken by a few can shape the future of all.

60. We are the global majority. As I said earlier, we must not simply live with the consequences of choices made elsewhere. We must help shape those choices.

61. Middle powers, such as Malaysia, can help keep dialogue alive when major powers cannot agree.

62. Regional organisations, such as ASEAN, can bring the perspectives of their people into global debates. We must have the conﬁdence to speak for our regions, not be spoken for.

63. I began by speaking about trust. Let me close where I began.

64. The question before us may appear simple, but in truth, it is profound.

65. When people are suﬀering, and when the world looks towards this Hall, will this organisation still answer the call for which it was created?

66. Actions speak louder than words, my esteemed Colleagues.

67. We must restore trust. Manage transformation.

68. Reform institutions that no longer serve current realities.

69. And we must ensure that the rules of the global system apply equally to all.

70. Malaysia will not turn away from the UN in its hour of diﬃculty. We will not abandon multilateralism just because it is imperfect.

71. We will do the work, to make it worthy of the trust placed in it.

72. Because we believe in multilateralism, most of all, when the alternative is a world ruled by power alone.

73. Eighty years ago, the founders of this organisation resolved to save succeeding generations from war.

74. We are those succeeding generations. And that promise now rests in our hands.

75. The world needs a UN that delivers.

76. One that ensures that international law is truly international. And guarantees that every region has a voice.

77. And above all, one that ordinary people can look to in their darkest hour, and still believe that it will act. That the world has not forgotten them.

78. Before concluding, we would like to oﬀer our most heartfelt gratitude to Secretary General Antonio Guterres.

79. As this will be the ﬁnal session of the General Assembly during his tenure, we thank him for leading the UN with unyielding dedication and patience through many unprecedented global upheavals.

80. These are the qualities we will need to face our future as an organisation.

81. And if there is anything that humanity has demonstrated throughout our history, it is our capacity to adapt.

82. My esteemed Colleagues, let us adapt and prove ourselves worthy of the promise entrusted to us.

Thank you.

Your Excellency, Khalilur Rahman, President of the General Assembly, Your Excellencies, Heads of State and Government, Your Excellency António Guterres, Secretary-General of the United Nations, Ladies and Gentlemen,

I congratulate you Mr. President, on your election as the President of the 81st Session of the  General  Assembly.  I  also  thank  the  President  of  the  80th  Session  of  the  General Assembly for her commendable leadership.

1.  Confidence  in  the  international  system  is  increasingly  declining.  International organisations are grappling with reduced capacity. Political and economic impunity is being entrenched. The UN Charter underscores resolving international disputes through  peaceful  means  and  the  obligation  of  States  to  pursue  diplomatic solutions, before resorting to escalation or the use of force. Notwithstanding, we continue to be inundated with images of suffering of innocent civilians, such as in Sudan and Eastern DRC, large-scale internal displacement, cross-border migration, and humanitarian crises across the world. These conflicts continue to undermine international  mechanisms  and  structures  established  to  maintain  international peace  and  security.  Hence,  we  commend  you,  Mr.  President  for  the  timely  and befitting theme for the 81st Session of the UN General Assembly: “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations That Delivers for All.”

2.  Namibia’s independence was born out of international solidarity, and is renowned as  a  UN  success  story.  This  is  a  testimony  to  the  effectiveness  of  the  UN. Therefore,  we  shall  not  be passive  observers  to  efforts  aimed  at  dismantling  or weakening the international system, that has served us over 80 years, albeit with some shortcomings. In this regard, we shall continue to call for peace over conflict, dialogue over confrontation, and peaceful coexistence over tensions.

3.  In  restoring  trust,  we  need  to  manage  transformation  of  the  United  Nations Security  Council,  based  on  equitable  representation,  in  its  decision  making processes,  to  reflect  contemporary  geopolitical  realities.  The  Common  African Position, as articulated in the Ezulwini Consensus and the Sirte Declaration, has also  been  re-affirmed  in  the  Pact  for  the  Future,  which  recognizes  Africa  as  a Special Case. The time has come for us to recognize that we have been negotiating for too long. And that it is such stalemates that erode trust in the United Nations.

4.  This fairness and justice should extend to the participation of women in decision making,  including  in  the  prevention  and  resolution  of  conflicts,  post-conflict reconstruction and peace building, in line with UN Security Council Resolution 1325 on  Women,  Peace  and  Security.  The  Women,  Peace  and  Security  Agenda  has contributed  positively  to  rehabilitation,  reconciliation  and  reintegration  efforts  in conflict-affected regions, serving as a core framework for stabilising post-conflict situations.  This  is  a  positive  undertaking,  which  should  be  emulated  by  other international and regional organisations and non-governmental organisations that are involved in peace support operations and peacebuilding efforts.

5.  Mr. President,

6.  Any system needs constant transformation to be effective. As we forge ahead with the  SDGs,  reform  of  the  international  financial  architecture  is  critical  to  a  more equitable and inclusive global economic order. Such reforms should create greater policy  space  and  access  to  financing,  to  enable  countries  to  expand  their economies  through  value  addition  to  their  natural  resources,  including  critical minerals, for our people to have full benefit of our resource. This will accelerate sustainable development, address inequality, create jobs for our youth and lift our populations out of poverty.

7.  In this context, we welcome the creation of the African Credit Rating Agency to be launched in Mauritius in October this year. This development is a building block of Africa  taking  ownership  of  her  development  and  prosperity  agenda.  It demonstrates progress in Africa’s ambition to drive impetus for the reform of the international financial architecture, in order to ensure a level playing field.

8.  Middle-Income  countries  continue  to  face  high  borrowing  costs,  limited  fiscal space,  debt  vulnerabilities,  climate-related  shocks  and  persistent  inequalities. Namibia  reaffirms  the  Sevilla  Commitments  as  an  important  step,  towards reforming  the  international  financial  architecture  and  strengthening  the  global partnership  for  sustainable  development.  The  system  must  thus  become  more inclusive, equitable and responsive to the realities of the Middle-Income Countries.

9.  The  world  is  experiencing  increasing  devastating  floods,  relentless  heatwaves, frequent hurricanes and prolonged periods of drought. At times, it feels that we

are at war with Mother Nature. At this point Namibia reiterates its solidarity with the government and people of Nepal following the recent floods in that country.

10. Namibia  continues  to  face  significant  climatic  challenges  as  a  result  of  climate change, including recurring droughts, rising temperatures, and growing pressures on agriculture and water resources. Yet, Namibia contributes less than 0.01 per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions and it bears a disproportionate share of the  impacts  of  climate  change,  like  other  developing  countries.  In  the  spirit  of climate justice: we call for a greater responsibility by those that have contributed most to global greenhouse gas emissions, including through increased support for countries  that  are  most  vulnerable  to  climate  impacts.  It  is  through  sustainable climate financing, that we will be able to achieve Sustainable Development Goal 13, to combat climate change.

11. Against this backdrop, it is very important to focus on water in 2026, particularly as climate change intensifies droughts, floods, desertification and land degradation across Africa. As an arid country, Namibia continues to promote the prudent use and conservation of water, integrated water resources management, groundwater recharge  and  greater  investment  in  sustainable  water  infrastructure.  We  also underscore  the  importance  of  implementing  the  Namib  Declaration,  adopted  at COP  11  in  Windhoek,  as  part  of  our  collective  response  to  desertification,  land degradation and drought. In this regard, we are pleased to inform that Namibia will host the Global Water Partnership Headquarters, first time to be located in the Global South.

12. In our capacity as co-chair with Senegal of the AU International High-Level Panel on the African Water Investment Program, Monday we convened a High-Level Side Event  on  water  investment  for  Africa  and  global  cooperation.  We  believe  its outcome is a meaningful contribution to the 2026 UN Water Conference later in the  year,  and  advances  stronger  global  partnerships,  investment  and  action  for sustainable water security.

13. The  Pact  for  the  Future,  which  was  co-facilitated  by  Namibia  and  Germany, provides  an  ambitious  framework  for  transforming  global  governance  and addressing  contemporary  and  emerging  challenges.  While  the  Pact  gives  due consideration for the interests and needs of future generations, its implementation has not been as effective as we had wished.

14. For Namibia, effective implementation of the key commitments of the Pact for the Future would be beneficial in accomplishing Namibian’s national priorities, namely: Agriculture, Sports, Youth Empowerment, Quality Education and Training, Creative Industries, Health and Social Welfare, Land, Housing and Sanitation. I wish to urge all member states to consider the implementation of the Pact for the Future as a crucial international priority for development.

15. As part of our development agenda, we are   preparing our young people for the emerging industries such as oil and gas, renewable energy, and Green hydrogen among others. Subsequently, this year we have introduced 100 percent subsidized registration  and  tuition  fees  for  Namibian  students  entering  universities  and Vocational Training Centers and encourage them to take appropriate courses. The government has established the National Youth Development Fund last year. As a result of this Fund, young people  have set up their own medical practices,  Law Firms,  milling  plants, poultry businesses  to  mention  a  few.  Thus  contributing  to job creation and poverty reduction.

16. Namibia also takes cognizance of the rapid advancement artificial intelligence (AI) in advancing human progress, in line with the Global Digital Compact. However, we call for the ethical, responsible, inclusive, and human-centered development, and  use  of  artificial  intelligence,  with  appropriate  safeguards,  to  ensure  that technological advancement complements and enhances human capabilities, rather than undermining them.

17. A  United  Nations  That  “Delivers  for  All”,  must  be  inclusive.  I  reaffirm  Namibia’s unwavering  solidarity  with  the  peoples  denied  their  right  to  self-determination. This position is firmly rooted in Namibia’s historical experience of the brutality of colonialism,  apartheid  and  occupation.  This  is  not  a  position  borne  out  of antagonism, but rather one grounded in Namibia’s longstanding commitment to justice,  solidarity,  and  the  rights  of  peoples  to  determine  their  own  destiny,  in accordance with the UN General Assembly Resolution 1514 of 1960.

18. The United Nations has a responsibility to advance a just and lasting resolution of the question of Western Sahara, consistent with the Charter of the United Nations and the relevant resolutions on decolonisation and self-determination. We support MINURSO’s  mandate,  and  the  holding  of  a  UN  backed  Referendum  in  Western

Sahara, for the Sahrawi people to finally exercise their right to self-determination. We  therefore,  call  upon  the  full  implementation  of  the  UN  Security  Council Resolution  2797  of  October  2025,  which  reaffirmed  the  need  for  a  mutually agreeable  lasting  political  solution  between  the  Polisario  and  the  Kingdom  of Morocco.

19. Namibia calls for the Palestinian people’s right to self-determination, freedom, and statehood. We further call for an end to the atrocities being committed in Gaza. The  establishment  of  an  independent  Palestinian  State  living  side  by  side  with Israel in peace and security, remains a vital goal that we must collectively pursue.

20. We call for the lifting of the unjustified economic embargo  against Cuba, which has had far-reaching consequences for the Cuban economy and the well-being of its people, including access to essential goods and services. We  call for the end to  the  energy  siege  on  Cuba,  and  her  removal  from  the  unilateral  list  of  States allegedly sponsoring terrorism.

21. From the forgoing and in the spirit of the Charter, for a United Nations that delivers for all, the UN has the responsibility to protect and facilitate the participation of all its members and observers  in its work

22. The adoption of the United Nations Resolution on the Transatlantic Slave Trade in March  2026,  is  the  beginning  of  a  journey.  A  journey  towards  truth, acknowledgement, healing and justice for millions of Africans and people of African descent,  whose  lives  were  forever  changed  by  slavery,  colonialism  and  other historic  injustices.  As  we  commemorate  the  25th  Anniversary  of  the  Durban Declaration and Programme of Action, we are reminded that racial discrimination must not have any place in our societies, and that restorative remedies, including reparations, must be put in place to address these historic injustices.

23. Namibia congratulates the outgoing Secretary-General, Mr. Antonio Guterres, as he nears the end of his tenure. We commend him for overseeing the largest part of the implementation of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, that has  energized  international  support,  including  the  actions  in  the  Pact  for  the Future.

24. Namibia stands ready to work with the incoming Secretary General. However, let me  point  out  that,  since  the  establishment  of  the  United  Nations  in  1945,  no woman has served as Secretary General of the organization. The leadership of the Organisation has yet to reflect the principle of gender equality, that it promotes across the international system. Namibia therefore, believes that it is time that a woman is elected as Secretary General of our Organisation.

25. The United Nations is the only platform through which all nations can collectively advance shared aspirations, achieve common goals and address global challenges. Namibia  will  remain  a  constructive  partner  in  strengthening  multilateral cooperation in restoring trust in the United Nations.

26. Let  us  therefore,  continue  to  defend  our  organization.  Let  us  collectively  place human dignity at the centre the United Nations, so as to restore trust, effectively manage transformation and deliver for all.

I thank you.

Mr. president. Mr. president of the general assembly, Mr. Secretary general ladies and gentlemen, heads of State and government. Ladies and gentlemen, heads of delegation. Ladies and gentlemen, I am taking the floor before this August assembly on behalf of my country. On behalf of His Excellency, the General of the Army, Abdourahamane Tchiani, President of the Republic of Niger, a head of state, to express the message of peace of the people of Niger, the sovereign people of Niger, a people that is committed to its dignity and to cooperation among nations. Mr. president, please accept the congratulations of Niger upon your election to the presidency of this 81st session of the General Assembly, as well as our thanks to your predecessor, Her Excellency Mrs. Angelina Baerbock, and Mr. Antonio Gutierrez, Secretary General of our organization, whose second term will conclude on the 31st of December.

Mr. president, the theme of this session, Restoring Trust, Managing transformation a United Nations that delivers for all, perfectly chimes with the concerns of those peoples aspiring to peace and progress, even while bombs and other devices of mass destruction are endlessly causing death and devastation in every corner of our planet. How can we restore trust and manage transformation in the world, so that the United Nations can effectively bring peace and good fortune to all peoples? How then, can we achieve this goal?
