Mr President, Your Excellencies,

Anne Frank was a teenage girl without power or influence. But she had a pen and a diary. A diary that would make its way into the world, and inspire millions of people. I think that one of the reasons people are so inspired by Anne, is that she had an unshakeable belief in the power of people to turn the tide so that good prevails. She wrote, ‘How wonderful it is that nobody need wait a single moment before starting to improve the world’. Those words are just as powerful and true today. This week is the perfect example of that.

I realise that the United Nations does not carry the most positive associations for everyone. And indeed, there is much that can and must be improved. But let us not forget what lay behind the founding of the UN, over 80 years ago: the realisation that doing nothing had led to the darkest chapters in human history. We now live in a different time. New generations have arisen. And we face new challenges. But when we look at the world today, we see  similar challenges as which preceded the founding of the UN.

We see that the international legal order is under pressure in more and more places, even though it is the very foundation of our freedom and prosperity. We see the unending human suffering in Gaza, Sudan and so many other places in the world. We see violations of international law and of human rights, which are in stark contrast to the UN’s aims. And we see institutions being undermined. Institutions that were established to protect people and populations. We must not be naive about the causes. These constant threats and attempts to dismantle the legal order are fuelled by people and groups with their own agenda. One that runs counter to the interests of everyone else. Yes: everyone. Even those who don’t feel directly threatened, because they think it doesn’t affect them. Sooner or later, everyone is affected. As we saw in the time before the UN.

When major powers choose to pursue only their own interests, it is tempting to respond defensively. But as Mahatma Gandhi taught us, ‘An eye for eye will only make the whole world blind.’ And so, it is time for us, the global community, to choose to pursue the common interest. Not by trying to build an entirely new world order. But simply by working together. The middle powers must take the lead in fostering such international cooperation. And everyone must be able to participate, including those countries who are currently too often left on the sidelines.

It is time that countries in Africa, Asia and Latin America had a fully-fledged place. Not only on the Equal Earth Map, but in the real world too. To start with, here in the UN, with improved African representation in the Security Council at the very least. Because if we want to preserve the UN for the future, we must change the balance of power in line with the changing times, and modernise our institutions. This means that we must focus on core tasks and stable financing, but also that we must work to protect the multilateral order with all our strength. Because international law either works for everyone, or for no one.

Take the attempts we’ve seen to undermine the International Criminal Court- which is based in my country, in my city. This undermines the international legal order as a whole. And that affects us all. This court was established to protect us against impunity. This court was built on the foundations of the Nuremberg and Tokyo Trials. In the words of the Nuremberg chief prosecutor, Robert H. Jackson, ‘one of the greatest tributes that power has ever paid to reason.’

Now, with the ICC under attack, the writing is truly on the wall. After all, how can you possibly be opposed to prosecuting the very worst crimes? I believe there can be only one response. To say: hands off the ICC, and all those other institutions that protect the international legal order.

Because the reality is that we still need to fight impunity. Not least through the Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression against Ukraine, which the Netherlands has offered to host in The Hague. Let me be absolutely clear: we cannot accept impunity.

In this fight, Ukraine has no choice but to defend itself. But Russia makes a choice every day to wage war. Russia must be held to account for its flagrant violations of the UN Charter. For the immeasurable suffering inflicted on so many victims and families in this senseless war.

Since the downing of flight MH17, the Netherlands has come to understand this only too well. Many others understand it too, with Russia threatening global food security, and millions of people experiencing the consequences.

History teaches us that the only way to resolve conflicts, is through justice. That was the idea underpinning the establishment, 80 years ago, of the International Court of Justice, the principle judicial organ of the United Nations. And it’s a conviction that is widely shared, as illustrated by the fact that more and more countries are finding their way to the ICJ.

So let us all continue to stand up for what we have built, and strengthen it further as we go forward.

Cooperation is the cornerstone of our history. And cooperation is what the world expects of us, now and in the future. Take the question of how we handle AI. We face a choice: do we let a small group of companies and countries take all the decisions, while the rest of us simply look on? Or do we decide, together – within the logical setting of the UN – what our future should look like.

It is also time for us to press forward together and tackle that other great challenge of our age: climate change. Nowhere on earth is the planet warming faster than in Western Europe. But in the Caribbean part of our Kingdom – including the countries of Aruba, Curaçao and St. Maarten – the effects of climate change have already been felt for much longer. And the same is true of many of your countries, as well. For too long, the consequences of climate change have been trivialised or simply denied. But after the horrors experienced by Nepal, and a long series of forest fires, the truth should be clear to everyone: the climate crisis will not just disappear if we pretend it doesn’t exist. We are living on borrowed time. And the generations that come after us will pay the price. If we want to prevent that, we must commit now to both mitigation and adaptation. We all know what needs to be done. Countless reports are agreed on that. We have all the technology we need. And fortunately, we are making progress.

Last year the electric vehicle market grew by 20 per cent. Wind power capacity grew by 14 per cent, and solar power by more than 30 per cent. This growth in renewable energy has exceeded even the most optimistic projections from 10 years ago. The challenge now is to accelerate this transition in all sectors and all parts of the world. And, at the same time, to reduce carbon emissions and phase out fossil fuels.

That is why the Netherlands and Colombia jointly organised the world’s first conference on ‘Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels’. This event in Colombia was attended by 57 countries. Together, these countries account for one-third of global GDP, one-third of energy demand and one-fifth of supply. And together, we worked to find concrete, practical solutions to take the transition forward.

But climate action requires everyone to contribute. In November we will gather at the COP in Türkiye. And I know that many of you don’t have high expectations. In my view, this can only be explained by the pessimistic idea that we are somehow powerless. But that is not true. We have the knowledge and technology to combat climate change. A better world really is within reach. Thanks to our joint efforts on the Sustainable Development Goals, 92 per cent of the world’s population now has access to electricity. Since 2015, we have doubled the amount of renewable energy we generate. And child mortality has dropped sharply, too. Climate action can be a catalyst for everyone to work together on solutions that concern us all.

We don’t need to reinvent the wheel. A lot of good things are happening already. For decades, the Netherlands has been working with partners around the world to develop climate-smart agriculture and future-proof water-management solutions. We are keen to share our knowledge and know-how, and we want to learn from what other countries are doing. There are so many great initiatives under way. But I also know there is much more to be done. The need to accelerate and scale-up our efforts is only too clear. And that demands our common commitment. The Netherlands wants to build practical partnerships with other countries. So we are once again making funding available for this purpose.

At the same time, we need to adapt to climate shocks that can no longer be avoided. And these adaptations will require major investment – both public and private. Because here too: we cannot do it alone. Today I call on all countries to stick to these ambitions. Because one way or another, a climate transition is coming. But we can decide how it will unfold. It can be chaotic, or it can be carefully planned – with an inclusive approach and economic benefits for all.

As I come to the end of my remarks, I have an even stronger sense of what Anne Frank was telling us. Because what she wrote is true: we have everything we need to change the world for the better and we don’t have to wait another minute. We aren’t starting from scratch. We’ve already come a long way. And the journey will continue, under the leadership of a new Secretary-General.

Secretary-General Guterres, thank you for all your years of hard work. You are leaving the UN at a turbulent time. But we can all take pride in the fact that, as we speak, more than 150 thousand men and women are serving under the blue flag. Giving vaccinations, providing food aid and serving in peace missions. Even in these difficult times, when darkness seems to be descending in many places on the high ideals of the UN.

But the light has not gone out. The torch of peace and justice still flickers and guides us. Just as it did in my country, more than 80 years ago.

Liberation from the tyranny of unbridled nationalism, racism and fascism came too late for Anne Frank. In my country, when it did finally come, it was brought by American, Canadian, British, Polish and other Allied soldiers, many of them not much older than Anne. Among their many resting places, far from their homes, is an American cemetery in Margraten, in the south of the Netherlands. A wall stands watch over their graves. And on it is inscribed a simple epitaph: 'To you from failing hands we throw the torch. Be yours to hold it high.'

Let us pledge, as a new generation, to always hold it high.

Thank you.

I am here with one message: We, who honor the UN Charter, must stand ready to make some tough calls.

Reform is necessary.

Not because the United Nations has failed.

But because it matters.

Today, our United Nations finds itself in a triple crisis.

It is a normative crisis, a financial crisis, and an institutional crisis.

Firstly, a normative crisis.

The fundamental rules that protect the integrity of sovereign states and prohibit the use of force, except in self defense, are threatened.

The number of ongoing wars is alarmingly high.

Most dramatically, the number of wars between states is the highest since the United Nations was established. Yet, this was the key motive for establishing this organisation in the first place: to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war.

International law is not charity to the weak. It is a common  investment in a system that reduces risk, friction, and costs for everyone, including the great powers.

Take freedom of navigation as an example. This long-standing principle, enshrined in our Convention on the Law of the Sea, benefits every state.

The Strait of Hormuz shows why: its closure raises energy prices, disrupts global supply lines and curbs growth far beyond the region itself —from petrol pumps in Minneapolis to Oslo, from Cape Town to Mumbai.

International law is not a menu you can choose from at will. It must be upheld universally. When we condemn Russia’s clear violation of international law in Ukraine, it is equally important to speak out against Israel’s violations of the same rules in Palestine. International law is only relevant if it is enforced.

There is no alternative to the two-state solution. At this GA, there has been a record number of Palestine-related meetings. The support for a Palestinian state has never been stronger, yet the situation on the ground is more dire than ever. We must act now with moral clarity, and ensure that the coming year becomes a year of implementation.

My message is this: Only if we apply international law to all people, in all places, and at all times, can we claim that these are universal rules.

Double standards quickly translate into no standards at all.

Secondly, the UN is in a financial crisis.

Major contributors are withholding or delaying payments.

Wars and security concerns diverts resources away from the fulfilment of our sustainable development goals.

And when resources are available, they too often come with strict earmarking.

We, the donors, should earmark less and allow more flexible use of resources.

Norway remains one of the UN’s ten largest donors.

We will use our funding to support and promote reform. Because we believe in investing in the UN.

We believe that active, constructive, implementation of the UN80 reforms is necessary for its future. This will be a key factor when we assess future voluntary contributions to agencies, funds and programs.

Thirdly, the UN is in an institutional crisis,

I am a strong believer in this organisation.

But I also recognise that over time, we have added excessive complexity to our United Nations. Too often, when we identify a new challenge or a new idea, we create a new agency, a new convention, a fund or a program to address it. Which then comes with secretariats, staff, resources and bureaucracies.

And on the ground, an average developing country hosts no less than 23 different UN organisations.

In the most vulnerable states, the number is even higher.

We also have ten human rights treaty bodies and eleven secretariats for global environmental treaties.

I pay tribute to the dedicated and serious staff that is representing us all out there in at times very difficult places,

But those who care about the UN must ask, Are we improving delivery, or just creating more fragmentation and duplication?

The United Nations derives its legitimacy from the sovereign equality of states. Yet many member states are struggling to keep pace and participate.

We must simplify. We must focus. We must improve our capacity to deliver as one and create more impact on the ground.

We, the member states, must give guidance to the Secretary-General in succeeding with the ongoing reform endeavour. At times, this might require a solid dose of tough love.

The cost of war affects us all.

Grain and fertiliser supplies, disrupted by Russia’s war against Ukraine, undermine food security, far beyond Europe’s shores.

Russia’s war against Ukraine and the conflict in the Strait of Hormuz teach us the same lesson: when might succeeds over right, we all pay the price.

Often, the consequences of war also come home to haunt the aggressor.

What was described by President Putin as a «special military operation», that would be over in days or maybe weeks, is now well into its fifth year. Likewise, there is no end in sight to the war in the Gulf.

Both wars remind us about the limitations of military power.

Military action is never the goal in itself. Clausewitz described war as the continuation of politics by other means.

If the war’s political goals cannot be achieved, war just becomes unnecessary death, destruction and loss. And, frankly, demonstrations of weakness.

The limited success of these and other ongoing wars   is in itself a strong argument for prevention, mediation, and peacebuidling. Diplomacy can work. If we allow it to.

We saw a good example of this this very week.

The agreement between our neighbour Denmark, Greenland and the United States serves as an example of how diplomacy can lead to a lasting solution that respects the interests of all parties while fully respecting their sovereign rights.

Colleagues,

We need to continue our quest to ensure that there can be no impunity for committing the most grave international crimes.

The International Criminal Court is one of the most important expressions of this noble quest. Together with so many likeminded countries, we will strengthen our resolve to defend and further develop the ICC.

Norway resoundingly rejects the calls for dismantling the International Criminal Court.

The triple crisis I have set out here  is no less than an existential crisis for the United Nations.

Yet, thankfully, to counter this, we have concrete proposals for reform on the table, the UN80 initiative.

The UN80 initiative is a test of our ability to build a stronger, more robust UN.

Norway supports the level of ambition the Secretary-General has set out for us. We support the proposals across all workstreams, including structural changes.

The UN80 process has already produced successes.

The Mandate Resolution laid the foundation for better joint decisions. We all agree that we must rationalize mandates, streamline reporting, and organize our work to allow for broad, effective participation.

Norway is proud to play our role in this process.

But we also need structural change. We need to deliver as one.

Some UN organisations overlap. They should be merged in order to serve our common interest. Unfortunately, too often Member States show vested interest, engage in turf battles, and are fearful of change.

Let me be clear: Reform will not succeed if we keep protecting the status quo.

Let us remind ourselves that we, the member states, are the owners of this organisation. Not the secreariat. With that comes responsibility.

The UN80 process needs to continue under the next Secretary-General.

We need to see this initiative succeed.

For an organisation of 193 states to function, we need a strong, independent Secretary-General that firmly advocates the principles of the UN Charter, with integrity and authority.

In a time of geopolitical tension, the Secretary General’s «Good offices» function becomes more important than ever before.

The next Secretary-General will face the formidable task of helping us lead the UN out of its current crises.

We need someone bold and transformative.

She must be able to build trust, to implement our decisions, lead meaningful reform, and improve effectiveness.

A true reform of this organisation must also address the composition and functioning of the Security Council. That is the common call of the majority in this room. The absence of Africa among the permanent seats in the Council is but one striking example.

Whilst striving to improve legitimacy, we must ensure that we do not reduce efficiency. We need a Security Council that is open, transparent and accountable in its deliberations. A Security Council that is both legitimate and effective, measured in its ability to actually take meaningful action.

There is no lack of challenges to be tackled:

While wars and geopolitical tensions dominate the agenda, we must not lose sight of our most important shared responsibility: to take better care of the planet on which we all depend.

Climate change, biodiversity loss and rampant pollution threatens life, property and prosperity everywhere.

The catastrophic floods that struck the Himalayas last month is yet another stark reminder of the growing risks associated with a changing climate.

The good news is that reducing emissions, and ensuring a more responsible management of the world’s natural resources is possible.

We already have the insights and technologies to make this transition possible. And they are increasingly competitive from an economic perspective, as seen by the fast falling cost of renewable energy.

But we can only succeed if we cooperate. We can not put fences around our own climate, biosphere, or deal with the ills of our oceans on our own.

We live in the era of artificial intelligence. As Secretary-General Guterres phrased it in his speech:

“We must control AI before it controls us”. I agree.

Colleagues, we should not panic.

But we must be determined.

There is nothing inevitable in this development. Artificial Intelligence is developed by humans and must remain under human direction, oversight and control.

It is becoming an integral part of our infrastructure. A part of almost all aspects of society and economy.

And as we have done so many times before, we must maximise the positive benefits of emerging technologies while curbing its darker potentials.

This week, Finland and Norway are appealing to businesses, governments and the UN alike to cooperate for responsible management of the opportunities and risks of AI.

Defence of essential human values goes beyond regulating technology.

For decades, we saw a growth in democratic governance, respect for rule of law and for human rights.

Sadly, this trend has now turned. Democratic backsliding, polarisation and weakening of our democratic shields challenges past achievements. Increasing economic inequality in countries exacerbates this trend.

We should take democratic backsliding very seriously. While these may seem to be domestic concerns, we know that the way states behave internationally reflects on their domestic politics. Authoritarian and exclusivist sentiments within

member states would therefore also affect our capacity to address our shared concerns.

The United Nations is one of humanity's greatest achievements.

Not because it created a perfect world.

It did not.

But because it helped spare us from a far worse fate.

For eighty years it has provided a space where nations can negotiate instead of fight, cooperate instead of confront, and build rules instead of yielding to raw power.

The world we know today is safer, more prosperous and more just because the United Nations exists.

The founders of the United Nations had witnessed two world wars and a global economic collapse.

They knew something we must never forget:

When law gives way to force, everyone loses.

When cooperation collapses, everyone pays.

When institutions fail, chaos follows.

They did not build the United Nations because they believed mankind was perfect.

They built it because they understood mankind is not.

They built it because they knew that without rules, without dialogue, without cooperation, history has a habit of repeating its darkest chapters.

That responsibility is now ours. Not only the Secretary-Generals.

Ours.

The United Nations belongs to the Member States.

We decide whether it succeeds or fails.

We decide whether reform advances or stalls.

The time for reports has passed.

The time for action is now.

It’s our turn to face the monsters of our time.

(END)

Mr. President,

Mr. Secretary-General,

Distinguished delegates,

Ladies and gentlemen,

I come before you from Nepal - a distant country in the Himalayas - carrying a close warning for humanity.

I wish I could stand here today simply to speak about development, democracy, peace and the hopes of a young nation.

Instead, I must speak about death and destruction of epic proportions.

About families waiting for loved ones who will never come home.

About communities searching through mud, rocks and water for people whose bodies may never be recovered.

About bridges, roads, schools, homes and livelihoods swept away in minutes.

And about a country whose steady progress to achieve Sustainable Development Goals has been interrupted.

====

Four weeks ago, the world saw the shocking images of the catastrophic flash floods that swept through Nepal’s mountain communities with ferocity many have called a “Himalayan Tsunami.”

The Bhotekoshi-Trishuli disaster was not just a local tragedy, it was a warning to the world.

And I ask you today: have we really heard that warning?

Nearly three years ago, standing in the shadow of our Mount Everest, the Secretary-General of the United Nations warned humanity about the madness of an impending climate disaster.

That cry from the rooftop of the world was not heard loudly enough.

We in Nepal heard it. Our communities heard it.

Scientists around the world heard it. They repeated it with evidence.

But we, the political leaders of the world, have been negligent to translate those warnings into action at the speed and scale that vulnerable people require.

Last month, we saw the tragic consequences.

A warming climate is destabilizing the fragile Himalayan ecology.

Melting permafrost are fracturing mountain slopes beneath the glaciers and accelerating the risks of ice-rock avalanche, floods, landslides and other cascading hazards.

The resulting devastation unleashed havoc on both sides of the Nepal-China border. The flood continued downstream towards India.

This tells us something fundamental:

Climate change does not recognize borders.

Glaciers and floods do not travel with a visa stamped on passports.

I am not here to complain but to share some suggestions.

First, I wish to express Nepal's deep gratitude to all those who came to our aid in the aftermath of the deluge.

Our immediate neighbors, India and China, offered prompt and generous assistance.

Other friendly countries, the United Nations system, humanitarian agencies, philanthropies and people around the world stood with Nepal.

To all of them, I say: thank you on behalf of the grateful people of Nepal.

Nepal now faces a massive task of recovery and reconstruction.

After at least 1400 confirmed deaths and over 6,000 people still missing, our rapid assessments peg physical recovery needs at about 10 percent of GDP.

As in rebuilding after past disasters like the 2015 Gorkha earthquake, we count on your solidarity and support.

But we must also understand why this disaster matters beyond Nepal.

Nepal contributes less than 0.1 percent of global greenhouse-gas emissions.

We did not create this crisis. Yet we are paying a colossal price for it.

Our glaciers are retreating. Our mountain slopes are becoming unstable. Our rivers are becoming less predictable.

And every major disaster threatens to erase years of development.

For Nepal, climate catastrophe is not just a humanitarian event, but a development emergency.

It destroys roads, bridges, schools, homes, farms and livelihoods.

It destroys clean energy infrastructure that we need to fuel our future.

And it forces a poor country to borrow money to repair damage it did not cause.

But we are not here to blame any country or continent.

We are not here to turn climate change into another geopolitical battlefield.

We are here to ask everyone to recommit to shared responsibility and solidarity.

Through the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, the international community has already agreed to the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities.

Those who have historically contributed more to the problem, and those with greater capacity to respond, must do more.

Climate Justice cannot just remain a beautiful phrase in a United Nations Document.

People of our country be allowed to build their future instead of constantly rebuilding their past.

The Hindu Kush Himalaya is home to nearly two billion people. These mountains provide water, ecosystems, agriculture and livelihoods to populations far beyond Nepal.

The Himalayas are not peripheral to the planet. They are part of the planet's life-support system.

That is why, as an urgent first step, we propose that we establish a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism, led by Nepal, India and China.

Through this mechanism, let us share satellite data and expertise.

Let us monitor dangerous glacial lakes.

Let us strengthen joint early-warning systems.

And when disaster strikes, let us coordinate assistance across borders.

Let the Himalayas become a laboratory of international cooperation, rather than a frontier of fragmented information.

Remarkable for a least developed country, Nepal is already playing a global role exceeding its ecological share.

We have restored forests to cover nearly half our territory.

We are installing hydro power at a pace enough to power all our clean energy needs and displace dirty sources abroad.

We are promoting electric mobility with an adoption rate to match parts of Europe.

We are strengthening climate adaptation at the local level. And we shall do more to withstand increased intensity and frequency of climate disasters.

But, Nepal cannot build resilience alone against a crisis made worse by the failure of global governance.

That is why this Assembly must note six words:

Relief. Rehabilitation. Reconstruction.

And also:

Responsibility. Reparation. Resilience.

The first three are what we need after disaster.

The second three are what we need to ensure that disaster does not become a permanent condition.

When a climate-driven disaster destroys the infrastructure of a poor country, the answer cannot simply be another mega loan or a patchwork of small grants.

We need adequate grant-based support from the world. The Loss and Damage Fund, the Global Environment Facility and other relevant financing mechanisms remain grossly inadequate.

Climate finance must not become a bureaucratic maze through which vulnerable countries spend years proving that they need help.

When the house is burning, we do not ask the family to complete fifty forms.

We act.

That is what climate justice must mean.

This brings me to a larger question:

What kind of international order do we want?

The United Nations was born from humanity's experience of horrific World Wars.

Its promise was that sovereignty would matter.

International law would matter.

The dignity of every human being would matter.

And the weak would not simply have to accept whatever the powerful decide.

Today, that international system is under strain.

Too often, military and economic power determines whose voice is heard.

Nepal believes we need a much fairer global economic order.

In 1994, UNDP’s Human Development Report conceptualized the notion of human insecurity.

It equated security with people rather than territories, and with development rather than arms. It called for the peace dividend to secure freedoms from fear and want.

The new majority government in Nepal, elected through the fairest and most peaceful elections in our history this March, has had to weather many international adversities since.

When a poor farmer in Nepal went to sow her seeds this monsoon, fertilizers didn’t reach her on time. When we wanted to pave a new highway, there was no bitumen. When a family sat down for an evening meal, there was shortage of cooking fuel.

On the one hand, there are melting glaciers and failing harvests to floods arriving without warning. On the other, a global supply chain punishes poor people for causes beyond reason.

Inter-continental missiles arrive on time. Rifles and ammunition cross borders, clear every bottleneck, meet each deadline. But a peasant in Nepal cannot procure his fertilizer or fuel at market price at a time of need.

We have built a world with flawless logistics for war and broken logistics for food.

And this is not Nepal's private misfortune. Ask Bangladesh. Ask Bhutan. Ask India. Ask the Maldives. Ask Pakistan. Ask Sri Lanka.  Ask any other country in our region and you will hear the same account: hit by the climate we did not warm, and hit again by the wars we did not start.

This tells us there is a lot more broken than meets the eye in the present order of global cooperation.

I am told I am the youngest Head of Government to address this Assembly this year.

I did not come here to make that the story.

I came to make sure that whatever else is said from this podium, one thing is said plainly: a country that is willing to pay should be able to buy, and a world that can deliver a weapon anywhere in seventy-two hours has no excuse for leaving a farmer without means for a decent livelihood.

This is why we continue to believe in multilateralism. This is why we need a United Nations in which the presence of small poor countries is felt, and we can work together towards just outcomes.

Climate justice is, therefore, not only about money.

It is about distributive justice - who bears the costs.

It is about procedural justice - who has a voice.

It is about whether the future of mountain communities, small island states, landlocked and least-developed countries, and generations yet unborn count equally.

Starting tomorrow at the “Sagarmatha to the Sea” side-event right here at the United Nations, Nepal is ready to help lead this conversation.

Mr. President & Excellencies,

We are at this General Assembly at a moment of profound global uncertainty — and with a renewed democratic mandate that reflects the aspirations of a new generation.

Our youth have demanded a politics of integrity and accountability.

This  generational  shift  is  not  only  a  national  story.  It  is  part  of  a  global awakening against conflicts, inequities, and lack of opportunities.

The commitment of my government  is clear: to build a state that delivers  — decent jobs, social protection, and a fair chance for every Nepali to thrive at home.

The  Nepal  floods  signal  a  future  shaped  by  rising  climate  extremes.  Our baselines are no longer relevant. And we must move from ad-hoc responses to a culture of preparedness.

Let us finance resilience, and invest in insurance and innovation.

Let us build stronger infrastructure and institutions.

Let us reduce fossil-fuel dependence.

Let us build systems that warn, alert and save lives.

Let us reform the order that leaves the weakest with the least power.

And when the next warning comes from the rooftop of the world:

Let us be ready to hear it, and ready to act.

Distinguished Delegates,

Ekamawir Omo. I bring you warm greetings from my people and my country.

We  meet  under  the  theme,  “Restoring  trust,  managing  transformation:  a  United  Nations  that

delivers for all.” For my country, that means ensuring no nation — regardless of size or distance

— is left behind as the world changes around us.

Let me begin by congratulating you on your election to preside over this eighty-first session. My

delegation assures you of our full support, and we thank your predecessor for the stewardship of

the eightieth session.

We also pay tribute to Secretary-General António Guterres. This is the last General Debate of his

tenure, and my country records its gratitude for a decade in which the smallest States were heard

more often than before.

I  have  travelled  far  to  speak  on  matters  that  may  seem  distinct,  but  are  united  by  a  single,

fundamental principle: the right of every people to be treated as an equal, and to speak for itself.

NAOERO NAME RESTORED

There are moments in the life of a nation when its people are called to remember who they have

always been. This is such a moment for us. And so I begin with something deeply personal to my

people and my country: our name.

For many years, the world has known our country as Nauru. Nauru is how our name sounded to

those who found it hard to say, and the world kept it. But it is not the name our people used among

themselves.

I rise on my first point not to announce a change, but to affirm a truth. Long before our country

took  its  place  among  the  family  of  nations—long  before  our  name  appeared  on  international

records—our people knew our homeland by one name: Naoero.

That name carries the memory of our ancestors, our language, and our identity. It has been there

all along. Never lost, never absent. Today, we restore Naoero.

We do not make this choice to erase our past. We make it because we honor it. We do so with

respect for our history, and with gratitude for the journey “Nauru” has carried us through to our

independence and our place on the international stage.

My  Government’s  priority  is  investing  in  our  people  and  our  future  generations.  Restoring  our

name gives back to them a piece of their inheritance. Because the identity handed down by our

own ancestors has a place in the community of nations. Because their history and language matter.

Because they too have the right to inherit a nation that knows itself, names itself, and speaks for

itself.

In light of this year's theme, let me say this: there can be no genuine trust and no true transformation

without respect for the identity, history, language, and right of every people to be treated as an

equal, and to speak for itself.

I take the opportunity now to convey my sincerest gratitude to the Secretariat, this Assembly, and

the many institutions and partners who have taken steps to recognise our restored name. It may

seem a small courtesy but it meant a great deal at home.

And so Mr President,

I say this with the greatest pride: Anga dei-Naoero (which means ‘I am from Naoero’). And so is

every person I have the honor to speak for today.

We take our seat under that name proud of where we have come from. Confident in who we are.

And determined to carry our name into the future.

What I ask of the world costs nothing. Join us in recognizing and respecting the identity that is

already ours.

Say our name. Naoero.

DEEP SEABED

Naoero is an ocean State. We are not merely guardians of the ocean, but rightful participants in its

future. For Naoero, the ocean represents both opportunity and responsibility. Never one without

the other. Both are essential, or the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea is left hollow.

Today,  I  focus  on  a  part  of  it  that  belongs  to  no  one—the  deep  seabed  area  beyond  national

jurisdiction.

The Convention established the International Seabed Authority and charged it with a clear legal

obligation to put in place regulations and regulate activities in parallel with sponsoring States. Its

role  is  not  to  determine  whether  deep  seabed  mining  is,  as  a  matter  of  public  policy,  a  correct

course of action.

Naoero joined trusting in the commitments set out in the Convention and the 1994 Agreement. For

fifteen years, Naoero has invested critical resources in sponsoring the exploration of a portion of

the  deep  seabed.  Our  sponsored  entity,  Nauru  Ocean  Resources  Inc,  has  contributed  about  one

petabyte of data — more than one-third of all Clarion-Clipperton Zone data held in the Authority’s

DeepData.

We  called  on  the  Authority  to  seek  an  Advisory  Opinion  on  the  responsibilities  of  sponsoring

States, and we followed it. We established a national regulator with the powers and due diligence

obligations that opinion requires.

At  every  stage,  our  decisions  have  rested  on  the  best  available  scientific  evidence,  on  the

Convention,  and  on  that  Opinion.  At  every  stage,  we  have  called  for  the  Mining  Code  to  be

finished. And when progress stalled, we looked to the 1994 Agreement and invoked the two-year

rule. We were told we were rushing. That was five years ago, and the rules remain unwritten.

We  are  participating  in  the  first  contentious  proceedings  before  the  Seabed  Disputes  Chamber,

because our obligations as a sponsoring State require legal clarity.

For fifteen years we have done everything a member State can do consistent with our obligations

as a sponsoring State. And we continue to wait.

There  is  a  general  understanding  within  the  Authority’s  Council  that  “nothing  is  agreed  until

everything is agreed”. And that the regulations will be adopted by consensus. Achieving that is a

great challenge for an institution whose members remain deeply divided on whether deep seabed

mining should proceed at all. A question the Convention never asked the Authority to decide.

Naoero welcomes every effort to ensure that seabed mineral development proceeds responsibly.

And I ask this Assembly to reckon with this: a principle declared in 1970, and a bargain struck in

1994 — both in this hall — still wait for the rules that would give them effect.

When a multilateral process cannot deliver, the world does not stand still. Those with the means

to act will not wait. And every year of delay makes that more likely, not less.

That is why the theme of this session matters. A multilateral system that cannot deliver for a State

like mine does not deliver for all. That holds here in this Assembly, and in any institution we build.

Naoero therefore calls upon the Authority to let the waiting end. Adopt the rules.

ECONOMIC STABILITY

My Government’s central purpose is to put Naoero on its own feet.

That work is under way. Our Trust Fund, to which we contribute more than ten per cent of our

revenue every single year, so that Naoero has something to stand on when these arrangements end.

Our fisheries. The seabed. Joining the Egmont Group. New revenue through our investment and

residence programmes. A virtual asset regulator built with full due diligence obligations before the

industry  it  regulates.  Our  valuable  partnerships.  And  behind  all  of  it,  investment  in  health,

education and sport, so that our people are not only better off but healthier and better prepared.

We  are  building  an  economy  that  does  not  depend  on  any  single  arrangement.  And  by  every

measure of fiscal discipline, we have done what was asked of us.

Yet the measure by which we are assessed sees none of it. It sees income, and nothing else. It does

not capture the full story of my nation: the true cost of our geographic isolation, the fragility of our

limited economic base, or the devastating impact a single disaster can have on our people and our

progress.

In  January  2027,  Naoero  will  be  considered  a  high-income  country  in  the  OECD  system.  That

reflects real progress. But progress should not be punished.

Because fifty-eight per cent of our revenue comes from bilateral arrangements that are not ours to

renew. Eighty-seven per cent of the food our people eat is purchased and imported. We have one

runway. One port. One road that connects everything we have.

None of that appears in how we are assessed.

That is why we strongly support the Multidimensional Vulnerability Index and the United Nations’

efforts to pilot the tool. Its full implementation is essential to ensuring that countries like ours are

fairly assessed and adequately supported. It recognises that vulnerability is complex, and it must

be seen, measured, and acted upon.

We  acknowledge  the  significant  progress  made  by  some  development  partners  and  financial

institutions in adopting vulnerability assessments and reviewing their eligibility criteria. The Asian

Development Bank (ADB) weighs vulnerability alongside income, and its own policy names my

nation as the clearest example of why income alone conceals what small island states face. As a

country that is ranked the fifth most vulnerable country in the world on the Index, and the most

vulnerable in the Pacific, we welcome these developments as positive steps.

But a gap remains. Not all have taken the necessary steps to truly recognise our realities. I therefore

urge all who have yet to do so, including the World Bank, to weigh vulnerability alongside income

in decisions on eligibility, as the ADB already does.

If the international community is truly serious about restoring trust and managing transformation,

it must demonstrate that commitment where it matters most: with those who are most vulnerable.

PARTNERSHIP

I turn to my final point. No country of our size stands alone. Naoero is a friend to all and an enemy

to none.

Naoero’s partnerships are not all of one kind. Some are born of kinship. Some of shared interests.

Some have been built through decades of cooperation. And some are grounded in the conviction

that when a wrong persists, it must be named and addressed.

Each  relationship  matters.  None  is  a  substitute  for  another.  And  none  comes  at  the  expense  of

another.

Small  States  are  increasingly  asked  to  choose.  Between  partners,  between  blocs,  between

competing  visions  of  the  world.  Naoero  will  not  be  made  to  choose.  We  will  work  with  every

partner who respects our sovereignty and our right to decide our own future. That is not neutrality.

It is independence.

Partnership does not mean agreement on everything. It means standing together where interests

align, and standing on principle where they do not.

A friend I speak for today has been waiting for justice. I am asking this Assembly to honour its

word, and I cannot  then fall silent when  that word  is broken for someone  else.  For  thirty-three

consecutive  years,  this  Assembly  has  called  for  an  end  to  the  embargo  against  Cuba.  Naoero

reiterates that call and we encourage dialogue grounded in full respect for sovereignty. Because

sovereign equality must be more than a principle written in the Charter.

Whatever  this  Assembly  intends  to  deliver,  it  will  be  delivered  through  partnership  and

cooperation, or not at all.

So let me extend an invitation to the members of this Assembly.

Invest  in  our  people.  Invest  in  an  economy  that  rests  on  more  than  a  handful  of  arrangements.

Invest in institutions that will outlast my Government and the next. Invest in the infrastructure,

connectivity and opportunities that distance has too often denied us.

What  Naoero  offers  this  Assembly  is  not  dependence,  but  participation.  Not  expectation,  but

contribution. Not a beneficiary, but a partner.

Invest with us, not simply in us.

Everything I have raised today concerns this Organization and what it has promised.

So does this:

The Security Council does not reflect the world as it is. It reflects the world as it was in 1945, when

most of the countries in this hall did not yet exist as sovereign States. Naoero therefore calls for

reform that expands both the permanent and non-permanent categories.

A body that speaks for all of us should look like all of us.

CONCLUSION

As I draw my statement to a close, the matters I have raised may appear separate. They are not.

Our name is about sovereignty. How we are measured is about justice. The deep seabed is about

opportunity and responsibility. Our partnerships are about standing as equals. One principle binds

them: the right of every people to be treated as an equal, and to speak for itself.

You  have  convened  this  Assembly  to  restore  trust,  manage  transformation,  and  deliver  for  all.

Trust  is  restored  when  promises  are  kept.  Transformation  is  managed  when  decisions  lead  to

action. And we deliver for all only when we deliver for the small.

Everything Naoero has asked for today was agreed in this hall long before I took this floor. I am

not asking this Assembly to be braver than it has ever been. I am challenging you to be as good as

your word.

Say our name.

Let the waiting end.

Let vulnerability be measured honestly.

Treat us as partners.

May God bless the Republic of Naoero, and may God bless the United Nations.

Mwa tubwa kor. I thank you.

speaker_post: Permanent Representative to the United Nations
text:
New Zealand Permanent Mission to the United Nations Te Aka Aorere

United Nations General Debate of the Eighty-First Session

New Zealand Statement delivered by Permanent Representative, H.E. Ms Victoria Hallum

Monday 28 September 2026

Over the past week, we have listened to leaders, ministers and representatives from every region of the world.

They have spoken of different priorities and  concerns. Yet they have  also  revealed  how  much  we  have  in  common. We  have been  reminded  that  the  biggest  challenges  we  face  do  not respect  national  borders. And  no  country,  however  large  or powerful, can address them alone.

It is clear we live in a more contested, fragmented and volatile world.

The number of active conflicts in the world has almost doubled in the past 20 years. The number of conflict-related deaths has reached levels not seen in decades.

Fundamental norms governing state behaviour are being violated with increasing impunity, contravening the UN Charter and other universally applicable rules of international law.

Core human rights that protect the well-being and dignity of our citizens are increasingly being ignored.

Humanitarian needs are growing faster than our collective ability to meet them.

After  decades  of  progress,  hard-won  development  gains  have slowed, and it is clear we will fail to meet most of the Sustainable Development Goals by their 2030 target.

Biodiversity  loss  and  pollution  are  impacting  key  natural resources in our oceans.

Natural  disasters  and  the  growing  impacts  of  our  changing climate  are  becoming  more  severe  and  more  visible.  In  our region,  these  pressures  are  already  affecting  lives,  livelihoods and long-term development prospects.

All of this is of grave concern to New Zealand, whose sovereignty, security  and  prosperity  depends  on  a  functioning,  inclusive multilateral  system,  grounded  in  agreed  rules  and  norms  with the UN Charter at its centre.

We regard the UN Charter – with its core principles of sovereign equality of states, territorial integrity, the prohibition of the use of force, and respect for human rights - as irreplaceable.

We  continue  therefore  to  invest  in  the  United  Nations,  and agreed  international  rules,  as  an  exercise  of  our  sovereignty, because we believe it is essential to our interests, and indeed the interests of all. In the face of rising volatility, we need the UN’s stabilising influence, and global solutions, more than ever.

Over recent years, New Zealand has spoken of the importance of  leadership.  New  Zealand  thanks  Secretary-General  Antonio Guterres for his service over the past ten years.

We  thank  you  for  your  visits  to  the  Blue  Pacific,  and  for  your attention to the unique situation of Pacific Islands countries and other Small Island Developing States.

We thank you also for starting the process of essential reform to put  this  vital  organisation  on  a  stronger  and  more  sustainable footing to deal with the challenges of the next 80 years.

Your assignment has not been easy.

As we prepare to appoint the next Secretary-General to lead the UN into the next phase, we should be clear about what this moment requires.

First and foremost, we call on the new Secretary-General to  be  a  courageous  guardian  of  the  UN  Charter  and  to assert the UN’s vital role on peace and security.

The United Nations was created to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war.

It  is  ultimately  the  responsibility  of  Member  States  to  prevent and resolve conflicts. We cannot outsource that responsibility.

But  we  need  a  Secretary-General  who  is  active  in  conflict prevention, mediation and peace-making.

The Secretary-General should never have to seek permission or forgiveness for acting to prevent or resolve conflict.

As  a  custodian  of  the  UN  Charter,  you  have  the  right  and  the obligation to speak up when its core norms are breached.

We expect you to do so in an objective, impartial, and consistent manner. We will support you when you do.

So  we  ask  you  to  be  active  in  seeking  an  end  to  the  horrific conflict in Sudan.

You must be bold in pressing for a sustainable and just end to Russia’s  illegal  invasion  of  Ukraine.  One  that  is  consistent  with Ukraine’s  sovereignty  and  territorial  integrity  and  the  core principles of the Charter.

You must be determined in your efforts to help alleviate the dire humanitarian  situation  in  Gaza.  We  ask  that  you  use  your influence  to  progress  a  fragile  ceasefire  into  a  sustainable, durable peace.

And you must be resolute in preserving conditions for a two-state solution. You must take the initiative, despite the challenges and entrenched views, to achieve a just and lasting resolution, where Israel  and  Palestine  can  live  side-by-side  within  secure  and clearly defined borders.

We urge you to use your good offices to secure a lasting end to hostilities in the Persian Gulf and restore freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, which is a right guaranteed under international law.

Of course, you cannot do this alone. For our part we, as Member States,  must  provide  you  with  the  tools,  the  resources,  and above  all  the  political  support  to  ensure  you  can  play  this  role effectively.

Parties to conflicts must  engage with you constructively and in good  faith;  while  global  and  regional  partners  with  influence must provide the necessary incentives for the parties to do so.

The  UN  Security  Council  needs  to  fulfil  its  responsibilities. Permanent  members,  in  particular,  must  act  in  a  manner consistent with their special responsibilities under the Charter.

Too  frequently  has  the  veto,  or  the  threat  of  the  veto,  been abused to block the Council from fulfilling its responsibilities, to the frustration, and sometimes despair, of the global community. Inevitably, the costs of this failure are borne by those caught in conflict.

This Assembly also has a legitimate and necessary role to play in maintaining  peace  and  security,  and  we  have  been  pleased  to see it step up on occasions when the Security Council has been stymied from acting.

For  our  part,  New  Zealand  will  continue  to  press  for  a  more effective,  credible,  transparent  and  representative  Security Council.  As  a  demonstration  of  our  continued  commitment  to collective security and the UN Charter, New Zealand is seeking a seat on the UN Security Council for 2039-40.

We ask the next Secretary-General to work with us to preserve the integrity of the global disarmament framework, particularly on  weapons  of  mass  destruction.  The  grave  dangers  of  the deterioration  of  the  global  nuclear  non-proliferation  regime should alarm us all.

New Zealand  was  deeply  disappointed  at  the  failure  to  reach consensus at this year’s Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty Review Conference.

After three consecutive Review Conference failures, we must all do what we can to preserve the health of the NPT and, indeed, strengthen it.

This  means  tackling  persistent  violations  and  cases  of  non-compliance. Iran is not in compliance with its nuclear safeguards obligations.  The  DPRK’s  nuclear  weapons  and  missile programmes continue to threaten its region and beyond.

Halting the NPT’s deterioration also requires concrete action from the Nuclear Weapons States to, at long last, chart a path towards total, verifiable, and irreversible nuclear disarmament.

We also call on you to safeguard the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, the “constitution for the oceans”, which provides the framework  within  which  all  activities  on  the  oceans  and  seas must  be  carried  out.    Compliance  with  these  universally applicable rules is essential, not only for maintaining peace and security,  but  also  for  protecting  prosperity  and  food  security, given the oceans' vital role in supporting trade.

Second, we call on the next Secretary-General to provide strong  leadership  across  the  UN’s  development  and human rights pillars.

The  authors  of  the  UN  Charter  understood  that  peace  and security cannot be sustained without creating the conditions for Member States to provide their citizens with prosperity and the full enjoyment of their human rights.

With significant changes in the global development cooperation landscape, we ask you to ensure the UN is clear about where its

comparative advantage lies, alongside the role of governments, regional organisations and International Financial Institutions.

Citizens  and  donors  expect  the  UN  to  operate  as  one,  with agencies  working  together,  through  a  strengthened  Resident Coordinator system. We will work with you to ensure the UN is more  coordinated  and  focused  on  strengthening  local  capacity and partnerships to address a country’s development needs.

The UN development system must remain relevant, responsive and accessible to all Member States based on need, rather than size, income level or location. We welcome progress in advancing the  UN’s  Multidimensional  Vulnerability  Index  and  want  to  see further  work  to  ensure  its  practical  application  across  the multilateral development system.

In  the  face  of  contracting  development  finance  flows  and increasing  debt  levels,  we  need  to  ensure  our  ambitions  are matched by more sustainable and predictable financing. This will inevitably  involve  moving  beyond  an  exclusive  reliance  on traditional sources and approaches.

As  Pacific  Islands  Forum  leaders  recently  reaffirmed  in  Palau, climate  change  remains  the  single  greatest  threat  to  the livelihoods, security and wellbeing of Pacific peoples.

While New Zealand will play its part, our efforts will mean little in  the  absence  of  determined  action  by  the  world’s  major emitters.

Rising  sea  levels  threaten  the  continued  viability  of  many communities  and  pose  a  threat  to  low-lying  island  states, including some of our Pacific neighbours.

The Political Declaration on Sea Level Rise, endorsed this week, is a demonstration of the UN’s ability to address contemporary challenges  affecting  its  members.  We  particularly  welcome  the Declaration’s  affirmation  of  the  preservation  of  maritime  zones and  the  presumption  of  continued  statehood,  notwithstanding sea-level rise.

to  defend We  also  expect international  humanitarian  law  and  international  human  rights law and its institutions.

the  new  Secretary-General

The promotion and protection of universal and indivisible human rights  is  fundamental  to  the  world  we  live  in  today  and  to  a collective  vision  of  our  future.  Societies  in  which  citizens  can enjoy  their  universal  human  rights  have  a  better  chance  of avoiding the descent into conflict that tragically impacts so many across the world today.

Over the past decade these norms have often been under threat, sometimes  through  neglect,  sometimes  through  deliberate  and sustained attacks.

The  rise  in  attacks  on  protected  individuals,  including  civilians and  humanitarian  and  medical  personnel,  needs  particular attention.

It is ten years since New Zealand co-led the adoption of Security Council Resolution 2286 on healthcare in armed conflict. Attacks on  medical  facilities  and  personnel  in  violation  of  international

humanitarian  law  have  grown  exponentially  worse  since  then. Few have been held accountable for these flagrant violations of international humanitarian law.

We ask you to help us reverse these trends, by drawing on the UN’s  unique  legitimacy  to  call  out  egregious  and  systematic violations of these norms, wherever they may occur and whoever may be perpetrating them, and by providing practical guidance and assistance to help Member States meet their obligations.

Third,  we  ask  the  new  Secretary-General  to  maintain momentum and ambition on UN reform.

Confidence  in  this  institution  depends  on  its  ability  to  deliver impact.  The  next  Secretary-General  must  work  with  Member States to chart an ambitious vision for the next phase of reform, while ensuring implementation of the decisions already taken.

At  a  time  of  multiple  and  overlapping  crises  and  growing constraints, we need a United Nations that is focused on its core tasks,  disciplined  and  accountable.  One  where  every  dollar delivers maximum impact.

One  that  measures  success  not  by  the  number  of  mandates  it creates  or  meetings  it  holds,  but  by  the  difference  it  makes  in people's lives.

Meeting this challenge means exercising your powers to achieve the most impact from the resources available.

It means demanding a culture of continuous improvement, one that focuses on effective implementation and results.

It  means  setting  the  highest  standards  for  performance  within the Secretariat and holding staff accountable for delivering.

In this regard, we ask you to demonstrate independence in your senior appointments. New Zealand has never accepted the right of any country to assert “ownership” of UN positions by virtue of its power and status.

We  encourage  all  Secretary-General  candidates  to  commit publicly to making senior appointments on the basis of merit.

Reform is a joint responsibility. We as Member States must avoid the trap of regarding reform as something that others will deliver for us and instead live up to our own responsibilities for building the organisation we need.

We cannot expect the UN to continue to lurch on, in a state of constant financial crisis. Member States must meet their financial obligations in full, on time, and without conditions, in accordance with their obligations under the Charter.

We need to focus our attention on the issues that really matter, and that can genuinely deliver benefits for our citizens.

Resolution  80/251  equips  Member  States  to  tackle  the  long-standing  challenge  of  mandate  accumulation  and  overload.    It commits us all to take a more disciplined approach to setting the Organisation's priorities. It provides the framework we need to create a more focused, coherent and impactful UN.

Yet  its  success  will  depend  on  whether  we  are  prepared  to act differently. If we aren’t prepared to make the necessary choices, we  will  be  left  with  an  ever-growing  set  of  responsibilities

supported  by  an  ever-shrinking  pool  of  resources.  That  will  do nothing  to  strengthen  confidence  in  the  UN's  relevance  or effectiveness.

Reform begins with us. It requires Member States to make the decisions that only Member States can make.

That is the only way we can truly achieve an organisation that is fit to meet the challenges that lie before us, and that our citizens need and expect.

Finally, we urge the next Secretary-General to ensure that the UN works for all states.

The  sovereign  equality  of  states  is  one  of  the  most  central principles  of  the  UN  Charter.  It  must  also  be  central  to  your approach.

The  fundamental  premise  of  the  United  Nations  is  that  every state,  regardless  of  its  size  or  circumstances,  has  a  stake  in shaping our shared future.

We also call on the President of the General Assembly to remain a steadfast champion of the voices, prerogatives, and interests of the entire UN membership across all pillars of its work.

The  next  Secretary-General's  leadership  in  these  areas will be essential. But we must also find it in ourselves to demonstrate leadership.

Ultimately, the health, relevance, and effectiveness of the United Nations  depends  primarily  on  its  members,  not  its  Secretary-General.  As  Member  States,  we  must  acknowledge  our  role  in

the  financial  and  legitimacy  crisis  facing  the  UN.  We  must  ask whether we have the collective will to change our behaviour?

Do we have the discipline to focus  our attention and resources on the issues that really matter to our citizens, and deliver impact in their lives? Do we have the honesty to admit what is working and what is not?

Do  we  have  the  will  to  invest  in  the  multilateral  system,  both politically and financially, to enable it to deliver results where we can truly make a difference?

Coupled with the courage to make bold and consequent decisions on UN reform that can deliver a more effective organisation?

Collective  action  has  changed  the  course  of  global  challenges before.

These achievements were not inevitable. They were the result of political  leadership,  persistence,  and  a  willingness  to  work together  despite  differences  to  build  understanding,  and compromise.

The  most  fundamental  step  we  can  all  take  to  revive  this organisation  is  to  unequivocally  recommit  ourselves  –  both  in words and in deeds - to the principles that the Charter requires us  to  follow  in  our  relations  with  other  states  -  respect  for sovereignty,  international  law,  the  pursuit  of  dialogue  and cooperation, and the peaceful settlement of disputes.

At a time when conflict is rising, trust is eroding, and geopolitical competition  is  intensifying,  we  should  not  conclude  that multilateralism has failed.

We should conclude that it is needed more than ever.

Thank you.

speaker_name: Sayyid Badr bin Hamad bin Hamood Albusaidi
text:
Your Excellency, President of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly

Heads and Members of Delegations,

I would like to extend my sincere congratulations to His Excellency Dr. Khalilur Rahman on  his  election  to  preside  over  this  session,  wishing  him  every success in carrying out his duties.

Ladies and Gentlemen

Dialogue is the true value capable of reminding us of what unites us, as well as its  being  the  optimal  means  of  overcoming  diLerences,  building  trust  and understanding, and resolving issues and crises.

We  would  like  to  aLirm  here  that  the  Sultanate  of  Oman  will  continue  its steadfast approach to ﬁnding peaceful and consensual solutions to disputes, based on the values and principles that help us achieve our shared goals of securing  security  and  stability  for  all  and  advancing  economic  development projects and prosperity for our peoples.

Mr. President, distinguished heads of state and government, distinguished delegates. I am appearing once again before this assembly on behalf of the Republic of Panama, a nation whose own geography defined its destiny. It's the bridge of the world and connects continents, cultures, and markets. At a time in history in which geopolitical fractures threaten to polarize us in a dangerous manner, Panama reaffirms its historic vocation to bring people together and seek common understandings. I must say that polarization is coupled with a large mass of people who feel that international organizations have forgotten the values and priorities of the majority of citizens. I'm referring to those who wish to progress in peace, to be able to work and return home safely.

Also, those who defend the institution of the family that has its own credo and a culture forged throughout the centuries that today is being called into question. The majority feel under pressure due to the actions of progressive multiculturalism, that a large part of society is not prepared to accept, almost under coercion. I'm a president that comes from a great nation, a crystal of different cultural heritages that forged a society that's open to the world, with a strong belief in peace. This was all achieved over many years without any imposition, so this means that it happened naturally. I'm convinced that the United Nations has immense potential in a world with so much volatility and such strong asymmetries. But it needs to take up, again, its leadership in order to engage in preventive actions and corrective actions.

I am a person who believes in and defends multilateralism, and I am convinced that peace and prosperity of nations must be grounded in international law as a guiding principle of relationships between nations. And these theoretical arguments must also be expressed with palpable results. We must recognize now that citizens do not believe that these types of meetings are that beneficial for them. And herein lies one of the reasons why we must restore trust. I want to give you a concrete example just to illustrate what I'm saying. Since 2021, this organization has been working on recommendations and calling out illegal migration across the Darien and established a basis of humanitarian aid, and it looked like more of a concentration camp in the midst of the 21st century.

However, in practical terms, the transit of people increased in 2022, and even more in 2023 and in the first six months of 2024. So it went from being uncontrolled migration and turned into huge illegal migration. People trafficking organizations linked to drug trafficking used and abused this space to transport more families, and the result of it was women and children, children ending up orphaned in one of the worst social disasters that my country can remember. In addition to this, we must add the ecological damage caused in a biodiversity reserve, the Darien Gap Reserve, and this has still not recovered. And this is a situation where there's more than a million people transiting across it, and since the first day I knew that we needed to resolve this issue individually, like I did, because this organization wasn't able to do it. And it's for this reason that at the beginning of my term I signed a memorandum of understanding with the government of the United States.

This, at the end of the day, is a border issue for the United States also, but it was taking place in Panama. And so in the second six months of 2024, with colossal effort being made by my country, we managed to oversee a 50% drop compared to the first six months of the year. In 2025, when restrictive measures were implemented in the United States and we worked in better coordination with one another, we saw a 99% drop. So this means halting one of the worst humanitarian disgraces that Panama has ever seen in its history, putting an end to family separation, and also we stopped criminals profiting. This description is something that should not be seen as an isolated criticism, but rather as an inflection point to understand the increasingly widening gap between what citizens expect and what they are able to obtain from this organization on issues such as illegal migration, for example. Ladies and gentlemen, in order to recover trust, we must make headway together on the key issues that benefit our citizens.

World trade, without a shadow of a doubt, is one of the best expressions of the freedom to produce, transport, and trade products from one nation to another. We're proud of being a country that connects the world through trade. Having the canal that unites two oceans, that transports goods from all countries of the world without any distinction, that is an icon of integration. This strategic canal for the free world, once again, is suffering the consequences of climate change. This is something that is a real paradox because we are a carbon-negative country and one of the very few carbon-negative countries in the world, but this does not mean that we don't have to face strong droughts followed by heavy rain that causes flooding. This leads us to a reflection that is, there's a lot of support for nations that assume the objective of decarbonization, but the fact is that we don't benefit from any type of economic aid, despite the fact that we remove more carbon from the world than we produce.

This is an endeavor of the United Nations to support responsible projects, both socially and environmentally, that represent real progress for our countries. We are a country that protects 33% of our territory and 54% of our seas.

Confidence and trust is won on the ground when institutions fulfill their promises, when international law is applied without selectivity, and when peoples see that the multilateral system delivers concrete actions and results. In terms of security, we will continue to work together with our allies to combat drug trafficking, which is a source of violence and social breakdown. We also staunchly support the government of Colombia in their measures to reduce the production of cocaine, which also affects Panama as a transit country. Ladies and gentlemen, in a world marked by strategic competition between the great powers, Panama, as a result of our history and beliefs, chooses to remain the meeting point where humanity can build a future of peace and shared development. We are a nation that hosts people from different cultures, that hosts birds, whales, and vessels from the entire world. Panama hosts the world, and we would like to invite all three nations who wish to see prosperity for their peoples and who wish to be more global in trade, but also more autonomous in decisions on their own traditions to work together. We also host investment with a new stage of national development to improve global logistics through the Panama Canal and also five high-quality global ports, including two of the largest in our region, in addition to the expansion of the services that we offer in terms of transporting hydrocarbons between the oceans.

This is a center that has recently been entirely acquired by the Panamanian state. As I have made clear in this statement, in terms of global trade and also investment in combating drug trafficking and terrorism, respecting sovereignty and peace, in all of these matters, all members of the United Nations can continue to count on Panama in this endeavor. In this war, there are no battlegrounds, no fronts Indeed, no fronts have been defined. There are no international rules governing these conflicts.

The enemy does not wear a uniform. The enemy hides among our people. There is no possibility to see surrender or to sign peace treaties in this context. And illegal businesses that range from smuggling, illegal mining, drug trafficking, human trafficking, extortion and killing. Consequently, the first thing we must do is isolate or pinpoint and identify the enemy. These organisations, these enemies are terrorist groups and they must be tackled for as what they are. That is justice. We can share universal principles and at the same time recognize that every people has its own story, its own history, its own culture, its own traditions, and the legitimate right to democratically define its own path. Those of us that come from nations that are constantly having to recover and get back on their feet.

We come here today absolutely sure of the fact that we can share great principles without ever turning our back on what we are We do not need to all think in the same way to have deep mutual respect for one another. The world does not require identical democracies. It requires legitimate democracies It does not demand nations that are all the same. It does not need cookie cutter nations. It needs truly free peoples. Thank you.
