NATIONAL STATEMENT

As delivered by

H.E. MA. THERESA P. LAZARO SECRETARY OF FOREIGN AFFAIRS

GENERAL DEBATE OF THE 81ST SESSION OF THE UNITED NATIONS GENERAL ASSEMBLY

26 September 2026, UNHQ, New York

(Theme: Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All)

We  meet  at  a  perilous  precipice—a  tumultuous  time  marked  by

profound upheaval, relentless uncertainty, and deep unpredictability.

More  than  fifty  active  conflicts  tear  at  the  fabric  of  nations.

Geopolitical  competition  strains  our  multilateral  institutions.  And  global

trust is fading precisely when we need it most.

Eighty-one  years  ago,  our  forebears  forged  this  Organization  to

save humanity from the scourge of war and reaffirm our shared dignity.

Today, we must ask: Have we honored that sacred compact?

When more than 645 million people face hunger, when our climate

remains in a state of emergency, and when our collective conscience is

stained by humanitarian catastrophes, reflection must give way to urgent,

united resolve.

We cannot continue down fragmented paths.

In an interconnected world, the disruption of maritime traffic in the

Middle  East  can  trigger  an  energy  emergency  in  the  Philippines,  more

than 3,600 nautical miles away. The war in Ukraine compounds a global

food crisis and economic shocks unseen since the Second World War.

Peace, therefore, is not merely the absence of war. It is our shared

and indivisible responsibility.

We  reiterate  our  call  for  an  immediate  and  sustained  ceasefire  in

Gaza,  the  protection  of  civilians,  the  release  of  all  hostages,  and  full

compliance  by  all  parties  with  international  law,  including  international

humanitarian law.

We urge all relevant parties to de-escalate, exercise restraint, and

return to the path of dialogue.

The  Philippines  reaffirms  its  consistent  and  principled  support  for

the inalienable right of the Palestinian people to self-determination.

We firmly believe that the two-state solution remains the only viable

path to lasting and durable peace—with Israel and Palestine living side by

side  in  peace  and  security,  and  all  others  respecting  their  peaceful

coexistence.

Peace is a daily choice.

It  requires  diplomacy,

justice,  respect

for

international

law,

confidence-building, and sustained investment in conflict prevention and

peacebuilding—with the United Nations at the heart of this effort.

Numbers and statistics can obscure the true magnitude of our trials.

Behind every metric is a human story.

Put a face to the climate emergency.

A single disaster can erase decades of hard-won progress.

Look to Nepal, bearing the heavy cost of rising temperatures despite

contributing less than 0.1 percent of global emissions.

Look to the Philippines—one of the world’s most climate-vulnerable

nations.

Since August alone, ferocious monsoons and storms have battered

our  islands,  affecting  more  than  2.7  million  families,  destroying  homes,

and shattering livelihoods.

We  share  these  vulnerabilities  with  many  developing  countries,

particularly small islands and coastal states.

Those who have contributed least to the climate crisis must not bear

its heaviest cost.

We call for the effective implementation of the Paris Agreement, the

full operationalization of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage,

and strengthened implementation of the Sendai Framework.

Put a face to the pursuit of sustainable development.

With the 2030 Agenda less than four years away, only 36 percent of

assessable SDG targets are on track.

Achieving  these  goals  requires  renewed  political  will,  stronger

partnerships with the private sector, reform of the international financial

architecture, and a United Nations Development System responsive to the

evolving needs and priorities of developing countries.

Consistent  with  the  Compromiso  de  Sevilla,  we  call  for  stronger

international  cooperation  to  mobilize  development  financing,  facilitate

technology transfer, and strengthen capacity building.

As a country that has newly attained upper-middle-income status,

the  Philippines  knows  that  income  classification  is  not  the  end  of  the

journey.

Our  metrics  must  evolve  to  capture  the  structural  vulnerabilities,

debt  burdens,  and  inequalities  that  continue  to  affect  middle-income

countries.

Put a face to the digital revolution—and to the rise of artificial

intelligence.

We stand at the dawn of an unprecedented technological era.

Harnessed responsibly, frontier technologies and AI can accelerate

sustainable  development,  optimize  resources,  and  bridge  deep  global

divides.

But AI also presents profound and systemic risks.

Without  robust  governance,  enforceable  ethical  standards,  and

strong  legal  guardrails,  it  could  deepen  inequalities  and  become  an

existential challenge.

We  echo  the  growing  call  across  industries:  we  need  robust  AI

governance, with enforceable standards—and we need it now.

Advanced capabilities must never be allowed to pose unacceptable

risks to human lives, human rights, or democratic integrity.

Effective  governance  must  also  address  deep  developmental

asymmetries.

We are not entering the AI era from the same starting point.

Managing  this  revolution  requires  closing  critical  gaps  in  digital

infrastructure,  computing  resources,  and  technical  expertise,  so  that

developing countries are not left behind.

We need AI systems that uplift the vulnerable, strengthen national

resilience,  promote  gender  equality,  and

foster  human-centered

partnerships—not exclusion and fragmentation.

Put  a  face  to  the  tireless  migrant  workers  and  seafarers  who

keep the global economy afloat.

Millions of migrant workers leave their homes in search of a better

life,  contributing  immeasurably  to  the  sustainable  development  of

countries of origin, transit, and destination.

They  are  entitled  to  full  human  rights  and  fundamental  freedoms,

regardless of status, and deserve steadfast protection from trafficking and

exploitation along perilous migration routes.

Among them, our seafarers form an indispensable lifeline of global

commerce.

Nearly 90 percent of world trade moves by sea, supported by close

to two million seafarers—more than 25 percent of whom are Filipinos.

They  are  essential  workers,  yet  increasingly  vulnerable  to  conflict

and attacks at sea.

Just recently, an incident in the Strait of Hormuz claimed the lives of

Filipino seafarers and injured many others.

Their tragedy reminds us: maritime security is human security.

Put  a  face  to  our  identity  as  an  archipelagic  and  maritime

nation, where open and secure seas are our lifeblood.

For  the  Philippines,  the  safety  of  ships  and  seafarers  cannot  be

separated from supply chains and global commerce.

Open and secure seas—free from interference and coercion—are

vital to our security, our economy, and our people.

International law must remain our guiding lighthouse, with UNCLOS

standing firmly as the constitution of the oceans.

Next year marks the 45th anniversary of UNCLOS and the Manila

Declaration on the Peaceful Settlement of International Disputes.

This  year  also  marks  a  decade  since  the  2016  South  China  Sea

Arbitral  Award—an  award  that  is  final  and  legally  binding,  and  that

demonstrates how international law provides States with peaceful means

to clarify rights and resolve differences.

The Philippines stands firm in its conviction that disputes must be

resolved through diplomacy and law, not violence and might.

International  cooperation  to  protect  maritime  security  must  also

extend to critical maritime infrastructure—the physical and digital nervous

system of our shared prosperity.

From  undersea  cables  carrying  99  percent  of  global  data,  to

strategic sea lanes and ports sustaining trade, to offshore facilities fueling

economies,  disruption  of  critical  maritime  infrastructure  can  send

shockwaves across borders.

Rather  than  waiting  for  threats  and  asking  who  should  respond,

States  must  explore  a  framework,  anchored  on  UNCLOS,  that  sets  out

clear

rules,

rights,  and  obligations  governing  critical  maritime

infrastructure.

All our advancements will falter if they are not anchored in universal

human rights and safeguarded from the shadow of modern threats.

Since  joining  the  United  Nations  as  a  founding  member,  the

Philippines has proudly stood with the vanguards of human rights.

We advocated decolonization and the elimination of discrimination

against women.

We advanced the rights of children, persons with disabilities, older

persons, Indigenous Peoples, and migrants.

And we called firmly for an end to apartheid and all forms of racial

discrimination.

We will continue to champion these timeless principles.

At  the  same  time,  we  must  secure  our  future  by  ensuring

responsible  behavior  in  outer  space,  reducing  space  threats,  and

preventing an arms race in outer space.

We  also  urge  a  renewed  and  rigorous  commitment  to  the  Non-

Proliferation Treaty—the cornerstone of the global nuclear disarmament

and non-proliferation architecture.

Restoring  trust  in  the  NPT  is  imperative  if  we  are  to  achieve  our

shared  vision  of  a  world  free  from  the  existential  threat  of  nuclear

weapons.

Closer to home, the Philippines’ own journey toward lasting peace,

exemplified  by

the  Bangsamoro  Autonomous  Region

in  Muslim

Mindanao, has taught us an invaluable lesson:

Lasting peace requires addressing the root causes of conflict,

empowering local communities, and ensuring that women are at the

center of peacebuilding.

Our world is evolving. So must the United Nations.

To remain effective, we must reform the Security Council to make it

more  representative,  transparent,  and  accountable—expanding  the

voices of developing regions across Asia, Africa, Latin America, and the

Caribbean.

As we look to the future, we are reminded that everything we strive

for ultimately depends on how we choose to navigate these trials together.

We need to reflect deeply on the promises of our Charter and on the

state of our fractured world.

We must actively seek collective pathways that transcend borders

and bridge divides.

And  above  all,  we  must  always  put  a  face  to  what  we  do—

remembering that every policy, every treaty, and every institutional reform

is ultimately about real human lives.

It is in this spirit that we voice a historic aspiration: the hope for a

woman  Secretary-General—a  leader  who  can  rally  nations  back  to

true multilateralism and deliver for all.

Thank you.

Mr. President, congratulations on your successful election as President for the 81st session of the UN General Assembly.

Secretary-General, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen,

Alii, and warm greetings from the people of Palau.

Secretary-General António Guterres, thank you for your leadership and service to the United Nations. Your climate leadership, steadfast defense of multilateralism, international law, human dignity, and the voices of the vulnerable carries special meaning for small island developing states.

I stand before this Assembly for a people whose future depends on a healthy ocean, a stable climate, and the sovereign right to determine their own path.

For us, sovereignty is lived - in our ability to feed our people from healthy oceans, power our homes independently from distant fuel markets, protect our shorelines from rising seas, and chart our own path.

It is a responsibility that grows more urgent each day, especially as UNEP’s latest findings make clear that the world is now certain to exceed 1.5°C. This reality must strengthen our resolve to deliver what we have promised and prepare our communities for the impacts science tells us are inevitable.

Small island states, young people, scientists, civil society, Indigenous communities, and responsible partners have already raised climate ambition, accelerated the shift to renewable energy, and exposed the true cost of inaction.

We have called for ambition that matches the science, demonstrated that ocean stewardship can protect nature while supporting livelihoods, and insisted on a stronger voice for small island states in the decisions that shape our future.

Pacific Leaders have charted a practical roadmap through Unlocking Blue Pacific Prosperity (UBPP). Launched at COP28 and reinforced by the Pacific Leaders’ Ocean Statement adopted in Palau, UBPP unites 22 Pacific countries and territories to mobilize accessible, catalytic investment for 100% sustainable ocean management, robust food systems, and resilient livelihoods—advancing our shared 30x30 commitment. We continue to seek and expand investment to UBPP to meet its goals and deliver lasting resilience for our communities.

Palau is translating that UBPP vision into national action. We launched our Sustainable Ocean Policy that commits to 100% effective, science￼based, and adaptive management of our ocean—balancing protection with production to deliver the optimal benefits for our people. In line with this effort, with support from partners like Japan, we

are working to develop fishing ports and other critical infrastructure to truly capture the value of the resources harvested in our waters.

As Chair of the Pacific Islands Forum and AOSIS, and through Palau’s leadership in the High‑Level Panel for a Sustainable Ocean Economy, we will continue to call for an ocean agenda that meets the scale of this challenge.

But, Mr President, the task now is delivery.

We need financing that reaches communities without adding debt; adaptation finance accessible to countries already bearing the costs of problems they did not create; and full support for loss and damage, and the special circumstances of SIDS.

This means grant‑based and concessional finance, grid readiness and storage, productive energy use, and support that respects our circumstances while enabling delivery at scale.

Those who contributed the least to this climate crisis, yet confront the worst threats of rising sea levels, must not be burdened with debt simply to purchase a life jacket for their survival.

International financial institutions must look beyond income and account for the vulnerabilities SIDS face: climate exposure, remoteness, narrow economies, and limited access to affordable finance. The Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS provides a strong roadmap for resilience, but it requires urgent, predictable, and scaled‑up support.

The Pacific Resilience Facility (PRF) is one practical answer. Endorsed by Pacific Leaders, PRF is the first Pacific‑led, owned, and managed regional financing facility dedicated to climate and disaster resilience — and the first international financial institution collectively owned by the Pacific, focused on turning resources into real, community‑level resilience. PRF reflects the kind of capital the world should support.

Resilience is also about safeguarding public health. I commend Palau’s First Lady for advancing efforts to combat tobacco and nicotine use, with a focus on youth. Her efforts led Palau to formally request the UN Secretary-General to initiate a WHO review of nicotine as a psychotropic substance. Globally, nicotine use claims over seven million lives annually with more than a billion trapped in addiction. Protecting our future requires expanding prevention, enhancing cessation support, and enacting strong policies to diminish the appeal and affordability of these harmful products.

No country should have to choose between the health of its children and the commercial interests of an industry built on addiction. We call for stronger international cooperation to protect young people from nicotine dependence and to put public health before profit.

Resilience must also transform how we power our homes, move our people, and connect our islands. Energy security is climate security, economic security, and national security.

Through the Manubada Call to Action, the Pacific reaffirmed a shared vision of a 100% renewable￼energy Blue Pacific and a just, inclusive, and equitable transition away from fossil fuels. This is not only about reducing emissions; it is about reducing vulnerability to imported fuel, external shocks, and prices we do not control.

Palau is carrying that regional commitment into national action. Our latest climate commitment targets a 44 percent reduction in fossil‑fuel use by 2035, supported by renewable energy generation and practical policies that make the transition affordable and reliable.

Our energy future reflects a larger truth: resilience requires partnership shaped by our priorities and respects our sovereignty. How we protect the ocean, confront climate change, and power our islands leads directly to how the world engages with us.

Partnership must never become pressure, and assistance must never come at the cost of a nation’s values, institutions, or freedom to choose.

Sovereignty is not isolation; it is the freedom to cooperate through mutual respect, transparency, accountability, dialogue, and international law.

This principle matters because we have seen what can happen when tensions build, when concerns are ignored, and when channels for dialogue are left too narrow for the challenges before us.

The Russia and Ukraine war is a painful reminder of the tragic human toll that occurs when diplomacy gives way to conflict, and how challenging it is to de-escalate tensions once violence erupts.

The Strait of Hormuz situation demonstrates how quickly disruption in an important waterway threatens international stability, energy security, and trade worldwide.

Reaffirming the primary responsibility of the UN Charter to maintain global peace and security, WE uphold the sovereignty of Bahrain, Jordan, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates, and condemn actions by Iran that jeopardize maritime security or aim to obstruct, close, or interfere with international navigation through the Strait.

At our Pacific Leaders Meeting in Palau, Leaders expressed deep concern that China’s ballistic missile test overflew several Pacific nations without adequate notice. Our region must never be treated as an empty expanse for strategic competition or tests of military power. The Pacific is home to peoples, communities, cultures, fisheries, and

ecosystems—it is the foundation of our security and our future, and a source of nourishment and a lifeline for the global community.

In the face of these risks, the Pacific way is to address tensions before they become crises; make room for dialogue before disagreement becomes conflict; seek inclusion rather than isolation; and uphold respect, restraint, and international law. The Pacific is our home, not a theater for geopolitical competition. It must remain an Ocean of Peace—where nations meet in cooperation, international law is respected, and the security of Pacific peoples is never compromised.

Palau is a friend to all. We choose our partners based on shared values of democracy, human rights, and rules‑based international order—principles that underpin our friendship with Taiwan, a trusted partner that can contribute even more fully if given space to do so.

The UN Charter begins with the commitment to "We the peoples," yet the UN marginalizes Taiwan's 23 million people, disregarding that foundational purpose. We stand with like￼minded partners in calling for the reversal of misinterpretations of rules and procedures that have constrained Taiwan’s meaningful participation in this body.

Under that UN Charter, small states are sovereign states with the right to determine their own future, choose their partners, and pursue development that serves their people. We urge all parties to preserve peace and stability, resolve differences peacefully, and choose dialogue over escalation.

Beyond politics and policy, one truth should unite us: our children, and their children, deserve a world that is safe, healthy, and clean.

For that reason, our discussions here and beyond must lead to action—action that protects the conditions in which every child can live, grow, and thrive.

We acknowledge, while not yet at the scale required, that the architecture is being built, political momentum is growing, and resources are beginning to mobilize — even amidst a complex geopolitical landscape. Our traditional wisdom reminds us: Msisichau e ng kmedang a meched — be strong and do not give up; the shore is near.

The promise of multilateralism is that even the smallest can be heard, and that many voices — shaped by different histories and experiences — can move toward a common shore. In Palau, we say: Tekoi el ua Iuul. Knowledge is like the ocean’s waves: it comes in many forms and sizes, yet no wave overpowers another, and all ultimately reach the same shore.

Let us leave this Assembly committed to a multilateralism that honors every voice, values every form of knowledge, and carries us toward a safer, healthier, and more peaceful world. Mesulang. Thank you.

Secretary-General, Excellencies, Distinguished delegates,

I bring you greetings from Papua New Guinea, a nation of extraordinary diversity, with more than 800 languages and cultures, united under one flag.

Papua New Guinea comes to this Assembly with profound respect for the Charter of the United Nations and for the principles and purposes upon which this great institution was founded.

The  United  Nations  reminds  us  that  whether  we  are  big  or  small  nations,  rich  or poor, developed  or  developing,  powerful  or  less  powerful,  we  are  all  members  of  one international community.

The  challenges  confronting  humanity  do  not  recognise  the  size  of  our  economies,  the strength of our militaries or the boundaries on our maps.

No nation can address them alone.

We  must  therefore  continue  to  work  together,  respecting  the  sovereignty  of  nations, upholding  international  law  and  the  United  Nations  Charter,  resolving  our  differences peacefully, and recognising that every nation, regardless of its size or economic strength, has a voice and a place in this Assembly.

For Papua  New Guinea,  and  for  the  small  island  nations  of  the Pacific,  multilateralism matters.

The  United  Nations  provides  a  place  where  the  smallest  nations  can  sit  alongside  the largest, where our voices can be heard, and where we can work together on the common challenges facing humanity.

At  this  time,  I  also  wish  to  acknowledge  Secretary-General  António  Guterres  as  he approaches the completion of his tenure.

On  behalf  of  the  Government  and  people  of  Papua  New  Guinea,  I  thank  Secretary-General Guterres for his strong and consistent advocacy for humanity.

At a time when our world has confronted war, displacement, poverty, inequality, climate change and many other challenges, he has consistently called for peace, human dignity, international cooperation and respect for the principles of the United Nations

He has demonstrated the qualities of a global statesman and has used his office to speak for humanity, including those whose voices are too often unheard.

Secretary-General Guterres, Papua New Guinea thanks you for your service to the United Nations and to humanity.

Your advocacy reminds us that beyond our national borders, political differences, cultures and beliefs, we belong to one human family and share one Earth.

It is in that spirit of our common humanity that I wish to speak about human rights, human freedom and, particularly, freedom of conscience, thought, religion and belief.

At the heart of human rights is a simple truth: every human being has inherent dignity and is entitled to fundamental freedoms.

From my Christian perspective, these freedoms are not gifts bestowed upon humanity by governments, institutions or powerful nations. They are God-given rights inherent in every human life.

And  because  these  rights  belong  equally  to  every  person,  we  have  a  responsibility  to respect and protect the rights of others, including those who may not look like us, speak like us, worship like us or believe what we believe.

The strength of a nation, a government, an economy, a technology or a religion should never be used to suppress the fundamental rights of another human being.

The might of military power must not suppress the weak.

The might of economic power must not suppress the poor.

The might of technology must not diminish human dignity or freedom.

And the might of a religious majority must never be used to suppress those who belong to a religious minority.

Human  rights  have  their  greatest  meaning  when  they  protect  those  with  less  power, minorities, vulnerable communities and individuals whose beliefs may differ from those of the majority.

We must therefore learn to live together with mutual respect.

We do not have to agree on everything.

We do not have to share the same religion, culture, political system or worldview.

But we must respect the humanity and fundamental freedoms of one another.

This principle is especially important when we speak about religion.

Papua New Guinea is a Christian nation, believing that Jesus Christ is our Lord, Saviour and soon-coming King. Christian principles have profoundly influenced our country, our communities and our institutions.

But our Christianity must never become an excuse to deny another human being freedom of conscience.

Section 45 of our Constitution guarantees every person freedom of conscience, thought and religion, and the practice of his or her religion and beliefs.

Our Constitution also protects people against being compelled to participate in religious observance and against attempts to force religion or irreligion upon another person.

Faith that is forced is no longer faith.

I  believe  freedom  of  choice  is  a God-given  right,  implanted  in  the conscience  of every human being. Our moral consciousness comes from God.

God does not compel worship. He calls people through love while allowing every person to exercise the freedom of choice He has given them.

True faith therefore cannot be imposed by force, fear, law or persecution.

A person must be free to believe.

A person must be free to worship.

A person must be free to change his or her belief.

And a person must also be free not to profess a religion.

The  Universal  Declaration  of  Human  Rights  recognises  this  principle  in  Article  18,  the right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion.

History  teaches  us  what  happens  when  governments,  institutions  or  majorities  use religion to suppress those who believe differently.

Human beings have been persecuted, expelled, imprisoned and killed because of their faith.

Humanity must learn from this history.

A Christian-majority nation must protect people of other religions.

A Muslim-majority nation must protect people of other religions.

A Hindu-majority nation must protect people of other religions.

A Buddhist-majority nation must protect people of other religions.

And every society must respect the rights of those who choose not to profess a religion.

The size of a majority does not diminish the human rights of the minority.

The United States of America, where this Assembly meets, expressed this principle more than two centuries ago through its First Amendment, which prohibits laws “respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof.”

Government  should  neither  impose  faith  upon  its  people  nor  prevent  people  from practising their faith.

Papua New Guinea supports this principle.

We are proudly Christian.

But the strength of our Christianity should not be demonstrated by suppressing another person’s beliefs.

It should be demonstrated by having the confidence to allow every human being freedom of conscience.

Humanity  can  be  diverse  in  culture,  religion  and  thought,  yet  we  must  be  united  in respecting and tolerating our differences.

Papua New Guinea knows something about diversity.

We have more than 800 languages and many different cultures and traditions.

Yet for 51 years as an independent nation, we have remained together as one Papua New Guinea.

We have disagreements and challenges. We do not claim perfection.

But our experience demonstrates something important:

Diversity does not have to mean division.

People can speak different languages and still belong to one nation.

People can come from different cultures and live under one Constitution.

And people can worship differently and still be neighbours, colleagues and fellow citizens.

Papua  New  Guinea  therefore  calls  upon  all  Member  States  to  defend  freedom  of conscience, thought, religion and belief.

And I respectfully extend this call to every nation that calls Papua New Guinea a friend, every  nation  with  which  we  have  a  bilateral  partnership,  and  every  nation  that  seeks friendship and engagement with us.

Look within your own borders.

Ensure  that  religious  minorities  are  not  persecuted,  suppressed,  intimidated  or discriminated against because they practise a religion different from that of the majority.

Whether a country is predominantly Christian, Muslim, Hindu, Buddhist or follows another religious  tradition,  the  faith  of  the  majority  must  never  become  an  instrument  for persecuting the minority.

This message is not directed at one country, one religion or one region.

It is a principle that must apply equally to all of us.

Because human rights cannot be selective. We cannot demand respect for our own rights while denying those same rights to others.

And we cannot ask the world to respect our beliefs while refusing to respect the freedom of conscience of another human being.

But there is a wider principle here.

This is ultimately about human dignity.

If  we  recognise  the  dignity  of  every  human  being,  then  we  must  also  consider  the conditions in which people live — and the Earth we will leave to our children.

The United Nations General Assembly has recognised the human right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment.

What value is freedom if a child has no clean water to drink?

What value is development if we destroy the environment that sustains human life?

And  what  inheritance  are  we  leaving  our  children  if  our  forests  disappear,  our  oceans become polluted and our climate becomes increasingly unstable?

There  is  one  reality  that  transcends  every  political,  economic  and  religious  difference between us:

We have only one Earth.

There is no other known habitable planet presently within the practical reach of humanity to which billions of people can simply relocate if we destroy this one.

This Earth is our common home.

Whatever our religion, nationality or political system, we breathe the same atmosphere.

We share the same oceans.

We depend upon the same global climate.

And ultimately, we share the consequences of what humanity does to this planet.

Think about the children of the world.

A child born today did not create climate change.

That child did not choose the wars of this generation.

That child did not create pollution or environmental destruction.

Yet that child will inherit the consequences of the decisions we make today.

We must therefore be custodians not only of the present, but also of the future.

Future  generations  cannot  stand  before  this  General  Assembly  today  and  argue  for themselves.

We must consider them when we make decisions about war and peace, development, energy, forests, oceans, minerals and the global economy.

Papua New Guinea understands this responsibility.

We are custodians of great tropical forests, extraordinary biodiversity and a vast ocean space.

For us, the environment is not an abstract international discussion.

It is where we live.

It is where we grow our food.

It is where we fish.

And it is the inheritance we must pass to our children.

In our interconnected world, decisions made in one country can affect people thousands of kilometres away.

Greenhouse gases do not recognise national borders.

Pollution carried by oceans does not stop at immigration checkpoints.

Wars can disrupt food, fuel, energy, trade and supply chains far from the battlefield.

Economic decisions made in the world’s largest economies can reach an ordinary family in a small developing country.

A mother buying food can feel the consequences.

A farmer buying fuel can feel the consequences.

A small business facing higher transport costs can feel the consequences.

And  developing  countries  trying  to  build  roads,  schools  and  hospitals  can  feel  the consequences.

This  is  why  leadership  in  powerful  nations  carries  responsibilities  beyond  national borders.

With greater power comes greater responsibility.

Papua  New  Guinea  respectfully  asks  the  leaders  of  the  world’s  major  powers  to remember the ordinary people whose lives can be affected by decisions made far away from them.

When wars disrupt food, fuel and trade, families far from the battlefield can experience higher prices and economic uncertainty.

When  the  climate  changes,  communities  that  have  contributed  relatively little  to  global greenhouse-gas emissions can nevertheless face rising seas, extreme weather, threats to food security and damage to livelihoods.

My appeal to leaders everywhere is simple:

Put human welfare ahead of war.

Put humanity ahead of narrow geopolitical interests.

Choose dialogue and peaceful settlement wherever possible.

Remember ordinary families when making major economic decisions.

Balance commercial interests with the welfare of people.

Use technology to advance human dignity, not diminish it.

Protect our planet while pursuing development.

And place the interests of our children and future generations at the heart of the decisions we make today.

Leadership is not measured only by the power a nation possesses.

Leadership is also measured by the responsibility with which that power is exercised.

Papua New Guinea does not claim to have all the answers.

We are a developing nation with challenges of our own.

But perhaps our position as a Pacific nation allows us to remind the larger powers of a simple reality:

No nation is so powerful that it can live apart from the Earth.

And  no  nation  is so  small  that  its people  should be  forgotten  when  decisions affecting humanity are made.

The military strength of a nation does not make the rights of another nation less important.

The size of an economy does not make the dignity of a poorer person less important.

Technological advancement does not diminish our obligation to protect human freedom.

And the size of a religious majority does not reduce the rights of a minority.

Power in all its forms must be exercised with responsibility.

We are many tribes.

Many languages.

Many churches.

Many cultures.

But one nation.

And perhaps Papua New Guinea can offer one simple thought to this Assembly:

You do not have to believe what I believe in order for me to defend your human rights.

Let governments govern for people.

Let churches preach.

Let mosques call their faithful to prayer.

Let temples welcome their worshippers.

Let people search their own consciences.

Let economies serve humanity.

Let technology serve humanity.

Let powerful nations exercise their power responsibly.

Let nations resolve their differences peacefully wherever possible.

And let no State compel the human soul.

We may have different religions, political systems, cultures and national interests.

We may be big nations or small nations.

We may be rich or poor.

We may possess different levels of military, economic and technological power.

But beneath those differences, we share something greater.

We share our humanity.

And we share one Earth.

This is our home.

We must protect it.

We must protect each other.

And we must leave our children a world better than the one we inherited.

Papua New Guinea will remain proudly Christian.

But we will also remain committed to freedom of conscience, thought and religion.

For ultimately, faith cannot be commanded by government. Faith must come from the heart.

God has given humanity the capacity to choose, and that freedom must be respected.

And God has entrusted this Earth to our generation only for a time.

Let us use our leadership wisely.

Let us pursue peace.

Let us uphold the Charter of the United Nations.

Let us respect the rights and dignity of every human being.

Let us work together — big nations and small.

Let us ensure that power, whether military, economic, technological or religious, is never used to suppress the rights of others.

Let us protect our common home.

And let us remember always the generations who will follow us.

On this note, I want to thank the United Nations and all those who have stood with Papua New Guinea over the last 51 years of our nationhood.

Amid  the  challenges  we  face  as  a  developing  nation,  we  are  growing  our  economy, opening our country through enabling infrastructure, working to provide quality education and health services for all, moving towards cleaner energy, conserving our forests and oceans, strengthening our independent judiciary and free-market economy, and opening our doors to genuine foreign investment.

I want to assure this Assembly that my Government is working to ensure that none of our 11 million people is left behind as we pursue development, opportunity and a better quality of life in our God-given homeland.

May God bless Papua New Guinea.

May God bless all nations and all peoples.

May God protect our children and the generations yet unborn.

And may the United Nations continue to defend peace, human dignity, freedom and the Earth that we all share.

Thank you.
