On  behalf  of  Senegal,  I  would  like  to  thank  your  predecessor  and  extend  to  you  my  warmest  congratulations,

together with my best wishes for success as you assume the presidency of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly.

I also reiterate our steadfast support for the Secretary-General, Mr. António Guterres, and his eﬀorts in the service of peace, development and human rights.

We  commend  his  leadership  of  the  Organization  and  wish  him  every  success  in  his  future  endeavors  as  his

tenure draws to a close.

Dear Colleagues,

As was the case last year, we meet once again against a worrying global backdrop.

The Organization is facing an unprecedented accumulation of complex global challenges.

In  this  context,  the  theme  of  this  session  aptly  captures  one  of  the  major  challenges  of  our  time:  “Rebuilding

trust, managing transformation: the United Nations at the service of all.”

The current crisis is undoubtedly a crisis of trust.

A crisis of trust between States; a crisis of trust in international institutions;

a  crisis  of  trust  in  the  ability  of  international  law  to  mobilize  collective  action  and  ensure  compliance  with  the

commitments agreed upon in the Charter of the United Nations; and, ﬁnally, a crisis of trust in the original promise

of the United Nations: to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war and to promote economic and

social progress for all.

The time has come to place this promise at the heart of the United Nations’ action.

If we do not want it to remain merely an ideal, it must once again become a reality for all.

Yet armed conﬂicts are multiplying.

The  wars  in  Ukraine,  the  Middle  East  and  Sudan,  the  crises  in  Haiti  and  Yemen,  and  conﬂicts  across  Africa,

including  the  expansion  of  terrorism  in  the  Sahel,  bear  witness  to  the  continued  deterioration  and  profound

weakening of international peace and security.

In  Gaza,  as  throughout  all  occupied  Palestinian  territories,  the  human  suﬀering  is  unacceptable,  and  the

systematic violation of international law is intolerable.

The time has come to act to put an end to the horror of massacres and destruction.

There  can  be  neither  viable  nor  lasting  peace  and  security  without  a  two-State  solution:  Palestine,  with  East

Jerusalem as its capital, and Israel, living side by side within secure and internationally recognized borders.

In  a  context  of  persistent  conﬂicts  that  fuel  the  arms  race,  weaken  disarmament  mechanisms  and  increase  the

risks  associated  with  new  technologies  and  the  exploration  of  outer  space,  Senegal  calls  for  a  collective

response.

Peace is not merely an aspiration.

It is a collective responsibility.

That is why, in my capacity as Chairperson of ECOWAS, I will spare no eﬀort to work for peace and security in the subregion, in cooperation with the African Union and the United Nations.

I am thinking in particular of the ﬁght against terrorism. It must be a common eﬀort, because terrorism is, by its

very nature, transnational.

The  Sahel  must  not  be  abandoned  to  its  fate.  Its  destabilization  will  aﬀect  neither  Africa  nor  other  interests

present in the Sahel without consequences.

I have not forgotten the worsening health crises; the Ebola epidemic reminds us of this.

Global inequalities are deepening. The climate emergency has become an even harsher reality, with its human,

economic and social costs continuing to grow.

On climate change and on the many other environmental threats of our time, we must act.

This is the ambition behind the Third United Nations Conference on Water, which Senegal will co-host with the

United Arab Emirates at the end of this year.

Lasting peace cannot be separated from development.

Forty years after the adoption of the Declaration on the Right to Development, we know what needs to be done

to achieve it: a profound reform of the international ﬁnancial architecture;

sustainable debt treatment;

fair global taxation;

better access to concessional ﬁnancing;

and, ﬁnally, implementation of the Seville Commitment as well as the Pact for the Future.

Senegal also believes in the transformative potential of new technologies, including the development of artiﬁcial

intelligence grounded in standards of ethics, responsibility and inclusion.

The  launch  of  our  ﬁrst  satellite  illustrates  our  determination  to  make  space,  digital  technologies  and  artiﬁcial

intelligence instruments in the service of human development.

Dear Colleagues,

We all know the challenges facing the Organization, including its precarious ﬁnancial situation, which aﬀects its

operational capacity and raises questions about its eﬀectiveness.

This is the case for peacekeeping operations. It is also the case for the Sustainable Development Goals, whose

implementation is facing considerable delays.

Faced  with  this  reality,  which  is  admittedly  far  from  encouraging,  some  may  be  tempted  to  consider

multilateralism an outdated model and to act outside our common mechanisms.

Senegal does not share this view.

On the contrary, it is precisely because the world is facing an unprecedented accumulation of crises that we need

a stronger, more representative and more eﬀective United Nations.

We will not resolve crises by further fragmenting the multilateral system.

We will not build peace through a logic of power politics.

We  will  not  guarantee  a  just  international  order  by  replacing  law  with  force.  That  would  jeopardize  the

Organization’s  fundamental  raison  d’être:  dialogue,  conﬂict  prevention,  the  peaceful  settlement  of  disputes,

cooperation and respect for international law.

In  this  spirit,  the  UN80  Initiative  oﬀers  us  a  historic  opportunity  to  undertake  the  structural  and  normative

transformations that are necessary.

But  reforming  the  United  Nations  should  not  mean  reducing  its  ambition.  It  should  make  the  Organization  less

bureaucratic  in  its  operations,  more  agile  in  its  actions,  more  eﬃcient  in  its  spending,  and  better  coordinated

between headquarters and the ﬁeld, so that it can better serve the peoples it represents.

Senegal supports this dynamic.

This is the meaning of our contribution to strengthening the United Nations system, with the construction, using

our own resources, of the United Nations House in the new city of Diamniadio, about thirty kilometers from Dakar.

This state-of-the-art platform will bring together all entities of the United Nations system on a single site, thereby

promoting greater coherence and eﬃciency.

But  a  stronger  Organization  also  requires  Member  States  to  honor  their  ﬁnancial  commitments  through  their

assessed contributions.

The years go by, yet our eﬀorts to reform global governance have still produced no signiﬁcant results.

The status quo on Security Council reform is evidence of this. We all agree that the composition of the Council no longer reﬂects the realities of our time.

We agree that its expansion must not result in greater inertia in its action.

But in the face of the legitimacy deﬁcit that characterizes the Council’s current conﬁguration, we must no longer remain in a time of observation; we must move into a time of urgency and action.

This  is  a  question  of  justice,  credibility  and  balance  within  the  international  system;  and  this  is  precisely  the

meaning of the Ezulwini Consensus, which reﬂects the common African position on Security Council reform.

In this spirit, Senegal is presenting its candidacy for a non-permanent seat on the Security Council for the 2032– 2033 term.

But  beyond  reform,  the  Organization  also  needs  experienced  leadership  to  guide  its  action  in  these  times  of

crisis and uncertainty.

It  needs  a  Secretary-General  capable  of  speaking  to  everyone,  listening  and  building  bridges  among  Member

States.

This is the vision championed by Mr. Macky Sall, former President of the Republic of Senegal. I therefore take this opportunity  to  renew  my  support  for  his  candidacy  and  reiterate  Senegal’s  request  for  support  from  Member

States.

As our Organization seeks to rebuild trust, Senegal continues to believe in a vision of a world founded on peace, justice, the dignity of every individual and human fraternity.

The world does not need unilateralist postures.

It needs a fairer, more inclusive and more eﬀective multilateralism.

Addressing our challenges requires bridges rather than walls.

Dialogue rather than confrontation.

Cooperation rather than isolation.

The rule of law rather than force.

It is in this spirit that Senegal will host the Youth Olympic Games.

This ﬁrst Olympic event in history to be held in Africa will bring together, from October 31 to November 13, 2026,

2,700 young athletes from 206 National Olympic Committees.

By  welcoming  the  youth  of  the  world,  Senegal  will  welcome  much  more  than  a  sporting  competition.  It  will

welcome a promise: that of a generation that wants to meet rather than confront one another, to surpass itself rather than divide itself, and to build together rather than oppose one another.

This is also the Olympic promise. And, ultimately, it is the promise of the United Nations: to make our diﬀerences

a strength, our diversity a source of richness, and our shared humanity the foundation of peace.

Conﬁdent  in  this  Olympic  message,  I  invite  all  Member  States  to  the  opening  ceremony  of  the  Youth  Olympic Games on October 31, 2026, and thank you for your kind attention.
