Madam president, excellencies, our world is undergoing a profound disruption characterised by great power, contestation, the wars in Ukraine, the Middle East, Africa. We're witnessing the rise of trade barriers. Supply chain disruptions, worsening climate change, and a new industrial revolution driven by digital technologies, biotechnology and renewable energy. This means we face both great peril and great promise. Yet we are in a more polarised and fractured world, and one that may be unable to protect the global commons at precisely the moment that we need that protection. Our inter-state relations are increasingly dictated by raw power, where the outcomes are determined on the basis of size, leverage and coercion.

And this poses obviously, a clear and present danger for smaller states like Singapore. But the point I wanted to make is that even the more powerful states would ultimately pay a price, because hard power on its own cannot secure supply chains, protect populations from pandemics, or stabilise a warming planet. Even big powers need partners to secure their long term national interests. The bilateral and regional arrangements can complement global frameworks, but on their own, they cannot replace shared rules that apply universally. A system built on individual coercive bargains would inherently be more volatile and more unstable. And therefore, our thesis today is that multilateralism offers a different bargain, one that is, in every state's enlightened national interest.

These shared rules and norms provide predictability. They constrain the capricious exercise of power, and they maximize autonomy even when power is unequally distributed. Actually the multilateral system today still works more often than the headlines would suggest. A few examples. The World Food Program feeds over 100 million people a year. The common ICAO standards enable 100,000 flights to operate safely every day with the ITU, our telecommunications networks and the internet continues to operate safely, smoothly on a planetary scale.

The question is, therefore not whether we need multilateralism, but how to make it fit for purpose. And I suggest three priorities. First, we all have to consistently comply with international law and the norms of multilateralism. Second, we need to reform existing institutions where needed. And third, we need to collectively formulate new rules and create new institutions for new technologies. Let me deal with the first point.

The consistent compliance with international law. Consider Unclose, the UN convention on the law of the sea. In fact, UN clauses, one of the great achievements of multilateral law making. It was concluded under the presidency of Professor Tommy Koh of Singapore, who called it the Constitution for the oceans. For over four decades It has set out the legal framework for activities in all our oceans and seas. But the current war in the Persian Gulf has put us close to a severe stress test.

The Strait of Hormuz is closed. We have to collectively reject this transit passage through straits used for international navigation is a right for all of us. It's not a privilege subject to fees and tolls. And this is customary international law, which means it is binding on all states whether or not they consider themselves parties to enclose how we deal with the Strait of Hormuz will have implications for navigational rights and freedom around the world. At stake is the legal architecture for freedom of navigation and overflight, and we cannot allow any single country to exercise a veto on these navigational rights and freedoms. Beyond the legal and political implications, the economic impact is also very stark.

The Strait of Hormuz carried around a fifth of the world's oil supplies, as well as critical supplies for other industries everywhere. Its disruption has meant higher energy prices for all of us broken disrupted supply chains and stranded seafarers. And this is why shared rules like enclose matter. Defending them is not just a matter of principle or debate. It is in our collective interests. The largest economies depend on the open sea lanes as much as the smallest.

And we in Singapore hold ourselves to the same standard. The Strait of Singapore is less than two nautical miles at its narrowest and yet nearly a quarter of the world's seaborne trade passes through the Strait of Singapore Singapore, Indonesia and Malaysia. The three littoral states of the Straits of Malacca and Singapore have worked with other users of these traits to keep the straits open, secure and accessible to everyone for decades, including through the cooperative mechanism on the safety of navigation and environmental protection in the Straits of Malacca and Singapore. Madam president, excellencies, the second point is that we should and must reform existing institutions and processes where necessary. In fact, free trade is another success story of the post-war multilateralism. Lower trade costs in these decades have boosted global real GDP by an estimated 6.8%, and in the case of low income countries, by around 33%.

Under the GATT and subsequently the WTO, disputes even between unequal powers could be settled by adjudication rather than the exercise of unilateral coercion But we all know the multilateral trading system has frayed. This year's WTO conference in Yaoundé could not even reach consensus on several key issues, including the moratorium on the customs duties for electronic transmissions, which lapsed tariffs and supply chain restrictions have also returned as instruments of coercion. The consequences of all this cannot be overstated for Singapore. Trade is three times our GDP. For many in this hall, access to markets and technology are absolutely essential for our development. When the rules governing trade are eroded, all of us will pay the price.

I know that consensus amongst 193 states is difficult, but it remains the gold standard. And I would ask all of you to recollect the BB, NJ agreement which entered into force this year. This is clear evidence that even in this time, we can still build common rules for shared challenges. And Singapore is proud that our ambassador, Vina Lee, presided over the negotiations that concluded this agreement by consensus. Having said that, even when consensus is elusive, we cannot allow collective action to be held hostage or to be paralysed. We need more flexible coalition of states and partners who are willing and able to move forward, whilst remaining open to others to join when they are ready.

Such coalitions already serve large and small economies alike The Rcep, the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership, is the largest trade agreement in the world. The Cptpp, the Comprehensive and Progressive Trans-Pacific partnership now stretches from Asia to Latin America to the United Kingdom, and in July 19th, small and medium sized trading nations of the Future of Investment and Trade Partnership met in Auckland. Not to negotiate a grand bargain, but to systematically reduce trade frictions and to strengthen supply chain resilience. Excellencies, this is not a retreat from multilateralism. It is a pragmatic and flexible effort to sustain cooperation when broader agreement is not yet possible, while remaining open for those who are ready to join later on. The objective remains the same to preserve the benefits of cooperation, widen participation over time, and ultimately bring these arrangements into the multilateral global architecture.

Third, we must collectively formulate new rules and be prepared to create new institutions, if necessary, for new technologies. Artificial intelligence, which we've heard so many times from the podium this week, is arguably the most urgent frontier AI offers with extraordinary potential, but its capability is advancing faster than our appreciation of its risks. There are fundamentally three categories of risk. First, the loss of control of autonomous systems. Second, that rogue actors could use AI to create bioweapons or other weapons of mass destruction or mass disruption. Third, the economic, the social the political.

Domestic disruptions are only just emerging. But excellencies, the genie is already out of the bottle. It is too late to call for a halt, especially given the superpower rivalry and the huge financial incentives for companies who already have frontier models. But let me offer a metaphor of driving a high performance car to drive a high performance car quickly and safely. You need a powerful engine. But equally, you need good brakes.

And especially if you are going to go beyond your neighborhood or cross boundaries, you need effective shared rules, traffic lights, insurance norms of behavior, seat belts. The engine is innovation. Every one of us has to continue to invest in science, the talent, and the infrastructure that will drive AI forward. For small states. This entails especially developing our people, equipping them with the skills necessary to master and deploy AI quickly, widely, at scale and safely. The real productivity gains from AI comes not from the IT department, but from our businesses and workers having the skills, the tools and the wherewithal to engineer their work processes.

Workflow by workflow. It is. That's where the cutting edge of value creation arises. But having said that, every powerful engine needs good brakes, safeguards as the capabilities of AI advance, our safeguards must keep pace. We need rigorous testing and evaluation before deployment. We need clear limits on what autonomous systems can do and mechanisms to intervene when they behave in ways we do not intend.

And since the risks from AI do not remain confined behind borders, it means we also need rules of the road that will form a shared global understanding of how we will collectively confront this challenge. Just as all of us instinctively understand traffic lights the same way, whether we're here in New York or in Beijing, Moscow or Singapore. Most importantly, human beings must ultimately remain in control and accountable. Let me give you an extreme thought experiment. Do you want the nuclear button to be in the hands of a human being or an AI? Think about that.

The scarce resource today is not legal architecture or technology. It is trust. Trust that the risks will be disclosed, that testing will be comprehensive and credible, and that cooperation will be inclusive and not be used to secure unilateral advantage. The technology has already become an arena for strategic competition precisely when international cooperation is most needed. Any durable international approach must give all states, all states a meaningful stake. Not only those who already have the most advanced models, or the deepest pockets, or the largest set of armaments.

So the question is how do we build trust? We begin with the science. Even where states have differences on governance, I believe it is possible for us to work together to collectively understand the capabilities and risks of AI models, to develop comparable methods for testing and evaluation, and to report serious incidents quickly across borders. We are not starting from zero. If you carefully go through what we already have today, the UN's Independent International Scientific Panel on AI already helps to establish a common understanding based on evidence The global dialogue on AI governance can help to translate that common understanding into common objectives, and the Itu's AI for Good Global Commission brings together leaders from government, industry and international institutions to discuss challenges and to come up with practical solutions. We must urgently establish common rules and safeguards for AI, and we should build on the many ongoing discussions in different formats and groupings And here I want to make a point The UN, the United Nations has a critical role to play in building convergence, because this is the only apex international institution with universal membership.

We must explore all options, including the idea of a UN framework Convention on AI safeguards. We may also need an international institution that can perform for AI some of the functions that currently exist for institutions that perform this. This function of setting common technical standards and the examples are the International Telecommunications Union, which provides all the International Atomic Energy Agency, which provides verification. Ultimately, the global Commons are best protected by collective action agreed through an inclusive process, and Singapore commits to contribute where we can. This week we joined the call for greater safety and security of frontier AI models, and I'm glad that this was led by Finland and Norway. We will continue to contribute through platforms such as the Digital Pillar for the Forum of Small States, and by making our governance frameworks and testing tools available to all.

But the work of building trust and laying the ground for global cooperation must begin now. Ultimately, powerful engines and good breaks and common rules do not stop us or slow us down. They give us the assurance and the confidence so that we can move faster and more effectively for the benefit of all our peoples. Madam president, excellencies, effective multilateralism requires institutions that can deliver, and that begins with a reform of the UN itself. I welcome the progress of the UN initiative. But reform must be strategic.

Not not merely. Fiscal reform must strengthen the equal standing of all members. The goal is not a smaller UN for its own sake, but one that delivers better and more equitably. In this session, we will appoint the 10th Secretary General of the UN. No one today under the age of 80, has lived in a world without the United Nations. But the UN has to earn the confidence of successive generations, and it does this through what it delivers, not what it declares on paper.

The next Secretary general must lead a UN that turns multilateral cooperation into practical results and communicates. This results in an effective way to all our people. Let me at this point, also pay tribute to Secretary General Antonio Guterres. He is a good man with the courage of his convictions, and he has ably steered this organization through some very difficult years of global division. He has been a consistent voice for the charter, for our climate and oceans, and for the rules that hold the global commons together. Finally, Madam President, effective multilateralism requires all countries to be prepared to contribute to the institutions that sustain it.

For Singapore, this begins with international law. The rule of law requires institutions to give it effect. Currently, the International Court of Justice has its fullest docket in its history, at precisely the moment when the relevance and effectiveness of international law is being questioned. States continue to bring their most serious disputes before the world's principal judicial organ. That's actually a good sign that demonstrates trust in the peaceful settlement of disputes and we must safeguard that trust. Singapore has nominated our ambassador for international law, Rina Lee, for election as a judge of the ICJ and as a tiny small state, Singapore has been a beneficiary, has been an active practitioner and a builder, a contributor to international law.

We now ask for the chance to serve the cause of the rule of law. Madam president, this is the case for multilateralism It's not some pie in the sky idealism, but a hard headed recognition that cooperation ultimately serves all of us. For every state, large or small a world governed by rules is infinitely better than one governed simply by the exercise of hard, crude power. In 1945, the founders of the UN hoped that the rules could restrain power. If we want to keep that hope alive, we must defend those very same rules that continue to serve us consistently everywhere across the globe. We have to adapt to a changing world, and we have to build new rules, new institutions and new processes where the challenges demand.

Thank you all very much.

Secretary-General of the United Nations,

Excellencies,

Distinguished Delegates,

I  stand  before  this  Assembly  conscious  that  I  speak  on  behalf  of a nation and a people whose future is being shaped in halls like this one.

I bring warm greetings from the people and Government of Solomon Islands, a nation of nearly one thousand islands stretching across as many miles of the Blue Pacific. Our people hold the same hopes as people in every land: to live in peace, and to raise their children in dignity.

Mr. President, I congratulate you on your election and assure you of the  full  support  of  Solomon  Islands.  I  also  commend  your

predecessor,  Her  Excellency  Ms.  Annalena  Baerbock,  for  her determined leadership of the eightieth session.

I  pay  special  tribute  to  Secretary-General  António  Guterres  as  he takes  part  in  his  final  General  Debate  in  office.  Mr.  Secretary-General,  you  have  been  a  true  champion  of  multilateralism  and  of Small  Island  Developing  States.  Your  unwavering  advocacy  on climate action and your repeated visits to our region told the world a simple truth: that the Pacific matters, and that our challenges, and how the world responds to them, remain a litmus test for us all.

We meet at a time when multilateralism is under serious strain, and when the notion that might is right appears to be making a return. Yet we continue to gather, in forums and dialogues around the world and here in the General Assembly, the pinnacle of multilateralism. That, in itself, is cause for hope.

National Priorities

For  my  people,  what  is  said  in  this  hall  is  measured  not  in declarations  but  in  results:  classrooms  with  teachers  and  books, clinics  with  medicines,  roads  that  reach  markets,  and  villages  that thrive. That is the lens through which Solomon Islands engages with the world.

My government is delivering a programme of national transformation. We are providing universal free education, so that no child is turned away from school because their family cannot afford the fees. We are strengthening our health system, with a renewed focus on tackling the scourge of non-communicable diseases, eradicating malaria and building a new national referral hospital.

We  are  prioritizing  energy  and  other  transformative  infrastructure, expanding roads, ports, airports and telecommunications to connect our scattered islands into one national economy. We are reforming

our  public  finance  systems  so  that  every  dollar  delivers  for  our people.  And  we  are  pursuing  constitutional  amendments  to strengthen our democracy. This is the agenda by which our people will judge my government.

International Peace and Security

Over  the  past  year,  the  international  community  has  faced  many challenges.  Protracted  armed  conflicts,  an  energy  crisis  and disruptions to global trade have been compounded by destabilization orchestrated by those who pursue their own selfish ambitions.

For small island economies, these are not distant events. Every rise in the price of fuel is felt in the cost of shipping, electricity, food and essential services, placing a heavy burden on communities that have no buffer against external shocks.

These tensions confirm what Solomon Islands has long understood: peace and security are inseparable from development. Neither can be secured without the other.

There  are  no  winners  in  war,  only  graves,  orphans  and  the  long labour of rebuilding what conflict has torn down.

There  is  no  substitute  for  dialogue,  diplomacy  and  peaceful negotiation. Solomon Islands calls on all parties to armed conflicts to protect civilians, return to the negotiating table and act in full respect of international law.

And it is why the world needs a stronger, more agile United Nations, one equipped to respond to the realities of today.

Transnational Crime, Illicit Drugs and Ocean of Peace

The Pacific faces a grave and growing threat. Transnational criminal networks  are  using  our  ocean  as  a  highway  for  illicit  drugs, undermining our sovereignty and national security, destroying young lives  and  tearing  at  the  fabric  of  our  communities.  Behind  every statistic stands a family, a community, and a young life robbed of its promise.

We will not allow criminal networks to profit from the vulnerability of our people. We are amending our Dangerous Drugs Act to introduce stiffer  penalties  as  a  deterrent,  and  we  are  strengthening  law enforcement  to  prevent  and  detect  these  crimes  and  to  hold perpetrators accountable.

In August this year, Solomon Islands acceded to the United Nations Convention  against  Transnational  Organized  Crime,  a  clear demonstration of our resolve to confront this threat.

These  are  costly  and  demanding  undertakings,  and  no  Pacific country  can  win  this  fight  alone.  We  call  for  stronger  international cooperation,  greater  information  sharing,  sustained  investment  in the  capacity  of  our  law  enforcement  agencies,  and  support  for prevention and rehabilitation.

Our  vision  of  a  peaceful  and  secure  Pacific  extends  beyond transnational crime. As enshrined in the Ocean of Peace Declaration, our  region  must  remain  free  of  nuclear  weapons  and  free  from destabilizing external influence.

In  keeping  with  that  vision,  my  government  has  proposed  a  treaty that would bind Pacific Island countries and like-minded partners to a firm, shared commitment to keep the Pacific an Ocean of Peace.

Artificial Intelligence and Emerging Technologies

Artificial  intelligence  and  emerging  technologies  present  both unprecedented opportunities and serious risks. They can accelerate sustainable  development,  transform  education  and  health  care, strengthen disaster preparedness, and open new economic pathways for developing countries.

But a widening digital divide threatens to leave developing countries further  behind.  For  my  government,  digital  transformation  is  not about  technology  for  its  own  sake;  it  is  about  connecting  our scattered islands and opening the modern economy to every Solomon Islander. The completion of 161 telecommunication towers across the country will lift national broadband coverage from 56 to 86 per cent, expanding  access  to  information,  education  and  digital  financial services.

The benefits of AI must be shared by all, not concentrated among a few. Its risks, including its use for non-peaceful purposes, must be governed  by  all,  not  left  to  a  few.  Solomon  Islands  therefore recognizes  the  need  for  an  inclusive  and  transparent  international governance framework on AI.

Climate Change

Year after year, Pacific leaders have stood at this podium and urged the world to act on climate change. And yet global action continues to fall short of what the science demands.

With every passing COP, the impacts grow more severe. Our islands are  being  lost  to  the  sea.  Disasters  are  more  frequent  and  more is  under  threat,  and devastating.  Food  and  water  security communities are being forced from their ancestral lands.

Solomon  Islands  knows  this  reality  first-hand.  This  year,  Tropical Cyclone  Maila,  a  Category  5  storm, tore  through  our  communities, destroying  homes,  schools,  infrastructure  and  livelihoods.  My

government has just approved US$9.38 million for shelter recovery. That is money our essential services urgently need, now diverted to deal with the impacts of this climate extreme.

Like  many  Pacific  Island  countries,  we  are  trapped  in  a  relentless cycle of response, recovery and rebuilding.

This is not sustainable, nor is it just. My people did the least to cause this  crisis,  yet  they  pay  its  earliest  and  heaviest  price.  That  is  the moral ledger that lies before this Assembly.

Last  year,  the  International  Court  of  Justice  confirmed  in  its landmark  advisory  opinion  that  States  have  legal  obligations  to protect the climate system.

Major emitters must make deep emission cuts and transition away from  fossil  fuels.  Climate  finance,  including  support  for  loss  and damage, must be grant-based and channelled through our national budget  systems.  Project-based  financing  of  climate  action  is unsustainable and out of step with the scale of a crisis we did least to cause.

Vulnerable  countries  should  not  have  to  choose  between  climate action and educating their children, caring for the sick or securing food  and  water. Yet  that  is  the  choice  we  face with  every  dollar  we spend.  We  therefore  call  for  the  full  capitalization  of  the  Pacific Resilience Facility and an ambitious and timely third replenishment of the Green Climate Fund.

Our  region  has  long  led  on  climate action,  and we  will  continue  to lead. The Pre-COP31 meeting, to be hosted in the Pacific by Australia in partnership with Fiji and Tuvalu, will bring the reality of climate change directly into the heart of the global process. I call on all Parties and partners to come to that meeting, and to COP31, with stronger commitments and concrete action. The communities on the frontline of the climate crisis deserve nothing less.

Sea-Level Rise

Solomon  Islands welcomes  the  convening  of  the  Second  High-Level Meeting  on  Sea-Level  Rise  and  the  adoption  of  the  first  political declaration on sea-level rise.

Every day, our people are defending their coastlines, strengthening their  resilience,  protecting  their  food  and  water  security  and  their cultural heritage, and, where there is no other choice, relocating.

But we cannot do this alone.

I  call  on  this  Assembly  to  match  the  courage  of  our  Pacific communities  with  collective  international  resolve:  to  scale  up adaptation and resilience finance and to support communities facing climate mobility needs.

Islands  reaffirms

Solomon that  maritime  boundaries,  once established and deposited in accordance with UNCLOS, together with the  rights  and  entitlements  that  flow  from  them,  shall  continue  to apply  notwithstanding  any  physical  changes  caused  by  climate change-related sea-level rise.

Ocean

The  ocean  is  not  simply  a  resource;  it  is  our  identity,  our  heritage and  our  future.  It  sustains  our  livelihoods,  our  culture  and  our economy.  We  do  not  own  the  ocean;  we  belong  to  it.  We  hold  it  in solemn trust for generations not yet born.

Yet our ability to benefit fully from our own ocean is undermined by illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing, which costs our region US$300 million every year. Solomon Islands is fighting back, working with the Forum Fisheries Agency and partners including Australia, France,  New  Zealand  and  the  United  States  to  strengthen surveillance and enforcement across our waters.

SDG  14  remains  among  the  least  funded  of  all  the  Sustainable Development Goals. With just four years left until 2030, the fourth United  Nations  Ocean  Conference  must  raise  the  bar  on  ocean finance  and  secure  the  ocean's  place  in  the  development  agenda beyond 2030.

Solomon  Islands  welcomes  the  entry  into  force  of  the  BBNJ Agreement and the preparations for the first Conference of the Parties in January. We look to that Conference to establish, without delay, the Secretariat and the institutional arrangements to implement the Agreement.

Plastic pollution is poisoning our ocean and our food. As negotiations resume in Bangkok, Solomon Islands calls for an ambitious, legally binding  treaty  that  addresses  the  full  life  cycle  of  plastics,  from production to disposal.

Youth, Women and Persons with Disabilities

Our  people  are  our  greatest  asset.  With  more  than  half  of  our population under the age of 25, my government is prioritizing legal frameworks  that  empower  young  people,  advance  gender  equality, and  strengthen  the  protection  of  women  and  children  against domestic violence.

We  welcome  global  progress  in  advancing  the  rights  and  full participation of women and persons with disabilities in the economy, and  Solomon  Islands  is  committed  to  accelerating  that  progress  at home.

There can be no sustainable development without equal opportunity for all.

International and Domestic Cooperation

Our  development  partnerships  play  an  indispensable  role  in infrastructure,  maritime  connectivity,  health  and expanding education, and in improving the lives of Solomon Islanders. I thank the  Governments  and  people  of  Australia,  China,  Japan,  New Zealand, the Republic of Korea and the United States, as well as the European Union, for their contributions to our national development.

South-South  cooperation  remains  an  important  complement  to Official  Development  Assistance.  Partnerships  among  developing countries have enabled us to share expertise, technology, innovation and practical solutions suited to our circumstances. The support of Papua New Guinea, Indonesia, India and our Pacific family embodies the true spirit of South-South solidarity, and we value it deeply.

We  also  acknowledge  the  partnership  of  multilateral  organizations, non-governmental organizations and our private sector in supporting development work in Solomon Islands.

At home, my government is working hand in hand with our churches to build stronger and more inclusive communities.

Cooperation and partnership, at every level and across borders, are critical  to  nation  building,  and  my  government  remains  fully committed to them.

Financing for Development

As  a  Small  Island  Developing  State,  our  vulnerability  remains  a fundamental  reality.  A  single  natural  disaster  can  erase  years  of investment and progress and push a nation backwards.

The  Multidimensional  Vulnerability  Index  captures  the  special circumstances of SIDS in a way that income measures alone cannot. We  call  on  international  financial  institutions  to  integrate  the  MVI into their financing decisions for SIDS without further delay.

Last year, the world spent more than US$2.9 trillion on its militaries. That is more than sixteen times all official development assistance. In less than 18 days, the world spends more on arms than developed countries provide in a full year of climate finance.

In the same year that military spending reached its highest share of global  output  since  2009,  development  aid  had  its  steepest  fall  on record. Bilateral aid to the least developed countries fell by a quarter.

This imbalance must be corrected. Redirecting even a small share of this spending would fully capitalize the Pacific Resilience Facility and the Loss and Damage Fund, secure the Green Climate Fund's third replenishment, and meet the ODA targets. The resources exist. What is missing is the will. The time to act is now.

LDC Graduation

Solomon  Islands  is  due  to  graduate  from  Least  Developed  Country status in 2027.

As part of our preparations, my government is pursuing an ambitious and proactive agenda that uses public-private partnerships to unlock investment  in  transformative  projects,  special  economic  zones  and key  sectors.  A  second  tuna  cannery  at  Bina  Harbour,  upgraded airports,  agricultural  treatment  facilities  to  support  trade,  and expanded road networks and maritime ports will shift the trajectory of our economy.

At  the  same  time,  my  government  is  strengthening  our  financial institutions  and  frameworks  to  improve  revenue  collection  and accountability,  so  that  we  can  sustain  our  development  priorities. These  reforms  reflect  our  commitment  to  a  strong  and  resilient economy  that  delivers  decentralized,  people-centred  development across the country.

Our ambition is clear: to graduate from LDC status with confidence, to  strengthen  the  foundations  of  our  economy,  and  to  ensure  that

development  delivers  lasting  opportunities  for  every  Solomon Islander.

UN Reform

As  the  United  Nations  marks  its  eighty-first  anniversary,  it  must continue to evolve to meet today's challenges while remaining faithful to its founding principles. The UN80 reform process must strengthen the  Organization's  effectiveness  and  relevance  without  diminishing its  presence,  services  or  support  in  the  most  vulnerable  regions, where assistance is needed most. Reform must enhance delivery, not reduce it.

The United Nations is not perfect, but it remains the cornerstone of multilateral  diplomacy  and  the  indispensable  platform  through which  nations  preserve  peace,  advance  sustainable  development, uphold international law and protect human rights.

Solomon  Islands  looks  to  the  next  Secretary-General  to  lead  with vision and to ensure that the Secretariat is accountable to all Member States,  serving  the  interests  of  small  and  large  States  on  an  equal footing.

Security Council Reform

Solomon Islands reiterates its support for comprehensive reform of the  Security  Council  to  make  it  more  representative,  transparent, accountable  and  reflective  of  today's  realities.  A  Council  with  a dedicated seat for Small Island Developing States would strengthen the legitimacy and effectiveness of the entire multilateral system.

The  veto  is  a  relic  of  1945.  Too  often,  it  has  been  used  to  shield violations of international law and to entrench the double standards that fuel conflict. At a minimum, the veto must never again be used

in  situations  of  genocide,  crimes  against  humanity  or  war  crimes. Ultimately, it should be abolished.

Peacekeeping

It is with great pride that Solomon Islands is once again contributing personnel to United Nations peacekeeping in South Sudan. Despite our small size, our participation reaffirms our enduring commitment to the Charter, to international peace and security, and to the noble work of peacekeepers serving communities affected by conflict.

I  thank  our  partners,  including  Australia  and  the  United  Nations Police, for their support. Solomon Islands looks forward to increasing its peacekeeping contribution in the coming year.

Decolonization

Leaving  no  one  behind  demands  that  we  complete  the  unfinished work  of  decolonization.  Solomon  Islands  reaffirms  its  longstanding support for the right to self-determination of the Kanak people of New Caledonia and the Maohi nui people of French Polynesia. The United Nations decolonization process must offer more than hope; it must provide  practical  pathways  to  the  full  emancipation  of  peoples  in Non-Self-Governing  Territories,  and  to  their  freedom  to  determine their own political future and development aspirations.

In  the  same  spirit,  I  turn  to  West  Papua,  whose  people  are  our Melanesian brothers and sisters.

Solomon Islands respects the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the  Republic  of  Indonesia,  and  we  value  our  friendship  with  its Government and people. It is precisely because of that friendship that we speak with candour. Reports of human rights violations in West

Papua have persisted for far too long. They must be independently verified, not left in dispute.

We therefore renew the call of Pacific Islands Forum Leaders for the Government of Indonesia to facilitate, without further delay, the long-awaited  visit  of  the  United  Nations  High  Commissioner  for  Human Rights to West Papua. Such a visit is an act of confidence between friends, and an affirmation that there is nothing to fear from the light.

Closing

Mr. President, in closing, the challenges of our time demand renewed solidarity, stronger multilateralism and genuine commitment to the principles  of  the  UN  Charter.  But  institutions  do  not  have  hearts; people do. Charters do not keep the peace; the men and women who honour them do. Beyond every declaration and commitment, each of us  carries  a  profound  responsibility:  to  be  agents  of  peace, champions of goodwill, and keepers of the fragile bonds of friendship among nations. The world has never needed that spirit more than it does today.

Mr.  President,  permit  me  a  word  from  the  Christian  faith  that  has shaped  my  people.  Our  Constitution  was  established  "under  the guiding  hand  of  God,"  by  a  people  "conscious  of  our  common destiny." We believe that is true not only of Solomon Islands, but of this whole family of nations.

We live in a time when division has become the calling card of the day. Nations are sorted into camps. Neighbours are asked to choose sides. Small States are too often treated as prizes to be won rather than partners to be heard. But the destiny of nations does not finally rest in this general assembly, nor in any capital, however powerful. King Solomon, among the wisest rulers of antiquity, wrote: "There are many devices in a man's heart; nevertheless, the counsel of the Lord, that shall stand."

That  truth  does  not  make  us  passive.  It  makes  us  humble,  and  it makes  us  accountable.  So  I  call  on  my  fellow  leaders  to  do  three things.

First,  let  us  ask  for  wisdom  before  we  ask  for  advantage.  When Solomon was offered anything he wished, he did not ask for riches, or  long  life,  or  the  defeat  of  his  enemies.  He  asked  for  "an understanding heart," so that he might judge his people well. I can think of no better prayer for every leader in this room.

Second, let us stay at the table. The same king taught that "in the multitude  of  counsellors  there  is  safety."  That  is  the  oldest  case  I know for what this Organization is meant to be: many nations, large and small, sitting together, because none of us sees far enough alone.

Third,  let  us  measure  greatness  rightly.  "Righteousness  exalteth  a nation." Not its arsenal, not its alliances, but its justice: how it treats the poor, the displaced, and the small.

Nations  rise  and  nations  fall.  The  purposes  of  God  endure.  Let  us choose cooperation over division, dialogue over confrontation, peace over hostility, and action over inaction. And let us lead as people who know we will answer for it one day.

Our national motto teaches us that “to lead is to serve”. In that spirit of service, Solomon Islands stands ready to do its part, as a willing partner and a committed Member of this Assembly.

May  God  bless  you  all,  and  may  God  bless  our  shared  family  of nations.

I thank you.

EXCELLENCIES,

DISTINGUISHED LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,

1.

I congratulate His Excellency Khalilur Rahman on his election as

President of the eighty-first session of the General Assembly.

2.

President Rahman assumes this responsibility at a moment that

demands principled and steady leadership, and he has Sierra

Leone’s full support.

3.

I  pay  tribute  to  His  Excellency  Secretary-General  António

Guterres, who is in the closing months of his mandate.

4.

He has served this Organisation with steadfastness, moral clarity

and the courage to speak difficult truths.

5.

I also commend Her Excellency Amina Mohammed, the Deputy

Secretary-General, for her exemplary service and distinguished

representation of Africa on the global stage.

6.

Nearly

twenty-five  years  ago,  Sierra  Leone  completed

disarmament and formally declared its civil war over.

7.

The  formal  declaration  matters,  but  peace  became  real  in

more practical ways: in the families that returned home, in the

communities that learned to live together again, in the citizens

who chose the ballot and in institutions that slowly earned back

confidence.

8.

The  United  Nations  stood  with  us  through  disarmament,

elections and the long work of peacebuilding.

9.

We  know  what  international  cooperation  can  make  possible

because we have lived it.

10.

That experience taught us that trust cannot be commanded by

declaration.

11.

Trust grows when promises are honoured, when the law protects

everyone,  when  institutions  serve  their  people,  and  when

citizens can see a future for themselves.

12.

Sierra Leone brings that lesson to this Assembly at a time when

trust  between  nations,

in

institutions  and

in  multilateral

cooperation is under profound strain.

13.

In this year’s theme, “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation:

A  United  Nations  That  Delivers  FOR  ALL,”  the  words  “FOR  ALL”

carry its defining moral weight.

14.

The  words  “FOR  ALL”  ask  not  only  whether  the  United  Nations

can act, but also whom its actions reach, whose voices shape

them, and whose dignity they protect.

15.  An institution may act quickly and still fail those it was meant to

serve.

16.  Delivery  worthy  of  the  UN  Charter  must  reach  those  furthest

from power and recognise the equal worth of every nation and

every human life.

17.

That is the standard by which the world will judge us.

18.

That  standard  begins  with  TRUST.  Trust  is  the  currency  of

multilateralism.

19.

Trust is gained when the law protects the vulnerable as firmly as

it restrains the powerful.

20.

International  law  must  not  change  with  geography  or  bend

according to the identity of the accused.

21.

In  the  Middle  East,  the  UN  Charter  and  international  law  must

guide  us.  Civilians  must  be  protected,  humanitarian  access

ensured, aggression and occupation ended, and freedom of

navigation safeguarded.

22.

The

inalienable  right  of

the  Palestinian  people

to  self-

determination  must  be  realised  through  a  viable  State  of

Palestine  living  alongside  the  State  of  Israel  in  peace  and

security.

23.

That same commitment to peace requires progress on nuclear

disarmament and non-proliferation through diplomacy.

24.

In  Sudan,  civilians  continue

to  endure  atrocities  and

displacement, underscoring the cost of delayed action.

25.

Sierra Leone calls for their protection, unhindered humanitarian

access,  accountability,  and  a  Sudanese-led  political  process

that  safeguards  the  country’s  sovereignty,  unity  and  territorial

integrity.

26.

In the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, agreements

have  not  yet  silenced  the  guns  or  allowed  millions  to  return

home.

27.  Across  West  Africa  and  the  Sahel,  terrorism  feeds  on  poverty,

exclusion, unemployment and weak institutions.

28.

These conflicts differ in origin and circumstance, but they carry

a common warning.

29.  Military action may contain a threat, but it cannot, by itself, build

lasting peace.

30.  When hunger, exclusion and despair deepen, insecurity takes

root.

31.

The  connection  between  peace  and  development  must

therefore move from our resolutions into our budgets.

32.

In 2025, global military expenditure reached almost 2.9  trillion

United  States  dollars,

the  eleventh  consecutive  annual

increase.

33.  Nations  have  legitimate  security  needs,  but  the  speed  with

which  the  world  finds  resources  for  war,  compared  with

prevention  and  development,  reveals  a  grave  disorder  in  our

priorities.

34.

The credibility of international law also depends on who has a

voice in applying it.

35.

That credibility weakens when the institutions entrusted with the

law preserve an unequal distribution of power.

36.

The Security Council still reflects the world of 1945. Africa, home

to more than 1.6 billion people and the subject of much of the

Council's work, still has no Permanent Seat.

37.  Africa seeks its rightful place because the Council cannot be

fully  legitimate  or  effective  while  an  entire  continent  remains

permanently absent from its highest level of decision-making.

38.  No durable global solution on peace, climate, food, energy or

technology can be built without African leadership.

39.

The  Common  African  Position,  espoused

in  the  Ezulwini

Consensus  and  Sirte  Declaration,  calls  for  no  fewer  than  two

Permanent Seats, with all the rights and privileges of permanent

membership, including the veto if it is retained, and five Non-

Permanent Seats.

40.  As  Coordinator  of  the  African  Union  Committee  of  Ten,  Sierra

Leone will continue to advance that position.

41.

Years  of  Intergovernmental  Negotiations  without  realising  the

reform have tested the credibility of the process.

42.

Before  this  session  concludes,  Member  States  should  have  a

consolidated model, which we committed to in the Pact for the

Future.

43.

Sierra  Leone  speaks  with  the  authority  of  service.  During  our

term on the Security Council in 2024 and 2025, we worked as a

voice of reason and a bridge across division.

44.  We convened the Security Council’s first high-level debate on

redressing

the  historical

injustice  against  Africa,  placed

conflict-related food insecurity at the centre of its agenda and,

with Guyana, co-drafted the unanimously adopted Resolution

2807  on  Youth,  Peace  and  Security,  strengthening  young

people’s role in conflict prevention and peacebuilding.

45.

Representation  becomes  meaningful  when

it  changes

decisions and improves lives.

46.

The  imbalance  within  the  Security  Council  is  also  present  in

International Financial Institutions, whose structures still bear the

imprint of an earlier age.

47.  Developing  countries  need

fairer  voting  power,  stronger

representation  and  increased  capital  within  these  institutions,

together  with  affordable  finance,  concessional  resources  and

fairer debt treatment.

48.

They  must  also  participate  equally  in  shaping  the  rules  of

international  taxation.  Sierra  Leone  therefore  supports  a  UN

Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation.

49.

Through ECOSOC, Sierra Leone will champion a development

system that responds more effectively to Africa’s priorities.

50.

Restoring  trust  and  delivering  for  all  must  also  embrace  the

unfinished cause of reparatory justice.

51.

In March, this Assembly adopted a resolution led by Ghana and

supported by the African Union and the Caribbean Community,

recognising the trafficking and racialised chattel enslavement

of Africans as the gravest crime against humanity.

52.

For Sierra Leone, this history is neither abstract nor distant.

53.

From  Bunce  Island,  in  our  own  river  estuary,  thousands  of

Africans  were  forcibly  transported  across  the  Atlantic  into

enslavement.

54.

Freetown, our capital, would later become a home for formerly

enslaved and liberated Africans. This history is woven into our

nation's identity.

55.

However,  the  consequences  did  not  end  with  abolition.  Their

legacy  continues  to  be  reflected  in  enduring  disparities  in

wealth, power and opportunity across our world.

56.

Reparatory justice is therefore not a plea for charity. It calls for

acknowledgement,  formal  apology,  the  return  of  cultural

heritage, fair redress and guarantees of non-repetition.

57.

Sierra Leone stands with Africa, the Caribbean and the wider

African diaspora in advancing this cause, not to remain captive

to the past, but to build a more just and equitable future.

58.

The  same  principle  of  fairness  applies  to  Africa's  critical

minerals.

59.  Critical  minerals  are  indispensable  to  the  global  energy

transition, yet too much value is still added elsewhere.

60.

Processing at source, fair value chains, technology transfer and

local  industry  would  turn  natural  wealth  into  skilled  work,

stronger economies and hope for our young people.

61.

The green transition must not reproduce the extractive terms of

the past.

62.

For the youth, this is immediate. A young person without work,

opportunity or a stake in the future becomes vulnerable to the

recruiter,  the smuggler  and  the  dangerous  journey across  the

Mediterranean.

63.

Jobs, skills and dignity are therefore part of any serious policy for

peace and development.

64.

Sierra Leone does not ask of the world what it does not demand

of itself. We carry these same principles into our work at home.

65.

Through  Feed  Salone,  we  are  increasing  domestic  food

production and strengthening food security.

66.

Through  Free  Quality  School  Education,  we  are  widening  the

path from the circumstances of a child's birth to the possibilities

of that child's future.

67.

In 2024, we enacted the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act and

subsequently championed the proclamation of 27 November

as the International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and

Forced Marriage.

68.  A  girl  in  Sierra  Leone  is  no  more  or  less  precious  than  a  girl

anywhere  else.  Protecting  her  childhood,  education  and

freedom is part of what development means.

69.  A  girl’s  future,  like  the  future  of  every  young  person,  will  be

shaped by forces already remaking our world: climate change,

artificial intelligence and the energy transition.

70.

The meaning of ‘FOR ALL’ becomes more urgent as we decide

how these transformations will be governed.

71.  Artificial  Intelligence  can  improve  education,  healthcare,

agriculture and public administration.

72.

It  can  also  widen  inequality  if  infrastructure,  knowledge  and

rule-making remain concentrated in a few countries.

73.  Developing  nations  must  help  shape  the  standards  that  will

govern technologies affecting their people.

74.  Climate  Change presents  the  same  moral  question  in  harsher

form: who benefits, who decides, and who pays?

75.

In Shenge, on Sierra Leone's southern coast, families watch the

sea take land, fishing grounds and the graves of their ancestors.

76.

For them, climate change is the disappearance of home in the

present.

77.

Those  who  contributed  least  to  the  climate  crisis  are  bearing

some of its greatest costs.

78.  Accessible  and  predictable  climate  finance,  support  for

adaptation, and effective arrangements for loss and damage

are obligations of justice.

79.

They are also investments in global stability.

80.

Fairness  in  transformation  depends  on  the  institutions  that

govern it.

81.

Sierra  Leone  therefore  supports  the  UN80  Initiative  and  wider

reforms

that  make

this  Organisation  more  effective,

accountable and responsive.

82.

Efficiency  matters  and  reform  must  preserve  the  capacity  to

act.

83.

The choice of the next Secretary-General offers another test of

institutional effectiveness and equality.

84.

In eighty years, every Secretary-General has been a man.

85.

The  women  put  forward  for  this  office  have  placed  their

competence beyond dispute.

86.  What  remains  is  the  will  of  this  Organisation  to  live  by  the

equality it asks of others and entrust a woman with its highest

office.

87.  Our  insistence  on  a  capable  United  Nations  comes  from

experience.

88.

For Sierra Leone, this Organisation is part of our living history. It

stood  with  us  when  our  country  was  broken  and  helped  us

make peace durable.

89.

In this Hall, a Small State has the same vote as a great power.

Imperfect  as  it  is,  that  equality  remains  one  of  humanity’s

boldest promises.

90.

Sierra  Leone  will  continue  to  contribute  personnel  to  United

Nations  peace  operations,  uphold  international  law,  support

mediation and peacebuilding, defend the rights of women and

girls, and serve as a bridge wherever Member States seek one.

91.  We will also continue to support the institutions of international

justice.

92.

In  this  regard,  Sierra  Leone  has  nominated  Professor  Charles

Chernor Jalloh, a distinguished international jurist, endorsed by

the African Union and ECOWAS, for election as a Judge of the

International Court of Justice.

93.  We respectfully seek Member States' support on 3 November.

94.

The United Nations was created in a world of unequal power,

yet it rests on a radical idea: nations differ in size and strength,

but their peoples do not differ in human worth.

95.  A United Nations that delivers ‘FOR ALL’ makes that equality felt

beyond this Hall.

96.  Nearly twenty-five years ago, Sierra Leoneans placed their trust

in peace because they believed tomorrow could be different.

97.

People around the world are asking something similar of us now.

98.

They  need  reason  to  believe  that  cooperation  still  works,  that

law still matters, and that promises made here will be honoured

in their lives.

99.

Let this session give them that reason.

100.  The words 'FOR ALL' should not remain at the end of this year’s

theme. They must become the measure of our work.

I THANK YOU.

President of the General Assembly, Secretary general. Your excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, as we're here talking about peace, international security and cooperation, thousands of people are dying victims of war hunger, violence, disease and injustice. It's as if we've lost our sense of humanity. It's not a future tragedy. The fact is that thousands, millions of people are dying as we're here. Right now, at this very moment, there will be mothers, fathers, children, entire families breaking up and asking themselves a question.

That's not an abstract one, a diplomatic one, or a geopolitical one. It's a fundamental question that they are asking with the most profound sense of humanity in a very human way. And that is, where are the United Nations? Where are the United Nations? This question, perhaps more than any other question, is the very reason we're here. And this is why I want to ask all of us here at this Assembly very seriously, with a strong sense of conviction, whether today we have an organization that is still relevant with a conviction to deal with the challenges that our humanity is dealing with.

That's the question, president. We are living through an extremely complex era where changes and challenges happen in a matter of seconds. These changes, and I think that we've all experienced them, overwhelm us. However, the most vulnerable people that suffer the most, the poorest people that don't have a voice and who we. Owe it to work for, are aspiring to something much more simple. They just want peace, security, jobs, freedom, and a safe future for their children.

And this is the greatest contradiction of our time. We have more capacities than ever before, but we also face challenges that no state can tackle alone. As the United Nations, we need to commit ourselves and work to redefine the international order so that we can prioritize the common well-being of the whole of humanity, regardless of whether of where they live and their condition guarantee the well-being of our brothers and sisters, the whole of humanity. We need a multilateral system that is able to listen, but also to make decisions, to safeguard present principles, to respect the sovereignty of states. But that at the same time understands that no state can resolve problems that know no borders alone. The fact is that the credibility of the United Nations is not something that we can build exclusively with resolutions.

On the contrary, its legitimacy is achieved when the organization is really, truly able to preserve and save people's lives and to ensure a decent future for all people. And this is something that El Salvador has firsthand experience in. Mr. president, for decades, my small but great country was known for a reality that it seemed impossible to change. The scourge of violence was deeply entrenched in our society. An entire nation was resigned to being condemned to live with this reality. After decades of institutional indifference.

In 2019, the El Salvadoran people opted for Nayib Bukele, our president, who is now known across the world, a young leader who dared to challenge something that an entire generation thought they were condemned to and strove to profoundly transform the reality of our country, regardless of the consequences or the criticisms he had received from the international community. El Salvador went from being the most violent country in the world, with. A murder rate of 103 people per 100,000 inhabitants. We as a country in peace, had more deaths than a country at war. So we moved from 103 murders per 100,000 inhabitants to 1.3 murders per 100,000 inhabitants in just five years. Unimaginable.

Just think about it. But we achieved that. Por eso. Thank you. So thanks to this, my country is now a benchmark for others who suffer from the same problem. The International Monetary Fund has said that improvements for security has strengthened trust in and, uh, the economic activity of my country.

And it's estimated the El Salvadorian economy will grow by 4.5% in 2026. So this has skyrocketed. And this is driven by investment, private consumption, remittances, tourism and inward capital flows. However, it would be a mistake to boil all of this down to numbers, because behind each and every number, these numbers that we have got used to when we say millions, um, they're not just numbers, they're millions of faces, individual people, individuals. So in my country, uh, that we're talking about a mother who no longer, uh, has to be scared about whether her children are coming home in the evening or not. Uh, a business owner who used to pay face so much anxiety that knew that their basket of mangoes that they, um, had to sell, they had to sell them for more than $10.

Because if they didn't sell them for more than $10, they wouldn't be able to pay their protection money and they'd get shot in the head. So now behind these figures, we have a business owner who's able to open their business without fear, somebody who's able to breathe easily and cross the city freely, and a child who's able to run around all of the streets of our country, streets and spaces that they weren't able to dream of going in before, and something more profound, even the fact is that we now have a society that has recovered hope, grounded in the ability to imagine a different future. This is what recovering security really means. It doesn't just mean reducing crime, it means giving freedom its rights, its rightful space back. And I'm talking about freedom for each and every one of our citizens and each and every person that visits our country. And when a society recovers its freedom to walk around, to work, to do business and to live and breathe without fear, a second transformation begins.

That is the recovery of trust. And this explains why El Salvador is now a benchmark for countries that are seeking support and looking for answers to their own security challenges. And it's not that our journey can be copied and pasted mechanically because there's no universal formula. Each situation needs to be resolved according to each country's individual experience However, there is a lesson that we believe can be a universal lesson, and that is that no nation should have to accept collapse and government impotence as their destiny, the destiny for their people. No country. El Salvador, no.

El Salvador has not come to this assembly to say that we've resolved all of our problems. No, we still got a lot to do. That would be false. To claim that we've come to say something much more profound. With determination, we have demonstrated that a problem that seemed irreversible could be tackled and turned around, regardless of whatever problem it is. And I want to be clear in line with the vision of my president, Mr. Bucheli, security is not the final destination.

It's just the departure point. In El Salvador We have placed education at the very heart of our national transformation, and we've done this because we believe that transforming a school ultimately leads to transforming someone's life, transforming our homeland. And with initiatives like the school two schools per day initiative, we are overhauling public education education comprehensively from early childhood to middle school and in healthcare. We've renewed infrastructure, modernized equipment and created digital care through Doctor S-v and, um We have managed to reach the length and breadth of our country, even the most forgotten corners, and providing immediate care for anyone who needs it, regardless of whether of wherever they live. Um, care is free and drugs are free too. And we are the first in the world to achieve this feat.

The vision of our first Lady, Gabriela Rodriguez de Bucheli, uh, is a profoundly human one. And that is that every boy girl, each and every young person, deserves to grow up in liberty to fully develop their potential and to have real opportunities to build the life that he or she wants for him or herself. Now, the efforts of our nation are focused on turning security into investment, investment into jobs and jobs, into social mobility technology, into opportunities and education, into skills and stability and to prosperity. Heading up alongside Estonia, the Global Dialogue on Artificial Intelligence Governance, El Salvador reaffirmed that this technology must expand um capacities and create opportunities to build environments that can be competitive in the future. Mr. president, the transformation that my country is experiencing has shown us that security, development and human dignity are not separate files. The fact is that without security, development is fragile.

Without development, it's very difficult to make security sustainable and without dignity. Neither of these things make any sense. The international community must understand that resolving these challenges, these global challenges, goes above and beyond, well beyond actually, uh, any resolutions, millions of resolutions on paper. Multilateralism that does not oblige countries to constantly choose between sovereignty and cooperation. Today, we have an historical and inexcusable challenge, and that is making multilateralism, uh, synonymous. Synonym again, with capacity to act.

El Salvador believes that the reform of the United Nations should not be restricted to reorganising its structures. We need an organisation that is agile, representative, effective and transparent that's able to, um, resolve contemporary challenges with the speed required. So enough with the conformism. Enough of, um, personal and national interests prevailing over the needs of the world and global crises. And enough, ladies and gentlemen. Enough with the bureaucracy.

Let us hope that. The next Secretary General of the United Nations is able to show leadership with absolute full independence and ability to engage in dialogue, moral authority, knowledge of the international reality, and with and and that they have a willingness to reform and a conviction that we need to reform to benefit humanity, like my president, Bill Kelly, regardless of the consequences, because one human life is worth it. Just a single life is worth the effort. El Salvador, in a short but historic period of seven years, made strong strides forward to change our reality, recovering our security, our spaces, trust, dignity. However, we did this while always fighting to safeguard our sovereignty because our sovereignty is not up for negotiation, our sovereignty. Is not, mustn't, must not be touched.

We are resolved to defend it because we spilt too much blood, recovering our sovereignty. I am convinced that each and every one of my compatriots within Our borders, as well as those outside of our borders, would be prepared to defend our homeland and our sovereignty with the highest level of commitment and sacrifice. Today, El Salvador wants to leave this assembly with four fundamental lessons. Number one. That nations are not condemned to eternally repeating their past. Two, the problems, even if they may seem impossible to resolve, are not impossible to resolve.

Number three, that the um challenge the size of a country with a very small country does not, um, determine the size of our responsibility. And that the future does not necessarily have to belong to those that have the most power. It belongs to those who dare to engage in transformations with a sense of determination. El Salvador's invitation to this General Assembly is very simple. Let us not give in. Let us not accept that war, poverty and violence are inevitable.

Let us not accept that this organization is, um, condemned to incapacity. And let us not accept that differences between nations are more powerful than what unites us. Today we must ask a vital question for the present and future of our nations. And that is what, Bill, what world do we want to build to ensure that nobody dies, that no innocent person has to suffer? So that the whole of humanity, regardless of their country, their origin, their social condition? Is able to prosper?

El Salvador already made a decision on our own future, and this is something I don't say lightly. Today we come here to declare loud and clear that change is possible not merely in words, but in deeds. It is possible to change, and we are doing this. We're demonstrating this through our actions and not with words. And we will continue to change. And we will not take a single step back because it's possible to do it.

We can thank you and may God bless all of you.

speaker_post: Minister for Foreign Affairs, Political Affairs, International Economic Cooperation and Digital Transition
text:
Mr. Secretary-General, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen,

San  Marino  is  the  world’s  oldest  Republic.  For  more  than seventeen centuries, we have survived not through military power, territorial  expansion  or  economic  might,  but  through  dialogue, respect  for  the  law,  neutrality,  and  the  conviction  that  the sovereignty of a small State is no less valuable than that of a great power.

Our  history  has  taught  us  a  simple  lesson:  when  power  is  not enough  to  protect  you,  rules  matter.  When  you  cannot  impose your  will,  dialogue  matters.  And  when  the  world  is  divided, institutions that bring States together matter.

This  is  why  multilateralism  is  not  an  abstract  concept  for  San Marino. It is a fundamental principle of our foreign policy, and, in many ways, a lesson drawn from our own history.

Our commitment to cooperation and shared rules is also reflected in our relationship with the European Union.

The forthcoming signing of the Association Agreement with the European  Union  on  19  October  will  mark  a  milestone  for  our country.

It  represents  a  historic  step  towards  closer  cooperation,  shared rules  and  greater  integration  with  the  European  Union,  while fully  preserving  our  sovereignty,  identity  and  institutional specificities.

For San Marino, this is not simply an agreement about economic relations. It is a long-term choice to deepen our engagement with Europe while preserving the distinctive character of our Republic.

It is a choice that reflects a principle at the heart of our history: cooperation  does  not  diminish  sovereignty.  For  a  small  State, cooperation,  rules  and  dialogue  are  precisely  what  allow sovereignty to be exercised and protected.

Today, that principle is under extraordinary pressure.

Eighty-one  years  ago,  the  United  Nations  was  created  to  save succeeding generations from the scourge of war.

Yet  today,  conflicts  are  multiplying.  Inequalities  are  deepening. Climate disruption is accelerating. Food and water are increasingly being  used  as  instruments  of  pressure.  And  the  rules  that  have governed international relations for decades are being challenged.

We are witnessing the use of force against sovereign States. We are witnessing  violations  of  international  humanitarian  and  human rights law.

At such a moment, the answer cannot be less multilateralism.

It must be more.

And it must be a multilateralism that works: one that protects the weak as well as the strong; one that applies the law equally; and one that gives every State, large or small, a meaningful voice.

Before  turning  to  the  challenges  before  us,  allow  me  to congratulate H.E. Dr. Khalilur Rahman on his election as President of the eighty-first session of the General Assembly.

San Marino supports the priorities of your programme and stands ready to cooperate fully with you and with all Member States in the year ahead.

I  also  wish  to  express  our  appreciation  to  Secretary-General António  Guterres  for  his  leadership  at  a  time  of  profound international  uncertainty,  and  for  his  continued  efforts  to strengthen the United Nations and the multilateral system.

There can be no world in which might makes right.

Sovereignty,  territorial  integrity,  political  independence  and  self-determination matter. These principles are not optional and they cannot  depend  on  the  size  of  a  country  or  the  power  of  a government.

There can be no impunity for violations of international law. The law must apply to all.

For San Marino, this is not an abstract principle. For small States, international law is our protection. It is the ultimate equalizer.

A rules-based international order allows every State, large or small, to have an equal voice and equal legal standing.

This is why San Marino strongly supports the Secretary-General’s UN80 initiative.

The  United  Nations  must  become  more  effective,  more  efficient and more responsive.

And reform must include the Security Council.

The  Council  must  better  reflect  today’s  world.  It  must  be  more representative, transparent and accountable.

San Marino is also a member of the Uniting for Consensus group and supports its efforts to promote a comprehensive and balanced reform  of  the  Security  Council,  based  on  greater  regional representation,  equitable  geographical  distribution  and  wider access to elected seats.

Reform must strengthen the voice of all Member States, including small States, and it must be achieved through broad consensus.

We support efforts to restrain the use of the veto, including the French-Mexican  initiative  and  the  ACT  Code  of  Conduct  in involving  mass  atrocities,  alongside  the  General situations Assembly veto initiative.

We  also  reaffirm  our  full  support  for  the  International  Court  of Justice. Its orders and judgments are legally binding. Respect for the Court is respect for the international legal order.

The next Secretary-General will carry a vital responsibility.

The United Nations must remain relevant and credible. Above all, it  must  remain  capable  of  protecting  people  and  upholding  the Charter.

San Marino stands ready to contribute.

I now turn to one of the most painful crises of our time.

The situation in the Middle East demands clarity.

San  Marino  unequivocally  condemns  terrorism,  including  the horrific attacks of 7 October 2023.

But  we  must  be  equally  clear  on  another  point:  the  Palestinian people  have  an  inalienable  right  to  self-determination  and  to their own State.

Statehood is not a reward for terrorism. It is a right.

At the same time, nothing can justify the collective punishment of civilians.

The suffering in Gaza cannot become the new normal.

We call for a permanent ceasefire and for full, safe and unhindered humanitarian  access.  Humanitarian  assistance  must  reach  those who need it. Civilian lives must be protected. UNRWA and other humanitarian organizations must be able to operate.

We call for the permanent disarmament of Hamas and other non-State armed groups, and for the withdrawal of Israeli forces from the Gaza Strip.

We  support  the  Palestinian  Authority  and  its  reform  efforts, including democratic elections.

We  urge  Israel  to  release  withheld  clearance  revenues  and  to facilitate  correspondent  banking  services  for  the  Palestinian Authority.

In  the  West  Bank  and  East  Jerusalem,  settlement  expansion, settler  violence,  land  appropriation,  demolitions  and  evictions rapidly  deteriorating  amid is must  stop. These  developments  undermine  the  possibility  of  a  viable Palestinian State.

The  Status  Quo  of  Jerusalem’s  holy  sites  must  be  respected.  All communities, including Christian communities, must be protected.

Escalation  across  the  region  threatens  international  peace  and security.

We  are  deeply  concerned  by  hostilities  involving  Iran  and  by threats  to  maritime  security  in  the  Red  Sea  and  the  Strait  of Hormuz.

Freedom of navigation is essential to global stability. International law, including UNCLOS, must be respected.

In  Lebanon,  we  call  for  full  respect  for  sovereignty  and  for  the implementation  of  Security  Council  resolution  1701.  Civilian infrastructure must be protected.

In Syria, we support an inclusive and peaceful political transition that  respects  sovereignty,  protects  civilians  and  strengthens institutions.

Peace  cannot  be  imposed  by  force.  It  requires  diplomacy  and dialogue. And it requires international law.

Europe  is  also  facing  a  war  that  continues  to  cause  immense human suffering.

San  Marino  condemns  Russia’s  ongoing  aggression  against Ukraine.

The bombardment of cities.

The killing of civilians.

Attacks on humanitarian workers.

The unlawful deportation of children.

These  are  not  simply  tragedies.  They  are  violations  of international law.

No State can be allowed to redraw borders by force.

San Marino therefore reiterates its call for a full, immediate and unconditional  ceasefire,  leading  to  a  comprehensive,  just  and lasting peace.

Any peace must respect Ukraine’s sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders.

From  Ukraine  to  Gaza,  from  Sudan  to  Syria,  from  the  Sahel  to Afghanistan, civilians continue to pay the highest price.

Women, Children, Older people. Families forced from their homes. Hospitals  and  schools  destroyed.  Food,  water  and  medicines denied.

International  humanitarian  law  was  created  precisely  for  these circumstances.

It  does  not  disappear  in  times  of  war.  It  is  not  suspended  by political convenience. It must be respected.

San  Marino  strongly  condemns  the  use  of  explosive  weapons  in populated areas and calls on all States to implement the Political Declaration on Explosive Weapons in Populated Areas.

Those  who  deliver  humanitarian  assistance  must  also  be protected. Aid workers and journalists are not legitimate targets.

San  Marino  also  reaffirms  its  commitment  to  the  Australia-led Declaration  for  the  Protection  of  Humanitarian  Personnel,  and calls  on  all  parties  to  armed  conflict  to  respect  and  protect humanitarian personnel and to ensure that  assistance can reach those in need.

San  Marino  therefore  reaffirms  its  commitment  to  the  Geneva Conventions, the Genocide Convention and the Rome Statute.

And  we  reiterate  our  unwavering  support  for  the  International Criminal Court.

The  Court  exists  because  the  gravest  crimes  cannot  go unanswered: genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity.

Accountability  is  not  an  obstacle  to  peace.  It  is  part  of  lasting peace.
