Recent political pressure and coercive measures against the Court, its officials and those who cooperate with it are deeply concerning. States Parties to the Rome Statute must defend the independence and integrity of the Court.

San Marino also reaffirms its historic commitment to the abolition of the death penalty, which it abolished in 1865. This reflects our enduring conviction that human dignity must be protected even in the face of the gravest crimes.

Justice cannot depend on political power.

Five years ago, the Taliban seized power in Afghanistan.

Five  years  is  too  long  for  half  of  a  population  to  be  denied  its rights.

Afghan women and girls continue to face systematic restrictions on education,  employment,  movement,  public  participation  and access to justice.

Girls  remain  excluded  from  secondary  and  higher  education. Women  are  increasingly  excluded  from  public  life.  This  cannot become normal.

San Marino calls for the full restoration of the rights of Afghan women and girls.

Education is a right. Work is a right. Participation in public life is a right. Dignity is a right.

These rights do not disappear because a government chooses to deny them.

The international community must continue to stand with Afghan women and girls.

Humanitarian access must also remain unhindered.

Afghanistan must not be forgotten.

Children  everywhere  deserve  protection.  Children  are  being killed,  maimed,  abducted  and  recruited.  They  are  losing  their homes, their schools and their futures.

San Marino remains firmly committed to the Children and Armed Conflict  agenda  and  supports  the  work  of  the  UN  Special Representative for Children and Armed Conflict.

Schools must remain safe places.

We  have  endorsed  the  Safe  Schools  Declaration,  the  Paris Principles and the Vancouver Principles.

We  call  on  all  States  to  strengthen  the  protection  of  children  in armed  conflict  and  to  ratify  the  Optional  Protocol  to  the Convention on the Rights of the Child.

The return of nuclear threats is another source of grave concern.

There  can  be  no  acceptable  nuclear  threat  or  acceptable  use  of nuclear weapons.

The  modernization  and  expansion  of  nuclear  arsenals,  together with growing military expenditures and the rapid development of artificial  intelligence  and  cyber  capabilities,  increase  the  risk  of escalation.

The consequences of nuclear use would be catastrophic.

San  Marino  remains  committed  to  a  world  free  of  nuclear weapons.

We  support  the  Treaty  on  the  Non-Proliferation  of  Nuclear Weapons. We also proudly uphold the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, which San Marino has signed and ratified.

Diplomacy must prevail over deterrence through fear.

Peace and security cannot be separated from development. Nor can development be separated from human rights.

Conflict  destroys  development  gains.  Poverty  fuels  instability. food,  water  and increases  pressure  on Climate  change communities.

We  must  also  not  overlook  the  devastating  humanitarian  and socio-economic  situation  in  Cuba,  where  prolonged  hardship  is placing an immense burden on the daily lives of the Cuban people.

We  must  therefore  treat  peace,  security,  human  rights  and sustainable development as parts of the same agenda.

The  SDGs  remain  our  common  commitment.  The  Pact  for  the Future provides an opportunity to strengthen multilateralism and accelerate implementation of the 2030 Agenda.

But commitments are not enough.

We need implementation, financing and accountability.

We  also  need  a  fairer  and  more  inclusive  international  financial architecture,  supported  by  adequate  resources  and  greater financial stability for the UN itself.

The triple planetary crisis - climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution - is already affecting peace and security.

Environmental  degradation  fuels  food  insecurity,  water  scarcity and displacement.

The Paris Agreement must be fully implemented.

The 1.5-degree goal must remain within reach, the transition must be just and no country should be left behind.

Food  security  must  also  remain  at  the  heart  of  our  collective efforts.

Conflict and climate shocks are driving hunger and malnutrition.

San  Marino  believes  that  reducing  food  loss  and  waste  is  one practical  contribution  to  a  more  secure  and  sustainable  food system.

We are also entering a new technological era.

Artificial intelligence and emerging technologies offer enormous opportunities, but they also create new risks.

Technology  must  serve  humanity.  It  must  not  be  used  to undermine  human  rights,  international  peace  or  international humanitarian law.

The rules must keep pace with innovation.

And where new technologies create new risks, our responsibility is not to look away, but to govern them.

This is why multilateralism matters.

Multilateralism is not an outdated idea. It is the only framework capable of managing an interdependent world.

No  country  can  address  today’s  challenges  alone,  protect  itself from climate change alone, prevent the proliferation of nuclear weapons alone or regulate global technology alone.

And no country can build lasting peace alone.

We need cooperation and institutions that work. And we need the political courage to uphold the rules we have created together.

For more than seventeen centuries, San Marino has shown that a small  State  can  preserve  its  independence  through  dialogue, respect  for  the  law  and  engagement  with  the  international community.

This is why San Marino will continue to defend the United Nations Charter, international law, human rights and multilateralism.

At a time when the world is tempted by division, we must choose cooperation. When force challenges law, we must stand firmly by the law.

And when despair is growing, we must choose peace.

San Marino will do its part.

Together, we must ensure that the United Nations remains what it was created to be: a shield for the vulnerable, a forum for dialogue and a guardian of peace, dignity and international law.

Thank you.

This partnership is one  in  which  national  institutions  are  strengthened  rather  than  bypassed  and  both governments and international organisations are mutually accountable for results.

Somalia  is  successfully  leading  on  its  own  national  development.  Our  government  is implementing  the  National  Transformation  Plan,  strengthening  public  financial  management, expanding domestic revenue, and investing in the capabilities of our national institutions.

For over five decades, our people have dreamed of choosing their leaders through their votes. The  last  such  election  was  held  in  1969.  Today,  we  are  determined  to  change  that  history. Through constitutional reform, we are laying the foundation for universal suffrage, accountable institutions, and a multi-party-political system that allows every Somali citizen to have a voice.

We engaged all Somali political leaders, Federal Member states, civil society, women, youth, and the diaspora to take part constructively in our hopeful political transition. Our aim is to become an effective democracy where differences are resolved through dialogue, law, and elections, not violence.

We  invite  the  United  Nations  and  our  international  partners  to  support  this  transition  by helping  to  strengthen  democratic  institutions  but  always  respecting  our  ownership  of  Somali democracy. This is a new progressive chapter where political power is determined by citizens guided by constitutional law and safeguarded by the rule of law.

That  is  how  we  are building  a  durable Somali state.  Ours  is  a  democracy  where  every  citizen has a  voice, where  every vote has value, and where  every  government is  accountable. That is our commitment to our people and to the world.

Somalia  also  continues  to  confront  international  terrorism  with  determination  and  with  the support of our international partners. We are strengthening our national security institutions, improving  force  generation,  developing  intelligence  capabilities  and  expanding  security cooperation  with our neighbours and the  rest  of the  world. But the  fight against  terrorism in Somalia must not be understood as Somalia’s responsibility alone. We stand on the front line of a struggle that directly affects regional and international security.

We  therefore  call  for  predictable  and  sustainable  support  for  Somalia’s  security  transition, including adequate financing for the African Union Mission in Somalia. is  narrowing,  while

pressure  on  states  to  choose  sides  is

steadily  increasing.  At  the  same  time,

disagreements

among

the  most

powerful

actors

are

increasingly

paralyzing

the  very

institutions

should  be  protecting  all  countries

equally.  The

traditional  system  of

international

justice

seriously

undermined  whenever  interests  prevail

over  law  and  the  same  rules  do  not

apply to everyone.

The greatest problem of today is not the

lack  of  rules  or  political  principles,  but

the fact that they were not respected in

the  past  or  now.    You  will  notice,  dear

friends, that today, with the exception of

a few countries, everyone speaks of and

invokes the UN Charter, the spirit of the

Charter, and the principles on which the

world  order  that  was  in  force  until

recently  was  based  on.  It  is  as  though

they  want  to  tell  us,  “Never  mind,  it

doesn’t count” — that the fact that in the

past  we  tore  down  and  violated  that

Charter,  by  which  we  opened  a

Pandora’s box which is impossible to be

closed, and today we would like, without

consequences,  to  return  to  the  future.

They  would

like

revitalize

observance of the very same principles

that  powerful  and  great  countries

trampled so brutally.

How many times over the past two days,

from this rostrum, have you heard calls

and  appeals  for  observance  of  the

principles  of  international  public  law,

particularly when it comes to the conflict

in  Ukraine,  while  the  majority  of  those

same

countries

shamelessly  and

recklessly  remain  silent  about  the  fact

that  they  themselves  participated  in

trampling the Charter and destroying the

foundations  of  the  international  public-

law system — and today they would, at

any cost, like to return to those principles

now  that  they  see  that  more  powerful

and stronger ones have resorted to the

very

same

violations

they

themselves carried out when they were

the  most  powerful  and  the  strongest.

Here  I  am  referring  to  all  the  countries

that recognized the unilaterally declared

independence  of  the  so-called  Kosovo

and,  without  any  basis  whatsoever  in

international

legal

documents,

attempted to seize 14 % of the territory

of  the  Republic  of  Serbia.  To  many  of

you, this may sound like a distant past,

but the wounds inflicted on international

public  law  are  becoming  ever  deeper

and  more  severe.  To  be  completely

precise, the order based on respect for

the  UN  Charter  and  the  law  founded

upon it no longer exists. It was destroyed

by those who tore apart the territories of

other countries for the sake of their own

political  and  economic  interests.  They

did  so  unscrupulously,  recklessly,  and

shamelessly.  Do  you  know,  esteemed

friends, what was, in fact, the reason —

the sole official and formal reason — for

the attack on the territory of the Republic

of  Serbia  and  the  Federal  Republic  of

Yugoslavia,  carried  out  by  19  NATO

countries?   You will not believe it. They

told  us

they  had  attacked  a

sovereign,

free,  and

independent

country  in  order  to  prevent  a  potential

humanitarian

disaster.

The

humanitarian disaster did not occur, and

I have still not managed to hear or see

where  a  similar  example  has  occurred

anywhere  in  the  world.  The  attack

against that small, yet free and freedom-

loving country, Serbia, of which I am the

proud president, was carried out with the

intention  of  finally  destroying  the  UN

order established after the World War II,

and of formally and informally confirming

the  dominance  of  at  that  time  unison

Western world, of America and Europe.

Do you know which countries took part

in  decision-making  in  the  UN  Security

Council  to  bomb  an  independent  and

sovereign country that had attacked no

other country? Not a single soldier, not a

single police officer from Serbia had set

foot on the territory of any other country,

and  yet  the  decision  was  made.  I  am

certain  that  most  of  you,  dear  friends,

who  are  among  those  best  informed

about  world  politics,  no

longer

remember  much  of  this  either  —  and

especially not the fact of who in the UN

Security Council voted for that decision,

or perhaps in the General Assembly. Do

not even try, because it is impossible for

you to remember. Why? Because such

a  decision  was  never  made  in  the  first

place, and to make things even worse,

no  one  ever  even  attempted  to  make

such a decision. They were so arrogant

and  so  powerful  that  they  trampled

everything in their path. From the Clinton

administration  to  the  administrations  of

numerous  European  countries.  That  is

precisely  why  Serbia  supports

actions  of

the  Administration  of

President Donald Trump and sees in his

work  an  opportunity  for  establishing  a

more  just  order  in  the  world  and  more

responsible attitude towards Serbia as a

close  American  ally  from  both  World

Wars.

And  what

they  did  not  know  or

understand  at  the  time  was  this:  they

trampled Serbia, but they did not defeat

it.  Serbia  rose  like  a  phoenix  from  the

ashes. And today, through its example,

it shows everyone in the world how the

international  public  order  is  preserved

and  how  international  public  law  is

protected.

Nevertheless,

consequences  of

that  brutal  attack

against  Serbia  are  enormous  and

particularly  visible  here

the  UN

General Assembly. Admittedly, they are

even  more  visible  on  the  numerous

battlefields  around  the  world.  Why?

Well,  because  the  principles,  of  any

kind,  no  longer  exist.  Those  who  once

trampled  them  have  no  moral  right  to

speak  about  them.  And  to  make  the

situation even worse, and the hypocrisy

even  more  visible,  it  is  precisely  those

very  people  and  those  very  countries

who  have  assumed  the  position  of

supreme  teachers  of  moral  and  every

kind  of  protection  of  the  values  of  the

modern  world.    The  most  difficult  thing

for  us  in  Serbia  is  when  we  see  in  our

surroundings the resurgence of Nazism

elevated

the  position  of  social

prominence,  especially  in  the  Republic

of Croatia, which is proud of its Nazi past

and  of  the  use  of  Nazi  slogans  and

symbols today. The Serbian people, as

people who suffered the most from Nazi

hands, cannot accept the revival of the

most

terrible  ghosts

from

the  past

responsible for the death of hundreds of

thousands of Serbs, Jews, and Roma in

monstrous  concentration  camps

like

Jasenovac. That is precisely why moral

lectures coming from such sources are

completely unacceptable to the Serbian

people and Serbia.

In addition, for four and a half years now,

I  have  been  listening  to  lectures  how

many in the West remain the last beacon

of democracy in the world, the protectors

not  of  Ukraine’s,  but  of  the  rules  and

principles of international law. And when

they raise their voices, thinking that they

are  being  highly  moral  and  that  their

positions  are  the  only  right  ones,  we

simply  smile  and  ask  ourselves:  “And

how did you treat Kosovo and Metohija

and  the  territorial  integrity  of  Serbia

which is guaranteed by the UN Charter

and  the  Resolution  of  the  UN  Security

Council 1244?” To that, either there is no

answer,  or  they  supposedly  give  us

some well-intentioned advice and tell us

not to look to the past, but to the future.

When we ask them, “Do you also say to

Ukraine  that  the  territories  they  are

fighting for are not important?”, we end

the pointless conversation and move on

to another subject. And I want to warn all

of you. All of you here who belong to the

Global  South.  Pay  the  utmost  attention

while  signing  all  the  agreements  with

great powers. That is how we signed the

famous  Brussels  Agreement  in  2013,

wishing  to  resolve  problems  between

Serbs  and  Albanians  in  Kosovo  and

Metohija  by  compromise.  All

obligations that were to be met by Serbia

have been met, and the only one that the

was  to  be  bet  by  Albanians,  the  one

about

the  establishment  of

Community  of  Serb  Municipalities,  has

not been met to this day. It is interesting

that  the  Agreement  was  accepted  not

only in the presence of the EU but it was

also confirmed with the signature of the

EU,  but

it  meant  nothing.  As

President of Serbia, for 10 years I have

been  facing  all  possible  tricks  and

pressures

give

up

on

full

implementation of what was signed. It is

a  lesson  to  us  Serbs,  but  also  to  all

others in the world who want to protect

their  country.  In  spite  of  everything,

Serbia  will  defend

its  country,

its

territorial  integrity,  the  UN  Charter  and

the  UN  Security  Council  Resolution

1244.

I wish to thank, individually, every of

107  states  that  has  not  recognized  the

unilaterally  declared  independence  of

the  so-called  Kosovo.  We  know  that

many  of

those  states  have  been

subjected to pressure, and we know that

maintaining  a  principled  position

sometimes  far  more  difficult  than  it

appears from the outside. Thank you for

being  consistent  in  not  recognizing  the

independence  of  a  part  of  Serbia’s

territory.

Serbia is on its European path and it will

have to do many more things in order to

become  a  full-fledged  member  of  the

EU.  We  are  grateful  to  the  European

Union, and in particular to the President

of the European Commission Ursula von

der  Leyen  and  to  the  President  of  the

European  Council  Antonio  Costa  for

every  kind  of  assistance  they  have

provided  to  our  country.  Although  full-

fledged  membership  to  the  European

Union  remains  a  strategic  priority,  we

cannot

ignore

prolonged

enlargement

fatigue,  both  among

certain  EU  Member  States  and  among

the  candidate  countries

themselves.

Serbia’s  European  path

is  a  clear

illustration of the length and complexity

of this process. We obtained candidate

status  in  2012  and  opened  accession

negotiations in 2014 – more than twelve

years  ago.  The  citizens  of  Serbia

therefore

rightly  expect  a  clearer

perspective  and  more  tangible  results

from a process in which our country has

participated for more than a decade. At

a time when the next enlargement of the

European Union does not appear likely

in  the  near  future,  we  have  sought  to

remain  constructive  and  to  propose

practical ways of overcoming the current

impasse.  We  have  therefore  proposed

that  the  Western  Balkans  be  gradually

integrated into the EU Single Market and

granted  access  to  the  Schengen  Area

even before attaining full membership in

the European Union. This would neither

serve  as  a  substitute  for  membership

nor  diminish  our  ambitions.  Rather,  it

would provide a concrete and pragmatic

way  forward,  enable  the  citizens  and

economies  of  the  region  to  experience

tangible  benefits  of  European

integration,  and  help  overcome

deadlock

in  which

the  enlargement

process has remained for far too long.

However,  a  stable  and

integrated

Europe,  of  which  Serbia  is  a  part,  and

our  European  path  do  not  mean

renouncing  the  traditional  friendships

thanks  to  which  Belgrade  is  one  of  the

few  European  capitals  from  which  one

can  fly  directly  to  the  United  States  of

America, the People’s Republic of China

and  the  Russian  Federation.  I  owe

special  gratitude  for  the  support  during

COVID  Pandemics  as  well  as

paramount  investment  in  Serbia  to  the

President  of  the  People’s  Republic  of

China  Xi  Jinping,  hoping  that  his  talks

with

the  President  Trump  will  be

productive  and  that  they  will  contribute

to the stabilization of the developments

in  the  world.  At  the  same  time,  we

nurture  ties  with  traditional  friends  and

partners

in  Africa,  Asia  and  Latin

America, with whom we recently marked

in Belgrade the sixty-fifth anniversary of

the  First  Conference  of  Non-Aligned

Countries,  held  in  our  capital  in  1961.

Our openness reflects our development

strategy,

our

history

our

understanding  of

the  world.  Serbia

believes  that  states  can  have  a  clear

course and interests of their own without

closing the door to those with whom they

do not agree on everything. After all, a

world  in  which  we  speak  only  to  those

who  think  as  we  do  would  have  little

need

for  diplomacy.  Freedom  and

independence  in  making  decisions  are

the highest values for Serbia.

We  must  anticipate  the  consequences

of a world in which force is once again

being  presented  ever  more  openly  as

the most reliable instrument of policy; in

which  military  budgets  are  growing,

conflicts  are  multiplying,  arms-control

mechanisms  are  weakening,  and

channels

of

communication

are

disappearing  precisely  when  they  are

needed most. We must therefore ask the

essential question: Where is the United

Nations  in  such  a  world?  The  Security

Council is often blocked precisely in the

crises in which it should be most active.

Other  parts  of  the  UN  system  face

financial

pressures,

overlapping

mandates,  bureaucratization  and  the

justified  demand  of  Member  States  to

see more concrete results.

These are real problems, and there is no

benefit  in  glossing  over  them.  Yet  it  by

no  means  follows  that  we  need  the

United  Nations  less.  We  may  need  it

more than ever; it simply must be more

effective,  more

focused  and  more

prepared to address the issues for which

it  was  created.  Over  the  past  eight

decades,  states  have  not  come  to  this

building because they shared the same

interests,  but because  they  understood

that  the  cost  of  settling  disagreements

by  force  of  arms  was  too  high.  That  is

why multilateralism came into being and

why we are here today. Serbia supports

the United Nations and reform of the UN

system  so  that  the  Organization  may

become  more  effective  and  better

adapted

today’s

realities.  We

advocate  a  more  representative  UN

Security  Council

through  greater

representation  of  developing  countries,

particularly

those

from

the  African

continent,  as  well  as  more  inclusive

regional representation and the addition

of  another  seat

the  Eastern

European  Group.  However,  without  a

genuine return to the principles on which

we have already agreed, I do not expect

progress in terms of this Organization’s

concrete results.

Peace is not the only test of our ability to

manage change. We are in the midst of

a  technological  transformation  whose

full  reach  we  are  only  beginning  to

understand.  Artificial

intelligence

already

changing

economy,

education, medicine, security, the labour

market  and  the  way  states  function.  It

can  bring  enormous  benefits

humanity.  It  can  also  deepen  existing

inequalities,  enable  new

forms  of

manipulation  and  create  security  risks

that  we  could  not  even  have  imagined

only  a  few  years  ago.  During  our

leadership

cycle

the  Global

Partnership  on  Artificial  Intelligence  –

GPAI, which Serbia chaired in 2025, one

of  our  priorities  was  to  ensure  that

technological

progress

remained

connected  with  security,  human  rights,

the  rule  of

law,  accountability  and

bridging the digital divide. The Belgrade

Ministerial  Declaration

received

support  of  44  Member  States  and  the

European Union and affirmed the need

for  safe,  sustainable  and  human-

centered artificial intelligence.

The  more

powerful

technology

becomes,  the  more  responsible  those

who manage it must be. We may have

cutting-edge

algorithms,

quantum

computers,  unmanned  systems  and

artificial

intelligence

capable

of

processing in a matter of seconds what

once took us years, but if, at the same

time, we allow the fundamental rules of

the  international  order  to  be  applied

selectively,  technological  progress  will

not make the world safer. It will merely

make us more technologically advanced

in  a  world  that  is  becoming  politically

less  predictable.  If  we  wish  to  manage

the  coming  transformation  responsibly,

we  must  first  reinforce  the  foundations

on  which  the  international  order  rests.

Those

foundations  are  simple:

sovereign equality of states, respect for

territorial integrity, the prohibition of the

use  of

force  except

the  cases

expressly  provided

the  UN

Charter,  and

the  obligation  not

change  the  rules  from  one  case  to

another.

Esteemed colleagues,

To  those  of  you  who  know  Serbia  and

our region, as well as those less familiar

with  this  part  of  the  world,  I  wish  to

express  my  gratitude  to  all  who  have

honored  Serbia  by  confirming

their

participation in the specialized exhibition

EXPO  2027,  to  be  held  next  year  in

Belgrade  under  the  theme  “Play  for

Humanity:  Sport  and  Music  for  All”.

Cultures,  science,  sport,  technology,

business  and  young  people  from  all

parts of the world will come together in

Belgrade,  and  I  look  forward  to  our

hosting  a  large  number  of  the  states

represented in this Hall today.

At  the  outset,  I  spoke  about  trust  and

responsibility, and that is where I wish to

conclude.  We  will  not  restore  trust

through  grand  declarations  if  we  then

continue  to  act  as  before.  Each  of  us

must  begin  with  our  own  decisions.

Serbia endeavors to do so by preserving

peace in its neighborhood, participating

in  peacekeeping  missions  far  from  its

borders, assisting others when they are

in danger, speaking even with those with

whom  it  disagrees,  and  fulfilling  the

commitments  it  undertakes.  What  will

restore  trust  in  international  law  and  in

the United Nations is more actions such

as those.

Thank you.

speaker_post: Permanent Representative to the United Nations
text:
Mr. Secretary-General, Excellencies, Distinguished Delegates,

I  bring  you  warm  greetings  and  best  wishes  from  His  Excellency  Salva  Kiir Mayardit, President of the Republic of South Sudan, the Government and the people of  South  Sudan,  together  with  a  message  of  peace,  unity,  development  and  an unwavering commitment to international cooperation.

I wish to congratulate you, Mr. President, on your election to preside over the Eighty-First Session of this esteemed Assembly. I also express South Sudan’s appreciation to the Secretary-General, His Excellency António Guterres, for his continued service to the United Nations and commitment to the principles of its Charter.

The  theme  of  this  Session,  “Restoring  Trust,  Managing  Transformation:  A United  Nations  that  Delivers  for  All,”  speaks  directly  to  the  experience  and aspirations of South Sudan. As the world’s youngest nation and the 193rd Member of  the  United  Nations,  South  Sudan  understands  both  the  promise  and  the responsibility of multilateralism.

South  Sudan  also  understands  that  trust  is  fundamental  to  peace:  trust  among citizens; trust between citizens and their institutions; trust among nations; and trust between Member States and the international institutions created to serve them.

South  Sudan  remains  committed  to  the  United  Nations  and  to  the  purposes  and principles of its Charter. We recognize and appreciate the contribution the United Nations has made to South Sudan, from humanitarian assistance and the protection of civilians to peacebuilding, development and institutional support.

However, restoring trust also requires honest reflection. Our experience has shown that  international  institutions  can  sometimes  be  slow  to  adjust  to  changing circumstances on the ground. Approaches designed to respond to conflict must be capable  of  evolving  as  nations  move  toward  peace,  recovery,  institution-building and national ownership.

For  South  Sudan,  therefore,  restoring  trust  must  mean  strengthening  partnership between  the  United  Nations  and  Member  States,  respecting  national  ownership, recognizing progress while acknowledging remaining challenges, and ensuring that international engagement ultimately strengthens the capacity of nations to assume responsibility for their own future.

To understand where South Sudan seeks to go, one must understand where South Sudan has come from. The history of South Sudan did not begin with independence on  9  July  2011.  It  was shaped  by  more  than  half  a  century  of  struggle,  sacrifice, displacement and an unwavering desire for freedom and self-determination. Dr. John Garang  de  Mabior  summarized  the  aspirations  of  that  struggle  when  he  spoke  of “freedom,  liberty,  equality,  justice,  human  rights  and  democracy.”  Those aspirations did not end with independence. They remain part of the ongoing work of nation-building.

The Comprehensive Peace Agreement of 2005 provided the political framework that transformed  decades  of  armed  struggle  into  a  peaceful  exercise  of  self-determination.  South  Sudan  therefore  continues  to  recognize  the  indispensable contribution of IGAD and our African brothers and sisters, as well as the support of the  Troika,  the  United  States,  the  United  Kingdom  and  Norway  and  the  wider international community.

South Sudan also remembers the extraordinary contribution of churches and faith leaders. During some of the darkest years of conflict, the churches remained with the  people.  They  educated  children,  assisted  displaced  communities,  mediated disputes and kept alive the belief that reconciliation was possible.

That tradition continued with the historic Ecumenical Pilgrimage of Peace to South Sudan  by  His  Holiness  Pope  Francis,  the  Archbishop  of  Canterbury  and  the Moderator of the Church of Scotland. Their message reinforced something South Sudan has learned through painful experience: Peace requires political agreements, but lasting peace also requires reconciliation, forgiveness and courage.

His Excellency President Salva Kiir Mayardit belongs to the generation that carried the struggle for liberation. Following the passing of Dr. John Garang, President Kiir assumed responsibility for safeguarding the Comprehensive Peace Agreement and leading the people of South Sudan toward the referendum on self-determination. In January 2011, the people of South Sudan spoke overwhelmingly through the ballot. And on 9 July 2011, President Salva Kiir Mayardit stood before the people as the flag of the Republic of South Sudan was raised for the first time.

Fifteen  years  later,  South  Sudan  has  travelled  a  difficult  road.  There  have  been achievements.  There  have  also  been  setbacks.  South  Sudan  experienced  internal conflict  shortly  after  independence.  Implementation  of  the  Revitalized  Peace Agreement has taken longer than originally anticipated. Economic and humanitarian challenges  remain  significant.  The  Government  does  not  deny  these  realities,  but neither  should  these  challenges  be  allowed  to  erase  the  progress  made  or  define permanently the identity of South Sudan.

Throughout  the  transition,  President  Kiir  has  repeatedly  made  one  commitment clear: he will not take South Sudan back to war. This commitment has guided his approach to the peace process and remains fundamental to his vision for the next chapter of South Sudan.

The mission before President Kiir today is therefore different from the mission of the liberation years. The liberation struggle sought to give the people of South Sudan the right to determine their destiny. The responsibility today is to consolidate peace, strengthen institutions and create the conditions through which the people of South Sudan can once again determine their political future through democratic means.

When the people of South Sudan voted for independence, they were voting for more than the creation of a new State. They were voting for a dream:

•  They dreamed of peace after generations of war;

•  They dreamed of schools for their children;

•  Healthcare for their families;

•  Roads connecting their communities;

•  Food security and economic opportunity;

•  Justice and equality;

•  Strong national institutions; and

•  A government whose authority ultimately derives from the will of its people. The difficulties of the last fifteen years have not extinguished those dreams. They remain alive among the people of South Sudan. And it is precisely for this reason that His Excellency President Salva Kiir Mayardit remains committed to paving the way towards general elections scheduled for December 2026. These elections are intended to mark the conclusion of the transitional period and provide the people of South Sudan the opportunity to democratically choose their leaders. We  recognize  that  important  work  still  in  progress.  Electoral  institutions  require adequate resources. Political dialogue must continue. Security arrangements must advance.  Civic  and  voter  education  must  reach  communities.  Women  and  young people  must  participate  meaningfully.  Refugees  and  internally  displaced  persons must  not  be  left  out.  And  an  environment  must  be  created  in  which  political competition can occur peacefully. The Government remains committed to working towards these objectives. For too long, South Sudan has often been seen internationally through the lens of conflict, humanitarian need and political crisis. President Kiir’s vision is to create

the conditions in which the world can once again see the people of South Sudan for who they truly are: a resilient people who struggled for freedom, voted peacefully for  independence,  and  continue  to  aspire  for  peace,  dignity,  democracy  and prosperity.

The people of South Sudan must increasingly speak for themselves. And they must speak through the ballot. Our journey therefore continues:

•  from liberation struggle to the Comprehensive Peace Agreement - to the

Referendum - to independence;

•  from conflict to peace; and now

•  from transition towards democratic governance.

The message of President Kiir remains clear: South Sudan must not return to war. Political  disagreement  must  be  addressed  through  dialogue.  Political  competition must never again become armed confrontation. The ballot must replace the bullet.

South  Sudan  recognizes  that  conducting  peaceful  elections  requires  security  and strong institutions. The Government bears the primary responsibility for protecting its citizens, maintaining public order and safeguarding the electoral process.

South  Sudan  therefore  continues  to  call  for  constructive  engagement  with  the Security  Council  concerning  restrictive  measures,  including  the  arms  embargo. South  Sudan’s  objective  is  not  militarization.  The  objective  is  to  develop professional, unified, disciplined and accountable security sectors operating under civilian authority and the rule of law.

South Sudan believes that accountability and national capacity should reinforce one another. We therefore call for the lifting of all restrictive measures. Sanctions must remain instruments for achieving clearly defined objectives; they should not become permanent substitutes for political engagement and institution-building.

South Sudan remains grateful for the contribution of the United Nations Mission in South Sudan. We recognize the men and women who have served under the United Nations flag, particularly those who have lost their lives in the service of peace. As South Sudan advances its transition, however, international engagement must also evolve.

President Kiir’s vision is not for South Sudan to remain indefinitely dependent upon international  peacekeeping.  The  objective  must  be  a  South  Sudan  capable  of sustaining  its  own  peace.  South  Sudan  therefore  calls  for  greater  emphasis  on

peacebuilding, institutional development and continuous capacity building. We are keen on establishing partnership:

•  Invest in South Sudan’s police and judiciary;

•  Invest in public administration;

•  Invest in education and healthcare;

•  Invest in infrastructure;

•  Invest in women and young people; and

•  Invest in the institutions that will sustain peace long after peacekeepers

have departed.

The  ultimate  measure  of  successful  peacekeeping  should  be  the  establishment  of conditions under which peacekeeping is no longer required. South Sudan therefore seeks a responsible transition from managing crises towards building lasting national capacity.

Peace  cannot  be  sustained  without  development.  At  independence,  South  Sudan inherited  extremely  limited  infrastructure  and  institutional  capacity.  Nation-building,  state-building  and  service  delivery  have  therefore  had  to  proceed simultaneously. His Excellency President Salva Kiir Mayardit has placed particular emphasis  on  agriculture,  infrastructure,  education,  healthcare  and  economic diversification.

South  Sudan  possesses  millions  of  hectares  of  arable  land,  significant  water resources, livestock, fisheries, natural resources and one of the youngest populations in  the  world.  South  Sudan  therefore  seeks  to  transition  progressively  from humanitarian dependency to self-reliance and to towards sustainable development and investment. For a farmer, a road to market is development. For a child, a functioning school is development. For a mother, access to healthcare is development. For a young person, employment  is  development.  And  for  South  Sudan,  development  is  one  of  the strongest foundations for lasting peace.

We therefore invite international partners and responsible investors to look beyond South Sudan’s current challenges and recognize its potential. Do not ask only what South Sudan needs. Ask what South Sudan can offer.

South  Sudan  continues  to  face  severe  consequences  from  climate  shocks  despite contributing minimally to global emissions. Recurrent floods, drought, displacement

and food insecurity are affecting millions of South Sudanese. South Sudan therefore reiterates  its  call  for  predictable  and  accessible  climate  financing,  investment  in adaptation,  resilient  infrastructure,  renewable  energy,  agriculture  and  technology transfer.  Climate  justice  must  be  reflected  not  only  in  commitments,  but  in implementation.

Women and young people remain central to President Kiir’s vision for South Sudan. The Revitalized Peace Agreement provided for 35 per cent representation of women in  public  institutions.  South  Sudan  continuous  on  working  to  translate  that commitment into meaningful participation at all levels. South  Sudan  also  has an  overwhelmingly  young  population.  These  young  people should  not  inherit the  conflicts  of  previous generations.  They should  inherit  the opportunities technology, entrepreneurship, agriculture and sports, that is the future they deserve.

of  peace:  Education,

vocational

training,

Decades  of  conflict  scattered  South  Sudanese  across  the  world.  But  the  South Sudanese diaspora should not be viewed only through the history of displacement. It is also an extraordinary national resource. Our national basketball team, the Bright Stars, demonstrated this before the world. South  Sudanese  whose  journeys  had  taken  them  across  different  countries  and continents came together under one flag. Under the leadership of Luol Deng and the South Sudan Basketball Federation, South Sudan qualified for the FIBA Basketball World  Cup  and  subsequently  for  the  Olympic  Games.  They  showed  the  world another image of South Sudan: not conflict; not displacement; but talent, discipline, unity and excellence. This experience offers a model for national development.

South  Sudanese  doctors  abroad  can  contribute  to  healthcare.  Engineers  can contribute to infrastructure. Academics can strengthen education. Entrepreneurs can invest and create employment. Technology professionals can connect South Sudan to the digital economy. And successful South Sudanese around the world can mentor another generation.

To  the  international  community,  we  need  to  create  strong  partnership  that  would enable  our  South  Sudanese  Diaspora  to  transfer  their  skills  and  professional experience; in  order to  contribute to  the  ongoing  development  in  the  Republic  of South Sudan.

To the South Sudanese Diaspora, our message is simple: South Sudan needs you. Bring your knowledge. Bring your experience. Bring your investment. Bring your

networks. Where physical return is not possible, allow your skills and experience to contribute to South Sudan.

The same spirit that brought South Sudanese athletes from around the world together under one flag can help bring South Sudanese expertise together for one national purpose. South Sudan’s greatest resource is ultimately its people, both at home and abroad.

South Sudan stands in solidarity with the people of Sudan. South Sudan and Sudan share  history,  families,  economic  interests  and  one  of  the  longest  borders  in  the region. South Sudan therefore reiterates and continues to support all efforts leading to the consolidation of peace in Sudan.

South Sudan knows from experience that military confrontation ultimately requires a  political  solution.  Even  the  longest  conflict  must  eventually  reach  a  negotiated settlement. South Sudan therefore supports regional and international efforts aimed at achieving peace in Sudan. Outstanding matters arising from the Comprehensive Peace Agreement, including border issues and the final status of Abyei, also require continued peaceful engagement between South Sudan and Sudan.

Restoring  trust  also  requires  reform  of  the  institutions  of  global  governance.  The composition of the Security Council does not adequately reflect realities of today; Africa with fifty-four Member States remains without permanent representation on the Council.

South  Sudan  therefore  reaffirms  its  support  for  the  Common  African  Position reflected  in  the  Ezulwini  Consensus  and  Sirte  Declaration.  Africa  must  be appropriately  represented  in  both  the  permanent  and  non-permanent  categories. Similarly, developing countries must have a stronger voice in international financial institutions and in decisions concerning development financing, debt, climate and technology.  Reform  does  not  weaken  multilateralism.  Reform  strengthens  its legitimacy.

Fifteen years after independence, South Sudan remains a young nation undertaking the  difficult  work  of  building  a  State  while  consolidating  peace  and  delivering development. The journey has not been easy. But South Sudanese have never been a people defined by easy journeys. The generation of liberation fought for freedom. The generation of the Comprehensive Peace Agreement secured the pathway to self-determination. The people of South Sudan chose independence through the ballot.

And  His  Excellency  President  Salva  Kiir  Mayardit  carried  the  responsibility  of leading South Sudan through the Referendum and into statehood.

Today, President Kiir’s vision is directed toward another historic responsibility: to preserve  peace,  strengthen  national  institutions  and  pave  the  way  toward elections  through  which  the  people  of  South  Sudan  can  determine  the  next chapter  of  their  nation.  This  is  ultimately  about  completing  the  promise  of independence. A South Sudan at peace with itself. A South Sudan governed through strong institutions. A South Sudan where political competition does not lead to war. A  South  Sudan  where  women  participate  fully.  Where  young  people  have opportunities. Where refugees can return home. Where the diaspora contributes to national  development.  And  where  children  grow  up  knowing  South  Sudan  not through memories of war, but through the possibilities of peace.

Dr. John Garang once challenged the people of South Sudan to “unite and dream together.” That dream did not end with independence. It continues. And today, the responsibility  of  President  Salva  Kiir  Mayardit,  his  Government,  the  political leadership  and  indeed  every  South  Sudanese  is  to  transform  that  dream  into  a functioning, peaceful and prosperous Republic.

To our international partners who stood with South Sudan during the struggle for peace, during the Comprehensive Peace Agreement, during the Referendum and at independence, we say: Stand with South Sudan again. But let this next chapter be a  partnership  that  strengthens  national  ownership.  A  partnership  that  builds institutions. A partnership that recognizes progress while helping address remaining challenges. And a partnership that enables South Sudan progressively to stand on its own.

For  South  Sudan,  restoring  trust  means  delivering  on  the  promise  of  peace. Managing  transformation  means  moving  from  conflict  to  institutions,  from dependency to national capacity, and from transition toward democratic governance. And a United Nations that delivers for all must ultimately help nations develop the capacity to deliver for their own people.

South  Sudan  remains  committed  to  the  United  Nations.  South  Sudan  remains committed  to  Africa.  South  Sudan  remains  committed  to  peace.  And  under  the leadership of His Excellency President Salva Kiir Mayardit, South Sudan remains committed to the long journey of transforming the sacrifices of liberation into the peace, dignity, development and democratic future for which the people of South Sudan have waited for generations. That is the promise of independence. That is the responsibility of this generation. And that is the future South Sudan seeks to build.

May the Lord Almighty bless the people of South Sudan. And may the Lord Almighty bless all nations represented in this Assembly.

I thank you.

text:
Mr. president, Mr. Secretary General, Heads of State and Governments. Ladies and gentlemen, it is a great honor for me to take the floor before this assembly on behalf of the government and the people of the Democratic Republic of Sao Tomé and Principe. Allow me, first of all to congratulate His Excellency, Mr. Khalilur Rahman on his election as president of the 81st session of the General Assembly, and to wish him every success in the discharge of his duties. I would also like to express our appreciation to Her Excellency, Miss Annalena Baerbock, for the work accomplished during the previous session of the General Assembly. Allow me to pay tribute to the Secretary General, His Excellency Mr. Antonio Guterres, for his commitment to peace, sustainable development, human rights and the strengthening of multilateralism at a time of great challenges. Excellencies, we live in a context marked by conflicts, geopolitical rivalries, economic uncertainty climate change, forced displacement, inequalities, transnational crime, and rapid technological transformation.

No state can face challenges of this magnitude alone. For Sao Tomé and Principe, this reality underscores the importance of an international order based on the charter of the United Nations International Law and the sovereign equality of states with principles applied universally and consistently. As a small island nation, we stand as a consolidated democracy and a state governed by the rule of law, grounded in peace, stability, and harmonious coexistence among our citizens. It is on the basis of this experience that we reaffirm our confidence in dialogue, diplomacy, cooperation and the peaceful settlement of disputes. Mr. president, for small island developing states, geographic, economic, financial and social vulnerabilities are compounded by the effects of climate change. In Sao Tomé and Principe, these impacts are already affecting our coastal areas, infrastructure, marine resources and livelihoods.

Despite our negligible contribution to global emissions. This reality reflects a profound climate injustice. Sao Tomé and Principe therefore reaffirms its commitments. Under the Paris Agreement, its nationally determined contribution and its National Adaptation Plan, while stressing that their implementation requires adequate, predictable and accessible resources. We also maintain that the vulnerability of small island states should be assessed beyond per capita income, taking into account their specific characteristics and structural constraints. In this context, we call for the Multidimensional vulnerability index to be translated into concrete eligibility criteria for concessional financing.

We likewise advocate for the full operational operation, rationalization of the fund for responding to loss and damage, and simpler, more effective access to the Green Climate Fund. The limited institutional capacity of vulnerable countries must not become an obstacle for to accessing the very instruments created to support them. In the case of Sao Tomé and Principe, this issue is particularly relevant following our graduation to middle income country status, which was an important milestone and a recognition of the progress achieved in human development. It nonetheless requires appropriate transition measures capable of consolidating these gains and shielding the country from external shocks. It is as part of this effort of consolidation and that the energy transition finds its place, a transition that is for us an economic, financial, social and environmental necessity. In an island economy dependent on imported fuel, the cost and reliability of electricity affect every sector.

The implementation of our Energy Transition Programme and the National Energy Compact should contribute to a cleaner, more affordable, secure and stable system. But it will require investment and international partnerships. Excellencies, food security and the strengthening of productive capacity are urgent priorities. We seek to reduce our dependence on imports, increase national production and ensure better market access for farmers so that a greater share of the value generated by quality products such as cocoa and coffee, remains in the country. If the land is essential to our food security, the sea and our biodiversity represent one of the broadest horizons for our development. The recognition of our territory by Unesco as a World Biosphere Reserve confirms the exceptional value of our natural heritage and reinforces our responsibility to protect it and make the most of it.

We aim to turn this wealth into opportunities for sustainable development through fisheries, the blue economy, research and nature based tourism that generates jobs and income for local communities. At the same time, in the face of threats posed by illegal fishing and transnational crime, Sao Tomé and Principe will continue to work with the states of the region and international partners to strengthen maritime security and promote a sustainable blue economy, thus preserving our resources for future generations. The preservation of these resources and the building of sustainable development ultimately depend on people and on the opportunities afforded to them. The future of Sao Tomé and Principe hinges on our ability to create opportunities for the next generation. Our priority is to ensure that young people have the conditions to study, work, start businesses, innovate and fulfil their life aspirations in their own country, in a nation of our size, every talent counts and every young person is an indispensable force for national progress. Likewise, the Santomean diaspora is an essential part of our human wealth and a strategic partner of the country.

We will continue to strengthen its ties with Sao Tomé and Principe, and to create the conditions for an even greater contribution to investment, entrepreneurship, knowledge transfer and national life. Mr. president, creating opportunities and ensuring truly inclusive development require strong institutions capable of guaranteeing peace, justice, respect for human rights and the participation of all in the life of the country. There can be no sustainable development without these conditions, nor without the full participation of women and men in political, economic and social life. It is in this context that 2026 is a year of particular significance for santomean democracy. On July 19th, our citizens took part in presidential elections, which were conducted peacefully and transparently, and led to the re-election of His Excellency, Mr. Carlos Vilanova, as president of the Republic. On September 27th, the people of Sao Tomé and Principe will return to the polls for the legislative, local and regional elections and will exercise their right to vote in large numbers.

These elections are marked by important innovations notably automatic voter registration and the first application of the parity law, which is a significant step towards strengthening the inclusion and participation of women. With women accounting for 41.4% of confirmed candidacies. Above the legal threshold of 40%, they will be able to assert a growing presence in decision making spaces. San Tomé and Principe reaffirms its commitment to constitutional order, political pluralism, fundamental freedoms and respect for the sovereign will of its citizens and will continue to pursue reforms aimed at strengthening justice, security, gender equality, human rights and trust in institutions. Inclusion and equality must also guide our response to the great transformations of our time. In the face of the rapid advance of artificial intelligence and the digital transition, Sao Tomé and Principe calls for international cooperation that enables developing countries to access the technology, knowledge, infrastructure and financing they need.

We advocate responsible technology governance centered on human dignity, transparency and fundamental rights, so that innovation translates into better opportunities and services for all. Excellencies. The experience of Sao Tomé and Principe as a small democracy also shapes the way we view representation at the international level. Africa today occupies a demographic, economic and political place that is not yet adequately reflected in the institutions where the most far reaching decisions are taken. It is in this area that reform of the Security Council becomes imperative. This is not a concession to Africa.

It is a matter of legitimacy, justice and effectiveness. An institution responsible for international peace and security cannot remain indefinitely based on a distribution of power inherited from another area. In the pursuit of greater historical justice and representation. Sao Tomé and Principe, therefore welcomes the recent decisions that recognize the historical gravity of the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans and promoted a more accurate cartographic representation of the size of the continent's correcting distortions that visually diminished Africa. These acts of recognition must translate into an international order in which Africa participates fully in shaping the future, rather than remaining merely in the position of responding to the decisions taken elsewhere. Mr. president, peace remains the very raison d'etre of the multilateral system.

Sao Tomé and Principe follows with concern the conflicts in Ukraine, the Sudan, the Sahel, the Great Lakes region, the Horn of Africa and the Middle East and calls for stronger diplomacy and protection of civilians in accordance with the charter of the United Nations and International law. We likewise call for respect for international humanitarian law, full humanitarian access and the release of hostages. We reaffirm our support for a two state solution that allows Israel and Palestine to live side by side in peace and security on the basis of international law and the relevant United Nations resolutions. We also followed with concern the persistence of the economic, commercial and financial restrictions affecting Cuba and call for their lifting for the benefit of the development and well-being of the Cuban people to whom we express our solidarity. Excellencies Sao Tomé and Principe will remain faithful to the charter of the United Nations international law, peace, human rights and multilateralism. Standing as a voice of dialogue and moderation, and as a committed partner for stability in the Gulf of Guinea.

On the eve of the elections in Sao Tomé and Principe, it is important to acknowledge the progress made in a challenging context. The government has launched reforms and made advances in infrastructure. The energy transition, digitalization and investment attraction, creating the conditions to mobilise resources needed to meet our population's most pressing needs, particularly in access to health, water, sanitation, justice and security, environmental protection and the infrastructure essential to development. As aligned with the national strategy based on Sustainable Tourism, 2026 2040, we thank all of our bilateral and multilateral partners who are supporting Sao Tomé and Principe in this process. However, the challenge before us is to turn these advances into concrete and lasting results, consolidating the foundations for more inclusive, sustainable and resilient development for which ensuring continuity and stability of governance and of governance is paramount. Mr. president, our vulnerabilities as a small island developing states do not define our horizon.

We therefore reaffirm our determination to turn challenges into opportunities through strategic partnerships based on shared responsibility and mutual benefit. And we reaffirm our capacity to contribute to peace, uphold the principles of the charter of the United Nations, and participate responsibly in building solutions to the challenges we collectively face We call on all Member States to continue building together a more representative, supportive and just international order founded on respect for the sovereignty of states, international law and equality of opportunity. It is in this spirit of peace, dialogue and hope that Sao Tomé and Principe will continue to shoulder its responsibility within the international community. Thank you, Mr. President.
