Secretary-General,

Excellencies,

Distinguished delegates,

Ladies and Gentlemen,

INTRODUCTION

Mr. President, let me congratulate you on the assumption

of the high office of President of the 81st session of the

General Assembly of the United Nations.

Expressing appreciation to your predecessor for her

stewardship of the 80th session of the General Assembly, I

wish her every success in her future endeavors.

Secretary–General, as you approach the conclusion of your

tenure, the Republic of Suriname commends the dedicated

service  to  humanity,  showcased  while  in  office.  We  also

remember  with  warmth  your visit  to  Suriname,  expressing

the importance of the United Nations’ engagement with our

country and the Caribbean region. We wish you well, in the

path before you.

Standing  before  this  Assembly,  I  am  reminded  that,  while

some efforts have been made from this rostrum over the past

year, these have not yet matched the scale of the challenges

confronting our world.

We  will  have  to  increase  and  strengthen  efforts  and

commitment

to

the  process  of

transformation  and

strengthening of the UN in order to restore the trust that our

organization  will  really  be  capable  of  delivering  peace,

inclusion and development in the world.

THE UNITED NATIONS AND MULTILATERALISM

Suriname

is

firmly  committed  to  the  upholding  of

International  Law,  as  we  depend  on  a  rules-based

international  order,  without  which,

like  many  other

vulnerable  nations,  we  simply  cannot  exist  as  sovereign

countries.

The  consistent  application  of  international  law  and  the

strengthening of its institutions is also essential to maintain

international peace and security, protect human rights and

ensure sustainable development for all.

INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY

As  mentioned  before,  the  international  community  is

experiencing  profound  uncertainty,  including  energy  and

food  security  crises,  leading  to  intensified  displacement  of

many people globally.

Armed  conflicts  continue  to  claim  innocent  lives,  while

geopolitical  tensions  escalate.  Children  are  living  through

unimaginable horrors. The United Nations has not been able

to prevent this or end the continuation.

Other  developments,  for  example  in  the  Strait  of  Hormuz,

demonstrate  how  quickly  wars  can  affect  energy  markets,

suddenly and steeply increasing the cost of energy, adversely

impacting  economic  and  social  developments

in  our

countries.

Common people suffer when food and energy prices rise, so

the quality of life of our people is directly threatened, even

by wars in regions far from their home.

Suriname, therefore, calls for a renewed commitment to the

purposes  and  principles  of  the  UN  Charter,  namely  the

peaceful resolution of disputes.

Dialogue is paramount for safeguarding a solid and proven

UN system. The people of Cuba, a Caribbean country, are

adversely affected by the current situation in their country.

Suriname calls on the parties involved to remain committed

to  dialogue  and  negotiation,  to  end  the  economic,

commercial  and  financial  embargo.  We  plea for  continuing

of negotiations in order to prevent further escalation and to

reach a resolution, that will benefit the people of Cuba.

We also call for sustained international support for Haiti to

restore  security,  constitutional  order  and  democratic

governance.  Suriname  supports  solutions  that  place  the

Haitian people at the center.

The  UN80

process

rightly

emphasizes  mandate

rationalization,

institutional  coherence  and  efficiency.

Reform  must  protect  and  improve  the  United  Nations'

capacity  to  deliver  and  also  make  the  system  easier  to

navigate.  It  should  not  reduce  support  where  it  is  most

needed.

Equally important, is the overdue reform of the Security

Council, hence Suriname reiterates its call for making it

more representative, more accountable and more capable

of acting.

Africa, the Republic of Suriname supports your demand,

for just permanent representation.  Likewise, we

underscore the relevance of a dedicated representation for

Small Island States and Low-Lying Coastal Developing

States.

CARICOM AND REGIONAL LEADERSHIP

Regional

and

international

partnerships

remain

indispensable to achieve our economic and social objectives

as Suriname continues to actively engage in various regional

bodies and mechanisms including CARICOM, CELAC, ACTO

and Brasilia Consensus.

As  Suriname  prepares  to  be  the  Chair  of  the  Caribbean

Community  (CARICOM)  in  2027,  we  are  also  committed  to

further strengthen our partnership globally in different areas

of shared interest.

Our  regional  priorities  are  practical:  food  and  energy

security,  climate  resilience,  improved  connectivity,  and

movement  of  skilled  people,  transportation  of  goods  and

services. These are essential to economic integration and to

our ability to withstand external shocks.

The  pursuit  of  restorative  justice  gained  new  momentum

with  the  adoption  of  the  resolution  on  Slavery  and

Transatlantic  Trafficking  of  Enslaved  Africans,  in  this  Hall

in March of this year.

This  development  is  relevant  for  Suriname.  And  equally

important for the countries of the Caribbean region.

The  discussion  is  no  longer  about  whether  slavery  and

colonialism have caused lasting consequences. We know we

are living them.

We increasingly must focus on how to overcome these effects

and on the question of what form reparation should take to

achieve  that.  How  will  countries  that  have  benefited  from

slavery and colonialism compensate the affected.

It  is  therefore  that  the  CARICOM  ten-point  plan  for

restorative justice is now of eminent importance.

SURINAME: CLIMATE LEADERSHIP AND CULTURAL HERITAGE

Suriname  occupies  a  unique  position.  We  are  carbon-

negative and remain the world’s most forested country with

over 90 per cent forest coverage.

High  Forested  and  Low  Deforestation  countries,

like

Suriname,  should  not  first  have  to  lose  forests,  before

climate finance institutions recognize the value of protecting

them.

Conservation  costs  cannot  be  borne  only  by  the  countries

protecting ecosystems whose benefits are shared globally.

I will continue my plea for just and effective climate finance,

because  our  forests  are  under  even  more  pressure  than

when I addressed this meeting last year.

I  stated  that  the  forest  faces  competition  of  rich  natural

resources like gold, diamonds and other precious minerals.

We are now confronted, however, with a new threat of people

who also want to clear parts of our rainforest for large-scale

agriculture.

At  this  very  moment  my  government  is  introducing  legal

and institutional measures to better protect our forests and

the immediate living environment of the Indigenous Peoples

and Tribal Communities. Their knowledge and participation

are important at all stages of development.

Last  year  at  this  rostrum  I  noted  that  Suriname  is

diversity.

At a time when diversity is too often manipulated as a source

of division, Suriname has chosen the path to recognize the

distinct histories of its people while strengthening their unity

and their shared responsibility for the future.

Our  experience  affirms  that  diversity,  when  grounded  in

equality,  mutual  respect  and  meaningful  participation,  is

not  an  adversity;  it  is  a  source  of  national  resilience  and

prosperity.

Last  month,  the  Republic  of  Suriname  observed  its  first

National  Heritage  Month  under  the  theme,  "Hoe  wij  hier

ook  samen  kwamen,  hoe  wij  samen  verder  gaan”,

meaning “However we came here, united we move forward”.

This  initiative  was  conceived  not  merely  to  celebrate  our

culture,  but  as  a  deliberate  national  undertaking  centered

on  growing  inclusion,  mutual  respect  and  unity.  This

process is also relevant for the global community.

SURINAME: ENERGY TRANSITION AND SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT

The  development  of  Suriname’s  offshore  natural  resources

including oil and gas, will present significant opportunities

to  accelerate  national  development  and  improve  the  well-

being of our people.

Yet, we are equally conscious that oil and gas cannot and

should not become the only foundation of our economy.

Our approach is therefore clear. We must transform

temporary resource wealth into lasting national prosperity

using resource revenues strategically to strengthen our

economy and make it more resilient, through

diversification.

Additionally, we will need to improve our energy security.

Although we are preparing for gas to shore, renewable

energy will be part of our national energy mix.

Besides  the  expected  economic  and  energy  transition,  we

must also prepare for the transformation driven by artificial

intelligence.

Only if we can implement AI responsibly, Suriname will be

able to benefit from the opportunities of this technology and

mitigate its risks.

With  only  four  years  left  to  achieve  the  Sustainable

Development  Goals,  we  may  question whether we  were  too

ambitious or if we should have done much more.

Political  will,

international  peace  and  accelerated

implementation  are  required,  supported  by  financing,

technology  and  partnerships  that  produce  measurable

results.

Equally important is to have a mechanism in place for global

commitments after 2030.

CLOSING: RECOMMITMENT TO THE CHARTER AND CALL TO ACTION

Mr. President, Excellencies, Distinguished Delegates,

Finally,  as  the  United  Nations  approaches  change  in  its

highest leadership, current realities and approved mandates

require  the  next  Secretary-General  to  portray  strong

commitment  to  multilateralism,  dialogue,  and  the  rule  of

law.

Many  capable  candidates,  including  women  leaders  who

have taken up the challenge, have been put forth and for the

first  time  in  history  we  have  a  female  candidate  from  the

Caribbean. CARICOM endorses this candidate.

We  are  at  that  time  in  history  where  trust  in  the  United

Nations must urgently be restored.

We  make  efforts  to  protect  our  forests,  use  our  natural

wealth  responsibly,  strengthen  the  Caribbean  Community

and promote dialogue.

We will do what we can and call on more influential members

of the United Nations, to help maintain peace.

Only a United Nations, capable of safeguarding international

peace and security will deliver for all.

I thank you.

Mr. President, Mr. Secretary-General, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen,

Every country that enters this hall brings its own concerns.

For some, security means protecting borders. For others, it means food, water, energy, or the future of their children. Many countries face all of these challenges at once.

That is why a world ruled mainly by power, rather than by rules, would be dangerous for everyone.

For smaller countries such as Slovakia, this is especially clear. But no country, large or small, is truly safe in a world where international law is ignored and institutions are weakened.

Sadly,  we  no  longer  need  to  imagine  such  a  world.  We  can  already  see  parts  of  it around us.

Trade is becoming less predictable. Security cooperation is more fragmented. The idea that every country should have a voice is under pressure.

And when rules are weakened, when cooperation is replaced by confrontation, all of us become more vulnerable.

But we still have a choice.

The  international  system  we  have  built  is  not  perfect.  It  can  be  slow.  It  can  be frustrating. At times, it does not deliver as quickly as people need.

But the solution is not to destroy it. The solution is to make it work better.

Slovakia is firmly anchored in the United Nations, NATO and the European Union. We believe in cooperation. But we also believe that institutions must produce real results.

Over  the  past  year,  Slovakia  has  hosted  several international  meetings  and  offered space  for  dialogue.  Where  we  can  be  useful,  we  are  ready  to  help  bring  parties together and support diplomacy within the UN framework.

Because when diplomacy stops, confrontation fills the space.

That is why, when we speak about the United Nations, I believe in evolution rather than revolution.

The  world  has  changed,  and  the  United  Nations  must  change  with  it.  The  Security Council should better reflect today’s realities and give a stronger voice to countries and regions that are still underrepresented.

Countries from the region often understand a crisis best. Giving them a stronger voice can help us act earlier and prevent escalation.

Slovakia  sees  its  engagement  in  UN  reform  as  part  of  its  responsibility  to  this Organization,  including  through  UN80  and  the  implementation  of  the  Pact  for  the Future.

Our responsibility to the wider international order is also reflected in our candidacy for the Security Council for 2028 and 2029.

We would be grateful for your trust and support.

If elected, Slovakia will focus on four priorities:

International law and the UN Charter;

Accountable security institutions;

The protection of strategic resources and critical infrastructure;

And the security challenges linked to digitalization and artificial intelligence.

I  fully  share  the  concern  of  the  United  Nations  about  the  inequalities  that  can  be created by unequal access to artificial intelligence.

It  is  in  our  common  interest  that  innovation  benefits  all  of  humanity,  not  only  the strongest economies or the biggest companies.

If AI is available only to a few, new divisions will appear. Entire communities may be left behind.

The  growing  use  of  AI-powered  weapons  and  autonomous  systems  also  requires urgent attention.

One principle must remain clear: machines should never be allowed to make life-or-death decisions on their own.

Just  as  the  international  community  developed  rules  for  nuclear,  chemical  and biological  weapons,  we  also  need  strong international  frameworks  for  new technologies. The United Nations can and should play a leading role in this effort.

AI is not only a potential threat on the battlefield. It is already having a negative impact on  society,  especially  in  education.  An  entire  generation  of  young  people  is  being affected. Recent assessments show declining test scores across the vast majority of countries.  This  is a  concerning  trend  that  deserves open  and  serious  discussion  on international platforms such as the United Nations.

At the same time, we should not see AI only as a risk. It can also be a tool for peace.

It can help us analyze information, identify patterns and overcome language barriers in  real  time.  It  can  support  better  decisions,  faster  responses  and  more  effective prevention.

With responsible use, proper human oversight and good governance, we can move this  technology  away  from  the  battlefield  and  towards  diplomacy,  mediation  and conflict prevention.

And prevention matters.

Every  conflict  we  prevent  saves  lives.  It  protects  development.  It  preserves  human dignity.

Once violence begins, every solution becomes harder, more costly and more painful.

There is no need to reinvent the wheel when we reform international institutions.

AI may be revolutionary, but we did not need to reinvent the personal computer in order to build it. The same is true in global politics. We should improve what already exists, not start again from zero.

But let's ask ourselves a simple question. What if we, as world leaders, simply started following the UN Charter again? Would reform even matter if we finally did our best for global peace?

Too many conflicts are still driven by the belief that political problems can be solved by force, by changing borders, violating sovereignty and ignoring international rules.

We need to reject this logic.

Leadership is not shown by the willingness to escalate. It requires the courage to de-escalate.

International rules may sound abstract in this hall. But on the ground, they are very real. They can mean the difference between life and death.

When these rules are ignored, civilians suffer. Communities are destroyed. Millions are displaced. Supply chains are disrupted. Prosperity is lost.

And there is an even deeper danger.

If  violence  becomes  normal  for  the  next  generation,  diplomacy  itself  will  become harder. What is difficult to solve today may become impossible tomorrow.

That is why our most urgent task must be clear: stop the violence, keep diplomacy alive, and prevent today’s conflicts from becoming tomorrow’s normal.

The  war  in  Ukraine,  now  in  its  fifth  year,  continues  to  bring  destruction  close  to Slovakia’s border.

Attacks on civilian areas and critical infrastructure remain unacceptable. A ceasefire is still distant and lasting peace even further away.

We  should  support  every  serious  diplomatic  effort  that  can  help  end  Russia’s  war against Ukraine and build a safe future for our neighbor.

Our  commitment  to  international  law  and  human  dignity  cannot  stop  at  Europe’s borders.

The same basic principles must guide us in the Middle East.

International  humanitarian  law  must  be  respected.  Civilians  must  be  protected. Humanitarian aid must reach those who need it, including in Gaza.

There can be no justification for terrorism, antisemitism, anti-Muslim hatred or calls to violence.

Israelis and Palestinians both deserve to live in security and dignity.

Slovakia  continues  to  support  a  negotiated  two-state  solution,  with  Israel  and  an independent Palestinian state living side by side in peace and security.

Other conflicts that are currently out of the spotlight must not escape our attention and  our  efforts  to  solve  them.  Take  for  example  the  civil  war  in  Sudan  that  has triggered the world’s largest humanitarian crisis.

Excellencies,

The first words of our Charter are “We the peoples of the United Nations”.

Today, we need that sense of shared responsibility again.

Armed conflicts have reached levels we have not seen since the Second World War. Civilians continue to pay an unacceptable price.

We already have institutions. We already have rules. We already have knowledge.

What we need now is the will to use them.

This year, the United Nations will choose its next Secretary-General.

Slovakia supports a transparent and inclusive process based on merit, with due regard to regional diversity and gender balance.

I would also like to thank Secretary-General António Guterres for his dedicated service and leadership during these difficult years.

The  next  Secretary-General  will  inherit  an  organization  under  serious  security, geopolitical, institutional and financial pressure.

But the future of the United Nations will not depend on one person alone.

It depends on all of us. On our will, courage and determination.

We “the people of the United Nations” should not leave the next generation a world where violence is normal and diplomacy is the exception.

Thank you.

Mr. President, excellencies, distinguished delegates,

At the outset, let me congratulate His Excellency Mr. Khalilur Rahman on his election

as  President  of  the  81st  session  of  the  General  Assembly,  and  I  wish  him  every

success in guiding this session.

Allow me to begin my speech by quoting the sentences that I delivered on behalf of

Slovenia,  on  behalf  of  vast  number  of  current  and  former  heads  of  states  and

governments who signed our declaration for this rostrum in 2012. I quote:

»  This  year's  theme  of  the  United  Nations  Assembly  is  peaceful  resolution  of

disputes... Last year we celebrated the sixtieth anniversary of the entry into force of

the  Convention  on  prevention  and  punishment  of  the  crime  of  genocide.  The

Convention was the fruit of the tireless efforts of the Polish jurist of Jewish descent,

Raphael Lemkin...

I would like to remind you that since the end of the Second World War alone; there

have  been  more  than  80  countries  witnessing  mass  atrocities.  At  least  53  million

innocent people lost their lives. Behind these numbers are concrete men and women,

as well as children. They had a future, but they were not allowed to live that future.

For  this  reason,  I  call  on  the  Member  States  of  the  United  Nations,  regional

organizations  and  the  United  Nations  system  to  develop  a  new  approach  and  a

strategy for the prevention of genocide and other mass atrocities...

In addition, an intergovernmental forum of like-minded states should be established

in order to propose a United Nations resolution that would give a clear mandate for

preparation and adoption of an appropriate legal mechanism – legal mechanism that

would give the concept of the "responsibility to protect" a new tool, a legal mechanism

that will enforce the prevention of crime, a mechanism that will enable a faster and

more effective response to acts of genocide and other mass atrocities...

I would like to inform you that this initiative also comes from international civil society.

The  Institute  for  Cultural  Diplomacy  has  gathered  thousands  of  supporters  at

international non-governmental organizations, among lawyers, students, journalists

and others...

As  early  as  1946,  Raphael  Lemkin  declared:  "Our  heritage  is  the  result  of  the

contribution of all nations." All nations, as well as the United Nations as a whole, have

great responsibility, as well as an enormous opportunity to prevent atrocities in the

future. We cannot escape history, but we can learn something from it... I firmly believe

that the mistakes we made yesterday we do not want to repeat tomorrow. We took

responsibility for this world from our fathers, and we have a great responsibility to

make it better for our children. I call on you to improve it by joining all our efforts for a

world free from genocide and other mass atrocities." End of quote.

After 14 years, I note that, despite the great initial support, our initiative has not been

realized. It has been drowned in new crises, in the incompetence and ignorance of

the individuals and institutions responsible, and  in the double standards that have

further marked the behavior of our United Nations. Today, we are even further away

from the goal we tried to achieve 14 years ago.

The  theme  of this  year's  session  is  therefore  actually  very well  chosen.  Restoring

trust. A United Nations that is here for everyone. Because: Trust begins with a simple

question:  do  we  apply  our  principles  consistently,  or  only  when  it  is  politically

convenient?

The United Nations was founded on universal principles: sovereignty, equal dignity,

the  rule  of  law,  the  peaceful  settlement  of  disputes,  and  the  protection  of  human

rights.

But principles lose their meaning when they are applied selectively.

Let us be concrete.

For decades, the United Nations has devoted significant institutional attention to the

question of Palestine. The General Assembly has adopted resolution after resolution,

while the Security Council and Human Rights Council have repeatedly addressed the

situation.

Let me be clear: the search for peace and security in the Middle East is of profound

importance, and the suffering of Palestinian and Israeli civilians deserves serious and

sustained consideration. Every civilian life matters.

But are we applying the same standard of urgency when victims are elsewhere?

Last year alone, over four thousand eight hundred Christians were killed because of

their  religion.  More  than  three  hundred  million  Christians  around  the  world  suffer

discrimination  and  persecution.  In  Iran,  the  criminal  theocratic regime  has  brutally

murdered tens of thousands of its own citizens this year alone.

After 1948, more than one million Jews fled or were expelled from Arab countries,

many amid persecution and violence.

Or consider Nigeria.

For  more  than  a  decade,  Nigerian  communities  have  faced  mass  killings,

kidnappings, the destruction of villages and places of worship, and the displacement

of hundreds of thousands of people. In return, this body produced a single Security

Council resolution. Not seventy. Not seventeen. One.

So, we must ask: if every civilian life matters, why does our urgency seem so different

from one crisis to another? This does not mean caring less about one crisis but caring

more consistently about all of them.

We must also be willing to ask difficult questions about how Palestine is discussed

and used politically. A majority position does not, by itself, determine what is right.

The right of a democratic state and its people to defend themselves against terrorism

must be recognized and upheld. Civilian suffering is tragic and must be addressed,

but it can never justify terrorism or the pursuit of political objectives through violence.

At  the  same  time,  criticism  of  government  policy  must  never  become  a  cover  for

antisemitism.

If civilian lives are equal, our attention should be guided by the scale, duration and

severity of suffering - not primarily by geography, political alliances, media visibility or

political influence.

These  principles  must  also  guide  our  approach  to  Belarus.  We  condemn  the

authorities’  systematic  repression,  arbitrary  detention  and  persecution  of  political

opponents, human rights defenders and independent voices. All political prisoners

must be released immediately and unconditionally, and those responsible for human

rights  violations  must  be  held  accountable.  Slovenia  stands  with  the  Belarusian

people and supports a peaceful democratic transformation founded on free and fair

elections, the rule of law and full respect for human rights. Belarus belongs in a free

and democratic Europe.

Selectivity  does  more  than  distort  our  attention.  Over  time,  it  destroys  institutions

themselves. The United Nations cannot defend the rule of law while silently watching

its  own  mandates,  procedures  and  institutions  become  instruments  of  political

convenience.

The rule of law must never become merely rule by law. It requires rules to be applied

impartially, consistently and transparently.

When  the  same  principles  are  invoked  strictly  in  one  case  and  conveniently

overlooked in another, we do not strengthen international law. We hollow it out.

And when institutions created to protect universal standards are instrumentalized for

political  purposes,  we  weaken  the  very  multilateral  system  they  were  created  to

defend.

This inconsistency is particularly difficult to ignore when we consider Iran. Executions,

including  those  involving  political  prisoners,  young  intellectuals  and  others  who

oppose the regime, demand serious attention. Yet there is often no sufficiently serious

condemnation of these executions or of the broader violations of human rights under

a system that seeks complete control over social, political and economic life.

The abuse of religion to justify or reinforce such control is another example of how

principles can be distorted when institutions and political power are placed above the

rights and dignity of individuals. Human rights cannot depend on whether the victims

are politically convenient to defend.

The  United  Nations  must  therefore  defend  not  only  its  institutions,  but  also  the

integrity of the principles those institutions exist to serve.

Russia’s  war  of  aggression  against  Ukraine  is  a  flagrant  violation  of  the  United

Nations Charter and a direct assault on the sovereignty and territorial integrity of a

Member State.

Russia's occupation and attempted illegal annexation of Crimea in 2014 challenged

a fundamental rule of our international order: territory cannot be acquired by force.

As Mustafa Dzhemilev, the leader of the Crimean Tatars, reminded us at yesterday's

Crimea Platform Summit, the international response to Russia's aggression in 2014

was too little, too late. Russia was never effectively stopped. Its impunity began in

Crimea. The full-scale invasion of 2022 was the consequence.

The Russian leadership chose this war. Russia is the aggressor. Ukraine is defending

its people and its independence.

For Slovenia, sovereignty and territorial integrity are fundamental to our own security.

If  a  powerful  state  can  seize  its  neighbour's  territory  by  force,  every  smaller  state

becomes less secure.

The United Nations has documented torture and executions of Ukrainian prisoners of

war  by  Russian  forces,  as  well  as  grave  abuses  in  occupied  territory.  Those

responsible must face justice.

Prisoners of war and civilian detainees must return home. Ukrainian children forcibly

transferred or deported must return to their families.

Our goal must remain a just and lasting peace, based on the United Nations Charter

and  Ukraine's  sovereignty  and  territorial  integrity.  Ukraine  must  participate  fully  in

decisions  concerning  its  future.  Any  settlement  must  provide  credible  security

guarantees against renewed aggression.

Slovenia  will  continue  to  support  Ukraine  on  its  European  path.  Ukraine's  future

belongs in the European Union.

A permanent member of the Security Council, entrusted with a special responsibility

for international peace, is waging a war of aggression against another Member State.

Russia's  permanent seat cannot place it above the Charter. Its veto cannot erase

aggression or responsibility for international crimes.

If this Organization wants to restore trust, it should begin by applying its own principles

consistently.

I therefore propose two things.

First,  this  Organization  should  strengthen  transparency  around  its  responses  to

crises. We should establish an independent mechanism, answerable to this Assembly

as a whole, that annually compares the scale, duration and severity of major crises

with the scale and nature of the international response. Not to dictate political verdicts,

but to make it impossible for us to remain unaware of our own patterns of selectivity.

Second, we should strengthen safeguards against the political instrumentalization of

United Nations mandates and institutions. Their credibility depends on transparent

procedures, consistent criteria and equal standards of scrutiny for all Member States.

The multilateral system was created to prevent power from replacing principle. We

must not allow political convenience to reverse that relationship  -  so that principle

becomes merely a language used by institutions when it serves political interests.

The answer is not to weaken multilateralism. It is to protect it from instrumentalization.

A  United  Nations  that  delivers  for  all  cannot  mean  an  organization  that  responds

loudly to some crises and quietly to others.

If we want to speak credibly of the United Nations that delivers for all, then we must

be prepared to ask a difficult question: does it really deliver for all?

For  those  living  through  war.  For  those  displaced  by  violence.  For  states  whose

concerns receive little international attention. For families struggling to build a future.

We will restore trust when a crisis matters because human beings are suffering, not

because the politics surrounding it are convenient.

And we will restore trust when the institutions of multilateralism are strong enough to

serve universal principles rather than political convenience.

But restoring trust is not only about correcting what is wrong today. It is about deciding

what kind of international system we are willing to pass on to those who come after

us.

Mr. President,

A United Nations that cannot uphold its own principles has no standing to ask the

world for its trust.

What we owe the people of the world is not sentiment. It is an institution consistent

enough, and far-sighted enough, to be worthy of their trust.

Thank you.

Madam/Mister President, Excellencies

I want to tell you about my grandmother, Alice.

Growing up in rural Sweden, as the seventh of eleven siblings, her opportunities were very

different from those of her brothers. Her parents expected her to focus first and foremost on

family life. Yet she was curious, capable and determined to build a life of her own.

A job at a local bank gave her not only an income, but also independence and confidence. There,

at the bank, she met many women with little to no experience with finances and were left

vulnerable when circumstances changed.

She wrote in her diary about some of the women she met – many of whom were recently

widowed – coming to the bank in tears because they didn’t know anything about their own family

finances. Some didn’t know how to fill out a withdrawal slip. One woman came to the bank

holding two safe-deposit keys without knowing which bank they belonged to.

My grandmother was as independent as a woman in that time and place could be. But she

worried deeply about the consequences for the women who were not.

During her life she witnessed extraordinary progress. But two generations later, far too many

women are still entirely economically dependent on men.

Madam/ Mister President

80 years ago, when Sweden joined the United Nations, the foundations of our modern society

were being laid.

1(12)

In the 1940s and 50s, Swedish women joined the labour market in large numbers. This was not

only a matter of principle – it also came from the realisation that our economy needed women in

the work force.

Women’s economic empowerment is a matter of freedom. When women work and earn their

own money, their self-determination grows.

Gender equality is not only the right thing to do, it’s the smart thing to do. When women work,

economies grow.

Each generation must fight for equality.

In 1919, the same year my grandmother was born, Sweden decided that women should have the

same right as men to vote. That very same year, women in Afghanistan were also granted the

right to vote.

More than a century later, the contrast between women’s freedoms in our two countries is as

striking as it is saddening. It is a painful reminder that progress is never irreversible. Rights once

gained can be lost.

Freedoms do not defend themselves. It is up to us to protect them, for women and girls

everywhere – and for generations to come.

When Sweden joined the UN in 1946, the world was emerging from the devastation of war. The

lesson from that catastrophe was clear: peace must not be taken for granted.

Defence of sovereignty and territorial integrity have been at the heart of Swedish foreign policy

ever since.

Eight decades later, these principles are once again being challenged. Bad faith, conflict and utter

contempt for our common rules are weakening the institutions that we built together. These are

times of upheaval.

2(12)

The number of armed conflicts is growing. And civilians are paying the price. In Ukraine, Sudan,

Yemen, Palestine, Lebanon, Myanmar, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and many other

conflict zones, millions are suffering.

Russia’s aggression against Ukraine is a blatant violation of international law. It strikes at the

heart of the very principles upon which the United Nations was founded.

Sweden’s support for Ukraine is felt deeply throughout our entire society. It comes from our

people, our civil society and the business community. We will support Ukraine for as long as it

takes.

Russia has not only violated the UN Charter, it has repeatedly violated international humanitarian

law and human rights law. Attacks targeting civilians, forcible transfer and deportation of

children, conflict-related sexual violence and torture – the list is far too long.

Ensuring accountability for these violations is crucial. If there is anything that we have learnt

from history, it is that there cannot be a just and lasting peace without accountability.

Sweden stands firmly behind the ICC, its independence and integrity, and recognises its vital role

not least in Ukraine.

Russia must also be held accountable for its breaches of the Chemical Weapons Convention,

both on and off the battlefield.

Russia’s war of aggression against a peaceful neighbour is one of the biggest strategic mistakes

and moral failures of the 21st century.

Four and a half years after launching its full-scale invasion, Russia has failed to achieve its

objectives. Its economy is under strain, and its casualty numbers are devastating. Ordinary

Russians are withdrawing their funds from the bank, and a substantial share of Russia’s young

people are dying on the front lines.

The impact of Russia’s war of aggression extends far beyond Ukraine. Russia intensified its

systematic attacks on civilian infrastructure and on vessels in the Black Sea this summer. This has

3(12)

once again disrupted global food supply chains, exacerbating an already dire situation for

vulnerable people across the globe.

To President Putin and Mr Lavrov I say this: the path to peace is clear, the choice should be easy.

Withdraw your troops. End this war.

Sweden has been an active contributor to the United Nations for 80 years. And we remain

committed. But as a staunch partner, we will continue to push for a UN that is more effective,

more transparent and better equipped to uphold the principles of its charter. A UN that is

resolute.

Sweden’s first peacekeepers, 300 of them, served this organisation during the Suez Crisis in 1956.

Since then, more than 80 000 Swedes have followed in their footsteps.

We have a long tradition of supporting mediation through the UN. It began in 1948 with the

UN’s first mediator, Sweden’s Folke Bernadotte.

We have long been a major donor of development assistance. And we remain devoted to tackling

global development challenges and contributing to urgent humanitarian efforts.

Sweden remains a generous donor. But development assistance alone will not be enough to meet

the challenges before us.

Reducing emissions to curb climate change is a common and global challenge, and is necessary to

safeguard and increase development gains in the coming decades.

Sweden will continue to promote climate action based on urgency and opportunity – urgency

based on what science tells us, opportunity based on the economic growth, jobs and

strengthened competitiveness that climate transition brings.

Given the state of the world, changes are necessary to ensure the UN’s central role in

international affairs and its ability to address today’s challenges.

4(12)

An efficient, effective, nimble and well-coordinated UN is urgently needed. Sweden strongly

supports the Secretary-General’s UN80 initiative and expects all UN entities to engage fully, with

a clear focus on improving delivery at country level.

We also expect Member States to give the UN adequate resources. Assessed contributions must

be paid in full and on time. As members, we also need to carefully consider institutional reforms

and align mandates with available resources.

UN80 is an opportunity to strengthen the UN’s impact across all three pillars, and to reinforce

the international system firmly grounded in the UN Charter and international law.

Sweden remains firm in its defence of the UN’s normative mandates on human rights, gender

equality and sexual and reproductive health and rights.

Everyone has the right to live freely and with dignity. To be who they are and to love whom they

choose. Sweden will always stand up for that freedom, and for equal rights of all.

A balanced expansion of the Security Council would strengthen its credibility and the legitimacy

of its decisions.

Sweden would like to see permanent and non-permanent seats added, and a fairer representation

of all continents on the Council.

Africa, home to 1.3 billion people and the largest regional bloc in the United Nations, has no

permanent seat. This is neither logical nor fair.

Furthermore, the veto should never be used to prevent the UN from acting against serious

violations of international law or in humanitarian disasters.

We must continue to strengthen our United Nations. To make this organisation stronger and

better equipped to prevent conflict and meet the challenges of tomorrow.

5(12)

We must continue to find common agreements, based on the fundamentals. Every country’s

sovereignty and territorial integrity. Prohibition of the use of force. Respect for international law,

human rights and humanitarian principles.

It is our shared responsibility to ensure that the UN remains relevant, effective and resolute. That

it becomes greater than the sum of its parts.

To show once again that we can turn the page on conflict and chaos and move toward peace and

prosperity.

Madam/ Mister President

This year also marks 65 years since Secretary–General Dag Hammarskjöld died. His integrity,

conviction and commitment to the vision and values of our organisation are still remembered.

Sweden continues to support the UN investigation aimed at clarifying the circumstances

surrounding Secretary–General Hammarskjöld’s death.

I would like to conclude with the words of Mr Hammarskjöld:

“It is no news to anybody, but we sense it in different degrees, that our world of today is more

than ever before one world.

The weakness of one is the weakness of all, and the strength of one – not the military strength,

but the real strength, the economic and social strength, the happiness of people – is indirectly the

strength of all.”

Thank you.

Mr. Secretary-General, Excellencies, Distinguished Delegates, Good evening.

I  warmly  congratulate  you  on  your  election  to  lead  the  eighty-first  session  of  this General  Assembly.  You  assume  this  high  office  at  a  defining  moment  for  our Organisation and for humanity. Seychelles assures you of its full support and wishes you every success in guiding our work.

Mr. Secretary-General,

As  this  is  the  final  General  Assembly  you  will  address  in  your  current  capacity, Seychelles extends its profound gratitude for your decade of dedicated stewardship. You have consistently championed a United Nations that is more effective, responsive, and grounded in the needs of the people we serve.

The theme of this session strikes at the core of our contemporary global crisis: trust has eroded, yet structural transformation is urgently upon us.

In a world increasingly fractured by geopolitical rivalry, the answer cannot be a retreat into isolationism. It must be a revitalized commitment to multilateralism. The United Nations  must  prove  that  dialogue  can  bridge  division,  that  international  law  must prevail over force, and that collective action achieves what unilateralism never can.

Seychelles approaches the world guided by an enduring, foundational principle: we are a friend to all, and an enemy to none.

Our commitment to non-alignment is not passive indifference; it is an active choice for peace. It is the conviction that principled diplomacy, mutual respect, and international law are the true foundations of global stability.

Small states like ours do not seek strategic competition—we seek shared solutions. This  requires  a  multilateral  system  that  is  principled  yet  practical,  ambitious  yet accountable, and representative yet effective. In short, a United Nations that delivers for all.

If  multilateralism  is  to  deliver,  it  must  first  secure  the  peace  upon  which  all  human progress  depends.  Without  peace,  sustainable  development  is  an  illusion.  Conflict destroys lives, uproots communities, and diverts vital resources away from healthcare, education, and climate resilience.

We must reject the normalization of perpetual conflict and the selective application of international law. International law must apply equally to all—without exception, bias, or double standards.

This principle is vital to maritime security. The oceans are the lifeblood of global trade. When  maritime  routes  are  threatened  by  piracy,  geopolitical  friction,  or  armed aggression,  the  shocks  ripple  far  beyond  regional  waters,  devastating  vulnerable island economies.

Freedom of navigation and maritime security must be preserved under international law. Small and vulnerable states should never bear the collateral economic costs of conflicts in which they have no part.

Furthermore,  we  firmly  reject  unilateral  coercive  measures  that  violate  international law and inflict disproportionate hardship on innocent populations.

Yet, our global architecture is failing to enforce these principles because its key organs remain outdated. The Security Council’s inability to act decisively in moments of global crisis undermines its very purpose. Its composition reflects a bygone era, not twenty-first-century geopolitical realities.

Reform  is  no  longer  a  matter  of  political  convenience—it  is  a  matter  of  institutional survival and legitimacy.

Seychelles reaffirms Africa’s unified position: our continent must hold no fewer than two permanent seats on the Security Council, with full prerogatives, including the veto for as long as it exists.

This  past  June,  Seychelles  proudly  celebrated  fifty  years  of  independence.  Half  a century of self-determination has taught us a fundamental lesson: size does not define sovereignty, and geography does not diminish dignity.

We may be a Small Island Developing State, but we sit as an equal participant in this hall.  Every  nation—regardless  of  population  or  economic  power—possesses  an inherent right to sovereignty, territorial integrity, and national dignity.

Today, however, sovereignty faces quiet, insidious threats. Transnational organized crime, drug trafficking, and illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing threaten our security, wreck our marine ecosystems, and steal from our people.

Because these threats are interconnected, our response must be equally integrated: stronger  international  intelligence-sharing,  expanded  maritime  surveillance,  and practical law enforcement support. It is unreasonable to expect nations safeguarding vast oceanic domains with modest budgets to meet standards set by heavily resourced states without providing them the tools to do so.

Resilience without resources is not resilience - it is merely survival. The same logic applies directly to the climate crisis.

For Seychelles, climate change is not a prospective debate; It is a daily reality that strikes at the very foundations of our society. Rising seas threaten our infrastructure, our coastal livelihoods, and our very territory.

The science is undisputed. The targets are clear. What remains missing is political will and  execution.  Major  emitters  must  display  greater  ambition,  while  all  nations  act according  to  their  responsibilities  and  capabilities.  Economic  growth  that  bankrupts the planet for future generations is not progress.

Seychelles  welcomes  the  Advisory  Opinion  of  the  International  Court  of  Justice  on climate  change,  reinforcing  that  climate  action  is  rooted  in  international  law, equity, and  intergenerational  justice.  Mitigation,  adaptation,  technology  transfer,  and  loss-and-damage funding are not acts of charity—they are legal obligations.

Our  survival  is  inextricably  linked  to  the  health  of  the  ocean.  Protecting  our  marine environment  is  an  economic  necessity.  As  an  early  ratifying  state  of  the  BBNJ Agreement, Seychelles looks forward to its first Conference of the Parties and urges all Member States to finalize their ratifications swiftly.

Yet, our ambitions are hampered by structural economic barriers. Frameworks like the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS and the Sevilla Commitment must be backed by  real  capital.  For  small  island  states,  debt  sustainability  is  a  matter  of  national survival.

We require affordable, accessible, long-term financing, meaningful debt relief, and the full  implementation  of  the  Multidimensional  Vulnerability  Index  (MVI).  Measuring  a nation’s development solely by GDP per capita ignores extreme exposure to climate shocks and geographic isolation. If international finance is to serve reality, it must first measure reality correctly.

Looking  ahead,  we  must  also  address  the  rapid  rise  of  artificial  intelligence  and emerging technologies.

While  these  tools  offer  immense  opportunities  for  development  and  ocean management,  they  also  risk  widening  the  global  divide  and  enabling  new  forms  of warfare and cybercrime.

We  must  ensure  technology  serves  human  dignity.  We  call  for  global  digital governance anchored in human rights, ethical standards, and international law—with the United Nations playing a central role in steering this transformation.

Excellencies,

Across every crisis we face, one fundamental truth endures: our ultimate duty is to the people  we  represent—our  families,  our  youth,  our  coastal  communities,  and  future generations.

Our nations represent a rich tapestry of cultures, languages, and political systems. But diversity need not breed division. Guided by our policy of friend to all and enemy to none,  Seychelles  believes  that  our  differences  can  be  the  dynamic  foundation  for stronger global cooperation.

Let us restore trust through deliberate action: By upholding the rule of international law unconditionally; By reforming our global governance institutions to reflect today’s world; By delivering equitable climate and development finance; and By protecting our shared oceans and climate.

Seychelles enters this General Assembly with deep humility, clear conviction, and an unshakable belief in the multilateral system. We may be a small nation, but our voice, our sovereignty, and our aspirations will never be measured by our size on a map.
