At the outset, I congratulate you, Mr. President, on assuming the presidency of

the 81st Session of the General Assembly.

It is an honour to address this Assembly for the first time, as Thailand marks 80

years of membership in the United Nations.

When  Thailand  joined  this  Organization,  the  post-war  international  order  was

still taking shape. Today, it is being reshaped once again.

Many of its old certainties are giving way. But what comes next is not yet settled.

We  are  seeing  many  transformations  taking  place.  Power  is  becoming  more

fragmented. Strategic competition is becoming sharper and international rules are under

strain.

At the same time, technology is transforming our societies, while climate change

is testing our resilience. Our institutions, however, are struggling to keep pace.

Confidence in our ability to work together is weakening.

That is why this year’s theme speaks directly to the task before us. Managing the

transformation requires trust: trust between countries, trust in the rules we share, and

trust that our institutions can deliver.

But trust cannot be taken for granted. It must be earned.

Trust weakens when principles are applied selectively. When countries have little

say in decisions that shape their future. And when promises made in this Assembly fail

to improve lives beyond it.

Rebuilding trust means addressing each of these concerns.

We  must  uphold  common  principles  consistently.  We  must  give  countries  a

genuine  stake  in  the  international  system,  including  a  stronger  voice  for  the  Global

South. And we must take shared responsibility for turning commitments into results.

The UN’s purposes remain as relevant as ever: to promote peace and security,

human rights and dignity, sustainable development and cooperation among sovereign

equals.

But we cannot build lasting peace if security is assured for some and denied to

others.  Universal  human  rights  lose  their  meaning  when  applied  selectively.

Development loses its purpose when prosperity remains in the hands of a few.

For Thailand, peace means more than the absence of war. It requires dialogue to

settle differences and respect for international law, so that all countries can live with

security and dignity.

The situation in Palestine continues to demand our attention. It reminds us that

the principles we uphold must protect people when they need them the most.

That  is  why  human  rights  must  be  universal  in  practice.  As  a  member  of  the

Human Rights Council, Thailand believes that our work must reach beyond resolutions

and make a real difference in people’s lives.

Development  must  be  people-centered  and  sustainable.  Growth  must  improve

people’s lives today without closing off the opportunities of tomorrow.

Consistent application of principles gives countries the confidence that they will

be  treated  fairly.  But  that  confidence  must  also  extend  to  how  decisions  are  made.

Countries need to know that their voices count.

Today the UN’s membership has become nearly universal. But representation has

not evolved at the same pace.

An international system cannot command trust if large parts of its membership

feel they have too little say in shaping it.

Rebuilding  trust  requires  shared  ownership.  The  United  Nations  must  reflect

today’s world, not the distribution of power eighty years ago.

That  is  why  Thailand  supports  Security  Council  reform  that  gives  developing

countries and underrepresented regions, particularly in the Global South, a greater role

in decision making.

Asia, too, must be better represented. For all its economic weight, Asia must be

able to help shape global decisions and carry more responsibility for the outcomes.

And representation must also mean that women have a meaningful voice in the

decisions  that  shape  our  common  future.  They  are  already  at  the  forefront  of  this

Organization’s  work  –  from  development  to  peacekeeping.  As  the  United  Nations

considers  its  next  Secretary  General,  maybe  it  is  time  that  this  representation  be

reflected at the highest level.

Representation and effectiveness must advance together. We commend

Secretary-General António Guterres for his commitment to reform, including through

the UN80 Initiative. We stand ready to work with his successor to carry this work

forward.

Having a stronger voice in global institutions means countries working together

on the problems closest to them. This is where regional cooperation has a vital role.

The United Nations must remain the centerpiece of the multilateral system. But

we cannot expect it to do everything. It cannot settle problems when Member States are

not willing to act.

Regional institutions can help turn that willingness into cooperation. They bring

countries  together  around  shared  challenges  and  translate  global  principles  suited  to

local realities.

In this way, regionalism becomes a building block of effective multilateralism.

ASEAN has demonstrated this for almost six decades. It has grown from five to

eleven members. We do not always agree. But we have learned to manage differences

and preserve space for cooperation.

For Thailand, that practical cooperation means serving as a trusted platform. We

want to leverage our strengths as a logistical hub and manufacturing base to connect

markets and supply chains across our region.

Our  conviction  is  that  together  we  should  combine  Asia’s  diversity  for  co-

creation, bringing together the different strengths of our countries to  promote shared

prosperity.

The same thinking should also extend beyond Asia. Thailand continues to pursue

free trade agreements with partners across regions, to expand trade and opportunities

for both sides.

Additionally, our Thailand–Africa Initiative seeks to deepen political, economic

and development cooperation -- to build partnerships of equals across our regions.

Institutions earn trust through what their members are prepared to do. A greater

voice must come with a willingness to contribute. Shared ownership therefore must lead

to shared responsibility.

The Charter begins with the words “We the peoples.”  Thailand believes that this

work must begin at home.

The  Sustainable  Development  Goals  (SDGs)  provide  us  with  an  important

framework that goes beyond development. Ultimately, they are about enabling people

to live in peace and dignity. Progress towards achieving the SDGs also shapes how we

are  building  a  strong  and  resilient  economy  and  how  we  remain  accountable  to  our

people.

Thailand will leverage our strengths. We are building upon our strong agricultural

base to be a source of food security for the world. Meanwhile, our Universal Health

Coverage ensures that people have access to affordable and quality healthcare, while

also developing Thailand into a medical and wellness hub.

Additionally,  our  energy  transition  efforts  take  Thailand  closer  to  meeting

climate obligations. And through our solar rooftop policy, we are also creating greater

economic opportunities for households by allowing them to sell excess electricity back

to the grid.

However, this responsibility goes beyond development.

Thailand’s humanitarian tradition demonstrates this conviction. In the late 1970s,

Thailand provided temporary refuge and assistance to large numbers of  Cambodians

fleeing violence and famine.

Today,  we  are  giving  displaced  persons  from  Myanmar  who  have  lived  in

temporary shelters in Thailand for decades greater opportunities to work and support

their families.

For the Rohingya transiting in Thailand, we have adopted a community-based

alternative to immigration detention for Rohingya children to better protect their rights

and access to services.

Our responsibility as a neighbor also means addressing the challenges in our own

neighborhood.

One of those challenges is the dispute between Thailand and Cambodia. We have

been through a difficult period. When I met with Prime Minister Hun Manet in May,

we sought to resolve difficult issues through bilateral dialogue, while rebuilding trust

and confidence in order to move forward together.

It is regrettable that Cambodia did not give dialogue a genuine chance and chose

a  different  path  by  initiating  compulsory  conciliation  proceedings  under  UNCLOS.

Nevertheless, Thailand is engaging in good faith. But our position is clear -- this process

concerns the delimitation of maritime boundaries only.

In the meantime, Cambodia must work with us to strengthen security along our

shared  border,  including  through  concrete  cooperation  to  combat  online  scams  and

demining. Our communities will not be safe if we do not make concrete progress on

these matters. Ultimately our shared border must be a place of shared prosperity, not

one that continues to bear the scars of conflict.

Let me be clear. Thailand has never sought conflict. But peace can only be built

when  we  work  together  in  earnest.  And  surely  this  will  require  genuine  effort  from

Cambodia.

That  same  commitment  guides  our  approach  to  Myanmar.    Thailand  supports

peace, national reconciliation and a durable solution that is Myanmar-led and Myanmar-

owned.

We believe in constructive and calibrated re-engagement, within ASEAN and in

coordination with relevant partners, while encouraging concrete progress on the ground.

In  both  cases,  our  responsibility  is  to  make  dialogue  possible  and  progress

achievable.

And  when  threats  cross  borders,  responsibility  must  be  shared  more  widely.

Thailand has stepped up efforts on prevention and suppression of narcotics through our

partnership with the UNODC, other regional and international organizations as well as

neighboring countries.

And through the Global Partnership against Online Scams, Thailand is bringing

together all the relevant stakeholders together to prevent these crimes.

Eighty years ago, in our first address to this Assembly,  the Kingdom of  Siam

affirmed that it “followed the path of peaceful settlement and friendly  co-operation.”

That path still guides Thailand today.

As a new international order takes shape, we must carry that spirit forward. No

country can write its future alone. And no international order can earn lasting trust if

too many countries feel that the system is written for them, but not with them.

A rules-based international order with shared ownership in shaping our common

future is the condition that will help rebuild that trust.

The future of the United Nations will depend on the trust we rebuild through our

actions today.

Let us give every nation reason to believe in the United Nations, and every person

reason to believe that the United Nations can deliver for them.

I thank you.

Excellency Mr. Khalilur Rahman, President of the United Nations General Assembly, Ladies and Gentlemen,

At the outset, allow me to congratulate His Excellency Mr. Khalilur Rahman on his election as President of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly.

We meet at a time when tensions are growing.

Conflicts are multiplying.

Trust is eroding.

And uncertainty is becoming part of our daily reality.

Over  the  past  several  days,  from  this  very  rostrum,  we  have  heard  many  delegations  speak  about  the importance of peace.

Peace remains our most fundamental responsibility.

But peace cannot be taken for granted.

It must be diligently built.

And it must be steadfastly protected.

And it must be passed on to future generations.

It is precisely in this spirit that Tajikistan initiated the proclamation of 2027–2036 as the International Decade of Strengthening Peace for Future Generations, which was adopted by the General Assembly resolution on 25 June 2026.

We are grateful to Member States, partners and the United Nations system for supporting this initiative of the President of the Republic of Tajikistan, His Excellency Mr. Emomali Rahmon.

The idea behind the Decade is simple:

Our responsibility for peace does not end with our generation.

We must work to resolve the conflicts of today.

But we must also prevent the conflicts of tomorrow.

Building on this vision, Tajikistan will convene a High-Level International Conference on Peace in Dushanbe in June 2027, in cooperation with the United Nations Alliance of Civilizations, the United Nations Youth Office and other partners.

The  Conference  will  help  launch  the  Decade  and  turn  our  shared  commitment  to  peace  into  practical cooperation.

Our position on conflicts and disputes is clear.

They must be resolved peacefully.

Through dialogue, diplomacy, negotiations and in accordance with the Charter of the United Nations.

In this context, the situation in Palestine remains a matter of deep concern to Tajikistan.

The continuing suffering of civilians must end.

We reiterate our call for a lasting ceasefire in Gaza and unhindered access to humanitarian assistance.

Our position remains principled and consistent:

A  just  and  lasting  peace  can  only  be  achieved  through  dialogue  and  diplomacy,  in  accordance  with international law and the relevant resolutions of the United Nations.

Tajikistan reaffirms its support for the establishment of an independent and sovereign State of Palestine, based on the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital, living side by side with Israel in peace and security.

But peace cannot endure in isolation.

It needs development.

Opportunity.

Inclusion.

And hope.

Lasting peace requires sustainable development.

Yet development remains deeply uneven.

Climate  change  is  accelerating.  Inequalities  persist.  And  too  many  countries  continue  to  face  structural barriers to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals.

For  developing  countries  —  particularly  mountainous  and  landlocked  developing  countries  —  these pressures are even greater.

We  therefore  need  stronger  international  solidarity  and  development  financing  that  is  more  accessible, predictable and adequate.

For Tajikistan, sustainable development begins at home.

Our  National  Development  Strategy  2030  remains  a  key  framework  for  economic  growth,  reducing vulnerabilities and improving the well-being of our people.

But development is not only about economic growth.

It is about people.

Opportunity.

And inclusion.

That is why Tajikistan continues to advance the empowerment of women and their meaningful participation in political, economic and social life.

It is also why we place growing emphasis on legal literacy.

In  2025,  the  General Assembly  proclaimed  2027  as  the  International Year  of  Legal Literacy,  following  an initiative of Tajikistan.

Respect for the law strengthens peaceful and inclusive societies.

But development also depends on something even more fundamental.

Something that connects people, economies, ecosystems and nations.

Water.

Mr.President,

The world remains far from achieving universal access to safe water and sanitation.

Progress is being made.

But not fast enough.

For Tajikistan, this challenge is both global and deeply national.

We are a mountainous country, home to thousands of glaciers and the source of major rivers that sustain communities far beyond our borders.

We know the value of water.

And we know its vulnerability.

For more than two decades, under the leadership of President of Tajikistan H.E. Emomali Rahmon, water has remained at the heart of our international engagement.

From the global Water Action Decades to the Dushanbe Water Process.

From the 2023 United Nations Water Conference to the global agenda on glacier preservation.

Our message has remained consistent:

Water requires cooperation.

And cooperation must lead to action.

The next two years will be decisive.

Later this year, the international community will gather for the United Nations Water Conference in Abu Dhabi.

In 2027, a high-level preparatory meeting will take place here at United Nations Headquarters.

And  in  2028,  we  will  gather  in  Dushanbe  for  the  United  Nations  Water  Conference  and  the  final comprehensive review of the Water Action Decade.

Member States will negotiate and adopt by consensus an outcome — the Dushanbe Water Framework.

This gives us an opportunity to assess what we have achieved, confront what remains unfinished, and decide how global water cooperation should move forward.

Because 2028 must not be an end point.

The conclusion of the Water Action Decade should mark the beginning of the next chapter of global water action.

The Dushanbe Water Framework can help us write that chapter.

A chapter focused on implementation.

On financing.

On technology and capacity.

On stronger partnerships.

And on protecting the sources of our water, including the world's rapidly changing glaciers.

Our objective is continuity, follow-up and implementation.

In  this  regard,  the  Dushanbe  Water  Process  can  help  sustain  that  momentum  beyond  2028,  connecting global commitments with national and regional action.

Our success will measured by the commitments we deliver.

We must also prepare for a world that is changing before our eyes.

Artificial intelligence is transforming our economies, our societies and the way we approach development.

As the Secretary-General recently reminded us:

“Used well, and shared widely, AI could compress decades of development into years.”

This is the opportunity before us.

AI should not become another source of division.

It should become a force for development, opportunity and reducing inequalities.

Last year, at the initiative of Tajikistan, the General Assembly adopted the resolution on the role of artificial intelligence in creating new opportunities for sustainable development in Central Asia.

This year, we took another step forward.

On August 31st, the General Assembly proclaimed the International Day of Safe, Secure and Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence, also at the initiative of Tajikistan.

Our message is simple:

Innovation must serve humanity.

Technological transformation is only one dimension of a rapidly changing world.

Old threats are also evolving.

And new ones are crossing borders faster than ever.

Terrorism and extremism. Cybercrime. Illicit trafficking in arms and narcotic drugs. Organized crime.

These threats know no borders.

Our response must be equally united.

Therefore,  the  Dushanbe  Process  on  Countering  Terrorism  and  its  Financing  has  become  an  important platform for international and regional cooperation.

We  will  continue  this  engagement,  including  by  convening  the  next  High-Level  Counter-Terrorism Conference in Dushanbe in 2027.

For our region, lasting security and sustainable development are also closely linked to Afghanistan.

Afghanistan needs peace, stability and economic opportunity.

Tajikistan will continue to support the Afghan people and constructive regional cooperation for a peaceful and stable Afghanistan.

When Tajikistan speaks about peace, we also speak from experience.

Next year, we will mark the 30th anniversary of the General Agreement on the Establishment of Peace and National Accord in Tajikistan.

That Agreement ended a devastating imposed civil war.

It was achieved through dialogue.

Through compromise.

And through the determination to put the future of the country above division.

The United Nations was an important partner in that process.

Three decades later, the same belief in dialogue continues to guide our relations with our neighbours.

Recent agreements with Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan have helped resolve long-standing border issues and opened a new chapter of cooperation in Central Asia.

Borders that once divided us can now connect us.

Our experience has strengthened our conviction:

Even  the  most  difficult  disagreements  can  be  resolved  when  there  is  political  will,  dialogue  and  mutual respect.

There is a wider lesson here.

Peace requires effective institutions.

And international cooperation requires an effective United Nations.

This is why Tajikistan supports the ongoing UN80 reform process.

Reform is not an end in itself.

It must make the United Nations more effective, agile, coherent and better able to deliver.

We support reducing duplication, improving efficiency and strengthening accountability, while preserving the Organization's ability to fulfil its mandates.

Member States must remain at the centre of this process.

A stronger UN also requires Member States willing to assume greater responsibility.

Tajikistan is ready to do so.

For the first time in his history, Tajikistan is seeking election to the United Nations Security Council for the 2028–2029 term.

We approach this responsibility with humility and determination.

We congratulate brotherly Kyrgyzstan on its election to the Security Council for 2027-2028 and look forward to its contribution to the work of the Council.

Tajikistan seeks to build on this growing engagement.

We would bring our own experience.

The experience of a country that has known conflict — and built peace.

That has faced difficult borders — and chosen dialogue and compromise.

A  country  that  shares  a  long  border  with  Afghanistan  and  understands  first-hand  the  importance  of prevention, stability and regional cooperation.

And a country that has consistently advanced practical multilateral initiatives on water, glaciers, counter-terrorism, sustainable development and peace.

For us, membership in the Security Council would not be about status.

It would be about responsibility.

Responsibility to uphold the Charter.

Responsibility to listen to all voices-large and small.

Responsibility to seek common ground where divisions persist.

And responsibility to contribute constructively to the maintenance of international peace and security.

We seek not simply a seat at the table.

We seek an opportunity to contribute.

To bring our experience.

To build bridges.

And to help advance the cause of peace.

We began with peace.

Let me end with peace.

The challenges before us are great.

But  they  are  not  greater  than  our  capacity  to  overcome  them  —  if  we  choose  cooperation  over confrontation, dialogue over division, and hope over fear.

The choices we make today will shape the world we leave behind tomorrow.

That is our responsibility.

To our peoples.

To one another.

And above all, to future generations.

Let us leave them not simply a world with fewer conflicts.

Let us leave them a world with more peace.

Tajikistan stands ready to do its part.

I thank you for your attention!

speaker_post: Permanent Representative to the United Nations
text:
Mr. President, Mr. Secretary-General, Excellencies, Distinguished Delegates, Ladies and Gentlemen,

First of all, I have the honour to convey, on behalf of the President of Turkmenistan,  His  Excellency  Mr.  Serdar  Berdimuhamedov,  greetings  and wishes of peace and prosperity to the peoples of your countries.

Allow me to congratulate you, Mr Khalilur Rahman, on your election as President of the eighty-first session of the United Nations General Assembly and to wish you every success in discharging your important responsibilities.

I would also like to express our appreciation to Ms Annalena Baerbock

for her leadership of the General Assembly during its previous session.

The current international environment requires all States to demonstrate a high degree of responsibility, political foresight and readiness for concerted action.  Rising  conflict  potential,  the  erosion  of  trust,  economic  instability, climate  risks  and  the  rapid  development  of  new  technologies  are  becoming increasingly  intertwined,  directly  affecting  the  security  and  well-being  of peoples.

In these circumstances, it is particularly important to uphold the common purposes enshrined in the Charter of the United Nations; ensure respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of States, their sovereign equality and non-interference  in  their  internal  affairs;  and  strengthen  the  rule  of  international law.

Turkmenistan firmly believes that the United Nations must continue to serve as the universal and legitimate foundation of international cooperation and  as  the  principal  mechanism  for  reconciling  interests  and  developing solutions in the areas of peace, security and sustainable development.

It is from this perspective that our country approaches the work of the

eighty-first session of the General Assembly.

Ensuring  international  peace  and  security  remains  a  key  priority  for Turkmenistan. The permanent neutrality of our country, recognized three times by  the  General  Assembly,  provides  a  practical  foundation  for  advancing political  and  diplomatic  methods,  preventive  diplomacy,  mediation  and  the peaceful settlement of disputes.

We  consider  it  essential  to  consistently  foster  a  culture  of  trust  and dialogue and to restore the legal and humanistic foundations of international relations.

In this regard, Turkmenistan intends to convene, under the auspices of the  United  Nations,  intergovernmental  consultations  on  the  elaboration  of  a Global  Peace  Strategy  founded  on  the  principles  of  peace,  security  and preventive diplomacy.

As  a  further  step  in  this  direction,  we  propose  proclaiming  a  United Nations  Decade  of  Dialogue  and  Preventive  Diplomacy.  We  believe  that such  a  Decade  would  lend  a  systematic  character  to  the  efforts  of  States  to prevent  conflicts,  build  trust  and  establish  sustainable  channels  of  political communication.

Turkmenistan  will  also  propose  the  establishment,  within  the  United Nations,  of  a  Group  of  Friends  of  Multilateralism  and  the  Sovereign Equality  of  States.  Its  activities  could  contribute  to  safeguarding  the fundamental  principles  of  the  Charter  of  the  United  Nations,  strengthening dialogue  among  equals  and  preventing  the  emergence  of  dividing  lines  in international cooperation.

We  attach  particular  importance  to  supporting  the  United  Nations Regional Centre for Preventive Diplomacy for Central Asia, headquartered in Ashgabat.  The  year  2027  will  mark  the  twentieth  anniversary  of  its establishment. We regard this milestone as a unique opportunity to take stock of the Centre's work and identify new avenues for its practical contribution to peace, stability and cooperation in Central Asia.

To this end, during the current session Turkmenistan will submit a further draft General Assembly resolution on the role of the Regional Centre. We trust that the document will reaffirm our shared interest in further strengthening its mandate and operational capacity.

In  consistently  promoting  education  and  scientific  cooperation  as important pillars of peacebuilding, Turkmenistan will continue its engagement with the United Nations on the initiative to establish a University of Peace and Neutrality.  As  a  practical  first  step,  we  will  begin  consultations  on  the establishment  of  an  Academic  Centre  for  Peace,  Neutrality  and  Preventive Diplomacy at the Institute of International Relations of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Turkmenistan.

Digital  transformation  is  becoming  an  increasingly  important  factor  in sustainability  and  development.  Artificial intelligence  offers  broad opportunities,  while  also  requiring  responsible  international  governance  to prevent its use to the detriment of peace, security and trust.

In  this  regard,  Turkmenistan  proposes  the  development,  under  the auspices of the United Nations, of an International Code for the Peaceful Use of Artificial Intelligence in International Relations and Diplomacy. To support this work, we propose convening in Ashgabat an international expert dialogue on digital trust and the responsible use of artificial intelligence.

Peace and development are inextricably linked. For Turkmenistan, a key priority  in  this  area  is  the  development  of  sustainable,  safe  and  inclusive transport systems.

The  proclamation,  at  the  initiative  of  Turkmenistan,  of  the  United Nations Decade of Sustainable Transport for 2026-2035 has launched an important mechanism for systematic work, coordinated by the United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs, to put into practice the Decade's Implementation Plan. Within the framework of this long-term undertaking, our country  will  continue  its  work  towards  the  creation  of  a  Global  Atlas  of Sustainable  Transport  Connectivity  -  a  comprehensive  analytical  and informational tool for assessing progress, identifying infrastructure gaps and coordinating international efforts.

During  the  eighty-first  session,  Turkmenistan  will  actively  support  the implementation  of  the  Awaza  Programme  of  Action  for  Landlocked Developing  Countries  for  the  Decade  2024-2034  and  the  Awaza  Political Declaration.  In  this  context,  we  particularly  welcome  the  election  of Turkmenistan as Chair of the Group of Landlocked Developing Countries for  2027-2028.  We  regard  the  confidence  placed  in  us  as  both  a  great responsibility and an opportunity to work together with the States of the Group to give fresh impetus to the practical implementation of the Awaza Programme of  Action  in  such  priority  areas  as  transport  and  energy  connectivity.  We proceed  from  the  need  to  translate  the  agreements  reached  into  concrete infrastructure, trade and investment projects.

We  propose  considering  the  establishment  in  Turkmenistan,  under  the auspices of the United Nations, of an International Centre for Sustainable Trade Logistics and Customs Cooperation. Such a Centre could serve as a practical  platform  for  harmonizing  procedures,  exchanging  best  practices, digitalizing  transit  and  expanding  developing  countries'  access  to  global markets.

Our country also proposes the establishment, under the auspices of the United  Nations,  of  a  transregional  transport  corridor  linking  South  and Central Asia with Europe through the Caspian Sea.

We  are  confident  that  its  development  would  help  diversify  routes, strengthen connectivity, expand trade and promote closer economic ties among the regions.

Excellencies, Distinguished Delegates,

Environmental security, climate change and the sustainable use of energy

resources are integral components of common security.

In this area, Turkmenistan will continue to promote multilateral dialogue by proposing the establishment of the Ashgabat Climate Dialogue - an open multilateral  platform  for  regular  political  and  expert  engagement,  the advancement  of  practical  climate  initiatives  and  the  strengthening  of international partnerships.

We believe particular attention must be paid to strengthening the climate resilience  of  regions  severely  affected  by  drought  and  water  scarcity.  This requires  coordinated  solutions  combining  modern  technologies,  financing, data exchange and regional cooperation.

In pursuance of the General Assembly resolution entitled "Key role of reliable and stable energy connectivity in ensuring sustainable development", Turkmenistan  will  continue  consultations  in  preparation  for  the  High-level Forum  on  Sustainable  Energy  for  All.  We  view  the  Forum  as  an  effective platform for developing practical approaches to ensuring a reliable, affordable and sustainable energy supply.

In the socioeconomic sphere, Turkmenistan will continue its active and responsible  work  as  a  member  of  the  United  Nations  Economic  and  Social Council for the period 2026-2028, as well as its constructive engagement in the work of the Council's subsidiary bodies.

Turkmenistan attaches great importance to the humanitarian dimension of  international  cooperation.  Lasting  peace  is  impossible  without  the  full participation of women and young people, the preservation of human dignity, mutual respect and equal opportunities.

Our country will continue to advance the Women and Peace and Security agenda,  including  by  developing  the  Central  Asian  Women's  Dialogue  and expanding its cooperation with the United Nations Peacebuilding Commission and UN-Women.

At  the  same  time,  we  will  support  the  activities  of  the  Central  Asian Youth Dialogue and promote the broader and more meaningful participation of young people in international and regional peace initiatives in accordance with the Youth and Peace and Security agenda.

Turkmenistan  regards  the  strengthening  of  international  law  as  an essential condition for a just and sustainable international order. We welcome the  consensus  adoption  of  the  General  Assembly  resolution  initiated  by  our country proclaiming 2028 the International Year of Law.

As  part  of  the  preparatory  process,  we  propose  convening  in Turkmenistan in 2027 an International Forum devoted to the interrelationship between international law, disarmament, neutrality, preventive diplomacy and sustainable  development.  We  believe  that  the  Forum  will  help  strengthen respect  for  the  Charter  of  the  United  Nations,  enhance  the  role  of  legal mechanisms and engage the younger generation in the study and development of international law.

Mr. President,

All  initiatives  of  Turkmenistan  are  united  by  a  common  purpose:  to strengthen peace and trust, advance cooperation among equals and create the conditions for a dignified future for present and succeeding generations.

We  stand  ready  to  work  with  all  Member  States,  the  United  Nations Secretariat and international partners towards the practical implementation of the proposals outlined above.

We  are  confident  that,  with  political  will,  mutual  respect  and commitment to dialogue, the international community can overcome existing differences and achieve tangible progress towards the purposes of the United Nations.

Turkmenistan will continue to firmly uphold the principles of permanent neutrality, good-neighbourliness, peacefulness and constructive engagement, contributing to the strengthening of the central role of the United Nations in international affairs.

Thank you

Mr. President, esteemed Secretary-General António Guterres, I'm going to speak to António Guterres. On a winter morning on January 1, 2017, you entered your office on the 38th floor of the Secretariat building, fully prepared to undertake the most demanding mission of your long and distinguished career. Throughout this remarkable journey, you have remained true to yourself: a compassionate and enlightened leader, tireless, humble, and approachable; neither dazzled by the promise of your office nor daunted by the immense weight of an unrelenting agenda, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. You brought to the office neither an ego in constant need of reassurance nor a vanity requiring daily attention. You have remained humble, honest, and steadfast in your principles, never losing sight of the millions of women and children who have been abandoned and forgotten, caught in the turmoil of wars unleashed by warlords. As these wars drag on and their human and material costs become ever more unbearable, the firefighters are blamed for failing to extinguish the very fires set by the arsonists themselves.

António Guterres, when you leave this building on December 31, 2026, you will take your place among the great Secretaries General, whose legacies will continue to inspire young people around the world to follow your example of service to those most in need. General Assembly, I congratulate you on your election to preside over the 81st Session of the General Assembly. You bring to this House the wisdom of 5 billion people— 60% of the world's population— representing some of the world's oldest and most sophisticated civilizations. Excellencies, at one time in history, waking up from the horrors of World War II, we were intoxicated with the dreams of a United Nations promising a new dawn for humanity. After the unimaginable World War II, started by Christian civilized Europe, we could not have hoped for anything less. But it seems that human beings can never really have enough wars, and never really learn lessons of history, never really care.

After the Holocaust came the glorious birth of the State of Israel, but then came the Palestinian Nakba, 1948. Over the following years, we read about the wars of partition, famines in South Asia, the Korean War, the onslaught in Cambodia, Laos-Vietnam, the infamous Khmer Rouge genocide, later the Bosnian genocide, Rwanda genocide, and so many other wars. Then came the end of Cold War, bringing us euphoria, celebration, new promises of peace. The Berlin Wall collapsed, apartheid ended, but the seeds of future wars were sown, just as NATO and Gorbachev inked the post-Cold War arrangements. The ink had not even dried, and NATO began its fast eastbound expansion. As expected, for more than 4 years we have had this devastating war in Ukraine, a war that now has backfired into Russia.

Excellencies, we are gathering in this hall of nations, countries, large and small, some insanely rich, too many shockingly poor, but all enjoying equal voting rights. Yet we know equality is an illusion. Some possess non-threatening antiquated guns, while few others have perfected their nuclear arsenals, now 100 times more destructive than the ones dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945. As primitive as they were then, these experimental bombs incinerated two cities, almost all living beings in them. Those unfortunate ones who survived the blast died long, painful deaths. Russia, U.S., China, France, the U.K. —all members of the NPT— were joined by four countries not members of the NPT: Israel, India, Pakistan, North Korea.

Yes, North Korea had a nuclear arsenal estimated to be around 100. And North Korean leaders seem to have learned lessons from Libya, Ukraine, and the ongoing Iran-Israel-Yes war. Dismantle your nuclear capabilities and you lose. The only deterrence you have against a nuclear power deciding to bomb you into submission. On June 30, 2019, President Trump traveled to DMZ in the Korean Peninsula. The mysterious Swiss educator leader of North Korea, half the age of the American president, walked halfway, and the two leaders engaged in an embrace that promised peace.

This is what leaders do to advance peace: they show courage, audacity. President Trump, you did the right thing. Friends are friends. We cherish and embrace our friends, never ignoring them or excluding them from the table. But we talk to adversaries so that we don't become enemies. We talk to enemies to prevent wars, and perhaps we become partners in peace.

Those countries amassing nuclear weapons keep us all living near imminent catastrophe. One day, any day, by accident, miscalculation, computer error, madness, or foolish strategic design, we could become the last human generation. All the while, the brandishing of these weapons reinforces adversity and fear, which create a high barrier to achieving rational cooperation necessary to fulfill our responsibility to future generations. Trillions of dollars are invested in perfecting forms of death. Instead, we invest in a fraction of these trillions in clean water: food, schools, clinics. No thought was given to the tens of millions of fellow human beings pushed back to extreme deprivation by COVID-19, Ukraine-Russia war, and as if innocent bystanders on the periphery had not suffered enough, we are presented with another catastrophe: the Iran war and disruption of vital waterways for trade.

We know the madness of Iranian leaders seeking regional supremacy, pouring fuel into the fire of religious extremism in neighboring countries to destabilize wealthy, stable monarchies. Iranian leaders launch unwarranted attacks against neighbors, destroying civilian industries, infrastructure. Iran's rationale for these attacks is that those countries host American bases. So is Iran going to launch waves of drones and missiles against U.S. bases in Europe? Can we change course? Can we stop slipwalking into wider wars?

My invitation to President Trump: be audacious, be unpredictable, be visionary. Invite all nuclear powers and all major conventional military powers and industries, without exception, to a summit somewhere, maybe a town in Portugal, to talk on no first strike. Enhance regular communication between leaders of the nuclear powers. Commitment on reduction of nuclear weapons toward total deactivation and destruction of nuclear arsenals over a decade. Be yourself, be President Trump, be audacious, be unpredictable. Do the unthinkable, and you will gain worldwide gratitude and respect.

The humanitarian situation in Cuba is heartbreaking. We understand that the U.S. has provided $100 million in emergency humanitarian assistance to Cuba through CARITAS. In keeping with the U.S. humanitarian tradition, and toward creating an environment conducive to normal, long-term Cuba-U.S. relations, trade relations between Cuba and the U.S. and the rest of the world could be improved. Regarding the situation in Israeli-occupied territories: Gaza and West Bank. Timor-Leste, joined with the vast majority of U.N. member states, to reaffirm our belief that the two-state solution is the only viable solution for Israelis to live in peace with themselves and with the Palestinians, and for the Palestinians to live in peace with themselves and with the Israelis. The risks are too high to continue an unstable status quo.

The opportunity to better sit before us, and the choice is an international order: falling to pieces or rising to peace. Regarding Western Sahara, we welcome the Moroccan proposal and the recent Security Council resolution as an opportunity for dialogue. As with any situation of this nature, the people directly interested must be consulted on the future status. We hope that a just, comprehensive settlement is reached between Moroccan authorities and the Polisario Front. Excellencies, please take some time to look at the situation in Sudan, the worst humanitarian crisis in the world today. Look at the situation in South Sudan, Democratic Republic of Congo, Afghanistan, Myanmar, Yemen.

These are not abstract. They are people. They are women. They are children, youth in their best years. They are parents. They are grandparents.

And they are a grand jury of humanity, indicting us all, leaders and business, of death. For you have celebrated the tens of billions of dollars in profits from wars and deaths that you are accomplishers too. How is it that we can scroll past the end of the wall before finishing our coffee? How is it that a child pulling pieces of his family from the rubble has become a deadline, a headline so we quickly skip, a notification we silence? A Tuesday. Behind each of the dead is not a statistic.

It is a mother who will spend the rest of her life searching for a face in a crowd that will never appear. It is a boy hiding in silence, learning before he can read that the wall outside his door wants him dead. It is a girl, pregnant by the man who came to destroy her home, carrying inside her both the violence done to her and the life she never shows. We tell ourselves we would never look away if we truly saw it. And yet we saw Rwanda and Bosnia happen right under U.N. watch. We see it every day, live in our pockets, in vivid color, and still, somehow, life goes on normally.

We finish our meetings, we plan our weekends, we grow inure to the killings of Palestinians. This is not a lack of information. We are drowning in information. We can live. We can livestream as it all happens. This is a lack of feeling, a numbness we have allowed to settle over us like dust.

All this happened before our eyes, but from the powers that can make the difference between life and death, there is no response. And worse, we witness diplomatic acrobatics to brush off the bombing of a school or a hospital, saying that it does not really violate international law because the terrorists, quote unquote, may be hiding in the basement of the building. I'm worried. Worried that we have started treating a catastrophe as something we can simply coexist with. Worried that the killing of civilians is casually being justified. Worried that total force now sounds more viable than diplomacy.

This very institution was founded on a promise, all through the archives here. Resolutions say a ceasefire must hold, a border must not be crossed, a civilian must not be a target. Many of those promises remain unmet, raising concern that the phrase" never again" has lost meaning. I do not have a plan that will end a war by tonight. But I know this: numbness is not neutral. Silence is not safety.

Every time we let the suffering of people become background noise, we let ourselves forget how small the distance really is, how little separates your daughter, granddaughter, niece from the girl in the refugee camp you saw on the news last night. How many children right now are learning that a wall at war is normality. The more we linger in this fog, the harder it becomes for the hiding child to believe the wall is not his enemy. These tragedies are not somebody else's tragedy. They are what we allowed, what we still allow, and what we will answer for. There is a painful cry for a better world order as we witness the weakening into irrelevance of multilateral institutions.

No country, regardless of size or power, can address today's interconnected challenges alone. Excellencies, leadership is not merely discovering the angriest instinct of the electorate and amplifying it. Leadership is sometimes telling our own supporters that they are wrong. It is explaining complexity when a slogan would be easier. It is asking people to consider tomorrow when they are angry about today. It is persuading citizens that humanity of others who may worship differently, speak another language, or vote for another party does not diminish their own freedoms.

Statementship requires patience, persuasion, courage to compromise. And above all, it requires an understanding that power belongs brings responsibility, not exemption. The Charter of the United Nations was not written to make the strong weak. It was written to prevent the strong from making the world unlivable. Soon we will elect a new Secretary-General. The regional rotation precedent must be preserved.

Africa had an unprecedented continuous rhetoric: Butrus Butrus-Gali, 1992-1996, Kofi Annan, 1997-2006. Now the Security Council will elect a Latin American as our Secretary-General for 2027-2032. And after more than 80 years of men at the helm of our organization, needless to say, we ought to have enough wisdom and elect a woman with unquestionable integrity, unblemished record, and in defense of human rights, a strong advocacy of gender equality and inclusion, rule of law, democracy, solid experience in senior management in national and multilateral institutions. Mr. President, Excellencies, for developing countries, particularly small island developing states and least developed countries, efficiency must translate into stronger delivery on the ground, not reduced essential support. Timor-Leste urges comprehensive reform, expansion in both the permanent and non-permanent categories, so that developing countries and historically underrepresented regions have a stronger voice in decisions concerning international peace and security. The veto is inconsistent with the sovereign equality of member states.

President, Timor-Leste reaffirms the principles of climate justice, common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities in the light of different national circumstances. Greater climate ambition must be accompanied by accessible, predictable finance: adaptation support, technology transfer, and capacity building. Artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies reshape our societies. Developing countries must actively participate in their governance and development. The Science for Development Summit 2026 was held in Delhi, August 2026, under the theme" Science in Service of Life." This was an initiative of myself and my brother, the Prime Minister of Timor-Leste, Excellency Kairala Shanana Guzmán.

We brought into Timor-Leste more than 20 Nobel laureates, scientists from around the world, leading thinkers to explore how science, technology, and innovation can be placed at the service of humanity and sustainable development. The same spirit of using knowledge, education, and human potential in the service of peace will also guide the chess for peace tournament played for Dili Timor-Leste in January 2027, jointly sponsored by my office and Mr. Keir San, former President of FIDE, International Chess Federation. It will bring together young people with over 100 chess masters from around the globe, using chess as a tool to promote education, dialogue, friendship, peace among generations. Mr. President, our accession to ASEAN, 26 October 2025, was a historic moment for our country, marking the culmination of a 14-year process that began in Timor-Leste, formally applied for membership in March 2011. Fellow ASEAN leaders provided us generally technical assistance, capacity building, and practical guidance, and they continue to do so. It is required of us strong institutions, capable public servants, effective implementation of ASEAN commitments across political, security, economic, and sociocultural communities.

Our foreign policy seeks friendship with all, and hostilities, none. We aim to maintain balanced constructive relations with all our major powers' development partners. Timor-Leste also brings the energy and aspiration of young population. Our young people are increasingly connected to the region and eager to learn, work, and contribute. As ASEAN works towards Community Vision 2045, Timor-Leste will support a united people center and resilient ASEAN. We will also support ASEAN centrality and constructive relations with all external partners.

We are a small island developing state, a least developed country, and a nation whose history demonstrates both the necessity and the possibilities of multilateralism. Last but not least, in parting, I want to share a selected message from children and youth who responded to my invitation a few days ago to write a few words expressing their hopes and dreams, so that they are here and they are listening back home in Timor-Leste. I selected 10 sentences for peace for the United Nations General Assembly, giving them a voice. And I begin, and I quote," From a country that has learned from war, Timor-Leste sends a message to the world. That is, peace is not just a dream, but a decision that we all have to choose." By Olguita, 16 years old.

We may look different, speak different languages, and come from different places, but we all bleed the same color. So why should our differences divide us? By Elizabeth, 16 years old." May we build a world where no child learns the sound of war before the sound of laughter, and where no dream is buried because someone else's hatred." By Emily, 16." Why should we choose hate and war when love is a choice?"

By Ira Bela, 12 years old." My voice may be small, but my request is simple. Let children grow up knowing the sound of peace, not the sound of war. Let them inherit schools, homes, and opportunities, not fear, destruction, and hatred. Let the leaders of today give the children of tomorrow a reason to believe in peace." By Victoria, 12 years old."

Let our differences be bridges between hearts, not walls between nations, so that every child can grow knowing the sound of laughter instead of the sound of war." Natalia, 17." Let every weapon fall silent so every child can grow up knowing the sound of peace." By Christian, 16." I only think that peace in the world begins within us. When we learn to love each other unconditionally, forgive sincerely, and respect each other despite our differences, the world will become a place full of peace, hope, and love."

By Melchi Videau, 12 years old." Peace is not merely the silence after conflict. Rather, it means we overcome everything peacefully. Let peace be the victory we seek and create a unity for humanity." By Clarissa, 14." Peace never exists on its own, but begins with us."

By Francisca, 14." For all the people who rule the world, children should not have to learn about all the worlds in our history class. We should learn about the names of the stars, the names of peacemakers, and how to reach planet Mars with deep, deep respect." Solomon. Excellencies, Nupasadu and Marsh. Excellencies, at the margins of the United Nations General Assembly, many of us, including heads of states and Nobel Peace Prize laureates, came together to launch the Global Declaration of Compassion.

The Prime Minister of Bhutan and I were among the declaration's first signatories joining its call for shared moral responsibility and greater accountability in global governance. As my friend and fellow Nobel Peace Prize laureate Kailash Satyarthi has said, we have globalized markets and technology. The time has now come to globalize compassion. But as a powerful force to reach justice and peace for all. I thank you, and God bless us all. En nombre de la Asamblea General.

Mr President of the General Assembly, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen,

I bring you greetings from His Majesty, King Tupou VI and the people of the Kingdom of Tonga.

Nine months into my service as Prime Minister, I stand here mindful that many Pacific leaders have come before me, raising the same warnings and making the same appeals.

Today, I am compelled to make them again.

The question before us is not whether the world has heard our message. It is why it has still not acted?

[Sovereignty and the United Nations]

We live in a world more connected than ever. But greater connection has not brought greater unity. We meet amid deepening division, geopolitical competition and rising conflict.

For Tonga, navigating such stormy currents is not new. As descendants of voyagers, “we have been in the survival business much longer than most appreciate.”

Under King George Tupou I, Tonga preserved its independence during an era of colonial expansion. Our Constitution of 1875 secured Tongans’ rights and freedoms more than seven decades before the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. It reflects our fierce determination to chart our own course.

That is the essence of our sovereignty. Multilateralism allows us to project the power of our ideas, rather than the might of our power. Tonga participates as an equal under the founding principle of the United Nations Charter: the sovereign equality of states.

This is how we must approach our theme, “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All.” Enduring trust is restored when commitments produce results.

True transformation is realised when our communities, economies and ecosystems can anticipate change and recover with greater strength. Small Island Developing States must not bear disproportionate costs for challenges they did little to create.

[United Nations Reforms]

Too much of the international architecture still reflects the world of 1945 rather than today’s realities. If the United Nations is to remain the principal vehicle through which sovereign nations confront global challenges, it must transform.

We need a United Nations that enables innovation and expands meaningful access to investment and technology, especially for Small Island Developing States too often excluded

from both. We need a stronger General Assembly and institutions that respond effectively to the needs of the majority of their members.

We cannot keep negotiating climate, biodiversity and the ocean in separate processes when they form an interconnected ecosystem requiring coherent solutions. Global processes must recognise the ocean–climate nexus and address these challenges together. International commitments must also be capable of implementation nationally.

We need a more inclusive and representative Security Council, equipped for today’s challenges and prepared to recognise the triple planetary crisis as a profound threat to peace and security. We need an international financial architecture that delivers timely, accessible financing to those most in need. Internationally pledged commitments must be acted upon urgently. Sovereign equality must be reflected in how these institutions listen, decide and deliver.

The next Secretary General must understand these realities. It is in this spirit that Tonga has nominated Ambassador Ivonne Baki of Ecuador. Her vision for a renewed and reformed United Nations speaks to the needs of vulnerable states. To restore trust, every Member State, large or small, must have a voice in shaping this Organisation’s future and a stake in its success.

[The Blue Pacific and an Ocean of Peace]

The Pacific region spans one third of the Earth’s surface. It is our home. Through the 2050 Strategy for the Blue Pacific Continent, we have set our own course and identified our priorities. Our Blue Pacific must be defined by those who call it home.

For Tonga, investing in the ocean and nature is foundational to our development ambition. Protecting and restoring them builds climate resilience, strengthens food security and enables a sustainable blue economy. The financing and partnerships we build around ocean and nature based solutions will help determine our future and sustain our people.

We declared our region an Ocean of Peace in 2025. It sends a clear message: the Pacific must not become a staging ground for military escalation or a battleground for major power rivalry. Our Ocean of Peace is more than the absence of conflict.

Our most pressing threats are already reaching our shores: transnational crime, illicit drugs, illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing, cyber threats, and the unresolved consequences of nuclear testing and radioactive contamination. We will use innovative technologies and work closely with trusted security partners to confront these threats, including through stronger regional cooperation and maritime awareness.

We are committed to protecting the rights of marginalised people and ending violence against women and girls. This year, Tonga ratified the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, reaffirming our commitment to dignity and equal participation for persons with disabilities.

Tonga also acceded to the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons and ratified the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty. In doing so, we completed the universalisation of the latter treaty in the Pacific.

[Climate Action and Resilience]

On climate, the Pacific is already drowning in a crisis that others continue to postpone addressing. The United Nations Environment Programme’s Limiting Overshoot report warns that exceeding 1.5 degrees Celsius could occur within the next few years. Crossing that threshold must not become an excuse for abandoning it. We must limit the extent and duration of any overshoot, peak as low as possible and return below 1.5 degrees as quickly as possible. Every fraction of a degree matters.

The Pacific loses an estimated US$500 million each year from cyclones and floods. Early warning systems give communities time to prepare and can reduce these losses. This sum may seem modest in global terms, but it is a heavy burden for Pacific nations. The financing to prevent such losses still falls short.

The Pacific Resilience Facility, our own mechanism for financing community resilience, needs a further US$328 million in pledges to reach its initial capitalisation target of US$500 million. Weather Ready Pacific, our regional mechanism supporting Early Warnings for All, needs a further US$160 million to reach its target. Tonga’s Climate Trust Fund, which provides funding directly to communities and disbursed its first grants this year, also needs significant support. We call on partners to invest in these Pacific-designed and Pacific-owned solutions.

Tonga stands behind the 2026 Pacific Islands Forum Leaders’ Belau Declaration and calls on all major emitters to act urgently. Climate action is a legal obligation. Meeting those obligations will require difficult decisions rooted in science. Climate leadership is not a popularity contest.

Seven of the nine planetary boundaries have been breached by human activity. Climate inaction is not an option. Tonga is accelerating its transition away from fossil fuels, expanding renewable energy and encouraging the shift to electric vehicles. For us, decarbonisation also means greater energy security and protection from global fuel price shocks. Explicit fossil fuel subsidies, estimated by the International Monetary Fund at US$725 billion, must be phased out.

International financial institutions and multilateral development banks must recognise the Multidimensional Vulnerability Index in eligibility and allocation decisions. The index must help unlock affordable and timely support before disasters strike. By any credible index, Tonga is among the world’s most vulnerable countries.

We call on all nations, especially the world’s largest emitters, to attend the Pre COP31 meetings in Fiji and Tuvalu this October. Come to the Pacific and confront what 1.5 degrees means for our water, our food, our homes and our people.

We welcome the General Assembly’s Declaration on Sea Level Rise, a significant achievement for the preservation of sovereignty and the first common text on sea level rise agreed by all Member States.

Our resilience must account for every hazard confronting our islands. In recent years Tonga has endured cyclones, flooding, earthquakes, volcanic eruptions and tsunamis. The developing El Niño intensifies weather patterns and strains water and food security. We need integrated warning, preparedness and response systems that protect communities against the full range of these risks.

[Protecting Our Ocean, Unlocking Prosperity]

Tonga has committed to protecting at least 30 per cent of our ocean by 2030. Our ratification of the Agreement on Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction extends that commitment beyond our waters, supporting the protection of marine biodiversity on the high seas. Its implementation must be fair and take account of the circumstances of Small Island Developing States.

Our task is to navigate a course that safeguards the ocean and unlocks its value for our people. This principle underpins Tonga’s Ocean Strategy: responsible management of ocean resources, stronger marine protection and a sustainable blue economy whose benefits reach our communities.

It is in this spirit that we intend to convene a Polynesian Ocean Summit in Tonga in May 2027, moving from shared ambition to practical action. We will bring governments, communities, scientists and partners together to strengthen ocean governance and generate lasting benefits for our people.

Our responsibility does not stop at the boundaries of our Blue Pacific Continent. Consider the humpback whale. Born in Tonga’s warm waters, it migrates to Antarctica to feed on krill before returning to the Pacific to breed. Tonga’s sanctuary protects whales here, but their survival depends on healthy ecosystems at both ends of that journey. What happens in the Southern Ocean near Antarctica is felt in Tonga’s waters. We invite partners to join us with practical commitments that recognise the interconnectedness of these ocean corridors.

[Energy Security and Technological Change]

The same principle extends across our development: interconnection must not become dependency. For Tonga, resilience means taking greater control of the forces shaping our future and turning the resources within our geography into greater self sufficiency.

When we import fossil fuels, we also import their volatility. Moving away from them is both a climate imperative and an energy security necessity. We are expanding renewable generation, improving energy storage and strengthening our electricity grid while exploring sources suited to our islands, including geothermal energy.

Tonga is not short of ambition: 70 per cent renewable electricity by 2030 and 100 per cent by 2035. We welcome partnerships that help turn these goals into reliable and affordable power.

The forces shaping our future are increasingly technological. Digital connectivity and rapid technological advancement are transforming how we live. They offer significant opportunities for large ocean sovereign states, but risk creating new inequalities and dependencies.

Those who benefit last from global change often bear its highest costs. We continue to live with that injustice through climate change. We cannot again be asked to adapt only after the systems have been built and the rules written.

For Tonga, submarine cables and satellite links are foundational infrastructure connecting our islands to global opportunities. Connectivity alone is not enough. Digital skills and secure, resilient systems must support it. We will protect children online and retain sovereignty over our national data.

Tonga does not need to be first in artificial intelligence, quantum computing or every technology that follows. But we will not simply endure global transformation. We will exercise sovereignty by helping shape the rules and norms that govern it.

We are looking beyond conventional development models, seeking new forms of finance through the responsible valuation of our natural and ocean assets while exploring the potential of frontier technologies. We will form the right partnerships and direct innovation towards our priorities in climate forecasting, public health, ocean management, clean energy and disaster preparedness.

The Pacific’s data, ocean, biodiversity, critical minerals and traditional knowledge must not power the next technological revolution while returning only a fraction of their value to our people. Small Island Developing States need meaningful access to emerging capabilities and a voice in how these technologies are governed and shared.

[Conclusion]

From experience, Tonga knows its challenges, and we will meet them with the determination that has always defined our people. We also know our strengths as a large ocean sovereign state. We are not asking for charity.

We will do our part. We simply ask that others do theirs: uphold the 1.5C degree threshold; help us protect the planet we all share and the ocean that connects us; ensure that everyone benefits from technological advancement; recognise the imbalance between the funds committed to our collective development challenges and those prepared for conflict; and uphold the rules and institutions that allow every nation to participate as an equal sovereign.

That is the promise at the heart of the United Nations. Not that all nations would be equal in power, but that no nation, however powerful, is more sovereign than another.

That is the multilateral system Tonga believes in: an international rules based order founded on the United Nations Charter and the equality of nations. That is the multilateral system we must preserve.

Mr President, I so submit.

Malo ‘aupito.
