In  every  conflict,  civilians  must  be  protected,  international  humanitarian  law  must  be respected, and humanitarian access must be ensured. Viet Nam supports the right of the Palestinian people to self-determination and the two-State solution, with an independent State  of  Palestine  living  peacefully  alongside  the  State  of  Israel,  in  accordance  with international law and relevant United Nations resolutions.

In the Asia-Pacific, nearly six decades of ASEAN’s development have demonstrated that countries  can  transform  suspicion  into  trust,  confrontation  into  dialogue,  division  into cooperation, and individual strength into collective strength.

In  that  spirit,  Viet  Nam  remains  steadfast  in  its  commitment  to  resolving  disputes, including those in the East Sea, by peaceful means and in accordance with international law, particularly the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea. Viet Nam is resolute in safeguarding its sovereignty, sovereign rights and jurisdiction. The seas and oceans  must  remain  spaces  of  peace,  cooperation,  connectivity  and  sustainable development.

In the same spirit of peace and respect for peoples’ right to development, Viet Nam has always stood in solidarity with the State and People of Cuba. We call upon the United States to end the unilateral embargo and sanctions and the energy blockade against Cuba, and to remove Cuba from the list of State Sponsors of Terrorism. We also call upon the international community to support Cuba in overcoming the sanction-driven crisis.

Second,  we  must  advance  development  that  is  equitable,  humane,  inclusive  and sustainable.

International commitments must be translated into action and bring people lives of peace, security, dignity and happiness. It is for this reason that the Pact for the Future and the 2030  Agenda,  our  promises  to  present  and  future  generations,  must  be  implemented earnestly and in full.

Commitments on financing for development, including the Sevilla Commitment, must be translated into concrete measures: expanding access to long-term financing at affordable cost,  supporting  countries  burdened  by  debt,  and  amplifying  the  voice  of  developing countries  in  international  financial  and  monetary  institutions.  The  multilateral  trading system  must  be  strengthened  in  an  open,  equitable  and  transparent  manner,  ensuring development opportunities for all countries.

Climate  action  must  be  accorded  its  rightful  place  in  development  cooperation, particularly through adaptation finance, technology transfer and a just energy transition. Development must be people-centered and leave no one behind. Growth must go hand in hand with social progress and equity, environmental protection and the safeguarding of people’s  livelihoods,  particularly  in  vulnerable  countries  and  communities.  Global progress must uphold the spirit of humanity in relations among nations, safeguard their legitimate interests, and respect differences in history, culture and development conditions.

Third,  we  must  proactively  shape  technology  governance  so  that  progress  serves humanity and our common development.

Science,  technology,  digital  transformation  and  artificial  intelligence  are  opening  up unprecedented  opportunities,  while  also  presenting  new  challenges.  The  future  of technology  does  not  automatically  guarantee  equity. Technological  progress  must  help narrow divides and expand development opportunities, rather than create new forms of dependency or new sources of conflict.

We need to develop inclusive, safe, transparent and accountable principles and governance frameworks to ensure that technology serves people, while respecting national sovereignty, digital sovereignty and the right to development. Developing countries must be able to participate  substantively  in  rule-making,  receive  support  for  infrastructure  and  digital capacity, and enjoy equitable access to the benefits of scientific and technological progress.

Viet Nam’s hosting of the Opening for Signature of the United Nations Convention against Cybercrime in Ha Noi in 2025 reflects our desire to make substantive contributions to global  digital  cooperation.  Viet  Nam  stands  ready  to  work  with  partners  to  strengthen cooperation and build capacity in preventing and combating cybercrime, so that people may live safely and benefit from technological progress.

Viet  Nam  also  stands  ready  to  support  international  initiatives  on  green  and  digital transformation and the development of effective governance frameworks, so that science and technology can truly become drivers of shared development.

Fourth, we must strengthen multilateralism and the central, indispensable role of the United Nations.

The strength of the United Nations does not lie in its ability to replace the responsibilities of States, but in its legitimacy and capacity to build consensus, establish norms, develop rules, and mobilize global efforts to address common challenges.

For the United Nations to adapt to the transformations of our time, Viet Nam supports efforts  to  reform  the  Organization,  particularly  the  General  Assembly,  the  Security Council and the Secretariat, with a view to enhancing effectiveness, prioritizing structural reform  and  streamlining  the  apparatus,  while  fully  harnessing  the  Organization’s advantages  in  advancing  global  agendas  and  safeguarding  the  interests  of  developing countries.

Mr. President,

The perspectives I have just shared are drawn from the experience of Viet Nam itself.

Viet  Nam’s  nearly  half-century  journey  alongside  the  United  Nations  mirrors  the transformation  of  our  own  country.  From  being  primarily  a  recipient  of  invaluable assistance during the years of reconstruction and Doi Moi, Viet Nam today is increasingly making  proactive  contributions  to  our  common  endeavors,  while  deepening  and broadening  our  substantive  relations  with  the  United  Nations.  Vietnamese  military personnel  and  police  officers  have  served,  and  continue  to  serve,  in  United  Nations peacekeeping operations, carrying our nation’s aspiration for peace to places where peace remains fragile.

Our tradition of independence and self-reliance provides the foundation for Viet Nam to strengthen  its  strategic  autonomy  and  proactively  pursue  international  integration. Looking towards our goal of becoming a developing country with modern industry and upper-middle income by 2030, and a developed, high-income country by 2045, Viet Nam is establishing a new development model based on productivity, quality and added value; with science, technology, innovation and digital transformation as key drivers; and with

economic growth closely linked to cultural development, social progress and equity, and environmental protection.

Autonomy also means proactively adapting and cooperating with the world on an equal footing.  Viet  Nam  therefore  pursues  the  consistent  foreign  policy  of  independence, autonomy,  self-reliance,  peace,  friendship,  cooperation  and  development,  and  of multilateralization and diversification of external relations. Viet Nam will remain steadfast in upholding the UN Charter and international law, promoting dialogue and the peaceful settlement  of  disputes,  and  deepening  its  participation  in  United  Nations  peacekeeping operations. Viet Nam is working together with fellow Member States to build a  united, self-reliant  and  resilient  ASEAN,  and  is  actively  preparing  to  host  APEC  in  2027, contributing to peace, cooperation and development in the region and the world.

As a member of the United Nations Human Rights Council, Viet Nam champions dialogue and cooperation in promoting and protecting human rights and in ensuring that all people can share in the fruits of development. Viet Nam stands ready to share its experience in poverty reduction, agricultural development and climate change adaptation, and to work with partners to broaden cooperation for common interests.

Mr. President, Excellencies,

The  world  will  continue  to  change.  The  direction  of  such  change  will  depend  on  the choices we make and the responsibilities we shoulder today.

Viet Nam chooses peace, cooperation and development. We will work steadfastly with all nations  to  strengthen  the  United  Nations,  uphold  international  law,  and  translate  our shared commitments into tangible benefits for our people.

Viet  Nam  believes  that,  with  a  strong  United  Nations,  together  we  can  build  a  more peaceful,  equitable,  inclusive  and  better  world  for  all.  On  this  journey,  Viet  Nam  will remain an active member, a trusted partner and a responsible nation, ready to contribute to the common endeavors of the international community.

Thank you.

text:
Mr. President of the General Assembly,

Mr. Secretary-General,

Excellencies,

Distinguished Heads of State and Government,

Ladies and Gentlemen,

I.

Introduction

I  have  the  honour  to  address  this  assembly  on  behalf  of  the

Government and People of the Republic of Vanuatu.

I bring with me the voice of a nation of more than 80 islands of many

indigenous communities and languages, and a nation whose identity

has been shaped by the ocean, by kastom, by faith, by resilience and,

above all, by our commitment to peace.

Mr. Secretary-General,

This session also carries a particular significance for us because it is

the  final  high-level  General  Assembly  of  your  tenure  as  Secretary-

General of the United Nations.

On behalf of the Government and people of Vanuatu, I wish to convey

our profound appreciation for your service to the United Nations and

your  engagement  with  the  people  of  the  Pacific.    Your  visits  to  our

region  reflect  an  understanding  that  the  concerns  of  small  island

development states deserve to be heard at the higher level.

Over  the  course  of  your  tenure,  you  have  led  the  United  Nations

through some of the most tumultuous periods in recent international

history.  You  have  stood  consistently  for  multilateralism  at  a  time

when multilateralism itself was under enormous pressure. Vanuatu

hopes that the next Secretary General will carry forward that  same

commitment to all member states, large or small.

Vanuatu comes to this 81st session of the General Assembly with a

simple message:

The  world  needs  the  United  Nations  more  than  ever,  and  the

United National must deliver for the people who depend on it.

The  theme  of  this  session  —  “Restoring  Trust,  Managing

Transformation:  A  United  Nations  That  Delivers  for  All”  —

therefore comes at an important moment. The 81st session opened

against  a  backdrop  of  profound  geopolitical  uncertainty  and  rapid

transformation.

For Vanuatu, developments in international system are never distant

or abstract. Their effects reach our villages, our markets, our schools,

our hospitals, our oceans and our homes.

II.

THE

INTERNATIONAL

POLITICAL

AND

SECURITY

ENVIRONMENT

The  international  political  and  security  environment  is  becoming

increasingly difficult.

We are witnessing geopolitical competition, strategic rivalry, armed

conflicts,  growing  military  expenditures,  economic  fragmentation,

technological  disruption  and  a  weakening  of  confidence

in

multilateral institutions.

The rules that were designed to provide predictability and stability are

increasingly being tested.

The prohibition against the use of force is being challenged.

International humanitarian law is being tested.

The peaceful settlement of disputes is being undermined.

And the authority of international institutions is being questioned.

For small States, this is deeply concerning.

Small States do not possess the military, economic or technological

capabilities of major powers. We do not have the ability to impose our

will through coercion.

Our security depends fundamentally on something else:

International  law,  multilateral  institutions,  diplomacy  and  the

equal sovereignty of States.

This  is  why  Vanuatu  has  a  profound  interest  in  the  success  of  the

United Nations.

The  Charter  begins  with  a  commitment  to  save  succeeding

generations from the scourge of war and reaffirms the equal rights of

nations  large  and  small.  It  establishes  sovereign  equality,  peaceful

settlement of disputes and the prohibition of the threat or use of force

as fundamental principles of international relations.

These are not merely legal concepts for Vanuatu.

They are our security architecture.

When international law is respected, a small State has protection.

When the Charter is respected, a small State has a voice.

When disputes are resolved peacefully, a small State does not have

to choose between submission and confrontation.

And when sovereignty is respected, independence has meaning.

We  therefore  cannot  accept  a  world  in  which  international  law

applies  differently  according  to  the  size,  military  strength  or

economic power of a State.

The Charter must apply equally to all.

The  security  environment

is  also  changing

in  ways  that  are

particularly important for the Pacific.

The  Pacific  Islands  are  increasingly  viewed  through  the  lens  of

strategic competition.

There is growing interest in our maritime spaces, our sea lanes, our

resources and our geopolitical location.

We welcome genuine partnerships.

But we also say clearly:

The  Pacific  must  not  become  an  arena  for  great-power

competition at the expense of Pacific priorities.

The security of the Pacific is not simply about military deployments

or strategic competition.

For us, security also means:

•

food security;

•  energy security;

•  water security;

•  health security;

•  economic security;

•  cybersecurity;

•  environmental security;

•  and  the  security  of  our  people  from  the  impacts  of  climate

change.

For Vanuatu, a cyclone that destroys a school is a security issue.

A  rise  in  food  and  energy  prices  as  recently  experienced  by  Middle

East conflict is a security issue.

A disrupted shipping route is a security issue.

A cyberattack against critical infrastructure is a security issue.

Sea-Level  rise  also  raises  fundamental  questions  on  sovereignty,

identity and security. Vanuatu joins its Pacific colleagues in affirming

the  continuity  of  statehood  and  the  preservation  of  maritime  zone

and sovereign right in the face of sear level rise. The rights and dignity

of  affected  persons  must  remain  at  the  center  of  international

response.

These are the realities faced by small island development states. We

therefore call for a broader understanding of international peace and

security — one that reflects the realities of small island developing

States, and we hope that these security issues are well understood

here at the United Nations.

III.  THE

INTERNATIONAL  ENVIRONMENT  AND  VANUATU'S

DOMESTIC REALITIES

What happens here in New York does not remain here in New York.

The decisions taken by major powers affect the smallest economies.

A conflict thousands of kilometres away can increase the price of fuel

in Vanuatu.

A disruption in international shipping can increase the price of food

in our islands.

A change in global interest rates can increase the cost of borrowing.

A crisis in international development finance can delay a school, a

hospital, a road or a climate-resilience project.

And  global  economic  uncertainty  can  affect  tourism,  investment,

employment and government revenue.

For Vanuatu, therefore, foreign policy and domestic development

are inseparable.

Our international diplomacy is ultimately about our people.

It is about whether a child in Tanna can attend school.

Whether a farmer in Malekula can bring produce to market.

Whether a family in Torba has access to reliable electricity.

Whether a community in Penama can recover quickly after a natural

disaster.

And whether our young people can find meaningful opportunities at

home rather than being forced to leave in search of them.

This  year,  as  Vanuatu  celebrated

its  46th

Independence

Anniversary,  we  reflected  on  how  far  our  country  has  come  since

1980.

Our independence was not given to us in a golden plate.

It was achieved through the determination, courage and sacrifice of

our people, supported by our brothers and sisters in the Pacific.

At our Independence celebrations, we were reminded once again of

the importance of solidarity — including the historic support of Papua

New Guinea during our struggle for independence.

Our  46th  Independence  anniversary  was  therefore  not  simply  a

celebration of the past.

It was a call to build the future.

The message of our national celebration was one of unity, national

pride,  resilience  and  determination  to  build  a  stronger,  more

prosperous Vanuatu for future generations.

And this is important in the context of our discussion today.

Vanuatu has experienced cyclones, earthquakes, volcanic eruptions,

economic shocks and other disasters.

Yet we continue to stand.

We rebuild.

We adapt.

We move forward.

Resilience  is  not  simply  something  Vanuatu  speaks  about.  It  is

something our people practise every day.

But resilience also requires international solidarity.

A  small  island  country  cannot  finance  all  of  its  resilience  needs

alone.

We cannot rebuild every road, bridge, school and hospital after every

disaster from domestic resources alone.

We  cannot  absorb  indefinitely  the  economic  consequences  of

external shocks.

And we cannot protect our people from a changing climate without

meaningful international cooperation.

Therefore,  when  we  speak  about  climate  finance,  development

finance, disaster resilience and sustainable development, we are not

asking merely for charity.

We  are  asking  for  partnership,  fairness  and  the  fulfilment  of

international commitments.

That partnership must include predictable and accessible finance for

adaption  and  for  addressing  loss  and  damage.  Access  to  such

finance  must  be  made  easier  for  the  small  island  state  and  must

respond to the needs of our communities.

We invite partners to support the Pacific Resilience Facility in bringing

the necessary resources to support resilience efforts in the Pacific.

At  the  same  time,  keeping  1.5  Degree  Celsius  is  vital  for  Pacific.  In

light  of  the  International  Court’s  Advisory  Opinion,  we  urge  all

members  to  give  effect  on  their  legal  obligations  through  stronger

climate actions and international cooperation.

We  are  also  deeply  concerned  by  the  developing  strong  El  Niño

event  in  the  Pacific,  which  threatens  to  bring  more  extreme  heat,

disrupted rainfall, drought and flooding across our region.

For  Pacific  Island  countries,  these  are  not  simply  meteorological

events;  they  affect  food  and  water  security,  agriculture,  fisheries,

health,

livelihoods  and  the  resilience  of  already  vulnerable

communities.

The international community must act before disaster strikes. We

call  for  stronger  regional  early-warning  systems,  pre-positioned

humanitarian  assistance,  rapid  access  to  climate  and  disaster

financing, and greater investment in resilient infrastructure and food

and water security.

The  Pacific  does  not  ask  the  world  to  prevent  El  Niño;  we  ask  the

world to help us prepare for it, withstand its impacts and recover

with dignity.

The Ocean is central to Vanuatu’s identity, culture, food security and

prosperity.  Protection of it is essential for the future of our people.

Climate change, damage to the ocean and the loss of biodiversity are

linked. We must address them together.

Vanuatu welcomes the entry into force of the BBNJ Agreement. It is

an  important  achievement  for  ocean  governance  and  multilateral

cooperation.

For  a  nation  whose  identity,  culture  and  prosperity  are  inseparable

from the ocean, the BBNJ Agreement represents an important step

towards  protecting  marine  biodiversity  beyond  national  jurisdiction

and  ensuring  that  the  benefits  of  our  common  ocean  heritage  are

shared fairly and sustainably.

Vanuatu  stands  ready  to  contribute  to  its  effective  implementation

and to strengthening international cooperation for the protection of

our  oceans  for  generations  to  come.  Since  the  Agreement  entered

into force on 17 January 2026, following its ratification by more than

sixty  States,  including  Vanuatu  and  our  Pacific  neighbours,  the

international  community  has  moved  into  a  critical  implementation

phase.

Vanuatu  looks  forward  to  that  first  Conference  of  the  Parties

advancing  the  operationalization  of  marine  protected  areas,

environmental  impact  assessments  and  the  fair  and  equitable

sharing of benefits from marine genetic resources, and we call on all

States yet to ratify the Agreement to do so without delay.

The Implementation of the BBNJ Agreement must respect sovereign

rights  and  take  full  account  of  the  special  circumstances  and

capacity constraints of small island developing states. It must enable

countries to participate effectively and equally benefit from it.

The  hosting  of  the  inaugural  Melanesian  Ocean  Summit  in  Port

Moresby, Papua  New Guinea,  this year arrives  at a  critical juncture

where, on one hand, we are faced with daily mounting challenges of

the detrimental effects of climate change, the alarming degradation

of  our  marine  biodiversity,  pervasive  marine  pollution,  and  the

overexploitation  of  our  vital  marine  resources.  Yet,  some  of  these

global  issues  have  already  escalated  to  a  level  where  ensuring

sustainability for future generations has become a critical concern,

highlighting the urgent need for improved management of our ocean

resources.

In

today's  world,  science  and

technology  and  economic

opportunities MUST also work closely with our traditional custodians

in our vast coastal area to maintain respect for nature.  Our culture

and tradition are deeply rooted in the ocean and hence our collective

wisdom  and  collaboration  to  address  the  core  issues  affecting  our

people's livelihoods today and reshape the future of our ocean and

the communities is extremely paramount.

IV.  MANAGING  TRANSFORMATION  —  WITHOUT  LEAVING  SMALL

STATES BEHIND

The world is entering a period of extraordinary transformation.

Artificial intelligence is changing economies and societies.

Digital technologies are changing the way governments operate.

Energy systems are changing.

Global trade is changing.

Demographic patterns are changing.

And  climate  change  is  transforming  the  physical  environment  in

which many of our societies exist.

The question before us is not whether transformation will occur.

It will.

The question is:

Who will shape that transformation, and who will benefit from it?

For Vanuatu, the answer must be clear.

Transformation must not create a new hierarchy between those who

possess  technology,  capital  and  influence  and  those  who  merely

experience the consequences.

We need an international system in which developing countries and

small  States  are  participants  in  transformation  —  not  simply

consumers of decisions made elsewhere.

Artificial intelligence provides one example.

AI  offers  enormous  opportunities  for  education,  healthcare,  public

administration,  agriculture,  climate  forecasting  and  economic

development.

But  without  appropriate  governance,  it  could  also  deepen  existing

inequalities.

Small States need access to technology.

We need digital infrastructure.

We need skills and capacity.

We need access to data and computing.

And  we  need  a  meaningful  voice  in  establishing  the  international

norms that govern emerging technologies.

The digital future must not become another form of dependency.

V. SMALL STATES: DEPENDENT, BUT NOT POWERLESS

There is a tendency to describe small States primarily in terms of our

vulnerabilities.

We are small.

We are geographically dispersed.

We are economically vulnerable.

We have limited institutional capacity.

We depend on international markets.

We depend on development partners.

We depend on international shipping.

We depend on imported fuel, food and manufactured goods.

And,  yes,  in  many  respects  we  are  dependent  on  the  international

system.

But dependence must not be confused with powerlessness.

Small States can lead.

Indeed,  history  has  shown  that  some  of  the  most  important

developments  in  international  law  and  global  governance  have

emerged  because  small  and  vulnerable  States  refused  to  remain

silent.

Vanuatu is proud of its contribution to the global climate debate.

We are proud of our advocacy for climate justice.

We  are  proud  of  our  role  in  advancing  the  recognition  of  the  legal

dimensions of climate change.

And we remain committed to ensuring that the voices of those most

vulnerable  to  climate  change  are  heard  in  international  decision-

making.

In this vein, the Vanuatu Government whole-heartedly thank all the

UN members who have supported us in this journey – especially here

at the UN General Assembly and the International Court of Justice.

Our experience demonstrates an important principle:

Influence  is  not  determined  solely  by  population,  territory  or

military power.

Influence can come from ideas.

It can come from moral authority.

It can come from coalition-building.

It can come from persistence.

It can come from international law.

And it can come from the ability to bring different regions and groups

together around a common cause.

This is the strength of the General Assembly.

Every Member State has a voice.

Every Member State has a vote.

And every Member State  — large or small — has a responsibility to

contribute.

The General Assembly is the most representative body of the United

Nations,  bringing  together  all  193  Member  States  on  the  basis  of

sovereign equality.

For countries such as Vanuatu, this principle is fundamental.

VI. HUMAN RIGHTS, SELF-DETERMINATION

The imposition of coercive economic measures, including unilateral

sanctions,  against  developing  countries  is  unfair  and  unjust.    Such

measures are in violation with the principles enshrined in the Charter

of the United Nations and adversely affects sustainable development

outcomes of countries such as Cuba.  In this respect, we consistently

call for the uplift of the economic embargo on the Republic of Cuba.

Peace and security cannot be separated from human rights.

Vanuatu remains deeply concerned about reports of serious human

rights violations affecting Indigenous Papuans in West Papua. United

Nations  Special  Procedures  have  also  raised  concerns  regarding

Indigenous  rights,  displacement,  cultural  rights,  environmental

impacts and the treatment of human rights defenders in Papua.

The  call  from  the  Pacific  Forum  Leaders  for  the  UN  Human  Rights

Commissioner visit to West Papua remains unheeded and needs to

be action.

Vanuatu  reaffirms  its  unwavering  support  for  the  decolonisation  of

Kanaky-New  Caledonia,  which  remains  a  Non-Self-Governing

Territory  under  the  purview  of  the  United  Nations.  We  reiterate  the

inalienable

right  of

the

Indigenous  Kanak  people

to  self-

determination  and  call  for  a  peaceful,  inclusive,  transparent  and

credible process, consistent with the Charter of the United Nations

and relevant General Assembly resolutions.

We  remain  concerned  by  persistent  socio-economic  disparities

affecting  the  Kanak  people,  including  inequalities  in  employment,

education,  income  and  access  to  economic  opportunities.  These

longstanding structural imbalances continue to constrain the full and

equitable  enjoyment  of  economic,  social  and  cultural  rights  by

Indigenous  Kanaks,  notwithstanding  the  Territory's  considerable

natural resources and economic potential. Reports from the FLNKS,

supported  by  independent  assessments,  point  to  the  enduring

effects  of  economic  marginalisation  and  uneven  development,

which may be understood as forms of structural violence insofar as

they limit meaningful participation in, and equitable benefit from, the

Territory's development. Addressing these disparities is essential to

fostering  social  cohesion  and  advancing  a  just,  inclusive  and

sustainable decolonisation process.

In this regard,  Vanuatu calls for the full implementation  of relevant

United  Nations  resolutions  on  the  Question  of  New  Caledonia  and

encourages  continued  engagement  and  constructive  dialogue

among  all  stakeholders,  including  the  administering  Power  and

representatives  of  the  Kanak  people.  We  further  reaffirm  the

important  role  of  the  Special  Committee  on  Decolonization  (C-24)

and  the  Fourth  Committee  in  advancing  the  realisation  of  self-

determination and ensuring that the rights, aspirations and interests

of  the  Kanak  people  remain  at  the  centre  of  the  decolonisation

process.

longstanding  historical  connection,

indigenous  ownership  and  seen  as  a  part  of  our  duty  as  ancestral

in  advancing  global  climate  action,

including through its support for our initiative before the International

We greatly value this partnership and France’s leadership on issues

of international importance. It is in that same spirit of mutual respect

and  commitment  to  international  law  that  we  respectfully  invite

VII. A UNITED NATIONS THAT DELIVERS FOR ALL

Trust is important for the United Nations credibility.

It cannot be restored through declarations alone.

Trust must be earned through action.

People  will  trust  the  United  Nations  when  they  see  it  preventing

conflict.

They will trust it when international law is respected.

They will trust it  when  humanitarian assistance reaches those who

need it.

They  will  trust  it  when  development  commitments  become  real

projects.

They  will  trust

it  when  climate  finance  reaches  vulnerable

communities.

They will trust it when small States are heard.

And they will trust it when the international system treats all nations

with equal dignity.

For  Vanuatu,  restoring  trust  also  means  restoring  confidence  in

multilateralism itself.

We  must  resist  the  temptation  to  conclude  that  because  the

international system is imperfect, it is therefore irrelevant.

The UN80 reforms currently implemented are paramount to rebuild

trust again at the UN and therefore needs to be managed diligently.

Vanuatu supports efforts to strengthen the United Nations.

But reform must preserve what is most important:

the principle of sovereign equality.

The United Nations cannot become an institution where the voices of

the  most  powerful  States  dominate  while  smaller  States  are

expected merely to follow.

Reform must strengthen the General Assembly.

It must make international institutions more accessible to developing

countries.

It must address the financing and capacity constraints facing small

delegations.

It must strengthen preventive diplomacy.

It must improve the implementation of international decisions.

It  must  ensure  that  the  development  pillar  remains  resourced  and

that implementation on the ground is effective and efficient.

And  it  must  ensure  that  international  law  remains  central  to  the

international system.

Vanuatu calls for a UN Security Council that is more representative,

transparent  and  accountable,  with  membership  and  working

methods  that  reflect  today’s  realities  and  give  all  regions  a

meaningful voice.

But reform cannot be limited to institutional structures.

The deeper reform we require is political:

a  renewed  commitment  by  Member  States  to  the  principles  we

have already agreed to.

The Charter does not need to be reinvented.

It needs to be respected.

VIII. CONCLUSION: THE UN CHARTER AS OUR COMPASS

Mr. President, Excellencies,

For Vanuatu, the United Nations Charter remains our compass.

It tells us that nations are sovereign equals.

It tells us that disputes must be settled peacefully.

It tells us that force must not be used against the territorial integrity

or political independence of States.

It tells us that nations must cooperate.

And  it  reminds  us  that  the  ultimate  purpose  of  the  international

system is not power for its own sake.

It is peace, justice, human dignity, development and cooperation

And it is a better future for succeeding generations.

These  principles  are  particularly  important  to  Vanuatu  because  we

know what independence means.

Our independence is not merely the absence of colonial rule.

Independence means the right of our people to determine our future.

It means sovereignty.

It means dignity.

It means equality.

And it means having an equal place in the family of nations.

That is why Vanuatu will continue to defend the multilateral system.

That is why we will continue to defend international law.

And that is why we will continue to speak for the principle that every

nation — regardless of size — matters.

We meet at a difficult moment in international affairs.

There are wars that remain unresolved.

There are communities facing humanitarian catastrophe.

There is growing geopolitical rivalry.

There is economic uncertainty.

There is climate disruption.

There is technological transformation.

And there is declining confidence in international institutions.

Yet  I  remain  convinced  that  this  is  precisely  the  moment  when  we

must choose cooperation over confrontation.

We must choose dialogue over division.

We must choose law over force.

We must choose solidarity over indifference.

And we must choose multilateralism over fragmentation.

Vanuatu  comes  from  a  part  of  the  world  where  our  ancestors

navigated  vast  oceans  using  the  stars,  the  winds,  the  currents  and

knowledge passed from generation to generation.

Today,  the  international  community  is  navigating  another  uncertain

ocean.

We need a compass.

The United Nations Charter is that compass.

It  provides  the  principles  by  which  we  can  navigate  a  world  of

competing interests while preserving our common humanity.

The  theme  of  this  81st  session  —  “Restoring  Trust,  Managing

Transformation: A United Nations That Delivers for All” — reminds

us of what is required.

But ultimately, restoring trust will depend not on the words we adopt

here, but on the actions, we take when we leave this hall.

Let  us  therefore  build  a  United  Nations  that  is  strong  enough  to

prevent  war,  fair  enough  to  protect  the  vulnerable,  courageous

enough  to  defend  international  law,  and  inclusive  enough  to  give

every nation a meaningful voice.

Let us build a United Nations where the concerns of a small island

nation in the Pacific and all over the world can stand alongside those

of the largest powers of the world.

Let  us  not  allow  division  to  rule  our  era.  Instead,  we  chose

cooperation.

We chose peace.

We chose justice.

We chose solidarity.

And we chose to renew our faith in the idea that  together, nations

can build a better world.

Vanuatu stands ready to do its part.

Thank you.

Climate change remains the single greatest threat to Samoa and the global

importance  as  an  authoritative  contribution  to  the  clarification  of  existing

the needs of the most climate vulnerable.  Resources intended for education,

health,  water  and  social  protection  are  now  diverted  to  disaster  recovery.

nation should have to borrow its way out of a crisis it did so little to create.

We  are  working  towards  a  whole-of-system

They are not two separate issues, but one and the same. Supporting the Yemeni government and strengthening its economic, security and military capacities is an investment in international peace and security. Protecting this strategic waterway is a shared regional and international responsibility which Yemen cannot shoulder alone.

It is the responsibility of every economy that depends on secure supply chains, energy security, and freedom of navigation. In this regard, we commend the initiative of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia to establish a multinational maritime defense coalition. This initiative reflects a deep appreciation and understanding of collective responsibility to protect navigation, deter threats and combat smuggling. The path to a secure at sea requires a stable Yemen. There is no stability in Yemen without restoring the state, sustainable peace cannot be achieved while an armed militia remains above the law and outside state authority, restoring the Yemeni state is restoring. The Yemeni state is not just a national interest, it is a direct contribution to regional security and stability and to the protection of one of the world's most vital maritime corridors.

Ladies and gentlemen our Yemeni people aspires to peace, but our people will not abandon their state. Our government is committed to peace, but it cannot accept that the armed coup becomes a fait accompli. There is no peace with arms outside state authority. Peace requires deeds, not words. 12 years of an incomplete peace have left millions. Millions of people enduring hunger, injuries, displacement.

Every statistic in Yemen's tragedy carries a human story. The world must not become accustomed to the suffering. Yemen as a great country, with its strategic location, its ports, its resources, its human capital. The challenge lies in unleashing those capabilities from the grip of war and transforming these capabilities into an engine for development. Today, the heroes of the Yemeni armed forces and all military formations, legitimate military formations are on the ground confronting these Houthi terrorist militias. In defense of our people, our land, our sovereignty, and our future.

Here, from this very podium, I salute them. I salute their struggle. They stand today to prevent much greater harm from reaching this world. I also address a message to our people, to our people, in particular in Sana'a and Saada and Hajjah and Hodeidah and ibn Dhamar in every governorate, city and village under. Houthi control. We tell them from here you are our people.

Your suffering is our suffering. Your rights are our responsibility. You will never be outside the national project of a Yemeni state, nor outside its future. Our struggle is not against any Yemeni citizen, nor against the sons of any region, governorate, any sect or social group. Our struggle is against an armed coup that has taken hostages, state and institutions that deepened the suffering of Yemen and Yemenis to serve Iran and its schemes. Restoring the state is not a victory for one Yemeni party over another.

It is the restoration of the rights of all Yemenis to their state and institutions, the Yemen through which we struggle belongs to all Yemenis. The state we seek to restore is your state. The future of Yemen will not be built by excluding any of its sons. Our cause is not merely about how to end the war, but to build what comes after it. We seek a safe, stable, prosperous Yemen that safeguards the dignity of its citizens, rebuilds its economy, provides education for its children, jobs for its youth, security for its families. Yemen.

That's a partner for its neighbors, a responsible guardian of its strategic location, a bridge for trade and cooperation between the Arabian Peninsula, the Horn of Africa and the wider world. That is the Yemen that we wish for the world to see. Not a man of war, but a Yemen of statehood, of humanity of opportunity, Yemen of the future. Ladies and gentlemen, the Yemeni people do not ask the world to fight their battle on their behalf. They are determined to restore their state, rebuild its institutions and confront terrorism in all its forms. What we ask is that the international community fulfill its responsibilities, implement its resolutions, stop the flow of arms and technologies to the militias, support our national capacities and economy.

The Yemeni government is capable of ending the threat posed by this terrorist group and protecting Yemen's ports and territorial waters. What we seek from the international community today is not a perpetual management of crises, but a strategic partnership that promotes security, stability and development for the benefit of Yemen, the region and international peace and security. We do not ask the world to build Yemen's future for Yemenis. We seek a partnership that supports the state and its institutions and invests in Yemen's people. For our part, we will continue to fulfill our responsibilities in reform, institution building and the rule of law. The international community can find in the Yemeni government a reliable partner.

We speak not only of what women Yemen needs from the world, but also of what Yemen can contribute to the world once it regains its security and its stability. Ladies and gentlemen, we express our deep appreciation to the brotherly kingdom of Saudi Arabia for its unwavering support for Yemen, its people and its government, and for the kingdom's comprehensive support to the state and its institutions. The Kingdom has borne and continues to bear significant burdens in support of Yemen's security and stability. These efforts will remain firmly engraved in the memory of the Yemeni people from this podium. The Republic of Yemen condemns the terrorist attacks carried out by the Houthi militias against the kingdom, targeting its territory, facilities and resources. We equally condemn their attempted targeting of Makkah Al-mukarramah, to which the hearts and prayers of Muslims turn.

We stand in solidarity with the kingdom and reaffirm Yemen's steadfast support for the kingdom's right to defend its territory, its citizens and its national interests. Ladies and gentlemen the Republic of Yemen reaffirms its unwavering support for the Palestinian people's right to freedom, dignity, and the establishment of their independent sovereign state. In accordance with international resolutions and the Arab Peace Initiative. We call for ending the suffering of the Palestinian people, protecting civilians and promoting stability in this world. We equally express our appreciation to the United Nations, the Secretary General and his special envoy, as well as all UN agencies for their support for their efforts. Rather, in support of peace and in assistance to the Yemeni people.

And we value the support of friends and partners standing by the Yemeni people. At the same time, we condemn the continued detention by the Houthi militias of UN personnel and humanitarian humanitarian workers. Those working for peace and humanitarian relief must never be held hostage of blackmail. I wish all the peoples of the world prosperity peace and development and we hope for a world that is more secure, just stable and prosperous. And in conclusion, I extend my congratulations to our great Yemeni people at home and abroad on the occasion. Today, on the occasion of the 60th of the anniversary of the Revolution of the 26th of September, we reaffirm our commitment to the values and objectives of the September and October revolutions and to the principles of our national struggle principles that are non-negotiable with determination of the Yemenis, their sacrifices and perseverance, Yemen will regain its security and its stability.

Bab el Mandeb, Bab el Mandeb will remain, as geography intended it to be, a bridge between peoples, a route for commerce and a gateway to peace Allow me to conclude this statement with words by a Yemeni poet expressing faith in the Yemeni people, Yemeni homeland and future, and affirming that Yemen belongs to its free people, not to Iran, nor to its proxies, he said. We are the land, its custodians and its inhabitants. To us it belongs, for we are its people, and its home today belongs to the people in yesterday. The glorious yesterday belongs to them as well. To them belong the future. History and time itself.

Long live Yemen, free, secure and great. May the peace and blessings be upon you all.

speaker_post: Minister for International Relations and Cooperation
text:
Mr Guterres, Secretary-General, Excellencies, Government, Ladies and Gentlemen,

Khalilur Mr of

Antonio

Heads

State

and

Mr President

Suggestion:  This  day  the  24th  of  September  is  a  national  day  immense significance in South Africa.

We call it Heritage Day. It is a day upon which recommit to not just a United but also a diverse nation. A day where we reassert that diversity is not a cause for division but celebration. Our strength is in our diversity.

In that spirit allow me Mr President to congratulate you in my mother tongue.

(Eka vuyimeri bya Riphabliki ya Afrika Dzonga, ndzi ku amukelesa eku hlawulweni ka  wena  ku  rhangela  Nhlengeletano  Hikwayo  ya  vu-81.  Ndzi  ku  tiyisekisa  hi nseketelo wa hina hinkwawo loko u ri karhi u hetisisa vutihlamuleri bya wena bya nkoka.) On behalf of the Republic of South Africa, I congratulate you on your election to preside over the 81st General Assembly. I assure you of our full support as you discharge your important responsibilities.

At  the  same  time,  Mr.  President,  with  this  being  the  valedictory  UN  General Assembly session for Secretary-General Antonio Guteress permit me to salute him  for  his  numerous  accomplishments  at  a  time  of  unprecedented  global challenges.

Sixty years ago, in the chambers of this Assembly, the United Nations adopted a resolution condemning apartheid as a crime against humanity.

The demise of apartheid freed the people of South Africa from racial segregation and slaughter, domination and deprivation, humiliation and exploitation.

But  it  was  not  only  the  people  of  South  Africa  who  were  unchained  when apartheid collapsed.

The end of apartheid also marked the end of a system that exported violence and instability across southern Africa.

Indeed, the fall of apartheid is a glorious story that attests to what multilateralism can deliver.

Since democratic South Africa took its place in this Assembly, we have pursued a  foreign  policy  anchored  in  Ubuntu  and  international  law,  dialogue  and multilateralism, and in the understanding that our fate is tied to the fortunes of our region and continent.

Millions more South Africans have access to education, electricity, water and sanitation,  housing  and  social  protection  than  they  did  at  the  dawn  of  our democracy.

We have built a united nation of a diverse people, steeled in their determination to never let history repeat itself.

In November 2025, South Africa classified gender-based violence and femicide as  a  national  disaster,  recognising  that  dealing  with  this  scourge  demands exceptional measures.

We have built a vibrant democracy capable of self-correcting and stepping back from the brink. A democracy strong enough to withstand and resist attempts at external supervision and tutelage.

After  the  2024  election,  political  parties  put  national  stability  above  narrow interests  and  formed  a  government  of  national  unity  within  two  weeks  of  the announcement of the results.

Since the dawn of our democracy, we have held no fewer than seven free and fair national elections.

As  we  speak,  South  Africans  are  preparing  once  again  to  exercise  their democratic right, this time in local government elections.

Again, the will of the people will prevail.

The  promise  of  democracy  and  international  cooperation  wanes  when  we cannot demonstrate that they can address inequality and insecurity. Compelled by  our  unenviable  position  as  the  world’s most  unequal  society,  South Africa made inequality a key focus of our G20 Presidency in 2025.

Today, the top 10 percent own roughly 75 percent of global wealth, while the bottom 50 percent own only 2 percent.

This extreme concentration of wealth at  the top and poverty at  the bottom is neither inevitable nor insurmountable.

Together with Brazil, Norway and Spain, South Africa calls on this Assembly to throw  its  weight  behind  the  establishment  of  an  International  Panel  on Inequality.

We know that inequality is at the heart of the rising appeal of politics founded on  hate  and  exclusion.  Across  the  world,  citizens  who  have  seen  little improvement  in  their  economic  fortunes  are  turning  to  ideas  diametrically opposed to the values of the UN Charter.

As we mark the 25th anniversary of the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action,  South  Africa  reaffirms  its  commitment  to  confronting  racism,  racial discrimination, xenophobia and all forms of intolerance.

We are determined to confront racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and all forms of intolerance through our Constitution, our laws and our institutions.

Dealing with the root causes and challenges of irregular migration is a shared responsibility of all countries of the world.

We  approach  our  leadership  of  a  regional  bloc  that  is  home  to  a  quarter  of Africa’s population – the Southern African Development Community (SADC) – with a firm resolve to champion greater regional integration, industrialisation and trade.

We want to increase trade among our countries so that our citizens can share in the prosperity of our region and our economies are better prepared to absorb the shocks of unilateralism.

If multilateralism works at regional level, then citizens have greater reason to believe it can work globally.

Our  governments  face  a  difficult  choice:  whether  to  meet  the  needs  of  their citizens or satisfy the expectations of creditors.

In  the  last  year  alone, African  countries  spent  roughly  the  same  amount  on servicing debt as is needed to close our infrastructure financing gap.

This  grim  reality  inspired  South  Africa’s  G20  Presidency  to  focus  on  debt sustainability.

The Africa Expert Panel report calls for an end to incrementalism.

It supports multilateral efforts to establish a Borrowers’ Club to counter-balance the  power  of  creditors  and  calls  for  greater  debt  transparency  and  greater scrutiny of credit rating agencies.

To us, Mr President, unsustainable debt betrays the promise of development and destroys the prospects for democracy.

With only 36 percent of the Sustainable Development Goals showing sufficient progress, we are running out of time!

Africa and much of the Global South need multilateral action to free resources absorbed by debt service and redirect them towards development.

We  must  close  the  financing  gap  for  the  2030  Agenda  and  meaningfully advance implementation of the African Union’s Agenda 2063.

Climate  disasters  and  extreme  weather  patterns  threaten  our  people,  our prosperity, and our hard-won development gains.

In  the  last  year,  two  million  people  in  SADC  suffered  the  combined  and debilitating impact of floods, cyclones, wildfires, and disease outbreaks.

Our  responses  are  severely  constrained  by  a  climate  finance  architecture stacked against developing nations.

Global action on disaster resilience and predictable financing for a just energy transition is essential if international cooperation is to deliver for all.

Our continent has the world’s largest reserves of critical minerals.

These  critical  minerals  can  help  bridge  the  gap  between  wealthy  and  poor nations and overcome the indignities of poverty and underdevelopment.

We insist, Mr President, that indeed Africa must have a stake in shaping the rules that govern the development and deployment of Artificial Intelligence.

We have a youthful population ready to play a key role in the beneficiation at source  of  critical  minerals  and  on  research  and  innovation  for  artificial intelligence.

Restoring trust in multilateralism demands that we demonstrate, as the United Nations, that the peaceful resolution of conflicts is still our mantra.

Unfortunately, much of what we see runs counter to this.

In  the  last  two  years,  the  world  spent  more  on  military  budgets  than  on resourcing this important body tasked with maintaining global peace.

We are reminded that meeting the SDGs by 2030, including ending hunger and expanding access to safe water and sanitation, would require no more than 5 percent of the 2.9 trillion US dollars spent on arms.

The result of the choice we are making is an arms race and a world as divided as it is dangerous.

We  see  the  consequences  in  Sudan,  which  is  today  the  worst  humanitarian crisis in the world.

We see the consequences in the Eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, Iran, Ukraine and elsewhere.

Humanitarian workers are caught in the crosshairs of today’s conflicts. When they are not being obstructed from reaching civilians in need, they are being killed in the line of duty.

To  restore  respect  for  international  law,  we  must  protect  those  who  deliver humanitarian assistance. That is why South Africa endorsed the Declaration for the Protection of Humanitarian Personnel, supported by nearly 120 states from all regions of the world.

Mr President

Eighty  years  ago,  the  first  resolution  of  the  General  Assembly  called  for  the elimination of nuclear weapons.

Later this year, South Africa will preside over the First Review Conference of the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons.

As  the  only  country  in  the  world  to  have  voluntarily  dismantled  its  nuclear weapons programme, South Africa stands ready to share this experience as a demonstration that,  with  political  will,  credible  and  verifiable  nuclear disarmament is achievable.

In our view, restoring trust in multilateralism will not happen without meaningful reform of global governance, principally the UN Security Council.

African  citizens  are  growing  weary  of  their  continent  being  consigned  to  the periphery of global governance.

Africa is home to nearly one-fifth of the world’s population and African countries together account for more than a quarter of UN member states.

Yet over the past decade, 70 percent of UN Security Council resolutions have concerned conflicts on the African continent.

If the future belongs to the young, then surely a continent that will be home to one in four of the world’s youth by 2030 deserves a bigger seat at the table.

South Africa therefore reaffirms its support for the Ezulwini Consensus and its call to end Africa’s relegation to the margins of global decision-making.

Permanent seats for Africa in the Security Council, with all the prerogatives of permanent membership, are long overdue.

Nowhere  is  the  need  to  uphold  our  shared  humanity  more  urgent  than  in Palestine.

The  rights,  dignity  and  humanity  of  Palestinians  cannot  be  treated  as conditional.

The State of Israel’s continued violations of international and humanitarian law constitute genocide, and we remain steadfast in our view that the international community must act decisively to end this impunity.

In  our  support  for  a  just  and  lasting  peace  and  a  two-state  solution,  in accordance with UN resolutions, South Africa is unwavering.

We  are  steadfast  in  our  longstanding  solidarity  with  the  people  of  Western Sahara.

We  reaffirm  their  inalienable  right  to  self-determination  and  support  a  just, lasting  and  mutually  acceptable  political  solution  consistent  with  international law and the principles of the United Nations Charter.

We are also deeply concerned by the wielding of economic weapons to coerce countries into abandoning their chosen development trajectories.

The suffering of the Cuban people should command our deepest solidarity.

We reiterate our call for an end to the blockade on the Cuban people.

The designation of Cuba as a State sponsor of terrorism, is similarly unfounded, and it should be removed from that list.

Unilateral  coercive  measures  have  negative  spillover  effects  that  seriously undermine third countries.

Similarly, we also call for the urgent removal of sanctions against Zimbabwe.

Our  current  reality  demands  that  we  act  collectively  to  protect  existing international  institutions  of  justice  from  sanctions  and  intimidation.  These institutions fulfil important mandates for the benefit of humanity.

As I conclude, Mr President,

South Africa leaves this podium with an important refrain:

The  South  African  nation  is  the  creation  and  heritage  of  the  international community.

South  Africa  today  stands  tall  in  the  family  of  nations  because  the  United Nations delivered on the promise of its Charter.

As  Member  States  we  must  continue  to  support  this  organisation,  our organisation,  because  as  President  Nelson  Mandela  said  in  his  inaugural Address to the United Nations General Assembly on 3 October 1994:

“The millions across our globe who stand expectant at the gates of hope look to this Organisation to bring them peace, to bring them life, to bring them a life worth living”

I thank you.

speaker_post: Minister for Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation
text:
President of the General Assembly,

Secretary-General,

Excellencies,

Distinguished Heads of State and Government,

Ladies and Gentlemen,

We congratulate you, Mr. President, on your election as the President of the

81st  Session  of  the  United  Nations  General  Assembly  and  pledge  our

cooperation  and  support  during  your  tenure.  We  also  commend  the

Secretary-General  for  his  strong  leadership  at  a  challenging  time  in  our

multilateral  system.  Zambia  salutes  His  Excellency  António  Guterres  for

reminding us that the answer to a more divided and multipolar world is not

less  multilateralism,  but  a  stronger,  fairer  and  more  representative  United

Nations.

The theme of this session, “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation:

A United Nations That Delivers for All,” is both timely and necessary.

Trust is the foundation on which international cooperation is built upon. Yet

today, trust in institutions, trust among nations and, most importantly, trust

between the institutions that serve the people, is under strain.

Trust means that the founding principles of the United Nations Charter must

be respected.

For Zambia, trust begins with keeping promises.

Trust means that international agreements must be honoured.

Trust means that development commitments must be financed.

Trust means that the voices of developing countries matter, in word and in

deed.

Trust  means  that  the  global  system  must  not  protect  the  interests  of  the

powerful, at the expense of the vulnerable.

And trust means that when the world agrees on a goal, we must have the

commitment to implement it.

The  world  is  undergoing  profound transformation.  Technology  is  changing

economies  and  societies.  Climate  change

is  reshaping

livelihoods.

Geopolitical  competition  is  altering  global  trade  and  investment  patterns.

Conflicts are causing massive displacements and humanitarian suffering.

And yet, Developing countries continue to confront a financing system that

does not adequately reflect  and respond to  their development needs. The

question before us is therefore, not whether transformation will happen, but

it is rather how we manage  transformation, who benefits from it, and whether

our multilateral institutions are capable  of delivering meaningful results for

ordinary people.

For Zambia, our answer is clear: we must restore trust by achieving results,

and we must manage transformation by ensuring that no country and no-one

is left behind.

Zambia's Democratic Journey and the 2026 Elections

Article 21 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights affirms that, “the will

of the people shall be the basis of the authority of government,” expressed

through periodic and genuine elections.

It is in this spirit that Zambia recently concluded its general elections, through

which our people exercised their constitutional right to choose their leaders.

We  thank  the  people  of  Zambia  for  their  participation  in  the  democratic

process and for renewing their confidence in our leadership. We also express

our sincere appreciation to the international Election Observation Missions

for their invaluable support and contribution to Zambia’s democratic process.

It is important to emphasize that Zambia is not at war. Zambia is a peaceful,

stable and sovereign nation, and the peaceful atmosphere that characterized

the country before, during and after the elections is a clear reflection of our

people’s  enduring  commitment  to  peace,  democracy,  national  unity  and

constitutional governance.

Despite  the  political  differences  that  naturally  accompany  a  democratic

election, Zambia has demonstrated that such differences can and must be

managed  peacefully  and  through  the  established  constitutional  and  legal

institutions. Our democratic process should never be mistaken for conflict or

instability.

We therefore reaffirm our unwavering commitment to preserving Zambia’s

long-standing  tradition  of  peace.  We  will  continue  to  ensure  that  political

differences are addressed through the due process of the law and will take

all necessary measures, within the confines of our Constitution and laws, to

prevent  political  disputes

from  degenerating

into  violence,  armed

mobilization, insurgency or the emergence of militia groups.

In  this  regard,  we  extend  a  sincere  invitation  to  cooperating  partners,

international  development  institutions,  investors,  the  private  sector  and

Zambia’s friends around the world to continue working with us in advancing

our  Grow  Zambia  Agenda.  Zambia  needs  partnerships,  investments,

innovation,  technology,  skills  and  sustained  development  cooperation  in

order to unlock its full potential.

We encourage our cooperating partners to view Zambia through the lens of

the  peace  and  stability  that  define  our  country,  and  to  deepen  support for

programmes

that  promote

inclusive  economic  growth,

job  creation,

infrastructure development, human capital development, agriculture, energy,

health and other priority areas of national development.

Our  message  is  clear:  Zambia  is  at  peace,  Zambia  is  open  for

partnership, and Zambia is ready to grow.

Zambia: A Stable Partner for Investment and Trade

Peace and stability provide the foundation for economic development.

Zambia  is  positioning  itself  as  an  attractive  destination  for  investment  and

trade,  with  opportunities  in  mining,  critical  minerals,  agriculture,  agro-

processing,  manufacturing,  energy,  infrastructure,  tourism  and  digital

services.

Our  ambition  is  to  move  beyond  the  export  of  raw  materials  and  primary

commodities  towards value  addition,  industrialization,  job  creation  and

technology transfer as key enablers of our economic transformation agenda.

We  welcome  investment  that  creates  jobs,  develops  skills  and  builds

sustainable value chains.

Our message to investors is: Come to Zambia. Invest with us. Produce

with us. Trade with us. Grow with us. Zambia is open for investment

Climate Change and Environmental Resilience; Water and Sanitation

For Zambia, climate change is not an abstract concept. Our people continue

to  experience  the  devastating  effects  of  droughts,  floods  and  changing

weather patterns, with significant impacts on agriculture, food security, water

availability, energy generation and livelihoods.

The effects of activities transcend our borders and yet our people and  the

coming  generations  may  pay  a  heavy  price.  Zambia  recognizes  that

countries such as ours cannot finance the climate transition alone, nor should

they. This is a collective moral responsibility of the international community,

especially the highest contributors to carbon emissions. This is to mitigate

the effects of climate change and protect lives and livelihoods.

Those who have contributed least to climate change must not be left to bear

its greatest costs.

We therefore call for predictable, accessible and affordable climate finance,

technology  transfer,  and  greater  investment  in  adaptation  and  resilience,

consistent with the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and

respective capabilities.

For  Africa,  adaptation  is  not  optional. Our  farmers  require  climate-resilient

agriculture;  our  communities  and  cities  need  resilient  infrastructure;  our

energy  systems  must  become  more  diversified;  and  our  water  resources,

forests and ecosystems must be protected. Zambia is ready to contribute to

global  climate  solutions,  but  those  that  have  contributed  least  to  climate

change must not bear a disproportionate share of its costs.

Water security is integral to climate resilience and sustainable development.

Zambia therefore attaches great importance to international cooperation on

water and has actively participated in the preparatory process for the 2026

United  Nations  Water  Conference.  Together  with  Finland,  Zambia  is  co-

chairing  the  Interactive  Dialogue  on Water  for  Cooperation,  focusing  on

transboundary  and  international  water  cooperation,  scientific  cooperation

and inclusive governance.

We remain committed to strengthening water security, climate resilience and

sustainable  management  of  natural  resources,  while  working  with  the

international  community  to  ensure  that  climate  and  water  action  delivers

tangible benefits for our people and future generations.

Health, Human Capital and Inclusive Development

Africa's youthful population is one of our greatest assets and represents an

enormous  opportunity  for  global  prosperity.  According  to  demographic

forecasts, one in every 4 youths on the globe will be African, by 2050. We

have a wealth of young Africans with the potential to become entrepreneurs,

scientists, engineers, farmers, innovators, artists and future leaders.

Our  responsibility  is  to  equip  them  with  quality  education,  relevant  skills,

access

to

technology,  entrepreneurship  opportunities  and  decent

employment,  so  that  they  can  become  active  drivers  of  economic

transformation and sustainable development.

We are alive to the fact that we should ensure that we keep this youthful and

productive population healthy in order to harness positive dividends.

In the health sector, Zambia has increased domestic budgetary allocations

from approximately 7 percent to over 10 percent, enabling the recruitment of

health  workers,  expansion  and  modernization  of  health  infrastructure,  and

improved  availability  of  essential  medical  supplies.  Recognizing  continued

vulnerability  to  epidemics,  Zambia  calls  for  the expedited  conclusion  of

negotiations on the Pathogen Access and Benefit Sharing Annex under the

WHO Pandemic Agreement, alongside strengthened access to technology

and preparedness capacities to detect and respond to future health threats.

Zambia is further making efforts toward building capacity for local Vaccine

Manufacturing.

In  Zambia,  we  have  taken  decisive  steps  to  expand  access  to  education

through the enactment of the Free Education Act, and the strengthening of

the  school  feeding  programme,  ensuring  that  more  children  can  access

education and remain in school without the burden of fees or hunger standing

in their way of learning.

Zambia  is  equally  committed  to  promoting  gender  equality  and  economic

empowerment  of  women  and  girls.  We  are  expanding  opportunities  in

education,  skills  development,  entrepreneurship,  financial  inclusion  and

leadership.  For  the  first  time  in  our  history,  Parliament  now  provides  for

proportional  representation  of women,  young  people  and  persons  with

disabilities, reflecting our conviction that their voices and experiences must

be heard in shaping the decisions that affect our nation.

We are also strengthening efforts to end child, early and forced marriage by

keeping girls in school and addressing the social and economic factors that

place  them  at  risk.  Zambia  has  demonstrated  that  progress  is  possible,

reducing child marriage prevalence from 29% to 23.9% in four years through

comprehensive  legal  reforms,  free  education,  school  re-entry  policy,

multisectoral support systems like the Keeping Girls in School initiatives and

targeted  economic  investments  such  as  our  expanded  Constituency

Development Fund. We need to continue building on these successes.

We therefore invite Member States to unite behind our global and continental

commitments to drive domestic action.

By investing in our people, particularly women, girls and young people, we

are  investing  in  Zambia's  future.  When  we  empower  our  people,  we

strengthen  our  nation;  and  when  we  invest  in  Africa's  young  people  and

women,  we  invest  in  the  prosperity  of  our  continent  and  the  world.  Our

commitment is to build an inclusive society in which every citizen, regardless

of  gender,  age  or  disability,  has  an  opportunity  to  participate  fully  in  our

country's economic and social transformation.

Sustainable Development and the 2030 Agenda

The  Sustainable  Development  Goals  remain  the  most  comprehensive

expression  of  our  shared  ambition  to  eradicate  poverty,  reduce  inequality

and build a sustainable future. Yet we  must acknowledge that progress is

uneven. The world cannot continue to adopt ambitious commitments while

developing countries struggle to finance their implementation.

For Zambia, the SDGs must translate into tangible improvements in the lives

of our people: a child receiving quality education; a mother accessing safe

healthcare;  a  farmer  having  reliable  water  and  markets;  a  young  person

finding  decent  employment;  a  family  having  access  to  electricity;  a

community having accessible roads; access to clean water and sanitation; a

small business gaining access to finance. That is what development means.

Sustainable Development Finance and Reform of the Global Financial

Architecture

Sustainable  development  cannot  be  achieved  without  addressing  the

persistent financing gap facing developing countries. High borrowing costs,

limited  fiscal  space  and  heavy  debt-servicing  obligations  continue  to

constrain  countries’  ability  to  invest  in  climate  action,  health,  education,

infrastructure and other development priorities.

We cannot expect countries to deliver more for their people while resources

available  are  increasingly  consumed  by  the  cost  of  debt.  This  is  not

sustainable, nor is it compatible with our collective commitment to leave no

one behind.

Zambia  has  undertaken  significant  fiscal  reforms  and  made  progress  in

restructuring our debt, to restore macroeconomic stability and create fiscal

space.  This  demonstrates  our  willingness  to  make  bold  decisions  when

needed.    At  the  same  time,  we  are  strengthening  domestic  resource

mobilization by expanding the tax base, modernizing tax administration and

combating  illicit  financial  flows.  We  cannot  continue  to  lose  resources

essential  to  Africa’s  transformation  while  being  asked  to  mobilize  greater

financing  for  development.  Africa’s  resources  must  work  for  Africa’s

development.

We support enhanced international cooperation on transparency, beneficial

ownership,  asset  recovery  and  the  prevention  of  illicit  financial  flows.  We

equally  support  stronger  international  tax  cooperation  through  the  UN

Framework  Convention  on  International  Tax  Cooperation,  to  ensure  fairer

taxing

rights  and  strengthen  domestic

resource  mobilization

for

development.

Zambia  therefore  calls  for greater  access  to  affordable  and  long-term

development finance, increased climate finance—particularly for adaptation

and  resilience—and  innovative  financing  mechanisms  to  mobilise  private

investment for sustainable development.

Africa needs a fairer and more responsive global financial architecture that

enables  developing  countries  to  finance  development  as  an  investment  in

our shared future.

Multilateralism, Geopolitics, Peace and Security

The  United  Nations  remains  indispensable  to  international  peace,  security

and sustainable development. However, its institutions must evolve to reflect

today’s geopolitical, economic and demographic realities. Zambia therefore

supports  meaningful  UN  reform,  particularly  of  the  Security  Council,

including  permanent  African  representation  in  line  with  the Ezulwini

Consensus  and  Sirte  Declaration.  We  also  support  reforms  to  global

economic and financial governance, that give developing countries a greater

voice in decisions affecting them.

Zambia  welcomes  the UN80  Initiative as  an  opportunity  to  strengthen

multilateralism  and  build  a  more  effective,  efficient,  equitable  and  fit-for-

purpose  United  Nations  and  acknowledge  the  commendable  progress

achieved so far.

As efforts are made to attain a more efficient and nimbler United Nations, we

must not lose sight of the most important aspect – the effectiveness of the

UN in delivering on its mandates. With each crucial question, we must ask

ourselves if the reforms will make the world safer and uplift the lives of the

most vulnerable in society. We take note of the proposed mergers of some

key  institutions  and  emphasize  on  the  importance  of  protecting  their

mandates.

We further note the changed landscape for international cooperation that has

seen significant declines in official development assistance, which has also

affected important UN programmes.  We, therefore, call on member states

to protect these institutions we trust by ringfencing crucial core funding.

In the face of rising geopolitical tensions and protracted conflicts, we reaffirm

our  commitment  to  dialogue,  diplomacy  and  the  peaceful  resolution  of

disputes in accordance with the UN Charter and international law. We further

support  African-led  solutions  and  stronger  cooperation  between  the  UN,

African  Union  and  regional  organizations  to  advance  conflict  prevention,

peacebuilding and collective security.

Conclusion

Zambia  remains  committed  to  peace,  democracy,  multilateralism  and

sustainable development.

We  believe

that  restoring

trust  requires  delivery;

that  sustainable

development requires genuine international partnership; and that managing

transformation requires inclusion.

We  call  for  an  equitable  global  system  that  provides  developing  countries

with  affordable  financing  and  policy  space  to  transform  their  economies,

strengthens climate action through adequate finance, expands opportunities

for  young  people,  and  reforms  international  institutions  to  reflect  today’s

realities.

Let us together strengthen peace through dialogue, respect for human rights,

democracy and the rule of law and ensure that the commitments made in

this Assembly, translate into tangible improvements in the lives of our people.

Zambia  stands  ready  to  work  with  all  nations  to  restore  trust,  manage

transformation and build a more peaceful, prosperous and equitable world.

I Thank You.
